<pb n="19"/>From Father Apa, who is of great honor, to the son, one portion of meat and food, beer, and spirits were offered once. May their people and wealth increase. Kye! From this royal palace in the outer Phimtsang region, the emanation of Gekser <note>likely a local deity or ancestral figure</note>, the great elder Gendun, the wise lady Drukmo, Ugyen Wangdzom, and their retinue provided meat, food, and beer once. By this gift, may they obtain virtuous Buddhahood. Father Apa Naktrong, who is moved by compassion, through great diligence in the Holy Dharma, established a connection by offering food and beer once. May he be born in the Pure Land of Avalokiteshvara. From Wengkhar Yulmo in the valley of beautiful water-patterns, Sonam Tenpa, who has entered the path of Holy Dharma, and Gekser <term>Metok</term> <gloss>Flower</gloss> Tashi Zangmo established a connection by offering food and spirits once. May they be born in the presence of Ugyen Pema. The master of scholars from the lineage of old, the Teacher Pekar and the youth Khipo, both performed service to the Dharma with food and spirits. May their merit increase like the limits of the sky. From the area of Themgnang-bi created in the cool land, the youth Kunzang in the prime of his life established a connection with the Dharma through food and spirits. The "Kumuda-flower" Karma Wangmo offers the moon-like beer of the <term>tsok</term> <gloss>feast gathering</gloss> to the Dharma. May she be enriched with wealth that never fades. The elder Gawa, who speaks the ancient Tsang language, offers service to the Dharma with food and beer once. May he have a long life without illness and may his enjoyments increase. From the Tagchu Monastery in the secluded mountains, those who have mastered the elephant of the mindful mind and who are practitioners of the vast expanse of the Great Perfection <note>original: "rdzogs pa chen po"</note>: led by the Master Sangdak Norbu, together with the renunciate meditator Tenzin Guru, the ascetic meditator Tashi, the meditator Karma who has abandoned worldly thoughts, and the meditator Ngawang Trinley—these ones of great merit offer to the Holy Dharma. May they be born in the presence of Samantabhadra. From Konbar Yulmo at the mouth of the "Elephant Spring," Pema Tsewang of great Dharma, Father Apa Druk Tsering who is moved by pure vision, Father Apa Druk Puntsok of great diligence, and the youth Kunlay endowed with destiny—these offered food together with spirits. By the great blessing of offering once each, may their people, wealth, and food, these three, flourish and increase. Meditator Tenzin Guru’s... 

<leaf-break/>

...the three of them performed service with southern beer <note>original: "lho chang"</note> once. May they possess enjoyments and may their people and wealth increase. Ngawang Tenzin, who possesses the talent of knowledge, and Sonam Chodzom, of faithful and good thoughts, these two established a connection with the Dharma with southern beer twice. The well-mannered Father Apa Tsewang and Jamyang Metok Pema Wangmo offered service to the Dharma with southern beer once. Sonam Trinley, strong as a buffalo, together with the daughter Bukri of perfect and unchanging faith, and the "Conch-leaf Flower" daughter Sonam, established a connection with the Dharma with southern beer twice. May they be born in the pure realm of Kechari <note>a celestial Dakini realm</note>. Father Dondrup, the great treasury of knowledge, offers southern beer once to the profound Dharma. Norbu Trinley, strong as a great lion, offered dried fish from the waters of India once as a service to the Dharma. By the virtue of this offering, may they all conquer and obtain the realm. Kye! From the Tsankhar Monastery on the white snowy mountains, Father Apa Druk Norbu of excellent speech and the "Mountain Valley Flower" daughter Chomo, these two performed service with southern beer once. May they be born in the lotus land of Sukhavati. From the stacked stone village of Dowali-phung in a beautiful valley surrounded by garlands of forest trees, Konchok of powerful activity, Sid-thal Tashi of great speed, the respectful lady Semcho Wangmo, the "Soft White Flower" Lhawang Dronma, and their retinue offered southern beer and one portion of beef. May they be born in the presence of the Buddha in the realm of bliss. The youth Tshechu-la, like a tree trunk, and the youth Ngoi-la, like a sandalwood tree, each established a connection once with southern beer. Father Apa Tsewang, Ngawang Druk Norbu, Sonam Trinley, Ngoi-la, and Tshechu-la together offered one portion of brisket. By the great virtue of this single offering, may they be born in the realm of Sukhavati. Druk-kyi Lhamo, of great clear results, and the daughter Karmo also established a connection with the Dharma by providing feast-beer. May they obtain the rank of the Victorious Vidyadhara. The mountain hermit ascetic Tsondru and the very compassionate Rinchen Wangmo, along with southern beer and spirits...

<pb n="20"/>...led by them, Drolma Lhamo of long-standing character, the very loving and compassionate Dekyi Chodzom, and the "Saffron Flower" daughter Yangdzin, established a connection with the Dharma through food and spirits. May they be born in Sukhavati in the future. Kye! From the Kurto region where the flowing water is beautiful like white hair, in the perfect city of Tashi Drak, the faithful Mother Kunga Wangmo, the "Golden Flower" Norbu Dzompa, and the delightful Wangchen Dondrup, these three offered southern beer and spirits twice, along with one portion of pork, to the Holy Dharma. May they be born in the presence of Pema Lingpa. Ugyen Tenzin, the great meditator whose mind is directed toward the Holy Dharma, and Dzompa Lhamo, who remembers the divine Dharma, these two offered food and spirits once. May they be born in the realm of Samantabhadra. Kye! From Lekshig-gang in Yulmo, where the tiers of the village are stacked like a great garden in a beautiful mountain valley, the "Silver Flower" Phagdor Wangmo offers food and beer once to the scriptures of the Dharma. Her servants Ngak Tsering and the very conscientious Mother Sang-dron, these two offered a connection of southern rice beer once. May they obtain the rank of liberation in the higher realms. Father Apa Tsewang of unchanging faith, Pekol-la like a sandalwood trunk, and the beautiful and faithful daughter Naka, these three provided southern food, tea, and beer. May they be miraculously born in the presence of the Victorious One. Mother Nyida of great virtuous thoughts offered a drink of fragrant tea once. May she be born in the presence of Ugyen Pema. Kye! From the great city of Domkhar in Yulmo, situated in the great cool land, Dechen Wangmo of great love and compassion, the "Udumbara Flower" Tashi Wangmo, the "Kumuda Flower" daughter Pemo, the "Flower of Great Joy" daughter Demchok-mo, the "Clear Flower" Tsewang Lhamo, the "Sky Flower" Dondrup Zangmo, and the "Sun Flower" daughter Khyi-mo—these girls provided feast-beer once. From the support of this virtuous mandala, may they obtain the supreme path of liberation in Great Bliss. Kye! From the village of Chama-dung, situated in the delightful garden valley of Nang-yer, Father Apa Druk-ga of great intention, the youth Dharma who possesses partial knowledge, and Mother Yoka-mo of long-standing character...

<leaf-break/>

...offered once. May they be born in the great realm of Tushita. Those who performed the service of the paper <note>original: "sho gu"</note> from the forest trees: Sonam Trinley, Norbu Trinley, Nakpo-la, Tamdrin Ngonser, the great gatekeeper Tenzin, Chodar, Dor-pun-tsok, Rinchen Wangmo, Tashi Drukgyal, the great gatekeeper Dophen, Konchok Wangyal, Tshechu-la, and Gnai-la—these eleven, having cast aside the exhaustion and fatigue of their magical labors, offered service of paper for the scriptures of the Victorious One. By this offering, may they be miraculously born in the presence of the Buddhas and receive their prophecy. Kye! From the great Tashigang in the very white East and from the very clear and cold Bagi in Yulmo, Trinley Norbu, who flies like a Garuda, offered southern beer twice with a faithful heart. May he be born in the realm of Abhirati. The meditator Rigzin, who has realized the meaning of emptiness, established a connection by providing southern beer six times. May he be born in the lotus realm of Ngayab <note>the Copper-Colored Mountain</note>. Now, well done, well done to all the patrons and their retinues! Happy, very happy are all those who have established a connection! To all those who performed service with a faithful heart: upon the good ground of the virtue of the white side, by everything offered, whether of great or small substance, may it be dedicated to the path of enlightenment. May the ocean of existence be dried by fire, and for us living beings, may the obstacles of the demons of wrong views be cleared away. May the great path leading to Tushita be seen. Having seen it, I pray that we may receive the prophecy. Kye! The great miraculous scribes who bring things to fruition, from Tashigang, Dungsum Phimtsang, Wangma-khar, and Kurto, gathered at the secluded mountain of Samten Choling in the presence of the qualified Guru, the leader of beings. All the secretaries assembled and constructed this. First, upon the beautiful soft white beaten paper, the emanation of the Victorious One, Pema Thugkha, established the first head-lines in the Sanskrit language. He called down the Wisdom Beings into the Commitment Deities. Trinley Wangchuk, Sherab Gyatso, and...
</translation>

<summary>This portion of the catalog lists numerous patrons, families, and practitioners from various Himalayan regions who provided offerings such as meat, beer, and paper for the production of the scriptures. It concludes by describing the assembly of scribes at Samten Choling and the ritual beginning of the manuscript's creation, initiated by Pema Thugkha.</summary>

<keywords>patrons, offerings, Yulmo, Samten Choling, Pema Thugkha, merit, paper production, scribes, dedication prayers, Southern beer</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="14"/>does not become pacified. Know that attachment to desires is exactly like that. Some who are afflicted by the disease of leprosy, suffering from the movement of worms beneath the skin, may rely entirely on the heat of a fire for the sake of comfort. Although it appears to be a momentary pleasure, the disease is not pacified; instead, the lymph-fluid increases the heat, and the stinging pain will grow. In the same way, although one may seem momentarily satisfied by indulging in the qualities of desire, craving will increase further and will never be sated. Therefore, know the nature of attachment to desires and reverse the craving for the objects of desire from the very beginning.

In that way, craving will increase, and there is no satisfaction. Therefore, immediately after explaining the definite cycle of attachment to desires, we come to the explanation of the actual path. This includes the detailed explanation of the common vehicle's path and a brief presentation of the entrance to the unique path and result of the Great Vehicle. Regarding the first, identifying the object of meditation through a general summary, and then explaining the stages of the five paths through a detailed exposition. For the first: To perceive the ultimate truth, cultivate familiarity with correct mental engagement toward all things. There is no other quality similar to that which possesses such excellence. The purpose is to see and realize the ultimate mode of being.
<column-break/>
All things comprised of matter and consciousness are called <term>composite</term> <gloss>samshrta</gloss> because they are assembled by causes and conditions. Furthermore, because they cease after the previous moment and the subsequent moment arises, they are constantly changing and perishing; thus, they are impermanent. Correspondingly, with correct mental engagement, one understands that all composite things—except for the Truth of the Path—are <term>contaminated</term> <gloss>sashrava</gloss>. These include the environmental world of the three realms, the physical senses, and the consciousness and mental factors, which are the five contaminated categories. Feelings associated with suffering are the <term>suffering of suffering</term>. Feelings associated with pleasure are the <term>suffering of change</term>. Feelings associated with neutrality are the <term>suffering of conditioning</term>. Among these, the suffering of suffering is known even by animals and the like. The suffering of change is seen by those with intelligence. Although the suffering of conditioning is the basis of all suffering, others do not recognize it, but the Noble Ones realize it. Regarding the statement "all phenomena are empty": although "emptiness" usually refers to being free from conceptual elaborations, here, the aspect of emptiness within the Truth of Suffering refers to being empty of discordant causes. This means that a creator such as <term>Ishvara</term> <gloss>the Almighty Lord</gloss> or causes like "Time" do not exist in the actual nature of things. One knows they are empty of such a creator and understands that things arise from the meeting of various suitable and harmonious causes and conditions.
<column-break/>
The essence of the path consists of untainted wisdom, meditative concentration, and ethical discipline. This path possesses the power to abandon the afflictions and brings about the attainment of the state of cessation. To generate certain knowledge in this way is the mental engagement with the aspect of the Truth of the Path. In the detailed explanation of the divisions of the five paths, there are two parts: showing the stages of the path for ordinary beings and showing the Noble Path along with its results. Within the first, there is the teaching on the qualities related to the Path of Accumulation and the qualities related to the Path of Preparation. First, regarding the necessity of abiding predominantly in ethical discipline and wisdom during the Path of Accumulation: even men of noble birth, fine appearance, and great learning are not venerable if they lack wisdom and ethical discipline. Therefore, one who possesses these two qualities should be honored even if they lack other qualities. Even if a person belongs to a noble royal lineage like a great Sal tree, or a noble priestly lineage like a great Sal tree, and thus has a supreme lineage, a beautiful and healthy body, and is highly trained in the eighteen sciences and worldly traditions, if they lack the wisdom that understands the path to liberation and the nature of reality, and if they lack the ethical discipline of pure conduct, they are not an object of veneration for the world including the gods.
<pb n="15"/>Furthermore, if one possesses the qualities of noble birth, appearance, and learning, it goes without saying. Even if one lacks those other qualities, if they possess these two—the wisdom that knows the path to liberation and the mode of reality, and the excellence of ethical discipline—they become a supreme object of worldly worship and veneration. Within that wisdom, there are three types: wisdom arising from hearing, from reflection, and from meditation. At this stage of the Path of Accumulation, the two wisdoms of hearing and reflection are primary. As for ethical discipline, while there are the infinite disciplines of a Bodhisattva, in this context, it refers to the <term>Pratimoksha</term> <gloss>Individual Liberation</gloss> discipline. To show that those on the Path of Accumulation must maintain equanimity toward the eight worldly concerns: The Knower of the World said to keep equanimity, making them not the objects of your mind—gain and loss, pleasure and pain, fame and insignificance, praise and blame—these are the eight worldly concerns. The Knower of the World, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, taught the necessity of equanimity toward these eight. Specifically: finding excellent possessions versus the poverty of not finding them; having a body free of disease and a comfortable mind versus discomfort; hearing pleasant reports spread by others versus unpleasant ones; and being directly praised versus being blamed.
<column-break/>
Because such actions will not come to help as friends, one should never perform sinful deeds even for the sake of others. Regarding the context of this verse: if one thinks there is no need to abandon sinful deeds because the results of committing them do not occur immediately: Though some sinful deeds committed may not cut immediately like a weapon, when the time of death arrives, the result of those sinful deeds will become manifest. For most sinful deeds, the result does not ripen immediately like a sharp weapon making a wound, but when the time of death, the intermediate state, or future rebirths arrive, whatever the ripening result of those sinful deeds may be, it will be experienced and become manifest. If you ask when the results of karma ripen: there are two types—karma not certain to be experienced and karma certain to be experienced. Within the first, there are "done but not accumulated" and "not done but accumulated." Among "done but not accumulated," there are three levels: great, medium, and small. Entering the preparation for a virtuous or non-virtuous deed but not reaching the actual act is "small." Entering the preparation but turning back with regret halfway through the actual act is "medium." Entering the preparation and completing the actual act, but feeling intense regret before the conclusion is "done but not accumulated."
<column-break/>
As for results to be experienced in other lifetimes: these are the weaker actions of the "done and accumulated" type, for which the time of occurrence is uncertain. Depending on whether they meet with similar activating conditions of virtue or sin, they may occur after two, three, or many lifetimes; this uncertainty is "to be experienced in other lifetimes." Even sinful actions that are certain to be experienced can be overcome by their remedies. In this text, the statement that the results of sinful deeds do not ripen immediately refers to the majority of karma, excluding those destined to be experienced in this very life. If one asks which will ripen first among both virtuous and sinful deeds: the Noble Ananda said, "In cyclic existence, that which is heavy, that which is near, that which is habitual, and that which was done first—among these, the former ones will ripen first." The meaning is: among all deeds ready to ripen, the one with the greatest strength will ripen first. If the strength of virtue and sin is equal, whichever mind—virtuous or sinful—is clearest and most reinforced at the time of death will ripen first. If the clarity is also equal, whichever has the stronger habituation from the past will ripen first. If that is also equal, then whichever virtuous or sinful deed was done first will ripen first, following the chronological order of when they were committed. Equal non-virtue and virtue...
</translation>

<summary>
This section discusses the futility of worldly desires using the metaphor of leprosy and explains the four noble truths, specifically focusing on the aspects of suffering, emptiness, and the path. It details the importance of ethical discipline and wisdom over social status, the eight worldly concerns, and the mechanics of how karma ripens over multiple lifetimes.
</summary>

Desire, Leprosy Metaphor, Four Noble Truths, Suffering, Emptiness, Path of Accumulation, Ethical Discipline, Wisdom, Eight Worldly Concerns, Karma, Ripening of Results, Ananda

<translation>
<pb n="124"/>possess a "state of attainment" <note>original: 有所得; refers to the error of grasping at a concept as a real entity</note>, so how do they differ from the old interpretations? Furthermore, they are even more excessive than others. This is because they previously grasped the old explanations of the Treatise on Numbers <note>Abhidharma</note>, and now they also grasp the new wisdom of the Three Treatises. This is simply adding one more view. The Master says this is like "adding feet to a drawing of a snake." One could say the more extensive their study, the more numerous their delusions. However, the intent of the sutras and treatises lies in quieting the mind to reach the original source; for this reason, one is called a <term>shramana</term> <gloss>ascetic or seeker</gloss>. Furthermore, one quiets it until reaching the state of "non-quieting" <note>where no effort to quiet the mind is required</note>. As for the statement about not refuting the "Middle-Provisional," those who embody the Way realize that this "provisional nature" <note>original: 性假; the provisional nature of inherent existence</note> is originally the Way itself. There is no need to refute it. If one wishes to refute it, would that not be refuting the Way? One must see this point most deeply. The reason we now speak of "refuting" is that people do not realize the established provisional nature is originally the Way. Therefore, they treat the Way as the non-Way. Now, we simply lead them to realize that the non-Way is the Way; thus we call it "refuting." In reality, nothing is refuted. Secondly, one must also know that the inherent nature is itself the provisional. Ordinary people are deluded and claim that the provisional forms an inherent nature. When the Buddhas observe it, nature is always provisional. Therefore, it is said that all worldly truths, if seen by the <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>the Thus-Come One; the Buddha</gloss>, <pb n="125"/> are always the supreme truth <note>original: 第一義諦; Paramartha-satya</note>. Thirdly, those who embody the Way know that this Way has never been "provisional nature." Provisional nature arises from dual conditions <note>original: 兩緣; referring to the relationship between causes and conditions</note>, just as the one Way has never been "absolute" or "conventional"; these arise from dual conditions. Fourthly, those who follow the teachings must recognize that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess unobstructed contemplation internally and limitless eloquence externally. They may speak of the provisional as nature, or speak of the provisional nature as being "not." Nature is provisional and "not-nature"; the provisional is nature and "provisional." If one clings to a single fragment of words, one loses the complete meaning. Such a person is not a student of the Three Treatises.
</translation>

<summary>Jizang criticizes scholars who treat Buddhist concepts as new objects of attachment, arguing that true understanding involves realizing that provisional nature and the Way are non-dual. He emphasizes that the "refutation" of concepts is a pedagogical tool to lead the deluded back to the original source where distinctions like nature and provisionality disappear.</summary>

<keywords>Jizang, Three Treatises, Middle-Provisional, nature and provisionality, shramana, Tathagata, supreme truth, non-duality, eloquence</keywords>

<pb n="165"/>A hunter was lying in wait in the mountains at night when he saw a small person, about two feet tall, walking alone along the bottom of a ravine. After a short while, another person of the same height arrived. They happened to meet and asked each other where they were going. The first one said, "I am going to visit Yang the Scar. I recently saw that his <term>qise</term> <gloss>complexion and aura</gloss> was dark and dim, with many unlucky omens." The second person said, "I am going for the same reason; what you say is not wrong." The hunter, knowing they were not human, gave a loud shout, and the two vanished. That night, he caught a large fox. On its forehead was a scar as big as a coin.

**The Dragon Plays with a Spider**

When Master Xu was the Magistrate of Qidong, there was a tower in the government office used for storing food. Items were often stolen and left in a mess on the ground. The family members were scolded several times for this, so they lay in wait to watch. They saw a spider as large as a bushel basket. They ran in terror to tell the Master. The Master thought it was extraordinary and every day sent the maidservants to throw food to it. The spider became increasingly tame; whenever it was hungry, it would come out and stay near 

<pb n="166"/>people, leaving only after it was full. After more than a year, the Master was once reading official documents when the spider suddenly came to crouch under his desk. Suspecting it was hungry, he was just calling for a servant to bring food when he suddenly saw two snakes flanking the spider, lying as straight as chopsticks. The spider curled its legs and shrunk its belly as if unable to bear its fear. In an instant, the snakes grew violently, becoming thicker than eggs. Just as the Master was about to flee in great terror, a massive clap of thunder erupted. The whole household was stunned and unconscious. After some time, the Master regained consciousness, but his wife and seven or eight servants and slaves had been struck dead. The Master was ill for over a month and soon passed away. The Master was an upright and honest man who loved the people; when he left office, the people collected money for his journey, and the sound of their weeping filled the fields.

Historian Wu says: I always thought the story of "The Dragon Plays with a Spider" was just a false rumor from the streets. Yet did it actually happen? I have heard that lightning strikes must target the wicked; why then did a law-abiding and good official suffer such a cruel fate? Is the Heaven's wrath not frequently misplaced?

<summary>Two supernatural tales: a hunter encounters mountain spirits foretelling a fox's fate, and a benevolent official's life ends tragically after a mysterious encounter involving a giant spider, snakes, and a fatal lightning strike.</summary>
<keywords>fox spirit, mountain spirits, omens, Master Xu, giant spider, dragon, lightning, karmic injustice, Qidong</keywords>

<pb n="50"/> understand words <note>original: "zhi yan"</note>. If one can understand the truth or falsehood of people's words and exhaustively examine the principles of things and events, then the mind becomes like a bright mirror. Only then can one use the Sage's method of observing people to examine others.

The Master said: "Reviewing the old and thereby knowing the new, one may then become a teacher."

"Reviewing" <note>original: "wen"</note> means to trace and unravel. "The old" refers to what was previously heard. "The new" refers to what is gained now. If in learning one can constantly practice what was previously heard and always have new realizations, then what is learned resides within oneself and its application is inexhaustible. Therefore, such a person can be a teacher to others. As for the "learning of memory and questioning" <note>referring to rote memorization</note>, there is no realization in the heart, <margin>Master Chen of Xin'an says: compared with</margin> and what is known is limited. <margin>Master Chen of Xin'an says: compared with</margin> This is the opposite of "inexhaustible application." Therefore, the Record of Learning <note>original: "Xue Ji," a chapter in the Book of Rites</note> mocks it as being insufficient to be a teacher to others. This exactly complements the meaning here. <margin>Master Zhu says: the learning of memory and questioning</margin> If one does not search for the principles within, then remembering ten items remains just ten items, and remembering a hundred items remains just a hundred items. This is something dead and fixed. "Knowing the new" means seeing within the "reviewing of the old"

<pb n="51"/> that these principles become increasingly refined and superior compared to before. By extending and stretching them, and by encountering a category and expanding upon it, the principles remain constantly alive and not dead. <note>Master</note> Gu says: In the Doctrine of the Mean, "reviewing the old and thereby knowing the new" does not mean reviewing the old and separately knowing the new; rather, it is in reviewing the old that one doubly gains the new. <note>Master</note> Qiu says: "Reviewing the old and thereby knowing the new" means reviewing the old to seek the new; otherwise, one cannot know the new. <pb n="61"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta> it was indeed the temple of Duke Huan. The Marquis of Chen said to Zigong, "Only now do I know how precious a Sage is." Zigong replied, "It is not as good as being devoted to his Way and implementing the goodness of his transformation." <margin>Revised according to the Shuo Yuan</margin>

After Yang Huo fled to Qi, he went from Qi to Jin and joined the Zhao clan. When Confucius heard of this, he said to Zilu, "The Zhao clan will likely suffer from disorder for generations." Zilu said, "Power does not originally reside with him, so how could he cause disorder?" Confucius said, "This is not something you know. Yang Huo is clever in his observations but lacks affection for benevolence. He was favored by Jisun, yet he planned to kill him; failing that, he fled to Qi. The people of Qi imprisoned him, so he escaped and returned to Jin. This means the two states of Qi and Lu have already cast off their illness. Zhao Jianzi loves profit and kills many; he will surely be charmed by Yang Huo's talk and follow his schemes. The end result of such calamity and defeat is not something that can be known in a single generation."

Ji Kangzi asked Confucius, "Now, in the twelfth month of the Zhou calendar, which is the tenth month of the Xia calendar, why are there still locusts <note>term: 螽; gloss: a type of migratory locust or grasshopper</note>?" Confucius replied, "I have heard that after the Fire Star <note>term: 火; gloss: Antares in the constellation Scorpio</note> sets, the hibernating creatures all go into hiding. Now, the Fire Star is still flowing toward the west. <margin>Zhengqi Hall edition</margin> 

<pb n="62"/> The official in charge of the calendar has made an error." Ji Kangzi asked, "By how many months is it off?" Confucius said, "By the tenth month of the Xia calendar, the Fire Star should have already disappeared. Since it is still visible, the leap month has been missed twice." <margin>See the Zuo Zhuan, 12th year of Duke Ai</margin>

King Fuchai of Wu intended to take Duke Ai of Lu to meet the Marquis of Jin. Zifu Jingbo replied to the envoy, saying, "When a King assembles the feudal lords, then a Hegemon leads the Marquises and Pastors to appear before the King. When a Hegemon assembles the feudal lords, then the Marquises lead the Viscounts and Barons to appear before the Hegemon. Now, while the lords are gathered, if you take my humble ruler to see the ruler of Jin, then Jin becomes the Hegemon. Furthermore, if your excellency summons the lords in the capacity of a Hegemon, yet treats yourself as a mere Marquis, what profit is there in that?" The people of Wu then stopped. Afterwards, they regretted it and imprisoned Jingbo. Jingbo said to Grand Secretary Pi, "In the tenth month, on the first 'xin' day, Lu will perform sacrifices to the High God and the former Kings, which will be completed by the last 'xin' day. For generations, we have held this duty; since the founding of Lu, this has never changed. If the ritual officials do not meet, they will say that Wu truly lacks ritual." This was reported to Fuchai, and he was sent back. When Zigong heard of this, he went to see Confucius and said, "The son of the Zifu clan is clumsy at persuasion."
</translation>

<keywords>Confucius, Yang Huo, Ji Kangzi, Zifu Jingbo, King Fuchai of Wu, calendar, Fire Star, ritual propriety, Zuo Zhuan</keywords>

<pb n="105"/>and since no physician can save them, then one should treat them using these methods. For things that can be obtained through effort, apply the effort to obtain them. For things that cannot be obtained, there is no harm in providing them through a clever ruse. For those who are poor and cannot obtain wealth, one might borrow from a rich man, or falsely claim a friend or relative has sent a gift of money out of concern for their hunger, and place it at the head of their bed. To give in this way brings joy; it is the primary strategy for curing the illness of poverty. For those who have not yet attained office, one might urgently pay the grain tax <note>to purchase a title</note> or falsely announce a recommendation. For those already in office, one might truly plot for a substantive appointment or falsely report a promotion <note>original: "tongyi," a change in official posting or promotion</note>. As for the longevity desired by the elderly, such words come from the mouths of astrologers, shamans, and physicians. Why should I be stingy with such words of praise? These are all cases of using a person’s own path to treat their own person. Nevertheless, while it is easy to treat various illnesses, it is difficult to treat poverty. The number of people in this world who worry about poverty until they fall ill, and whose illness becomes incurable, is nearly as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges River. How can I possibly borrow the grain of the Imperial Granary or the gold of Guo Kuang <note>a famously wealthy figure of the Han Dynasty</note>? If I could give all these people my Mustard Seed Garden, <pb n="106"/>would such a joyful thing make them suddenly and completely recover?

Medicines that the heart deeply loves

The third category: a person whom the heart deeply loves can serve as medicine. When the human heart has a private love, it must be concentrated on something. It often happens that a ruler cannot obtain this from a minister, nor a father from a son; instead, a person who is extremely distant, remote, or seemingly unworthy of love becomes the focus of one's spirit and the very essence of one's life. This is the object of one's concentrated affection. It might be a charming wife or a beautiful concubine, or perhaps a close companion or a young favorite, or even a most intimate friend. To long for them and not obtain them, or to obtain them and not be close to them, can lead to illness. Even if the cause of the illness was unrelated to this, once a person reaches a state of painful distress and boredom, they will inevitably think of the person they privately love. If they are suddenly brought together, like a fish returning to water, there is no one who will not find their ears and eyes cleared and their spirit suddenly invigorated.
</translation>

<summary>Li Yu concludes his discussion on using desired objects to cure illness, noting the difficulty of curing poverty, before introducing the third category: the presence of a beloved person as a powerful remedy for the spirit.</summary>
<keywords>psychology, poverty, wealth, official rank, deception, love, companionship, spirit, Mustard Seed Garden</keywords>

<pb n="24"/><meta>continues from previous page</meta> Master Dao’an heard of this from afar. He placed a bramble cane inside a bamboo tube, sealed it, and sent it to Fayu. When Fayu opened the seal and saw the cane, he immediately said, "This is because of the monk who drank alcohol. I have been negligent in my instruction and leadership, causing my teacher to worry from so far away." He then struck the signal mallet to gather the assembly, placed the tube in front of them, and burned incense to show his respect. Prostrating on the ground, he ordered the <term>Karmadana</term> <gloss>the duty-distributor or monastic administrator</gloss> to strike him three times with the cane. He shed tears as he reproached himself. Both the clergy and the laity within the region were moved to sighs of admiration. Because of this, the number of people who exerted themselves in their spiritual practice was very great.

The Eulogy says: Alas! If people today were to open a seal sent by an elder like Dao’an, those who would not smash the tube and break the cane while speaking arrogant words would be few indeed. Between the sagely teacher and the worthy disciple, even after a thousand years, I still hold these two gentlemen in high esteem.

### Performing Repentance Rituals for the Teacher

During the Jin dynasty, Fayu of Xiapi lost both parents at a young age. He was famous for his filial piety in serving his stepmother. Later, he left the home life and served the <term>Sramana</term> <gloss>monk</gloss> Danyin as his teacher. Once, Yin became critically ill. Fayu then prayed with sincere devotion and performed repentance rituals for seven days and seven nights. On the seventh day, he suddenly saw five-colored light illuminating the doors of Yin's room. Yin felt as if someone were shaking him with a hand, and his illness was immediately cured.

### Standing in Snow Above the Knees

During the Wei dynasty, Shenguang’s learning and understanding were unsurpassed in his generation. When the Great Master Bodhidharma arrived from the Western Regions <note>referring to India</note>, Shenguang went to serve him as his teacher. Bodhidharma never spoke to him. One night, there was a great snowfall. Shenguang stood on the garden steps, and by dawn, the snow reached above his knees. Bodhidharma looked at him and asked, "You have stood in the snow for a long time; what is it you seek?" Shenguang wept and said, "I only wish for the Monk to open the gate of ambrosia <note>the nectar of immortality/the Dharma</note> and broadly deliver all living beings." Bodhidharma said, "The supreme and wonderful Way of all Buddhas is reached through diligent practice over vast eons, doing what is difficult to do and enduring what is difficult to endure. Even then, one may not reach it. How can you, with a light and shallow mind, hope for the True Vehicle? Your hard labor is in vain." Hearing these instructions, <pb n="25"/> Shenguang felt encouraged. He used a blade to cut off his own arm and placed it before Bodhidharma. Bodhidharma said, "When the Buddhas sought the Way, they forgot their own forms for the sake of the Dharma. Now that you have cut off your arm, your seeking may indeed be acceptable." Shenguang said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the teacher to pacify my mind." Bodhidharma said, "Bring your mind here, and I will pacify it for you." Shenguang said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly impossible to find." Bodhidharma said, "I have finished pacifying your mind for you." He then transmitted the Dharma to him, and Shenguang became the Second Patriarch <note>known as Huike</note>.

> The Eulogy says: The Second Patriarch obtained the Dharma truly because his sincerity was perfect and his internal potential had ripened. It was like a needle meeting a magnet; it was not necessarily because he cut off his arm. If a foolish person were to imitate this <note>literally "knitting the brows" like a famous beauty</note>, they would only be applying effort to the knife and chopping block. Alas! If transmitting the Dharma required cutting off arms, then the patriarchs would have no whole skin left. If becoming a Buddha required burning the body, then the saints would have no living flesh left. Cut off the arm of afflictions and burn the body of ignorance. I hope those who practice Chan will exert themselves in this.

***

### ->Self-Reproach Upon Leaving the Teacher<-

During the Tang dynasty, Qingjiang realized at a young age that life is like a phantom or a bubble. He took Vinaya Master Danyi as his personal preceptor. He recited the scriptures and laws, understanding everything he saw. Those who knew him said, "This is a thousand-mile colt <note>a prodigy</note> of the monastic gate." He once had a slight disagreement with his teacher, left him, and traveled to various places. After attending many Dharma assemblies, he reproached himself, saying, "I have traveled half the world, yet those who are like my original teacher are rare indeed." He then returned. At a time when the monks were assembled, he carried a bramble branch on his back and cried out, "So-and-so <note>referring to himself</note> throws himself once more before the Monk, wishing only for your compassionate acceptance." Whenever Master Danyi scolded him, Jiang would shed rain-like tears and repent. He said, "In the past, my thoughts were ignorant; now, my heart has reached realization. I hope the Monk will bestow joy through great mercy." He begged piteously four or five times. Master Danyi took pity on him, and they became teacher and disciple as before. After Master Danyi passed away, he served National Teacher Huizhong and was secretly transmitted the essentials of the Mind.

> The Eulogy says: To leave a sage and then realize one's error, and to endure scolding without retreating, can be called both wise and sincere. That he eventually received the Mind Seal, was it not because of this? Those of shallow faith leave forever over a small grudge and harbor resentment over a slight scolding. To meet a bright teacher in vain—what benefit is there in the end? It is like meeting an Emperor but failing to obtain a single office. How regrettable!

</translation>

<summary>This text details the extreme devotion and humility required of disciples toward their teachers, featuring the famous story of Huike cutting off his arm for Bodhidharma and the self-reproach of Qingjiang. It emphasizes that true spiritual progress comes from inner sincerity and overcoming ego rather than merely physical sacrifice.</summary>

<keywords>Bodhidharma, Huike, Shenguang, Second Patriarch, Dao'an, Fayu, Qingjiang, Danyi, filial piety, pacifying the mind, Zen Buddhism, monastic discipline, teacher-disciple relationship</keywords>

Later, he left the home life and served the <term>Sramana</term> <gloss>monk</gloss> Danyin as his teacher. Once, Yin became critically ill. Fayu then prayed with sincere devotion and performed repentance rituals for seven days and seven nights. On the seventh day, he suddenly saw five-colored light illuminating the doors of Yin's room. Yin felt as if someone were shaking him with a hand, and his illness was immediately cured.

### Standing in Snow Above the Knees

During the Wei dynasty, Shenguang’s learning and understanding were unsurpassed in his generation. When the Great Master Bodhidharma arrived from the Western Regions <note>referring to India</note>, Shenguang went to serve him as his teacher. Bodhidharma never spoke to him. One night, there was a great snowfall. Shenguang stood on the garden steps, and by dawn, the snow reached above his knees. Bodhidharma looked at him and asked, "You have stood in the snow for a long time; what is it you seek?" Shenguang wept and said, "I only wish for the Monk to open the gate of ambrosia <note>the nectar of immortality/the Dharma</note> and broadly deliver all living beings." Bodhidharma said, "The supreme and wonderful Way of all Buddhas is reached through diligent practice over vast eons, doing what is difficult to do and enduring what is difficult to endure. Even then, one may not reach it. How can you, with a light and shallow mind, hope for the True Vehicle? Your hard labor is in vain." Hearing these instructions,
pages.25:
Shenguang felt encouraged. He used a blade to cut off his own arm and placed it before Bodhidharma. Bodhidharma said, "When the Buddhas sought the Way, they forgot their own forms for the sake of the Dharma. Now that you have cut off your arm, your seeking may indeed be acceptable." Shenguang said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the teacher to pacify my mind." Bodhidharma said, "Bring your mind here, and I will pacify it for you." Shenguang said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly impossible to find." Bodhidharma said, "I have finished pacifying your mind for you." He then transmitted the Dharma to him, and Shenguang became the Second Patriarch <note>known as Huike</note>.

> The Eulogy says: The Second Patriarch obtained the Dharma truly because his sincerity was perfect and his internal potential had ripened. It was like a needle meeting a magnet; it was not necessarily because he cut off his arm. If a foolish person were to imitate this <note>literally "knitting the brows" like a famous beauty</note>, they would only be applying effort to the knife and chopping block. Alas! If transmitting the Dharma required cutting off arms, then the patriarchs would have no whole skin left. If becoming a Buddha required burning the body, then the saints would have no living flesh left. Cut off the arm of afflictions and burn the body of ignorance. I hope those who practice Chan will exert themselves in this.

***

### ->Self-Reproach Upon Leaving the Teacher<-

During the Tang dynasty, Qingjiang realized at a young age that life is like a phantom or a bubble. He took Vinaya Master Danyi as his personal preceptor. He recited the scriptures and laws, understanding everything he saw. Those who knew him said, "This is a thousand-mile colt <note>a prodigy</note> of the monastic gate." He once had a slight disagreement with his teacher, left him, and traveled to various places. After attending many Dharma assemblies, he reproached himself, saying, "I have traveled half the world, yet those who are like my original teacher are rare indeed." He then returned. At a time when the monks were assembled, he carried a bramble branch on his back and cried out, "So-and-so <note>referring to himself</note> throws himself once more before the Monk, wishing only for your compassionate acceptance." Whenever Master Danyi scolded him, Jiang would shed rain-like tears and repent. He said, "In the past, my thoughts were ignorant; now, my heart has reached realization. I hope the Monk will bestow joy through great mercy." He begged piteously four or five times. Master Danyi took pity on him, and they became teacher and disciple as before. After Master Danyi passed away, he served National Teacher Huizhong and was secretly transmitted the essentials of the Mind.

> The Eulogy says: To leave a sage and then realize one's error, and to endure scolding without retreating, can be called both wise and sincere. That he eventually received the Mind Seal, was it not because of this? Those of shallow faith leave forever over a small grudge and harbor resentment over a slight scolding. To meet a bright teacher in vain—what benefit is there in the end? It is like meeting an Emperor but failing to obtain a single office. How regrettable!

The gentleman embodies the virtue of Heaven and Earth’s love for life, and thus deliberates on legal cases and delays executions. This is the intent of Inner Truth. When a legal case is about to be finalized, he deliberates on it; when a death sentence is about to be carried out, he delays it. Only then can he fully satisfy the hearts of men. Regarding legal cases, he deliberates to seek an exit from within the sentence; regarding death, he delays to seek life from within the execution. The concern for punishment shown by <note>Emperor</note> Shun, the weeping over criminals by <note>Emperor</note> Yu, the prayer over the hunting nets by <note>King</note> Tang, and the burying of bleached bones by King Wen—if these did not arise from the sincerity of the original heart, who could have been moved by them? The Way of utmost sincerity can step through water and fire, crack metal and stone, and move Heaven and Earth. How much more, then, does it affect men? How much more does it affect the ghosts and spirits? The King listens to the case, the Three Dukes listen to it, and the Minister of Justice <note>original: Sikou</note> listens to it; this is the deliberation of legal cases. After ten days the officials listen again, and after thirty days they report to the superiors; this is the delaying of executions. Deliberating on cases is the image of the <term>Dui</term> <gloss>Lake/Joy</gloss> trigram; delaying executions is the image of the <term>Xun</term> <gloss>Wind/Gently penetrating</gloss> trigram. Speaking of the six lines of the single hexagram, they form an inner void; <pb n="135"/>speaking of the second and fifth lines of the two constituent trigrams, they form an inner solid. Both are images of <term>Fu</term> <gloss>Truth/Trust</gloss>. Furthermore, the lower trigram is joyful to respond to the upper, and the upper trigram is penetrating to comply with the lower; this also contains the meaning of trust. Inner Truth is that which is trusted in the heart. That which is trusted in the heart is that which is trusted in <term>Li</term> <gloss>Principle</gloss>. Having a vision of Principle and trusting it is the means by which one trusts the heart. Among the sixty-four hexagrams, there is not a single hexagram or a single line that does not take trust as its pivot. Without trust, the center is not void; and if it is not void, how can it be made solid? Vacuity is what allows for solidity; the soft being trusted by the hard. Joy and penetration are the means to achieve vacuity. Trust reaching even to pigs and fish is the mutual resonance of vacuity. Crossing the water in a wooden boat is the mutual assistance of vacuity. Its reality is Principle. Principle is Heaven; it is the reason why the heart is a heart. This is what is meant by "beneficial to persist."

# High-Minded and Wise Scholars Will Naturally Use This to Correct Themselves

## Instructions for Dong Zhiguang

The student Dong Sizhang <note>The secular name of Dong Zhiguang</note> was born and raised in a wealthy and noble household, yet he early on developed the mind to seek liberation from the cycle of birth and death. This is surely the result of the inner scenting power of his habitual practice of <term>Prajna</term> <gloss>transcendental wisdom</gloss> and superior karmic connections from past lives. He first studied under Great Master Yunqi <note>Also known as Lianchi Zhuhong, a prominent late Ming dynasty master of the Pure Land and Chan schools</note>, who transmitted to him the <term>Pure Land</term> <gloss>Sukhavati</gloss> Dharma gate. Recently, he visited me, the Old Man, at Shuangjing, wishing to receive the <term>Upasaka</term> <gloss>layman</gloss> precepts. He openly confessed his deep and heavy karmic obstacles and sinful deeds, wishing to seek the essential points for escaping suffering and asking what kind of cultivation he should practice to extinguish his transgressions. 

I, the Old Man, therefore instructed him, saying: Since you already know your roots of sin are deep and heavy, the ancient virtuous ones taught people to dissolve old karma according to the situation and strictly avoid creating new misfortunes. For sentient beings with heavy karma, the Buddha opened the gate of <term>repentance</term> <gloss>Kshama</gloss>, which is the most convenient way to escape suffering. A verse says:

> All sins are like frost and dew,
> The sun of wisdom can dissolve them.
> If one wishes to practice repentance,
> Sit upright and mind the <term>True Mark</term> <gloss>Dharmata; the ultimate reality of all phenomena</gloss>.

This is the correct practice; all other methods are auxiliary means. The original nature of sentient beings and the Buddha <pb n="11"/> is equal; originally it is without defilement and has no marks of birth, death, coming, or going. It is only because of the initial lack of enlightenment and the delusion regarding one’s own original nature that it is called <term>Ignorance</term> <gloss>Avidya</gloss>. Because of ignorance, all kinds of false thoughts arise, leading to various inversions <note>distorted perceptions of reality</note> and the creation of various karmas. One falsely takes on the sufferings of birth and death within the <term>Triple Realm</term> <gloss>the realms of desire, form, and formlessness</gloss>. This is all because ignorance prevents one from understanding one's own mind, causing one to be turned by false thoughts. 

It is like a person in a deep sleep having various nightmares. There are all kinds of environments and all kinds of terrors, with many sufferings that are hard to endure. Yet, once they wake up and search for the things in the dream, they are completely unobtainable. Therefore, sentient beings fallen into the dream of ignorance follow false thoughts and inversions, creating various karmas and bringing suffering upon themselves. Looked at with waking eyes, how could those states of inversion be found? 

Existing now within this dream of ignorance, how can one dissolve old karma? One must use the light of wisdom to illuminate and break through ignorance, believing that one's own mind is originally pure and not being driven by false thoughts and inversions. Then, all karmas will have no cause, for false thoughts are the very cause of all karmas. Why is this? It is because since the beginningless past, one has been deluded about one's own original mind, life after life...
</translation>

<summary>Master Hanshan instructs a lay disciple, Dong Zhiguang, on the nature of repentance and the dissolution of karma. He explains that sin and suffering are like a dream caused by ignorance, which can only be dispelled by recognizing the original purity of the mind through wisdom.</summary>

<keywords>Hanshan Deqing, Dong Zhiguang, repentance, karma, ignorance, True Mark, original nature, Pure Land, Buddhist precepts, dream metaphor</keywords>

Thus, fire flames upward and water moistens downward; they follow the rising and falling of <term>yin</term> and <term>yang</term>, and soil cannot restrain them. Wood and metal are the flowering and fruiting of soil. Their natures contain a mixture of water and fire. Therefore, wood as an object is born when soaked in water and produces fire when burned, yet it remains inseparable from them. This is because it obtains the flowering of the soil, floating at the intersection of water and fire. Metal as an object obtains the essence of fire from the dryness of the soil and obtains the essence of water from the moisture of the soil. Thus, water and fire depend on each other without mutual harm; when melted, metal flows but is not consumed. This is because it obtains the solid essence of the soil at the boundary of water and fire. Soil is that which brings things to their beginning and their end. It is the substance of the earth and the finality of transformation. It is that through which water and fire rise and fall, <pb n="121"/> and it is the substance that encompasses all things without omission. Master Zhang’s explanation of how metal, wood, water, fire, and soil are produced is an unchanging principle.

From this, the invalidity of the fatwa of those who opposed it is known. Thus, if anyone issued a fatwa opposing that fatwa, they have retracted that fatwa and have acknowledged their error. Their signatures have been written above this, confirming the fatwa of the Mufti <unclear>so that the brothers may know</unclear> who see this response. upon the best of Allah's creation, and upon his family and companions, the guides of the nation, and upon the scholars who are the inheritors <note>referring to the prophetic tradition that scholars are the heirs of the prophets</note>, and those who follow them until the Day of Resurrection. <pb n="15"/>their mother. The male and female share equally in this, because they are her brothers and sisters through her mother; and brothers through the mother share equally with their sisters <note>in Islamic inheritance law, siblings through the mother share equally regardless of gender, unlike other siblings where males receive a double share</note>, as is well known. Thus, if they were to divide the inheritance of a son of a sister through the mother and maternal aunts through her, they do not divide it such that the male receives the portion of two females. End quote.

It is apparent from both the <term>Tuhfa</term> <gloss>The Gift, likely referring to Tuhfat al-Muhtaj</gloss> and the <term>Nihaya</term> <gloss>The End, likely referring to Nihayat al-Muhtaj</gloss> that their statement "equally" is a condition for both the children of the child through the mother and for the maternal uncles and maternal aunts through her. This is explicitly stated in the <term>Sharh al-Rawd</term> <gloss>Commentary on the Meadow</gloss>, as you have learned from its phrasing. However, the matter is not so; rather, their statement "equally" is a condition for the children of the child through the mother only. The exception then becomes apparent. Then they mentioned the reason for the exception, until he said: As for the maternal uncles and maternal aunts through the mother—meaning the brothers of the deceased’s mother and her sisters through her mother—they are excepted from the aforementioned rule as you have learned. It follows from their exception that they inherit with the male receiving the portion of two females, because they occupy the status of the mother, as is explicitly stated in the primary texts, let alone others. If they were to inherit the portion of the mother as if she were the deceased, they would divide it according to the number of their heads <note>per capita</note>. 

Jamal al-Ramli <note>a prominent 16th-century Shafi'i jurist</note> followed this in his <term>Nihaya</term>, and their teacher Zakariya al-Ansari preceded them in <term>Sharh al-Rawd</term>. His phrasing was: "And an exception to that is made for the children of the brother through the mother, and the maternal uncles and maternal aunts through her; they do not divide it such that the male receives the portion of two females, but rather they divide it among themselves equally, as will be known from what follows in his speech." End quote. 

I understood it as such so that we do not judge that to be an oversight. End quote. And God knows best. According to the Hanbalis, the maternal uncle is prioritized over all other uterine relatives <term>dhawi al-arham</term>. If the male and the female are from the same side, such as the children of a daughter being in the same degree, and one of them precedes the other in reaching the heir, that one is prioritized. Otherwise, they inherit through both, such as the daughter of a daughter of a daughter of a son of a daughter, as if the son of Zaid’s daughter married the daughter of his other daughter and they had a daughter; or the daughter of a paternal sister who is the daughter of a maternal brother, as if Zaid’s brother through his mother married his sister through his father and they had a daughter; or the daughter of a maternal uncle who is the daughter of a paternal uncle, as if Zaid’s maternal uncle married his paternal aunt and they had a daughter. Note: <insert>they are equal in it</insert> This is taken from our statement "descendant."

<pb n="16"/>In the case of descending generation after generation, etc., until the intermediary between the uterine relatives and the heir, the lower heir is considered among the first. He said in <term>Kashf al-Ghawamid</term> <gloss>Uncovering the Obscurities</gloss> by the grandson: The mother’s father occupies the status of the mother, and the father’s father’s mother occupies the status of the father’s mother, and the mother’s father’s mother occupies the status of the mother’s father. End quote. If the intermediary were not considered, the mother’s father’s mother would occupy the status of the heir, who is the mother, and thus she would be equal to the mother’s father, but no one holds this view. Thus, what is found in the <term>Fatawa</term> <gloss>Legal Opinions</gloss> of the scholar Ibn Hajar regarding his making the son of the maternal aunt equal to the maternal uncle is subject to review. 

It is understood from our statement "according to his inheritance from him" as a residuary <term>asaba</term> or as a fixed share <term>fard</term> that the intermediary is considered in bringing down the portion of the heir to the uterine relative, since the residuary and fixed shares are actualized in the connected descendants. He said in <term>al-Fath</term> <gloss>The Victory/Opening</gloss>: The summary of this is that you raise the lower descendant generation by generation, and for the higher ancestor, you do the opposite. End quote. Therefore, I said after that: meaning the portion of the heir descends to the descendants connected to him, etc. Also, there might be a uterine relative at the end of the descendants, such as the daughter of the son of a daughter of a son, and the son of the daughter of that daughter. If the intermediary were not considered, he would be excluded because he is not an heir of this heir. But it is not so; rather, the portion of the granddaughter <note>daughter of the son</note> descends to her descendants three times, then the portion of the son descends to his daughter, and the portion of the daughter to her son. And God knows best.

The author, may God grant him enjoyment of it, said: This is the end of what I intended to transcribe from the aforementioned book during my journey to the Honored Mecca for the Pilgrimage <term>Hajj</term> in the year 1232 <note>1817 CE</note>, so that it may be a reference for me in case of need, as it is the summary of the statement of that commentary. And because it was not possible for me to take the original work with me; otherwise, that would have been better because it mentions additional clarification and explanation, and mentions chapters on examples of the classes of heirs, their branches, their differences, the rulings of the return <term>radd</term>, the principles of their mathematical problems and examples, and the school of the People of Relationship <term>Ahl al-Qarabah</term> <gloss>a school of thought in uterine inheritance</gloss> and its branches. I ask God Almighty to benefit the people of Islam by them both. May God bless our master Muhammad and his family and all his companions and grant them peace. Amen. Finished.
</translation>

<summary>
This text concludes a legal treatise on the inheritance rights of uterine relatives (dhawi al-arham), discussing the methodologies of prominent Shafi'i and Hanbali jurists. The author notes he transcribed this summary during his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1817 CE as a portable reference for complex estate division.
</summary>

— In a jar, in a jar with spirits!... The heir of the Tsars of All Russia is floating in spirits like a little frog! — he suddenly burst into such wild laughter that a shiver ran through Peter’s body. He thought again: "Madman!" — and felt that loathing, akin to an unearthly horror, which he always felt toward spiders, cockroaches, and other vermin.

But in that same instant, the horror turned to rage: it seemed to him that his son was laughing at him, deliberately "playing the fool" in order to shut himself off and hide his villainies.

— What else is inside you? — he proceeded again with the interrogation, as if not noticing what was happening to the Tsarevich.

The latter stopped laughing as abruptly as he had begun; he leaned his head back against the chair, and his face turned pale and haggard, like that of a dead man. He looked at his father silently with a senseless gaze.

— When you had hope in the rabble, — Peter continued, raising his voice and trying to make it sound calm, — did you not send someone to the rabble to speak of that rebellion, or did you not hear from anyone that the rabble wants to revolt?

Alexei was silent.

— Answer! — Peter shouted, and his face was jerked by a convulsion.

Something flickered in Alexei's face as well. He forced his lips open with an effort and pronounced:

— I have said everything. I will say no more.

Peter struck his fist upon the table and leaped up.

— How dare you!...

The Tsarevich also stood and looked his father straight in the eye. Again they became like one another with a momentary and seemingly ghostly resemblance.

— Why do you threaten, father? — Alexei spoke <pb n="535"/> quietly. — I am not afraid of you; I am afraid of nothing. You have taken everything from me, ruined everything, both soul and body. There is nothing more to take. Except perhaps to kill. Well then, kill! It is all the same to me.

And a slow, quiet smile twisted his lips. It seemed to Peter that in this smile there was infinite contempt.

He roared like a wounded beast, threw himself upon his son, seized him by the throat, threw him down and began to strangle him, trample him with his feet, and beat him with a cane, all with that same inhuman roar.

In the palace, people woke up, grew frantic, and began running about. But no one dared enter the Tsar's presence. They only turned pale and crossed themselves, approaching the doors and listening to the terrifying sounds that carried from within: it seemed as if a beast were gnawing on a man there.

The Empress was sleeping in the Upper Palace. They woke her. She came running, half-dressed, but she also did not dare to enter.

Only when everything had finally grown quiet did she open the door slightly, peer in, and enter on tiptoe, stealing in behind her husband’s back.

The Tsarevich lay on the floor unconscious; the Tsar was in an armchair, also nearly in a faint.

They sent for the personal physician Blumentrost. He calmed the Empress, who feared that the Tsar had killed his son. The Tsarevich had been beaten severely, but there were no dangerous wounds or fractures. He soon regained consciousness and seemed calm.

The Tsar was worse off than his son. When they moved him — almost carrying him in their arms — to the bedroom, he was seized by such convulsions that Blumentrost feared paralysis.

But by morning he felt better, and in the evening he had already risen and, despite the entreaties of <term>Katenka</term> <gloss>Empress Catherine I</gloss> and the warnings of the physician, ordered a boat to be brought and set out for St. Petersburg. The Tsarevich was carried alongside in another closed boat.

On the following day, the 14th of May, a second manifesto regarding the Tsarevich was announced to the people, in which it was stated that the Sovereign had been pleased to promise his son forgiveness, "if he should bring true repentance in all things and conceal nothing;

<meta>continues from previous page: the claim of the existence of unbearable hardship in walking between the two mosques, as they mentioned in the following question, is false and explicitly so.</meta> <translation>
<pb n="12"/> Rather, what compelled the claimant to make such an assertion was ignorance of its meaning, combined with deception in the question <note>referring to a formal legal query or fatwa request</note>, as will be explained later. This is coupled with a lack of desire for divine reward and a love for ease and luxury. Consider this: if a sick person is able to endure a hardship equivalent to walking in rain and mud—as previously mentioned—then how can a healthy person not endure a hardship that is less than that? This is an undeniable logical analogy. Indeed, if there were a distribution of <term>riyals</term> <gloss>silver coins</gloss> at the old mosque, would you see those claiming "hardship" staying behind because they lack the strength to endure it? Or would you find them to be the first to rush toward it? Success in returning to the truth is from God. Amen.

### The Ninth Matter: Clarifying the Ruling on the impermissibility of multiple Friday prayers in this specific case.
It is not hidden from any person of knowledge that our <term>Shafi'i</term> <gloss>one of the four major schools of Sunni Islamic law</gloss> Imams—may God be pleased with them—only permitted the multiplication of Friday prayers due to necessity and need. This necessity is defined as "the certainty of the difficulty of gathering," as will be cited from *al-Tuhfah* <note>referring to Tuhfat al-Muhtaj by Ibn Hajar al-Haytami</note>, in order to repel the constraint resulting from "unbearable hardship." It is well known that every necessity is measured according to its extent. They identified causes for the difficulty of gathering: either due to fighting <note>civil strife or danger</note>, the narrowness of the place due to the large number of worshippers, or the distance of the town's outskirts. They established strict conditions for each of these causes that must be certainly present.

The condition for "narrowness of the place" is that there is certainly no place in the town of the Friday prayer that can accommodate them. Furthermore, the relied-upon position—as in *al-Tuhfah* and *al-Nihayah*—is that the criterion is the number of those who usually attend the Friday prayer, not those who actually attended, whether the place is a mosque or otherwise. The certainty of the lack of a place is verified when no place for the Friday prayer exists at all, when it is impossible to expand the existing prayer site, or when it is impossible to roof an unroofed area if praying in the sun <column-break/> results in a hardship that is certainly unbearable.

The certain absence of these aforementioned conditions is the "excuse" alluded to by our Master <term>al-Ghazali</term> <gloss>the famous 11th-century jurist and theologian</gloss> in his statement: "If their gathering in one congregational mosque is excused <note>literally: becomes difficult/impossible</note>, then it is permitted in two mosques, etc." For the meaning of "excuse" is the total impossibility of the matter, not merely a suspicion that there is no space, nor a mere claim of narrowness without verifying the aforementioned meaning with certainty—rather, such claims are a "strike in the dark" <note>an idiomatic expression for guesswork</note> and a pursuit of comfort and luxury.

Furthermore, the condition of "distance of the outskirts" is either that the distance requires traveling from dawn until the time of the Friday prayer, or that the person cannot hear the call to prayer from the top of the minaret—as explained in the seventh matter—or the presence of "unbearable hardship" according to its definition in the eighth matter. Thus, the certainty of the difficulty of gathering is not established except through these mentioned restrictions and conditions. As for the statement in *al-Tuhfah*, "the certainty of their difficult gathering," it refers to the existence of one of those causes with its specific conditions. The same applies to every statement by al-Ghazali. 

When the need is verified—meaning the existence of what we mentioned—know that they have defined the "difficulty of gathering" arising from one of those causes as "unbearable hardship." The author of *al-Tuhfah* said: "The criterion for difficulty is that it contains a hardship that is usually unbearable." The end. This hardship is what constitutes constraint and necessity, as previously mentioned in the eighth matter, and as will be cited here from <term>al-Qamuli</term> <gloss>a noted Shafi'i jurist</gloss>, who stated this explicitly with its evidence. Similarly, the answer of the <term>Mufti</term> <gloss>jurisconsult</gloss> of Mecca cannot be used as evidence for the validity of multiplication in this specific case, because it mentions the conditions of "need" and "hardship" which <column-break/> are not found in the actual reality of the case, as has been established in these matters repeatedly and will be clearly known from the eleventh matter to come. These traits clearly indicate their stubbornness against the truth and that they have no motive other than establishing the multiplication <note>of Friday prayers</note>, by any means, through any path, and according to any school of thought—even if it is through a void <note>invalid</note> method, as will be known from their words. This is an undeniable logical analogy. Indeed, if there were a distribution of <term>riyals</term> <gloss>silver coins</gloss> at the old mosque, would you see those claiming "hardship" staying behind because they lack the strength to endure it? ### The Ninth Matter: Clarifying the Ruling on the impermissibility of multiple Friday prayers in this specific case.
It is not hidden from any person of knowledge that our <term>Shafi'i</term> <gloss>one of the four major schools of Sunni Islamic law</gloss> Imams—may God be pleased with them—only permitted the multiplication of Friday prayers due to necessity and need. This necessity is defined as "the certainty of the difficulty of gathering," as will be cited from *al-Tuhfah* <note>referring to Tuhfat al-Muhtaj by Ibn Hajar al-Haytami</note>, in order to repel the constraint resulting from "unbearable hardship." It is well known that every necessity is measured according to its extent. They identified causes for the difficulty of gathering: either due to fighting <note>civil strife or danger</note>, the narrowness of the place due to the large number of worshippers, or the distance of the town's outskirts. They established strict conditions for each of these causes that must be certainly present.

The condition for "narrowness of the place" is that there is certainly no place in the town of the Friday prayer that can accommodate them. Furthermore, the relied-upon position—as in *al-Tuhfah* and *al-Nihayah*—is that the criterion is the number of those who usually attend the Friday prayer, not those who actually attended, whether the place is a mosque or otherwise. The certainty of the lack of a place is verified when no place for the Friday prayer exists at all, when it is impossible to expand the existing prayer site, or when it is impossible to roof an unroofed area if praying in the sun <column-break/> results in a hardship that is certainly unbearable.

The certain absence of these aforementioned conditions is the "excuse" alluded to by our Master <term>al-Ghazali</term> <gloss>the famous 11th-century jurist and theologian</gloss> in his statement: "If their gathering in one congregational mosque is excused <note>literally: becomes difficult/impossible</note>, then it is permitted in two mosques, etc." For the meaning of "excuse" is the total impossibility of the matter, not merely a suspicion that there is no space, nor a mere claim of narrowness without verifying the aforementioned meaning with certainty—rather, such claims are a "strike in the dark" <note>an idiomatic expression for guesswork</note> and a pursuit of comfort and luxury.

Thus, the certainty of the difficulty of gathering is not established except through these mentioned restrictions and conditions.
