<translation>
<pb n="533"/>clever the ministers are, Alexander Nikolaevich <note>Tsar Alexander II</note> does not trust them completely. To assist them, he has called upon the famous Doctor Liprandi <note>Ivan Liprandi, a high-ranking official known for his role in domestic surveillance and suppressing the Petrine circle</note>, who treats with heroic remedies and will undoubtedly bring things to a tragedy sooner. The great consolation of governmental Petersburg now is the people and the people's attachment to the Tsar. They threaten the revolutionary youth with the people. "The Tsar need only wave his hand, and the students will be no more." Yes, undoubtedly they will be no more; but on the next day, the nobility in all of Russia will also be no more, and along with the nobility, the entire officialdom will fall under the axe; you yourselves, dear fellows, will perish. Well then, try waving that hand! And there will remain the people and the Tsar. But what will this Tsar do with this people? For our Tsar is bureaucratic, a Tsar of the nobility, not a <term>Zemsky</term> <gloss>land-based or representative of the common people</gloss> Tsar. He himself will drown in noble blood, only to give way to some new Pugachev <note>Yemelyan Pugachev, leader of a massive peasant uprising in the 18th century</note>! Would it not be better to try the methods of Nicholas <note>Tsar Nicholas I, known for his autocracy</note>: the whip, the gallows, and Siberia? They are good methods. But they will hardly help you now. For fear has been killed in Russia. Nowadays people will go to the place of execution laughing at you. Even for cowards, there is no advantage in recoiling before your terror. In Russia now there is a fear more terrifying: the fear of the people's retribution. And if one must choose between the axe or the gallows, then naturally it is better to fall with the consciousness of a noble feat than as the victim of a fatal popular misunderstanding.

You have one more remedy: war. A national war against the Germans, in alliance with Italy and France, perhaps even for the freedom of the Slavs, if only to avoid giving freedom to the Russian people. Yes, indeed, to go to war against the Germans is a good and, most importantly, a necessary Slavic cause; in any case, it is better than strangling the Poles to please the Germans. To rise up for the liberation of the Slavs from under the Turkish and German yoke will be a need, a necessity, and a sacred duty of the liberated Russian people. But you, the enemies of Russian and Polish freedom, what kind of freedom will you give the Slavs? Or do you want to repeat the old, shameful deception for the hundredth time? Having satisfied no one and resolved nothing at home, upon what will you lean? Even the army you will have to <pb n="534"/>maintain on credit through foreign subsidies. And you will only serve as a means for the goals of others; you yourselves will gain nothing, while you will ruin Russia completely. Or perhaps you are counting on her exhaustion? Do you think, perhaps, to pacify her with hunger? Look out, do not be mistaken in your calculation: war did not hinder the Pugachev rebellion nor the Novgorod riot here.

But all our efforts are in vain. Neither war, nor the tricks of a mock-liberal (?) ministry, nor overt reaction will help you. The people have awakened and are waiting for their hour; you yourselves contributed to their awakening. By flirting with them and inciting them against the young educated generation, you yourselves awaken in them the consciousness of strength, and they will take by force that which you do not wish to give voluntarily.

For a peaceful outcome to the present inevitable crisis, there is only one remedy: a <term>Zemsky Sobor</term> <gloss>Assembly of the Land</gloss> representing all the people, and within it, the resolution of the <term>zemskoe</term> <gloss>common land/national</gloss> cause. This is the only salvific means in the hands of the Tsar. But he does not wish to use it. This means he wants blood.

When rulers ruin a country, private individuals must take up the work of salvation. To all true conservatives who have the intellect to understand and foresee necessary events, to all merchants, priests, and nobles, to military and civil officials who love tranquility and peace and wish to preserve life, property, wives, sisters, and children, to all to whom the prosperity and glory of Russia are dear, I would advise thinking hard about this. For not much time remains for free reflection. And it would not be bad if they, having come to an agreement, formed among themselves a massive conservative society, which I would suggest they name: "the society for the salvation of Russia from Tsarist nearsightedness and from criminal ministerial charlatanism," and let them raise their voices in unison in favor of the <term>Zemsky Sobor</term> as the sole means for preventing a bloody, destructive catastrophe.

And for us, the revolutionary party, what is to be done? We too shall unite and stand under the banner of the "People's Cause" <note>Narodnoye Delo</note>.
</translation>

<summary>Bakunin warns that the Russian autocracy's attempt to use the peasantry against the revolutionary youth will lead to a total social collapse and noble bloodshed. He argues that only an all-national representative assembly (Zemsky Sobor) can prevent a violent revolution.</summary>
<keywords>Alexander II, Liprandi, Pugachev, Zemsky Sobor, Slavic liberation, revolutionary party, People's Cause, Russian nobility, social crisis</keywords>

<pb n="26"/>all the people are sustained, just as a <term>fetus</term> <gloss>embryo</gloss> is sustained through its navel in the womb of its mother. Shining in the Torah like the crescent of the moon, they do not cease to study the words of the Law; the words of the Torah do not cease from their mouths, just as the waters of the river that goes out from Eden do not cease. And seventy sages surround it like a circular threshing floor, whose treasuries are full of the holy tithes, vows, and free-will offerings. They fence them about with the study of the Law, and for all who seek salvation and comfort, it is said to them in the language of the assembly: since they are compared to roses, their scent is pleasant. They have the strength to labor in the Torah and its paths. **Your navel is a rounded goblet, let it not lack mixed wine; your belly is a heap of wheat, hedged about with lilies.** The heads of your assembly and its leaders, who for the sake of your merit, provide for the whole world. They are like a fortress of ivory, and through them, the people of the House of Israel are conquered and returned to the Master of the world. Your scribes are full of wisdom like pools of water, and they know how to calculate the accounts of the intercalations, fixing the leap years and determining the heads of the years and the beginnings of the months according to the knowledge of the Sanhedrin. The place of the court is like the House of Judah, similar to King David who built the fortress of Zion, which is called the Tower. And the Lebanon, which every teacher who stands upon it can see all the towers of Damascus. And your people are like a tower of <unclear>Shab</unclear>. **Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim; your nose is like the tower of Lebanon looking toward Damascus. Your head crowns you like Carmel, and your flowing locks are like purple; a king is held captive in the tresses.** The teacher is not withheld from the righteous head, like Elijah the prophet who was zealous with his zeal and slew the false prophets at Mount Carmel, and brought the people back to the fear of the Lord, God of Hosts. And the poor of the people who walk with a bowed head are destined <pb n="27"/> to be clothed in purple, just as Daniel was clothed in the city of Babylon and Mordecai in Shushan, because of the merit of Abraham who previously acknowledged the Master of the world, and by the righteousness of Isaac whom his father bound in order to sacrifice him, and by the piety of Jacob who peeled the rods. It shall be added unto you like a full star. And he shall be occupied with you like purple. **A king is bound in the tresses. How beautiful and how pleasant you are, O loved one, with all your delights!** Solomon the King said: How beautiful are you, O assembly of Israel, at the time when you accept the yoke of My kingdom, when I chastise you with sufferings for your sins and you accept them with love. They appear in the faces of those who are pampered. How I shall reward you and how I shall delight you, O beloved among the nations. **Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts are like clusters.** And at the time when the priests spread their hands and bless their brothers, the House of Israel, their fingers are spread out like the branches of a palm tree, and their stature is like a date palm. They stand face to face before the priests, their faces bowed to the earth. Indeed, the answer of Judah was: I will rise like a palm tree. I will hold to <column-break/> its clusters. **I say: I will climb the palm tree and lay hold of its fruit. May your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the scent of your breath like apples.** The Lord said through His Word: I will go up and test Daniel to see if he can stand in the trial, just as Abraham his father stood, who is compared to a palm branch, in ten trials. And they were all proven through Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, to see if they could stand in the trial. I will redeem the people of the House of Israel for the sake of their merit, for they are compared to clusters of grapes. And the names of Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah shall be heard in all the earth. Their fragrance shall be like the scent of the apples of the Garden of Eden. **And your palate is like the best wine.** And she revealed her finger. And your palate is like the best wine. **It goes down smoothly for my beloved, flowing gently over the lips of those who sleep.** The assembly of Israel said: How sweet are the words of the Law upon the decree of the Word, just as they were received by their fathers. It is compared to new wine and old. It follows the paths that were prepared before Him, just as the fathers and the ancient righteous ones walked. They raise the dead, which is like a man who speaks in his sleep.
</translation>

<summary>This portion of the Targum to the Song of Songs provides an allegorical interpretation of the physical descriptions in the biblical text, linking them to the Sanhedrin, the patriarchs, and the merit of Daniel and his companions. It emphasizes the spiritual nourishment of the Torah and the future rewards for Israel's faithfulness during times of trial.</summary>

<keywords>Targum, Song of Songs, Allegory, Sanhedrin, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, Azariah, Torah study, Priesthood, Resurrection of the dead</keywords>

I will redeem the people of the House of Israel for the sake of their merit, for they are compared to clusters of grapes. And your palate is like the best wine. **It goes down smoothly for my beloved, flowing gently over the lips of those who sleep.** The assembly of Israel said: How sweet are the words of the Law upon the decree of the Word, just as they were received by their fathers. <pb n="56"/>melodious, sorrowful, and enchanting songs, or for noble character, or for the delicate craftsmanship of the paw, or for extraordinary guidance and useful assistance, or even for the harmfulness that necessitates extreme caution and precise cunning; thus it is prioritized in mention for those reasons. And what is more wondrous than the magpie <note>original: *al-‘aq‘aq*</note>, with the accuracy of its senses, the intensity of its caution, and its excellent discernment? Furthermore, there is no bird on earth that protects its eggs more fully, with greater defense and subtler knowledge than it. ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan <note>the third Caliph, reigned 644–656 CE</note>, may God be pleased with him, said: "Everything loves its offspring, even the bustard," though the bustard is used as a proverb for stupidity. Yet the magpie, despite its proficiency in means and its speed in snatching, does not employ these traits for what benefits it. How many a heavy, precious necklace and noble, costly earring has been snatched from the hands of people, only for it to be thrown away after circling in the air, or tucked away and never looked at again. Al-Asma‘i <note>a celebrated Arab philologist and scientist, 740–828 CE</note> claimed that a magpie once stole a precious beaded necklace <term>sikhab</term> <gloss>a necklace made of scented beads or cloves</gloss> belonging to some people. The owners of the necklace seized a Bedouin woman who was with them. While she was being beaten, dragged, and cursed, the magpie passed by with the necklace in its beak. They shouted at it, and it dropped the necklace. The Bedouin woman, recalling her safety after having been afflicted by another calamity, said:

> The day of the necklace is among the wonders of our Lord,
> It is as if He rescued me from a town of evil.

She meant the settled people among whom she had stayed. There is no harm in mentioning what arises, provided it does not belong to those long chapters containing nothing but abstract analogies and pure dialectic <term>kalam</term> <gloss>speculative theology</gloss>, for such things are not easy to hear, nor do souls find joy in reading them. A professional scholar or one seeking divine reward and merit might endure that, but whenever we find a topic that can be adorned with elegant, eloquent poetry and novel reports, we take the trouble to include it and narrate it all for the benefit of the reader. For this reason, we permitted ourselves to say what we said in the chapter on fire. I shall write to you after this—since I have perhaps bored you with lengthiness and led you upon the most difficult mounts and roughest paths by mentioning a significant portion of the discourse of the theologians <term>mutakallimun</term>—and I do not think I should increase your weariness or make you exhaust your energy by starting the discourse on camels, cows, sheep, lions, wolves, donkeys, gazelles, and the like, which I intend to write for you. Rather, I will start with the smaller, shorter, and more concise chapters, and the most pleasant of them, so that you do not leave the first chapter without being eager for the second, and likewise for the third and fourth, until the end of what I shall write for you, God willing. We shall begin with what concerns the sparrow, then we shall take up the mention of the mouse <pb n="57"/> and the scorpion, and the enmity between them along with their other traits; then the discourse on the scorpion and the beetle and the friendship between them; then the discourse on the cat; the discourse on the hedgehog; then the discourse on mosquitoes and fleas; then the discourse on lice and children; then the discourse on the monitor lizard and the dabb-lizard; then the discourse on the jerboa and the hedgehog; then the discourse on vultures and Egyptian vultures; then the discourse on the eagle and the rabbit; then the discourse on ticks and frogs; then the discourse on the bustard and similar creatures.

Before this chapter, we shall mention chapters of elegant poetry suitable for study and encouraging vigor, making the reading of long books worthwhile. Were it not for my low opinion of those who pretend to seek knowledge in this time, and those who feign the patronage of books in this age, I would not have needed to coax them, entice them, reconcile their souls, and encourage their hearts—despite the many benefits of this book—with this long training and these frequent apologies. It is as if the benefit I provide them is something I receive from them, and as if my desire for their improvement is the desire of one who seeks their worldly gains. 

Yet, I have not mentioned anything from the long chapters, and I have moved toward mentioning the difference between the Jinn and mankind, and between the angels and the prophets, and the difference between the female and the male, and the difference between them and that which is neither female nor male, until our discourse extends to the superiority of the human being over all types of animals. We shall mention nations and eras, destinies and lifespans, and the measures of intellects through sciences and crafts. Then the discourse will cover the nature of the human being from the time it was a drop of fluid <term>nutfah</term> until it is consumed by anxieties. If you become bored with the book and find the reading heavy, you are then excused. I have no ruse for you except to present it to you in the finest form and turn you through various arts, so that you do not leave the argumentation of the Wise Quran except for the traditional Hadith, and you do not leave the Hadith except for authentic poetry, and you do not leave elegant authentic poetry except for a current, pertinent proverb, and you do not leave a current proverb except for philosophy and rarities that experience has validated, examination has highlighted, and proof has unveiled—the wonders for which souls have a passion and toward which sound minds have a strong longing. For this reason, I wrote it for you and directed it to you, seeking reward through you. So look into it with the eye of an impartial peer and scholar, or the eye of a seeker of guidance among students and followers. For if you find the book I have written for you to be contrary...
</translation>

<summary>Al-Jahiz discusses his authorial method, emphasizing the use of poetry, anecdotes, and variety to keep the reader engaged despite the serious theological and scientific content. He lists upcoming topics including small animals like magpies, mice, and scorpions, as well as broader philosophical distinctions between humans, Jinn, and angels.</summary>
<keywords>magpie, bustard, Al-Asma‘i, literary style, pedagogy, Jinn, human superiority, Jami' al-Hayawan</keywords>

<pb n="19"/>When they set their hearts on the love of power, and are unable to obtain it through themselves and their own merit, they squander their fortunes, baiting and corrupting the masses in every way. Once they have made the people greedy for bribes and handouts through this mindless craving for reputation, then democracy is destroyed, and it is transformed into a rule of violence and the law of the fist <note>original: "χειροκρατία"</note>. For the multitude, having become accustomed to eating the property of others and basing their hopes for a living on the possessions of their neighbors, when they find a high-spirited and daring leader who is excluded from the honors of the state due to poverty, then they establish the rule of the fist. Gathering together, they commit massacres, banishments, and redistributions of land, until, having become thoroughly brutalized, they find a master and a monarch once more. This is the cycle of constitutions <note>original: "πολιτειῶν ἀνακύκλωσις"</note>, this is the ordinance of nature, according to which political systems change, are transformed, and return again to the same point. A person who has clearly recognized these things might perhaps be mistaken regarding the exact timing when speaking of the future of a constitution, but concerning where each state stands in its growth or its decay, or in what direction it will change, he would rarely be deceived, provided he makes his declaration without anger or envy. Furthermore, regarding the Roman constitution, it is through this specific understanding that we may best come to know its formation, its growth, and its peak, and likewise the reverse change that will follow from these. For if any other constitution, as I have just said, follows a natural course, this one too has its formation and growth according to nature from the beginning, and will have its change into its opposite according to nature as well. This will be visible through what is to be said hereafter. For now, we shall make a brief mention of the legislation of Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note>. For such a discussion is not irrelevant to our purpose. He, having considered each of the aforementioned <pb n="20"/> things to be fulfilled by necessity and nature, and having reasoned that every simple form of constitution founded upon a single power is precarious, because it quickly turns into its own characteristic and naturally following vice. For just as rust is a natural plague to iron, and wood-worms and borers to timber, by which they are destroyed from within even if they escape all external harm; in the same way, a certain vice grows naturally within and follows each constitution. For kingship there is the so-called monarchical way <note>referring here to tyranny</note>; for aristocracy, the way of oligarchy; and for democracy, the brutal rule of the fist. Into these, it is impossible for all the aforementioned systems not to undergo transformations over time according to the logic just described. Lycurgus, having foreseen this, did not establish a simple or uniform constitution, but gathered together all the virtues and characteristics of the best systems, so that no single part, by growing beyond what is necessary, should turn into its inherent vice. Instead, by the power of each being pulled in opposite directions by the others, no part should lean or incline too far in any direction, but being held in equilibrium and balanced, the constitution should remain for a long time like a ship sailing against the wind. The pride of kingship is restrained by the fear of the people, who were given a sufficient share in the government. The people, in turn, do not dare to treat the kings with contempt because of their fear of the elders <note>The Gerousia or Council of Elders in Sparta</note>, who, having been selected based on merit, would always incline themselves toward justice. Thus, the side that was being weakened by remaining faithful to traditional customs would always become greater and heavier through the influence of the elders.

<summary>Polybius describes the cyclical nature of political decay, moving from democracy to violent mob rule and back to monarchy. He explains how Lycurgus of Sparta countered this by creating a balanced, "mixed" constitution to prevent any single branch of government from becoming corrupt.</summary>
<keywords>Polybius, political cycles, anacyclosis, Lycurgus, Sparta, Roman constitution, mixed government, checks and balances, political decay, democracy, oligarchy, monarchy</keywords>

<pb n="183"/> <note>The word "stainless" <note>original: "Niranjanam"</note> was concluded on the previous page.</note> Through constant practice, one certainly sees it within three days. By the mere sight of it, that practitioner burns away a multitude of sins. || 189 || 190 ||

Commentary—One should contemplate that <term>Niranjana</term> <gloss>the stainless</gloss> known as the <term>Hamsa</term> <gloss>Swan</gloss>, possessed of nectar-like rays and sixteen digits, located in the cavity of the skull at the head. By performing this practice constantly for three days, the manifestation of the stainless one will certainly appear to the practitioner. Through mere sight, that practitioner will burn away all fallen states. || 189 || 190 ||

Root Text—The future reveals itself and the purification of the mind truly occurs. Even if performed for a moment, it burns away the five great sins. || 191 ||

Commentary—By performing this meditation, the inspiration of future matters will occur; that is, matters that have not yet arisen will be revealed, and the purification of the mind will take place. Through mere meditation, the practitioner burns away the five great sins at that very moment. || 191 ||

Root Text—The planets become favorable and all calamities perish. Obstacles are pacified and one obtains victory in battle. || 192 || The <term>siddhis</term> <gloss>supernatural powers</gloss> of <term>Khechari</term> <gloss>moving in the sky</gloss> and <term>Bhuchari</term> <gloss>moving on the earth</gloss> occur from seeing the milk-white Moon. Through meditation alone <pb n="184"/> everything occurs, there should be no doubt here. || 193 || Through the yoga of continuous practice, a human becomes a <term>siddha</term> <gloss>perfected being</gloss>. Truly, truly, and again truly, he certainly becomes equal to me. This supreme Yoga Scripture is the giver of perfection to yogis. || 194 ||

Commentary—By meditating on the Moon located in the head, all planets become favorable, all calamities are destroyed, obstacles are calmed, and victory is gained in war. The perfection of <term>Khechari</term> and <term>Bhuchari</term> is obtained, there is no doubt in this. By performing this yoga practice constantly, the practitioner certainly becomes a perfected being. O Parvati! I say truly, truly, and repeatedly, that he will become equal to me, there is no doubt in this. This supreme yoga is the giver of perfection to yogis. || 192 || 193 || 194 ||

The Description of Raja Yoga
Root Text—Beyond this is the divine-formed thousand-petaled lotus. It stands outside the body known as the <term>Brahmanda</term> <gloss>the egg of Brahma/the macrocosm</gloss> and grants liberation. || 195 || Its name is Kailas, where <term>Mahesha</term> <gloss>the Great Lord Shiva</gloss> dwells; it is called <term>Akula</term> <gloss>beyond family or form</gloss>, imperishable, and free from decay or increase. || 196 ||
</translation>

<summary>These pages describe the benefits of meditating on the lunar disc within the skull, which grants prophetic vision, planetary favor, and equal status to Shiva. It then introduces Raja Yoga and the thousand-petaled Sahasrara lotus, identified as the spiritual Mount Kailas.</summary>

<keywords>Niranjana, Hamsa, five great sins, Khechari siddhi, Bhuchari siddhi, Raja Yoga, Sahasrara, Kailas, Mahesha, Akula</keywords>

<pb n="54"/>and the action of existing things arises from the attribute of pervasive knowledge. 

However, knowledge is of two types: one is that which is called knowledge according to common convention <note>original: "bi-hasb-i 'urf"</note>, and the other is that which is not called knowledge according to common convention. Both categories belong to the category of knowledge according to the Masters of Truth <note>the Sufi gnostics</note>, for they witness the permeation of the essential knowledge of God—Glorified is He—into all existing things. 

Of the second category—which is not conventionally considered a "knower"—is water, for example. We see that it distinguishes between height and depth; it turns away from height and flows toward depth. Similarly, it penetrates into the interior of a body and arranges the exterior of the visible body, and so forth. It is a property of knowledge to flow according to the requirements of the receptivity of the receiver and to not oppose it. However, in this particular degree, the degree of knowledge has appeared in the form of nature. By this same analogy, knowledge permeates all other existing things—indeed, all perfections 

<pb n="55"/> that follow existence permeate all existing beings.

<note>The following is a poetic quatrain presented in a table format in the manuscript.</note>
| | |
|---|---|
| That which follows existence in all existing things: | |
| Existence, with the attributes that were hidden within it, | Brought the essences of the world into being. |
| The secret of a description, because it was receptive to it, | Became manifest according to the capacity of the essence. |

Just as the reality of existence, by virtue of its absolute purity <note>original: "sarafat-i itlaq"</note>, permeates the essences <note>term: "dhawat"</note> of all existing things in such a way that within those essences it is identical to those essences—just as those essences were identical to it <note>in the divine foreknowledge</note>—so too His perfect attributes, in their totality and absoluteness, permeate all the attributes of existing things. This occurs in such a way that, within the context of their attributes, they are identical to their attributes, just as their attributes were identical to those perfect attributes within the essence of those perfect attributes. For example, the attribute of knowledge, within the context of the knowledge of one who knows particulars, is identical to the knowledge of particulars; and within the context of the knowledge of one who knows universals, it is identical to the knowledge of universals.
</translation>

<summary>Jami explains how divine knowledge and attributes permeate all levels of reality, even in seemingly inanimate things like water. He argues that all worldly attributes are specific manifestations of God's absolute and perfect attributes.</summary>
<keywords>knowledge, existence, permeation, attributes, essences, nature, particulars, universals, Sufi metaphysics</keywords>

Just as the reality of existence, by virtue of its absolute purity <note>original: "sarafat-i itlaq"</note>, permeates the essences <note>term: "dhawat"</note> of all existing things in such a way that within those essences it is identical to those essences—just as those essences were identical to it <note>in the divine foreknowledge</note>—so too His perfect attributes, in their totality and absoluteness, permeate all the attributes of existing things. This occurs in such a way that, within the context of their attributes, they are identical to their attributes, just as their attributes were identical to those perfect attributes within the essence of those perfect attributes. For example, the attribute of knowledge, within the context of the knowledge of one who knows particulars, is identical to the knowledge of particulars; and within the context of the knowledge of one who knows universals, it is identical to the knowledge of universals.

<pb n="13"/>The son, having followed in the footsteps of his dear father,
Bestows many benefits upon my fatherland.
He presides over the afflicted, and kindly helps
Needy men, and is ready to bring aid to the wretched.
He once provided green pastures for my Muses <note>The author uses the Muses to represent his poetic inspiration and education</note>,
And continually benefited my studies.
For these things, may Almighty God one day grant him
The celestial joys of eternal life.
You will skillfully imitate these examples of your kin;
Express the character of your renowned ancestors, distinguished groom.
Thus your praise will grow, thus your lineage will become
Brighter, and thus your fame will be perennial.
But since you weigh these matters more wisely through your own self,
Let our songs cease from their admonition.
Just as a strong horse born of strong seed
Does not fear the clatter, nor flee from dismal arms,
Not otherwise will you follow the deeds of your famous parents,
Nor allow your own natural talent to degenerate.
Great joys deservedly sustain your mind,
Bride, because that man comes into your chambers.
Not I, even if I should surpass the Pylian Nestor <note>A legendary king of Pylos in the Iliad, famous for his extreme age and wisdom</note> in speaking,
Or if I were greater in eloquence than Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the most famous Roman orator</note>,
Could I recount all the things that the glory of such a groom
Demands to be brought forth according to his merit.
Why then, my Muse, do you not rather leave the young
Husband, and seek the face of the chaste maiden?

<pb n="14"/>Greetings, renowned nymph <note>The bride is poetically addressed as a nymph to emphasize her beauty and grace</note>, the ornament of feminine modesty;
Greetings, great glory of the virginal choir.
May He himself prosper the most holy laws of your marriage bed,
He who was the first patron and author of the bridal chamber <note>A reference to God as the institutor of marriage</note>.
He who first devised the weddings of the sweet torch <note>The wedding torch was a classical symbol of the marriage ceremony</note>,
And who is said to love the sacred flames of the bed.
May he peacefully bless the treaties of your couch,
Euphrosyne <note>The name of the bride</note>, a girl worthy of so great a man.
Rare is your beauty, and the excellence of your form
Is so great that it makes you surpass all other women.
You lift your dark blue eyes toward the lofty airs
Quite often, and you shine entirely with a golden color,
Just as is frequently accustomed to be in the clouds
Colored by the shining light of the Sun opposite them;
Or like the dewy mother <note>Aurora, the Goddess of the Dawn</note> who drives away the stars of heaven
And leads the day from the Eastern axis.
Such color is seen on your face; hardly do lilies
Stained with purple blood blush so much for me.
Divine modesty adorns your beautiful countenance;
You are gentle, and you lack all rudeness.
An ivory neck lets down golden-haired locks,
And flowery wreaths polish your hair.
Your arms are whiter than snowy privets;
Each limb displays its own adornment.
You also, Groom, be cheerful, be glad with all your heart,
Because she seeks your embraces.
</translation>

<summary>This wedding poem praises the groom's virtuous ancestry and personal character before turning to celebrate the beauty and modesty of the bride, Euphrosyne. The author uses classical allusions to Nestor, Cicero, and the goddess Aurora to elevate the couple's status.</summary>
<keywords>epithalamium, marriage, Johann Hartlieb, Euphrosyne, Memmingen, virtue, beauty, ancestry</keywords>

## Report of Mr. Johannes Waser, Pastor at Dynhart.
->From Jesus the Physician, health comes from no other source!<-

<note>A large ornamental initial letter E is decorated with floral and leaf motifs.</note>
**Honorable**, highly learned Mr. Brother-in-law Doctor Ziegler, etc.
Since I have heard that the third description of the bath at Urdorff is to be prepared for the press, I also wish to share what has been observed by me during the time of my fifteen-year pastoral service at Urdorff. This famous bath is heartily good for the <term>Calculo</term> <gloss>stone</gloss>, for it softens and drives out stone, sand, and grit from the kidneys and bladder, as many other honest persons besides myself have experienced in deed. For <term>Cholericis</term> <gloss>those suffering from bile</gloss>, or the jaundiced, it is also excellently suited, from whom it has carried away a mass <note>original: "Wust"</note> of waste, of which the witnesses are for the most part still living at this time. For <term>Febricitanten</term> <gloss>those suffering from fever</gloss> (of whatever kind they may be), it was beneficial. Many wasted away, tubercular, and lung-diseased persons have been brought there in litters due to weakness, who after completing the cure were able to ride home on horseback fresh and healthy. To the ruined and indigestive stomach it brings again an excellent appetite and creates a desire for eating. It <term>Acuire</term> <gloss>sharpens</gloss> and strengthens the eyes most wondrously, so that many persons who had to use glasses or spectacles before the bath-cure could afterwards write, read, and perform other business without them. I also well remember respectable people of standing who visited it on account of infertility and afterwards excellently praised the <term>efficaciam</term> <gloss>efficacy</gloss> and joyful effect. To this blessing of God, my successor, Mr. Pastor Wirtz, also gives testimony. Precious at that place for the bath is a helpful, charming, friendly, and lovely host and innkeeper; where the fault lies in the place, all attraction is lost.

<pb n="14"/><note>A woodcut ornament features symmetrical scrolls and floral motifs.</note>

### I.

Come here! You friends, come here! Shown to you here
Is an excellent bath; which has long been praised
By the highly learned Stumpff; who spoke of it with fame;
Kircherus, world-renowned, highly esteemed by the learned,
In his book of wonders; about it has written
Mr. Doctor Gessner too; since then it has kept
Its ancient praise and fame. It has three springs,
Whereby one may see how manifold is
The grace of the Great Physician. The first carries sulfur,
The second copper; from the third spring comes
The healing, good alum. There one finds at all times
Food, drink, and everything that delights the soul and mind.

->Well-meaningly added for his beloved brother the Doctor<-
->By<-
->**Christoph Ziegler, Doctor.**<-

<note>A small decorative border made of repeating floral patterns.</note>

### II.

After God the Lord had stirred at Urdorff
Three healthy waters, the foundation was laid.
<margin>1526.</margin> For its proper use, by Mr. Steiner indeed,
<margin>1583.</margin> Mr. Johann Ziegler was however the true master builder.
Who did lead and equip this precious bath,
And also excellently adorned it for honorable bathing guests
With its amenities, just as one desires.
Mr. Jacob Ziegler, who was a highly learned doctor
<margin>1620.</margin> And well-experienced, has shown us two times
<margin>1662.</margin> In print, from what minerals,
Out of three springs, this water is powerful:
He knew this through the wondrous chemistry <note>original: "Chimey"</note>.
</translation>

<summary>A testimonial from Pastor Johannes Waser regarding the medicinal successes of the Urdorff baths, followed by poetic tributes from Christoph Ziegler detailing the bath's history and mineral composition.</summary>

*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
The wave of the Scamander <note>a river near Troy</note> will be witness to his great virtues,
Which spreads far and wide into the rapid Hellespont,
Whose path he will narrow with heaps of slaughtered bodies,
Making the deep rivers warm with mingled carnage.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Finally, even the prey given over to death shall be a witness,
When the smooth tomb, heaped up with a high mound,
Shall receive the snow-white limbs of the struck-down maiden <note>Polyxena, sacrificed to the ghost of Achilles</note>.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
For as soon as chance has given the weary Achaeans <gloss>Greeks</gloss> the power
To loosen the Neptunian bonds of the Dardanian city <note>the walls of Troy, built by Neptune</note>,
The high sepulcher shall be moistened with the blood of Polyxena,
Who, like a victim falling under the two-edged steel,
Shall drop her headless body on a kneeling knee.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Therefore come, join the desired loves of your souls,
Let the husband receive the goddess in a happy covenant,
Let the bride be surrendered at last to the eager husband.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
When the nurse revisits her at the rising light,
She will not be able to encircle her neck with yesterday's thread <note>a reference to the swelling of the neck after the consummation of marriage</note>.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Nor shall the anxious mother, saddened by the separate sleeping
Of her discordant daughter, cease to hope for dear grandchildren.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Foretelling such happy things for Peleus in days of old,
The Fates <note>original: "Parcae"</note> sang these songs from their divine breast.
<pb n="197"/>For in person, the heaven-dwellers used to visit chaste homes
Quite often, and show themselves to the mortal assembly,
While piety was not yet despised.
Often the father of the gods <note>Jupiter</note>, revisiting his shining temples,
While the annual rites came on festive days,
Beheld the chariots of the Cretans racing on the ground.
Often wandering Bacchus <note>original: "Liber"</note> from the highest peak of Parnassus
Drove the Thyades <gloss>Bacchic devotees</gloss> crying "Euan!" with flowing hair,
When the Delphians, rushing eagerly from the whole city,
Received the god with joyful smoking altars.
Often in the death-bearing contest of war, Mars <note>original: "Mauors"</note>,
Or the mistress of rapid Triton <note>Minerva</note>, or the Rhamnusian virgin <note>Nemesis</note>,
Being present, exhorted the armed troops of men.
But after the earth was stained with unspeakable crime,
And everyone banished justice from their greedy minds,
Brothers soaked their hands in brotherly blood,
The son ceased to mourn his dead parents,
The father wished for the funeral of his young son,
So that he might freely enjoy the flower of a young stepmother,
The impious mother, casting herself beneath her unknowing son,
Did not fear to defile the ancestral gods <note>original: "Penates"</note> with impiety.
All things right and wrong, mingled in a wicked madness,
Turned the righteous mind of the gods away from us.
Therefore they do not deign to visit such assemblies,
Nor do they suffer themselves to be touched by the clear light of day.

<summary>The Fates conclude their prophecy regarding the marriage of Peleus and Thetis, foretelling the bloody exploits of their son Achilles and the sacrifice of Polyxena. The poet then contrasts the ancient age of divine intervention with the current age of human depravity and moral decay.</summary>

he will lay low the bodies of those born of Troy with his hostile sword.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
The wave of the Scamander <note>a river near Troy</note> will be witness to his great virtues,
Which spreads far and wide into the rapid Hellespont,
Whose path he will narrow with heaps of slaughtered bodies,
Making the deep rivers warm with mingled carnage.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Finally, even the prey given over to death shall be a witness,
When the smooth tomb, heaped up with a high mound,
Shall receive the snow-white limbs of the struck-down maiden <note>Polyxena, sacrificed to the ghost of Achilles</note>.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
For as soon as chance has given the weary Achaeans <gloss>Greeks</gloss> the power
To loosen the Neptunian bonds of the Dardanian city <note>the walls of Troy, built by Neptune</note>,
The high sepulcher shall be moistened with the blood of Polyxena,
Who, like a victim falling under the two-edged steel,
Shall drop her headless body on a kneeling knee.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Therefore come, join the desired loves of your souls,
Let the husband receive the goddess in a happy covenant,
Let the bride be surrendered at last to the eager husband.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
When the nurse revisits her at the rising light,
She will not be able to encircle her neck with yesterday's thread <note>a reference to the swelling of the neck after the consummation of marriage</note>.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Nor shall the anxious mother, saddened by the separate sleeping
Of her discordant daughter, cease to hope for dear grandchildren.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Foretelling such happy things for Peleus in days of old,
The Fates <note>original: "Parcae"</note> sang these songs from their divine breast.
pages.197:
For in person, the heaven-dwellers used to visit chaste homes
Quite often, and show themselves to the mortal assembly,
While piety was not yet despised.
Often the father of the gods <note>Jupiter</note>, revisiting his shining temples,
While the annual rites came on festive days,
Beheld the chariots of the Cretans racing on the ground.
Often wandering Bacchus <note>original: "Liber"</note> from the highest peak of Parnassus
Drove the Thyades <gloss>Bacchic devotees</gloss> crying "Euan!" with flowing hair,
When the Delphians, rushing eagerly from the whole city,
Received the god with joyful smoking altars.
Often in the death-bearing contest of war, Mars <note>original: "Mauors"</note>,
Or the mistress of rapid Triton <note>Minerva</note>, or the Rhamnusian virgin <note>Nemesis</note>,
Being present, exhorted the armed troops of men.
But after the earth was stained with unspeakable crime,
And everyone banished justice from their greedy minds,
Brothers soaked their hands in brotherly blood,
The son ceased to mourn his dead parents,
The father wished for the funeral of his young son,
So that he might freely enjoy the flower of a young stepmother,
The impious mother, casting herself beneath her unknowing son,
Did not fear to defile the ancestral gods <note>original: "Penates"</note> with impiety.
All things right and wrong, mingled in a wicked madness,
Turned the righteous mind of the gods away from us.
Therefore they do not deign to visit such assemblies,
Nor do they suffer themselves to be touched by the clear light of day.

76. Likewise, is a mother excluded from her legal portion <note>original: "legitima"</note> through an express pupillary substitution <gloss>the naming of a substitute heir for a minor</gloss>? We affirm this.

->Donellus on the law "By prayers" in the Code regarding substitutions for minors and others.<-

77. A man can make a testament by military law both for himself and for his son, or for the son alone even if he has not made one for himself: which testament will be valid if the father happens to die either during military service or within a year of service.

->Law "In fraud" 15, paragraph "likewise both for himself" in the Digest on military testaments.<-

78. Finally, a soldier can appoint an heir by his bare will, even by signs, in whatever way he wishes or is able; likewise, he can appoint an heir for a specific time, and another after that time.

->Law "In fraud" 15, paragraph 1, and paragraph "a soldier" 4 in the Digest under this title.<-

79. Here a question can be proposed: Why can an heir be written by a civilian <term>paganus</term> <gloss>a non-soldier or civilian</gloss> under a condition, but not starting from or ending on a specific day? We shall investigate the reason.

->Law "Under condition" 73 in the Digest on the institution of heirs, law "inheritance" 3, 4.<-
->Digest on the institution of heirs: Cujacius in the commentary on the Code regarding<-
->military testaments, folio 325.<-

80. Hence, although soldiers have neither employed the legal number of witnesses nor observed other solemnities of testaments, they nevertheless make a valid will, provided it is established that a testament was made.
<margin>at the beginning of the Institutes on military testaments.</margin>

81. Therefore, if the soldier whose goods are being questioned before you spoke in such a way, after calling men together for the purpose of testifying to his will, that he declared whom he wished to be his heir and to whom he would grant freedom, he can be seen to have testified in this manner even without writing, and his will must be held valid.

->Law 24, paragraph "if therefore" in the Digest on the testament of a soldier.<-

82. Indeed, if he has noted anything in his scabbard or on his shield with letters glowing with his own blood, or has inscribed it in the dust with his sword at the very time when he left his lot of life in battle, a will of this kind ought to be stable.

->Law "a soldier" 15 in the Code on the testament of a soldier.<-

<pb n="19"/>
83. Just as a soldier can grant an inheritance by bare will, so also can he take it away.
Law "In fraud" 15, paragraph "Just as however" 5 of the Digest on the testament of a soldier.

84. Likewise, a soldier is permitted to make several testaments; but whether he made them at the same time or separately, they will all be valid if he has specifically expressed this: nor will the earlier one be broken by the later one.
Law "it was complained" 19 on the testament of a soldier.

85. An elegant question can be discussed here as occasion permits: Whether a civilian's testament, perfected earlier, is broken by a later imperfect one in which those coming from intestacy are appointed heirs, if a son was passed over in the later one? Having inspected the legal truth in this, we shall strive to defend the negative with all our strength.
Law 7 of the Digest on children and posthumous heirs; Law 16, paragraph 1 of the Digest on common substitution.

86. A soldier’s testament is also not broken by the birth of a posthumous child <note>agnatio posthumi</note>, provided that when the soldier passed over the posthumous child, he knew his wife was pregnant.
Law 9 and Law 10 of the Code on the testament of a soldier.

87. Likewise, even if he was unaware his wife was pregnant, if he was of such a mind that he wished whoever might be born to him to be disinherited, the testament is not broken.
Law 7 of the Digest on the testament of a soldier.

88. A soldier's testament is also not broken if he has adopted a son <term>arrogaverit</term> <gloss>adopted a person who was legally independent</gloss>, or if a grandson has succeeded to the place of a son.
Law "the same is" 8 of the Digest on the testament of a soldier.

89. Likewise, if a soldier who is a head of a household <term>paterfamilias</term>, having made a testament only concerning his camp-acquired property, has given himself over to be adopted, his testament is nonetheless valid, as if by a new expression of will.
Law "the same" 23 of the Digest under this title.

90. However, these benefits concerning the making of last wills are granted only to those who are occupied in expeditions.
The second to last law of the Code on the testament of a soldier.

91. It is disputed whether those soldiers who are in camps, in the trenches, or in winter quarters, or stationary camps, or in garrisons, away from the battle line and away from the danger of battle, are permitted to testify by military law? We judge it more true that it is permitted.
Cujacius in the commentary on the Code regarding the testament of a soldier.

<keywords>military law, testament, inheritance, pupillary substitution, posthumous heirs, adoption, battle, legal privilege</keywords>

Given from my study at Altdorf <note>original: "Museo Altdorphino"</note> on the day before the Academic Festival, held in the church sacred to Saints Peter and Paul, by which this most flourishing Academy was to pass into a University on the following day; I pray and vow from the innermost fibers of my soul that it may thrive and flourish in this bloom and honor forever. In the year of restored Salvation 1623.

-> To the Kind Reader <-

I truly confess, wise reader, that many—indeed, very many—errors are present in this collection, not only light ones but also grave ones that offend grammatical purity. Such is the case in the fifth decade <note>a section or group of ten items</note> regarding <term>tēs eudaimonias</term> <gloss>concerning happiness</gloss> in the preface, where <term>infamis</term> <gloss>infamous</gloss> appears instead of <term>infamibus</term> <gloss>for the infamous</gloss>. ## FAVORING FRIEND.

Whom shall I call you, Friedrich, so skilled?
With what titles shall I adorn you, Friedrich, you who are skilled
With sufficient dignity? Truly amazed,
I do not know; I doubt, truly amazed,
That anyone is more blessed with a divine genius than you,
More blessed with a divine judgment.
What? Should you not deservedly be called—
Who? A *second Tirynthian Hercules*?
By Pollux! Not undeservedly would you be called that—
Who? A *second Tirynthian Hercules*.
Do you wish? I will show you, and you will give faith to my words.
What, I ask, is the celebrated <term>Sophia</term> <gloss>Wisdom</gloss>? Is she
Not the pious mother of the liberal
Arts? And she brought forth more beautiful
Daughters, whom you seize with a more celebrated
Love of a more celebrated intellect.
Among the others, <term>Dejanira</term> <note>the wife of Hercules in mythology</note>,
Especially more sweet in her form
And also more virtuous than the rest,
Is through your every limb...

<pb n="10"/>### XLIV.

Furthermore, the Jews, in order to maintain the same cycle of seasons in each month, add an entire month whenever the number of <term>Epacts</term> <gloss>the difference in days between the solar and lunar years</gloss> exceeds thirty days.

### XLV.

The Epacts are the eleven differential days between the Solar year of 365 days and the Lunar year of 354 days. These must subsequently increase if we allow several years of this kind to flow from a single common beginning without compensation.

### XLVI.

And thus arises that Lunar year which I previously called <term>Embolimæus</term> <gloss>intercalary</gloss>. Since it is so tempered by the motions of the Moon that even the months of common years, regarding the enjoyment of perpetual seasons, are by its benefit restored in some way to the laws of solar revolutions; the entire form of such years is deservedly considered composite, and the years themselves are to be held neither as purely Lunar, nor even as solar, but as Luni-Solar.

### XLVII.

Finally, some Civil years are more unrestricted than others. The Olympiad years are completed sometimes in 360, sometimes 361, or 362 days, and likewise others in 390, 391, or 392 days. The Nabonassar years, or Egyptian years, have 365 days, like the Common Julian year: but without any intercalation.

### XLVIII.

Therefore, that reckoning of years is quite wandering if it is compared with the Julian form. For the Egyptian year does not find a certain and perpetual beginning there, but once any four-year period has elapsed, it differs from the Julian years by an entire day, because of the intercalary day which every fourth Julian year receives, but the Egyptian does not admit.

### XLIX.

Hence its beginning runs backward through all the months of the Julian year, until 1460 Julian years are finished and 1461 Egyptian years are completed. For then both return to one common beginning. <pb n="11"/> These things I had to say concerning Time, according to the nature of my purpose, concluding with the verses of Master Cramer:

> If you always measure fleeting time with your fingernails and finger,
>    time will never pass away idle.
> Tomorrow's hour is not yet here, yesterday's cannot be recovered
>    for a thousand talents: if you wish to live, live today.

<pb n="12"/>They prepare everything: the house bustles on all sides with unaccustomed work. Then Father Abraham, with all things now duly prepared, binds raw sandals around his <note>Isaac's</note> tender feet, and takes up the fate-bearing sword with its gleaming hilt. This blade, as they tell it, was first beautifully forged from solid iron by the clever mind of Lamech’s son <note>Tubal-cain, the first smith</note> through the newly discovered art of smithing. He had delivered it to his father, and Father Noah then preserved it in the safe ark when God overwhelmed the vast world and all its peoples with waves. From there, all his descendants joyfully received it, and Terah himself left it thus to his son Abraham. When these things were done, he entrusts the faithful reins of the household to Sarah and bids her guard the rest of the home. She nods to his command and seeks her son; she delays him with her voice just as he is attempting to follow his dear father. Now she bids him cover his golden hair, now his chest; now she charges him to keep the gods <note>the Divine</note> in mind and to hold God before his eyes above all else with frequent gaze. For the upright, she says, their rewards remain; these the Ruler of high Olympus loves, these he cares for. Thus she speaks, and pours out tears between every word. But the son replies: Now, dear mother, farewell; farewell, best of mothers. Behold, my father calls, behold he calls; farewell, you rooftops. When he had spoken thus, he turns his steps likewise, leaving his mother weeping and often wishing—whether love persuaded her, or perhaps the forebodings of a worried mind—to wrap her arms around his snowy neck.

<pb n="13"/>She, however, followed him as he departed with such words: Go, go, our glory; enjoy the favor of the gods; with them as companions may you leave this home, and with them may you return. Thus, therefore, having now left the dear city of their fatherland, the son and father enter the greening fields. The servants follow behind them, leading the bowed beast of burden, and they tire it out much with staff and goad. From here they enter joyful valleys and are covered by various trees, pursuing their way under high foliage. The Zephyrs <note>west winds</note> accompany them from behind as they go, and charming birds rise up and greet them with their song. Meanwhile, Father Abraham, through the pleasant greenery, relates many things concerning primeval religion and faith. In the beginning, he recounts the origins of the spacious world: how God fashioned the spheres of heaven out of nothing, and once separated the earth from the wandering waves, and bound all things so beautifully in concordant peace. Then he sings of the wickedness of Satan, and the crimes of the first parent <note>Adam</note>, and the Seed to come in the rolling years who shall take vengeance on Satan and overturn the depths of hell; and who shall crush the head and coil the dark breast of the Serpent, flowing with much gore, through the gloomy caverns. Then he tells how He submerged the whole world beneath the sea because of the sins of men and the foul heats of lust; or in what way and with what voice God revealed himself to the fathers and ancestors, or with what speech he spoke to them; and he lays open the remaining deeds of the ancients in a long sequence.
</translation>

## THEOLOGICAL APPROBATION

*These Universals, most learnedly proposed along with their side-arguments <term>parerga</term> <gloss>supplementary philosophical points</gloss> drawn from the whole of Philosophy, and illuminated by the splendors of the most serene House of Bavaria, will be most rightly published in print for the common benefit of studious youth and the most useful exercise of the religious lord defending them.*

-> JOHANN OSWALD VON ZIMMERN, Doctor and <-
-> Professor of Sacred Theology, Licentiate of Both Laws <note>Civil and Canon Law</note>, Academic <-
-> Pro-Chancellor, and currently Theological Dean. <-

***

## PHILOSOPHICAL APPROBATION

*This Dispute concerning Universals in genus and species proposes a solid and clear doctrine of the same, and at the same time, with the annexed side-arguments, provides abundant material for further disputation; wherefore it is worthy to be printed for this purpose.*

-> LEONARD LERCHENFELDT of the Society <-
-> of JESUS, Professor of Moral Philosophy and <-
-> Dean for the time being. <-

<pb n="24"/><note>A decorative horizontal border of repeating ornamental floral and knotwork patterns sits at the top of the page.</note>

# TO THE REVEREND, RELIGIOUS, AND MOST LEARNED LORD DEFENDER OF UNIVERSAL PHILOSOPHY IN THE UNIVERSALS.

*Let others build up for themselves beautiful Wisdoms <note>original: "Sophias"</note>,*
*As if grooming shining Rachels <note>referring to the biblical Rachel, representing the contemplative life</note>,*
*Let them fashion their brows and shape them with a needle,*
*Refine their cheeks with learned trifles,*
*And paint their brides with sterile labor.*
*At these things my Wise Man laughs; he seizes*
*The sister, the eloquent mother Leah <note>referring to the biblical Leah, representing the active or fruitful life</note>.*
*Rachel displeases him: Leah, he says, gives*
*The universal dowry, she gives birth to the universals.*
*I have seen forms swell under Daedalian <gloss>skillfully wrought</gloss> chisels,*
*Born to stir up envy.*
*I have seen bulls ordered to be silent by a Sarmatian <note>Polish or Northern</note>*
*Wound: the threatening pillars of harbors,*
*Built in the water-flowing Triple-City <note>possibly referring to a specific city like Passau or a symbolic structure</note>:*
*Causes supported by the favor of demigods:*
*Gods playing in a physical bath:*
*Small particles from a more blessed urn:*
*The worlds of Alexander the Great <note>original: "Pellaeos mundos"</note> while Asia stood amazed.*
*I have seen clouds give birth to great things;*
*The Pious heirs of the heavenly spheres.*

<column-break/>

*The Lion of Stagira <note>Aristotle</note> will roar in a Pygmy fashion.*
*The Lyceums <note>Aristotelian schools</note> will learn the price of shadows.*
*Our man says: I want the bleary-eyed sister.*
*Though Leah is not bleary-eyed, even if she is believed*
*To be so by one whose own eyes are dim; she is not bleary-eyed.*
*How is it that she brings forth Species? To us,*
*Leah is lovely, and a noble Nymph:*
*The mother of both Lineage and pedigrees:*
*The goddess of beautiful Differences.*
*Now let Rachel boast of the light favors of the Graces,*
*And glass dolls, and Accidents*
*On a parchment brow, the roses of cheeks,*
*The brief riches of youth.*
*Not so, not so does Leah offer from her own.*
*She does not need borrowed vapors;*
*She has learned to shine with native elegance;*
*Taught to blush with no other dye*
*Than that which is Property <note>original: "Proprium", a logical term for an essential attribute</note> for the One, which she is and has.*
*Rachel displeases. Rich Leah promises*
*The universals; you deliver the universals.*

***

->Out of the debt of Religious honor and love.<-

->Applauded by<-

FATHER GREGORY MAGIUS, Professed Canon Regular of the
Order of St. Augustine in Gars, Student of Sacred
Theology and the Canons.
</translation>

Ah! for your endeavors, beloved one, when a select company

The rostrums of your own accord, and weighs with silent mind the prizes
With which everyone who is yours wishes to see you adorned at once.

->Master Samuel Schultetus, of Hamburg.<-

Is it so, Friend, that all discover the omen
Of your noble name, while you present the easy pledges
Of your genius? Just as the Phrygian lion, led by fierce
Savage-power, does not harm all the wretched race of beasts,
To whom wise nature granted weakened strengths
Of body, but rather pursues the rabid ones with ferocious
Ardor, by which he may test his deeds that prove his fame.
So also, Friend, you bring forth the monuments of your manly genius,
Defending the swelling material concerning the Essence of Spirit <note>original: "de Pneumatis Esse"</note>,
And scorning all things with a lesser investigation.
Well done! I pray for your undertakings and for fates favoring your studies!

->These things I wrote for the sake of our most sincere friendship.<-

->**Otto Helle of Lübeck.**<-

58. Those things are mixed in which God is worshiped by the body and the soul, internally and externally at the same time, such as prayer, praise, thanksgiving, reading, and honorable speech concerning divine matters.

<margin>Luke 10.</margin>
59. Therefore, whoever is content with mental prayer and rejects vocal prayer as if it were useless is in error. Such a person dares to prefer every prayer performed by the mind alone over every prayer which is also expressed by the voice. For although Mary Magdalene is said to have chosen the better part compared to Martha, because the latter gave herself to action and the former to contemplation: yet most truly that which is said of Magdalene, the Church proclaims concerning the most blessed Virgin Mary, as one who joined both together and excelled greatly in both. Thus, clearly, he who prays with affection alone does better than he who only mumbles with his lips. Yet he who offers prayers to God in both ways undoubtedly surpasses him.

<margin>
Proverbs 30.
Jeremiah 22.
</margin>
60. **THESE ARE THE THREE** things through which the earth is moved, to which Jeremiah cries out a third time. For sobriety sustains the man approaching God, justice leads him, and piety brings him through to the end toward which he strives.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 25.</margin>
61. Who denies that these three are indeed difficult? But they are beautiful, in which even the spirit of God finds pleasure; they are approved before God, whom sobriety invites, justice holds, and piety places upon a throne. And just as they are before God, so they are also before men, among whom surely the first wins admiration, the second benevolence, and the third reverence. For we admire the chaste and sober, we love the beneficent, and we deem the religious worthy of special honor.

<margin>
Ecclesiasticus 25.
Proverbs 30.
Ecclesiasticus 4.
</margin>
62. There are three other types which I wish our soul hated, just as the soul of God does. Three insatiable things: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life <note>original: "concupiscentia carnis, concupiscentia oculorum, et superbia vitae"</note>; a triple wedge marching with a hostile face against the ranks of the God of Israel; a triple cord drawing toward certain destruction, which undoubtedly could only be broken with difficulty (if at all) by those who trust in their own strength.

63. But (thanks be to God) our force is no less strong in pulling us back from ruin, while temperance extinguishes the lust of the flesh, generosity curbs the lust of the eyes, and humility strikes down the pride of life.

<pb n="13"/>64. Man (over whom they contend) is placed in the middle between these battle lines; to whichever side he turns, its victory is certain.

65. This is the order of the struggle: first of all, the flesh must be subdued, and he who serves it still clings to the beginnings; pride always remains for the last, which, even if cast down a thousand times, nevertheless keeps rising again, and is sometimes stronger the more powerful the force that prostrated it.

<margin>
Isaiah 22.
1 Corinthians 15.
</margin>
66. Since, however, there is mention of labor and battle, let the memory of reward and payment immediately occur; we are compelled to say this: we worship God in vain, we follow justice in vain, and they act foolishly who do not eat and drink, being about to die tomorrow, if there is no reward for a deed rightly done, and if no punishment is prepared for the sinner.

<margin>Psalm 61.</margin>
67. Furthermore, God could be judged more cruel than just or merciful (let there be no blasphemy in the word) if He is moved by anger but not by grace; if He brings punishments upon the iniquitous, the impious, and the sinners, but establishes no rewards for the just, the pious, and the hardworking.

<margin>
Proverbs 24.
Ecclesiasticus 35.
Romans 2.
2 Corinthians 5.
Revelation 22.
</margin>
68. If, however, a reward and wage will be given to each one according to the fruit of his works, it is a wonder why the merits of good works are denied.

> Therefore let us live soberly, justly, and piously; that is, let us strenuously apply ourselves to every kind of good works in this world, awaiting the blessed hope, namely the reward of eternal happiness, which He may deign to grant us—and previously our merits—who is the beginning, fountain, and origin of all good things, as well as the end and goal: God blessed forever, Amen.

<note>A small decorative trifoliate ornament.</note>

<note>A second small decorative trifoliate ornament.</note>

->**Praise be to God.**<-
</translation>

<summary>This concluding section of the manuscript argues for the necessity of both internal and external worship while categorizing the virtues of sobriety, justice, and piety against the vices of lust and pride. It affirms the theological position that good works receive a divine reward, concluding with a prayer for eternal happiness.</summary>
<keywords>prayer, sobriety, justice, piety, vices, good works, merit, rewards, Mary and Martha, temperance, humility, salvation</keywords>

<pb n="11"/><meta>continues from previous page: Titius, a citizen of the City of N., with</meta> children both above and below the age of puberty, departs by the fates <note>meaning he died</note>. For these children, <term>Tutores</term> <gloss>guardians for those under puberty</gloss> and <term>Curatores</term> <gloss>guardians for those above puberty</gloss> are immediately appointed by the Magistrate. But having become more skilled for the sake of business, which they had begun to learn in their fatherland, they depart for other places of the earth. In the meantime, the guardians of the minors sell their houses—the only property they have—due to urgent necessity and not without a decree from the Magistrate of that place.

It is now asked whether, under these circumstances, a <term>gabella</term> <gloss>tax or duty</gloss> can be taken or deducted from the received price or the money immediately placed at interest and still subject to contributions, which money the minors neither ask to be sent to them, nor do the guardians and debtors wish to send it to those who may one day ask for it without the prior knowledge of the Magistrate.

### CASE XX.

Titius leaves a son as successor to a <term>feudum</term> <gloss>fief or feudal estate</gloss>, to whom, when he seeks the renewal of <term>investitura</term> <gloss>investiture or formal possession</gloss> after a year and twenty days, the Lord of the fief opposes him with a <term>fatalium exceptio</term> <gloss>an objection based on a legal deadline</gloss>. That is, that the time for seeking the renewal of investiture has slipped away, and consequently the <term>Vasallus</term> <gloss>vassal</gloss> has lost the fief.

It is asked whether this objection can be struck down, notwithstanding the text of the second book of Feuds, chapter 24, and similar laws.

I affirm that it can.

->APPENDICES<-

<pb n="12"/>### APPENDICES

### I.

<note>A large ornamental initial letter N begins this section.</note> They do not explain themselves with sufficient consideration who, while rightly granting power over sacred matters to the Princes of the <term>Augustana Confessio</term> <gloss>Augsburg Confession</gloss>, say that <term>jus Episcopale</term> <gloss>Episcopal right or power</gloss> is possessed by them.

### II.

And likewise that our Princes bear a double persona: namely, the Ecclesiastical and the secular.

### III.

But also that Episcopal rights are exercised by them by way of a <term>contractus fiduciarius</term> <gloss>fiduciary contract</gloss>, or as if from a deposit, or <term>usufructuarie</term> <gloss>by way of usufruct or temporary use</gloss>.

### IV.

Finally, that the right of our Princes concerning sacred matters consists in <term>lex Diaecesana</term> <gloss>diocesan law</gloss> and the law of jurisdiction. See the public manuscript lectures of the Magnificent Lord Strauchius on <term>Regimen Ecclesiasticum</term> <gloss>Ecclesiastical Government</gloss>, special part, title 1, paragraph 3 and following, where he pursues this argument in his own most subtle manner. Join with this the same author's Dissertation on Statutes by the Sovereign Prince, in the section on the Constitutions of Princes, paragraph 36.

### V.

Lutherans and Calvinists are not proven to be heretics simply because they are addressed by the names of their authors <note>meaning the names of Luther and Calvin</note>. The same author argues this in his public manuscript lectures on the sixth law of the Code regarding heretics and Manichaeans, against the scholars of Dillingen.

<note>A decorative printer's ornament featuring a central circular motif with scrollwork and floral elements serves as a tailpiece at the bottom of the page.</note>
</translation>

<summary>This portion of the legal dissertation concludes the case studies with a dispute over property taxes for minors and the expiration of feudal investiture deadlines, followed by a series of legal appendices regarding the ecclesiastical authority of Protestant princes and the status of Lutherans and Calvinists.</summary>
<keywords>guardianship, gabella, fief, investiture, Augsburg Confession, Episcopal right, Strauchius, Lutherans, Calvinists, ecclesiastical law</keywords>

<pb n="102"/>Although the natural state of the primordial mind has never been something to be seen from the beginning, cut through the root of whoever is the viewer or the act of viewing! Although the natural state of the primordial mind has never been something to be meditated upon from the beginning, let the essence of the meditating awareness rest in the Great Pervasiveness! Although the natural state of the primordial mind has never been an action from the beginning, let it rest in the unfabricated and relaxed state where there is neither action nor the choice to accept or reject! Although the natural state of the primordial mind has been spontaneously present from the beginning, let the mental longing for a result to be accomplished rest in the freedom from conceptual elaboration! If the yogi who maintains it in this way gains stability in the natural state, the delusions of the mental afflictions are purified and the result of Buddhahood is attained. Thus he spoke. 

Again, this was offered to the great scholar Nyima Drakpa, arranged according to the thirty letters of the alphabet: 
<term>Ka</term>: The self-arising realization of the unborn. 
<term>Kha</term>: Within the state that is clear like the sky. 
<term>Ga</term>: That awareness which is without denial or proof. 
<term>Nga</term>: Is the state of knowing that I have no true existence. 
<term>Ca</term>: Through practice that is without fabrication. 
<term>Cha</term>: Until the <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss> is attained. 
<term>Ja</term>: Accomplish the meaning of acting for the <leaf-break/> benefit of others. 
This song of experience on the thirty letters of the alphabet was written as it dawned in the mind. Thus he spoke. 

Again, in the year of the Pig, when the Interior Minister <term>Nangso</term> <gloss>a local administrative title</gloss> Sonam Gyalpo passed away in Lhalung, his wife and son, the <term>Chomze</term> <gloss>religious practitioners</gloss>, requested that the master come to lead the funeral rites. At that time, his schedule did not allow it, so he sent a relic that had emerged from his own teeth, along with this series of instructions to comfort the minds of the Minister’s wife and son: 

To the Triple Gem, the reliable objects of refuge, I bow and go for refuge. To the Lord, mother, and son who have had a deep karmic connection since previous times, please listen. Wherever one looks on the earth, under the sky, in the cardinal or intermediate directions, in the center or the periphery, for all sentient beings of the three realms, there is no time of escape from the suffering of death; it is the destination for everyone. Father <leaf-break/> and mother alike, rising up in succession, there is no end to the depths of suffering. Now that you have found this precious human body, cast away all mundane affairs and exert yourself in the Dharma; this is your eternal purpose. All these temporary affairs are of an illusory nature; whatever you do will not help, so meditate on impermanence within your being. Abandon the affairs of this life and accomplish your eternal purpose. If you are to achieve the great goal, do it now, for there is no knowing what will happen in the next life. At this time when you have your own autonomy, abandon distractions and busywork, and exert yourself in the practice of these profound instructions of the self-arising Great Perfection! This will lead to happiness here and joy in the next life. As for your current kingdom, protect it with the Dharma of a loving mind. If you benefit all sentient beings, happiness will come to you. Hold these instructions of the <term>Be-ban</term> <gloss>the bee-monk</gloss> Pema Lingpa in the center of your heart! Around the pig month, I will be there; at that time, priest and patron shall have a detailed discussion. 

<pb n="103"/><note>The following describes the lineage successor.</note> When the Great Knowledge-Holder <term>Metok</term> <gloss>Flower</gloss> was performing alms-gathering, at a delightful place called Bi in the southwest border of the monastery of Pema Lingpa, he gave this introduction through poetry to the Khampa mendicant Rinchen Zangpo: 

The unconditioned nature of mind is the great sky. The natural conceptualizations of elaboration are a continuous chain. The six objects and the ground display illusory forms. Does the Khampa see that which, being without truth, destroys the path to happiness, like the moon in water or a mirage? 

So he spoke, and the other replied: 
Upon the ground of firm, unchanging faith, the branches of the wish-fulfilling tree of devotion flourish. I pray that the fruit of compassionate needs and desires may ripen. 

In response, he spoke this again: Like the king of birds <note>the Garuda</note> with wings <leaf-break/> spread wide. 

Aha! Having studied and contemplated in a non-sectarian way, the furthest reaches of the doubting mind were cut. Knowing what to adopt or reject regarding Dharma and non-Dharma, the peak of one's purpose is unmistakable, aha! Spurred by the reminder of impermanent death, having developed renunciation and weariness toward the delusive nature of cyclic existence, the peak of one's purpose is unmistakable, aha! Knowing that all worldly actions and deeds are without point, resting in the state of non-action, the peak of one's purpose is unmistakable, aha! Seeing the suffering of all who possess wealth, yet finding that having no wealth is a great ornament for the mind, possessing the noble wealth of contentment, the peak of one's purpose is unmistakable, aha! Taking awareness as the support for one's own benefit, training in the Bodhichitta that benefits others, turning the minds of oneself and others toward the Dharma, the peak of one's purpose is unmistakable, aha! The expanse of reality is free from conceptual elaboration, and awareness is unborn and free from extremes; having reached the limit of realizing the View, the peak of one's purpose is unmistakable, aha! The natural state of bliss, clarity, and non-thought, where the object and subject of meditation <leaf-break/> are one. 

Relying on the teacher, the pure vision that awakens the karmic potential of the fortunate is the main priority for certain yogis who dwell in the land of Tibet. I ask you to offer a brief praise to them. This time, I, a yogi, have arrived at Bumthang, which is difficult to reach. I have met one such as you, the Lord Pema Lingpa, who is difficult to meet. You have granted the instructions of the Profound Dharma, the Gathering of All Intentions. I have tasted the sacred substances that bring liberation through tasting. I am happy, aha! I am joyful, aha! I, the yogi Lhawang Drakpa, have come upon the path of empty-clarity without grasping. From the mountain pass of naked seeing, free from extremes, I looked toward the unobstructed, translucent state, and I met the guru of the spontaneously present natural state. I requested the oral instructions on the inseparability of appearance and emptiness. I offered the mandala of the relaxed six senses. Through the pure merit of former times, I have met such an essence of the realization of the All-Good <term>Samantabhadra</term>. Through the power of the prayers I make now, may we never be parted throughout the eon. I am happy!
</translation>

<summary>This collection of instructions by Pema Lingpa outlines the view of the Great Perfection (Dzogchen), emphasizing the unfabricated nature of the mind and the importance of preparing for death. It includes an alphabetical song of realization and a poetic exchange between the master and a visiting yogi regarding the certainty of the path.</summary>
<keywords>Pema Lingpa, Dzogchen, Great Perfection, Mind Nature, Impermanence, Thirty Letters, Nyima Drakpa, Lhalung, Funeral Instructions, Samantabhadra</keywords>
