and recollection.

Explanation of the text.
The title of the book *On Memory and Recollection* indicates its subject matter; the single chapter is completed in two parts.

### Part One
Treats of memory.
I. To remember <note>original: "memorari"</note> and to recollect <note>original: "reminisci"</note> are not the same: because those with good memories, such as the gifted, are not always good at recollecting.
II. Memory is not of the future or the present, but of the past: for hope or opinion concerns the future, and sense perception concerns the present; but memory concerns a past act: which is neither sense nor opinion.
III. Memory is an affection <note>original: "passio"</note> of something when time has passed.
<margin>Corollary. Supposition.</margin>
IV. Only those things that perceive time are remembered.
V. Understanding does not occur without a <term>phantasm</term> <gloss>mental image</gloss>: and therefore the intellect does not understand without continuous time.
VI. Memory is an affection of the primary sense <note>the common sense</note>. He proves this because it belongs to that sense to know time; therefore it belongs to it to remember: for the sense knows motion, time, and magnitude. Whence he admits memory to belong to the intellect by accident: insofar as it receives a phantasm from the sense.
VII. These sayings are proven because even non-intelligent beings remember, such as brute animals.
VIII. Not all animals have memory.
IX. Although the species <gloss>mental form</gloss> of a thing is present, memory does not concern the species itself, but the absent thing. He proves this because if a painting or a seal represents a past thing, so does the species in the imagination. He proves this first because those in great motion do not remember, such as the drunk or the sick, because the species are hindered. 2. Children do not remember because species are hindered due to their flux. 3. Old men do not remember well because, due to excessive dryness, they do not receive the species well. 4. Because those who understand quickly retain and remember poorly.
X. Memory is not of that species <note>itself</note>: because then it would be of the present.
XI. It seems that memory is of the present: because memory belongs to the sense itself, and sense is of the present. 2. Because the species is in the imagination like a painting on a wall: and the painting is present to the viewer. 3. If the common sense can be of the absent, then so can the exterior sense.
XII. These points are resolved: because although the species, as a certain thing, is present in the mind, yet as it is representative of another, it is of an absent thing: he explains the mode of representing of the species as in the text.
XIII. Memory is increased and preserved through frequent meditation: for the soul is made more capable if it remembers many times.

### Part Two: On Recollection
XIV. Recollection is not memory, nor is it sensing or understanding something anew: the second is proven because memory does not occur when one understands or senses something anew: therefore neither does recollection. The antecedent is clear because memory requires the interruption of past time: and so memory supposes there to have been a prior act or habit. But it differs from memory because in recollection, forgetfulness intervenes.

XV. To remember or to recollect is not merely to know something again: but to know that one had previously known or seen it.
XVI. The mode of recollecting occurs through this: just as one motion of the soul occurs after another, so it apprehends one after another. And so when we recollect, we are moved from one act to another by meditating through similarity or contrast.
XVII. Why do we sometimes recollect easily from a long time ago, and not what was done yesterday or the day before? He responds that this is because recollection occurs through the apprehension of something that is useful for apprehending <note>the target memory</note>.
XVIII. First Corollary: we certainly recollect from that principle from which the things to be recolled began. Second Corollary: We recollect well-ordered things more easily than disordered ones.
XIX. Why is it that someone wishing to recollect cannot do so at one time, and then later, without seeking it, recollects spontaneously? He responds because the one wishing has many apprehensions that are not useful for that recollection: and later an apprehension comes spontaneously that is useful for apprehending.
XX. One wishing to recollect should think of the places in which they were.
XXI. The best mode of recollecting is through division, as in: "I was there that week," and by dividing by days, I may easily find what I did from one to the next.
XXII. Why do those who have the starting point of recollection not recollect? He responds because that principle is indifferent to many things.
XXIII. Why do we sometimes recollect defectively? It is responded that just as it happens in natural things, so also in things of the will.
XXIV. Time contributes to recollecting: so that one knows past time to be past; yet both memory and recollection occur without a certain time: although they understand things in proportion to time.
XXV. It happens that one errs in recollection, and this is both on the part of the thing and on the part of the time.
XXVI. Memory differs from recollection because although other animals besides man remember, they do not recollect; the reason for this is that recollection occurs through discourse <note>reasoning</note>.
XXVII. Recollection is a bodily affection: the first sign of this is that many wishing to recollect and being unable to are troubled: especially in the melancholic: and it is just as with the angry, whose motions they cannot easily settle; and because of strong imagination, we do not cease from the memory of certain things.
XXVIII. The second sign is that those having large upper parts <note>of the body or head</note> remember poorly. The third sign is that children and old men are poor at remembering: children due to excessive motion, old men due to a lack of motion.

### Annotation
1. Primary sensitive part, that is, the common sense.
16. Order contributes greatly to memory: whence one about to commend something to memory should always study to review it in the same order: otherwise, if he orders it now this way, now that, he will confuse himself.
The precepts which Aristotle handed down here concerning memory,
</translation>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
younger [writers] have followed more accurately: Rhetoricians and Orators have enriched them, as may be seen in Cicero and Fabius <note>Quintilian</note>: for artificial memory consists most especially in places, images, their comparison, and the order employed. Indeed, in our time, some have handed down [treatises on] artificial memory.
12. Antiphon, being of an unsound mind, thought those things were truly done which were only imaginary to him.

### Whether memory and recollection differ.
### Article I.

That species is reserved in the soul: and he who saw it can think of him: and then he is said to remember. This being supposed, know that memory is understood in four ways: for the memorative power itself is called memory; similarly, the organ that preserves the species is called memory; and fourthly, memory is used for the act of remembering: and thus we speak here of memory. And thus memory is twofold, namely, intellectual and sensitive. ¶ And six things are required for memory: namely, three representing things and three represented things, according to Buridan. The represented things in the prior example are the king seen, the vision, and the past time in which he saw him: of all these, the soul must have species, images, and likenesses if it wishes to remember.

Note II. That foundation being laid, the difference between remembering, recollecting, and forgetting can easily stand. For if the species are strongly impressed and totally reserved in the soul, so that immediately upon noticing them, they move the power to a repeated cognition of the thing: then through these species, memory occurs. Or these species are weakly impressed, or lost by length of time or another cause, and corrupted and totally abolished and removed from the power that incorporates species: and then we are said to forget. Or they are only weakened, not entirely lost, but confused and fragile, still sticking a little in the memorative organ, not sufficient by themselves to move the power unless with the apprehension of another thing and with help, by which it may be elevated and actuated: and then through these species we recollect. Add, however, that memory generally extends itself to recollection.

The title of the book *On Memory and Recollection* indicates its subject matter; the single chapter is completed in two parts.

### Part One
Treats of memory.
I. To remember <note>original: "memorari"</note> and to recollect <note>original: "reminisci"</note> are not the same: because those with good memories, such as the gifted, are not always good at recollecting.
II. Memory is not of the future or the present, but of the past: for hope or opinion concerns the future, and sense perception concerns the present; but memory concerns a past act: which is neither sense nor opinion.
III. Memory is an affection <note>original: "passio"</note> of something when time has passed.
<margin>Corollary. Supposition.</margin>
IV. Only those things that perceive time are remembered.
V. Understanding does not occur without a <term>phantasm</term> <gloss>mental image</gloss>: and therefore the intellect does not understand without continuous time.
VI. Memory is an affection of the primary sense <note>the common sense</note>. He proves this because it belongs to that sense to know time; therefore it belongs to it to remember: for the sense knows motion, time, and magnitude. Whence he admits memory to belong to the intellect by accident: insofar as it receives a phantasm from the sense.
VII. These sayings are proven because even non-intelligent beings remember, such as brute animals.
VIII. Not all animals have memory.
IX. Although the species <gloss>mental form</gloss> of a thing is present, memory does not concern the species itself, but the absent thing. He proves this because if a painting or a seal represents a past thing, so does the species in the imagination. He proves this first because those in great motion do not remember, such as the drunk or the sick, because the species are hindered. 2. Children do not remember because species are hindered due to their flux. 3. Old men do not remember well because, due to excessive dryness, they do not receive the species well. 4. Because those who understand quickly retain and remember poorly.
X. Memory is not of that species <note>itself</note>: because then it would be of the present.
XI. It seems that memory is of the present: because memory belongs to the sense itself, and sense is of the present. 2. Because the species is in the imagination like a painting on a wall: and the painting is present to the viewer. 3. If the common sense can be of the absent, then so can the exterior sense.
XII. These points are resolved: because although the species, as a certain thing, is present in the mind, yet as it is representative of another, it is of an absent thing: he explains the mode of representing of the species as in the text.
XIII. Memory is increased and preserved through frequent meditation: for the soul is made more capable if it remembers many times.

### Part Two: On Recollection
XIV. Recollection is not memory, nor is it sensing or understanding something anew: the second is proven because memory does not occur when one understands or senses something anew: therefore neither does recollection. The antecedent is clear because memory requires the interruption of past time: and so memory supposes there to have been a prior act or habit. But it differs from memory because in recollection, forgetfulness intervenes.

XV. To remember or to recollect is not merely to know something again: but to know that one had previously known or seen it.
XVI. The mode of recollecting occurs through this: just as one motion of the soul occurs after another, so it apprehends one after another. And so when we recollect, we are moved from one act to another by meditating through similarity or contrast.
XVII. Why do we sometimes recollect easily from a long time ago, and not what was done yesterday or the day before? He responds that this is because recollection occurs through the apprehension of something that is useful for apprehending <note>the target memory</note>.
XVIII. First Corollary: we certainly recollect from that principle from which the things to be recolled began. Second Corollary: We recollect well-ordered things more easily than disordered ones.
XIX. Why is it that someone wishing to recollect cannot do so at one time, and then later, without seeking it, recollects spontaneously? He responds because the one wishing has many apprehensions that are not useful for that recollection: and later an apprehension comes spontaneously that is useful for apprehending.
XX. One wishing to recollect should think of the places in which they were.
XXI. The best mode of recollecting is through division, as in: "I was there that week," and by dividing by days, I may easily find what I did from one to the next.
XXII. Why do those who have the starting point of recollection not recollect? He responds because that principle is indifferent to many things.
XXIII. Why do we sometimes recollect defectively? It is responded that just as it happens in natural things, so also in things of the will.
XXIV. Time contributes to recollecting: so that one knows past time to be past; yet both memory and recollection occur without a certain time: although they understand things in proportion to time.
XXV. It happens that one errs in recollection, and this is both on the part of the thing and on the part of the time.
XXVI. Memory differs from recollection because although other animals besides man remember, they do not recollect; the reason for this is that recollection occurs through discourse <note>reasoning</note>.
XXVII. Recollection is a bodily affection: the first sign of this is that many wishing to recollect and being unable to are troubled: especially in the melancholic: and it is just as with the angry, whose motions they cannot easily settle; and because of strong imagination, we do not cease from the memory of certain things.
XXVIII. The second sign is that those having large upper parts <note>of the body or head</note> remember poorly. The third sign is that children and old men are poor at remembering: children due to excessive motion, old men due to a lack of motion.

The civil law comes from Laws, Plebiscites <gloss>decrees of the common people</gloss>, Senate decrees, the decrees of Emperors, and the authority of the Jurisprudents <gloss>legal experts</gloss>. According to Law 7, in the beginning of the <term>Pandects</term> <gloss>the Digest of Roman law</gloss>, title *On Justice and Law*, it is not entirely clear to which of these parts our action owes its birth. However, there is no doubt that its formulated words and the solemn formula by which it was necessary to propose the case in ancient times must be attributed to the legal experts, based on the argument in Law 2, paragraph 6, of the <term>Pandects</term>, title *On the Origin of Law*.

### §. VII.

The proximate efficient cause or foundation is a Right established in another's property, or a servitude, whether personal or real; or rather, the injury and wrong that is inflicted when one person seeks either to completely deprive another of the exercise of a servitude due to him, or at least to hinder him so that he cannot exercise his right quietly. For since an action is a complaint according to the final Law of the <term>Pandects</term>, title *On Summoning to Court*, and since no one can complain unless he suffers an injustice which he desires to be corrected by a Judge, it follows that the foundation of the Confessory action is not so much the Right in another's property itself, as it is the injury inflicted concerning that Right.

### §. VIII.

This action can be tested by one who, while holding a Right in another's property belonging to himself or to his estate, is either entirely deprived of its exercise or is at least hindered in its quiet use. For just as a person claims a physical thing <note>original: "rem corporalem vindicat"</note> if, being the Owner, he lacks the exercise of Ownership power while another is in possession; similarly, it is permissible to use the Confessory action for one whose exercise of a Right in another's property has been either completely misappropriated or at least whose quiet use has been interrupted by the act of another. Since, however,

Therefore, when *Ulpian* says in Law 2, § 1, and Law 6, § 3, *If a servitude be claimed*, that the action belongs to no one other than the Owner of the estate, it is clear he is speaking only of Real servitudes; since in personal ones, a Right in another's property is sufficient without an estate. But if there are several Owners of a dominant estate, each one claims the whole <note>original: "in solidum"</note> and not just a part, according to Law 6, § 4, *If a servitude be claimed*. This is not given to a USUFRUCTUARY <gloss>one who has the right to use and enjoy the fruits of another's property</gloss> according to Law 1, at the beginning, and Law 5, § 1, *If a Usufruct be sought*; for although he also holds a right in another's property, because the dominant estate does not belong to him by right of ownership, he therefore cannot claim a servitude belonging to that estate; he can, however, sue those hindering the Usufruct. This, however, must be understood regarding a direct claim <note>original: "directâ vindicatione"</note>; for that he may proceed by a <term>utilis actio</term> <gloss>useful or equitable action</gloss> is declared by Law 1, § 4, *On Remissions*. Furthermore, since it happens that he who holds a Right in another's property is either entirely deprived of the exercise of his right, or exercises it but not securely and quietly, it follows that this action is given to an Owner whether possessing or not possessing, according to Law 6, § 1, *if a servitude be claimed*; to the latter so that one may recover lost possession, to the former so that he may securely exercise the servitude, based on the argument of Law 5, the last paragraph, *if a usufruct be sought*.

19. Truly, it is clear that even this reasoning concludes nothing other than that the Angels did not exist before the third day; yet it by no means follows that they were created on that very day.
20. Since, therefore, none of these opinions rests upon certain foundations, we conclude with Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian from Alexandria</note> in the first book of *On First Principles* <note>original: "περὶ ἀρχῶν" (Peri Archon)</note>:
> It is contained in the Ecclesiastical preaching that there are certain Angels of GOD; but when these were created is not distinguished with sufficient clarity.

## APHORISM III.

->*Angels are spirits, intelligent and wise, good, holy, and powerful, destined for the ministry of GOD for the salvation of men.*<-

### I. EXPOSITION.

1. Since the human tongue falters in matters remote from the senses, some sort of description of the Angels—those most blessed minds which are as far removed from the senses as possible—should suffice for us, such as this one which our aphorism has just delivered.
2. It describes the Angels as they were from their first origin, and establishes their *Genus* as *Spirits*.
3. To these same beings it attributes concrete *accidents* or *Qualities*, such as intelligence, wisdom, goodness, holiness, and power. We wish all these predicates to be understood restrictively and within their own kind, not absolutely. For as soon as you compare these to the spirituality, intelligence, and goodness of GOD, a difference reveals itself as great as that which lies between the infinite and the finite; between essential holiness and goodness and that which is accidental <note>In philosophy, "essential" refers to a being's core nature, while "accidental" refers to qualities that can change or be bestowed</note>; between the Creator and the created; and between the immutable and the mutable.

<summary>The author concludes that the exact timing of angelic creation is not clearly revealed in scripture, citing Origen. He begins a new aphorism defining the nature and qualities of angels as created spiritual beings.</summary>
<keywords>Origen, On First Principles, angelic nature, spirit, accidents vs essence, theology</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="11">
<meta>continues from previous page: and between the immutable and the mutable intercedes holiness, goodness, and the rest.</meta>
4. *Their office is reported to be twofold: one is considered in respect to GOD, the other in respect to men.*

->CONFIRMATION.<-

5. Scripture itself confirms this nature of the Angels, and specifically I. *that they are Spirits*. 1. By calling them *Spirits* simply, in Psalm 104:4, and Hebrews 1: *last verse*. Are they (the Angels) not all ministering spirits? 2. By *denying them matter*, because they do not have flesh and blood, Ephesians 6:12; or flesh and bones, Luke 24:39.
6. II. It attributes *concreated qualities* to them: And that the *Angels are Intelligent*, the woman of Tekoa says: My lord, she said, is wise according to the wisdom of an Angel of GOD, so that he may know all things that are on the earth, 2 Samuel 14:20.
7. They are called *Good* by the Creator himself. For GOD saw all things that He had made, and behold, they were all very good, Genesis 1:31. Since the Angels were made by GOD (as stated above in aphorism 1), they are therefore good by the goodness of creation, as theologians like to say.
8. They are called *Holy*, Luke 9:26, Acts 10:22.
9. They are *Powerful* in virtue, Psalm 103:20; to say nothing here of the wonderful works of the Angels which sufficiently demonstrate their power, as seen above in aphorism 1, thesis 9, and the names of principalities, powers, virtues, and thrones which they are assigned in scripture.
10. III. The *Office* which they perform in respect to GOD is the celebration of His name. For the Cherubim and Seraphim sing: Holy, Holy, Holy, etc., Isaiah 6:3. Also, the execution of His commands. Hence thousands of thousands minister to Him, and ten hundred thousand stand before Him, Daniel 7:10. Psalm 103:20-21 speaks of both aspects of this office.

<summary>This page provides scriptural evidence for the definition of angels as immaterial spirits possessing wisdom, holiness, and power. It also outlines the primary angelic duty as the worship and service of God.</summary>
<keywords>Scripture, Woman of Tekoa, Cherubim, Seraphim, angelic hierarchy, ministering spirits</keywords>
</translation>

Paragraph 3 of this title. This constitution of Marcus was finally removed by custom, by which at Rome tutors were given either by the Prefect of the City <note>the "Praefectus Urbi"</note>, specifically for the children of illustrious persons <note>referencing Law 1, Code on the Guardianship and Curatorship of Illustrious Persons</note>, or by the praetor according to his jurisdiction. In the provinces, however, they were given by the governors or by magistrates at the governor's command. Paragraph 4 of this title. This custom was later changed again by Justinian, who entrusted that right to the defenders of the cities <note>the "defensores civitatis"</note> together with the bishop of the same city or other magistrates. Paragraph 5 of this title; Law 30, Code on Episcopal Hearings; and Cujas in his later notes on this.

Today, however, the ordinary magistrate of each place grants a tutor, and not only when a guardianship has ended, as in civil law <note>Law 5, "If a tutor," Code on the Risk of Tutors; final paragraph of this title</note>. But also every year, according to the constitution of Charles V issued in the year 1548, he demands an account from the tutors; the Canon Law does not resist this <note>Clementine 1, "On religious houses," chapter 1, "On sick Clerics"</note>. According to Saxon law <note>the "ius Saxonicum"</note>, the nearest heirs demand an account every year. Book 1, Landrecht <gloss>territorial law</gloss>, article 23; Fachsius, difference 17; Reinhard, difference 7.

(e) Because it is a matter neither of command <term>imperium</term> <gloss>the power to command</gloss> nor of jurisdiction <term>iurisdictio</term> <gloss>the power to administer law</gloss>. Law 6, paragraph 2, "On guardianships"; Law 23 at the end, "On the excuses of tutors." It belongs only to the person to whom either the law, a Decree of the Senate <term>Senatusconsultum</term>, or the Prince has granted it. The beginning of the Institutes on this title; Law 1, paragraph 2; Law 8, "On tutors and curators"; Law 1, "On his office." There is a dissertation of the Doctors after the gloss on said Law 6, while they attribute this to "mixed command" <term>mixto imperio</term>. Muscornius, in his treatise on jurisdiction, says otherwise: that it is sometimes of the nature of jurisdiction and sometimes of command. Bellonus, in his first "Supputations," section 2, determines it to be a matter of permission.

Pragmatic Question 3, numbers 33, 63. Nor to a minor <note>said question, numbers 8, 10</note>. Nor to a mute person or a deaf person. Law 1, paragraph "the mute," "On guardianships." said question 3, number 49, whom Manzius follows with doubt in his second question, number 1. Nor can it be granted to someone suffering from a perpetual illness, since he himself is under care. Nor to a slave, because he is held as dead in civil law <note>Law 32, "On the Rules of Law"</note>. Nor to a debtor or a creditor <note>Authentica "of the minor," Code on those who give tutors</note>. Nor to a husband <note>Law "the husband," Code on guardianship</note>. It is otherwise in Saxon Law, by which a wife is found under the guardianship of her husband. Book 1, Landrecht, article 31.

These persons being excepted, guardianship can be deferred to anyone, and since it is a public office <note>The beginning of the Institutes on the excuses of tutors</note>, it is necessary to the extent that a tutor can even be compelled by the seizing of pledges <note>Law 5, Code on those who give tutors</note>. Saxon Law also proves this. Book 1, Landrecht, article 47, where the gloss is accepted. Law at the end, in the beginning, Code on the administration of tutors; by argument of Law 28, Code on decurions, book 10. And indeed, it is performed for free, unless the tutor is poor <note>Law 33 "from tutors," final paragraph on the administration of tutors; also Law 15</note>, but even then for the purpose of exhibiting accounts or other excuses about which we shall treat in the following disputation.

(g) Not only by virtue of the office but also at the petition which is offered by the free will of blood relations, in-laws, or friends. Law 2, "Those who seek tutors"; Laws 4, 5, 10, Code of the same title. Or they are held to provide it, as a mother is, unless she wishes to be excluded from the succession according to the Tertullian Decree of the Senate <term>Senatusconsultum Tertyllianum</term>. Said Law 2, paragraph 1. Even if she is a natural mother. Law at the end, Code on guardianship. And all those who are called to the succession of a deceased ward <term>pupillus</term>. Law 10, Code on legitimate heirs. Likewise, freedmen. Said laws.

(h) Law 6, paragraph 1, "On guardianships"; for time is not a method for introducing or removing an obligation. Law 77, "On the Rules of Law." (i) Said law, paragraph 1.

</translation>

### CHAPTER IV.
#### Concerning
# The Division of Nobility
# On the Classification of the Nobility. <note>original German: "Von des Adels Eintheilung"</note>

§. 1. More than one division of Nobility occurs. **Plato** divided it into four species: the first consists of those born from distinguished, good, and just ancestors. Secondly, those whose parents were noble and princes, he called by the same name. Thirdly, he wanted those to be called noble whose ancestors were famous in reputation and opinion, whether from clearly executed military deeds or from the crowns of contests. Finally, he esteemed the most excellent kind of Nobility to be when someone excelled by the greatness of their own soul. Compare **Plutarch**, book 10, *Against Nobility*.

§. 2. **Aristotle**, in book 1 of the *Rhetoric to Theodectes*, chapter 5, distinguishes between the Nobility of the Race and that of the City, along with Private nobility; he says the splendor of the former belongs to those who are indigenous and most ancient, and whose first leaders were illustrious; also that many from that race have stood out as distinguished in matters that are sought after. Private nobility, however, comes from either men or women and is the legitimate procreation from them.

§. 3. **Gregory of Nazianzus** makes a threefold kind of nobility: one which draws its origin from above, as are all who are created in the image of God; the second, which proceeds from blood; the third is recognized from virtue and vice. Oration 18; compare Oration 28.

§. 4. **Piccolomini** says that six grades of Nobility can be established: He makes the first Divine Nobility. (2) Metaphysical. (3) Inspectoral. (4) Civil. (5) Physical. (6) Of Fortune. However, a little later he contracts these into only four forms, namely: Divine, Moral, Natural, and Nobility of Fortune. Divine nobility, as he says, approaches God most closely; Moral nobility, which he also names nobility of the soul, consists in the composition of character and the habit of virtue. Natural nobility

When they were contending with one another over the kingdom, Danaus killed the sons of Aegyptus by the handiwork of his daughters, except for one or two; for he had received an oracle that slaughter threatened him from one of them. From there, landing at Rhodes, he dedicated a statue of Minerva Lindia. From here he also traveled to Argos, and Helanor, who was then reigning at Argos, handed the kingdom over to him (but he himself, having taken possession of that region, called the inhabitants Danaans after his own name). But because that region suffered from a lack of water, since Neptune <note>Poseidon</note> had angrily dried up the springs of Inachus because he <note>Inachus</note> had testified that the land belonged to Minerva, Danaus meanwhile sent his daughters out to fetch water. One of these, Amymone, while searching for water, threw a spear at a stag and hit a sleeping Satyr; therefore, awakened from sleep, he was seized with a wondrous desire to couple with the girl. Furthermore, the sons of Aegyptus, having set out for Argos so that they might restrain their mutual hostility, encouraged one another and pleaded that the daughters of Danaus be given to them in marriage. Therefore, he selected Hypermnestra, the eldest of the daughters, for Lynceus, and Gorgophone for Proteus. For Aegyptus had raised these from his wife Queen Argyphia. However, among other things, sacred and spiritual items are excepted, as they cannot be sold in themselves without the sin of sacrilege and <term>simony</term> <gloss>the selling of church offices or spiritual things</gloss>. The agreement of resale <note>original: "pactum retrovendendi"</note> and the resale itself is approved by law if it is done without fraud. A sale under a <term>lex commissoria</term> <gloss>a clause dissolving a contract if terms are not met</gloss> or an <term>addictio in diem</term> <gloss>a provisional sale that can be canceled if a better offer arrives by a certain date</gloss> are considered absolute.

### XVI. Remaining Onerous Contracts.

Not only a real <term>census</term> <gloss>a tax or ground rent attached to property</gloss>, but also a personal one is licit; and it is licit not only when it is irredeemable, but also when it is redeemable on the part of the buyer as well as the seller. "Dry exchange" <note>original: "cambium siccum", a form of usury disguised as currency exchange</note> cannot produce a just profit. The justice of a real exchange, whether local, manual, or by letters <note>original: "per litteras", such as bills of exchange</note>, is easily maintained. A contract of partnership can be made so that one party contributes the capital <note>original: "fortem"</note> and the other contributes labor or industry. For a game to be valid, it is required among other things that there be an equal risk on both sides; and for a wager <note>original: "sponsio"</note>, an equal condition for the bettors. A lessor must primarily guarantee the preservation of the thing leased. A depositary <note>one who holds property for another</note> is sometimes held liable for slight negligence. *Law 12, Digest on deposits.* A loan for use <note>original: "commodatum"</note> cannot be demanded back in itself before the time has elapsed for which it was granted. If a thing loaned for use perishes by chance without the fault of the borrower, the loss falls on the owner. *Final Law, Digest on loans for use.* A <term>precarium</term> <gloss>a grant of use at the will of the grantor</gloss> is not ended by the death of the one granting it. A wife’s non-sworn <term>fidejussio</term> <gloss>suretyship or guarantee</gloss> for her husband is void. Even rights can be pledged or mortgaged.

Injury is the violation of another's right. One type is "real," which is committed by the unjust laying on of hands; another is "verbal," which is committed through words, letters, writing, or an insulting picture. *Law 15, Digest on injuries and libelous pamphlets.* One type is slight, another is atrocious; the type is to be determined from the act, the place, the person, and other circumstances. *Paragraph "atrox", Institutes on injuries.* No injury is done to one who is willing, unless

I ask, indeed, let them explain to me whether the diversity of meanings depends on the consonants alone, or truly on the vowels? No less must the leaders of the Churches and Pastors be reverently obeyed in the Lord. 2 Thessalonians 3:3, 14. Hebrews 13:17. Yet not absolutely, but conditionally, insofar as and as long as they hear the voice of the Supreme Shepherd Jesus Christ, correctly set forth His word, and contain themselves within the boundaries of their vocation. <translation page="14">
<meta>continues from previous page: should invite us to...</meta>
such great sobriety <note>original: "sobrietatem"</note> that we would not even allow drunkenness <note>original: "ebrietatem"</note> to be named among us. AP. Above all, the most shameful deeds and the most foolish behaviors of drunkards should drive us away from the habit of immoderate drinking. For from what outrages do they abstain? They cast off all shame, they are inflamed by illicit lust, they bring forth the secrets of the soul, they wallow in filth, they walk with no moderation in their step, they stagger, they vomit in the manner of beasts, and they harass all the best people
<margin>
*Isaiah 5.*
</margin>
with slanders; they do not look upon the work of God, nor do they consider the works of His hands. Indeed, once they have weakened the body with immense engorgement, and are exhausted by the perpetration of works of darkness, they collapse as if lifeless; like pigs they
<margin>
*Chrysostom, On Prayer, Book 2.*
</margin>
lie prostrate on the ground, so that it can be most truly said: A DRUNKARD IS A LIVING CORPSE. Finally, let us be moved by the profane men, the <term>Ethnici</term> <gloss>pagans/Gentiles</gloss>, who altogether condemned this detestable and abominable vice, so much so
<margin>
*Athenaeus, Book 10.*
</margin>
that Solon <note>an Athenian lawmaker and one of the Seven Sages of Greece</note> judged that a ruler should be punished with death if he were caught drunk. And among the Indians, it was not permitted for a king to reach the point of drunkenness while drinking. Among the Persians, however, this was granted to the king on only one day, on which they sacrificed to the sun. NEPH. And I remember reading that Pittacus of Mitylene <note>another of the Seven Sages of Greece</note> passed a law that if anyone committed any outrage while drunk, he should be punished with a double penalty. AP. If, therefore, those men who were ignorant of God so
<margin>
*Ephesians 5; Hosea 4; Augustine; Origen.*
</margin>
greatly condemned, avoided, and punished this crime, what I ask you do you think we Christians ought to do? NEPH. Let us strive never to be intoxicated with wine, in which there is <term>asōtia</term> <gloss>profligacy/debauchery</gloss>; let us despise and avoid drunkenness, which takes away the heart and the memory, which dissipates the senses and confuses the intellect; and which makes a beast out of a man, an
<margin>
*Ignatius, Epistle 11 to the Ephesians.*
</margin>
infirm person out of a strong one, and a fool out of a wise one. Let us burn with the zeal for sobriety and temperance; and let us reflect that the final times are even now at hand; let us revere and fear the long-suffering of God, lest we despise the riches of His goodness and patience.
</translation>

<translation page="15">
Let us also remember that our bodies are the temple of God, and the instrument of the Spirit who dwells within us. AP. Sobriety and temperance
<margin>
*1 Corinthians 3; 2 Corinthians 6; Galatians 5.*
</margin>
are the fruits of the Spirit; but drunkenness and luxury are the nurses and promoters of all vices, the receptacles of all kinds of filth. Just as smoke drives away bees, so does <term>crapula</term> <gloss>excessive drinking/the resulting hangover</gloss> drive away the Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts. NEPH. And just as clouds and rains always follow the South Wind, so do diseases of the soul and the animal nature follow drunkenness. COM. Is it then plainly not allowed to drink at all? AP. Certainly it is, if moderation is not absent. For honor must be given to the body,
<margin>
*Colossians 2.*
</margin>
so that it may be fed with sufficient food, not immoderate and superfluous, and we must take care lest we be found to be the murderers of our own bodies. COM. I understand at last that nothing is more destructive to a man than <term>temulentia</term> <gloss>intoxication</gloss>. AP. Therefore, brother, heal this disease in yourself; separate this vice from yourself, and flee the company of wine-drinkers as if fleeing a shipwreck. TRIC. For shame! Are you not embarrassed, Comasta <note>the name likely derives from the Greek word for a reveler or participant in a "komos"</note>, that you allow yourself to be corrupted by their persuasion? AP. Come, get up Comasta, let us go, do not listen to these men. COM. Farewell, you fellow drinkers, I must depart and take care so that I may become a man; but if you are wise, take an example from me.

## THE END.

<note>An ornate woodcut tailpiece features symmetrical scrollwork and floral designs, possibly acanthus leaves, forming a heart-like central shape.</note>

<margin>III. Member of this dispute.</margin>
It remains for us to attach the form of the feudal judgment, which is common with Civil Law: for a citation must be made, a petition exhibited, the dispute contested, and there are other things belonging to the Judicial order: <note>marked by Ardizona in said chapter 238, part 2; Blancus in said chapter 1, book 4, no. 116; Duarenus chapter 21, no. 1; Zasius in said part 1, no. 26; Wesenbeck in said chapter 17, no. 10; Curtius in said part 7, no. 17; Hartmann Hartmann, title on feuds in practical observations, observation 42.</note> Unless in certain cases something else is specially observed. <note>section "strenuus," title 1, book 2, Feudal Law; Raynaudus, Baldus, Ravenas, Alvarotus no. 11; Isernia and others, in the said penultimate section, title 55, said book 2, Feudal Law.</note>

### XCIII.

Namely in cases of proofs, where women are clearly not admitted to give testimony: <note>section "On the ancient," at the end, Title 32, book 2, Feudal Law; and there Cujas book 4, title 35; see also law "ex eo," Digest: On Witnesses; Novel of Leo 48.</note> Likewise five witnesses are required to prove ingratitude: <note>chapter "un." and there the Doctors, title 57, said book 2, Feudal Law; otherwise two suffice, as in proving an Investiture, section "si quis," title 26, book 1, Feudal Law.</note> and if there is a contention between the Lord and the Vassal, neither offers the <term>Iuramentum calumniae</term> <gloss>oath of calumny/good faith</gloss>, even if one or the other tenders it: <note>section "in quibus," title 33, book 2, Feudal Law.</note> Then, if the plaintiff does not prove his case, the defendant is not immediately acquitted, but a defense is still granted to him through a <term>Sacramentum</term> <gloss>oath</gloss>: <note>sections 2 and 3, title 4, and sections 1, 2, and 3 of said title 26, book 1, Feudal Law; section "Item placet," title 15, book 2, Feudal Law; note Borcholt chapter 7, no. 48.</note> indeed, sometimes to the Defendant and sometimes to the plaintiff, at the discretion of the Judge, an oath is given or remitted. <note>section "Sacramentum," and final section, said title 33, book 2, Feudal Law; note Cujas book 1, Feudal Law title 1, section "similarly," at the end, and book 4, title 36.</note>

### XCIV.

This sworn defense, or this oath enjoined or permitted for the sake of defense, is either simple, when one person swears alone, such as the Lord against the Vassal, <note>section "if indeed a feud," title 4, book 1, Feudal Law; and there Cujas book 1, title 1, section "similarly."</note> and the Vassal against the lord, if for instance when a controversy of investiture is moved he can prove that he possessed the feud for a year with the Lord's knowledge and without his contradiction: <note>section "if however anyone," end of Title 26, book 1, Feudal Law; Cujas in said section "similarly," and title 28.</note> or it is due to a lack of proofs with twelve <term>Sacramentalibus</term> <gloss>oath-helpers/compurgators</gloss>, that is, co-swearers, who from kinsmen or others

### XCV.

Another is the armed defense, used in these books: which is established through a duel and single combat: <note>section "if a Knight," with the gloss title 27, and section 3, Title 39, book 2, Feudal Law; section 1, title 2, book 3, Feudal Law; in the more correct books.</note> And yet another which was formerly permitted by way of an Ordeal rather than a defense, in a very superstitious manner, by touching glowing iron, and likewise by the walking through of waters, <note>See Münster everywhere, and other Histories here and there.</note> which the Feudalists call an exploration: both of which, as being plainly contrary to humanity and piety, we deservedly detest. <note>Damhouderius notes in Criminal Practice, chapter 42.</note>

### XCVI.

What if the peers, who were present at the time of the investiture, later ceased to be Peers; if a dispute arises between the Lord and the Vassal, are they still held to be suitable witnesses? Certainly, from whatever cause they ceased to be peers. <note>single chapter Title 19, book 2, Feudal Law; where Cujas and others discuss this.</note>

### XCVII.

What if the Peers are absent, or contumacious <note>willfully disobedient to a summons</note>? Those, unless they are far away, are to be waited for: <note>gloss of Baldus, Laudensis, number 26; Alvarotto, Praepositus, Afflictis and others in chapter 1, Title 2, book 2, Feudal Law; Ardizona notes in said chapter 138, section "Where indeed someone possesses."</note> but these <note>the contumacious</note> are to be plainly ignored. <note>Baldus in said chapter 1; argument from the law "if to a legatee" section 1, Digest: on trust-bequests of freedmen; Curtius part 2, member 2, on the feuds of Laymen, number 25.</note>

### XCVIII.

When a sentence has been passed, is it possible to appeal in feudal cases? It is variously debated: but it has prevailed that one can, and indeed to the next superior, if there be one, or to the ordinary judge to whom the matter is subject.

<note>Text at the end of title 22, and section "Witnesses," title 26, book 1, Feudal Law; Raynaudus in the said penultimate section.</note>

Another is the armed defense, used in these books: which is established through a duel and single combat: <note>section "if a Knight," with the gloss title 27, and section 3, Title 39, book 2, Feudal Law; section 1, title 2, book 3, Feudal Law; in the more correct books.</note> And yet another which was formerly permitted by way of an Ordeal rather than a defense, in a very superstitious manner, by touching glowing iron, and likewise by the walking through of waters, <note>See Münster everywhere, and other Histories here and there.</note> which the Feudalists call an exploration: both of which, as being plainly contrary to humanity and piety, we deservedly detest. <note>Damhouderius notes in Criminal Practice, chapter 42.</note>

### XCVI.

What if the peers, who were present at the time of the investiture, later ceased to be Peers; if a dispute arises between the Lord and the Vassal, are they still held to be suitable witnesses? Certainly, from whatever cause they ceased to be peers. <note>single chapter Title 19, book 2, Feudal Law; where Cujas and others discuss this.</note>

### XCVII.

What if the Peers are absent, or contumacious <note>willfully disobedient to a summons</note>? Those, unless they are far away, are to be waited for: <note>gloss of Baldus, Laudensis, number 26; Alvarotto, Praepositus, Afflictis and others in chapter 1, Title 2, book 2, Feudal Law; Ardizona notes in said chapter 138, section "Where indeed someone possesses."</note> but these <note>the contumacious</note> are to be plainly ignored. <note>Baldus in said chapter 1; argument from the law "if to a legatee" section 1, Digest: on trust-bequests of freedmen; Curtius part 2, member 2, on the feuds of Laymen, number 25.</note>

### XCVIII.

When a sentence has been passed, is it possible to appeal in feudal cases? It is variously debated: but it has prevailed that one can, and indeed to the next superior, if there be one, or to the ordinary judge to whom the matter is subject.

<note>Text at the end of title 22, and section "Witnesses," title 26, book 1, Feudal Law; Raynaudus in the said penultimate section.</note>

### XXXIII.

As concerns the case in section 30, the cause of the litigation there is the detention of the property which Paul seeks back from Maevius. He assigns the reason for seeking it as being that he mandated Maevius to carry his property to Pomponius so that he might keep it, and if Pomponius refused, Maevius was to guard it for as long as it took for him to seek it back. Paul's intention is founded in *Law 1, paragraph 12, [under the title] On Deposit,* where the action of mandate, rather than the action of deposit, is granted to him. We shall yet propose other examples.

### XXXIV.

The things said thus far have shown us actions arising from contracts; we must now look at a case where partly a contract and partly a delict <gloss>a civil wrong or offense</gloss> produces the action. For instance, Sempronius leased his house to Titius. This consensual business having been completed, they go together to visit the leased house. But after they are inside the house, Sempronius, without any ambiguity of words, beats Titius with a club placed behind the door, out of a hatred previously conceived against him. Having thoroughly thrashed him, he ejects him out of doors and no longer grants the power of inhabiting the house. Because Titius has endured this with an unwilling stomach <gloss>with great resentment</gloss>, he does not wish to bear the matter without any vengeance, and so he hastens to approach a judge and intends to sue Sempronius.

### XXXV.

Furthermore, because in the proposed case two facts or distinct acts offer themselves, why should two separate remedies of Law not also be obtained to pursue the double aim or end of the intention? For two things are involved here, one of which is a contract, the other a delict, which differ greatly and bring forth two separate petitions. Or rather, a double object of grievance and offense, resulting from the double fact and action performed, is brought into judgment. The first object of dispute
</translation>

<translation page="20">
is the denied habitation of the house which the plaintiff seeks. Either for this reason, because it was so agreed between them that he should inhabit it for a certain price to be paid at a determined time, the plaintiff's intention is founded in *Laws 7, 8, and 9 of the Digest, [under the title] On Letting and Hiring.* The other matter of litigation, or the second object that creates the lawsuit, is the beating, for which the plaintiff seeks a civil pursuit. He desires to bind the defendant to pay him such and such an amount, for the reason that, without any justification or occasion given, the defendant received the plaintiff injuriously enough with blows. Therefore, his intention is founded in *Section 10 of the Institutes, On Injuries,* and the estimatory action of injuries <note>an action where the court estimates the damages based on the severity of the insult and injury</note> is granted to him.

### XXXVI.

Another example follows, where only a delict is vindicated, which shall be the following: namely, a certain shoemaker hired a musician living at Altdorf <note>a university town near Nuremberg</note> so that he might cheer him and his companions with the help of music. Consent now being given by both parties, the musician came at the prearranged time with his companions joined to him, and he played the strings as long as it was permitted to do so by the permission of the magistrate. The time having now elapsed, the musician refused to play further. Because this displeased the shoemaker, he did not stand long meditating on what should be done, but with one blow he broke his <term>pandura</term> <gloss>a three-stringed lute or similar instrument</gloss>. But indeed, since the musician cannot endure this, he therefore calls the shoemaker to the tribunal. But by what action will he be able to proceed against him?

### XXXVII.

Here again the fact, whether it be promissory or of a delict, must be sought so that we may know what creates the lawsuit between the parties. This truly consists in the fact that the shoemaker damaged the musician's lute, the damage of which the musician desires to avenge before the judge, because the shoemaker performed this injurious act against the musician without any fault or occasion given. And so he intends to bind him to the provision of the damage caused. Surely the intention of the musician is founded in *Section 13 of the Institutes, On the Aquilian Law* <note>the Roman law governing compensation for property damage</note>.
</translation>

<summary>These pages explore complex legal scenarios involving multiple causes of action, such as cases combining contract disputes with physical assault or property damage. The author demonstrates how to identify the correct legal foundations for seeking restitution and damages under Roman law.</summary>
<keywords>mandate, deposit, contract, delict, lease, assault, property damage, Aquilian Law, Altdorf, legal procedure</keywords>

demonstrated that a human corpse, filled rather liberally with wine a few hours before strangulation, was opened by the same <term>Bartholin</term> <gloss>Thomas Bartholin, a famous Danish physician and anatomist</gloss>. For once this body was dissected, neither the lacteal veins were visible anywhere, nor did the thoracic ones overflow with any chyle. He confirms that the heart indeed sought the wine, as much from a fearless mind despising death, as from the fierce bile flowing out from the mammary vessels. Thus, we recently saw that it represents a milky color from milk during public anatomical demonstrations in a <term>molossus</term> <gloss>a large breed of dog</gloss> well-nourished with milk before strangulation, and dissected by the Most Noble Lord Doctor <term>Faschius</term> <gloss>Sebald Fasch</gloss> in the anatomical theater. For once this was opened, the lacteals, the <term>receptaculum chyli</term> <gloss>receptacle of the chyle</gloss>, and the thoracic duct immediately came forth so swollen, white, and glistening that all who were present were seized with stupor and the greatest admiration.

Various observations by authors confirm that the insertion of the thoracic lacteals varies in different subjects. Bartholin, departing slightly from <term>Pecquet</term> <gloss>Jean Pecquet, the discoverer of the thoracic duct</gloss> here, proves through various experiments that a solitary branch under the esophagus, thymus, thoracic artery, and left clavicle is poured into the left axillary vein. Pecquet, on the contrary, asserts that this thoracic duct is divided into two branches from the third spine of the back, of which the left tends toward the left clavicle and the right toward the right. > *I would have sacrificed <note>an idiomatic expression for finishing a task</note> had not the bifurcating path of the lacteals wandering through the spine of the thorax recalled my wondering eyes to itself again with its persistent white swelling.*

#### Paragraph I.

Just as a real annuity <term>census realis</term> redemable only on the part of the seller (provided it is bought at a just price, namely by virtue of the Imperial constitutions: 5 florins of annual return for one hundred florins) is a lawful and non-usurious contract according to *Extravagantes* 1 and 2, *On Buying and Selling*. So an annuity irredeemable on the part of the seller (even with the same aforementioned price intervening) is not free from the stain of usury. This was confirmed by Emperor Charles V in the constitution published at Augsburg in the year 1548, under the title **On Usurious Contracts** <note>original German: "Von wucherlichen contracten"</note>, **paragraph "and after the redemption-guilders"** <note>original German: "und nachdem die wiederkauffs Gulden"</note>. For this quality is inherent in annuities of this kind: that the seller may redeem even against the will of the buyer, nor can he bargain to the contrary, nor can the faculty of redeeming ever be prescribed, not even by the space of one hundred years, at least according to canon law. If, therefore, in the instrument of obligation, mention of perpetuity: **unredeemable** <note>original German: "unablößlich"</note> has been made, then irredeemability must be understood and accepted in respect to the buyer or creditor, not the seller or debtor.

### From Civil Law.

#### Paragraph I.

A well-worn question in law is whether the profit of a dowry by force of a pact or statute falls to the survivor if the other dies before the physical union <term>copula</term>? For the negative side, it is commonly brought forward that a dowry is not owed where the burdens of marriage do not exist, according to Law *Si pater* 76, at the end of the Digest, *On the Right of Dowries*. We shall respond affirmatively, however, if nothing was expressly cautioned regarding time in the pact or statute. For consensus, not cohabitation, makes the marriage; the text in Law *Cum fuerit* 15, Digest, *On Conditions and Demonstrations* supports this part, where a legacy left under the condition of marriage is owed immediately as the woman is led <note>into the husband's house</note>. Nor does the said Law 76 stand in the way, because it disposes of a case where

<translation page="9">
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
conveniently, nor could all cases be settled by him, they distinguished other smaller parts into <term>Centenae</term> <gloss>Hundreds</gloss>, or specific villages and districts, by a praiseworthy institution. They assigned individual governors to each <term>Centena</term>, called <term>Centgraven</term> <gloss>Hundred-Graves or Hundred-Counts</gloss>, and joined to these again other helpers and deputies who went by the name of <term>Centenarii</term> <gloss>Centenarians</gloss>, so that in this way the burden was shared with others, and the task became lighter for the Count who was not equal to it alone. <term>Beatus Rhenanus</term> agrees with us in book 2 of his German Affairs, where he says: the regions were divided into Hundreds, whence the name of the <term>Centenarius</term>. That magistrate, who presided over the <term>Centena</term>, was subject to the Count. Moreover, just as we said a little before that traces of the ancient German <term>Pagi</term> <gloss>districts or cantons</gloss> exist among us today, so too it must not be thought that the word <term>Centena</term> has entirely vanished through the length of time. For near Heidelberg, by the testimony of the same <term>Rhenanus</term>, a trace of the <term>Centena</term> still appears in several places, and the use of this word has remained even to our own times.

§. 3. Indeed, in <term>Franconia</term> and the <term>Palatinate</term>, the word <term>Centena</term> seems to have another meaning today, while they understand by <term>Centena</term> criminal jurisdiction and high justice <note>original: "merum Imperium"</note>, and thus the punishment of capital crimes. From this, what is called in other places <term>Hals-</term> or <term>hohe Gerechtigkeit</term> <gloss>neck-justice or high justice</gloss>, they themselves call <term>Centgerechtigkeit</term> <gloss>Hundred-justice</gloss>. They name him to whom such judgment belongs a <term>Centherrn</term> <gloss>Lord of the Hundred</gloss>; the assessors of the same criminal judgment, <term>Zentschöpffen</term> <gloss>Hundred-jurors</gloss>; and finally, those who are subject to such judgment, they call <term>Zentbare Unterthanen</term> <gloss>subjects liable to the Hundred</gloss>. Regarding this matter, <term>Berneggerus</term> may be consulted. But it is so far from the case that modern customs have imposed a different meaning on the word <term>Centena</term> from the old use, that it rather exactly reflects the very ancient institution of the Germans, by which they divided the districts into <term>Centenae</term>, or as we just said, and placed over each <term>Centena</term> a judge, whom they called a <term>CentGraffen</term>, with his <term>Centenarii</term> and <term>Scabini</term> <gloss>lay judges or jurors</gloss>. For what prevents one from being allowed to call the Count of the <term>Centena</term> a <term>Zentherrn</term>, or the judgment held in the <term>Centena</term> before the Count and <term>Centenarii</term> a <term>Zentgericht</term> <gloss>Hundred-court</gloss> or <term>Zentgerechtigkeit</term>? The <term>Scabini</term>, called <term>Schöpffen</term> by the Germans, from the Teutonic verb <term>schaffen</term> <gloss>to do or provide</gloss>, because the <term>Scabini</term> must diligently take care that no injury is done to anyone in the <term>Centena</term>, and must procure the advantage of the <term>Centena</term> in all ways.
</translation>

<translation page="10">
They are so named (for all those err who derive that word either from the Hebrew <term>Shabbat</term> <gloss>Sabbath/rest</gloss> with <term>Besoldus</term>; or from the <term>Scamnis</term> <gloss>benches</gloss> on which they were accustomed to pronounce sentence, with <term>Beckmann</term>; or with others from elsewhere) who were given as helpers to the Count of the <term>Centena</term> along with the <term>Centenarii</term>, and what forbids calling them <term>Zentschöpffen</term>; or calling the men who belonged to the same <term>Centena</term> <term>Zentbare Unterthanen</term>?

§. 4. We said in §. 2 that the <term>Centenarii</term> are to be derived from the <term>Centenae</term>, so that it might be clear that we are not pleased by the opinion of those men—who are many in number and of the greatest authority—who wish our <term>Centenarii</term> to be understood as Counts of the Hundreds and so named from the number one hundred. Thus, to produce at least one out of many, the Famous <term>Berneggerus</term> says: <term>Zentgraffen</term>, as if you were to say, Centenary Counts, that is, the presidents and princes of a hundred-man court, who are also called <term>Centenarii</term> in the ancient laws of the Germans. But we assert that Mr. <term>Berneggerus</term> relies on an insufficiently certain hypothesis, and that neither were a hundred Counts once added to the Princes elected in the council, nor are the Counts of the Hundreds themselves ever understood by the term <term>Centenarii</term>. For that passage of <term>Tacitus</term> which he cites for himself: <note>from Tacitus, Germania 12</note> "Princes are also elected in the same Councils, who administer justice through the Districts and villages. A hundred companions from the common people are present for each, serving as both counsel and authority," <term>B. Reinesius</term>, a man never to be spoken of without praise, has proved to be faulty. He showed that <term>Certi</term> <gloss>certain/fixed</gloss> should be substituted for <term>Centeni</term> <gloss>one hundred each</gloss>. It is clear from this that he himself wandered into a common error with others, and having presupposed this false hypothesis, fell with several others into a false opinion concerning the Centenary Counts. We know from <term>Tacitus</term> and other authors that the ancient Germans, if they were about to enlist soldiers, chose a hundred youths from each district. But what then? Is it to be gathered from this that a hundred companions were also joined to a Prince in civilian dress <note>original: "Togato Principi"</note>? Truly, the patrons of the contrary opinion seem to have gathered thus and compared <note>original: "κατ’ ἄλληλον"</note> that passage about the hundred youths elected from individual districts in time of war (and afterwards named from that number of a hundred for the sake of honor, as <term>Tacitus</term> hints) with this one about the hundred companions. Although this was, as it were, their first falsehood <note>original: "πρῶτον... ψεῦδος"</note> and stood as the cause of such a notable error for them, nevertheless those two passages are very different.
</translation>

<summary>These pages discuss the etymology and historical administrative structure of the German Centena or Hundred, arguing that the term Centenarius refers to a deputy of the district rather than a count governing a hundred men. The author critiques previous scholars like Berneggerus for misinterpreting a passage in Tacitus regarding the number of companions assigned to local princes.</summary>

<keywords>Centena, Hundred, Centenarius, Tacitus, German law, legal history, Franconia, Palatinate, administrative districts, etymology, Centgraven, Scabini</keywords>

### XV. <term>Nazōraios</term> <gloss>The Nazarene</gloss>

JESUS is so called by a gentilic name from Nazareth, a city of Galilee and the homeland of his parents. Regarding the application of this name to Christ, a three-fold different explanation is given. By some he is called a Nazarene as if separated and consecrated to the Lord, from Judges 13:7 and Genesis 49:26. To others, the eleventh chapter of Isaiah, verse 1, is a help. A third group joins both passages. And here different people look to different roots. There is the root <term>natsar</term> <gloss>to guard, to fashion, to plant</gloss>; there is also <term>nazar</term> <gloss>to separate, to sanctify</gloss>. Whence <term>nazir</term> and in Chaldean <term>nazira</term>, a Nazarene. We do not deny that both apply to the Lord, yet we feel that he had this name here derived from the city and common homeland. It is also written in various ways. Sometimes <term>Nazōraios</term> in Matthew, Luke, and John; but Mark exhibits it with another termination, <term>Nazarēnos</term>, as it is also found elsewhere. It is therefore used interchangeably, just as I say <term>Essaios</term> and <term>Essēnos</term> <gloss>Essenes</gloss>. We do not deny that it is also found written <term>Nazarenos</term>, since that could have happened due to the negligence of the painters or the corruption of the Greek language—as, alas, in Greece itself the inhabitants do not know Greek! We shall append a monument of this fact from Crusius, who collects the letters of learned men and reports several in book 3 of his *Turco-Graecia*, page 216 and following, from which it will suffice to have noted only the following one:

> Lord Theodosios, dear brother-in-law, and brother in holiness, and lord priest, greetings in Christ. Know, Lord Theodosios, that since we took up our dwelling after the exile of my wife, the mother died a good death.

III. Just as the motion of the eagle, the serpent, and the ship is smooth and without noise, so the arts of men in seducing her who is an <term>Almah</term> <gloss>maiden</gloss> or virgin are hidden and secret. IV. It is equally difficult to know whether she who still remains hidden with her parents is an <term>almah</term> <gloss>maiden</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: עלמה</note> and has not granted a man access to herself, as it is to know the way of an eagle in the sky, etc. V. The guarding of virgins is difficult because the arts of men, by which they lay snares for them, are concealed, etc. <note>Compare the distinguished Saubert in his dissertation on this passage, chapter 2; and Spanheim in his Gospel Doubts, 34, section 18 and following. Add to these Leonhard Hutter, Common Places, Diexod. article 23, latter question, pages 864 and 865; Jacob Martini, book 3, On the Three Elohim, chapter 43; and Blessed Walther, Vindication of the passage Jeremiah 31:22, against his opponent, page 73 and following.</note> Let us assume, however, that in that passage of Proverbs a comparison of a prostitute and an adulteress is established; nevertheless, the word <term>almah</term> could still signify a virgin there and be understood <term>doxastikos</term> <gloss>according to opinion</gloss> or <term>eironikos</term> <gloss>ironically</gloss>. Nor is that manner of speaking unusual in the Holy Scripture, where someone is called not by what they truly are, but what they seem or are believed to be, or what they sell themselves as, or what they had been before. Whence our Blessed Luther says:

> The Jews would gain nothing, he says, except this: that the name <term>almah</term> there signifies such a young woman whom everyone regards as a virgin, and who wears a virgin's wreath and name, and presents herself as a virgin, even though she may be a prostitute. Which abuse of the name surely does not at all remove its proper and genuine meaning even in that place, as all endowed with a sound mind will easily understand.

Therefore, we have so far proved that this passage of Proverbs does nothing to support the sense which the Jews attribute to the word <term>almah</term>. And since these same people, refusing to yield to divine truth, explain the same word in Isaiah 7 in that perverse sense and simultaneously appeal to the passage in Proverbs, they do what most lazy Sophists are accustomed to: when they dispute some controversial matter, they take as granted the very thing under controversy and thus mock the opponent. We conclude now with a once great Theologian and Philosopher, Doctor Jacob Martini, that the word <term>almah</term> in our passage signifies nothing other than a virgin hidden from the sight of men, concealed and secret, and thus entirely untouched, of whose modesty and integrity there is no doubt—especially since it is preceded by the letter <term>He</term> <note>The Hebrew definite article</note>, which, as Galatinus rightly advises, makes the word signify determinately
</translation>

<translation page="16">
and specifically. For it is worthy of note, says the praised author, that in the entire *Holy Scripture* this word **ha-almah** <note>original Hebrew: העלמה</note>—written specifically with the article, namely with the letter **He**—is found only three times, and is always used of a virgin: *Genesis 24 verse 43; Exodus 2 verse 8; and Isaiah 7 verse 14.* Since, therefore, the first two to whom **ha-almah** is attributed were virgins, who will doubt that this word, used in the same way by Isaiah in his prophecy, denotes a pure virgin? Especially since the Jews cannot demonstrate from any other passage that **ha-almah** is used for a married woman. Finally (which even Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> hands down), that sign given by Isaiah had to be truly miraculous; but for a young woman to conceive by a man (and thus with the loss of virginity) and bear a son is no miracle, since it happens naturally and thus occurs daily. Let the Jews therefore concede, whether they will or no, that the sign given by the Prophet was none other than that, contrary to the way of nature, a virgin would conceive and bear a son by the miracle of GOD alone. <note>Blessed Jacob Martini, said book 3, page 243 and following.</note>

If we obtain this by our vowing, each of us will have cause to congratulate himself and rejoice after the course of the year.

the son himself <note>Symmachus the Younger</note> testifies and rejoices in <note>original: "1. Ep. 44"</note> Book 1, Epistle 44. To this, the rhythmic writer of the <term>Fasti</term> <gloss>The Festivals</gloss>, Naso <note>Ovid</note>, subscribes and courteously introduces this rite when he says:

> In spotless garments they go to the Tarpeian heights,
> And the people themselves are the same color as their festival.
> Now the new <term>fasces</term> <gloss>bundles of rods symbolizing authority</gloss> lead the way, new purple shines;
> And the conspicuous ivory chair feels new weights. <note>original: "1. Fast. v. 10"</note>

Indeed, there was also a custom of "tasting," and as it were, imbuing and auspiciously beginning one's duties on that very day. Drusus, the Prefect of the City, ascended the tribunal to take the omens; Nero took the omens on the Calends of January; the Emperor Maximianus immediately made what he had hoped for in the future a completed act. Regarding the former, Tacitus the writer of the Augustan History <note>original: "liber 4. annales caput 36"</note> testifies; regarding the second, Suetonius <note>original: "caput 46"</note>; and regarding the latter, the Panegyrist. <summary>This page compares Roman inaugural customs with Christian traditions, arguing that while political and religious renewals happen at the New Year, true prosperity comes from God's grace rather than omens.</summary>

Internal works are to acknowledge the depravity and corruption of nature, to confess oneself guilty of divine wrath and eternal punishments, and to grieve for sins from the soul.

To take refuge in the mercy of GOD offered in Christ, and to firmly and certainly establish that through Him the remission of sins and the right of approaching the heavenly inheritance is given.

To devote one's whole self to the service of GOD, and to apply oneself to this with the whole mind, so that all plans and actions of life serve the glory of the divine name and the utility of the Church.

### LXVII.
External works, however, are those which strike the eyes and the exterior senses.

### LXVIII.
These are either of words, such as teaching the gospel, invoking GOD in dangers, giving thanks to the same for benefits, and issuing a confession of faith.

<translation page="18">
since you expect a magnificent one, what is more magnificent than this King, whom the Angels applaud from the heavens, whom Kings adore in the cradle, and to whom they offer gold, frankincense, and myrrh, the gifts of kings. If you desire one fighting and triumphing, what is stronger, what more glorious than this Hercules, who already in the cradle tamed the ancient serpent, and was born and revealed for this purpose: that he might destroy the works of the devil and restore to its place whatever the fury of the infernal Prince had shattered. Here you see a Lamb indeed, but one who is to take away the sins of the world; a lamb, but one who is at the same time the greatest Lion of the tribe of Judah. You believe that the dry rod of Aaron blossomed, sprouted leaves, and bore fruit; why do you not also believe that a virgin could give birth? You believe that the great Goliath was slain by little David, the lion was torn apart by Samson, and the Philistines were routed; why do you not also believe that by this little Hercules in the cradle, and by the seed of the woman, the head of the serpent was crushed? Omnipotence performs what human impotence cannot, and what lack of faith cannot grasp. Rightly indeed does Saint Augustine judge these cradles more venerable than your temple in Jerusalem, repeating:

> *O manger, more venerable and holy than the temple of Solomon itself! Let the Jerusalem temple shine with gold, let it glitter with Cherubim, the ark of God, lampstands, tables, and golden vessels; let it be adorned with the most spacious courts, with sacrifices, and the ministry of priests, yet it is inferior to the Bethlehemite manger.*

Your fathers in the desert bore many and deadly plagues from the fiery serpents; and when Moses had raised a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign, whoever among those struck looked upon it was healed. Behold, truly, here in the cradle hides the tamer of those fiery serpents, and the bronze serpent himself, who was later raised up on the sign of the cross: look upon him and you see! But alas, you seed of the snake, seed of vipers, you do not wish to recognize the blessed seed of Abraham, the seed of the woman. The most holy Infant complains of you unbelievers: The ox has known
</translation>

<translation page="19">
his owner, and the donkey the manger of his lord; but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood. After the Jews, approach the cradles of our Hercules, you born of the gentiles, whom this infant, long desired by the nations, called a people when they were not a people. The Magi <gloss>Wise Men</gloss> — whether Persians or Chaldeans — go before you, and with a star as their guide, they approach the Savior of the nations as well. *Indeed, those cradles do not shine with precious paintings, here purple and scarlet do not radiate, nor whatever* the Chinese <note>original: "Seres"</note> *taught the skilled hand to spin, whatever* Babylon *wove with ingenious comb, whatever* the Tyrians *dyed, whatever* the Phrygians *stitched, whatever* the Milesians *sheared;* yet those cradles are nonetheless those of the King of Kings and Lord of Lords, the King who will shatter the kings of the earth with an iron rod. If you believe, gentiles, that Minerva was born from the brain of Jupiter; then believe also that this God was born of God. If you believe that Jupiter made Danaë pregnant through a golden shower, believe also that the Spirit of God overshadowed the virgin so that she might carry a womb and bear a son. If you believe that your Hercules subdued the immense monsters of men and beasts, overcame the Erymanthian boar, squeezed the bull in a wrestling match with Antaeus, routed the Stymphalian birds, fought with the Amazons, defeated the three-bodied Geryon, tamed the horses of Diomedes, cleansed the stable of Augeas, struggled with the dragon of the Hesperides, fought to the end with the Lernaean Hydra and the three-headed Cerberus; then believe also that this our heavenly Hercules has conquered the world, death, the devil, and hell, and has trampled his and our enemies under his feet, cast out evil spirits with a word, calmed the winds and waves with a command, healed lepers, the deaf, and the blind with a touch, and put to flight every kind of disease and death with a simple order.

I have summoned, after the Christians, even the Jews themselves; I have summoned the nations to the cradles of our Hercules. It is time that I myself approach. Grant, Boy Jesus, that I may only from a distance [approach] your manger
</translation>

<summary>
These pages present a theological comparison between the infant Christ and the mythological Hercules, arguing that Christ's humble birth fulfills biblical prophecy and surpasses pagan legends. The author addresses both Jews and Gentiles, urging them to recognize Christ as the true tamer of the "ancient serpent" and the ultimate victor over sin and death.
</summary>

<keywords>
Hercules, Jesus Christ, Nativity, typology, Jewish-Christian relations, pagan mythology, Saint Augustine, miracles, Labors of Hercules, symbolism
</keywords>
