### XLII.

This pleasure is nothing other than a certain subsequent perfection of human functions, commending them with a certain singular sweetness.

### XLIII.

Therefore, just as theoretical happiness excels practical happiness, so also theoretical pleasure surpasses practical pleasure.

### XLIII I.

<margin>
See the last chapter of book 1 of the Ethics and chapter 7 of book 10 of the Nicomachean Ethics.
</margin>
Furthermore, from the preceding points this is also clear: that Aristotle saw both the excellence and the dignity of human nature, as well as its corruption. This is evident while he confesses that a desire for divinity and immortality is implanted in man by nature; and yet he says that divinity does not belong to man insofar as he is man. But truly, he did not know the cause of this matter, much less the way of obtaining immortality through the MESSIAH: for this is entirely owed to revelation, as the most learned Zwinger <note>Theodor Zwinger, 1533–1588, a Swiss physician and humanist scholar known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> most beautifully noted on chapter 7 of book 10 of the Ethics.

### XLV.

Nor is there any reason why we should reject the doctrine of Aristotle concerning human happiness on the grounds that it is less in agreement with our Christian religion.

### XLVI.

For besides what we said above,
</translation>

<translation page="15">
<margin>
Homily: To young men, on how they might profit from Greek literature. <note>original: "ὁμιλ: πρὸς τοὺς νέους ὅπως ἂν ἐξ ἑλληνικῶν ὠφελοῖντο λόγων"</note>
</margin>
that the philosopher disputes on this matter philosophically, his opinion ought to be commended to us on this name alone: either the philosopher says the same things—that is, things congruent with heavenly truth—and the consensus is profitable; or he says different things, and the comparison is profitable. We use here the words of Saint Basil the Great, a witness in this matter greater than any exception.

### XLVII.

Finally, the philosopher does not contradict himself, even though in the first book of the Nicomachean Ethics he asserts that practical happiness is the highest good, while in the last book he maintains and contends that theoretical happiness <note>original: "θεωρητικὴν εὐδαιμονίαν"</note> is superior to it.

### XLVIII.

For just as in the first book, with respect to practical happiness, he regards the composite man <note>original: "τὸν σύνθετον ἄνθρωπον," referring to the union of soul and body</note>, so in the tenth book, regarding theoretical blessedness, he considers the mind <note>original: "τὸν νοῦν"</note>, which he says is most of all the man.

### XLIX.

From all these things at last, I judge it to appear more clearly than the midday light, as the saying goes, that what Cicero said is most true: that all authority of philosophy—that is, the doctrine concerning life and morals—consists in procuring a blessed life, and therefore its dignity and excellence are supreme and admirable.
</translation>

<summary>These pages conclude the argument that Aristotelian ethics, specifically the distinction between practical and contemplative happiness, remains valuable to Christian scholars. It reconciles Aristotle's focus on the intellect with the Christian need for revelation through the Messiah, ending with a Ciceronian praise of moral philosophy.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Happiness, Pleasure, Contemplation, Messiah, Theodor Zwinger, Basil the Great, Cicero, Moral Philosophy</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: and also that the poor do not exercise envy against the rich,</meta>
and pursue them with a hatred that will erupt into the certain ruin of the Republic. For we see that in the states of all Republics, various kinds of men are found, who of their own accord depart into diverse classes, as it were; so that the illustrious and wealthy constitute one, the weaker and poor another, and finally a third consists of those who walk the middle path and exist as a temperament <gloss>moderating force</gloss> between the illustrious and the poor. But by what method these classes are to be composed, so that the city is rendered quiet and each part of the city may enjoy its own happiness: here is the task, here is the toil.

<margin>Aristotle, Politics, Book 5, Chapter 1.</margin>
The illustrious or wealthy persuade themselves that because they excel the rest in splendor, they are simply superior, and that by right and merit, unequal things are owed to them as unequals. On the contrary, the poor, measuring all things by liberty, concede no inequality. By this vain persuasion of men—as if his own right were not granted to each—the states of Republics are changed most of all, which was already long ago excellently proven by Aristotle.

Writers record of Solon <note>Athenian lawmaker, c. 630 – c. 560 BCE</note> that, in order to make the citizens friendly to himself and to be declared a legislator by them, he said: He would bring laws equal for all, and for that reason, by the greatest zeal and will of all, the judgment of making laws was permitted to him. For the common people thought he spoke of the mean <gloss>middle point</gloss> of the matter—to borrow this from the schools—while the Aristocrats <term>Optimates</term> thought he spoke of the mean of the person. If the citizens persist in these precipices, and do not wish to remit anything of their own right, which they boast of so laboriously, it is easily evident that contentions of this sort are joined with the internal destruction of the Republic, and do not cease until one side is oppressed.

Indeed, neither side, whether the poor or the rich be considered, is accustomed to seek equality and inequality from true principles. It is a common assertion of the Philosophers that virtue alone makes a distinction between the commoners and the illustrious; so that the latter may shine forth among the rest, and the former may live content with their humbler lot. But who could persuade the minds of those who, blinded too much by self-love, are driven hither and thither? Nor is the matter so clear that it holds no further doubt.

<margin>Aristotle, Politics, Book 6, Chapter 3.</margin>
Aristotle himself, dealing with Democracy, confesses it is extremely difficult to so order the people that all participate equally in the communion of rights. For although the weaker look to nothing else by this equality of theirs than that they not be oppressed by the wealthier, you will nevertheless notice the diverse purposes, zeals, propensities, inclinations, inventions, arts, and rules of the more powerful.

Lest we dwell longer on this question, and to explain in a few words the mind of the Philosopher, which is found more than once in his work *The Politics*,
</translation>

<translation page="13">
these things must be added: namely, that harmony can be obtained between the poor and the rich if the legislator always takes greater care for the middle-class citizens than for the extremes; for then the Republic will be maintained as if in an equilibrium. But if this proceeds less according to wish, another way must be attempted: namely, that the rights themselves be properly mixed, so that both parties preside over affairs and concede a little to each other in turn. Let there be added also the other duties of humanity and signs of benevolence, whether in gesture or in speech; let one promote the advantages of the other and avert disadvantages; perhaps in this way such a Republic will fare well enough, as long as no one can complain of being either oppressed or despised, but all live among themselves with equal right.

What we have said so far regarding the mixing of a Popular state with an Aristocratic one is explained more fully, beyond the *Politics* of Aristotle and Plato, by Greek and Latin writers who treat Democratic and Aristocratic affairs even to the point of nausea. For to repeat our opinion again: among the ancients, a Popular state was never found unless tempered by the arts of the Aristocrats <term>Optimates</term>. We shall not speak at present of the changes and various attempts by which the Athenian Republic was vexed. Therefore, Thucydides, Demosthenes, and Isocrates must be turned over diligently. In Roman history, Halicarnassus <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus</note>, Plutarch, and Dionysius are to be commended; but no one surpasses the labors of Livy in learning the characters of the Aristocrats.

§. 13. The signs for recognizing the state of a Republic are not rarely confused. If the power of Kings were contained in external apparatus and splendor, the King of Poland would certainly surpass all the Princes of Europe in Majesty, whom the leading men <term>proceres</term> venerate like servants. But his power is closed within narrow limits. Indeed, that which is permitted to him in Ecclesiastical matters is meager: it is a crime to condemn a knight to death except in the assemblies <term>comitia</term>. Regarding the waging of war or entering into a treaty, there is a common care with the Senate: he cannot even in the Senate, without the consent of the rest of the nobility, promulgate new laws, command an extraordinary tax, mint money, name a successor, and other things which most adorn the Royal dignity. And to finish in a few words: the rights of Majesty are exercised by the aristocrats rather than by the King. Marcin Kromer <note>Polish historian and cartographer, 1512–1589</note> has followed this out diligently and successfully.

<margin>Kromer, Book 2, The Polish Republic <note>original: "Rep. Pol."</note></margin>
Lorraine was formerly distinguished by the title of a Kingdom; in most recent times, a certain part of it began to be held as a fief from the German Empire, yet so that it acknowledged no superior: regarding which matter they do not permit us
</translation>

<summary>These pages discuss the necessity of social harmony between the rich and poor, suggesting a strong middle class and a "mixed" government as the best way to maintain stability. The author uses the limited power of the Polish monarchy as a case study for how actual sovereignty can reside with the nobility rather than the king.</summary>
<keywords>social class, Aristotle, Solon, mixed government, Democracy, Aristocracy, Poland, Marcin Kromer, Lorraine, sovereignty</keywords>

# THE SUMMA, BOOK I

### Concerning the impediments of this work on the part of the artist's body. Chapter IV.

We have already determined for you the impediments of this work in general. Now, however, we shall address you with a more specific discourse in this chapter, and we shall relate to you all those impediments most fully and in order. We say, therefore: that if anyone does not have his organs complete, he will not be able to reach the completion of this work by himself—for example, if he were blind or had his limbs amputated—since he is not aided by the members which, as ministers of nature, are the means through which this art is perfected. Furthermore, if the artist's body is weak and sickly, such as the bodies of those with fever, or lepers whose limbs fall away, or those laboring in the final stages of life, or old men of decrepit age, he will not reach the completion of the art. The artist is therefore hindered in his intention by these natural bodily incapacities.

### Concerning impediments on the part of the artist's soul. Chapter V.

We have set before you a single chapter in which we related in absolute and manifest discourse the impediments depending on the artist's body. It remains for us to relate briefly the impediments on the part of the soul itself, which most greatly hinder the completion of this work. We say, therefore, that he who does not have natural talent <note>original: "ingenium naturale"</note> and a soul subtly searching into natural principles, the foundations of nature, and the crafts which are able to follow nature in the properties of her action, will not find the true root of this most precious science. Such are many who have a stiff neck <note>a metaphor for stubbornness or lack of intellectual flexibility</note>, empty of talent in every investigation, who can scarcely understand common speech and likewise learn common works of the populace with difficulty. Besides these, we also find many to have a soul easily believing any fantasy, but what they believe they have found to be true is entirely fantastic, wandering from reason, full of error, and removed from natural principles; for their brain, filled with many smoky vapors, cannot receive the true intention of natural things. There are also others besides these who have a mobile soul, shifting from opinion to opinion and from will to will, like those who now believe this and want the same thing without any foundation of reason. Yet a little after that, they believe another thing similarly and want another thing. And these are so mobile that they can scarcely finish the smallest part of that which they intend, but rather leave it diminished. There are likewise others who cannot see any truth from natural things any more than beasts, such as the mentally captured <note>feeble-minded</note>, the insane, and children. There are others who despise science and do not think it exists; whom this science likewise despises and repels from the end of this most precious work. And there are those who are slaves serving money, affirming this wonderful science themselves, but fearing to set aside the necessary expenses. Therefore, although they affirm it and investigate it according to reason, they do not arrive at the experience of the work because of the greed for money. To these, therefore, our science does not come. For how could he who is ignorant or has neglected to investigate science arrive at it easily?

### Concerning external impediments hindering the work of this art. Chapter VI.

We have reduced to two chapters all the impediments delaying the end of this art which arise from radical principles according to the nature of the artist of this most precious business. It is appropriate, then, that we finally relate the impediments arriving from the outside, from contingent fortunes and accidents by which this most glorious work is hindered. We see, therefore, certain astute and ingenious men, not at all ignorant of the works of nature, and of those things in which it is possible
</translation>

These men, however, being oppressed by extreme poverty, are forced to postpone this excellent <term>magisterium</term> <gloss>mastery or Great Work</gloss> due to the lack of means. There are also many others besides those just mentioned who are curious, detained by various cares and anxieties of this world, occupying themselves entirely with every secular business; from these our precious science flees again. Now, therefore, it is sufficiently clear to you from the preceding chapters what the impediments are that distract from this art.

For that which is not attained through natural talent is aided in its defect through doctrine. It is necessary, therefore, for the artist to be helped by the highest investigation and industry. Likewise, he would help an error in an instant from the science acquired through natural doctrine, which he could not avoid through industry alone; since art is aided by talent, and talent is likewise aided by art.

It is similarly necessary for him to be of a constant will in the work, so that he does not presume to attempt now this, now that; because our art does not consist in, nor is it perfected by, a multitude of things. For there is one stone, one medicine, in which the <term>magisterium</term> <gloss>mastery</gloss> consists, to which we add no foreign thing, nor do we diminish it, except that we remove what is superfluous in the preparation. It is also necessary for him to insist upon the work diligently until its consummation, so that he does not leave the work cut short; because he would acquire neither science nor profit from a diminished work, but rather despair and loss. It is also expedient that he not be ignorant of the principles and primary roots of this art, which concern the being of the work; for he who is ignorant of the beginning will not find the end. Furthermore, what most object regarding the efficacy of the dodecatemories, Gassendi also objects in his *Physics*, section 2, book 6, chapter 2, page 724. Abdias Trew candidly admits this error of the Astrologers in his *Disputations on Medical Astrology*, thesis 36: <note>original: "Quod quatuor qualitatibus elementaribus pollere & differre ab invicem inferunt Astrologi, majori faciunt absurditate, quam si asinum iisdem qualitatibus pollere cum equo dicant, quod uterque, & ut Homerus loquitur, μώνυξ sit."</note> That the Astrologers infer these signs possess and differ from one another by the four elementary qualities is a greater absurdity than if they were to say a donkey possesses the same qualities as a horse because each is, as Homer says, "single-hoofed." And yet some Astrologers attribute so much to this fiction that they fill both sides of the page with it, prognosticating a future season to be either warmer or colder based on how many planets are found in notably hot or cold signs. But by the rule above, the liver is subject not to Saturn, but either to Venus according to the mind of Ptolemy and the Paraphrast Proclus, or to Jupiter according to Cardano; therefore, it will not be corrupted by Saturn itself. <meta>continues from previous page: is imposed as a fine for an offense.</meta> Thus the Phocians were accused by the Thebans and condemned in the common council of Greece to pay so great a sum of money that it could not be paid. Finally, in desperate circumstances, since they were being deprived of their fields, children, and wives, they were driven to plunder that most celebrated Temple of Apollo at Delphi. From this later erupted the greatest wars, by which all Greece was subjected to the yoke of the Macedonians. Justin writes concerning this in Book 8, chapter 1. A no less grave danger is to be feared from that Avarice which is seen in private matters, namely when either individual Magistrates or the entire order of Magistrates draw the goods of private citizens to themselves by force, deceit, and under some pretext.

## XIII.
Indeed, since this **Avarice** stands out above the rest as a frequent cause of ruin, a King will act most safely if he exacts small taxes in portions, with the consent of the estates, having demonstrated the necessity of the financial situation; if he maintains ordinary taxes and does not easily command new ones. Adam Conzen <note>original: "Adamus Conzenius"</note> states this in Book 9 of his Politics, chapter 8, section 4. This is especially true since no vice is found to be more foul in Princes and those governing the Commonwealth than **Avarice**. *To hold the Commonwealth for profit is not only base, but even wicked and nefarious*, says Cicero. Indeed, it is even repugnant to nature itself; hence the same author says:

> To take something away from another, and to increase one's own advantage by the disadvantage of another human being, is more contrary to nature than death, than poverty, than pain, than the other things which can happen either to the body or to external things. For it removes the fellowship and society of men: For if we are so affected that each person plunders or violates another for the sake of his own gain, that society of the human race, which is most according to nature, must necessarily be torn apart.

## XIV.
Harrowing **Ambition** of those handling the scepters is often accustomed to produce a plague in Commonwealths equal to, or even greater than, **Avarice**. From Ambition, as if from a <term>Lerna</term> <gloss>a many-headed Hydra</gloss> of evils, besides wars—of which it is the torch—infinite other evils also leap forth, and it often brings the greatest plague and destruction to the Ambitious themselves. For although **Avarice** also stands as a frequent cause of war, yet far
</translation>

<translation page="10">
more persistent in this regard is Ambition. Indeed, wicked causes seize each man for battles, yet the lust for dominating holds the principal place, says *Adam Conzen in Book 10 of his Politics, chapter 8.* Hence *Thucydides* rightly said: The cause of all evils is the desire for power arising from ambition. And *Polybius*, a most weighty writer, says that after some city has overcome and struggled through many great dangers and has already ascended to leadership and power: It is manifest that when favorable fortune, not used with moderation, has fixed its seat there, luxury creeps into the morals, and Ambition and obstinacy into the minds of Men, both regarding the Magistrates and regarding others. Once these evils have grown strong, they will be the beginning of a change for the worse, arising from honors sought through Ambition or denied.

XV. Moreover, many do not judge themselves to be blessed in every part until they can enlarge their Kingdom by adding new Provinces to old ones, being ignorant that according to *Seneca in Epistle 113*, to command oneself is the greatest Command <note>original: "Imperium"</note>. Nor do they pay attention to the most certain destruction of their own Provinces resulting therefrom: For while they are not content with their own limits and gape for more provinces, they often lose those things which they have already placed in safety. An example is the Cities of Greece, which while they each desired to command individually, they all lost their command. *Justin, Book 8, chapter 1.*

XVI. Therefore, it is from the mouth of Truth what *Thucydides* says in the description of the *Seditions of Corcyra*: The cause of all evils is the desire for power and Ambition. From these passions all calamity is born. Thence have come atrocious wars continued in a perpetual series from the beginning of the world's creation. Inflamed by this, Alexander pursued all Asia with fire and sword, and Cyrus previously devastated Ionia. Demosthenes is said to have once remarked: if two paths were open, one to the underworld and the other to the throne, he would choose the one that led to the underworld. I believe he did not speak sincerely, but nevertheless he showed the most miserable Ambition of those who, through labors, dangers, and wounds, climb to a slippery, tottering summit, shaken by lightning and winds, where they can neither stand firm nor depart.
</translation>

The author emphasizes that excessive taxation and the lust for territorial expansion lead to internal ruin and external defeat.</summary>
<keywords>Avarice, Ambition, Taxation, Phocians, Thucydides, Cicero, Political Corruption, Greek History, Sovereignty</keywords>

From Ambition, as if from a <term>Lerna</term> <gloss>a many-headed Hydra</gloss> of evils, besides wars—of which it is the torch—infinite other evils also leap forth, and it often brings the greatest plague and destruction to the Ambitious themselves. For although **Avarice** also stands as a frequent cause of war, yet far
pages.10:
more persistent in this regard is Ambition. Indeed, wicked causes seize each man for battles, yet the lust for dominating holds the principal place, says *Adam Conzen in Book 10 of his Politics, chapter 8.* Hence *Thucydides* rightly said: The cause of all evils is the desire for power arising from ambition. And *Polybius*, a most weighty writer, says that after some city has overcome and struggled through many great dangers and has already ascended to leadership and power: It is manifest that when favorable fortune, not used with moderation, has fixed its seat there, luxury creeps into the morals, and Ambition and obstinacy into the minds of Men, both regarding the Magistrates and regarding others. Once these evils have grown strong, they will be the beginning of a change for the worse, arising from honors sought through Ambition or denied.

XV. Moreover, many do not judge themselves to be blessed in every part until they can enlarge their Kingdom by adding new Provinces to old ones, being ignorant that according to *Seneca in Epistle 113*, to command oneself is the greatest Command <note>original: "Imperium"</note>. Nor do they pay attention to the most certain destruction of their own Provinces resulting therefrom: For while they are not content with their own limits and gape for more provinces, they often lose those things which they have already placed in safety. An example is the Cities of Greece, which while they each desired to command individually, they all lost their command. *Justin, Book 8, chapter 1.*

XVI. Therefore, it is from the mouth of Truth what *Thucydides* says in the description of the *Seditions of Corcyra*: The cause of all evils is the desire for power and Ambition. From these passions all calamity is born. Thence have come atrocious wars continued in a perpetual series from the beginning of the world's creation. Inflamed by this, Alexander pursued all Asia with fire and sword, and Cyrus previously devastated Ionia. Demosthenes is said to have once remarked: if two paths were open, one to the underworld and the other to the throne, he would choose the one that led to the underworld. I believe he did not speak sincerely, but nevertheless he showed the most miserable Ambition of those who, through labors, dangers, and wounds, climb to a slippery, tottering summit, shaken by lightning and winds, where they can neither stand firm nor depart.

<meta>continues from previous page: for a supreme Prince</meta>
<note>Page number 5 is centered at the top, flanked by two floral typographical fleurons.</note>

->X.<-

The constitution of Charles the Fat <note>original: "Caroli Crassi"</note> *concerning the Roman expedition* from the year 890 is suspicious and devoid of both credit and truth. Even if this were not evident from the clause added to the constitution which manifesty betrays its defect, nevertheless the single word *Feud* <note>original: "Feudi"</note> inserted there, and the rest of the character of its style, being inconsistent with that age, would clearly demonstrate it.

---

->XI.<-

The *constitution on tournaments* attributed to Henry the Fowler <note>original: "Henrici Aucupis"</note>, the first King of Germany from among the Saxons, dated to the year 938, is spurious. This is because the style is repugnant and does not suit the logic of the times, and also because it names circles <note>administrative districts</note> not yet known and illustrious dignities not yet established, such as Burgraviates, the Palatinate of Thuringia, and the Principality of Pomerania, to say nothing of other signs of forgery.

---

->XII.<-

The origin of the Electors is incorrectly ascribed to the age of Otto the Great, as is done by Christoph *Gewoldus*, a Bavarian Counselor and otherwise a very learned man. He undoubtedly followed Martin *Polonus*, whom they believe to have been nearly the first author of that opinion.

---

->XIII.<-

The tradition of Frederick Barbarossa <note>original: "Friderico Aenobarbo"</note> being trampled underfoot by Pope Alexander III <note>original: "Alexandro Magno Pontifice"</note> is deservedly to be exploded, just as that other matter which the common folk report regarding his death—that he was submerged in a river—is to be numbered among fables. For the contrary is clear from the *Diary of Thageno*, in which no such thing is produced. Only Otto *of Saint Blaise*, as far as I know, stands
</translation>

<translation page="10">
<note>Small leaf-like typographic ornaments flank the page number 6.</note>
for the common opinion. All others, whoever are more accurate, are either silent or disagree.

### XIV.

That Hatto, Archbishop of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinum"</note>, was devoured by mice is false; the argument concerning the tower visible today in the Rhine, which they mostly bring forward to confirm their opinion, is utterly inept and does not sustain the worthiness of proof at all.

### XV.

That the Emperor Henry VII of Luxembourg was removed by Francis Paulinus, a monk of the Order of Saint Bernard, by means of a host dipped in poison, is a common opinion. Yet it is not without merit that it is doubted, because Conrad *Vecerius*, who described his life most diligently, reported no such thing.

### XVI.

It cannot be proved by certain and undoubted monuments that the Emperor Charles IV alienated the Kingdom of Burgundy beyond the Jura, or Arles <note>the Kingdom of Arles</note>. Nor can the assertors of the contrary opinion bring forth or demonstrate a diploma of such alienation, although it is otherwise well known that he was a little too liberal not only toward the French, but also toward the Rhenish Princes.

### XVII.

<margin>
Germany, chapter 28, in the book on the Origin of the Bohemians.
</margin>
Those are absurd who think the Bohemians received their name from some King Bohemus. To this also belongs the error of those who write that they were a Gallic people, among whom are Cornelius *Tacitus* and Johannes Matthias *from the Sudetes* <note>original: "à Sudetis"</note>, to whom Melchior *Goldastus* otherwise owes very much. But there are just causes which urge us the less to agree with them
</translation>

<summary>This page critiques various historical myths and legal forgeries involving Holy Roman Emperors and European origins. The author refutes legends such as Hatto's Mouse Tower, the poisoning of Henry VII, and the Gallic origins of the Bohemians.</summary>
<keywords>Charles the Fat, Henry the Fowler, Frederick Barbarossa, Hatto of Mainz, Henry VII of Luxembourg, Charles IV, Bohemians, historical forgeries, Roman Expedition, tournaments, Electors</keywords>

This is because the style is repugnant and does not suit the logic of the times, and also because it names circles <note>administrative districts</note> not yet known and illustrious dignities not yet established, such as Burgraviates, the Palatinate of Thuringia, and the Principality of Pomerania, to say nothing of other signs of forgery.

---

->XII.<-

The origin of the Electors is incorrectly ascribed to the age of Otto the Great, as is done by Christoph *Gewoldus*, a Bavarian Counselor and otherwise a very learned man. He undoubtedly followed Martin *Polonus*, whom they believe to have been nearly the first author of that opinion.

---

->XIII.<-

The tradition of Frederick Barbarossa <note>original: "Friderico Aenobarbo"</note> being trampled underfoot by Pope Alexander III <note>original: "Alexandro Magno Pontifice"</note> is deservedly to be exploded, just as that other matter which the common folk report regarding his death—that he was submerged in a river—is to be numbered among fables. For the contrary is clear from the *Diary of Thageno*, in which no such thing is produced. Only Otto *of Saint Blaise*, as far as I know, stands

for the common opinion. All others, whoever are more accurate, are either silent or disagree.

### XIV.

That Hatto, Archbishop of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinum"</note>, was devoured by mice is false; the argument concerning the tower visible today in the Rhine, which they mostly bring forward to confirm their opinion, is utterly inept and does not sustain the worthiness of proof at all.

### XV.

That the Emperor Henry VII of Luxembourg was removed by Francis Paulinus, a monk of the Order of Saint Bernard, by means of a host dipped in poison, is a common opinion. Yet it is not without merit that it is doubted, because Conrad *Vecerius*, who described his life most diligently, reported no such thing.

### XVI.

It cannot be proved by certain and undoubted monuments that the Emperor Charles IV alienated the Kingdom of Burgundy beyond the Jura, or Arles <note>the Kingdom of Arles</note>. Nor can the assertors of the contrary opinion bring forth or demonstrate a diploma of such alienation, although it is otherwise well known that he was a little too liberal not only toward the French, but also toward the Rhenish Princes.

Therefore, Samson did not strictly kill himself, as he would have done if he had run himself through with a sword or dashed his head against a column; but he permitted himself to be crushed along with the enemy. and that he <note>Calvin</note> had openly undertaken <note>the contention</note> in the fourth place, and thus while Luther was alive, he was never suspected among the Saxons. <note>Public Acts, pages 3, 4, 5</note>. Hence, the most illustrious Prince, FREDERICK IV, in the same year [15]89, in order to thoroughly investigate the doctrine of Krentzheim, proposed in an assembly of Priests the Table of the Lutherans on the difference of the Dogmas of Luther and Calvin etc., printed at Wittenberg in the year of our Lord 1575. He aminedly exhorted him to return a simple and direct written response, expressed point by point. <note>Acts, pages 7, 82</note>. He did this, albeit unwillingly, acting rightly in the same manner as the theologians of Rostock, Oels, Frankfurt, and Saxony judged, using the phrases and words of our own people (i); and he delivered this confession of his to the MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE on nearly the last day of September. <note>Acts, pages 82, 24b, 25b, 65b, 98. Report, page 26</note>. FREDERICK IV then took care to refer it on the fifteenth day of the following April, in the year [15]90, to the Rostock theologians; in the month of January of the year [15]91 to the theologians of Oels; adding two speeches of Krentzheim delivered in the general Assembly by the mandate of FREDERICK IV in excuse of Calvinism. Finally, in the month of April, he saw to it being brought to the Academy of Frankfurt. All of these men, turning over this confession and the remaining writings most diligently from head to heel <note>from beginning to end</note>, condemned Leonhard Krentzheim for Calvinism in the Articles on the Holy Supper and the Person of Christ in the judgments and annotations sent back. <note>Acts, pages 24b, 28, 43, 65, 92, 98</note>.

> (i) He speaks indeed with us, and yet holds with the Calvinists; the voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau. <note>Acts, pages 19, 21</note>.

### X.

Nor did the theologians in the villages of Bärsdorf and Cuniz judge differently concerning Krentzheim; and in the sight of all, when the MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE, moved by their prayers, called the Pastors of the Duchy of Legnica <note>original: "Ducatus Lignicensis"</note> into public judgment with Krentzheim toward the end of this year [15]91, which was instituted on the fifteenth day of January, they were constant in this opinion in both voice and writings. <note>Acts, page 87</note>. Indeed, our subject <note>Krentzheim</note> responded with many words to the chapters brought against him and attempted to clear himself of the crime, but the Prince in no way approved the response. Instead, he sent the exhibited written testimony of his contrary will once again to the Academy at Frankfurt. Krentzheim, having been summoned to the Court on the twentieth day of June, took home the opinions and questions of this University, which had been sent back from Frankfurt on the third day of May of the same year, by the grant of the Judge, who was the Prince's Prefect; and at the seventh morning hour of the following day, he returned them, adorned with a written and plausibly colored response.

Truly, this plausible response was vehemently rejected by all, for the reason that both the explanations and the modes and formulas for explaining the Article on the Holy Supper—which *Martin Gosky*, formerly Pastor of St. Mary's Church, had excerpted from Krentzheim’s orations held in the assemblies of Pastors and had read publicly in the presence of all the Pastors—proved and showed him to be entirely suspect. For this reason, the Frankfurt theologians were consulted a third time by the Most Illustrious Prince through letters written on the eleventh day of July; but since Krentzheim, even in this writing, had responded with little integrity to the things that were asked, they could not rest easy. Instead, on the thirty-first day of June <note>likely July</note>, having transmitted their judgments to the Prince, they again judged him suspect of Calvinism. <note>Acts, pages 109, 110b</note>.

XI. Hardly had this judgment been sent back when there reached the ears of the Most Illustrious Prince not only the reformation instituted by the Administrator of the Electorate of Saxony, Frederick Wilhelm, but he was simultaneously informed that certain letters of Leonhard Krentzheim had been written to Master Urban Pierius—Pastor at Wittenberg and General Superintendent of the Electorate of Saxony, who was vehemently suspected of Calvinism (k)—and were found in his study and kept in the desk of Duke FREDERICK WILHELM. Incited by these things, the MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE resolved to refer this controversy to the Saxon theologians as well. To ensure Krentzheim was evidently convicted of his errors, the Most Illustrious Prince first twice requested his letters most kindly from the Administrator; having obtained them by a second letter, he read them greedily and at once discovered in them the most certain signs of perverse doctrine. <note>Acts, page 116</note>. Therefore, after FREDERICK IV saw that this discord could in no way be suppressed by tolerating and prolonging it, but would cause great detriment to the Church unless it were matured and put to rest, he called Master Martin Mirus and Master Georg Müller from Saxony to settle this controversy in letters composed on the 6th day of February in the year [15]93 to the Most Illustrious Duke of Saxony, Frederick Wilhelm. <note>Acts, pages 141, 142</note>. and that he <note>Calvin</note> had openly undertaken <note>the contention</note> in the fourth place, and thus while Luther was alive, he was never suspected among the Saxons. <note>Public Acts, pages 3, 4, 5</note>. Hence, the most illustrious Prince, FREDERICK IV, in the same year [15]89, in order to thoroughly investigate the doctrine of Krentzheim, proposed in an assembly of Priests the Table of the Lutherans on the difference of the Dogmas of Luther and Calvin etc., printed at Wittenberg in the year of our Lord 1575. # PARADOX VII.

## Although the <term>Lunula</term> <gloss>little moon or lune</gloss> (a part of the circle) was long ago reduced to a square space by Hippocrates of Chios, the <term>quadrature</term> <gloss>squaring</gloss> of the circle has nevertheless not yet been discovered to this very day.

### DECLARATION.

<term>Tetragonism</term> <gloss>the process of squaring</gloss>, or the Squaring of the circle, has hitherto been attempted chiefly in two ways: either Geometrically through lines, or Arithmetically through numbers. In the former way, the <term>Lunula</term> was long ago reduced to a square space by Hippocrates of Chios; however, the circle itself could in no way be squared, neither Geometrically nor Arithmetically, up to this very day.

### DEMONSTRATION.

No one, if they have rightly understood his demonstration, will deny that the quadrature of the <term>Lunula</term> was most correctly discovered by Hippocrates of Chios, for it is as follows: Let the Circle *a, b, c, d* be drawn, and upon its diameter *b, c* let the Square *b, e, f, c* be established, whose Diagonal
</translation>

<translation page="13">
is *b, d, f*. <note>See Figure VI.</note> Let the semidiameter *g, i, d* also be dropped, perpendicular to *b, e*, which will bisect both the semicircle *b, d, c* and the Diagonal *b, d, f* at point *d*. Then, with point *d* made the center and with the interval *d, b*, let another circle be described through points *b, e, f*, and let the straight line *d, c* be connected. Since, moreover, in the right-angled Triangle *b, e, f*, the side *b, f* subtends the right angle *b, e, f*, its square will be double the square of *b, e* or *e, f* according to the 47th proposition of the first book of Euclid. And consequently, Circle *b, e, f* will be double the circle *a, b, d, c* according to the 2nd proposition of the twelfth book of Euclid; and the semicircle *b, e, f* will be double the semicircle *b, a, c*, and the quadrant *b, g, d, c* will be equal to the same semicircle *b, a, c*. Therefore, when the common segment *b, g, c, i* is taken away, the lune *b, a, c, g* remains, equal to the Triangle *b, i, d*. If that Triangle is squared according to the last proposition of the second book of Euclid, the Lune *b, a, c, g* will be squared. But it is clearly evident from the most recent writings of Geometers that the circle has not been reduced to a square space, either by lines or by numbers, to this very day. Hippocrates indeed, by the same reasoning with which he had completed the quadrature of the Lune (a part of the Circle), persuaded himself that the whole circle could also be squared, and therefore attributed the discovery of the Tetragonism or Squaring of the Circle to himself. But in truth, as ingeniously as he had restored the Lune to a square space, he was so foully deceived in the squaring of the Circle, as is evident to anyone from Father Caspar Schott's <term>Technica Curiosa</term> <gloss>Curious Techniques</gloss>, Book VIII, section 1, my pages 600 and 601; and from Christopher Clavius's <term>Opera Mathematica</term> <gloss>Mathematical Works</gloss>, Volume II, Book VIII, page 189. Nay, it is credible, says Blancanus in <term>Aristotelis Loca Mathematica</term> <gloss>Mathematical Passages of Aristotle</gloss>, that Hippocrates recognized this fallacy (which he used in squaring the circle) and concealed it on account of the subtlety of the discovery. Not otherwise has it happened with the most recent attempts at the Squaring of the Circle, in which, when they are rightly examined, a false reasoning is usually detected, so that many today consider Tetragonism to be absolutely impossible; compare the <term>Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensium</term> <gloss>Reports of the Scholars of Leipzig</gloss> for the month of September in the year 1687, page 524. Therefore, although the Lune (a part of the Circle) was long ago reduced to a square space, the quadrature of the Circle has nevertheless not yet been found to this very day. Which Was to be Demonstrated.

### XXI.

Therefore, parents succeed to their children who die without children or surviving brothers and sisters equally; however, if brothers or sisters joined to the deceased on both sides <note>on both the paternal and maternal sides</note> are left, they succeed <term>in capita</term> <gloss>per person</gloss>; but with the children of these brothers or sisters, they succeed by the right of representation <term>in stirpes</term> <gloss>by lineage/branch</gloss>.

### XXII.

Parents of different lines from the paternal and maternal side, established in an equal degree but unequal in number, divide the inheritance of the deceased today not by a man's portion <note>per capita</note> but by consideration of the lineage, without distinction of the goods left by the deceased.

### XXIII.

It is a known point of law that brothers and the sons of brothers joined to the deceased from only one side are excluded by all ascendants.

### XXIV.

An adoptive father will not be able to be the heir of his adoptive son whom he does not have in his power, although a son of this kind may succeed him.

### XXV.

I would say otherwise concerning him into whose power the adopted person passes, to whom succession is granted just as to an <term>arrogator</term> <gloss>one who adopts a person who is legally independent</gloss> in the goods of a grown adopted son, as to a legitimate and natural father.

### XXVI.

Natural parents succeed to their children whom they have legitimized by a subsequent marriage, or by a prince’s rescript, or by offering to the <term>curia</term> <gloss>the local municipal council</gloss>, just as to natural and legitimate children.

### XXVII.

By the same reasoning as natural and illegitimate children succeed their parents, so these parents in turn succeed them; namely, the natural father and his ascendants succeed to two-twelfths of the natural son's estate, but the mother and ascendants from the maternal line succeed to the whole.

### XXIIX.

I believe there is no doubt that those born from incest and condemned coitus, if they cease to be among the living, have neither father, nor mother, nor any of the ascendants as a successor.

### XXIX.

These things concern the succession of those standing in the direct line: when these are lacking, collaterals in the oblique line succeed, whose succession extends as far as the tenth degree.

### XXXII.

Is a <term>consanguineous</term> <gloss>half-brother from the same father</gloss> also excluded from those joined on both sides in feudal law? The accepted opinion is that he is to be admitted to the fief of the deceased along with the brother joined on both sides.

### XXXIII.

Brothers succeed each other in a paternal fief, but not so in a new fief; rather, the fief reverts to the lord. However, sisters of both are incapable of succeeding.

### XXXIV.

If only the children of brothers joined on both sides remain, and no uncles survive, are they called to the succession of the deceased uncle <term>in capita</term> or <term>in stirpes</term>? It has been maintained in both the new and old law that they are called <term>in capita</term>, and this is true.

### XXXV.

If the deceased left no brothers or sisters joined from both sides, nor their children, but only <term>uterine</term> <gloss>half-siblings from the same mother</gloss> or paternal ones, then these are admitted to the brother's inheritance,

### XXXVI.

Not indeed so that paternal goods go to paternal relatives and maternal goods to maternal relatives, as in the old law; but between paternal and uterine relatives, if they exist together, the inheritance of the deceased shall be divided equally; if only one type exists, they shall obtain the whole inheritance.

### XXXVII.

Those adopted by ascendants from both the paternal and maternal lines succeed each other transversely, as do those <term>arrogated</term>, although these are by no means included under the name of <term>cognates</term> <gloss>blood relatives</gloss>.

### XXXIIX.

Collaterals reaching each other by a natural bond through the father enjoy no right of succession; however, it is a settled point of law that those joined through the maternal line succeed each other, even if one is natural and the other legitimate.

### XXXIX.

Illegitimate children <term>spurij</term> born of one and the same father, but from different mothers, are prohibited from succeeding each other; which no one will affirm concerning <term>ὁμογαστρίοις</term> <gloss>born of the same womb</gloss> illegitimate children.

### XL.

Among incestuous brothers, and likewise those adopted by a stranger, there is no succession.

### XLI.

After brothers and the children of brothers, those who are closer in degree are called <term>in capita</term>, so that equals in degree are admitted equally without difference of sex.

From the distance, cries of anguish from women and children were heard from time to time, whenever unscrupulous marauders had forced access to their hiding places and plundered them or took them captive.

The Pâlem do not differ significantly in their physical appearance from the Somraï and Gâberi; they are strong, proportionately built, and often tall figures with a more or less black skin color, which generally shows no nuances leaning toward reddish or yellowish, and they also seem for the most part to understand the Bagirmi language.

The sky had become heavily overcast with clouds, and thunder rolled on all sides as we set up our night camp at the feet of some <term>Delêb</term> palms <note>Borassus aethiopum, or African fan palm</note> without any other tree cover. I spent half the night with the surgical treatment of the wounded. I sewed the flesh wounds together with horsehair and bandaged the more serious injuries as well as I could. Yet many had penetrating chest and abdominal wounds or opened shoulder and hip joints, and several gave up the ghost during the night.

The next morning (June 1st), we set out an hour before sunrise and crossed, likewise in an approximate easterly direction, a lowland with lush grass growth which was described to me as a <term>Komodûgu</term> <gloss>river or watercourse in the Kanuri language</gloss>; it showed swampy ground at the deepest points and small puddles here and there, and according to the people, it is said to stretch north toward Mul and northwest toward the Ba Ili. We had passed a similar, grass-rich, treeless valley, which was abundant with water in the summer and seemed to extend from southeast to northwest, toward evening the day before. Both, as well as the valley-like lowland near Murki and another located south-southwest of Gundi which we saw later, seem to be parts of the swamp network from which the Ba Ili eventually develops. An hour after sunrise we turned south, passed numerous scattered and barricaded homesteads which already belonged to Gundi, moved beyond the center of this main settlement of the Tummok tribe, and camped at 8 o'clock in the morning. Immediately everyone went into the

# BOOK VI, CHAPTER 6. SLAVE HUNTS.

surrounding area to look for roofs and coverings from huts, poles and fences, wooden mortars, and other household utensils—in short, all the necessary requirements for a dwelling. The insolent slaves of the King and his highest dignitaries also returned richly laden, but my people had only captured a piece of straw fence, which was at most sufficient for the wall of a hut, and for the time being we had to make do with a dwelling made of leafy branches. While the morning had been overcast with a weak southeast wind, the sky cleared up around midday, so that I gave myself over to the hope of a rain-free night. But the rains had become so frequent over time, and I could so little afford damage to my meager belongings, that I did not lie down to sleep without concern when neither Almâs nor Hammu had succeeded in finding a hut roof in the vicinity during the afternoon.

An evil night followed, the beginning of which has remained in my memory as particularly repulsive. Without suspecting it, we had erected my provisional hut on a termite mound that had not yet risen above the level of the surrounding area, and at night the hated little creatures paid me a most unwelcome visit. I had barely spent half an hour in a restless sleep on my bed—which was always laid out directly on the ground, and I had been suffering from severe rheumatic pains since Somraï—when I awoke and felt a strange sensation on the skin of my entire body. At first I tried to ignore it and fall back asleep, but since my pains promised me no peace anyway, I decided to get up and light a light. The latter was no easy procedure, for although I had fashioned a lamp out of a small bowl of butter by means of a scrap of <term>Châm</term> <gloss>unbleached cotton cloth</gloss> rolled into a wick, our cooking fire had gone out, and I had to ignite dry rags using the priming powder of one of our flintlock muskets. At last I had light, and now by the dim glow of the primitive lamp, I saw my bed flooded by thousands upon thousands of white termites, a great many of which I had already crushed. My shirt and the surface of the bedroll were covered with the insects squashed into a pulp, and ever new swarms of them...

<summary>Upon arriving in Gundi, the expedition plunders local huts for building materials. Nachtigal describes a miserable night spent suffering from rheumatism and a termite infestation in his makeshift shelter.</summary>
<keywords>shelter construction, termites, illness, flintlock musket, camp life, Gundi</keywords>
</translation>

Regarding these grudges, it is like this: the grudges of women are the lowest of all. If one person has entered inside and another also enters, they will undoubtedly kill one another without hesitation. As for the statement that one must carry five hundred <term>karshapana</term> <gloss>a type of silver or copper coin</gloss> to enter, that is also true, for it is certainly needed for her clothes and ornaments. As for the statement that the house should be cleaned after seven days have passed, that is also true; whether it is done earlier or later, what conflict could there be? As for the statement that those who enter and exit for the sake of men shall not be examined, that is also true; since she is not a common prostitute, if one were to examine those who enter and exit for the sake of men, who would ever enter her house? Then the assembly granted her those five supreme conditions, and she was enjoyed by the assembly. When the Licchavis of Vaishali began to enter her house to take their pleasure as they desired, some of them, because they were so overwhelmed by sensual desire, became free from passion the very moment they saw her. Others became so through mere touch. Thus, none of them performed the manly act. She thought, "These are not real men; I must devise a method." Having thought this, she stayed in various places <note>the text breaks here as she prepares to observe different men</note>

<leaf-break/>

"The one called Amrapali <note>literally: Protector of Mangoes</note> is perfectly endowed with beauty and youth, knows the sixty-four arts, and is worthy of being enjoyed only by a god." He <note>King Bimbisara</note> said, "Sakyong, if that is so, let us go to Vaishali. I shall take pleasure and delight with her." Sakyong replied, "The Licchavis of Vaishali have been enemies who have sought to harm us for a long time; they will surely come to harm you." The King said, "Wise ones, men possess the courageous heart of a hero, so let us go." Sakyong said, "Your Majesty, if you place such great importance on a matter of no purpose, then go." Entering a chariot, he set out for Vaishali together with Sakyong. Having gradually reached Vaishali, Sakyong stayed in a grove. As the King entered Amrapali's house, the sound of a bell arose. The Licchavis of Vaishali became agitated and a clear cry went out, "Wise ones, an enemy of ours has entered, sound the bell!" A great noise arose, and King Bimbisara <note>original: Gzuk-can Snying-po</note> asked Amrapali, "Good lady, what is this?" "The Lord's house is being searched." "For what reason?" "For the sake of the Lord <note>referring to the King</note>." "What should be done? Shall I flee?" "Lord, do not be displeased. When seven days have passed, they will search the house, so for these seven days, please enjoy yourself happily. Do as you please, and when seven days are up, I shall know the time."
</translation>

<translation page="89">
He played with her, delighted with her, and took his pleasure as he desired. Eventually, Amrapali became possessed of a sentient being <note>she became pregnant</note>, and she said to King Bimbisara, "Lord, a sentient being has entered me." He gave her a piece of fine cotton cloth and a signet ring, saying, "If it is a girl, she is yours. If it is a boy, wrap him in this cotton cloth, hang this signet ring around his neck, and bring him to my presence." He then departed, entered his chariot, and set out with Sakyong as the bells were ringing. The Licchavis said, "Wise ones, the enemy has appeared, let us pursue him!" Five hundred Licchavis, experts with the bow, pursued King Bimbisara. Sakyong saw them and said, "Lord, the Licchavis of Vaishali are coming. Shall I fight with them, or shall I drive the chariot?" The King replied, "I am weary, so I will drive the chariot; you alone must fight with them." As he began to fight with them, the people of Vaishali recognized him...

<leaf-break/>

"Wise ones, whoever the father of this one is, he is our enemy!" they said, and they struck him even more. Later, when he told his mother everything that had happened, she thought, "The Licchavis of Vaishali are extremely cruel and powerful; there is a danger that he might be killed." While she was thinking such things, she saw many merchants carrying goods and heading for Rajgir <note>original: Rgyal-po'i Khab</note>. She said to them, "Stamp your containers with this signet ring and go; you will not have to pay customs duties. Also, take this boy to the royal palace, hang this signet ring around his neck, and leave him at the gate of Rajgir." They agreed to do so. She also gave the boy a pearl necklace and said, "Son, when people gather for the King's business, place this pearl necklace on his feet, and then sit in his lap as if afraid. If anyone says, 'This boy does not know how to be afraid,' then say, 'Does a son have any fear of his father?'" He gradually reached Rajgir with the merchants. They bathed him, attached the signet ring, and left him at the gate of the royal palace. He then went to where the King was...
</translation>

<summary>
These pages narrate King Bimbisara's secret visit to the courtesan Amrapali in Vaishali, their brief union, and the subsequent birth and journey of their son to the palace in Rajgir.
</summary>

<keywords>
Bimbisara, Amrapali, Vaishali, Licchavis, Rajgir, signet ring, pregnancy, merchants, customs duties
</keywords>

<translation page="386">
abide in the words one thousand and eight times, or even one hundred and eight times. Having performed the recitation, and having stayed in a state of fasting day and night, offer the rosary to the <term>Muni</term> <gloss>Sage/Buddha</gloss> on the seventh day. Perform the recitation as before. Match that measurement exactly. Then, recite over the rosary. Stay right there that night. On a ground spread with <term>kusha</term> grass, the mantra-knower should sleep. Whatever dreams are seen—if virtuous dreams are seen, the dreams are certainly a sign. One should achieve accomplishments <term>siddhi</term> by that. If Buddhas, <term>Sravakas</term> <gloss>Disciples</gloss>, or <term>Pratyekabuddhas</term> <gloss>Solitary Realizers</gloss> are seen in the dream, the practitioner of mantra will achieve results. One must certainly perform that ritual. If one sees the form of a monk or various beautiful images of Brahmins—if those dreams are seen, the rosary should be offered in that same way. The practitioner of all the purposes of mantra will certainly achieve them without doubt.

From the Great Extensive Mahayana Sutra of the Pitaka of the Bodhisattvas, from the Fundamental Ritual of the Bhagavati Arya Tara with Upward-Bound Hair <note>original: "rGyal pa gyen brdzes"</note>, the tenth chapter on the extensive ritual of the painted cloth banner <note>original: "ras ris"</note>, the chapter on the ritual of the counting rosary, is complete.

Then again, the Blessed One Shakyamuni, having looked once more at the great mandala of the assembly possessed of all things, spoke to the Great Bodhisattva Arya Avalokiteshvara: "Great Being, there are special rituals to complete the chapters of your knowledge-mantras, and there are knowledge-accomplishments for the application of fire-offering <term>homa</term> rites..."

<column-break/>

...abandoning living beings <note>ensuring the ground is free of insects</note>, and having properly prepared the area with sand. Then, the rim should be like a lotus, in the form of a circular mandala on all sides. Or, with effort, make it four-sided with three tiers. The peaceful and the increasing types are also correctly proclaimed here. For the wrathful <term>abhichara</term> rites, in the center of the ground, make a <term>vajra</term> <gloss>ritual thunderbolt</gloss> with two or three points. The fire pit <term>kunda</term> should be two cubits <term>hasta</term> in width. Prepare it in a clean direction. Likewise, perform it on the banks of a river. In the directions of a single teaching, in cemeteries, or in empty houses, the fire-offering <term>homa</term> should be well-prepared. Likewise, at the peaks of mountains, and always in empty temples, and likewise in great wildernesses—whatever the places of accomplishment are, they were spoken of by the Supreme Person <note>the Buddha</note>. For all fire-offering actions, those are spoken of as the locations. Sitting upon a bundle of <term>kusha</term> grass measuring one cubit, there the mantra-knower should especially perform the fire-offering rites. By staying in that very place, there is no doubt of swift accomplishment. By facing East or North, perform the peaceful and increasing rites. The wrathful rites are in the South; the mantra practitioner should avoid those <note>for general practice</note>. Facing East brings the accomplishment of peace, and facing North brings the increasing rite. By those means, the mantra-knower should always begin the recitation of the knowledge-mantra. Use <term>bilva</term>, <term>arka</term>, <term>aslatta</term>, and <term>nyagrodha</term> wood for the increasing rites. For wrathful rites, use dry wood, and those that are spicy, sour, or sharp. All of those should be avoided; the Sages always forbade them.
</translation>

<translation page="387">
For peaceful and increasing rites, moist wood is most auspicious. Likewise, for wrathful rites, dry wood, spicy, sour, and sharp types are used. If those specific types of fuel wood <term>samidhs</term> are not available, one should always examine the wood available. Examine them for two tips <note>split ends</note>. Use <term>kusha</term> grass that is green, oily, and resembles the neck of a peacock. Always spread such <term>kusha</term> grass in a circle. For peaceful and increasing rites, it should be like emerald. Likewise, the Supreme Victors have forbidden the performance of sinful <note>wrathful</note> actions with dry grass here. With stainless, pure water, always free of insects, perform the sprinkling purification <term>prokshana</term> on all sides. Having circumambulated to the right <term>pradakshina</term>, ignite the fire with diligence. Perform the ritual touching of water <term>achamana</term> according to the rite. Having made a lamp of proper measure from the roots of pure grass, and then having formed a fist <note>a specific mudra</note>, ignite the fire with effort. It should not be done with the wind of the mouth, nor ever with the hem of one's clothing. One must avoid using the lower robe or upper robe. It is not pleasing to extinguish the fire with the wind of the hand using other clothes. Use a pure fan or a cloth; one may also fan with a jewel. By this correctly arising wind, when the fire is made even, the mantra-knower should ignite the fire. Being in meditative absorption for the sake of the fire-offering, then with the hand that is not the right <note>the left</note>, perform the sprinkling purification. Then, with cow's butter <term>ghi</term>, give three poured offerings <term>ahuti</term>. Then, offer prostrations to all the Buddhas and...

<column-break/>

...prepared. For the peaceful rite, the color is white; this is always praised by the Supreme Victors. If one performs the fire-offering with a white fire, the mantras will be accomplished. Likewise, one who desires the accomplishments of the increasing rite always uses the color white. Black and the color of smoke, as well as pale grey, are for sinful <note>wrathful</note> actions. By changing these three colors, these are the three types of accomplishment. Other colors like the color of clouds, if seen on that ground of the teaching, the mantra practitioner will have no accomplishment. If such colors or various different colors are seen when the fire burns, one must begin the rites again. Recitations should be performed once more. If the mantra is accomplished, then by seeing the ritual of the action, one enters the fire-offering again. For the dismissal and the invitation, the fire mantra should be... recited. Having examined it well before, request this mandala to depart. The actions of invitation are also to be done right there. The behavior of the fire and its form should be performed in front of the painted cloth banner <term>ras ris</term>. The previous Tathagatas have said that the mantras will be accomplished there. All actions praised by the Victors should be done in that very place. Other actions are to be performed, but especially those sinful actions which are despised by the Supreme Victors and which contradict or are reviled by the world. The stages of the rising, the wheel-turning <term>chakravartin</term>, and the Bodhisattva grounds...
</translation>

<summary>This text details the ritual requirements for mantra recitation and fire-offerings (homa), focusing on dream omens, site selection, and the specific materials like wood and grass types required for different ritual aims. It emphasizes the importance of purity and the correct physical execution of igniting the ritual fire according to Buddhist tantric traditions.</summary>
<keywords>fire offering, homa, siddhi, mantra, kunda, kusha grass, samidh, ritual purity, Tara, Avalokiteshvara, dreams, iconography</keywords>

<translation page="214">
A bodhisattva does not focus intently on their own mind, nor do they focus intently on the minds of others. Why is that? In that way, the stream of the bodhisattva's mind is known through primordial wisdom <term>jnana</term>. The stream of the mind is known through mindfulness. It is known through intelligence. The stream of the mind is known through realization. The stream of the mind is known through discriminating awareness <term>prajna</term>. The stream of the mind is known through the intellect. The stream of the mind is without afflictions; the connection to habitual tendencies <term>vasana</term> is completely severed; it is pure, stainless, luminous, blameless, not harsh, and undisturbed; it knows all phenomena as appearances. It knows how to engage in accordance with the mental activity of all sentient beings. Shariputra, this entry of the mind into the knowledge of such phenomena is called the bodhisattva's higher cognition of the minds of others and the perfection of the activity of primordial wisdom. Shariputra, what is the bodhisattva's higher cognition of recollecting past lives, and what fulfills the activity of the primordial wisdom of higher cognition? Shariputra, in this regard, a bodhisattva [recollects] the births of all sentient beings in all the infinite world systems of the ten directions—one birth, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty...

<leaf-break/>

They also recollect their own roots of virtue arising from previous causes. They also recollect the causes of the roots of virtue of others. They dedicate their own roots of virtue toward enlightenment. Having recollected the roots of virtue of other sentient beings, they cause them to generate the mind of enlightenment <term>bodhicitta</term>. Whatever causes of previous pleasure and pain existed, they rely on them as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and without a self. Because they rely on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, they are not arrogant about their form. They are not arrogant about wealth. They are not arrogant about attendants. They are not arrogant about power. They do not desire and are not arrogant about being a universal monarch <term>chakravartin</term>. They do not desire and are not arrogant about the state of Shakra <note>Indra</note>. They do not desire and are not arrogant about the state of Brahma. They do not desire and are not arrogant about being a world protector. They do not desire and are not arrogant about any kind of birth. They do not possess a mind that desires any pleasures, kingly realms, or the happiness of power, except for intentionally assuming existence in order to bring sentient beings to maturity. Because they rely on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, [their] previous...
</translation>

<translation page="215">
...they are ashamed of, embarrassed by, and critical of the behavior of the afflictions. Even for the sake of their life, they do not perform actions that would become non-virtuous roots through present things. They also dedicate and expand their previous roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment. In order to gather all present roots of virtue, they completely abandon incompatible dedications. To ensure that the lineage of the Buddha, the lineage of the Dharma, and the lineage of the Sangha are never interrupted, they dedicate everything toward omniscience through the power of perfectly generated mindfulness. That mindfulness of theirs is also highly blessed by the blessing of the expanse of phenomena <term>dharmadhatu</term>. It is very stable through reasoning. It is not distracted because they have purified meditative concentration <term>dhyana</term>. It is without harm because it is highly blessed by calm abiding <term>shamatha</term>. It is without error because it is perfectly held by special insight <term>vipashyana</term>. Because it is direct perception, it is not ordinary. Because mindfulness is unimpaired, it is without forgetfulness...

<leaf-break/>

...because they have perfectly meditated on these four bases of miraculous power <term>riddhipada</term>—which are the phenomena that have been attained: desire, effort, intention, and investigation—they manifest miraculous powers. They experience many varieties of the display of miraculous power. Those displays of miraculous power are also mastered for the sake of looking after sentient beings. Through whichever form, strength, blessing, or display of miraculous power sentient beings are to be tamed, they demonstrate that very display of miraculous power. Through whichever appearance of form and color sentient beings are to be tamed, they demonstrate that very appearance of form and color. Whether it is the appearance of the form and color of a Buddha, the appearance of the form and color of a solitary realizer <term>pratyekabuddha</term>, the appearance of the form and color of a hearer <term>shravaka</term>, the appearance of the form and color of Shakra, the appearance of the form and color of Brahma, or the world...
</translation>

<summary>
These pages describe the advanced meditative states and higher cognitions of a bodhisattva, specifically the ability to know others' minds and recollect past lives without personal arrogance. The text details how a bodhisattva utilizes miraculous powers and various forms to skillfully guide and tame sentient beings.
</summary>

<keywords>
bodhisattva, higher cognition, past lives, miraculous powers, siddhis, dedication of merit, mindfulness, dharmadhatu, four bases of miraculous power, skillful means
</keywords>

The stream of the mind is without afflictions; the connection to habitual tendencies <term>vasana</term> is completely severed; it is pure, stainless, luminous, blameless, not harsh, and undisturbed; it knows all phenomena as appearances. Shariputra, what is the bodhisattva's higher cognition of recollecting past lives, and what fulfills the activity of the primordial wisdom of higher cognition? Shariputra, in this regard, a bodhisattva [recollects] the births of all sentient beings in all the infinite world systems of the ten directions—one birth, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty...

They dedicate their own roots of virtue toward enlightenment. Having recollected the roots of virtue of other sentient beings, they cause them to generate the mind of enlightenment <term>bodhicitta</term>. Whatever causes of previous pleasure and pain existed, they rely on them as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and without a self. Because they rely on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, they are not arrogant about their form. They are not arrogant about wealth. They are not arrogant about attendants. They are not arrogant about power. They do not desire and are not arrogant about being a universal monarch <term>chakravartin</term>. They do not desire and are not arrogant about the state of Shakra <note>Indra</note>. They do not desire and are not arrogant about the state of Brahma. They do not desire and are not arrogant about being a world protector. They do not desire and are not arrogant about any kind of birth. They do not possess a mind that desires any pleasures, kingly realms, or the happiness of power, except for intentionally assuming existence in order to bring sentient beings to maturity. <translation page="352">
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
transformed into <note>referring to a ritual transformation or visualization</note>. Medicines are to be eaten, and water is to be constantly drunk. One will not be overcome by old age or death, and will be protected forever. Make a crown from the hair of a thief, and to that, the syllable <term>HUM</term> should be joined. The practitioners of yoga take up the skull-cups of the five Buddhas. By making a skull-cup the size of five fingers, one wears it as a crown. From the nature of Method and Wisdom, a hair-belt should be wound twice. Carry ashes for the sake of the hair-offering; this is maintained by the conduct of a yogi. The sound of the <term>damaru</term> <gloss>hand-drum</gloss> is the recitation. To know the meditation on the <term>khatvanga</term> <gloss>ritual staff</gloss> is Wisdom itself. Through the conduct of the <term>vajra</term> and the skull-cup, these are the recitation and the meditation. Utterly abandon greed, delusion, fear, anger, and the fruit of shame. Having abandoned these dualities through one's own self, one should perform the conduct without doubt. Having given the gift of the body, then afterwards, perform the conduct perfectly. Because of the investigation of what is a worthy recipient and what is not, one should not give the gift <note>implying a state of non-conceptual equality where such distinctions are dropped</note>. Food and drink should be eaten just as they are found. Because of the conceptualization of what is pleasant and unpleasant, one should not have even a grain of attachment. The practitioner should not form concepts about what is food and what is not, likewise about what is drink and what is not, or about where to go and where not to go. Any student who has found accomplishment and perfect wisdom...

<leaf-break/>

To someone who shows their clothes, show the trident. To someone who shows their breast, show the junction <note>possibly the solar plexus or a specific energy center</note>. To someone who shows their teeth, show the mouth. To someone who shows a frown, tell them to loosen their topknot. To someone who shows their forehead, show the back of the head. To someone who shows the sole of the foot, one should play with the <term>ldo</term> <gloss>possibly a specific ritual gesture or object</gloss>. By the signs and the responses to the signs, one distinguishes by the <term>samaya</term> <gloss>sacred bond/vow</gloss>. To that, the <term>yogini</term> said: Oh, the son of great compassion! If a rosary is shown in the hand, it is the speech saying "Let us gather." If the rosary is handed over, it is a good ascetic practice dwelling in the <term>samaya</term>. That which is called the external gathering, staying in the domain of the excellent, in that gathering, whatever the <term>yogini</term> says, all that should be done. O Blessed One, where are the places of gathering? The Blessed One replied: The <term>pitha</term> <gloss>place</gloss> and the <term>upapitha</term> <gloss>near-place</gloss>, the <term>kshetra</term> <gloss>field</gloss> and the <term>upakshetra</term> <gloss>near-field</gloss>, the <term>chandoha</term> <gloss>gathering place</gloss> and the <term>upachandoha</term> <gloss>near-gathering place</gloss>, likewise the <term>melapaka</term> <gloss>meeting place</gloss> and the <term>upamelapaka</term> <gloss>near-meeting place</gloss>, the <term>pilava</term> <gloss>drinking place</gloss> and the <term>upapilava</term> <gloss>near-drinking place</gloss>, the <term>shmashana</term> <gloss>charnel ground</gloss> and the <term>upashmashana</term> <gloss>near-charnel ground</gloss>. These are the twelve stages, the Lord who is the master of the ten stages. This should not be spoken of by others. O Blessed One, what are the places?
</translation>

<translation page="353">
The Blessed One replied: The <term>pitha</term> is explained as Jalandhara. Likewise is Oddiyana. The <term>pitha</term> is also Kollagiri. Likewise is Kamarupa. The <term>upapitha</term> is called Malava and Sindhunagara. The <term>kshetra</term> is explained as Mummu, which is the number of the creator <note>possibly a numerical code for the location</note>. Devikota is likewise a <term>kshetra</term>, the number of the iron-worker. The <term>upakshetra</term> is called Kuluta, and likewise Arbuda, and Godavari the bestower of wind. These are the summarized <term>upakshetra</term>. The <term>chandoha</term> are Harikela, those born within the salt ocean, Lampaka, Kanchi, and likewise Saurashtra. The <term>upachandoha</term> is Kalinga, the island endowed with gold, and Konkana is also an <term>upachandoha</term>; these are spoken of in summary. The <term>pilava</term> is in the city, and also the <term>upapilava</term> dwells at the edge of the village, Caritra and Kosala, and the city of young Vindhya. O <term>Vajragarbha</term> of great compassion, the <term>upapilava</term> is near those. The <term>shmashana</term> is the attained assembly, and the <term>upashmashana</term> is the shore of the ocean. The shore of the pond in the garden is said to be the <term>upashmashana</term>. For the sake of the benefit of all sentient beings, the <term>Vajra</term> of the <term>Yogini Tantra</term>, the excellent gathering of the <term>yoginis</term>, even during the day...

<leaf-break/>

All sentient beings will come under that power. This is the seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Certainty of Signs and Places. Then, the mandala of the <term>yoginis</term> will be explained. Meditate on the <term>bhaga</term> <gloss>source of phenomena/womb</gloss> in the realm of space. As for the meditation in the center, first is the mandala as appropriate, just as the deities arise. The mandala of earth and water comes first, then as appropriate the fire, and with the deities, the great wind. Just as the meditator arises, the mandala itself is born from the source of phenomena <term>dharmodaya</term>. The two leaps are without fault, becoming one from the filaments, and the triangle is spoken of as the outer. In the center of that, meditate on the essence of the fifteen seats of the dead. Above that is the moon. Above the moon is the seed-syllable itself. Afterwards, it is pressed down by the conqueror of demons. From the union of the two comes great bliss. The <term>ali</term> <gloss>vowels</gloss> dwell in the form of the moon. The <term>kali</term> <gloss>consonants</gloss> appear in the form of the sun. From the union of the moon and sun, the lady Gauri and the others are well known. The moon is the mirror-like wisdom. The seventh of the seven is the wisdom of equality. The seed-syllable and hand-symbol of one's own deity should be spoken of as the wisdom of discernment. All becoming one is the wisdom of all-accomplishing effort. The perfect purity of the realm of phenomena is told by the wise through the five aspects <note>referring to the five Buddha wisdoms</note>.
</translation>

<summary>These pages detail the specialized conduct, secret sign languages (choma), and sacred geography (pithas) of the Yogini Tantra tradition, concluding with the beginning of a chapter on mandala visualization.</summary>
<keywords>yogini, tantra, pithas, sacred geography, choma, mudra, mandala, five wisdoms, samaya, vajra</keywords>
