They prepare everything: the house bustles everywhere with the unaccustomed work.
Then Father Abraham <note>original: "Abramus"</note>, now that all things have been duly prepared,
Wraps raw sandals <note>leather bindings</note> around the tender soles of his feet,
And takes up the fate-bringing sword with its gleaming hilt.
This blade, once (as they say) with a skillful mind, the son
Born of Lamech and Zilla <note>original: "Lamecho & Sella genitus"</note>, by the first discovery of the smith’s art,
Had beautifully forged from solid iron: and he
Had handed it to Father Noah <note>original: "Noe"</note>: Then Noah himself,
When God <note>original: "DEVS"</note> overwhelmed the vast world and all its peoples
With the flood-waters, had preserved it in the safe ark.
From there, all his descendants joyfully received it:
And Terah <note>original: "Thares"</note> himself thus left it to his son Abraham.
When these things were done: he commends the faithful reins <note>of the household</note> to Sarah <note>original: "Sarae"</note>:
And bids her protect the rest of the house: she nods
To his command: and seeks her son: she delays him with her voice
As he is just now attempting to follow his dear father.
Now she commands him to cover his golden hair, now his chest:
Now to care for the Gods above: and before all things to bring God
Before his frequent gaze. For those who are upright, she says, their rewards remain:
These the Ruler of high Olympus <note>a classical epithet for God</note> loves: these he cares for.
So she speaks, and pours out tears between every word.
But the son: Now dear mother, farewell, farewell best of mothers:
Behold he calls, behold my father calls: farewell to you, our home.
When he had spoken thus: he turns his tracks alongside him,
Leaving his weeping mother, who often wished
(Whether love persuaded her: or perhaps a foreboding of a troubled
Mind) to wrap her arms around his snow-white neck.
</translation>

<translation page="13">
She, however, followed him as he departed with such a voice:
Go, go, our glory: may you enjoy the favor of the blessed divinities:
And with them accompanying you, may you leave home, and with them may you return.
   So therefore, now that the dear city of their homeland was left behind,
Both the Son and the Father enter the greening fields.
The servants follow behind them, leading the bowed
Beast of burden: and they tire him out much with staff and knotty club.
Next they enter joyful valleys: and are covered by various
Trees: and they pursue their way beneath the high foliage.
The West Winds <note>original: "Zephyri"</note> accompany them from behind as they go:
And charming birds rise up and greet them with their song.
   Meanwhile Father Abraham, through the pleasant greenery,
Relates many things concerning the first religion and faith.
In the beginning he recounts the origins of the spacious world:
How God created the spheres of heaven out of nothing,
And once separated the Earth from the wandering waves:
And bound all things so beautifully in concordant peace.
Then he sings of the crime of Satan <note>original: "Sathanae"</note>, and the transgressions of the first parent <note>Adam</note>,
And of the Seed to come, as the years roll by,
Which shall take vengeance on Satan: and shall overturn the lowest hell <note>original: "auernum"</note>.
And how He shall crush the head and coil the breast of the Serpent,
Flowing with much gore, through the dark caverns.
Then, how He submerged the whole world in the sea
Because of the sins of men, and the foul heats of lust.
Or in what manner, and with what voice, God revealed
Himself to the fathers and ancestors, or with what face he spoke to them:
And he unfolds the remaining deeds of the ancients in a long sequence.
</translation>

<summary>Abraham prepares for the journey to sacrifice Isaac, taking a legendary sword forged before the Flood. As they travel, Abraham instructs Isaac in the history of creation, the fall of man, and the prophecy of the serpent-crushing Savior.</summary>
<keywords>Abraham, Isaac, Sarah, Noah's sword, creation, Satan, prophecy, salvation history, Lamech</keywords>

*These Universals, most learnedly proposed along with their side-issues <note>original: parergis</note> drawn from the whole of Philosophy, and illuminated by the splendors of the most serene House of Bavaria, shall most rightly be published by the press for the common utility of studious youth and the most useful exercise of the religious lord defending them.*

-> Professor of Sacred Theology, Licentiate of Both Laws, <-

# TO THE REVEREND, RELIGIOUS, AND MOST LEARNED LORD, DEFENDER OF UNIVERSAL PHILOSOPHY IN UNIVERSALS.

*Let others build up for themselves beautiful Wisdoms,*
*Like shining Rachels <note>referring to the biblical Rachel, representing the contemplative life</note> adorning themselves,*
*Let them build up their brows, fashion them with a needle,*
*Polish their cheeks with learned trifles,*
*And paint their brides with sterile labor.*
*At these things my Wise Man laughs; he seizes*
*The sister, the eloquent mother Leah <note>referring to the biblical Leah, representing the active life and fecundity</note>.*
*Rachel displeases: "Leah," he says,*
*"gives a universal dowry, she gives birth to all things."*
*I have seen forms swell under a Daedalean chisel,*
*Born to incite envy.*
*I have seen bulls commanded to be silent*
*By a Sarmatian wound: the menacing piers*
*Of harbors, built in the wave-flowing Triple-City:*
*Causes supported by the favor of demigods:*
*Gods playing in a physical bath:*
*Small particles of a more blessed urn:*
*The worlds of Alexander the Great <note>original: Pellaeos mundos</note> while Asia stood amazed.*
*I saw the clouds bring forth great things;*
*The Pious heirs of the celestial spheres.*

<column-break/>

*The Lion of Stagira <note>Aristotle</note> will roar in a Pygmy fashion.*
*The Lyceums will learn the price of shadows.*
*"I want the bleary-eyed sister," says Our Man.*
*And yet Leah is not bleary-eyed; though she may be*
*Believed to be so by one who is bleary-eyed, she is not.*
*How so, she who brings forth the Species? Fair*
*To us is Leah, and a noble Nymph:*
*Both the mother of the Genus, and of lineages:*
*The goddess of beautiful Differences.*
*Now let Rachel boast the light favors of the Graces,*
*And glass dolls, and Accidents,*
*The roses of the cheeks on a parchment brow,*
*The brief riches of youth.*
*Not so, not so does Leah offer from her own.*
*She does not need borrowed vapors;*
*She has learned to shine with native elegance;*
*Taught to blush with no other rouge,*
*Than that which is Proper <note>a play on the logical "Property"</note> to the One, which she is, and has.*
*Rachel displeases. Wealthy Leah promises*
*Universals; you, sir, deliver the Universals.*

***

-> Out of the debt of Religious honor and love. <-

-> He applauded: <-

FATHER GREGORY MAGIUS, Professed Canon
Regular of the Order of St. Augustine in Gars,
Student of Sacred Theology and the Canons.
</translation>

### To the Very Excellent and Most Distinguished
## LORD RESPONDENT, a friend to be honored among few.

<note>A large decorative initial S begins the first poem.</note>

Thus at last, providing fame forbids committing the monuments
of tireless labor and the gifts of an excellent mind to the earth;
nor does it threaten small names,
Alas! for your endeavors, beloved one, when the select cohort
of both the young and the old beholds you
ascending the pulpits of your own accord, and weighs in silent mind
 the prizes <note>term: "brabea"</note> with which it wishes to see you
adorned at the same time, as one who is entirely yours.

->M. Samuel Schultetus, of Hamburg.<-

---

Is it thus, Friend, that everyone discovers the omen of your noble name,
while you present the easy pledges of your
genius? Just as the Phrygian lion, led by fierce
savagery, does not harm the wretched race of beasts,
to whom wise nature granted weak strengths
of body, but rather pursues the rabid with fierce
ardor, by which he may test the deeds that prove his fame.

In all your sojourning:

## LORD RESPONDENT, a friend to be honored among few.

<note>A large decorative initial S begins the first poem.</note>

Thus at last, providing fame forbids committing the monuments
of tireless labor and the gifts of an excellent mind to the earth;
nor does it threaten small names,
Alas! for your endeavors, beloved one, when the select cohort
of both the young and the old beholds you
ascending the pulpits of your own accord, and weighs in silent mind
 the prizes <note>term: "brabea"</note> with which it wishes to see you
adorned at the same time, as one who is entirely yours.

->M. Samuel Schultetus, of Hamburg.<-

while you present the easy pledges of your

<meta>continues from previous page: If you say...</meta>
that they worship a false god, or indeed the true one but not in the proper manner, then it will be permitted to use external worship, provided we use it in a different manner than they do.

58. Those things are mixed in which God is worshiped simultaneously with body and soul, internally and externally, such as prayer, praise, thanksgiving, reading, and honorable speech concerning divine matters.

<margin>Luke 10.</margin>
59. Therefore, one errs who, content with mental prayer, rejects vocal prayer as useless, and dares to prefer all prayer made by the mind alone over all prayer expressed also by the voice. For although Mary Magdalene <note>the sister of Martha, often identified with the contemplative life</note> is said to have chosen the better part than Martha, because the latter gave herself to action and the former to contemplation: yet the Church most truly proclaims of the most Blessed Virgin Mary that which is said of her <note>Magdalene</note>, as one who joined both and excelled most highly in both. Thus, he clearly does better who prays with affection alone than he who only murmurs with his lips. Yet he who offers prayers to God in both ways undoubtedly surpasses him.

<margin>
Proverbs 30.
Jeremiah 22.
</margin>
60. **THESE THREE** things are those by which the earth is moved, to which Jeremiah cries out a third time <note>a reference to Jeremiah 22:29, "O earth, earth, earth"</note>. For sobriety <note>temperance/restraint</note> sustains the man approaching God, justice leads him, and piety brings him through to the end toward which he strives.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 25.</margin>
61. Who denies that these three are difficult? Yet they are beautiful, in which even the Spirit of God takes delight, approved before God, whom sobriety invites, justice holds, and piety places upon a throne. And just as they are before God, so also are they before men, among whom the first certainly wins admiration, the second benevolence, and the third reverence. For we admire the chaste and sober, we love the beneficent, and we deem the religious worthy of special honor.

<margin>
Ecclesiasticus 25.
Proverbs 30.
Ecclesiasticus 4.
</margin>
62. There are three other types which I wish our soul had hated just as the soul of God does. Three insatiable things: the concupiscence <gloss>lust/strong desire</gloss> of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life; a triple wedge marching with a hostile face against the ranks of the God of Israel, a triple cord drawing toward certain destruction, which undoubtedly could be broken only with difficulty (if indeed it can be) by those who trust in their own strength.

63. But (thanks be to God) this [strength] of ours is no less strong in drawing us back from ruin, while temperance extinguishes the concupiscence of the flesh, generosity bridles the concupiscence of the eyes, and humility casts down the pride of life.

<summary>The author argues for the necessity of combining internal and external worship, using the figures of Martha, Mary, and the Virgin Mary as examples. He contrasts the virtues of sobriety, justice, and piety with the three worldly lusts.</summary>
<keywords>vocal prayer, mental prayer, Mary and Martha, sobriety, justice, piety, concupiscence, pride</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="13">
64. Between these battle lines man (over whom they contend) is placed in the middle; to whichever side he turns, its victory is certain.

65. This is the order of the struggle: that first of all the flesh must be tamed, for he who serves it still lingers in the beginnings; pride always remains for the last, which, if it should be cast down a thousand times, yet rises up again, and is sometimes stronger the more powerful the forces were by which it was prostrated.

<margin>
Isaiah 22.
1 Corinthians 15.
</margin>
66. SINCE, HOWEVER, there is mention of labor and battle, let the memory of reward and payment also immediately occur; we are forced to say this: we worship God in vain, we follow justice in vain, and they act foolishly who do not "eat and drink for tomorrow we die," if there is no reward for a deed rightly done, and if no punishment is prepared for the sinner.

<margin>Psalm 61.</margin>
67. Furthermore, God could be judged more cruel than just or merciful (let there be no blasphemy in the word) if He is moved by anger but not by grace; if He inflicts punishments on the unjust, the impious, and sinners, but establishes no rewards for the just, the pious, and the hardworking.

<margin>
Proverbs 24.
Ecclesiasticus 35.
Romans 2.
2 Corinthians 5.
Revelation 22.
</margin>
68. If, however, a reward and payment will be given to each one according to the fruit of his works, it is a wonder why the merits of good works are denied.

> Therefore, let us live soberly, justly, and piously; that is, let us strenuously apply ourselves to every kind of good work in this age, awaiting the blessed hope, namely the reward of eternal happiness, which He may deign to grant us—and previously our merits <note>suggesting grace precedes and enables merit</note>—He who is the beginning, fountain, and origin of all good things, as well as the end and goal, God blessed forever, Amen.

<note>A small decorative trifoliate ornament.</note>

<note>A second small decorative trifoliate ornament.</note>

->**Praise be to God.**<-

<summary>The text concludes by discussing the spiritual struggle against pride and the flesh, asserting that the necessity of good works is tied to the reality of divine judgment and eternal reward. It ends with a prayer for a life of sobriety, justice, and piety.</summary>
<keywords>spiritual warfare, pride, merits, good works, reward and punishment, grace, doxology</keywords>
</translation>

<meta>continues from previous page: Titius, a citizen of the City of N., with four shillings</meta>
and with children, both adult and minor, departs this life.
For these children, <term>Tutores</term> <gloss>legal guardians for minors under puberty</gloss> and <term>Curatores</term> <gloss>guardians for those over puberty but under legal age</gloss> are immediately appointed by the Magistrate. However, having become more skilled for the sake of business, which they had begun to learn in their homeland, they depart to other regions of the land. In the meantime, the guardians of the minors sell their houses, which are the only assets they possess, out of urgent necessity and not without a decree from the Magistrate of that place.
*It is now asked whether, under such circumstances, a tax* <note>original: "gabella"</note> *can be taken or deducted from the price received or from the money immediately placed out at interest* <note>original: "foenori locata"</note> *and still subject to contributions, which the minors neither request to be sent to them, nor which the guardians and debtors wish to transmit to those who might eventually request it without the prior knowledge of the Magistrate.*

### CASE XX.

Titius leaves a son as successor to a <term>feudum</term> <gloss>fief or feudal estate</gloss>. To this son, who seeks a renewal of the <term>investitura</term> <gloss>the formal legal transfer of the fief</gloss> after a year and twenty days, the Lord of the fief raises the <term>fatalium exceptionem</term> <gloss>an objection based on a legal deadline</gloss>, namely, that the time for seeking the renewal of investiture has elapsed, and consequently the <term>Vasallus</term> <gloss>vassal</gloss> has lost the fief.
*It is asked whether this objection can be refuted, notwithstanding the text of the second book of the Feuds, chapter 24, and similar laws.*
I affirm it can.

<note>original: "ΠΑΡΕΡΓΑ" (Parerga); minor or supplementary works</note>

<summary>This page discusses the legalities of taxing the estate of minor heirs who have moved abroad and whether a vassal forfeits his fief by missing the one-year deadline for renewing investiture.</summary>
<keywords>guardianship, estate tax, gabella, feudal law, investiture, legal deadlines, succession</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="12">
# <note>original: "Π Α Ρ Ε Ρ Γ Α" (Parerga); Supplementary Legal Observations</note>

### I.

<note>A large ornamental initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note>
Those who, while rightly granting power over sacred matters to the Princes of the Augsburg Confession <note>the primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church</note>, say that Episcopal right <note>original: "jus Episcopale"</note> is possessed by them, do not extricate themselves with sufficient consideration.

### II.

Likewise, they claim that our Princes bear a double persona, namely, an Ecclesiastical and a secular one.

### III.

But also, that Episcopal rights are exercised by them by way of a <term>contractus fiduciarii</term> <gloss>fiduciary contract</gloss>, or as if from a deposit, or <term>usufructuariè</term> <gloss>by way of usufruct, using another's property</gloss>.

### IV.

Finally, they claim that the right of our Princes regarding sacred matters consists in <term>lex Diaecesana</term> <gloss>diocesan law</gloss> and the law of jurisdiction. See the Magnificent Lord Strauchius's public manuscript lectures on Ecclesiastical Governance <note>original: "de Regimine Ecclesiastico"</note>, special part, title 1, paragraph 3 and following, where he pursues this argument in his own most subtle manner. Add to this the same author's Dissertation on Statutes by the Supreme Prince, in the <term>Digest</term> <gloss>Pandects</gloss> on the Constitutions of Princes, paragraph 36.

### V.

Lutherans and Calvinists are not proven to be heretics by the fact that they are addressed by the names of their authors. The same author in his public manuscript lectures on the 6th law of the Code regarding heretics and Manichaeans against those of Dillingen.

---

-><note>A printer's ornamental tailpiece featuring a central circular motif with surrounding scrolls and floral patterns.</note><-

<summary>This page critiques various legal and theological interpretations of the ecclesiastical authority held by Protestant princes and addresses the classification of Lutherans and Calvinists in relation to heresy.</summary>
<keywords>Augsburg Confession, Episcopal right, Ecclesiastical Governance, Strauchius, Lutherans, Calvinists, heresy, jurisdiction</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="102">
Although the natural state of the primordial mind has been without anything to see from the beginning, cut through the root of whoever is the viewer and the act of viewing! Although the natural state of the primordial mind has been without meditation from the beginning, let the essence of the meditator's awareness rest in great pervasiveness! Although the natural state of the primordial mind has been without conduct from the beginning, let it rest in an unaltered and relaxed state without the duality of action and rejection! Although the natural state of the primordial mind has been spontaneously present from the beginning, let the desire to achieve a result rest in the state free from conceptual elaboration! If a yogi who maintains it in such a way attains stability in the natural state, then having purified the delusions of the mental afflictions, the result of Buddhahood is attained. Thus it was said. 

Furthermore, this was given to the great resident scholar Nyima Drakpa, arranged according to the thirty letters of the alphabet:
**Ka**: The primordial unborn realization is self-arising. 
**Kha**: From the state that is clear like the sky, 
**Ga**: In that awareness which is without negation or proof, 
**Nga**: I rest in the state of knowing there is no self-entity. 
**Ca**: By means of this practice which is without artifice, 
**Cha**: Until the unadulterated <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss> is attained, 
**Ja**: Accomplish the meaning of the noble lord...

<leaf-break/>

...in that way. This melody of experience based on the thirty letters of the alphabet was written as it dawned in the mind. Thus it was said. 

Furthermore, in the Year of the Pig, when the Internal Minister <note>Tibetan: nang so</note> Sonam Gyalpo passed away in Lhalung, the Internal Minister Chodze, the mother, and the son requested that [Pema Lingpa] should come to lead the funeral rites. However, at that time he was unable to attend. Sending a sacred relic that had emerged from his own tooth, he wrote this series of instructions to comfort the minds of the Minister Chodze, the mother, and the son:

To the Triple Gem, the reliable objects of refuge, I prostrate and take refuge. 
Lord, mother, and son, you who have deep karmic connections from the past, please listen. Wherever one looks on the earth, under the sky, in the directions or the intermediate points, in the center or the borders, for all sentient beings of the three realms, there is no time of escape from the suffering of death. It is the destination for everyone. Like a father...

<leaf-break/>

...likewise, rising gradually, suffering is without end. Now that you have found a precious human body, cast away all worldly activities! If you apply yourself to the Dharma, it will be your eternal companion. All the temporary activities of this life are of an illusory nature; whatever you do, they are of no help, so contemplate impermanence in your heart! Rather than the activities of this life, accomplish your eternal companion. If you are to achieve the great purpose, do it now; there is no certainty as to what will happen in the next life. In this time when you have your own autonomy, cast away distractions and busyness! Apply yourself to the practice of these profound instructions of the self-arising <term>Dzogchen</term> <gloss>Great Perfection</gloss>. This will bring happiness now and joy in the future. Even this current kingdom, if you protect it with the Dharma of a compassionate mind and benefit all sentient beings, happiness will come to you. You, the monk Pema Lingpa's advice, hold it in the center of your heart! I will also come around the pig month. At that time, priest and patron shall discuss the matters in detail. 
</translation>

<translation page="103">
The Lineage Holder <note>Tibetan: gdung tshob</note>, the Great <term>Vidyadhara</term> <gloss>Knowledge-Holder</gloss>, while performing his flower alms-round at a delightful place called Bi, on the southwest border of the monastery of Pema Lingpa, gave this introduction to the Khampa mendicant Rinchen Zangpo through the gate of poetry:

The unconditioned nature of mind is the great sky. 
The natural thoughts of conceptual elaboration are a continuous chain. 
The six objects show the illusory forms of the ground. 
Since these lack truth, they scatter the path of bliss. 
O Khampa, do you see it like a reflection of the moon in water or a mirage? 

Thus he spoke, and [the Khampa] requested: 
On the stable ground of unchanging faith, 
The branches of the wish-fulfilling tree of devotion flourish. 
Please let the fruit of compassionate needs and desires ripen. 

In response, he spoke this: 
The King of Birds, the Garuda, with wings...

<leaf-break/>

**Ang**: To study and contemplate without partiality to any school, 
To cut through the depths of the doubting mind, 
To know what to adopt or reject regarding Dharma and non-Dharma— 
This is to not mistake the peak of the future goal, **Ang**! 
By the reminder of impermanence and death, 
To the nature of the delusions of <term>samsara</term> <gloss>cyclic existence</gloss>, 
The arising of renunciation and weariness— 
This is to not mistake the peak of the future goal, **Ang**! 
All the various worldly actions 
Are known to be meaningless deeds. 
To rest in the state of non-action— 
This is to not mistake the peak of the future goal, **Ang**! 
Seeing the suffering of all who possess wealth, 
The lack of wealth is a great ornament of the mind. 
To possess the noble wealth of contentment— 
This is to not mistake the peak of the future goal, **Ang**! 
Taking the base of one's own benefit as awareness, 
Training in the <term>Bodhicitta</term> <gloss>Awakening Mind</gloss> that benefits others, 
Turning the minds of oneself and others toward the Dharma— 
This is to not mistake the peak of the future goal, **Ang**! 
The <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>expanse of reality</gloss> is free from elaboration. 
Awareness is unborn and free from extremes. 
Reaching the limit of the realized View— 
This is to not mistake the peak of the future goal, **Ang**! 
The natural state of bliss, clarity, and non-thought, 
Where the object of meditation and the meditator...

...because there are some yogis in the midst of the Land of Snows, Tibet, who focus primarily on pure vision where the fortunate karmic potential is awakened by relying on the fierce [practice], I ask that you compose a brief praise for them. This time, I, the yogi, found the [treasure] of the Vase of Medicine <note>Tibetan: sman bum</note> at Thang, which is difficult to find. I met a Master like you, Pema Lingpa, who is difficult to meet. You granted the instructions of the profound Dharma, the *Assembly of All Intentions* <note>Tibetan: dgongs pa kun 'dus</note>. I tasted the sacred substances that liberate through tasting. I am happy! I am joyful! I, the yogi Lhawang Drakpa, have come upon the path of empty-clarity without grasping. From the mountain pass of naked seeing that is free from extremes, I looked over at the unobstructed and transparent state, and I met the Guru of the spontaneously present natural state. I requested the oral instructions on the inseparability of appearance and emptiness. I offered the mandala of the relaxed six senses. Through pure merit in the past, I have met such an essence of the realization of <term>Samantabhadra</term> <gloss>The Primordial Buddha</gloss>. Through the aspiration prayers I have made now, may we never be separated for aeons. I am happy!

Although the natural state of the primordial mind has been without anything to see from the beginning, cut through the root of whoever is the viewer and the act of viewing! Although the natural state of the primordial mind has been without meditation from the beginning, let the essence of the meditator's awareness rest in great pervasiveness! Although the natural state of the primordial mind has been without conduct from the beginning, let it rest in an unaltered and relaxed state without the duality of action and rejection! Although the natural state of the primordial mind has been spontaneously present from the beginning, let the desire to achieve a result rest in the state free from conceptual elaboration! If a yogi who maintains it in such a way attains stability in the natural state, then having purified the delusions of the mental afflictions, the result of Buddhahood is attained. Thus it was said. 

Furthermore, this was given to the great resident scholar Nyima Drakpa, arranged according to the thirty letters of the alphabet:
**Ka**: The primordial unborn realization is self-arising. 
**Kha**: From the state that is clear like the sky, 
**Ga**: In that awareness which is without negation or proof, 
**Nga**: I rest in the state of knowing there is no self-entity. 
**Ca**: By means of this practice which is without artifice, 
**Cha**: Until the unadulterated <term>dharmakaya</term> <gloss>truth body</gloss> is attained, 
**Ja**: Accomplish the meaning of the noble lord...

<leaf-break/>

...in that way. This melody of experience based on the thirty letters of the alphabet was written as it dawned in the mind. Thus it was said. 

Furthermore, in the Year of the Pig, when the Internal Minister <note>Tibetan: nang so</note> Sonam Gyalpo passed away in Lhalung, the Internal Minister Chodze, the mother, and the son requested that [Pema Lingpa] should come to lead the funeral rites. However, at that time he was unable to attend. Sending a sacred relic that had emerged from his own tooth, he wrote this series of instructions to comfort the minds of the Minister Chodze, the mother, and the son:

To the Triple Gem, the reliable objects of refuge, I prostrate and take refuge. 
Lord, mother, and son, you who have deep karmic connections from the past, please listen. Wherever one looks on the earth, under the sky, in the directions or the intermediate points, in the center or the borders, for all sentient beings of the three realms, there is no time of escape from the suffering of death. It is the destination for everyone. Like a father...

<leaf-break/>

...likewise, rising gradually, suffering is without end. Now that you have found a precious human body, cast away all worldly activities! If you apply yourself to the Dharma, it will be your eternal companion. All the temporary activities of this life are of an illusory nature; whatever you do, they are of no help, so contemplate impermanence in your heart! Rather than the activities of this life, accomplish your eternal companion. If you are to achieve the great purpose, do it now; there is no certainty as to what will happen in the next life. In this time when you have your own autonomy, cast away distractions and busyness! Apply yourself to the practice of these profound instructions of the self-arising <term>Dzogchen</term> <gloss>Great Perfection</gloss>. This will bring happiness now and joy in the future. Even this current kingdom, if you protect it with the Dharma of a compassionate mind and benefit all sentient beings, happiness will come to you. You, the monk Pema Lingpa's advice, hold it in the center of your heart! I will also come around the pig month. At that time, priest and patron shall discuss the matters in detail.

(2) Tabulated Explanation by Position, Phenomenon, and Contemplative Practice

| Scripture | Interpretation | Position | By Phenomenon | By Contemplative Practice |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Neither arising nor ceasing | Ordinary people before attaining the Path. Death here and birth there; this is the position of arising and ceasing. True Emptiness is apart from this. | | Causes arise, causes fade. | The "imaginary nature" is empty; there is nothing to arise or cease. <note>Contemplation of Non-arising</note> Delusory phenomena. |
| Neither defiled nor pure | Bodhisattvas on the Path. Staining obstructions are not yet exhausted, but pure practices are already cultivated. This is the position of defilement and purity. True Emptiness is apart from this. | | Following the flow, emerging from obstructions. | The "dependent nature" of defilement and purity; having no self-nature despite following conditions. <note>Contemplation of No-form</note> Dependent origination. |
| Neither increasing nor decreasing | The Buddha-fruit after the Path. Afflictions exhausted is "ceasing," and virtues perfected is "increase." True Emptiness is apart from this. | | Obstructions exhausted, virtues perfected. | The previous two contemplations illuminate └─┘ neither increase nor decrease. <note>Contemplation of No-nature</note> True Emptiness. |

(3) Tabulated Explanation of the Eight Negations from the <term>Madhyamaka Shastra</term> <gloss>Treatise on the Middle Way</gloss>

**No arising:** All phenomena have no arising. Why? Because it is seen by the eyes of the world. For instance, the grain at the beginning of the <term>kalpa</term> <gloss>aeon</gloss> does not arise. Why? Because apart from that initial grain, the current grain cannot be obtained. If the current grain existed apart from the initial grain, there would be "arising," but in reality, it is not so; therefore, there is no arising.

**No ceasing:** The grain at the beginning of the <term>kalpa</term> does not cease. Why? If it ceased, there should be no grain today, but in reality, there is grain; therefore, there is no ceasing.

**No permanence:** All things are not permanent. Just as when a grain produces a sprout, the seed is transformed and destroyed; therefore, there is no permanence.

**No discontinuity:** All things are not discontinuous. Just as from the grain there is a sprout, there is no discontinuity. If there were discontinuity, there would be no succession.

**No oneness:** All things are not one. Just as the grain does not become the sprout, and the sprout does not become the grain. If they were one, but in reality they are not; therefore, they are not one.

**No difference:** All things are not different. If they were different, why distinguish between the grain's sprout, stem, and leaf, rather than saying a tree's sprout, stem, or leaf? Therefore, they are not different.

**No coming:** All things do not come. Just as the sprout within the grain comes from nowhere. If it came, the sprout would have to come from another place, like a bird coming to perch in a tree; but in reality, it is not so; therefore, there is no coming.

**No going out:** All things do not go out. If there were a going out, one should see the sprout emerge from the grain like a snake emerging from a hole; but in reality, it is not so; therefore, there is no going out.

37

<keywords>Eight Negations, Madhyamaka Shastra, arising and ceasing, contemplative practice, three natures, grain metaphor</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="52">
<meta>continues from previous page: surpasses the Lesser Vehicle.</meta>
The Lesser <note>the path of disciples and solitary realizers</note> is called "excellent," but that which transcends the causal stages is called "most supreme." Because obstacles are exhausted and virtues are perfected, achieving the ultimate rank of the fruit <note>attainment of Buddhahood</note>, it is called "most supreme."

The term "karma" <note>original: "ye"</note> refers generally to the functional activities of the three wheels <note>body, speech, and mind</note> of all Buddhas. This means the "most supreme karma" is the "most supreme as karma." Two interpretations are available:
1. "Omniscient" refers to the karma of the mind. "Supreme and unobstructed" refers to the karma of the body. "Supreme in saving the world with compassion" refers to the karma of speech. "One who is supreme" refers to the person who possesses these virtues, namely the Buddha.
2. Distinguishing by the two benefits <note>benefit for oneself and benefit for others</note>: "Most supreme karma" is the general heading for the specific categories like omniscience. It manifests the virtue of self-benefit. Within this, internally there is the wisdom of omniscience, and externally there is the unobstructed form. The *Srimala Sutra* <note>original: "Shengman jing"</note> says: "The Tathagata's physical form is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise." This passage follows that meaning. "Saving the world" and the other phrases specifically manifest the virtue of benefiting others. One who is perfected in these two benefits is called the Buddha.

Third, distinguishing by the three virtues:
1. "Most supreme karma" is the general heading.
2. "Omniscience" manifests the Buddha's virtue of Great Wisdom.
3. "Physical unobstructedness" clarifies the Buddha's virtue of Great Concentration <note>original: "ding"</note>. This means relying on concentration to trigger supernormal powers, manifesting form without obstruction.

<summary>This page defines the "Most Supreme" nature of the Buddha through his activities and virtues. It categorizes the Buddha's excellence using the three modes of karma, the two types of benefit, and the three great virtues of wisdom, concentration, and compassion.</summary>
<keywords>Buddha, Most Supreme, Karma, Three Wheels, Two Benefits, Three Virtues, Wisdom, Unobstructed Form</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="53">
<header>General Commentaries on Various Treatises, Part Two</header>

3. "Saving the world" and so on explains the Buddha's virtue of Great Compassion. The *Compendium of the Great Vehicle* <note>original: "She dacheng lun"; Sanskrit: Mahayanasamgraha</note> explains the virtues of the Buddha's Enjoyment Body <note>original: "shouyong shen"; Sanskrit: Sambhogakaya</note> using only these three.

Fourth, explaining according to the text:
This passage only clarifies the Reward Body <note>Sambhogakaya</note> and Emanation Body <note>Nirmanakaya</note>, because the Dharma Body <note>Dharmakaya</note> is included within the Dharma Jewel. "Most supreme" is as explained in the first interpretation. 

Regarding the "omniscience" of functional activity, there are two types:
1. Omniscience of True Wisdom: This relates to the Mind as Suchness <note>original: "xin zhenru men"</note>, containing virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
2. Omniscience of Conventional Wisdom: This relates to the Mind as Birth and Death <note>original: "xin shengmie men"</note>, regarding the distinctions of dependent origination. 
When the principle <note>absolute truth</note> and the measure <note>phenomenal truth</note> are perceived equally, it is called non-erroneous omniscience. 

Regarding "unobstructed form": 
The Tathagata's physical body is sovereign and unobstructed in many ways, as described in the Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharmas in the *Flower Adornment Sutra* <note>original: "Huayan jing"; Sanskrit: Avatamsaka Sutra</note>. Here, four types are briefly distinguished:
1. Unobstructedness of the large and small: Every single sense organ pervades the Dharma Realm, yet they do not destroy the specific nature of the organs. The text is not confused regarding the characteristics of the organs.
2. Unobstructedness of mutual use: The various organs perform each other's functions without hindering one another.
3. Unobstructedness of principle and phenomena: This means that while the physical form is manifested brilliantly, it does not obstruct the fact that the entire substance is empty of nature. This profound principle...

<summary>The text continues the technical breakdown of the Buddha's virtues, focusing on the distinction between True and Conventional Wisdom. it introduces the concept of unobstructed physical form, drawing on the Flower Adornment Sutra to explain how a Buddha's physical presence interacts with absolute reality.</summary>
<keywords>Great Compassion, Reward Body, Dharma Body, True Wisdom, Conventional Wisdom, Suchness, Birth and Death, Flower Adornment Sutra, Unobstructed Form, Principle and Phenomena</keywords>
</translation>

1. Omniscience of True Wisdom: This relates to the Mind as Suchness <note>original: "xin zhenru men"</note>, containing virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
2. Omniscience of Conventional Wisdom: This relates to the Mind as Birth and Death <note>original: "xin shengmie men"</note>, regarding the distinctions of dependent origination. 
When the principle <note>absolute truth</note> and the measure <note>phenomenal truth</note> are perceived equally, it is called non-erroneous omniscience. 

Regarding "unobstructed form": 
The Tathagata's physical body is sovereign and unobstructed in many ways, as described in the Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharmas in the *Flower Adornment Sutra* <note>original: "Huayan jing"; Sanskrit: Avatamsaka Sutra</note>. Here, four types are briefly distinguished:
1. Unobstructedness of the large and small: Every single sense organ pervades the Dharma Realm, yet they do not destroy the specific nature of the organs. The text is not confused regarding the characteristics of the organs.
2. Unobstructedness of mutual use: The various organs perform each other's functions without hindering one another.
3. Unobstructedness of principle and phenomena: This means that while the physical form is manifested brilliantly, it does not obstruct the fact that the entire substance is empty of nature. This profound principle...

# Description of the Six Chakras
## Page 61

For this reason, he qualifies the Lord of All <note>original: <term>Sarvesha</term></note> by calling him <term>Hamsa</term> <gloss>the Swan/Soul</gloss>. This Lord of All is the form of the mantra consisting of the sequence of these syllables. As stated in the <term>Prapancha Sara</term>: "That known as Reality is pure consciousness. From its proximity to the light, it desires to divide; becoming dense, it reaches the state of the <term>bindu</term> <gloss>point/seed</gloss> at a certain place. In time, that <term>bindu</term> splits in two. The <term>bindu</term> is the right side, and the left side is the <term>visarga</term> <gloss>emanation/two dots</gloss>. Thus, the right and left parts are distinguished as male and female. The sound <term>Ham</term> is said to be the <term>bindu</term>, and <term>Sah</term> is known as the <term>visarga</term>. The <term>bindu</term> is called the Male <note><term>Purusha</term></note>, and the <term>visarga</term> is known as Nature <note><term>Prakriti</term></note>. The <term>Hamsa</term> consists of the Male and Nature; this entire world consists of that."

This is clearly stated in the first chapter of the <term>Mahakali Tantra</term>: "Within the void of the thousand-petaled lotus, adorned with a divine gateway, in the middle of the lunar mandala, above the two letters of the <term>Hamsa</term>, it shines like pure crystal, radiant with pure moonlight," and so on. Here, the phrase "above the two letters of the <term>Hamsa</term>" makes it very clear. Alternatively, he is known and famous by the name <term>Hamsa Parama</term> <gloss>the Supreme Swan</gloss>. Indeed, the author himself stated in the forty-eighth verse that "some call this the form of the <term>Hamsa</term>," thus giving it the name <term>Hamsa</term>. Or, by taking the compound <note>original: <term>karmadharaya</term></note> "he who has <term>Hamsa</term> at the end and who is Supreme," and following the grammatical rule of dropping the middle term, we arrive at <term>Hamsa-Parama</term>. This means he is known by the name <term>Paramahansa</term>. Thus it is said in the <term>Agama Kalpadruma</term>: "This one, in the form of <term>Paramahansa</term>, is joined with all things moving and unmoving."

The phrase "an overflow of the wave-series of all happiness" <note>original: <term>sakala-sukha-santana-lahari-parivaha</term></note> means that "all happiness" refers to every kind of joy; its "extension" is its expansion; that itself is a "series of waves" <note><term>lahari</term></note> which is "overflowing" or rising up everywhere, being revealed as something that lasts through subsequent times. Consequently, in the form of a series, he is characterized by all-pervasive and all-encompassing happiness. It was stated previously that this <term>Hamsa</term> is situated below the Supreme Shiva.

43
</translation>

<translation page="62">
# Description of the Six Chakras
## Page 62

The followers of Shiva call it the place of Shiva; the groups of Vaishnavas call it the Supreme Person <note><term>Paramapurusha</term></note>; some others call it the place of <term>Hari-Hara</term> <gloss>Vishnu and Shiva conjoined</gloss>. Others, great sages who take delight in the nectar of the Goddess's lotus feet, call it the place of the Goddess; yet others call it the stainless place of Nature and Person <note><term>Prakriti-Purusha</term></note>.

44

By knowing this place, the best of men, with his own mind controlled, shall not be born again in the world of change <note><term>Samsara</term></note>; he is no longer bound in the three worlds. His power shall be complete...

Because all deities, beginning with <term>Hamsa</term>, reside in this pericarp, he explains that it is the place of the deity to be worshipped by all practitioners, whether they follow Shiva, Shakti, or others. Regarding "the place of Shiva" <note><term>Shivastanam</term></note>: the followers of Shiva say this lotus is the place of Shiva. "Supreme Person": that this is the place of the Supreme Person Vishnu is established by the grammatical suffix implying "belonging to." Regarding "some": those who worship <term>Hari-Hara</term> are both Shaivas and Vaishnavas. These "some others" are distinct from those who worship only Shiva or only Vishnu; they call it the station of <term>Hari-Hara</term>. Thus, with the intention of saying that not all Shaivas or Vaishnavas call it exclusively the place of Shiva or Vishnu, he mentions "others" who are inclined toward the worship of the Couple. Or, "other" great sages who are practitioners of the <term>Hamsa</term> mantra call it the place of Nature and Person <note><term>Prakriti-Purusha</term></note>, because the <term>Hamsa</term> consists of the two forms of Nature and Person and resides there. This is merely an illustration; it should be understood that since this place is the seat of the Supreme <term>Bindu</term> which contains all deities, whoever worships a particular deity calls it the place of that deity.

44

He describes the fruit of knowing the Thousand-Petaled Lotus <note><term>Sahasrara</term></note> in the phrase "By knowing this place." The idea is that one gains knowledge of this station with all its parts and sub-parts. "With his own mind controlled": this means one whose own mind is steadily fixed there. "He shall not be in the world of change": the meaning is that he becomes liberated. The reason is given in the qualifying phrase "he is no longer bound in the three worlds." "Bound" means tied by the snares of <term>Maya</term> <gloss>illusion</gloss> in the form of merit and demerit. As stated in the <term>Bhagavata</term>: "While actions are being performed, he thinks of himself as the qualities; that is his worldly bondage and his dependence."
</translation>

<summary>These pages explain the symbolic identity of the Hamsa mantra as the union of male and female principles and clarify that the Sahasrara chakra is perceived as the abode of various deities depending on the practitioner's sectarian path. Knowledge of this center is said to lead to liberation from the bonds of karma and rebirth.</summary>
<keywords>Hamsa, Bindu, Visarga, Prakriti, Purusha, Sahasrara, Shiva, Vishnu, Hari-Hara, Liberation, Samsara, Tantra</keywords>

### Chapter Twenty-one
->Chapter Twenty-one. 48<-

She has very beautiful teeth, she is eternal, and she has full, high breasts. She is situated in a triple-bent posture <note>original: "vibhanga", a graceful curve in iconography</note>, the slayer of the buffalo demon <note>Mahishasuramardini</note>. (25)
Her touch is as soft as a long lotus stalk, and she is endowed with ten arms. One should meditate on the trident in the right hand, then the sword and the discus in order. (26)
She holds a sharp power <note>term: shakti, a spear-like weapon</note> in the left arm, along with a shield, a full bow, and she is marked by the noose and the goad. (27)
One should place the bell or the supreme <unclear>axe</unclear> likewise on the left side. Her limbs are sprinkled with red sandalwood paste, and her garments and coverings are red. (28)
Seated upon a lion is the Supreme Goddess, worshiped by Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva. The Great Illusion <note>Mahamaya</note> is also seated upon a corpse, and stays upon a red lotus seat. (29)
One should meditate on Durga seated on a lion, the giver of supreme liberation. Shiva is the corpse, Mahadeva <note>the Great God</note> is the corpse, Brahma is the red lotus. (30)
Vishnu is known as the lion; these are the vehicles of great energy. O Goddess, their worship is never performed in their own original forms <note>as independent deities in this context</note>. (31)
Having taken another form, these three have attained the state of being vehicles. Sometimes she stays on the Shiva-corpse, sometimes on the red lotus. (32)
Sometimes, O Supreme Goddess, she dwells on the back of the lion <note>original: "keshari", the maned one</note>. At the time of desire <note>ritual union</note>, the Lion-Rider dwells upon the Shiva-corpse. (33)
Now hear of the beloved group of companions of this Queen of the Buffaloes <note>Mahisha-Mahishi, an epithet of the Goddess</note>. (34)

Thus ends the Twenty-first Chapter in the illustrious Kamivilasa Tantra.

<summary>This page describes the iconography of Mahishasuramardini, detailing her ten weapons and her symbolic mounts, where major gods like Shiva and Vishnu take the form of her seat or vehicle.</summary>

</translation>

<translation page="63">
->Now the Twenty-second Chapter.<-

The Illustrious Tatpurusha <note>an aspect of Shiva</note> said:

Chanda, Chandavati, Vidya, Chamunda, Chandanayika, Ugrachanda, Prachanda, Chandograh, and Chandanasika. (1)
Surrounded by these powers <note>shaktis</note>, hear now of the Lion-Rider, the victorious one; I shall speak the mantra of the Slayer <note>of the demon</note> which grants liberation. (2)
After extracting the seed of illusion <note>term: Maya-bija, the syllable Hrim</note>, then the words "Durge Durge." After that the word "Rucha," O auspicious one, and at the end the beloved of fire <note>term: vahni-vallabha, the ritual exclamation Svaha</note>. (3)
There is no mantra superior to this target in the Tantra, O beautiful-eyed one. I shall now speak to you the great ten-syllabled mantra after extracting it. (4)
After extracting the seed of illusion, then the word "Durge," O dear one. The wife of fire <note>Svaha</note> is at the end; this is considered the giver of all success. (5)
Having extracted the seed of illusion, then "Durgayai," and placing the wife of fire at the end, if one chants this even once, (6)
Having gathered ten million kinsmen, he goes to the abode of Vishnu <note>Vaikuntha</note>. "Durge Durge" is likewise spoken, followed by the wife of fire. (7)
This knowledge is the Great Knowledge <note>Mahavidya</note>, the giver of the fruits of the four aims of life <note>virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation</note>. After extracting the seed of illusion, the beloved of fire is at the end. (8)
This is your most excellent knowledge, the faultless mantra of the Slayer. "Hrim Durge" is the subsequent mantra, the giver of the four aims. (9)
"Hrim Durge Rakshani" <note>Protectress</note> is the phrase, then the syllable "Namah." After extracting the seed of illusion, the wife of fire comes next. (10)
The fourteen-syllabled knowledge is devoid of all faults. "Hrim Durge" is the subsequent mantra, the giver of the four aims. (11)

<translation page="10">
<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'N' begins the dedication.</note>

**THERE IS NO ONE WHO WOULD DENY** that your father, Lord Philipp, Count of Gleichen, is worthy of being celebrated with the praises of a hero and with Latin verse <note>original: "carmine Ausonio"</note> on account of his most famous virtues and the singular piety he showed toward God. Since I am not endowed with such eloquence as to be able to adorn his shade <note>an allusion to the spirits of the departed</note> according to his dignity, and yet I have descended into this arena, I pray that no one attributes it to me as a fault. For it is fitting to favor even those with modest talents, even if they do not achieve everything. However, generous Counts, I have chosen to dedicate this poem to you, although it is a slight gift <note>original: "Leuidense munus"</note>, and I pray that you receive it with a calm and serene countenance. If you continue as you have begun, in no way deviating from your father's virtues, you will one day be celebrated with a similar eulogy. Therefore, apply yourselves so that you do not degenerate or wander from the footprints of your father. From Mühlberg, on the 11th of May, in the year of the birth of the Virgin, 1544.

### FUNERAL POEM FOR THE ILLUSTRIOUS
### AND FAMOUS COUNT, etc.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'L' begins the poem.</note>

**S**orrowful elegy, put on your garments again now,
   And wish to have a name that truly fits you.
Philipp has departed from the living, he who was high-born
   Of the Gleichen line, who was a father among the rest.
Therefore, a new grief occupies the brothers from that moment, and their cheeks
   Now again, and their whole faces, they drench with tears.
And thus at home in the ancestral house of the castle, Sigismund
</translation>

<translation page="11">
Grieves for his brother, full of mournful love.
But you, Ernest, having set out for the household gods of Speyer,
Groan for the fate of your brother under a foreign sky.
And just as you were recently following the pious arms of the Saxon,
A fighter with combined forces: those of the Hessian.
Meanwhile, the Fate, cruel and unjust, snatched away
Your brother, whose name is Grace <note>the Latin name *Gratia* often refers to Johann/Hans, or could here be a specific reference to a family name element</note>, in a wretched funeral at home.
With the Emperor now holding a council, a welfare
Which I pray brings welcome gifts of peace.
With the Duke of Saxony and you visiting it, you now lose
Philipp in a similar way at home.
Therefore, Ernest, you deservedly shed heavy tears,
And you have a just and grave cause for weeping.
You too, children, sad about the death of your parent,
Are weeping, and heavy grief holds your hearts.
Just cause brings forth for you immense complaints,
And anyone finding fault with these has no reason.
Until now you wept for your deceased mother and your uncle Johann,
You weep for both of them now along with your father.
And the castle, sad, now mourns each one, having lost
Its father, and the river Ora mixes its waters with your tears.
What need is there for many words, everything is full of grief,
And every subject has cause to weep with reason.
We also, who inhabit the shores of the nearby Weida <note>original: "VVcite"</note>,
Weep for you, famous Philipp, with a lamenting lyre.
We weep and sing the praises of your renown in these
Verses, though they may be unpolished and rude.
</translation>

<summary>This text contains a dedication by Wendelin von Helbach to the Counts of Gleichen, followed by an opening funeral elegy for Count Philipp, detailing the family's grief and the mourning of the surrounding region.</summary>
<keywords>Count Philipp of Gleichen, Funeral Elegy, Wendelin von Helbach, Mourning, 1544, Saxon nobility</keywords>

Since I am not endowed with such eloquence as to be able to adorn his shade <note>an allusion to the spirits of the departed</note> according to his dignity, and yet I have descended into this arena, I pray that no one attributes it to me as a fault. For it is fitting to favor even those with modest talents, even if they do not achieve everything. However, generous Counts, I have chosen to dedicate this poem to you, although it is a slight gift <note>original: "Leuidense munus"</note>, and I pray that you receive it with a calm and serene countenance. If you continue as you have begun, in no way deviating from your father's virtues, you will one day be celebrated with a similar eulogy. Therefore, apply yourselves so that you do not degenerate or wander from the footprints of your father. From Mühlberg, on the 11th of May, in the year of the birth of the Virgin, 1544.

### FUNERAL POEM FOR THE ILLUSTRIOUS
### AND FAMOUS COUNT, etc.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'L' begins the poem.</note>

**S**orrowful elegy, put on your garments again now,
   And wish to have a name that truly fits you.
Philipp has departed from the living, he who was high-born
   Of the Gleichen line, who was a father among the rest.
Therefore, a new grief occupies the brothers from that moment, and their cheeks
   Now again, and their whole faces, they drench with tears.
And thus at home in the ancestral house of the castle, Sigismund
pages.11:
Grieves for his brother, full of mournful love.
But you, Ernest, having set out for the household gods of Speyer,
Groan for the fate of your brother under a foreign sky.
And just as you were recently following the pious arms of the Saxon,
A fighter with combined forces: those of the Hessian.
Meanwhile, the Fate, cruel and unjust, snatched away
Your brother, whose name is Grace <note>the Latin name *Gratia* often refers to Johann/Hans, or could here be a specific reference to a family name element</note>, in a wretched funeral at home.
With the Emperor now holding a council, a welfare
Which I pray brings welcome gifts of peace.
With the Duke of Saxony and you visiting it, you now lose
Philipp in a similar way at home.
Therefore, Ernest, you deservedly shed heavy tears,
And you have a just and grave cause for weeping.
You too, children, sad about the death of your parent,
Are weeping, and heavy grief holds your hearts.
Just cause brings forth for you immense complaints,
And anyone finding fault with these has no reason.
Until now you wept for your deceased mother and your uncle Johann,
You weep for both of them now along with your father.
And the castle, sad, now mourns each one, having lost
Its father, and the river Ora mixes its waters with your tears.
What need is there for many words, everything is full of grief,
And every subject has cause to weep with reason.
We also, who inhabit the shores of the nearby Weida <note>original: "VVcite"</note>,
Weep for you, famous Philipp, with a lamenting lyre.
We weep and sing the praises of your renown in these
Verses, though they may be unpolished and rude.

<header>PRO A. CLVENTIO.</header>

who had coveted Sassia’s wealth, considered that he must seek a remedy at home for the delay that was being brought to his marriage. For although he had an infant son by Novia, his other son—born of Pappia—was being educated with his mother at Teanum Apulum, which is eighteen miles from Larinum. He suddenly summoned the boy to Teanum without any reason, a thing he was not accustomed to doing except during public games or festival days. The wretched mother, suspecting no evil, sent him. Although he had feigned that he was setting out for Tarentum, on that very day the boy, who had been seen in public in good health at the eleventh hour <note>about 5:00 PM</note>, was dead before nightfall, and on the following day, before dawn, he was cremated. Rumor among the people announced this great grief to the mother sooner than anyone from Oppianicus' household did. When she heard at the same time that not only had her son been taken from her, but also the duty of performing his funeral rites, she came to Larinum immediately, distraught, and there performed the funeral anew for her son, who had already been buried. Not ten days had passed when his other infant son was killed. Therefore, Sassia married Oppianicus immediately, with a spirit now joyful and strengthened by the best hope; and no wonder, for she saw herself appeased not by nuptial gifts, but by the funerals of her sons. Thus, whereas others are accustomed to be more covetous of money because of their children, he thought it pleasant to lose his children for the sake of money. I sense, judges, that because of your humanity, you are vehemently moved by these great crimes which I have briefly demonstrated. With what heart, then, do you think those men were, who not only had to hear about these matters but also to judge them? You are hearing about a man concerning whom you are not the judges; about one whom you do not see; about one whom you can no longer hate; about one who has satisfied both nature and the laws, whom the laws have punished with exile and nature with death. You hear not from an enemy, and you hear without witnesses.</translation>

<translation page="55">
<header>ORATIO</header>

You hear, while those things which can be said most copiously are being stated by me briefly and in outline. They were listening to a case about which they were bound by oath to deliver their verdict; about a man whose wicked and depraved countenance they were beholding in his presence; about one whom they hated for his audacity; about one whom they considered worthy of every punishment. They were hearing from the accusers; they were hearing the words of many witnesses; they were hearing while P. Canutius, a most eloquent man, was speaking about every point gravely and at length. And is there anyone who, upon learning these facts, could suspect that Oppianicus was crushed by the judgment and that, as an innocent man, he was circumvented? I will now state the remaining points in a heap, judges, so that I may arrive at those matters which are closer and more connected to this case. I ask you to keep in mind that my purpose here is not to accuse a dead Oppianicus, but, since I wish to persuade you that the judgment was not corrupted by him, to use this as the starting point and foundation of the defense: that Oppianicus, a most wicked and guilty man, was rightfully convicted. For he gave a cup to his wife, Cluentia, who was the aunt of this man Habitus, and suddenly, in the midst of drinking, she exclaimed that she was dying in great pain, and she lived no longer than she spoke; for she died in that very conversation and outcry. And in addition to this sudden death and the cry of the dying woman, all the other signs and traces of poison that are usually present were found in the body of the dead woman. With the same poison he killed his brother, C. Oppianicus. Nor is this enough; although in this very fraternal <term>parricidium</term> <gloss>murder of a relative</gloss> no crime seems to have been omitted, he nonetheless fortified his path beforehand with other crimes so that he could arrive at this nefarious deed. For when Auria, his brother's wife, was pregnant and it seemed that her delivery was approaching, he killed the woman with poison, so that with that one woman,</translation>

<keywords>Oppianicus, Sassia, Cluentia, Habitus, parricidium, murder, poisoning, judicial integrity</keywords>

But in the opinion of <term>Riccioli</term>, it descends from <term>παρὰ τῷ χεῖσθαι</term> <gloss>from the act of pouring</gloss>, a derivation that pleased the Stoics in particular, according to <term>Philo</term> in his work <term>On Incorruptibility</term>, and the author <term>Achilles Tatius</term> in his commentary on <term>Aratus</term>. 

In this way, it will signify confusion and many things mixed together or aggregated at once. But writers vary greatly in its origin as well as in its meaning. The Gentiles, besides <term>Aristotle</term> (who interprets it regarding place), seem commonly to have determined that it denotes matter unbegotten and existing before all Gods, or, as <term>Plato</term> speaks, before all things were made. Certainly, almost all who mention it agree equally that the <term>principium C. N.</term> <gloss>principle of the nature of things</gloss> is indicated by it. Yet what that is, and how it was established and constituted, is no more agreed upon among them than it is among clocks. Regarding this, as well as the order in which individual elements or bodies were separated or distinguished from it, see <term>Riccioli</term> or our own <term>Roeschelius</term>. <term>Burnet</term> sets it out in such a way as to establish the firstborn—as it were—of chaos, and its twins: Night and Tartarus, that is, the upper and lower body. The former he makes a dark air, impenetrable by the rays of the sun; the latter he makes Tartarus, or the abyss. Then he posits that Night, being pregnant, likewise bore twins: namely Earth and Aether, or the sublunary Heaven, that is, the region of purer air. Anyone can see, I think, that this most ingenious author <term>Aristophanes</term> gives much of his own into this. For besides the fact that neither a sign nor a trace of the distinction between aether and heaven appears in him, nor could an atmosphere be conceived at that time when the terrestrial globe was fashioned, with no vapors existing; furthermore, Night and Tartarus are not said by him to be generated from Chaos, but to have existed simultaneously with Chaos. Finally, he ascribes immense bays to Erebus, which he joins with the abyss and Tartarus—bays that certainly could not be described except incongruously regarding the terrestrial-aerial sphere, which scarcely accounts for itself as a point with respect to the Universe. These inconveniences, and others similar to them, all vanish of their own accord if it is said that <term>Aristophanes</term> held <term>Night, Tartarus, and Erebus</term> not as different offspring of Chaos, but as its parts, or rather its adjuncts or affections. Thus, Chaos signifies the matter, Night the darkness and privation of light, Tartarus the horrific confusion, and Erebus the vast emptiness or the </translation>

<translation page="16">measure, and denote them. It is as if he had wanted to say that the Chaos was an immense and boundless, and likewise formless, vastness; not unlike how the author of the Book of Wisdom says that God made the world from invisible and formless matter; or, as the Doctor of the Gentiles <note>St. Paul</note> speaks, that the ages were adjusted by the word of God, so that things visible might be made from things invisible. Or, if one must speak from the corpuscular philosophy, supported by experience and the firmest reasoning, [one would say that] the primary and infinite matter occupied the immense space with the force of its atoms.

§. XVI. These things are entirely conformable to the Mosaic narrative and agree excellently with the pronouncements and traditions of both Greek and barbarian philosophers. We will not be more laborious in citing these, since the Lord Master <term>Tentzel</term> has already occupied this entire province. We urge rather that <term>Aristophanes</term> clearly proclaims that the race of Gods did not exist before Love had mixed all things. That stars should be understood by these Gods, the formula of speaking <term>γένος ἀθανάτων</term> <gloss>the race of the immortals</gloss> proves more clearly than the midday sun; a term no one of the ancients—whether Pythagoreans, Platonists, or Peripatetics—ever applied to sublunary things. So much so that, although the <term>Pseudo-Hermes</term> states and maintains that nothing in the world dies, he nevertheless does not use the word <term>ἀθάνατον</term> <gloss>immortal</gloss>. The passages by which this assertion could be demonstrated are infinite; however, two may suffice: one from <term>Aristotle</term>, who says that all nations attribute the supreme place to the Gods, for the reason that <term>ὡς τῷ ἀθανάτῳ τὸ ἀθάνατον συνηρτημένον</term> <gloss>the immortal is connected to the immortal</gloss>; another from <term>Ocellus Lucanus</term>, asserting with an elegant simile that the course of the moon is the isthmus between mortality and immortality. Nor do the mythologists and cyclic poets say or teach anything else, for they all proceed in explaining their <term>Theogonies</term> <gloss>genealogies of the gods</gloss> in such a way that they narrate the creation or production of the Gods and the Theogony in a continuous series, with no space of time interposed. Regarding <term>Plato</term> and the Platonists, the same is most evident, so that to wish to declare it laboriously would be a waste of effort.

Nevertheless, we cannot help but add from <term>Proclus</term> that he calls the Gods the new and recent creators and producers of animals; elsewhere, however, he asserts that the same is the <term>Ὀρφικὸν ᾠὸν</term> <gloss>Orphic egg</gloss> and the <term>τοῦ πλάτωνος ὄν</term> <gloss>that which is of Plato</gloss>. These latter points not only show that the ancients understood nothing else by the egg than Chaos itself, but they also reveal the foundation or the occasion of the opinion regarding the pre-existence of antemundane matter. Namely, because whatever Gods they spoke of besides the supreme God—whom they called the one, the good, <term>ἀνουσίαον</term> <gloss>without substance/essence</gloss>, and endowed with non-essence—such as the stars, demons, or indeed the very mind and Soul of the World, they believed to be entities produced by the supreme God. Yet they believed these recently produced Gods received the matter from which they fashioned sublunary bodies as already prepared and existing. They could not help but posit matter as eternal, because before the time that began as soon as the mundane bodies were produced, there was mere eternity.

§. XVII. That <term>Aristophanes</term> says Night laid the first wind-egg does not hinder the truth, and shows only that he did not sufficiently grasp the Mosaic doctrine, nor could he attain to the incubating or brooding of the Divine Love; thus, he adorned the opinion according to the capacity of his own intellect. So that this single difficulty cannot at all cause us to refrain from subscribing to the opinion—having dismissed <term>Burnet’s</term> archaeology—that was sufficiently demonstrated by <term>Hugo Grotius</term>, <term>Edmund Dickinson</term>, <term>Jacob Tollius</term>, and <term>Adam Tribbechovius</term>.</translation>

<summary>This section examines the etymology of "chaos" and its interpretations by classical philosophers and theologians, ultimately arguing that these classical accounts, including those of Aristophanes, largely mirror the Mosaic account of creation if understood through a proper philosophical lens.</summary>
<keywords>Chaos, Mosaic narrative, Aristophanes, Theogony, Matter, Creation, Philosophy, Ancient Theology</keywords>

### XL.

And a pact is considered again either in itself, or insofar as it is confirmed by law, or as it is added to a contract immediately.

### XLI.

The former is called a nude <note>original: "nudum" - a bare or informal agreement lacking legal enforceability</note> pact, whereas the latter are not called nude. Since these do not rest upon the nude terms of the agreement, but rather either adhere to a contract or have an assisting law, no one fails to see that they cannot be placed in the class of nude pacts. *Bachovius in his notes on the Disputations of Treutler.*

### XLII.

And these also can be called "clothed" <note>original: "vestita" - agreements supported by a cause or legal formality</note> without inconvenience; for although these words do not exist in the Law, it can hardly be denied that the thing itself exists. However, when the matter is clear, we must be lenient regarding words, by the *argument of law 17 of the Digest concerning laws.*

### XLIII.

A nude convention is that which rests on the mere end of an agreement, *law "if to you" 27, Code concerning hiring and letting*, or, what is the same thing, that which consists in the pure and simple terms of a convention.

### XLIV.

And it is called so because it is naked of a cause or business, *the said law "are accustomed" 15, Digest concerning prescribed words*, which also formally distinguishes this convention from a contract. Whence it is also called a simple convention in *law "ancestral" 6, Code concerning the Law of dowries*, and merely a pact in *law "greater" 23, Code concerning pledges and mortgages.*

### XLV.

For example, if it is agreed that you sell me your house, this convention stands in the nude terms of the agreement; but if it is agreed regarding the thing and the price, this convention is no longer

<summary>This page defines the distinction between nude (informal) and clothed (formally supported) pacts, explaining that simple agreements lack the legal cause required to form a binding contract.</summary>
<keywords>nude pact, clothed pact, convention, contract, Bachovius, Treutler</keywords></translation>

<translation page="11">

called a convention, because a business has been added which produces a civil obligation. A contract has been concluded, which is called purchase and sale, in the beginning of the law concerning purchase and sale, and in law "agreed pacts" 72, in the beginning of the Digest concerning the contracting of a purchase.

### XLVI.

Thus, if I agree with you that you should lend me money, or that you exchange your Cornelian estate for my house, up to this point, besides the nude convention and the nude agreement, nothing has been done. But as soon as you count out the money to me, or deliver the Cornelian estate to me, or I deliver my house to you, a business intervenes besides the convention, and in that case, a loan contract is made, in the beginning of the law concerning the ways in which an obligation is contracted by a thing; but this, indeed, is an exchange, *law "natural" 5, paragraph 1, Digest concerning prescribed words.*

### XLVII.

It is doubted whether the name "pact," pronounced simply, signifies a nude pact. I affirm this by *law "of the law of nations" 7, paragraph 5, Digest concerning pacts.* Those who think otherwise are moved by the above-mentioned law "by traditions" 20, there "not by nude pacts," in the Code concerning pacts. But Hunnius satisfies these in his resolutions on Treutler, Disputation 9, question 5.

### XLVIII.

A nude pact, however, is either express or tacit, which is understood from the actions of the contracting parties, and it is said to be entered into by the thing itself in *law 2, Digest concerning pacts; law 32, Digest concerning partnership*. We have one example of this in *law 2, paragraph 1, Digest concerning pacts*: he who has returned a bond to a debtor is understood to have tacitly agreed not to sue. Another is in *law 3, Digest under the said title*, where he who returns a pledge is believed to have remitted the right of the pledge, not the debt itself.

<summary>This page illustrates the transition from a nude convention to a binding contract through performance and explains the nature of tacit versus express pacts.</summary>
<keywords>contract, obligation, purchase and sale, loan, exchange, Hunnius, tacit pact, express pact</keywords></translation>

The *Inaugural Dissertation on Malignant Fever of the Most Illustrious Licentiate* J. C. Wolff of Servest, formerly my most pleasant colleague, held at Wittenberg under the Excellent Doctor Berger, Public Professor there and venerable preceptor, will shed light on this opinion.

However, for a more relaxed degree of fermentation, the sick person does not feel those discomforts.

A proclivity to sleep is also an effect of the viscosity, thickness, and scarcity of the animal spirits and other liquids, or even of compression of the brain. Nevertheless, somnolence is not an inseparable attribute of <term>Hemicrania</term> <gloss>migraine</gloss>, as the previously praised Piso seems to hint. But excessive vigils otherwise urge, and that on account of the atrocity of the pains. A cold sweat occurs, insofar as the glandular context and tone on the surface of the body is too relaxed, whence an easy exit for the serum is open by any given gate; and it is cold where the humors, and especially the blood, pass through the small canals so slowly that they cannot produce that agitation which represents heat to the mind, then on account of the solid parts, among which the heart holds primacy, relaxing from a constrictive motion. With the nervous genus corrupted, and the humors also corrupted, what good shall we hope for from the stomach? XII. If we now recall to mind all the things said thus far with a little more curiosity, what great *dangers* do we not see present for the sick? And what even greater ones do we not fear, not without the support of reason? We do not hesitate to affirm that <term>Hemicrania</term> <gloss>migraine</gloss> is a most dangerous disease, in whatever way it behaves. Indeed, both the affected part is most sensitive and must provide help to the economy of the body, and the producing causes are extremely grave. Moreover, the disease is most difficult to cure, both because its various causes must be torn out by the roots before it can be removed, and because hardly any remedy can be found to reduce the solid parts, which are twisted against nature, to a state according to nature. But above all, it is the fact that only half of the head is affected that renders the evil stubborn. For a remedy, however much it may wash the affected place, will work sparingly, seeking an exit where it finds the least resistance of all. I pass over the fact that what is assumed is not specifically determined here or there, but is distributed through the whole body by the law of circulation. Wherefore *External Hemicrania*, where medicines immediately touch the affected part, bids us be more secure, unless caries of the skull is joined to it.
