XVII. He who denies that *ens* <gloss>being</gloss> as such is the object of Metaphysics, because all things that are handled in this discipline, such as first principles, axioms, hypotheses, primary definitions, the doctrine of primary substance and its operations and attributes, cannot be recalled to this, should also deny that a natural body as such is the object of Physics, because not all things treated in Physics are natural bodies, for example, matter, form, nature, place, time, quantity, quality, sound, sight, and so on. Even though not everything belongs to any discipline that this or that person designates.

XVIII. Whoever said that he who wishes to use abstractions in other philosophical disciplines besides Mathematics abstracts the mind from truth, because things must be known as they are found in the nature of things, not as certain things are or can be abstracted from them, was either playing with ambiguity or did not understand abstraction.

XIX. There is great debate among the ancients whether virtue can be learned, with some affirming it is given to the good by nature and denied to the wicked, while others assert it is acquired through practice and doctrine. Plato seems to agree with the former at times and with the latter at other times; but there is no doubt that virtue is established and perfected by nature (if it is not inherently depraved) and by precepts, exercise, and instruction: what the ancients called <term>φύσιν, λόγον καὶ ἄσκησιν</term> <gloss>nature, reason, and practice</gloss>: which are as necessary in virtue as in the arts, and even in crops, for which one needs rich soil, good seeds, and the farmer's diligence. Ludovicus Vives, *on chapter 1, book 19 of the City of God, column 1141; add Augustine in the stated book, chapter 4, column 1148.* The Philosopher elsewhere: Plutarch, the treatise *Whether Virtue is Teachable, page 370.*

XX. Everyone always desires the good: Plato in *Hipparchus*. For all good things are useful: the same in *Meno*.

XXI. Poverty, the sister of a good mind, as Petronius says in the *Satyricon, page 94*, seems preferable to riches; for it teaches all arts, wherever it touches anyone, says Plautus in the *Stichus. Add Seneca, epistle 15, and Theocritus.* For usually Necessity and Sobriety accompany them, and it makes men attentive and circumspect, whereas good fortune and opulence beget negligence. Hence, the intellect is sharpened, from which the arts arise. Indeed, as Apuleius says, it has never inflated anyone with pride, nor depraved anyone with power, nor brutalized anyone with tyranny; it neither desires nor can tolerate the delicacies of the belly and loins. For these and other crimes are the usual companions of wealth; and although we read that even the poorest men have committed the greatest crimes, many were not poor, but beggars; this distinction is provided by Aristophanes in *Plutus, page 11*:

> The life of a beggar, which you speak of, is to live having nothing,

<keywords>Metaphysics, Physics, Virtue, Poverty, Nature, Philosophy, Wealth</keywords></translation>

### XXII. Hesiod teaches in these verses that the care of human affairs lies with the <term>Genii</term> <gloss>guardian spirits</gloss> by the permission of the supreme Emperor:

> For there are noble spirits upon the earth,
> holy, the averters of evil, guardians of mortal men,
> who watch over judgments and wicked deeds,
> clothed in mist, wandering everywhere over the earth:

It is probable, therefore, that some of the <term>Genii</term> <gloss>guardian spirits</gloss> act as envoys or tribunes to care for peoples and regions: Theodoret holds that these are Archangels (on chapter 10 of Daniel, cited by Besold). Certainly, that the Lord Michael presides over my Poland is made credible by the fact that, before the victory against the Lithuanians, which was obtained without a single Pole being killed, he was seen in Poland, as the histories attest; hence, a Basilica was eventually built to him in Lublin. What of the fact that this kingdom extends most vastly toward the North, and thence, according to the dictum of Scripture, comes evil; that is, the greatest part of the <term>Alastores</term> <gloss>avenging spirits</gloss> are stabled there. Hence, Nicephorus Gregoras writes that the Chaldeans considered Orcus <gloss>the underworld</gloss> to be the prince of the farthest and adjacent earthly inheritance, which fell to him by lot: <term>τῆς ἐσχάτης καὶ περιγείου λήξεως ἀρχηγόν</term> <gloss>the leader of the outermost and earthly lot</gloss>.

### XXIII. Among men, he who has been raised by the gift of fortune to opulence, and elevated to the changeable throne of a kingdom and a swinging tribunal, lives rarely accessible and with attendants kept far away in certain inner chambers of his dignity, says Apuleius in *On the God of Socrates*.

And among the Persians, that the person of the King is hidden under the guise of Majesty is testified by Justin (book 1, page 10) and Herodotus (Clio); they seem to have received this custom from the Chaldeans. For among them, Ninus, the son of Semiramis, satisfied with the empire elaborated by his parents, laid aside the studies of war, and as if he had exchanged sex with his mother, he rarely seen by men, grew old among a crowd of women. His descendants also followed that example and gave responses to the nations through intermediaries (Justin, loc. cit., page 4). They themselves indulged only in the pleasures of the body, and especially those that are more immersed in matter than others, which the senses of touch and taste provide, and they led a life not unlike that of a sea-lung <note>a primitive biological reference to a life of low activity</note>. Much more rightly, Emperor Leo says in *Tactica* (ch. 16, §. 21, p. 245): <term>οἱ ἀναβαλλομένοι καὶ ἀπρόσιτοι καὶ τοῖς ὑπηρέταις αὑτῶν κελεύοντες ἀνακόπτειν τοὺς οὕτως προσερχομένους, πολλῶν καὶ μεγάλων εἰκότως ἁμαρτάνουσι πραγμάτων</term> <gloss>Those who are procrastinating and inaccessible, and who order their servants to turn away those who approach, deservedly err in many great matters</gloss>. Nor is there any reason for Apuleius to say (loc. cit.) that association breeds contempt, and that rarity itself procures admiration for things; let us hear Synesius, *Oration on Kingship* (p. 20), arguing as Petavius translates: *No one has yet despised the sun, although what is there that is seen more frequently?* Therefore, the King, if he is to be true, and otherwise he cannot...

<summary>The author explores the roles of guardian spirits, the historical precedents for royal seclusion among the Persians and Chaldeans, and the importance of accessibility for rulers.</summary>
<keywords>Guardian spirits, Archangels, Poland, Michael, Kingly duty, Nicephorus Gregoras, Synesius, Inaccessibility</keywords></translation>

<translation page="14">

### XXX.

Nor does it hinder [our position] that the Church in this life is subject to immense miseries, is deformed by many scandals, and is still weak, carrying about many signs of guilt, whence it has need of constant prayer, as witnessed by Psalm 32, verse 6, and concerning which it is said in the Lord’s Prayer, Matthew 6, verse 12: "Forgive us our debts." For it is adorned with the remission of sins, the Son of God sanctifying Himself for it (John 17, verse 19). And by His merit He covers its remaining filth, applying His righteousness to it, and granting it the Holy Spirit, who ignites new light and life in the hearts of the faithful. This ornament is that gilded garment in which, according to Psalm 45, verse 10, the queen stands at the right hand of this king, and which the same Psalm affirms, in verse 14, to be internal and not to be beheld by human eyes.

### XXXI.

But other, rotten and dead members are spoken of, and they are trees that are withered and barren (Ezekiel 20, verse 47); a fruitless fig tree having nothing "but leaves only" (Matthew 21, verse 19); foolish virgins who, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them (Matthew 25, verse 2); tares, and the children and seed of the Devil (Matthew 13, verse 38; Genesis 3, verse 15); men, that is to say, not reborn nor holy, even if they agree regarding the doctrine as far as the foundation is concerned. For they live without repentance and faith, and are not quickened and governed by the Spirit of Christ, even if they dwell in the external society of the pious. Yet, who would call those in whom Christ does nothing but dead members of Christ and the Church?

### XXXII.

But if they are not only secure hypocrites, but also dissent from the foundation and doctrine of truth, and become either defenders or approvers of false doctrine that overturns the foundation, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3, verse 5), and if they pertinaciously persist in those manifest errors, which the true Church judges to be condemned according to the standard of the Prophetic and Apostolic writings: then we maintain that they are not even to be considered dead members, but altogether as <term>ἀναθέμασι</term> <gloss>accursed things</gloss></translation>

<translation page="15">and blasphemers, and that they are outside the Church, even if they dare to arrogate to themselves the title and name of the Church, which the <term>Pontificij</term> <gloss>Papists</gloss> indeed do diligently. Because it is written, Galatians 1, verses 8 and 9: "If anyone preaches another Gospel, let him be <term>ἀναθέμα ἔστω</term> <gloss>accursed</gloss>."

### XXXIII.

That the holy ones, however, can also have some errors, but [errors] that do not overturn the articles of faith (for some build gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundation, while others build wood, hay, and stubble, as witnessed by Paul in 1 Corinthians 3, verse 12), is manifest from the example of the Apostles. In them, both before and after the resurrection, even though they had seen before their eyes the beginnings of new and eternal life and the restoration of our nature in the glorified body of Christ, there was such darkness and infirmity that they still dreamed that the Kingdom of the Messiah would be political (Acts 1, verse 6), and many wished for Levitical worship to be retained (Acts 15, verse 1).

### XXXIIII.

And too blind and unhappy is the arrogance and <term>φιλαυτία</term> <gloss>self-love</gloss> from which many suffer if we think there is nothing of infirmity in us, that we are ignorant of nothing, but are perfect and omniscient. For it is most true what Paul says, 1 Corinthians 13, verse 9: "We know in part, and we prophesy in part." And verse 12: "Now we see through a glass and in a riddle."

### XXXV.

But the pious, and those who are teachable, when admonished, return to the way, just as it is certain that the Apostles finally abandoned their dreams about the corporal Kingdom of the Messiah and the necessity of circumcision and other Levitical rites, having received the Holy Spirit, whom they did not resist—unlike the stubborn Jews—against conscience and so many and such great testimonies of the truth.

### XXXVI.

NOR do we, differing about the Church in the manner of which it has been spoken, dream of some Platonic <term>Idea</term> <gloss>Ideal form</gloss> or city existing nowhere on earth, and which consists only in the image of the mind; nor do we consider it to wander in darkness among <term>Andabatae</term> <gloss>gladiators who fought blindfolded</gloss>.</translation>

<summary>This section continues the discussion on the nature of the Church, distinguishing between the true, sanctified members of the Church and those who are merely external members or hypocrites. It further clarifies that while the Church is subject to human weakness and error, it remains the true body of Christ, distinct from heretical or "Platonic" conceptualizations of the Church.</summary>
<keywords>Ecclesiology, Remission of Sins, Holy Spirit, Hypocrites, False Doctrine, Apostolicity, Messiah, Platonic Idea</keywords>

## Q. III.

### *Does quantitative number pertain to Intelligences?*

The substances that theologians call Angels, metaphysicians name Intelligences. It is debated here regarding them: whether a quantitative number can be attributed to them. We stand firmly for the negative side, using such a shield: Where there is no quantity, there is no quantitative number. In intelligences, there is no quantity. Therefore. Do you doubt the minor premise? You do well: for always to doubt is always to inquire into a greater truth. But do you attack it? Attack it, provided you do not overcome it. For does quantity not belong only to material and corporeal things? Do you deny it? You strike against the philosophical principles; you rise up against Aristotle himself; against truth itself. Look at the species of quantity: the continuous is that whose parts are joined by some common boundary; the discrete, on the contrary, has parts that are neither joined nor fitted together by any such boundary (Aristotle, book of Categories, concerning quantity). Where, I ask, are there any parts in Intelligences? If these existed, they would surely make the very substance of the Angels either partible or divisible, they would surely give the intelligences themselves an extension of parts, they would surely consist of a body, they would surely participate in matter along with form, all of which are absurd. I add this as well: quantitative number is listed among the common sensibles (Aristotle, book 2 of On the Soul, chapter 6, text 64). If, therefore, intelligences are sensible, they must surely be perceived by the senses. Otherwise, with the thing that falls under the sense removed, the sense itself must necessarily be removed. But sense does not exist except in a body, and it is concerned with bodies (Aristotle, book of Categories, concerning quantity). But who, endowed with sound reason, would ever call Angels bodies?</translation>

You infer that quantity, although not predicamental, is nevertheless given in *Angels* as an intelligible quantity, such that our intellect conceives one thing in them that is not another? Indeed, the divine Intellect makes things conformable to its concept; but the human intellect itself is conformed to things. How then will you be able to form a quantity for yourself where there is no quantity at all? How will you be able to conceive one part distinct from another where there are absolutely no parts given, and therefore, how could distinct ones be given? Certainly, when you conceive a thing in this way, your intellect represents to you not a reality, but a figment of the brain and the imagination.

### §. 22.

In surgery, there is nothing that helps hectic patients. For venesection is just as harmful as purgation to all diseases arising from inanition <note>emptiness/wasting</note>, such as hectic fever, according to <term>Forestus</term>, who in *Book 4, Observation*, reports that he noted a noble matron with hectic fever who, after having her vein opened by an empiric, died shortly thereafter. Another person afflicted with hectic fever, ignoring the warnings of <term>Forestus</term> and persuaded by a surgeon and a charlatan, also allowed a venesection; and on the following day, after taking a single pill of <term>precipitato</term> <gloss>precipitated mercury</gloss> from a quack, died on the same day.

### §. 23.

In pharmacy, many praise metallic medicines, asserting that because they are more generous, they restore almost every patient to health, let alone the hectic. But <term>Sennertus</term>, in *On the Agreement and Disagreement of Chemists, Chapter 18*, affirms that <term>Spirit of Salt</term> and similar things, which can be exhibited more safely than metallic ones, can often cause the greatest harm when used, as they consume the natural humidity by drying it out; and therefore, he argues that their use should be guarded against in dry bodies (such as are those of hectic patients). This may be said with better reason regarding the metallic medicines, with which many boast they have cured hectic patients, and which are in common daily use. On the same foundation, <term>Bravo de Sobremonte</term>, in *Medical Resolutions* (fol.), disapproves of the rashness of <term>Paracelsus</term>, who uses a single diaphoretic in every fever, and thus also in hectic fever: [this is] contrary to the indication that demands nutrition, not a vehement dissipation of moisture. He also cannot help but find fault with <term>Helmontius</term>, because he uses the same diaphoretic</translation>

<translation page="15">of <term>Paracelsus</term>—which is indeed drying and heating, and consumes the vital forces no less than the hectic fever itself—even though he solemnly affirms in his book on fevers that it performs its effects imperceptibly and without sweat, and that it cures a hectic patient within the course of a month.

### §. 24.

<term>Poterius</term> also presses his thumb to this when he testifies from his own experience in *Book 2 on Fevers, Chapter 25*, that he cured a fifty-year-old suffering for four years from a slow fever of the hectic type with <term>Magnetic sugar</term>. He restored another of the same sort to health within a month by giving his <term>antihectic</term> in a conserve of roses twice a day. <term>P. J. Faber</term> joins him in asserting the same utility of metallic substances for hectic patients, recounting in *Curation of Various Diseases, Curation 14*, a desperate case of hectic fever [treated with] the use of <term>Spirit of acid Salt</term> and <term>Tincture of Sun</term> <gloss>gold extract</gloss> extracted with rectified <term>Oil of Salt</term>. I also know those for whom dry <term>Salt</term> is in use for essentially moistening the withered body of hectic patients. Others praise the <term>Balsam of Life</term>, as they call it, which they prepare thus: They take two and a half ounces of <term>Salt</term>. They melt two drachms of the purest <term>Gold</term>. They pulverize it, extract it with <term>Spirit of Salt</term>, and abstract it to the consistency of oil. They instill this into one drachm of pulverized <term>Salt of Pearls</term>. Mix in a marble mortar, dry over a slow fire, and regenerate gradually until it acquires a purple color. They exhibit from five to ten grains in a restorative broth quite often; and from this they hope that the substantial moisture consumed by the hectic heat will be restored, as if by an essentially moistening substance being substituted.

We embrace a healthier opinion on curing hectic fever, as much as possible, together with <term>Sennertus</term>. ### XXVII.

Item: if he does not administer justice to the Vassal, he is restricted by the same loss.

And regularly, if the lord commits a felony against the Vassal, through which, if the Vassal had committed it, he would lose the fief, he forfeits the ownership of the feudal property.

### XXIX.

However, because the mention is made by us mostly regarding that loss of the Fief which deprives the Vassal, it is not inconvenient to add here that there are some cases in which the Vassal does not lose the fief, even if the loyalty, which joins both the Vassal and the Lord, does not exist and is not provided.

### XXX.

For instance, if the lord of the fief is excommunicated, banned, a condemned heretic, guilty of treason <note>original: "laesae Maiestatis reus"</note>, etc.

### XXXI.

Item: if against honesty, possibility, or another immoderate command</translation>

### XXXII.
Fiefs being lost for various reasons, it is a question: Do Fiefs open entirely and indistinctly to the Lord? Or, according to the variety of the causes, sometimes to the lord, sometimes indeed to others? Which is more true.

### XXXIII.
It is asked whether the power of renouncing a fief is free, or whether it ought to depend on the consent of the lord? Which seems uncivil, for it is permitted to renounce gains.

### XXXIIII.
Therefore, the fief being renounced, it returns, in the case where it is new, to the Lord, notwithstanding that loss may occur to the children therefrom; but in the case where it is paternal or ancient, it devolves to the male children, or to the agnates <note>relatives on the male side</note>, if they are lacking.

### XXXV.
A brother renouncing a fief in favor of a brother, to whom it was later assigned, and he died without heirs, is not excluded from the fief.</translation>

Since the right education of youth is the foundation of the entire Republic, it prevents and stands against, through the solicitous care of education—the foundation, as it were—any possibility that the structure built upon it might develop cracks, threaten ruin, or be entirely shaken and collapse. Whoever has not seen or heard the public specimens of such great and provident care for the Schools, issued by the Most Ample Senate, must be regarded as being in great ignorance of the affairs of Wrocław <note>original: "Vratislaviensium"</note>.

I am not ignorant of what was done six years ago in our Magdalenian School. While elsewhere things were then either growing sparse or those places were bitterly grieving their own emptiness, our school was seen not only to be built up higher and amplified—with new stories added, and with the third furnace <note>original: "Hypocaustum"</note> as well as the boarding rooms <note>original: "cubicula Convictorum"</note> facing South and North providing a pleasant and delightful atmosphere—but also to have the number of its students increased with eagerness. I will not mention other recognized experiments of care regarding the School: among which you might not undeservedly include the convenient separation of the lower ranks. By this, it was brought about that students could not interfere with one another or with the Masters, and that the confusion of languages, or of voices, might not avert the ears or minds of some from the study of letters, as those two Emperors, Theodosius and Valentinian, say. (Code, Book 11, Title 18.)

I shall state here, or touch upon only lightly, those things which, long deliberated beforehand, have only recently been very prudently and usefully established regarding the two principal Schools, namely our Magdalenian school. There, one truly discerns divine and human things, to use a Plautine word. They piously command that divine worship and prayers, for the health of the public Schools, be religiously continued no less in the public assemblies of the Temples than in those of the Schools</translation>

<translation page="8">in the beginning of the Constitutions: that all things are managed well and competently if the beginning of the matter is made decent and pleasing to **GOD**. (Novellae VI, Justinian, in the Preface to Epiphanius, Patriarch of Constantinople.) Human affairs, which are established, are committed to be carried out both to the civil Magistracy and to the Order of Scholastic Masters. The former testifies that it has undertaken, and will undertake, care and thought as much for the Persons as for the Things pertaining to the School.

<margin>III.</margin>
Regarding Persons: *when it increased and amplified the octonary number of our College by the addition of three new members, one in the highest and two in the lower ranks, according to a vow—[members] who had hitherto labored in misery—at all hours, [it] augmented and amplified [the number] of colleagues.*

<margin>IV.</margin>
Regarding Things: *when it partly doubled and partly increased the salaries of the teachers, and when it deemed that the studies of the students should be excited and inflamed by distributing prizes for diligence after public examinations; indeed, it has already recently begun to excite and inflame them.* 

<margin>V.</margin>
*Which munificence and liberality of the Magnificent Senate, who among those who either teach or learn could fail to embrace and kiss with grateful hearts? Among them, I truly give and hold the greatest thanks to **GOD** and the **Magistracy**, and I will hold and shall owe them for as long as I remain in this image; nor would I wish for anything more than to recover several years already passed (I cannot complain that my strength has failed) with this sole purpose: that I might be able to sufficiently prove and demonstrate my gratitude and desire to serve to **GOD**, the **Magistracy**, and this noble **Republic**, my nurturer and promoter. After this care of the Magistracy, Doctrine and Discipline are committed to the order of Masters. We find the former distinguished*</translation>

> It is held in ecclesiastical preaching that there are certain Angels of GOD, but it is not sufficiently clearly distinguished when they were created.

## APHORISM III.

->*Angels are spirits, intelligent and wise, good, holy, powerful, destined for the ministry of GOD, for the salvation of men.*<-

### I. EXPOSITION.

1. Since human language stammers when dealing with matters removed from the senses, let a moderate description of the Angels—those most blessed minds, as removed as possible from the senses—suffice for us, such as our aphorism has just provided.
2. It describes the Angels as they were from their first origin, and it establishes their *Genus* as *Spirits*.
3. To them it attributes *accidents* or concrete *Qualities*, such as intelligence, wisdom, goodness, holiness, and power. We intend for all these predicates to be understood restrictedly and in their own kind, not absolutely. For as soon as you compare these to the spirituality, intelligence, goodness, etc., of GOD, as great a difference presents itself as exists between the infinite and the finite, between the essential and the accidental, between the Creator and the created, and between immutable and mutable holiness, goodness, and so forth.
4. *It reports that their duty is twofold; one part is considered with respect to GOD, the other with respect to men.*

<summary>The text reviews various theological opinions on the timing of the creation of angels, ultimately adopting Origen's view that their precise origin is not explicitly revealed in scripture, followed by a formal definition of the nature of angels.</summary>
<keywords>Angels, Creation, Origen, On First Principles, Spirit, Essence, Accidents</keywords></translation>

<translation page="11">accidental, between the Creator and the created, between the immutable and the mutable holiness, goodness, and the rest.
4. *It reports that their duty is twofold; one part is considered with respect to GOD, the other with respect to men.*

->CONFIRMATION.<-

5. Scripture itself confirms this nature of the Angels, and indeed confirms that Angels are *Spirits*. 1. By calling them simply *Spirits*, Psalm 104:4, Hebrews 1, *last verse*: Are they not all (the Angels) ministering spirits? 2. By denying them *matter*, in that they do not have flesh and blood, Ephesians 6:12; nor flesh and bones, Luke 24:39.
6. II. It attributes *concreated qualities* to them. And the woman of Tekoa says that Angels are *intelligent*: My lord, she says, is wise according to the wisdom of an Angel of GOD, so that he knows everything that is on the earth, 2 Samuel 14:20.
7. They are called *good* by the Creator himself. For GOD saw all things that He had made, and behold, they were all very good, Genesis 1:31. But the Angels were made by GOD, see above, aphorism 1. Therefore they are also good, by the goodness of creation, as the theologians like to speak.
8. They are called *holy*, Luke 9:26, Acts 10:22.
9. They are *powerful* in virtue, Psalm 103:20: not to mention here the works of the Angels, which sufficiently demonstrate their power, which is to be admired, see above, aphorism 1, thesis 9, and the names of principalities, powers, virtues, and thrones, which they receive in scripture.
10. III. The *duty* which they perform with respect to GOD is the celebration of His name. For the Cherubim and Seraphim sing: Holy, Holy, Holy, and so forth, Isaiah 6:3. And the execution of His commands. Hence thousands of thousands minister to Him, and ten times a hundred thousand stand before Him, Daniel 7:10. Psalm 103:20, 21 speaks of both of these duties.

<summary>This page confirms the nature and duties of angels through scriptural references, establishing their existence as spiritual beings, their intelligence, goodness, holiness, and power, and their specific roles in praising God and executing His commands.</summary>
<keywords>Angels, Scripture, Spirit, Goodness, Holiness, Power, Cherubim, Seraphim, Divine Service</keywords></translation>

XIX. Since it is the duty of the supreme powers to preserve the true worship of God and to protect the people under the true religion, and since such protection often cannot be provided without the aid of arms, those who rule can hardly afford to lack the virtue of courage. *The Republic ought to be fortified and adorned not only by religion and justice but also by arms and military discipline,* according to Isaiah the Pontiff in *Florilegium*, ch. 3. Consequently, a Queen, sufficiently armed with the shield of saving religion, must also be equipped with arms; if the aforementioned religion is defended by their use, the assaults of enemies are repelled, and more powerful forces are warded off by the lesser, such arms are not wrongly called pious. *And this courage, which defends the fatherland from barbarians through war, or protects the weak, or shields allies from brigands, is full of justice.* Ambrose, *On Duties*.

Tomyris, having gathered her forces, clashed with Cyrus in such a way that this battle is said to have been the fiercest of all among the barbarians; Herodotus, book 1. built in a square, covered with silk and most precious cloths, and surrounded on all sides by railings, outside of which the spectators stand. A small door provides access to this tower or shrine; connected to it is another area where, on one side, there are twenty books and, on the other, twenty-five books, bound most preciously, which contain the life and laws of Muhammed and his companions. In the lowest part of the tower, the aforementioned man adds, the underground sepulchre of Muhammed is shown, in which certain of his friends are likewise buried, namely Haly, Othmann, Abubecer, and Homar; the two highest of whom were companions of Muhammed. These things, I say, Varthema testifies as an eyewitness. Moreover, that others have commonly persuaded the public—perhaps more out of hatred for the religion than a pursuit of truth—that the sepulchre of Muhammed hangs under the vault of the temple by a magnet, or was driven to the underworld by lightning, is shown to be far from the truth by the most consistent report of men returning every year from Medina to Egypt, and by the accepted accurate floor plan, which includes an explicit diagram of the entire temple. Prosper Alpinus also mentions this, in the following manner: It was built alongside the tombs of his father-in-law and his son-in-law, with a simple but precious stone; then it is fortified by a square-perimeter enclosure. The enclosure that closest surrounds the tomb is of lower structure and contains a diamond inserted into the inner face of the wall, which they proclaim to be the most noble of all that the sun sees, in magnitude and appearance, and through the reflection of rays captured from the sun, it shines upon the ark of the lying Muhammed like a celestial brightness. A veil, splendid with gold and gems, adorns the intermediate partition. The Byzantine emperors solemnly send this to Medina, and when it is carried in public procession through the city of Cairo, the Viceroy of Egypt and the nobility, as well as several myriads of the people, follow it reverently outside the gates. Outside these enclosures of the sepulchre, the monument of Fatima, daughter of Muhammed, [is seen], and the cases of several sacred books are visible.

### CHAPTER IV.
#### Concerning
# The Division of Nobility
# On the Division of the Nobility.

§. 1. A single division of nobility does not exist. <term>Plato</term> divided it into four species, the first of which consists of those who are born of illustrious, good, and just ancestors. Then, he called those noble whose parents had been noble and princes of the same. Thirdly, he wanted those to be called noble whose ancestors had been famous in fame and reputation, whether from clearly conducted deeds of war or from crowns of contests. Finally, he considered the most excellent genus of nobility to be when someone excelled by himself through greatness of soul. Compare <term>Plutarch</term>, book 10, *Against Nobility*.

§. 2. <term>Aristotle</term> distinguishes between the nobility of the lineage and that of the city, along with private nobility, in book 1 of his *Rhetoric to Theodectes*, chapter 5, such that he says the former's splendor lies in being indigenous and most ancient, and the first illustrious leaders; and that many from that lineage have also stood out in matters that are sought after. Private nobility, however, is from either men or women and legitimate procreation from them.

§. 3. <term>Gregorius Nazianzenus</term> makes a triple genus of nobility: one which draws its origin from above, as are all who are created in the image of God; the second, which proceeds from blood; the third is recognized from virtue and vice. Discourse 18; compare discourse 28.

§. 4. <term>Piccolomineus</term> says that six degrees of nobility can be established: first, he makes it of divine nobility; (2) Metaphysical; (3) Inspecting; (4) Civil; (5) Physical; (6) Of Fortune. Which, however, he shortly after contracts into only four forms, namely divine, moral, natural, and the nobility of fortune. Divine, as he speaks, approaches God most closely; Moral, which he also names the nobility of the soul, consists in the composition of morals and the habit of virtue. Natural</translation>

Danaus had fifty daughters, and Aegyptus an equal number of sons. When they contended among themselves for the kingdom, Danaus killed the sons of Aegyptus, save for one or two, by the agency of his daughters; for he had received an oracle that his death was imminent at the hands of one of them. Struck by fear, by the counsel of Minerva he was the first to construct a ship, which he named from the number of his daughters a *pentēkontoros* <note>a fifty-oared ship</note>, and having placed his daughters on board, he fled. From there, landing in Rhodes, he dedicated a statue to Minerva of Lindus. Thence he betook himself to Argos and the kingdom was handed over to him by Helanor, who was reigning at Argos at that time (and having taken possession of that region, he called the inhabitants Danaans after his own name). But because that region suffered from a scarcity of water, since Neptune, in his anger, had dried up the springs for Inachus—because he had testified that it was the land of Minerva—he sent out his daughters in the meantime to fetch water. One of them, Amymone, searching for water, threw a spear at a deer and struck a sleeping satyr. Wherefore, awakened from sleep, he was seized with a wondrous desire to possess the girl. But at the arrival of Neptune, the satyr took to flight. Amymone, however, lay with him, and to her Neptune revealed the springs of Lerna. Furthermore, the sons of Aegyptus set out for Argos to restrain the mutual enmity between them; they exhorted one another and begged that the daughters of Danaus be given to them in marriage. Then Danaus, partly because he little trusted their promises, and partly because he remembered the injury of his flight and exile, having agreed to the nuptials, began to distribute the girls by lot. Therefore, he chose Hypermnestra, the eldest of the daughters, for Lynceus, and Gorgophone for Proteus. For Aegyptus had fathered these from his wife, Queen Argyphia. From then on, each chose his lot.

But the girls who were Ethiopians, because they were namesakes to Memphis, by no means wished to be joined among themselves by lot. For Clitus, born of a Tyrian mother, married Clite; Sthenelus, Sthenele; and Chrysippus, Chrysippe. And from Caliadis and the naiad nymph, twelve sons were born, along with as many daughters of Polyron the naiad. These are the names of the former: Eurylochus, Phantes, Peristhenes, Hermus, Dryas, Potamon, Cilleus, Lixus, Imbrus, Bromius, Polyctor, and Chthonius. ### XVI. Other Onerous Contracts.

Not only is the real <term>census</term> <gloss>ground rent or annuity</gloss> permitted, but also the personal one, and not only the irredeemable one, but also the redeemable one, both on the part of the buyer and the seller. A dry exchange <note>referring to a bill of exchange that hides usurious interest</note> does not know how to produce just profit. The justice of a real exchange, whether local, manual, or by letter, is easily preserved. A contract of partnership can be made so that one contributes capital, the other industry. For a valid game, among other things, it is required that the risk be equal on both sides; and for a wager, there must be equal conditions for the bettors. The lessor must especially provide for the preservation of the leased thing. A depositary is sometimes liable for slight fault. <note>Law 12, Digest on deposit.</note> A loan for use cannot be reclaimed by itself before the time elapsed for which it was granted. If a borrowed thing perishes by accident without the fault of the borrower, it perishes for the owner. <note>Law final, Digest on loan for use.</note> A precarious grant is not ended by the death of the grantor. A non-sworn suretyship of a woman for her husband is void. Even rights can be pledged or mortgaged.

II. As for the place in Matthew 18:17, to which the Protestor appeals several times, it is likewise <term>kenē askopa</term> <gloss>empty and aimless</gloss> in relation to this argument of Augustine. For it does not speak of the interpretation of Scripture at the whim of the Church or of controversies, but precisely of private injuries and offenses. But let it be so. Let us grant to some Papist Exceptors that it can also be understood in a broader sense regarding injuries that are done to the whole Church and to God himself, namely, through the perverse interpretation of Scripture and through heresies. Indeed, we ought to hear the Church; but it is not to be heard simply and in all things. No less must we reverently obey the leaders and pastors of the churches in the Lord (2 Thessalonians 3:14; Hebrews 13:17), yet not absolutely, but conditionally: insofar as and for as long as they hear the voice of the chief Pastor, Christ Jesus, correctly propose his Word, and keep themselves within the bounds of their calling. One must not believe or obey simply and in all things without any <term>dokimasia</term> <gloss>testing/examination</gloss> (that is, the examination of interpretations, dogmas, and rites proposed by others according to the standard of the divine Word), and without any discernment of all things, as if with closed eyes. It is just as the Pharisees were teachers and interpreters who were to be heard in part, insofar as they sat in the seat of Moses (Matthew 23:2), but in part were not to be heard, but avoided, insofar as they brought forth the leaven of their own doctrine and human traditions, infecting the healthy sense of Scripture (Matthew 16:6, 12).

Therefore, we maintain that there is absolutely no church on earth, whether it be particular or universal, that is not perpetually and simply bound to the written Word of God, and that is not held to derive and explain to others who ask, the reason for both its dogmas and</translation>

<translation page="16">its rites. Thus, pastors are not to be obeyed except at the altars, or not except in the Lord, as the Holy Scriptures speak. Nor is any of their dogmas to be held as a fundamental article of faith whose solid and open foundations we have not first discovered in the Word of God itself. Even if we know for certain that the Church in which we live is true, and that the pastors we hear are orthodox, yet we should not believe either them or these others absolutely. For it is possible that even a true Church and even orthodox teachers may hallucinate in interpreting the Scriptures, gradually deflect from the truth, and begin to put forward erroneous opinions, as happened to many churches in the times of the Old and New Testaments.

One must not believe or obey simply and in all things without any <term>dokimasia</term> <gloss>testing/examination</gloss> (that is, the examination of interpretations, dogmas, and rites proposed by others according to the standard of the divine Word), and without any discernment of all things, as if with closed eyes. It is just as the Pharisees were teachers and interpreters who were to be heard in part, insofar as they sat in the seat of Moses (Matthew 23:2), but in part were not to be heard, but avoided, insofar as they brought forth the leaven of their own doctrine and human traditions, infecting the healthy sense of Scripture (Matthew 16:6, 12).

Therefore, we maintain that there is absolutely no church on earth, whether it be particular or universal, that is not perpetually and simply bound to the written Word of God, and that is not held to derive and explain to others who ask, the reason for both its dogmas and
pages.16:
its rites. Thus, pastors are not to be obeyed except at the altars, or not except in the Lord, as the Holy Scriptures speak. Nor is any of their dogmas to be held as a fundamental article of faith whose solid and open foundations we have not first discovered in the Word of God itself. Even if we know for certain that the Church in which we live is true, and that the pastors we hear are orthodox, yet we should not believe either them or these others absolutely. For it is possible that even a true Church and even orthodox teachers may hallucinate in interpreting the Scriptures, gradually deflect from the truth, and begin to put forward erroneous opinions, as happened to many churches in the times of the Old and New Testaments.

III. Thus, to say something about the Pauline passage: the *Church is the pillar and foundation of the truth*, but because of the Holy Scripture which it faithfully embraces, guards, commends, teaches, explains, and propagates. If it retreats from this, it is not only not the firmament of truth, but it even loses the truth itself.

Hence, the true Church interprets Scripture from Scripture. With <term>Tertullian</term> in his book *On the Flesh of Christ*, it receives nothing that anyone introduces from their own mind outside of Scripture; with <term>Hilary</term>, it does not bring an understanding of the sayings, but draws it back from Scripture. It pronounces on articles of faith only from the one Holy Scripture and according to its perpetual analogy, in this way above others:

In the parables of Scripture, it does not rashly urge other things outside the intended scope. It does not allow theological allegory to be argumentative, or rather, it does not constitute and build up dogma from mere figures and allegories, according to <term>Jerome</term>. Whatever in divine discourse cannot be properly referred either to the honesty of morals or to the truth of faith, it recognizes as figurative, with <term>Augustine</term> in *On Christian Doctrine*, book 3, chapter 10. Or, when the absurdity of the letter clashes with other clearer places of Scripture, or with articles of faith, it corrects it by the benefit of figures so that the meaning is retained, not the literal <term>rhēton</term> <gloss>the spoken/literal word</gloss>. Therefore, from figuratively spoken things, and those that treat a matter incidentally, it appeals to the seat of some article. For it extracts nothing from those more obscure matters that cannot be found said more plainly elsewhere, according to <term>Augustine</term>, *On Christian Doctrine*, book 2, chapter 6. so much to sobriety, that we would not suffer drunkenness to be even named among us. AP. Primarily, let the most shameful deeds of drunkards and their most inept behaviors drive away from us an immoderate habit of drinking. For what crimes do they abstain from? They cast aside all shame, they are inflamed with illicit lust, they bring forth the secrets of the soul, they wallow in filth, they walk without any control of their steps, they stagger, they vomit like beasts, they attack all the best men with slanders, they do not look to the work of God, nor do they consider the works of his hands. Now, indeed, when they have weakened their bodies with immense gluttony, and are exhausted by perpetrating the works of darkness, they collapse as if lifeless, lying prostrate on the ground after the manner of swine, so that it can be most truly said: A DRUNKARD IS A LIVING CORPSE. <margin>Isaiah 5.</margin> <margin>Chrysostom, On Prayer, book 2.</margin> Finally, let us be moved by profane men, the <term>Ethnici</term> <gloss>heathens/pagans</gloss>, who altogether condemned this detestable and abominable vice, so much so that Solon judged that a prince should be punished with death if he were discovered drunk. And it was not permitted for a king among the Indians to arrive at drunkenness through drinking. Among the Persians, however, this was granted to the king on only one day, on which they sacrificed to the sun. <margin>Athenaeus, book 10.</margin> NEPH. And I remember reading that Pittacus of Mitylene, not the least of the seven Greek Sages, passed a law that if any drunkard committed any crime whatsoever, he should be punished with a double penalty. AP. If, therefore, those who were ignorant of God so highly condemned, avoided, and punished this wickedness, what, I ask, do you think we Christians should do? <margin>Ephesians 5. Hosea 4. Augustine. Origen.</margin> NEPH. Let us strive so that we are never inebriated with wine, in which is <term>asōtia</term> <gloss>dissoluteness/profligacy</gloss>: let us despise and avoid drunkenness, which takes away the heart and memory, which dissipates the senses and confuses the intellect; and which makes a beast out of a man, a weakling out of a robust person, and a fool out of a prudent one. Let us instead burn with a desire for sobriety and temperance; and let us think that these are the very last times; let us revere and fear the long-suffering of God, lest we despise the riches of his goodness and patience. <margin>Ignatius, Epistle 11 to the Ephesians.</margin>
</translation>

<translation page="15">
that we squander them. Let us also remember that our bodies are the temple of God, and the instrument of the Spirit who dwells within us. AP. Sobriety and temperance are fruits of the Spirit; but drunkenness and luxury are the nurses and patrons of all vices; they are the receptacles of every kind of filth. <margin>1 Cor. 3. 2 Cor. 6. Galatians 5.</margin> Just as smoke drives away bees, so does intoxication drive away the Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts. NEPH. And just as clouds and rain always follow the south wind, so do the diseases of the soul and the animal nature follow drunkenness. COM. Therefore, must one not drink at all? AP. Certainly, if moderation is absent. One must hold the body in honor so that it is nourished with sufficient food, not immoderate and superfluous, and we must take care lest we be found the murderers of our own bodies. <margin>Colossians 2.</margin> COM. I understand now at last that there is nothing more ruinous to man than drunkenness. AP. Therefore, brother, heal this disease in yourself; separate this vice from yourself, and flee the company of wine-drinkers as if it were a reef. TRIC. Oh! Are you not ashamed, Comasta, to allow yourself to be corrupted by the persuasion of these men? AP. Come, arise Comasta, let us go; do not listen to them. COM. You tipplers, farewell; I must go and take care, so that I may become a man; truly, if you are wise, take an example from me.

There is another armed defense used in these books: which is instituted through a duel and single combat: a. And there is still another which, by way of trial rather than defense, was formerly permitted in a very superstitious manner, by touching red-hot iron, and likewise by water-walks, b. which the Feudists call an exploration: Both of which we rightly detest, as they are clearly contrary to humanity and piety. c.

### XCVI.

What if the peers <term>pares</term> <gloss>feudal equals who act as jurors</gloss>, who were present at the time of the investiture, later cease to be peers; are they still held to be suitable witnesses if a dispute arises between the Lord and the Vassal? Certainly, for whatever cause they may have ceased to be peers. Chapter "un." Title 19, book 2, Feudal Law, where Cuiacius and others [agree].

### XCVII.

What if the peers are absent, or contumacious? The former, unless they are far away, are to be awaited: a. the latter, however, are clearly to be disregarded. b.

<note>a. gloss Baldus, Laud, number 26; Aluarius, Praepositus, Afflictis, and others in chapter 1, Title 2, book 2, Feudal Law; notes Ardizo, in the said chapter 138, paragraph "Where however one possesses." b. Once the sentence is passed, can one appeal in feudal cases? It is debated in various ways: but it has been established that one can, and indeed to the nearest superior, if there is one, or to the ordinary judge to whom the matter is subject.

has arrived at him on the occasion of the mandate, he should restore it; see <term>lex</term> 10, paragraph 2, and <term>lex</term> 20, the beginning of <term>mandate</term>.

### XXXIII.

Regarding the case in paragraph 30, the cause of the litigation there is the detention of the property, which Paulus seeks back from Mævius, and he assigns the reason for seeking it because he mandated that Mævius carry that property to Pomponius so that he might guard it, and if Pomponius refused, Mævius should guard it for as long as it took until he might seek it back. The intention of Paulus is founded in *Digest 16.3.1.12, "On Deposit,"* where the action of <term>mandate</term> is granted to him, and not in truth [the action] of <term>deposit</term>. We shall propose still other examples.

### XXXIV.

So far, the things said have shown us actions arising from contracts; now we must look at a case where, in part, a contract and, in part, a tort produces an action. For Sempronius rented his house to Titius; this consensual business being completed, they go together to visit the rented house, but after they are inside the house, Sempronius, without any preamble of words, because of hatred previously conceived against him, beats Titius with a club placed behind the door, throws the heavily bruised man outside, and does not grant [him] the power of inhabiting [the house] any longer. Titius, because he endured this against his own stomach <note>i.e., unwillingly or with great resentment</note>, does not wish to endure the matter without any retaliation, and thus he hurries to approach the judge and intends to summon Sempronius.

### XXXV.

However, because in the proposed case two different deeds or acts present themselves, why should they not also obtain two separate legal remedies for pursuing a double scope or end of intention? For two things are involved here, of which one is the contract, the other a tort, which differ greatly and put forward two separate petitions; or, a double object of grievance and offense, from the deed and the double action performed, is brought into court, the first object of the dispute [is...disceptationis]</translation>

<translation page="20">
<header>❦:) 20. (:❦</header>

<note>Two mirrored floral ornaments or fleurons flank the page number.</note>

the denied habitation of the house, which the plaintiff intends, and even for this reason, because it was agreed between them that for a certain price, to be paid at a determined time, he might inhabit it; the intention of the plaintiff is founded in *Digest 19.1.7, 8, 9, "On Locating and Hiring."* The other matter of the litigation, or the other object which makes the lawsuit, is the beating, which the plaintiff pursues in a civil manner, and wishes to bind the defendant to pay him so much or so much, because of this, namely, that without any reason or opportunity given, he quite injuriously received the plaintiff with blows; therefore, his intention is founded in *Institutes 4.4.10, "On Injuries,"* and an estimatory action for injuries is granted to him.

### XXXVI.

Another example follows, where a tort alone is vindicated; that indeed will be the following: namely, a certain cobbler hired a musician living in Altdorf so that he might exhilarate him and his associates with the help of music. a disgraced person is appointed by a deceased uncle, does the claim of an inofficious will <note>original: "querela inofficiosi testamenti"; a legal action to challenge a will that excludes close relatives without just cause</note> belong to the children of the brothers by virtue of this right of representation? It might seem so from the decision of the aforementioned Novella 118, which generally substitutes children into the place of their parents; yet, with Zoesius on the title of the Digest *On the Inofficious Testament*, number 26, we will maintain the negative, based on the law *Fratris* 21, Code *On the Inofficious Testament*, § 1, Institutes of the same. For although in the Novellae the children of brothers are admitted to the inheritance of an uncle along with the brothers, this only proceeds if he dies simply intestate, not if the will is overturned by a complaint of inofficiousness. Furthermore, the children of brothers succeed to a deceased uncle by the right of representation only if they were conceived while he was alive; otherwise, they will not be admitted to his goods, for they are not linked to him by any kinship, law 1, § *Si quis proximior*, Digest *Whence the Relatives* <note>original: "unde cognati"</note>. Unless an access to the succession is opened by the right of transmission, and that from the right of deliberating (namely, if their parent dies within a year's time from the day of knowing that the inheritance had been deferred to him), law *Cum in antiquioribus* 19, Code *On the Right of Deliberating*, and Brunnemannus there.

# ON THE LORD'S SUPPER.

and is exhibited, but only where His word is, as in the Lord’s Supper, in or with the bread and wine.

<margin>II.</margin>
Secondly, those things which we have said until now concerning the majesty of Christ—who is true God and man, filling all things everywhere—have this use and bring us this benefit: that in all afflictions we may approach our Christ, our high priest, with all the greater confidence and implore His aid, regarding Him as present everywhere, not only as to His divinity but also as to His humanity. For whatever evil happens to us, it is not to be understood as something occurring by chance or without His foreknowledge or will. He is truly with us; He sees and knows all things. The same One also directs and governs all things. And since He favors all who believe in Him and call upon Him in faith, He does not concede nor permit anything adverse to befall them, unless He knows that it is salutary for them and useful for attaining heavenly goods. Thus, if we are endangered in water, in fire, in prisons, or are overwhelmed by any calamity, we can and ought always to stir up our faith and prayer to God in this way: by knowing that Christ, true God and man, is not far from us, situated in some peculiar place in this external heaven far distant from us, having perhaps no care for us, but that He is with us in His humanity as well as His divinity, in water, in fire, in prison, and in every calamity. And provided we embrace and call upon Him in true faith, He will never allow us to perish.

<margin>III.</margin>
Finally, the knowledge of the majesty of Christ, in that He is everywhere and fills all things not only by His divinity but also by His humanity, brings us this use and benefit: that we may walk all the more religiously in the fear and obedience of God, and avoid sins and crimes with all the greater diligence. For if that majesty, namely Christ, true God and man, acts perpetually with us and around us, and to us...
</translation>

<translation page="18">
# SERMON OF JOHANNES KARG ON THE LORD'S SUPPER.

is present wherever we may be, and assiduously observes all our thoughts as well as our actions, we certainly ought, with good reason, to stand in awe and fear of such a majesty, and live all the more cautiously. Many suppose that if they can so cover and hide the things they do wickedly, that they do not reach the eyes and conscience of any human, they have provided well for their own affairs. Meanwhile, they do not think that Christ Himself is present, who sees everything, and who will, without doubt, not leave evil deeds unpunished. Who would not say that a servant is foolish in the extreme who thinks he is doing well if the things he is treacherously committing against his master are hidden from the conscience and eyes of his fellow servants and the rest of the household, while meanwhile, he does not care about the conscience and sight of his own master, who is present and sees all things? Therefore, let us not confound or disturb the presence and sight of Christ our Savior, but rather let us honor and gladden Him. And so that His presence may be more for our consolation than for our terror and destruction, let us endeavor not to offend the present eyes of that majesty with sins and crimes,

->but let us walk through faith in the fear and obedience of God, so that we may be governed by the favor and grace of Christ, and be preserved forever. Amen.<-
</translation>

<summary>This section discusses the theological implications of Christ's omnipresence—both divine and human—arguing that this truth serves as a source of comfort in affliction and an incentive for living in moral obedience.</summary>
<keywords>Christology, Omnipresence, Lord's Supper, Divine Providence, Faith, Moral Obedience</keywords>

They distinguished them into smaller parts by means of <term>Centenae</term> <gloss>Hundreds, a district unit</gloss>, or certain villages and districts, by a praiseworthy institution, assigning to each <term>Centena</term> individual prefects, called <term>Centgraven</term> <gloss>Hundred-counts</gloss>, and adding to these others as helpers and deputies, who went by the name of <term>Centenarii</term> <gloss>Hundred-men</gloss>, so that the duty, which the Count alone could not bear, might become lighter once the burden was partitioned among others. B. Rhenanus agrees with us in book 2 of his *History of the Germans*, saying: "The regions were distinguished by <term>Centenae</term>, whence the name <term>Centenarii</term>." The magistrate who presided over a <term>Centena</term> was subject to the Count. But as we said a little earlier that the traces of the <term>Pagi</term> <gloss>districts</gloss> of the ancient Germans still exist among us today, so we must not think that the word <term>Centena</term> has completely vanished with the passage of time. For near Heidelberg, as the same Rhenanus testifies, a trace of the <term>Centena</term> still appears in several places, and the use of this word has remained right down to our own times.

§. 3. Indeed, in Franconia and the Palatinate, the word <term>Centena</term> seems to have a different meaning today, as they understand by <term>Centena</term> criminal jurisdiction and "pure empire" <note>original: "merum Imperium," legal term for the power to punish crimes</note>, and consequently the judgment of capital crimes. And from this: what is called "neck-justice" or "high justice" <note>original: "Hals- vel hohe Gerechtigkeit"</note> elsewhere, they themselves call <term>Centgerechtigkeit</term> <gloss>Hundred-justice</gloss>, and they call him to whom such judgment pertains <term>Centherrn</term> <gloss>Hundred-lord</gloss>, and the assessors of the same criminal court, <term>Zentschöpffen</term> <gloss>Hundred-jurors</gloss>, and those who are subject to such judgment, <term>Zentbare Unterthanen</term> <gloss>Hundred-liable subjects</gloss>. On which matter, see Berneggerus. But it is so far from the case that modern customs have imposed a meaning on the word <term>Centena</term> that is other and different from the ancient use, that it rather reflects precisely the most ancient institution of the Germans, by which they divided the <term>Pagi</term> into <term>Centenae</term>, or what we have just spoken of, and placed over each <term>Centena</term> a judge, whom they called <term>CentGraffen</term> <gloss>Hundred-counts</gloss>, with his <term>Centenarii</term> and <term>Scabini</term> <gloss>jurors/magistrates</gloss>. For what prevents one from calling a Count of a <term>Centena</term> a <term>Zentherr</term> <gloss>Hundred-lord</gloss>, or a judgment held in a <term>Centena</term> before a Count and the <term>Centenarii</term>, a <term>Zentgericht</term> <gloss>Hundred-court</gloss> or <term>Zentgerechtigkeit</term> <gloss>Hundred-justice</gloss>? The <term>Scabini</term>, called <term>Schöpffen</term> <gloss>jurors</gloss> by the Germans, from the Teutonic verb <term>schaffen</term> <gloss>to manage/ensure</gloss>—because the <term>Scabini</term> must diligently ensure that no injustice is done to anyone in the <term>Centena</term>, and procure the advantage of the <term>Centena</term> by all means—</translation>

<translation page="10">are so named (for they are mistaken, as many as derive that word either from the Hebrew <term>שבת</term> <gloss>Sabbath</gloss> with Besoldus, or from <term>Scamnis</term> <gloss>benches</gloss>, on which they were accustomed to pronounce sentence, with Becmannus, or with others from elsewhere), who were given to the Count of the <term>Centena</term> as helpers along with the <term>Centenarii</term>, to call them <term>Zentschöpffen</term> <gloss>Hundred-jurors</gloss>; or to call those men who belonged to the same <term>Centena</term> <term>Zentbare Unterthanen</term> <gloss>Hundred-liable subjects</gloss>, what forbids it?

§. 4. We said in §. 2 that <term>Centenarii</term> are to be derived from <term>Centenae</term>, so that it would be clear that we do not approve of the opinion of those who are numerous in number and great in authority, who wish the Counts of the <term>Centenae</term> to be understood by our <term>Centenarii</term> and to be so called from the hundredth number. For thus, to produce only one from many, the famous Berneggerus: "<term>Zentgraffen</term>, as if you were to say 'Hundred-counts,' that is, presidents and princes of a hundred-man court, who are also called <term>Centenarii</term> in the ancient laws of the Germans." But we assert that Mr. Berneggerus does not rely on a sufficiently certain hypothesis, and that neither were "hundreds" of counts ever added to the Princes chosen in the council of old, nor are the Counts of the <term>Centenae</term> themselves ever understood by the <term>Centenarii</term>. For since that passage of Tacitus which he cites for himself: "Princes are chosen in the same councils, who render rights through districts and villages. One hundred companions from the people are present as counsel and authority," the man who is never to be spoken of without praise, B. Reinesius, has convicted it of being a mistake and shown that for <term>Centeni</term> <gloss>hundreds</gloss>, <term>Certi</term> <gloss>certain</gloss> is to be substituted, it is evident from this that he himself shared the same error with others and, with this false hypothesis presupposed, fell into the false opinion regarding the <term>Centenarii</term> counts along with many others. We know from Tacitus and other authors that the ancient Germans indeed chose one hundred youths from each district if they were to draft soldiers. But what then? Is it to be concluded from that, that one hundred companions were also joined to the Prince in civilian life? The defenders of the contrary opinion indeed seem to have concluded thus and <term>κατ’ ἄλληλον</term> <gloss>mutually</gloss> to have confused this passage regarding the one hundred youths chosen from individual districts at the time of war, and named from that hundredth number for the sake of honor afterward, as Tacitus implies, with this one regarding the "hundred" counts. But although this was as it were their "first lie" <note>original: "πρῶτον ψεῦδος"</note> and became the cause of such a notable error for them, these two very different passages</translation>

<summary>The author discusses the etymology and function of the German administrative units known as Centenae, arguing against the historical interpretation that these were overseen by a hundred-fold group of counts.</summary>
<keywords>Centena, Centenarii, Centgraven, Scabini, judicial districts, German history, Tacitus, etymology</keywords>

Finally, the dispute and expostulation of the Jews regarding the changing of the writing. For if it had been without the י <term>yod</term> and ו <term>vav</term>, the writing would have remained doubtful, and the crowd of high priests would have had a handle and opportunity to excuse themselves regarding the explanation.

XIII. *Iησȣ͂ς* <gloss>Jesus</gloss>, in its origin, is Hebrew; it is said to be from either יהושע <term>Yehoshua</term> or ישוע <term>Yeshua</term>. For he who was called יהושע <term>Yehoshua</term> in <note>Haggai and Zechariah</note>, is elsewhere called ישוע <term>Yeshua</term> (Ezra 2:2; Neh. 7:7), and Joshua or יהושע <term>Yehoshua</term> is elsewhere called ישוע <term>Yeshua</term> (Neh. 8:17). It is derived from the verb ישע <term>yasha</term> in the <term>Hiphil</term> <gloss>causative stem</gloss>, which signifies to make safe, to save, to preserve, and to vindicate. The name has its origin in the action performed. Just as we read many things in Scripture, such as *Jacob* being called <term>Yaakov</term> <gloss>supplanter</gloss> from עקב <term>aqav</term> <gloss>heel/to supplant</gloss>, because he had supplanted his brother in the birthright. By the same reasoning, Christ receives his name from the wonderful and truly stupendous work of salvation, so that he is called *Iησȣ͂ς*, *Salvator* <gloss>Savior</gloss>, or *σωτήρ* <gloss>Soter/Deliverer</gloss>, which signifies more than the Latin *servator* <gloss>preserver/protector</gloss>, as *Cicero* himself acknowledges. *Second Action against Verres:* "I have seen him inscribed at Syracuse not only as the patron of that island but also as Soter." How much is this? It is so great that it cannot be expressed by a single Latin word. He is truly the *Soter* who has granted salvation. From this arose the Greek *Iησȣ͂ς*, which is read and written in Latin with two syllables, adding the letter S. For the Greeks add that same letter to the end of foreign names.

XIV. Here, if anyone likes, let them venerate the religion and subtlety of the *Jesuits*, who write JHESUS instead of JESUS, or by abbreviation with three letters, IHS, and so that no superstition is lacking, they even place a cross above it. Those good fellows wrongly introduce the H into Latin, not attending to the fact that the aspiration H is present in neither the Greek nor the Hebrew language. For it is not a Latin word, but is made in imitation of the Greek diction, whence it preserves almost the same inflection in oblique cases. But this is not new concerning the Jesuits; for I remember, and I knew, the name of the *Rector* of a Jesuit College, in a place not undistinguished, who was shouting loudly while he was inspecting the register in a state of near-admiration, as he read the students and other Lutherans</translation>

<translation page="16">as they were reading the Greek and Hebrew sentences placed before them, when the good director himself could scarcely speak Latin, and hardly even that. For, intending to ask what lodging I had, he fashioned another word according to a foreign character: "What is your *Quartirium* <gloss>quarters/lodging</gloss>?" But I forgive him most willingly, on account of his generosity. Furthermore, Galatinus is a witness that there are some who esteem the name *Iησους* as identical with the tetragrammaton, JEHOVAH: such that a Ψ <gloss>psi</gloss> is inserted, which error is surely not light. It is derived from the verb ישע <term>yasha</term> in the <term>Hiphil</term> <gloss>causative stem</gloss>, which signifies to make safe, to save, to preserve, and to vindicate. The name has its origin in the action performed. Here, if anyone likes, let them venerate the religion and subtlety of the *Jesuits*, who write JHESUS instead of JESUS, or by abbreviation with three letters, IHS, and so that no superstition is lacking, they even place a cross above it. <translation page="3">that the day had passed; on this day, he says, the ancients were accustomed to wish and pray that they might be allowed to live through the year happily <note>Latin: "annare perannare"; a formulaic expression for enduring through the year</note>, and they applied themselves diligently to ensure that they would not even name things dire, sad, or deadly; instead, they spoke only good words, abstained from all quarrels, and discussed only joyful and friendly matters among themselves.

Although this honor paid to the invocation of Anna Perenna was neither trivial nor worthy of scorn, the worship of Janus was preferred to it. For we find in the archives of antiquity that Janus was the first to be invoked in all sacrifices and prayers, and that he was accustomed to be placed before all other gods, and even before Jupiter himself. Because he was the first in Italy to build temples to the gods and establish the rites of sacred things, he deserved perpetual prayer in sacrifices. And since the beginning and the end have the greatest power in all affairs, they wished for Janus to be the leader in sacrificing, says Cicero <note>original: "liber 1 de Natur. Deorum."</note>.

We, who are called and are Christians, are so far from simply subscribing to the formulas of the heathens, as if we did not have ones that are equally good or better, that we rather seriously condemn everything that the idolatry of the Gentiles drew in erroneously, and we deem that only that part—especially in this vow—is to be retained which seems to be derived from and composed of the year. If we obtain [this] with our vow while praying, each of us will have that for which he may congratulate and rejoice in himself after the course of the year.

And we know that such vows were looked after, primarily by the flamens <note>priests of ancient Rome</note>, in the temples. But what were those who sat at the helm of the Republic doing around this time? Consuls and senators were being ordained; once ordained, they entered upon their offices and, for the sake of an omen, tasted [the work of their office]. This can be seen in the choice of the father of Symmachus, a man of marvelous eloquence and knowledge. In the country and in retirement, he was mourning the injury of his lost home, but through frequent votes and finally through orators sent [to him], the Senate summoned him to a new honor. And they were then the Calends, on which the year is opened, as the son himself testifies and rejoices <note>original: "1. Ep. 44."</note>.</translation>

<translation page="4">himself testifies and rejoices <note>original: "1. Ep. 44."</note>. To this, Naso <note>Ovid</note>, the prolific writer of the *Fasti*, subscribes, and he introduces this rite in a friendly manner when he says:

> The people go to the Tarpeian heights in untouched robes,
> And the people themselves are of one color with their festival.
> Now the new fasces <note>symbols of magisterial authority</note> lead the way, the new purple shines;
> And the ivory <note>the curule chair</note> feels new weights of distinction. <note>original: "1. Fast. v. 10"</note>

There was also a custom of tasting, and as it were, imbuing and happily inaugurating offices on that very day. Drusus, the Prefect of the City, ascended the tribunal to take the auspices; Nero took the auspices on the Calends of January; Emperor Maximian immediately completed what he had hoped for in the future. Tacitus, the writer of Augustan history, testifies to this regarding the former <note>original: "liber 4. annales caput 36."</note>, Suetonius regarding the second <note>original: "caput 46."</note>, and the panegyrists regarding the latter. The habit and custom of Christians does not stray far from this time, who in certain places, around the same turning points of the year, integrate and restore their collegia of senators. And they seem to do so more rightly than the ancients. For we believe that the eternal Son of God was born at that time, the <term>Logos</term> <gloss>Word</gloss> of the eternal Father, who by His merit and satisfaction designated and established us as heavenly citizens and nobles. However, we transmit the other custom of tasting and imbuing businesses and occupations—assigned to each—as <term>aparchas</term> <gloss>first-fruits/offerings</gloss>, and, if I may say so, into disuse: knowing that the paternal grace of God, entreated by our prayer, can, if He wills, make every month and every day of the month prosperous for us, and that the certain commencement of work on the first or any other day helps us nothing at all.

The most praised Emperors, the divine Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, seem to have recognized this; they wished, by a salutary rescript, that the days of the January Calends be devoted to leisure and be an <term>apodeixis</term> <gloss>demonstration/display</gloss>, a fact which is not unknown to the priests of the law and the learned <note>original: "Novellae 8. L. omnes Dies. 7. caput de Feriis XII, liber 3."</note>. Perhaps so that to divine worship and sacred things, there...</translation>

### LXIII.
Of these, some are internal, others are external.

### LXIIII.
The internal works are: to acknowledge the depravity and corruption of nature, to confess oneself guilty of divine wrath and eternal punishments, and to grieve from the soul for one's sins.

### LXV.
To take refuge in the mercy of GOD offered in Christ, and to establish firmly and certainly that through Him the remission of sins and the right to enter upon the heavenly inheritance are given.

### LXVI.
To dedicate oneself entirely to the obedience of GOD, and to apply oneself with one's whole mind to this: that all the plans and actions of life may serve for the glory of the divine name and the utility of the Church.

### LXVII.
The external works, indeed, are those which strike the eyes and the exterior senses.

### LXVIII.
Some concern words, such as to teach the Gospel, to call upon GOD in dangers, to give thanks to Him for benefits, and to issue a confession of faith.

### LXIX.
Others concern deeds: such as to hear the Word, to use the sacraments ordained by GOD, to give alms, and to lay down one's body for the assertion of the truth and the glory of Christ, if there be need, by martyrdom.

If all things are implicitly in scripture, which Pistorius says on page 35, therefore this too will be held implicitly in it: that nothing is to be believed outside the word of God. 4. For Christian faith and the word of God are related. 5. Which Pistorius will not deny, who wrote expressly that he would prove all his points from Holy Scripture alone. 6. And Bellarmine, although he speaks insidiously, nevertheless admits (lib. 1 de verbo Dei, c. 1) that the prophetic and apostolic books are a certain and stable rule of faith. 7. And nothing is brought forward today by the Pontificians in the matter of religion that the Jesuits do not attempt to prove from some scripture: a fact which is evident from their disputations. <translation page="14">

### XLII.

Which pleasure is nothing other than a certain perfection following human functions, recommending them with a singular sweetness.

### XLIII.

Therefore, just as theoretical happiness excels the practical, so too does theoretical pleasure surpass the practical.

### XLIV.

<margin>See the last chapter of Book 1 of the Ethics and chapter 7 of Book 10 of the Nicomachean Ethics.</margin>
Furthermore, from what has been said, it is also clear that Aristotle perceived both the excellence and the dignity of human nature, as well as its corruption, when he admits that a desire for divinity and immortality is implanted in man by nature, yet he says that divinity does not belong to man as man. But indeed, he did not know the cause of this, much less the way to obtain immortality through the MESSIAH. For this whole matter is owed to revelation, as the most learned Zwinger has most beautifully noted on chapter 7 of the 10th book of the Ethics.

### XLV.

Nor is there any reason that we should reject Aristotle’s doctrine on human happiness because it may be less in agreement with our Christian religion.

### XLVI.

For besides what we said above, that the philosopher disputes philosophically about this matter, his opinion ought to be commended to us for this single reason: whether the philosopher says the same things—that is, things consistent with heavenly truth—and then the consensus is beneficial; or whether he says different things, and then a comparison is beneficial, to use the words of St. Basil the Great, a witness in this matter greater than any exception.

</translation>
<translation page="15">

<margin>Homily to the young on how they might profit from Greek literature.</margin>

that the philosopher discusses this matter philosophically, his opinion ought to be commended to us for this single reason: that either the philosopher says the same things, that is, things consistent with heavenly truth, and then the consensus is beneficial; or he says different things, and then a comparison is beneficial, to use the words of St. Basil the Great, a witness in this matter greater than any exception.

### XLVII.

Finally, the philosopher does not contradict himself, even if in the first book of the Nicomachean Ethics he asserts that practical happiness is the highest good, while in the last book he maintains and argues that theoretical happiness <term>θεωρητικὴν εὐδαιμονίαν</term> <gloss>contemplative happiness</gloss> is superior to it.

### XLVIII.

For just as in the first book, with respect to practical happiness, he considers the composite man <term>τὸν σύνθετον ἄνθρωπον</term> <gloss>the composite man</gloss>, so in the tenth book, regarding theoretical blessedness, he considers the mind <term>τὸν νοῦν</term> <gloss>the mind</gloss>, which he calls the "man in the highest sense" <term>μάλιστα ἄνθρωπον</term> <gloss>most truly man</gloss>.

### XLIX.

From all of which I judge it to appear clearer than the midday sun, as the saying goes, that what Cicero said is most true: that all authority regarding the pursuit of the blessed life consists in philosophy, that is, in the doctrine of life and morals, and that therefore its dignity and excellence are supreme and admirable.

</translation>

<summary>These pages conclude the discussion on Aristotelian ethics, comparing practical and theoretical happiness and arguing that despite his lack of Christian revelation, Aristotle's philosophical insights regarding human nature and the blessed life remain valuable and consistent with truth.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Theoretical Happiness, Practical Happiness, St. Basil the Great, Cicero, Human Nature, Immortality</keywords>
