For besides what we said above, that the philosopher disputes philosophically about this matter, his opinion ought to be commended to us for this single reason: whether the philosopher says the same things—that is, things consistent with heavenly truth—and then the consensus is beneficial; or whether he says different things, and then a comparison is beneficial, to use the words of St. Basil the Great, a witness in this matter greater than any exception.

### XLVII.

Finally, the philosopher does not contradict himself, even if in the first book of the Nicomachean Ethics he asserts that practical happiness is the highest good, while in the last book he maintains and argues that theoretical happiness <term>θεωρητικὴν εὐδαιμονίαν</term> <gloss>contemplative happiness</gloss> is superior to it.

### XLVIII.

For just as in the first book, with respect to practical happiness, he considers the composite man <term>τὸν σύνθετον ἄνθρωπον</term> <gloss>the composite man</gloss>, so in the tenth book, regarding theoretical blessedness, he considers the mind <term>τὸν νοῦν</term> <gloss>the mind</gloss>, which he calls the "man in the highest sense" <term>μάλιστα ἄνθρωπον</term> <gloss>most truly man</gloss>.

### XLIX.

From all of which I judge it to appear clearer than the midday sun, as the saying goes, that what Cicero said is most true: that all authority regarding the pursuit of the blessed life consists in philosophy, that is, in the doctrine of life and morals, and that therefore its dignity and excellence are supreme and admirable.

We see indeed that in the states of all Republics, various kinds of men are found who depart of their own accord into different classes, as it were, so that they constitute one group of the illustrious and the rich; another of the more humble and the poor; and finally a third, those who walk the middle path and exist as a sort of temperament between the illustrious and the poor. But by what method these classes should be composed so that the state may be rendered quiet, and every part of the state may enjoy its own happiness, this is the task, this is the labor.

<margin>5. Pol. 1.</margin>
The illustrious or the rich persuade themselves, while they surpass the rest in splendor, that they are simply superior and that, by right and merit, unequal things are owed to those who are unequal. Conversely, the poor, measuring all things by liberty, concede no inequality. Because of this vain persuasion of men, and as if one’s own right is not attributed to each, the status of Republics is changed in the highest degree, which was long ago excellently proven by Aristotle.

Writers record of Solon that, in order to make the citizens friendly to himself and to be declared legislator by them, he said he would bring forth laws equal for all, and from this, the authority to enact laws was permitted to him by the highest zeal and will of all. For the common people thought he spoke of the equality of the thing, if we may borrow this from the schools; the Optimates <gloss>Aristocrats</gloss> thought he spoke of the equality of the person. If citizens remain in these precipices and are unwilling to remit anything of their own right, which they boast of so laboriously, it is easily clear that such contentions are joined with the internal ruin of the Republic, nor do they cease until one side is oppressed.

Truly, neither party, whether the poor or the rich is considered, is accustomed to derive equality and inequality from true principles. It is a common assertion of philosophers that only virtue makes the distinction between the plebeians and the illustrious, so that the latter may shine among the others, while the former live content with their humbler lot. But who could persuade this to minds that are too blinded by self-love and are agitated here and there? Nor is the matter so clear that it no longer holds any doubt.

<margin>6. Pol. c. 3.</margin>
Aristotle himself, while dealing with Democracy, confesses that it is very difficult to organize the people in such a way that all participate equally in the communion of rights. For although the humbler sort look at nothing else in this equality of theirs than that they not be oppressed by the richer, yet you will notice the diverse proposals, pursuits, propensities, inclinations, inventions, arts, and rules of the more powerful.

So that we may not dwell longer on this question, and may explain in a few words the mind of the philosopher, which is found more than once in his work *Politics*</translation>

<translation page="13">, these things must be added: that harmony can indeed be obtained between the poor and the rich if the legislator always has a greater care for the middle citizens than for the extremes, for then the Republic will be held as if in equilibrium. If this proceeds less according to one’s wishes, another path must be undertaken, namely that the rights themselves be properly mixed, that both parties preside over affairs, and that each concedes a little to the other. Let other duties of humanity and signs of benevolence be added, whether in gesture or in speech; let one promote the advantages of the other and decline their inconveniences, and perhaps such a Republic will fare well enough, while no one can complain of being oppressed or despised, but all live among themselves with equal right.

What we have said thus far about mixing a Popular state with an Aristocratic one, Greek and Latin writers—who treat of Democratic and Aristocratic affairs even to the point of nausea—explain more fully beyond the Political works of Aristotle and Plato. For to repeat our opinion again: among the ancients, a Popular state was never found unless it was tempered by the arts of the Optimates <gloss>Aristocrats</gloss>. Let us not speak for the present of the mutations and various attempts by which the Attic Republic was vexed. Therefore, Thucydides, Demosthenes, and Isocrates must be diligently unrolled. In Roman history, Halicarnassus, Plutarch, and Dionysius are to be commended; but no one surpasses the labors of Livy in thoroughly learning the characters of the Optimates.

§. 13. Signs of recognizing the status of a Republic are not rarely disturbed. If power were contained by external apparatus and splendor, the King of Poland would certainly surpass all Princes of Europe in Majesty, whom the nobles venerate like slaves. But his power is closed within narrow limits. Indeed, it is small that is permitted to him in Ecclesiastical matters; it is a crime to condemn a knight to death, except in the assemblies. Concerning waging war and entering into a treaty, there is common care with the Senate; he cannot even in the Senate, without the consent of the rest of the nobility, promulgate new laws, command a tax outside of the ordinary, mint money, nominate a successor, and whatever other things most adorn Royal dignity. And to finish in a few words: the rights of Majesty are exercised by the optimates rather than by the King. Cromer has executed this diligently and happily.

will you be reminded, and you will rouse yourself toward an excellent desire for all honorable arts. Whatever is contrary to these arts, you will cast aside and despise. You will judge those things not only unworthy of the man you must prove to be in the future, and of the sort of man we all augur you will be, but entirely unworthy of any human being. Since he is the uncle of your parent, and since he has loved you not unremarkably from your early age, and since he has been accustomed to embrace all his kin with a certain incredible affection, he nevertheless followed a different path in honoring you. He gave the honor not to kinship or family, but to you yourself, who strive to illustrate the name of your family. And as beginnings present themselves, the outcome will confirm the zeal. Behold, you have, Alfonso, a field in which your virtue, born of vigils and already confirmed by the habit of doing good, may range. This is the province, most worthy of your genius and your best thoughts and studies, toward which you were exercising yourself and toward which your cares were directed. Show what the excellence is not only of your will but also of your industry. Bring forth from your spirit those noble qualities which you have collected since childhood, so that you might reflect the ancient glory of your people and the virtue present in your own house. It is not, believe me, a labor for one who thinks well, to do

well. For what is placed within ourselves does not depend on anything else, nor is it assumed from the outside. In that, what stands in the way of the deed itself following the will? Now virtue itself invites, it entices, and it affects those who study it with every desire and with all rewards. <header>BOOK I. OF THE SUMMATION</header>

Concerning the impediments to this work, on the part of the artist's body. Chapter IV.

We have now determined for you, in a general way, the impediments to this work. Now, however, we shall address you with more specific discourse in this chapter, and we shall relate to you more openly all those impediments, fully and in order. We say, therefore, that if anyone does not have his organs complete, he will not be able to reach the completion of this work by himself, as for example if he were blind or maimed in his extremities, since he is not aided by those members through whose medium this art is perfected, as if they were ministers of nature. But if the artist’s body is weak and ill, such as the bodies of those suffering from fever or lepers—whose members fall away—or those laboring in the extremities of life, and the elderly already of decrepit age, he will not reach the completion of the art. By these natural impotencies of the body, therefore, the artist is hindered in his intention.

Concerning the impediments on the part of the artist's soul. Chapter V.

We have provided for you a previous chapter in which we related, in absolute and manifest speech, the impediments depending upon the part of the artist’s body. It remains for us to relate briefly the impediments on the part of the soul itself, which most greatly hinder the completion of this work. We say, therefore, that he who does not have natural talent and a soul that searches subtly into natural principles, the foundations of nature, and the crafts that can follow nature in the properties of its action, will not find the true root of this most precious science. There are many such who have a stiff neck and, in all their searching, a mind void of talent, who can scarcely understand common speech, and who likewise learn common works with difficulty. Besides these, we also find many who have a soul that easily opines any fantasy whatsoever; but what they believe they have found to be true is entirely fantastic, deviant from reason, full of error, and remote from natural principles, since their brain, filled with many fumes, cannot receive the true intention of natural things. There are also, besides these, others who have a mobile soul, shifting from opinion to opinion and from will to will, like those who now believe one thing and desire the same, without the foundation of any reason. Yet a little while after, they similarly believe and desire another thing. And these are so mobile that they can scarcely finish the least bit of that which they intend, but rather they leave it diminished. There are likewise others who cannot see any truth in natural things, no more than beasts, such as those deprived of their mind, the insane, and children. There are also others who despise science and do not believe it to be: whom this science similarly despises, and repels them from the end of this most precious work. And there are those who are slaves, serving money, who affirm this marvelous science, but fear to interpose the necessary expenses. And therefore, although they affirm it and investigate it according to reason, they do not arrive at the experience of the work on account of avarice. To these, therefore, this science of ours does not reach. For how could one who is ignorant, or who has neglected to investigate the science, easily arrive at it?

Concerning the external impediments, hindering the work of this art. Chapter VI.

We have reduced to two chapters all the impediments retarding the end of this art, which are from the radical principles, according to the nature of the artist of this most precious business. It is therefore useful for us at last to relate the impediments supervening from the outside, and from contingent fortunes and accidents, by which this most glorious work is hindered. We see, therefore, some who are astute and talented, in no way ignorant of the works of nature, and of those things in which it is possible</translation>

<translation page="139">
<header>OF THE PERFECTION OF GEBER.</header>

to follow the principles and works, and for whom there is also a search that is not fantastic, in all things which are regulated by the motions and actions of nature beneath the lunar circle. These, however, oppressed by extreme poverty, from the lack of funds, are forced to postpone this excellent masterwork. There are also many others besides those just mentioned who are curious, detained by various cares and anxieties of this world, occupying themselves entirely with every secular business, from whom this precious science of ours again flees. Now, therefore, it is sufficiently clear to you from the aforementioned chapters what are the impediments distracting from this art.

<note>A decorative drop cap C begins the paragraph.</note>We conclude, therefore, from what has been said, that it is necessary for the artist of this work to be learned and perfect in the sciences of natural philosophy, because no matter how much money and naturally profound talent and desire for this craft he may have, he will not acquire its end unless he has attained natural philosophy through doctrine, because what is not obtained through natural talent is provided for by doctrine. Therefore, the artist must be aided by the deepest searching and industry. For on account of doctrine, no matter how much science he may have acquired, unless he is also aided by natural industry, he will not be invited to such precious banquets. For he would amend his error in a moment through his industry—for which he would not know how to apply a remedy—if he were founded only on doctrine; and he would similarly amend an error in a moment from the science acquired through natural doctrine, which he could not avoid by industry alone; for art is aided by talent, and talent is likewise aided by art. And it is similarly necessary for him to be of a constant will in the work, so that he does not presume to attempt now this, now that: for in a multitude of things our art does not consist, nor is it perfected. For it is one stone, one medicine, in which the masterwork consists, to which we add no extraneous thing, nor do we diminish it, except for what we remove as superfluous in the preparation. It is also necessary for him to persist diligently in the work until its completion, so that he does not leave the work truncated: because he would acquire neither science nor profit from a diminished work, but rather despair and loss. It is also useful for him not to be ignorant of the principles and main roots of this art, which are of the essence of the work: for he who is ignorant of the beginning will not find the end. And we shall tell you all those principles in complete speech, and also, to the prudent, sufficiently open and manifest, according to the requirement of this art of ours. It is similarly useful for the artist to be temperate and slow to anger, lest he suddenly dissipate and destroy what has already been begun due to a surge of anger. Likewise, let him guard his money, and not distribute it vainly with presumption, lest if by chance he does not find the art, he is left in misery and the desperation of poverty: or lest by chance, when he has already approached the end of this masterwork through his investigation, his funds are consumed, and the wretched man violently abandons the true end on account of poverty. As it is with those who in the beginning, through their investigation, prodigally exterminate their whole treasure, and when they are at the end, they no longer have anything from which to work. Hence, such people are doubly buried in sorrow, both because they dissipated their money in useless things, and because they lose the most noble science they had immediately investigated. For it is not necessary to consume your goods, because you will arrive at the completion of the masterwork for a low price (if you are not ignorant of the principles of the art, and have correctly understood those things which we have handed down to you). If, therefore, you have lost your money by not heeding our warnings, which we have written for you in this booklet, open and manifest, do not unfairly gnaw at us nor heap blasphemies upon us, but impute it to your own ignorance and presumption. Therefore, this science does not suit a poor or needy person well, but rather it is</translation>

### XXXI.

It is evident that gout takes its origin from phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note> by the phlegmatic nature of the patient, the whitish color of the joint, a persistent dull pain accompanied by an edematous tumor, the nature of the food previously ingested, and finally by the paroxysm returning every day <sup>a</sup>.
<sup>a</sup> Pereda in Paschalis, Book 1, Chapter 61.

### XXXII.

Gout rarely arises from melancholy <note>original: "melancholia"</note>. If, however, it does originate from black bile <note>original: "humore atro"</note>, it is dangerous, both because it causes much more disturbance than other forms and because it lasts longer and does not yield easily to medicines. The signs by which it is revealed are deep pain with a sense of heaviness, a blackish color, a cold and dry temperament, age verging toward the elderly, and a cycle of exacerbations returning on the fourth day. The urine is for the most part thin and watery at the beginning, but later it is black and moderately thick, and the sediment within it is sometimes dark, sometimes mixed, as Paulus Aegineta testifies in Book 3, Chapter 78.

### XXXIII.

Finally, if gout proceeds from a varied mixture of humors, the signs will arise in a varied and mixed manner.

### XXXIV.

Regarding the prognosis, it is known from the nature and condition of the aforementioned factors. Generally, however, it must be affirmed that all gout is difficult to cure.

### XXXV.

Nevertheless, young people can be cured <sup>a</sup>, even if they have inherited the condition, as can those in whom hardened tophaceous calluses <note>original: "calli tophacei"</note> do not yet appear around the joints <sup>b</sup>, provided they enjoy physical labor and have regular bowel movements. These people, having found a prudent physician, can be saved.
<sup>a</sup> Felix Plater, in Observations, Book 2, page 473. <sup>b</sup> Hippocrates, Aphorisms 6, 49 and 55.

### XXXVI.

Conversely, elderly people can scarcely be cured, those who around the joints</translation>

<translation page="11">
<margin>a Hippocrates, Book 2, on diseases of the external parts.</margin>
have such hardened calluses, of which the poet writes:
> Medicine knows not how to loosen knotty gout.
Likewise those who live luxuriously and have a dry bowel, as Galen teaches in *On the Composition of Medicines according to Places*, Book 10, Chapter 2. Nor can those be cured for whom it is hereditary <sup>a</sup> due to an innate imbalance of the brain and weakness of the joints, unless they have countered this evil in a timely manner during their youth.

### XXXVII.

Gouty pains are for the most part stirred up in the spring and autumn, as Hippocrates teaches in Aphorism 55 of Book 6. Whatever the case, gouty illnesses, once the inflammation has been calmed over a period of 40 days, generally end, provided (as Galen says in his commentaries) the physician has not erred in his work and the patient has obeyed him in all things.

### XXXIIX.

Otherwise, by reason of the path and the outcome itself, this malady generally ends in one of four ways: either it is resolved, which happens most frequently; or it matures, which is rare; or it sometimes hardens; or it is transferred to vital organs, from which it has ended in many as dropsy <note>original: "hydropicum morbum"</note>, and in some as asthma, as Aëtius testifies.

### XXXIX.

From these things already said, it appears that gout takes its origin from diverse causes and also ends in diverse ways: by reason of its origin, one is hot, such as that arising from blood and bile; another is cold, such as that which arises from phlegm and black bile; another possesses a mixed nature, according to the proportion of the causative matter; one is curable, while another is in no way curable.

It highlights that while gout is generally difficult to treat, younger patients or those without hardened joints have a better chance of recovery, and it describes the typical outcomes of the disease, including potential complications like dropsy or asthma.</summary>

Concerning which, Justinus, book 8, chapter 1. A no less heavy danger is to be feared from that Avarice in public affairs which is seen in private matters, when, namely, either individual Magistrates or the whole order of Magistrates draw the goods of private citizens to themselves by force, deceit, and under some pretext.

## XIII. 
However, since this **Avarice** exists as a frequent cause of ruin compared to others, a King will act most safely if he exacts small tributes in parts, with the consent of the estates, having demonstrated the necessity for monetary matters, maintains the ordinary, and does not easily command new ones. Adam Contzen, book 9 of his Politics, chapter 8, § 4. Especially since, among Princes and those governing the Commonwealth, no more loathsome vice is found than **Avarice**. *For to treat the Commonwealth as a source of profit is not only shameful, but also wicked and nefarious*, says Cicero. Indeed, it is even opposed to nature itself; hence the same author says:

> To take something away from another, he says, and to increase one's own advantage at the inconvenience of a man, is more against nature than death, than poverty, than pain, than other things which can happen either to the body or to external affairs. For it destroys the fellowship and society of men: if we are so affected that each one, for his own gain, despoils or violates another, it is necessary that this society of the human race, which is most in accordance with nature, be torn apart.

## XIV. 
Not rarely, **Ambition** of those who wield the scepter is accustomed to generate a pestilence in Commonwealths equal to, indeed almost greater than, **Avarice**; from which, as from a Lerna of evils, beyond the wars of which it is the torch, infinite other evils also spring forth, and it is often accustomed to bring the greatest pestilence and destruction upon the Ambitious themselves. For although **Avarice** also exists as a frequent cause of war, far</translation>

<translation page="10">nevertheless, Ambition is more persistent in it. Wicked causes do indeed drive everyone to their own battles, yet the lust for ruling holds the primacy at home, says *Adam Contzen, book 10, Politics, chapter 8*. Hence *Thucydides* rightly said: The cause of all evils is the desire for power out of ambition. And *Polybius*, a most weighty writer, says: After any city has overcome and struggled through many and great dangers, and has already risen to primacy and power, it is manifest that where favorable fortune is not used with moderation, it fixes its seat in that city, and luxury creeps into its morals, and ambition and obstinacy into the minds of men, both concerning the Magistracy and concerning others. Where these evils have once prevailed, they will be the beginning of a change for the worse, from honors sought or denied through Ambition.

XV. Many, however, do not judge themselves blessed in every respect until they can enlarge their Kingdom by adding new Provinces to old ones, unaware that, according to *Seneca, epistle 113*, to rule oneself is the greatest Empire. Nor do they attend to the most certain destruction of their own Provinces resulting therefrom: for while they are not content with their own limits and covet more provinces, they often lose those which they have already placed in safety. By way of example, the Cities of Greece, which, while each desired to rule, all lost their power. *Justinus, book 8, chapter 1.*

XVI. Therefore, that saying of *Thucydides* in his description of the Corcyrean sedition is from the mouth of Truth: The cause of all evils is the desire for power and Ambition. From these affections, every calamity is born. Thence, atrocious wars have been continued in a perpetual series from the beginning of the created world. Inflamed by this, Alexander followed all of Asia with fire and sword, and Cyrus had previously devastated Ionia. Demosthenes is once said to have said: If two paths were open, one to the infernal regions, the other to the throne, he would choose the one that led to the infernal regions. I believe he did not speak sincerely, but it nonetheless shows the most miserable ambition of those who, through labors, dangers, and wounds, ascend to a slippery, trembling summit, agitated by lightning and winds, where it is not possible to stand firm, nor to depart from there.</translation>

<summary>This text examines the destabilizing roles of Avarice and Ambition within Commonwealths, citing historical examples such as the pillaging of the Temple of Delphi and the consequences of Alexander the Great's conquests.</summary>
<keywords>Avarice, Ambition, Commonwealth, Politics, Cicero, Thucydides, Adam Contzen, power, corruption</keywords>

XLIX. You might not incongruously call <term>PICTORIAL ART</term> either its daughter or its sister, the true and genuine kind, in which Zeuxis, Apelles, and Parrhasius excelled in the past, and Dürer in our own age. Whatever is artistic in their paintings, they owe uniquely to mathematical proportions. Dürer himself proves this sufficiently in his most learned German work. Indeed, other craftsmen—statue-makers, goldsmiths, architects, military commanders, captains, and gunners for the artificial firing of pellets at fixed targets—cannot do without these same principles.

L. Finally, I come to <term>CANONICS</term> or <term>MUSIC</term>, specifically the <term>Harmonic</term> variety, which is the science of sound estimable by number. This is the contemplation and practice of harmony, or an order composed of sounds and intervals, considering the rationale of apparent concords, and applying the judgment of the senses throughout, so that the ears might appear to have been placed before the mind, according to Plato. Whatever this <term>HARMONIC</term> theory teaches, it demonstrates everything by mathematical principles. Among the ancients, many excelled in this: Euclid, Aristoxenus, Ptolemy, and Boethius, the musicians.

LI. But from those theoretical foundations, another <term>PRACTICAL</term> branch composes songs that possess charm in sound or harmony and elegance in singing. In this field, many emulate the supreme artist Orlando [di Lasso].

LII. Finally, <term>ASTROLOGY</term> also does not wish to be separated from the mixed mathematical disciplines. Astronomy is present as either its handmaid or mistress, teaching to what good those astronomical observations and contemplations can be put, if we look at them through the distinction of times, just as it has wonderfully and uniquely aided in chronographical matters</translation>

There is no need to reject it, if many superstitions of the Arabs and many other less sound minor precepts are cut away, and only those things are retained that admit of either reason, experience, or both together.

LIII. In this class, others also count <term>CHIROMANCY</term> <gloss>palm reading</gloss> and <term>METOPOSCOPY</term> <gloss>physiognomy of the forehead</gloss>. The former teaches the method of recognizing signs and characters in the human hand and judging them skillfully, while the latter is the art of divining from the forehead. We have primary patrons and authors for these: Taisnier, Johann de Indagine, Rothmann, and Thaddaeus Haggecius.

<note>Page number 5 centered at the top, flanked by two floral typographical fleurons.</note>

->X.<-

The <term>constitution regarding the Roman expedition</term> of Charles the Fat, in the year 890, is unreliable and lacks both credibility and truth. Even if this were not evident from the clause added to the constitution, which clearly reveals its defect, the mere insertion of the word <term>fief</term> and the remaining character of the style, which is foreign to that age, clearly demonstrate its falsity.

->XI.<-

The <term>constitution on tournaments</term> of Henry the Fowler, the first German King of the Saxons, dated to the year 938, is a forgery. This is because the style is discordant and does not conform to the conditions of the times, and also because it names circles not yet known and illustrious dignities not yet instituted, such as Burgraviates, the Palatinate of Thuringia, and the Principality of Pomerania, to omit other indications of falsehood.

->XII.<-

### XIV.

It is false that Hatto, Archbishop of Mainz, was devoured by mice. The argument regarding the tower in the Rhine, which is still visible today and which people generally bring forth to confirm their opinion, is entirely inept and does not sustain the dignity of proof in the slightest.

### XV.

The common opinion is that Emperor Henry VII of Luxembourg was destroyed by a poisoned host given to him by Francesco Paulino, a monk of the Order of Saint Bernard. This is doubted, and not without cause, because Conrad Vecerius, who described his life most diligently, recorded nothing of the sort.

### XVI.

It cannot be proven by certain and indubitable documents that Emperor Charles IV alienated the Kingdom of Burgundy Transjurane, or Arelatense. Nor are the supporters of the contrary opinion able to produce or demonstrate a document of such alienation, although it is otherwise known that he was somewhat too liberal, not only toward the French but also toward the Rhenish Princes.

### XVII.

<margin>Germany, chap. 28 in the book on the origin of the Bohemians.</margin>
They are absurd who think the Bohemians derived their name from some King Bohemus or other. The error of those who write that they were a Gallic people belongs in the same category; among these are Cornelius Tacitus and Johannes Matthias à Sudetis, to whom Melchior Goldast otherwise owes much. But there are just causes that urge us not to agree with them.

That Samson was a <term>Nazarite</term> <gloss>one consecrated to God by vow</gloss>, who from birth was dedicated to God for the redeemer of Israel, can be gathered from the preceding sections. What a <term>Nazarite</term> or <term>Nazariteship</term> <gloss>state of being a Nazarite</gloss> is, is described at length in Numbers 6. The narrow page forbids citing everything here. Let the eager reader look there. Nevertheless, the most numerous and principal aspects of the <term>Nazariteship</term> seem to be referable to these three heads: (1) That they should not drink wine or strong drink, or anything else that could intoxicate. <term>Sicera</term> <gloss>strong drink</gloss>, as Peter Martyr notes in his commentary, was called by the Jews water that was poured onto pressed grapes after the wine was expressed, and when that had fermented, it retained some flavor of wine, and was the same as that which we call secondary wine, and which in Upper Saxony is called <term>Lauer</term> <gloss>dregs/weak wine</gloss>. (2) That they should not cut their hair, but throughout the whole <term>Nazariteship</term> should let it grow. (3) That they should not defile themselves with funeral mourning, not even at the death of a father. A vow of such a kind Paul also seems to have taken in Acts 21. Samson was therefore from his very first birth a holy and public person; he was such even in his death. (2) Regarding what Samson did, some things have been said in the doctrine concerning the object; namely, after he had judged the people of Israel for some time, having been captured by the Philistines and deprived of his eyes, he was cast into prison. There he recovered the grace of God and the power of his <term>Nazariteship</term>, and thus, in his recovered vocation, he redeemed the people of Israel and liberated his fatherland from the enemies by whom it was oppressed. He fought bravely, he conquered, and he sealed his victory with his own death. (3) Where this occurred, the sacred history teaches, namely in a public place where the Philistines had gathered to celebrate a festival to the false god <term>Dagon</term> <gloss>Philistine deity</gloss>, where God was mocked, and Samson, that chosen Prince of God, was held in derision. Not a few think this house was the temple of <term>Dagon</term> itself, because of the size, which is not to be presumed in a private house</translation>

<translation page="19">private; for three thousand men were in the upper part of the house. The place, therefore, was not narrow; which also proves all the more that those extraordinary powers were so immense that they were clearly to be judged incomparable. (4) By what aids he did this is clear from the prayers, namely by supernatural aid, the special grace of God, and clearly divine assistance. (5) Finally, it must be seen how that man of God, a judge of the people and therefore a public person, liberated his people and avenged the deprivation of his eyes and the injury brought upon himself and God through this. Clearly, he seized the opportunity given to him: for when he saw that every hope of victory without his death was vain, he chose to perish in mutual destruction rather than leave the glory of God stained, his fatherland without liberty, and his enemies without vengeance. He sought therefore victory with accompanying death as one called to it, and he preferred to render the life bestowed and granted to him to God and his country, rather than to retain it unjustly.

->§. 19.<-

Samson, therefore, did not kill himself properly, as he would have done if he had run himself through with a sword or dashed his head against a column; but he allowed himself to be overwhelmed with the enemy. Nor did he kill himself by moral imputation, because he primarily intended to kill the Philistines and seek vengeance for his eyes. Secondarily, however, and only permissively, he involved himself in that same slaughter, which he could not escape. This was, indeed, of great fortitude, as Cornelius a Lapide says on this passage. Not inappropriately, therefore, does Ambrose say of him in epistle 70 on this passage:
> *Samson conquered himself in death; and although indeed he was incomparable in this life, yet in death he conquered himself, and bore an insuperable spirit, so that he despised, and as it were held for nothing, the end of life which is fearful to all.*
It was therefore of virtue that he closed the day with a number of victories, and found not a captive end, but a triumphal one. Finally, not with weapons,</translation>

<translation page="10">and openly took up [this contention] in the fourth year, and thus, while Luther was alive, he was never suspected of this among the Saxons. H. and M. in the Public Acts, pages 3, 4, 5. Hence the Most Illustrious PRINCE, FREDERICK IV, in that same eighty-ninth year, in order to investigate Krentzheim’s doctrine, proposed in the assembly of priests the Table of Lutherans concerning the difference between the dogmas of Luther and Calvin, etc., printed at Wittenberg in the year of our Lord 1575, and he urged him in a friendly manner to return a response that was express, simple, and straightforward to each point in writing. Acts, pages 7, 82. He did this, though reluctantly, yet by acting correctly—as the theologians of Rostock, Oels, Frankfurt, and Saxony judged—using the phrases and words of our own people <note>(i)</note> and handed this confession of his to the MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE on nearly the last day of September. Acts, pages 82, 24b, 25b, 65b, 98. Report, page 26. FREDERICK IV then caused it to be sent to the Rostock theologians on the fifteenth day of April of the following year, 1590, and in the month of January of the ninety-first year to the theologians of Oels, with two of Krentzheim’s orations added, which were delivered at the general convention by the mandate of FREDERICK IV in excuse of Calvinism. Finally, in the month of April, he had it sent to the Academy of Frankfurt. All of these, pondering this confession and the remaining writings most diligently from beginning to end, condemned Leonhard Krentzheim in the transmitted judgments and annotations for Calvinism in the Articles concerning the Holy Supper and the Person of Christ. Acts, pages 24b, 28, 43, 65, 92, 98.

> (i) He speaks indeed with us, yet he holds with the Calvinists; the voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau. Acts, pages 19, 21.

### X.

The theologians in the villages of Bärsdorf and Cuniz judged no differently concerning Krentzheim, and in the sight of all, when the MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE, moved by their prayers, around this ninety-first year, called the pastors of the Duchy of Legnica with Krentzheim into a public trial, which was instituted on the fifteenth day of January, they remained constant in this opinion in both voice and writing. Acts, page 87. Our man indeed responded with many words to the charges brought against him and attempted to purge the crime, but the Prince by no means approved of the response, and he sent the testimony of the contrary will he had interposed, exhibited in writing, once again to the Academy of Frankfurt. Krentzheim, summoned to the hall on the twentieth day of June, took the judgments of this University and the Questions, which had been sent back from Frankfurt on the third day of May of that same year, to his home with the permission of the Judge, who was the Prefect of the Prince, and on the seventh hour of the morning of the following day he returned them with a written and speciously adorned response.</translation>

<translation page="11">Acts, pages 102, 103. But this plausible response was vehemently protested by all, as both the explanations and the methods and formulas of explaining the Article concerning the Holy Supper, which *Martin Gosky*, formerly pastor of the Marian church, had excerpted from Krentzheim’s orations delivered in the conventions of pastors, and had publicly read aloud in the presence of all the pastors, argued and taught that he was entirely suspect. For this reason, the Frankfurt theologians were consulted a third time by the Most Illustrious Prince via letters written on the eleventh day of July; but since Krentzheim had also responded poorly in this writing to those things that were asked, they could not acquiesce, but on the thirty-first day of June, with the judgments transmitted to the Prince, they once again deemed him suspect of Calvinism. *Acts, pages 109, 110b.*

# PARADOX VII.

## A <term>lunula</term> <gloss>crescent shape</gloss> (a part of a circle), although it was long ago reduced to a square area by Hippocrates of Chios, the <term>quadrature</term> <gloss>squaring</gloss> of the circle has not yet been found to this day.

### DECLARATION.

The <term>tetragonism</term> <gloss>squaring of a square</gloss>, or <term>quadrature</term> of the circle, has hitherto been attempted chiefly in two ways, either Geometrically through lines, or Arithmetically through numbers: by the former method the <term>lunula</term> was long ago reduced to a square space by Hippocrates of Chios, but the circle itself, in no way, neither Geometrically nor Arithmetically, could be squared to this day.

### DEMONSTRATION.

That the quadrature of the <term>lunulae</term> was most correctly discovered by Hippocrates of Chios, no one will deny, if they have properly grasped his demonstration, for it is as follows: Let a circle *a, b, c, d* be drawn, and upon its diameter *b, c* let there be constructed a square *b, e, f, c* whose <term>diagonius</term> <gloss>diagonal</gloss></translation>

<translation page="13">is *b, d, f* (see Fig. VI). Let there also be drawn a semidiameter *g, i, d*, perpendicular to *b, e*, which will bisect both the semicircle *b, d, c* and the diagonal *b, d, f* at point *d*. Therefore, having made *d* the center and *d, b* the interval, let another circle be described through points *b, e, f*, and let the straight line *d, c* be connected. Now, since in the right-angled triangle *b, e, f*, the side *b, f* subtends the right angle *b, e, f*, its square will be double the square of *b, e* or *e, f* by 47 of the first of Euclid. And consequently, the circle *b, e, f* will be double the circle *a, b, d, c* by 2 of the twelfth of Euclid, and the semicircle *b, e, f* will be double the semicircle *b, a, c*, and the quadrant *b, g, d, c* will be equal to the same semicircle *b, a, c*. Therefore, the common segment *b, g, c, i* having been removed, there remains the <term>lunula</term> *b, a, c, g*, equal to the triangle *b, i, d*. Which triangle, if it is squared according to the last of the second of Euclid, the <term>lunula</term> *b, a, c, g* will be squared. But that the circle to this day has not been reduced to a square space, neither by lines nor by numbers, is clearly evident from the most recent writings of geometers. Hippocrates indeed persuaded himself that by the same reason by which he had completed the quadrature of the <term>lunula</term> (a part of a circle), the whole circle could also be squared, and therefore he attributed to himself the discovery of the tetragonism or quadrature of the circle. But in truth, how ingeniously he had reduced the <term>lunula</term> to a square space, so shamefully he hallucinated in squaring the circle, as is plain to anyone from Father Caspar Schott’s <italic>Technica Curiosa</italic> Book VIII, § 1, my page 600, 601, and Christopher Clavius’s <italic>Mathematical Works</italic> Volume II, Book VIII, page 189. Indeed, it is credible, says Blancanus in <italic>Aristotelian Mathematical Topics</italic>, that Hippocrates recognized this fallacy (which he used in squaring the circle) and, on account of the subtlety of the discovery, concealed it. It happened no differently with the most recent attempts at the quadrature of the circle, in which, when they are properly examined, a paralogism <note>logical fallacy</note> is for the most part detected, so that many today judge the tetragonism to be absolutely impossible; see the <italic>Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensium</italic> <note>Journal of the Learned of Leipzig</note> for the month of September, the year 1687, page 524. Therefore, although the <term>lunula</term> (a part of a circle) has long since been reduced to a square space, the quadrature of the circle has nevertheless not yet been found to this day. but this does not extend to the nephews of brothers and sisters.

### XXI.

Therefore, parents succeed to their children who have died without children, brothers, and sisters, equally, along with the surviving brothers or sisters of the deceased who are joined on both sides, counting by heads; however, they succeed together with the children of these, by right of representation, counting by lines of descent.

### XXII.

Parents of different lines, from the paternal and maternal, placed in an equal degree, divide the inheritance of the deceased today not according to their individual portion, but having taken the line of descent into account, without distinction of the goods left by the deceased.

### XXIII.

It is a point of known law that brothers and the sons of brothers who are joined to the deceased on one side are excluded by all ascendants.

### XXIV.

An adoptive father cannot be the heir of his adopted son whom he does not have under his power, although a son of that kind succeeds to him.

### XXV.

I would say otherwise concerning him into whose power the adopted person passes, to whom, just as to the <term>arrogator</term> <gloss>one who adopts a person already in their own right</gloss> regarding the property of a pubescent adopted son, succession is granted as a legitimate and natural father.

### XXVI.

Natural parents succeed to their children whom they have legitimized by subsequent marriage, or by the rescript of a prince, or by presentation to the court, in the same way as natural and legitimate children.

### XXVII.

In the same way that natural children and illegitimate children succeed to their parents, so these succeed to them in turn: namely, the natural father and his ascendants succeed to their natural son for two ounces <note>a fraction of the inheritance, typically 2/12ths</note>, but the mother and those ascending from the maternal line [succeed] to the whole.

### XXIIX.

I believe there is no doubt that those born from incest and condemned coitus, if they cease to be among the living, have neither a father, nor a mother, nor any of the ascendants as a successor.

### XXIX.

These are the rules concerning the succession of those who consist in the direct line: when these are lacking, the collaterals succeed in the oblique line, whose succession extends to the tenth degree.

### XXX.

But whether the succession of agnates in the succession of an ancient fief is limited to certain degrees or proceeds to infinity, the opinions of doctors vary due to discrepant texts, which I believe ought to be reconciled by a covenant of distinction.

### XXXI.

Brothers and sisters <term>ἀμφιθαλεῖς</term> <gloss>full brothers and sisters, born of the same father and mother</gloss> joined on both sides, with those joined only by one side excluded, are called to the inheritance of a predeceased brother counting by heads; the children of predeceased full brothers, but not others, are called together with these by right of representation, counting by lines of descent.

<summary>This page defines inheritance hierarchies for parents, collaterals, and adopted or legitimized children, including distinctions between full and half-blood relations.</summary>
<keywords>succession, parents, agnates, full siblings, representation, legitimacy, inheritance law</keywords>
</translation>

### XXXII.

Does a half-brother <term>frater consanguineus</term> <gloss>brother related through the father only</gloss> also get excluded by those joined on both sides in the law of fiefs? The received opinion is that he is to be admitted to the fief of the deceased along with the full brother.

### XXXIII.

Brothers succeed one another in a paternal fief; in a new one, this is not the case, but the fief reverts to the lord; however, sisters of either are incapable.

### XXXIV.

If only the children of full brothers exist, and no paternal uncles are living, are they called to the succession of the deceased uncle by heads or by lines of descent? It has been established that they are called by heads, both in new and old law, and this is true.

### XXXV.

If the deceased has left no brothers or sisters joined on both sides, or their children, but only uterine <note>related through the mother</note> or paternal [siblings], then these are admitted to the inheritance of the brother.

### XXXVI.

Not, indeed, so that paternal goods are deferred to the paternal side and maternal to the maternal, as in the old law; but the inheritance of the deceased is divided equally between the paternal and uterine [relatives] if they are present at the same time; if only one side is present, he obtains the entire inheritance.

### XXXVII.

Those adopted by ascendants from both the paternal and maternal lines succeed one another collaterally, as do the <term>arrogati</term> <gloss>those adopted under the power of another</gloss>, even though they are not contained under the name of blood relatives.

Collaterals related to each other by a natural bond <note>illegitimate blood relation</note> do not enjoy any right of succession; however, it is a point of certain law that those connected through the maternal line, even if one is natural and the other legitimate, succeed to one another.

Illegitimate children <term>spurij</term> <gloss>children born out of wedlock</gloss> born from one and the same father but different mothers are prohibited from succeeding to one another; which no one would affirm regarding <term>ὁμογαστρίοις</term> <gloss>children of the same mother</gloss> illegitimate children.

### XL.

Among incestuous brothers, and also those adopted by a stranger, there is no succession.

### XLI.

After brothers and the sons of brothers, those who are closer in degree are called by heads, so that those equal in degree are admitted equally without difference of sex.

### XLII.

So much for the succession of those touching the deceased by kinship: to whom

<translation page="262">It was also spoken thus:
The manifestation of the reality of sound is not something that truly exists, as it is completely empty. Although one becomes fully satisfied by sound, there is no sound that is self-arising. I offer the wisdom that arises from sound as an offering. I offer it with body, speech, and mind. Because it is pure from the very beginning, self-arising, I offer medicines compounded from eight thousand roots, as well as substances such as <term>rasayana</term> <gloss>rejuvenating elixirs</gloss>. These are the substances of the five families and five pledges, fulfilled through the five wisdoms. To liberate all sentient beings of the six realms, this nectar eliminates the five poisons. To the blessed ones—the five families of Father and Mother, the brothers and sisters of the Bodhisattvas, the Kuntuzangpo Father and Mother, the six sages, and the gatekeepers with their consorts and the assembly of <term>Dakinis</term>—I offer this pure nectar and sacred substance as a pleasing offering. May you look upon us with compassion and be pleased; please grant the supreme miraculous accomplishment. In the stainless, pure nature of the sky, many signs of deluded thought gather like masses of clouds. To clearly illuminate them with the sunlight of wisdom, I realize the meaning of purity and make this offering. The wondrous <term>torma</term> <gloss>ritual offering cake</gloss> and the five qualities of desire, the suchness...

<leaf-break/>

...the maker and the noble ones, the washerman and the dancer, make ink with human blood. Write the heart-mantras of each of the nine deities with a pen made from a supreme leg bone. Invoke the presence of the <term>bandha</term> <gloss>skull-cup</gloss> to be seated. That supreme, great Vajra family, holding the Vajra and bell, possesses both method and wisdom. May it be seated as the mudra of symbols. The crescent-moon mandala is the space of the Mother. The <term>bandha</term> is the body of the Sugata. The seed syllables are the speech of the Sugata. The butter lamp is the mind of the Sugata. Surrounded by the light of the nine wisdoms and adorned with substances, I circle around. To clarify the wisdom of meditative concentration, I write it plainly even while depending on the eyes. To clarify the wisdom of attachment, I place it before the eyes. Investigating the mind in the phenomena that are not observed, and through the power of the generosity of the wisdom-eye, may everything be blessed correctly. From the higher investigation, having marked everything, I contemplate the seed syllable that transforms into anything. In the past, in the time that has gone by, the great self-investigation—in the scriptures of the Tathagatas, in the manner of wanderers, previously...</translation>

<translation page="263">...it occurred. At that time, all sentient beings became extremely angry and fierce. Calling out and falling, they became extremely wicked and angry. To those who are extremely angry and fierce, peaceful means do not bring benefit. Therefore, all Tathagatas act as wrathful deities through the essence of wisdom and method. If the wrathful display of the wrathful ones burns the three worlds, there is no need to speak of what happens when all Buddhas are enraged. Possessing great compassion, the Vajrasattva Tathagata, to purify those who are hostile to the vows, reveals the mudra of the charnel ground dance. Having made the lotus and precious jewels present, that which is indicated by the magical signs of <term>Demchok</term> <gloss>Chakrasamvara</gloss>, that which is the arising of the blissful sovereign of the basic space, is the light of the great self-knowing wisdom. Like a gathering of the fires at the end of an aeon, light resides within the form of the physical body. The gathering of blazing ones is contemplated. It was also spoken thus: The Father and Mother who imprint bliss are revealed in the mudra. Bliss, the bewildering state of non-duality. Bliss, the exhaustless, various activities...

<leaf-break/>

...and for the sake of taming the untamable without exception, consume flesh, bones, and so forth. I am the Great Blood-Drinker. For all those bound by the net of cyclic existence, within the ocean of gathered great red blood, I revel with the assembly of <term>Dakinis</term>. Without being attached to evil desires, the enemies and obstacle-makers who are hostile to the vows must be liberated by the power of direct presence. <term>Shri vajra kara mukha shara ya namo. Om shri vajra raga samaya namo. Om shri vajra khatvanga prachamaya ya namo. Om shri vajra ghanta jala ya namo. Sarva buddha gata bandha dana ma karo mi. Maha yogini. Ati pu ho. Prati dza ho. Dza hum bam ho. Shri Heruka aina. Dhupe, Pushpe, Dipa gandhe, balingdha, prati dza ho. Hri bandha kha kha khahi khadza hum bam ho. Shri Heruka. Maha vajra. Aveshaya, aveshaya, praveshaya, praveshaya. Prati dza ho. Shri bandha khahi khahi. Dza hum bam ho. Shri Heruka. Maha vajra sarva dushtan. Samaya mudra. Mara kha khahi khahi. Hridaya sipa hum phat. Shri Heruka. Maha mansa, maha rakta, maha tsitta, maha basuta, maha pancha amrita, maha argham drati</term>.</translation>

<summary>These pages contain liturgical instructions for ritual offerings, including the preparation of substances like nectar and torma, the visualization of wrathful deities, and the application of sacred mantras to achieve the liberation of beings.</summary>
<keywords>Tantra, Heruka, Dakini, ritual offerings, blood-drinker, mandala, wisdom, liberation</keywords>

<translation page="88">As for the grudges, it is like this: because the grudge of a woman is lowly, if one were to enter while another is inside, they would undoubtedly kill one another. What was said about paying five hundred <term>karshapana</term> <gloss>units of currency</gloss> to enter is also true, and it is undoubtedly necessary for her clothing and ornaments. 

What was said about the house being vacated after seven days is also true; even if it is done sooner or later, what conflict is there in that? What was said about not inquiring about the men coming out or going in is also true; this is a courtesan, so if one were to inquire about men coming out or going in, who would enter her house? Then the assembly granted her the five supreme conditions, and she was enjoyed by the assembly. When the Licchavis of Vaishali began to enter her house for their own pleasure, some, out of strong attachment to sensual objects, became free of desire the moment they saw her. Others were free of desire merely upon touching her; no one could perform the act of a man with her. She thought, "These are not men, so I shall arrange a method." As she lived in various places,

<leaf-break/>

Amrapali, who was perfect in beauty and youth, possessed of the sixty-four arts, and suitable for the enjoyment of gods alone, resided there. She said, "Your Majesty, if that is the case, then travel to Vaishali. There, we shall enjoy ourselves to our heart's content." He said, "The Licchavis of Vaishali have been enemies who have long caused harm and retaliated; if I go, they will cause you harm." The king said, "Wise ones, people are courageous, so I will go." She said, "If you are insistent on going for a fruitless goal, then you may go." He boarded a carriage and departed for Vaishali with the king. Arriving gradually in Vaishali, the king stayed in a pleasure grove. The king entered Amrapali’s house. After a while, the sound of a bell rang out. The Licchavis of Vaishali became agitated, saying, "Wise ones, a person who is not our friend has entered, and the bell has rung." As the noise grew loud, King Bimbisara asked Amrapali, "Lovely one, what is this?" "Your Majesty, they are inspecting the residence." "For what reason?" "For your sake." "What shall we do? Shall we flee?" "Your Majesty, do not be displeased. Your Majesty, stay for seven days and..."</translation>

<translation page="89">...staying for seven days, you will enjoy yourself, and you will know the time." 

He played, rejoiced, and engaged in pleasure with her. After some time, Amrapali became pregnant and said to King Bimbisara, "Your Majesty, I have conceived." He gave her a signet ring and said, "If it is a girl, it is yours. If it is a boy, put this signet ring around his neck and bring him to me." When the time came, she boarded a carriage and departed with the king, but the bell rang out. They said, "Wise ones, the enemy has emerged, pursue him." Five hundred Licchavis with arrow-spoked wheels chased after King Bimbisara. Seeing this, the king said, "Your Majesty, the Licchavis of Vaishali are coming. Shall we fight them, or shall I drive the carriage?" He said, "I am exhausted, so you drive the carriage, and you alone shall fight them." As he began to fight with them, the Vaishalis recognized him

<leaf-break/>

"Wise ones, whoever our enemy is, that is his father," and they struck him even harder. When he arrived in due time, he told his mother everything that had happened. She thought, "The Licchavis of Vaishali are cruel and powerful; if he stays, there is a place where he might be killed." While she was thinking this, she saw many merchants carrying goods, traveling to Rajagriha, and she said, "With this signet ring, you will be exempted from taxes and duties. Take this boy to the king's palace, place this signet ring around his neck, and leave him at the gate of Rajagriha." They agreed, saying, "We shall do just that." She also gave the boy a pearl necklace and said, "Boy, when you gather where the king is needed, place the pearl necklace on your feet and sit in a lap in fear. If anyone says, 'This boy does not know how to be afraid,' then say to them, 'Does a boy ever have fear of his father?'" He traveled gradually with the merchants to Rajagriha. They bathed, tied the signet ring on, and left him at the gate of the king's palace. He then went to where the king was...</translation>

<summary>This passage recounts the story of the courtesan Amrapali, her relationship with King Bimbisara, and the birth of their son, who is sent to the king's court in Rajagriha to escape the hostility of the Vaishali Licchavis.</summary>
<keywords>Amrapali, King Bimbisara, Vaishali, Licchavis, courtesan, court intrigue, Rajagriha</keywords>

<translation page="386">The 108 positions of the pulse <note>or points of focus</note>. Having recited one hundred or even one, along with eight, remain fasting through the day and night. On the seventh, offer the rosary to the sage. Recite it just as before.

The measurements must be made equivalent. Then, recite the rosary completely. On that very night, stay there. On the ground covered with <term>kusha</term> <gloss>sacrificial grass</gloss>, the mantra practitioner should sleep. Whichever dreams are seen, if one sees an auspicious dream, it is the certain manifestation of the dream. Through that, the accomplishment <term>siddhi</term> will be realized. If the practitioner sees Buddhas, Shravakas, or Pratyekabuddhas in a dream, the mantra will be accomplished with fruits. Perform that ritual with certainty. It is unerring due to being perfectly grasped by superior insight <term>vipashyana</term> <gloss>insight meditation</gloss>. It is not common because of direct perception. <translation page="107">One will be protected from all attackers, enemies, malevolence, and negative deeds. Never again will fear arise from anyone anywhere, and one will be completely liberated. Moreover, one will no longer be stained by the defilement of negative deeds. If you mix <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pills with sesame oil, smear them on your face, and appear before a king, you will be embraced like a son and will receive great joy, and all fear of a wrathful king will be pacified. If you smear it on your body, even if the body is destined to be killed, it will not be harmed by weapons but will instead break into pieces. If an arrow is shot, it will not land on your body, and the bow will break. If you tie a <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pill around your neck and enter wild places, mountains, or dense, difficult-to-traverse forests, all fears from bandits, tricksters, thieves, <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>, <term>rakshasas</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, humans, non-humans, vicious wild animals, venomous snakes, and poisons will not arise; they will not be there. If you tie it to your right shoulder, you will be victorious over others in every respect. You will become a great object of reverence in all places. Everyone will possess great power and diligence.
<leaf-break/>
All those food items will be summoned and will come; wherever you desire them, they will come there. If you go to a perfume shop, all the goods in the shop will come to you. If you clap your hands at the door of a brewery, all the pots of beer will come to you. If you clap your hands at the door of a granary, all the grain will be summoned. If you enter the house of a sugar producer and touch their equipment, all the sugar cane juice and slabs of brown sugar will come to you; they will be sent wherever you desire. If you clap your hands at the city gate during the twilight, everyone residing in the city will be awakened from their sleep. If you tap on an enemy’s door, they will be driven away. If you throw it into the house of a weapons maker, the weapons and armor will become frozen and stiff. If you tap on a king’s door, all opposing parties, enemies, and vicious sentient beings will be bound, frozen, and stiffened. If you smear it on a conch shell and blow it from a high place, wherever the sound is heard, one will be completely liberated from fighting, strife, harm, disputes, magic, black magic, poisons, and diseases. If you blow it at the city gate, pestilence, harm, and the</translation>
<translation page="108">crushing of the poor will not occur, and one will suppress the opponent. If you tie it to your left shoulder, you will become highly honored by all men, women, boys, and girls, and everyone will look upon you with desire. You will become a great object of offerings. Many purposes will be accomplished. If you tie it to your right calf, you will be able to travel a thousand leagues without becoming tired. If you hold a <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pill in your mouth and, with your right hand, recite the "Hook of Meaningful Intent" for mustard seeds and draw them forth without speaking any other words, you will become a high-ranking person. In whichever direction you focus your thoughts, if you cast the mustard seeds toward the direction where the men, women, boys, and girls are, they will immediately be summoned and will arrive. Even if they are residing a hundred leagues away, they will surely come within three days without doubt. If you tie a <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pill to your right or left hand, wherever you touch, wealth, grain, gold, jewels, pearls, conch shells, coral, refined gold, silver, clothing, and all such ornaments will be summoned and come to you; whatever you desire will come. If you enter a kitchen and clap your hands at the door of the cooking area, all the cooking and the cooking vessels
<leaf-break/>
will be completely pacified. If you blow it in a cattle pen, all the milk will be extracted. It will go wherever you desire. If you blow it in a sheep or goat pen, all the sheep and goat milk will be extracted, and it will go wherever you desire. If you blow it in the middle of a great gathering of people, everyone will become naked and all their clothing will be summoned. If you smear it on a clay drum and beat it on a high veranda, all cold, wind, and hail will be bound and scattered, and they will not do any harm. Hail will be stopped within a hundred leagues all around. If you blow it throughout the entirety of a city or region, all diseases, pestilence, harm, and violence will be pacified. All fighting, strife, disputes, and disputes will be thoroughly pacified. All fears of poverty and famine will be thoroughly pacified. Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of various kinds of needs will be accomplished; it should be applied to all of them. Then, in common with all sentient beings, it will pacify all fourth and increasing diseases, destroy all negative deeds, thoroughly pacify all pestilence and harm, thoroughly pacify all places of famine, and [pacify] <term>bhutas</term> <gloss>spirits</gloss> and <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>.</translation>

Many purposes will be accomplished. If you tie it to your right calf, you will be able to travel a thousand leagues without becoming tired. If you hold a <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pill in your mouth and, with your right hand, recite the "Hook of Meaningful Intent" for mustard seeds and draw them forth without speaking any other words, you will become a high-ranking person. In whichever direction you focus your thoughts, if you cast the mustard seeds toward the direction where the men, women, boys, and girls are, they will immediately be summoned and will arrive. Even if they are residing a hundred leagues away, they will surely come within three days without doubt. If you tie a <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pill to your right or left hand, wherever you touch, wealth, grain, gold, jewels, pearls, conch shells, coral, refined gold, silver, clothing, and all such ornaments will be summoned and come to you; whatever you desire will come. If you enter a kitchen and clap your hands at the door of the cooking area, all the cooking and the cooking vessels
<leaf-break/>
will be completely pacified. If you blow it in a cattle pen, all the milk will be extracted. It will go wherever you desire. If you blow it in a sheep or goat pen, all the sheep and goat milk will be extracted, and it will go wherever you desire. If you blow it in the middle of a great gathering of people, everyone will become naked and all their clothing will be summoned. If you smear it on a clay drum and beat it on a high veranda, all cold, wind, and hail will be bound and scattered, and they will not do any harm. Hail will be stopped within a hundred leagues all around. If you blow it throughout the entirety of a city or region, all diseases, pestilence, harm, and violence will be pacified. All fighting, strife, disputes, and disputes will be thoroughly pacified. All fears of poverty and famine will be thoroughly pacified. Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of various kinds of needs will be accomplished; it should be applied to all of them. Then, in common with all sentient beings, it will pacify all fourth and increasing diseases, destroy all negative deeds, thoroughly pacify all pestilence and harm, thoroughly pacify all places of famine, and [pacify] <term>bhutas</term> <gloss>spirits</gloss> and <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>.

<translation page="352">
[… ] prepared. Medicine is for eating. Water is for constant drinking. One is not oppressed by the force of aging or death, and one is always protected. Make a crest from the hair of a thief.

To this, one must apply the <term>Hum</term> <gloss>seed syllable</gloss>. The practitioner of yoga should properly hold the skulls of the five Buddhas. The size of the skull should be five finger-widths. By doing this, one holds the crest. From the nature of <term>Upaya</term> <gloss>skillful means</gloss> and <term>Prajna</term> <gloss>wisdom</gloss>, the hair belt is worn in two loops. Wear ashes for the sake of offering to the hair. The yogi holds to these practices. The sound of the small drum <term>damaru</term> is the recitation.

The <term>Khatvanga</term> <gloss>tantric staff</gloss> is the meditation on wisdom. Through the practice of the <term>Vajra</term> <gloss>thunderbolt/diamond</gloss> skull, these are recited and meditated upon. Desires, ignorance, fear, and anger—the fruits of shame—are completely abandoned.

Having personally abandoned the two <note>referring to conceptual duality</note>, one should practice without doubt. After giving the gift of the body, one should correctly perform the conduct. By practicing according to those who are capable and those who are not, therefore one should not give gifts. Eat whatever is obtained, whether it is food or drink. To avoid the conceptual thoughts of pleasant and unpleasant, one should not have attachment. Do not discriminate between what is to be eaten and not eaten, between conduct and non-conduct, or between walking and not walking. The practitioner of mantra should not have conceptual thought. Which student has attained the <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>accomplishment</gloss>? Truly...
<leaf-break/>
Regarding showing garments, their three points are well explained. Whoever shows the breasts, their limit is well explained. Whoever shows the teeth, their mouth is well explained. Whoever shows a frown, it should be said that the topknot should be loosened. Whoever shows the forehead, their back is well explained. Whoever shows the soles of the feet, by reversing, one should play. Through the <term>Mudra</term> <gloss>hand gesture</gloss> and the reply of the <term>Mudra</term>, one is differentiated through the <term>Samaya</term> <gloss>sacred bond</gloss>. To this, the yogini says, "Wonderful, son, you have great compassion! If one shows a garland in the hand, it is said that one should gather." If the garland is explicitly offered, one remains in the <term>Samaya</term> and the vows are good. That which is called the external gathering is the place of good conduct. To that, the yogini says, "Do whatever is said." "O Bhagavan, what is the place of gathering?" The Bhagavan replied, "The place and the near-place, the field and the near-field, the <term>Chandoh</term> <gloss>sacred site</gloss> and the near-<term>Chandoh</term>, likewise the gathering and the near-gathering. The <term>Pitha</term> <gloss>sacred site/seat</gloss> and the near-<term>Pitha</term>. The charnel ground and the near-charnel ground. These are the twelve lands. The Lord of the ten lands is the protector. This should not be spoken of by others. O Bhagavan, the place..."</translation>

<translation page="353">
...and so on, what are they?" The Bhagavan replied, "The place is explained as <term>Jalandhara</term>. Likewise, it is <term>Oddiyana</term>. The place is <term>Kollagiri</term>. Likewise, it is <term>Kamaru</term>. The near-place is said to be <term>Malava</term>. It is <term>Sindhunagara</term>. The field is explained as <term>Mummuni</term>. The field is the number of those who act. <term>Devikota</term> is likewise a field. The field is the number of the <term>Lachpa</term> <gloss>a specific regional category</gloss>. The near-field is said to be <term>Kuluta</term>. Likewise, it is <term>Arbuda</term>, and the <term>Khabai</term> mountain, bestower of the supreme <term>vayu</term> <gloss>wind/breath</gloss>. The near-fields are summarized. The <term>Chandoh</term> is <term>Harikela</term>, and those born within the salt ocean, <term>Lampaka</term> and <term>Kanci</term>. Likewise, it is <term>Saurastra</term>. The near-<term>Chandoh</term> is <term>Kalinga</term>, the island containing gold, and <term>Konkana</term> is also a near-<term>Chandoh</term>. This is summarized. The <term>Pitha</term> are the cities and those residing at the edge of the <term>Pitha</term> villages, <term>Caritra</term> and <term>Kosala</term>, the city of the <term>Bindha</term> youth. The <term>Vajra</term> essence is great compassion. The near-<term>Pitha</term> are those. The charnel ground is the supreme <term>Sangha</term>, and the edge of the charnel ground ocean. The edge of the park pond is said to be the near-charnel ground. For the sake of all sentient beings, the <term>Vajra</term> of the <term>Yogini Tantra</term>, the good gathering of the <term>Yogini</term>, even during the day...
<leaf-break/>
...the sentient beings fall under the power of those. This is the seventh chapter, the Chapter on Signs and Places. 

Then, the Mandala of the <term>Yogini</term> will be explained. In the space of the sky, one should contemplate the <term>Bhaga</term> <gloss>womb/source</gloss>. In the center, what is to be meditated upon is the mandala, in order as they appear, the gods as they manifest. The mandala, the earth and water are first. According to what is appropriate, the <term>Agni</term> <gloss>fire</gloss>, and the great wind from the gods, and how the meditator appears, is the mandala born from the source of phenomena. The two extras are without faults. One arises from the stamen. It is said to be the outer part of the triangle. Inside that, one should contemplate the nature of the seat of the fifteen dead. Above that is the moon. Above the moon is the seed syllable. Afterwards, one is suppressed by the conqueror of the <term>Mara</term> <gloss>demonic forces</gloss>. From the bowing of the two, there is great bliss. <term>Ali</term> <gloss>vowels</gloss> remain in the form of the moon. They make manifest in the form of <term>Kali</term> <gloss>consonants</gloss>. From the union of the moon and sun, the white and others are famous. The moon possesses the mirror-like wisdom. The seventh of the seven possesses equality. The seed syllable and hand emblem of one's own deity should be spoken of as individual discrimination. Everything becomes one, the exertion. The perfection is the pure <term>Dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>expanse of reality</gloss>. By the ritual spoken by the wise, the five aspects...</translation>

<summary>These pages outline tantric behavioral conduct, including the use of specific implements like skulls and drums, and detail the geography of sacred sites (Pitha, Chandoh) for gathering. The text concludes by beginning a technical description of the Yogini mandala and its symbolic components.</summary>
<keywords>Vajrayana, Yogini Tantra, sacred sites, Pitha, Chandoh, Mandala, Vajra, Mudra, Samaya, tantric conduct</keywords>

<translation page="10">Adorned with a wheel of light,
She stirs the masses of her own radiance.
Homage to her, radiant with great joy,
She who wears a crown of light-garlands.
With the laughter of <term>Tuttare</term> <gloss>the second mantra of Tara</gloss>,
She brings demons and the world under her control.
Homage to her who is able to summon
The entire host of those who protect the earth.
By the <term>Hum</term> <gloss>a sacred seed-syllable</gloss> of her shaking, frowning face,
She completely liberates all from poverty.
Homage to her, crowned with a crescent moon,
Adorned with all that blazes brightly.
From her hair, <term>Amitabha</term> <gloss>Buddha of Infinite Light</gloss>
Constantly emits rays of great light.
Homage to her who dwells in the center
Of a garland of fire, like the fire at the end of the eon.
Right leg extended,
<leaf-break/>
Left leg drawn in, surrounded by joy,
She completely destroys the ranks of the enemy.
Homage to her who strikes the surface of the earth
With her palms and beats it with her feet.
With the <term>Hum</term> <gloss>sacred seed-syllable</gloss> and a frowning face,
She shatters the seven levels.
Homage to her who is blissful, virtuous, and peaceful,
Whose sphere of activity is Nirvana <gloss>the cessation of suffering</gloss>.
Endowed with the <term>Om</term> and <term>Svaha</term> <gloss>sacred mantras</gloss>,
She truly destroys all great sins.
Homage to her who is surrounded by joy,
She completely shatters the bodies of the enemies.
With the ten-syllable mantra arranged in speech,
She is the liberator born from the <term>Hum</term> of wisdom.
Homage to her who stamps her feet in <term>Ture</term>,
She who is the seed-syllable in the form of <term>Hum</term>,
Shaking Mount Meru.</translation>

<translation page="11">Mandara and the piercing one,
She makes the three worlds tremble.
Homage to her who holds in her hand
The deer-marked <gloss>moon</gloss> emblem of the celestial ocean.
By twice uttering <term>Tare</term> and the syllable <term>Phat</term>,
She clears away all poisons without exception.
Homage to her who is the king of the gods' host,
Resorted to by gods and <term>kimnaras</term> <gloss>mythical celestial musicians</gloss>.
With the glory of armor that delights from all sides,
She dispels conflict and bad dreams.
Homage to her whose two eyes are bright
With the light of the full sun and moon.
By twice uttering <term>Hara</term> and <term>Tuttare</term>,
She clears away highly violent epidemic diseases.
Homage to her who, by arranging the three suchnesses,
Is perfectly endowed with the power of peace.
She destroys the host of ghosts, zombies,
<leaf-break/>
And <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>; she is the supreme <term>Ture</term>.
This praise of the root mantra
And these twenty-one homages.
Any intelligent person who is truly endowed with devotion
To the goddess, and who recites this with great faith,
Whether rising at dusk or at dawn,
By remembering it, they are granted total fearlessness.
All sins will be completely calmed,
And all lower realms will be destroyed.
Seventy million victorious ones
Will quickly grant empowerment.
They will attain greatness beyond this,
And will proceed to the ultimate state of Buddhahood.
Her poison is the great, fierce one,
Whether dwelling on a seat or moving elsewhere.</translation>

<summary>This text contains the concluding verses of the Twenty-One Praises of Tara, describing her various manifestations, mantras, and the benefits of reciting the prayer. It emphasizes her power to overcome obstacles, diseases, and negative spirits, and the promise of spiritual attainment for the devoted practitioner.</summary>
<keywords>Tara, Praises, Mantras, Buddhas, Protection, Nirvana, Empowerment</keywords>
