She is the liberator born from the <term>Hum</term> of wisdom.
Homage to her who stamps her feet in <term>Ture</term>,
She who is the seed-syllable in the form of <term>Hum</term>,
Shaking Mount Meru.
pages.11:
Mandara and the piercing one,
She makes the three worlds tremble.
Homage to her who holds in her hand
The deer-marked <gloss>moon</gloss> emblem of the celestial ocean.
By twice uttering <term>Tare</term> and the syllable <term>Phat</term>,
She clears away all poisons without exception.
Homage to her who is the king of the gods' host,
Resorted to by gods and <term>kimnaras</term> <gloss>mythical celestial musicians</gloss>.
With the glory of armor that delights from all sides,
She dispels conflict and bad dreams.
Homage to her whose two eyes are bright
With the light of the full sun and moon.
By twice uttering <term>Hara</term> and <term>Tuttare</term>,
She clears away highly violent epidemic diseases.
Homage to her who, by arranging the three suchnesses,
Is perfectly endowed with the power of peace.
She destroys the host of ghosts, zombies,
<leaf-break/>
And <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>; she is the supreme <term>Ture</term>.
This praise of the root mantra
And these twenty-one homages.
Any intelligent person who is truly endowed with devotion
To the goddess, and who recites this with great faith,
Whether rising at dusk or at dawn,
By remembering it, they are granted total fearlessness.
All sins will be completely calmed,
And all lower realms will be destroyed.
Seventy million victorious ones
Will quickly grant empowerment.
They will attain greatness beyond this,
And will proceed to the ultimate state of Buddhahood.
Her poison is the great, fierce one,
Whether dwelling on a seat or moving elsewhere.

<translation page="14">Just as that does not become peaceful, you should know that attachment to sensory desires is also like that. A person afflicted by leprosy is tortured by the movement of insects under their skin, and in an attempt to find relief, they lean entirely toward the warmth of a fire. Although this appears to provide temporary relief, the illness does not subside; instead, the heat causes the lymph to spread, which increases the pain. Similarly, by relying on sensory pleasures, one may feel temporarily satisfied, but craving will expand further, and one will remain insatiable. Therefore, you should know that attachment to sensory desires is like that, and you should reverse from the very beginning the craving that is attached to sensory pleasures.

Because it causes craving to expand and there is no satisfaction, after the section on the certainty of attachment to sensory desires has been explained, the path itself is explained. This includes a detailed explanation of the common path and a brief indication of the uncommon path of the Great Vehicle and the entrance to its fruition. Regarding the first, there are two parts: identifying what is to be cultivated through a summary, and explaining the sequence of the five paths through a detailed explanation. Regarding the first, it is: "To behold the ultimate, cultivate the mental engagement that is in accordance with reality toward phenomena." There is no other virtuous quality that exists like that. The purpose is to see and realize the reality of the ultimate.

<leaf-break/>

Phenomena included within the conditioned and the knowing are called "conditioned" because they are composed of causes and conditions. Furthermore, because they produce subsequent states and then cease in an instant, they are impermanent because they are constantly changing and decaying. In accordance with that, mental engagement that is in accordance with reality, and all conditioned phenomena other than the Truth of the Path, are contaminated. This includes the receptacle of the world, the environment included in the three realms, the sense faculties, the body, and the consciousness and mental factors, which are all contaminated. Those associated with painful feeling are the suffering of suffering. Those associated with pleasant feeling are the suffering of change. Those associated with neutral feeling are the suffering of conditioning. The suffering of suffering is known even by animals and the like. The suffering of change is seen by individuals possessing intelligence. The suffering of conditioning, although it is the basis of all suffering, is not known by others, but is realized by the noble ones. Saying "all phenomena are empty," although in general this often refers to emptiness being free from conceptual elaboration, here, the emptiness of the aspect of the Truth of Suffering refers to being empty of incompatible causes. Therefore, it is impossible in the nature of reality that a creator, such as Ishvara and the like, or those who speak of time or causes as the creator, have produced them; one understands them as empty of such creators. By suppressing the various compatible and appropriate causes and conditions,

<leaf-break/>

The nature of this—the wisdom free from contamination along with ethical discipline and meditative concentration—is endowed with the power to abandon afflictions and is what enables one to attain the state of cessation; being certain of that is the mental engagement with the aspect of the Truth of the Path. Regarding the detailed explanation of the five paths, there are two parts: showing the sequence of the path of ordinary beings and showing the path of the noble ones along with its fruition. The first includes showing the qualities associated with the path of accumulation and showing the qualities associated with the path of preparation. Regarding the first, showing that one must place supreme importance on ethical discipline and wisdom on the path of accumulation: "Even those individuals endowed with high caste, beauty, and learning are not respected if they lack wisdom and ethical discipline. Therefore, whoever possesses these two qualities is worshipped even if they lack other virtues." Although individuals who are of royal caste like a great sala tree, or of brahmin caste like a great sala tree, and thus are of superior caste, who are handsome and healthy, and who possess extensive learning in the eighteen branches of knowledge and other conventional arts, if they lack the wisdom to practice the nature of reality and know the path of liberation, and if they lack the ethical discipline to remain in the purity of what to adopt and what to discard, they are not objects of respect or worship for the world, including the gods. Furthermore, if one possesses caste,

</translation>
<translation page="15">beauty, and learning, need it even be said? Whoever possesses those two virtues—wisdom that knows the nature of reality and the path of liberation, and perfect ethical discipline—even if they lack other virtues, is a holy object of the world’s offerings and respect. Regarding wisdom, there are three types: wisdom born of hearing, wisdom born of contemplation, and wisdom born of meditation. In this context of the path of accumulation, wisdom born of hearing and wisdom born of contemplation are primary. Although there are limitless bodhisattva vows, in this context, it refers to the ethical discipline of individual liberation. Regarding the need for one on the path of accumulation to balance conceptual thoughts regarding the eight worldly concerns: "O knower of the world, whether gain or lack of gain, pleasure or displeasure, fame or lack of fame, or praise and blame, do not allow these eight worldly concerns to be the object of your mind; balance them." The Fully Awakened Buddha, the knower of the world, commanded that the eight worldly concerns must be balanced. That is, the gain of perfect resources versus the lack of gain, being destitute; having a healthy body and a happy mind versus displeasure; hearing pleasant reports passed from one person to another versus unpleasant reports; and being directly praised versus being blamed.

<leaf-break/>

So that it does not become a companion in the future, one should never perform negative deeds for the sake of others. The connected meaning of this stanza: If one thinks that because the result of performing negative deeds does not occur immediately, there is no need to abandon them, it says: "Although some negative deeds that have been performed do not cut like a weapon at that very moment, when the time of death arrives, the result of the negative deed that has been performed will become manifest." The results of most negative deeds that have been performed, unlike a wound inflicted by a sharp weapon, do not ripen or cut immediately. However, when the time of death, the intermediate state, or a future life arrives, the result that is the maturation of the negative deed will be experienced and will become manifest. If one asks how long it takes for the result of karma to ripen, there are two types: karma that is not certain to be experienced and karma that is certain to be experienced. The first includes two: karma that has been performed but not accumulated, and karma that has been accumulated though not performed. The first has three levels: great, medium, and small. Engaging in the preparation for virtuous or non-virtuous karma but not reaching the main act is "small." Engaging in the preparation but turning away with regret before reaching the middle of the main act is "medium." Engaging in the preparation, completing the main act, but having intense regret before the conclusion is...

<leaf-break/>

"Karma that will be experienced in another lifetime" refers to karma that has been performed and accumulated but is of lesser strength; since the time of its occurrence is not certain, it is not certain whether it will appear after two, three, or many lifetimes, depending on whether or not it encounters the catalysts of similar virtue or non-virtue. This is what is meant by "experienced in another lifetime." Even negative karma that is certain to be experienced can be suppressed by antidotes. In this text, the statement that the result of negative karma does not ripen immediately refers to most karma, excluding karma that is experienced in the current lifetime. If one asks, among those results of virtuous and non-virtuous karma that are ready to ripen immediately, which ripens first? Venerable Ananda said: "Regarding karma in cyclic existence, whichever is heavier, whichever is closer, whichever has been practiced, or whichever was performed first, from among these, the former will ripen first." The meaning is that among the karma of both virtue and non-virtue that is ready to ripen, the karma that has greater strength ripens first. If the strength of virtue and non-virtue is equal, the one supported by the state of mind at the time of death—whichever is more clear—ripens first. If their clarity is equal, the one for which there was greater habituation in the past ripens first. If that is also equal, whichever was performed first ripens first, in accordance with the order of the time it was performed. If non-virtue is equal, and virtue...

</translation>

<summary>This passage details the dangers of attachment to sensory desires, the cultivation of mental engagement with reality, and the nature of the paths to liberation, including the ethics of the path of accumulation and the mechanics of karmic fruition.</summary>
<keywords>Sensory desire, suffering, emptiness, Truth of the Path, path of accumulation, ethical discipline, eight worldly concerns, karmic fruition</keywords>

Phenomena included within the conditioned and the knowing are called "conditioned" because they are composed of causes and conditions. Furthermore, because they produce subsequent states and then cease in an instant, they are impermanent because they are constantly changing and decaying. In accordance with that, mental engagement that is in accordance with reality, and all conditioned phenomena other than the Truth of the Path, are contaminated. This includes the receptacle of the world, the environment included in the three realms, the sense faculties, the body, and the consciousness and mental factors, which are all contaminated. Those associated with painful feeling are the suffering of suffering. Those associated with pleasant feeling are the suffering of change. Those associated with neutral feeling are the suffering of conditioning. The suffering of suffering is known even by animals and the like. The suffering of change is seen by individuals possessing intelligence. The suffering of conditioning, although it is the basis of all suffering, is not known by others, but is realized by the noble ones. Saying "all phenomena are empty," although in general this often refers to emptiness being free from conceptual elaboration, here, the emptiness of the aspect of the Truth of Suffering refers to being empty of incompatible causes. Therefore, it is impossible in the nature of reality that a creator, such as Ishvara and the like, or those who speak of time or causes as the creator, have produced them; one understands them as empty of such creators. By suppressing the various compatible and appropriate causes and conditions,

<leaf-break/>

The nature of this—the wisdom free from contamination along with ethical discipline and meditative concentration—is endowed with the power to abandon afflictions and is what enables one to attain the state of cessation; being certain of that is the mental engagement with the aspect of the Truth of the Path. Regarding the detailed explanation of the five paths, there are two parts: showing the sequence of the path of ordinary beings and showing the path of the noble ones along with its fruition. The first includes showing the qualities associated with the path of accumulation and showing the qualities associated with the path of preparation. Regarding the first, showing that one must place supreme importance on ethical discipline and wisdom on the path of accumulation: "Even those individuals endowed with high caste, beauty, and learning are not respected if they lack wisdom and ethical discipline. Therefore, whoever possesses these two qualities is worshipped even if they lack other virtues." Although individuals who are of royal caste like a great sala tree, or of brahmin caste like a great sala tree, and thus are of superior caste, who are handsome and healthy, and who possess extensive learning in the eighteen branches of knowledge and other conventional arts, if they lack the wisdom to practice the nature of reality and know the path of liberation, and if they lack the ethical discipline to remain in the purity of what to adopt and what to discard, they are not objects of respect or worship for the world, including the gods. Furthermore, if one possesses caste,

beauty, and learning, need it even be said? Whoever possesses those two virtues—wisdom that knows the nature of reality and the path of liberation, and perfect ethical discipline—even if they lack other virtues, is a holy object of the world’s offerings and respect. Regarding wisdom, there are three types: wisdom born of hearing, wisdom born of contemplation, and wisdom born of meditation. In this context of the path of accumulation, wisdom born of hearing and wisdom born of contemplation are primary. Although there are limitless bodhisattva vows, in this context, it refers to the ethical discipline of individual liberation. Regarding the need for one on the path of accumulation to balance conceptual thoughts regarding the eight worldly concerns: "O knower of the world, whether gain or lack of gain, pleasure or displeasure, fame or lack of fame, or praise and blame, do not allow these eight worldly concerns to be the object of your mind; balance them." The Fully Awakened Buddha, the knower of the world, commanded that the eight worldly concerns must be balanced. That is, the gain of perfect resources versus the lack of gain, being destitute; having a healthy body and a happy mind versus displeasure; hearing pleasant reports passed from one person to another versus unpleasant reports; and being directly praised versus being blamed.

So that it does not become a companion in the future, one should never perform negative deeds for the sake of others. The results of most negative deeds that have been performed, unlike a wound inflicted by a sharp weapon, do not ripen or cut immediately. The first includes two: karma that has been performed but not accumulated, and karma that has been accumulated though not performed. The first has three levels: great, medium, and small. Engaging in the preparation for virtuous or non-virtuous karma but not reaching the main act is "small." Engaging in the preparation but turning away with regret before reaching the middle of the main act is "medium." Engaging in the preparation, completing the main act, but having intense regret before the conclusion is...

"Karma that will be experienced in another lifetime" refers to karma that has been performed and accumulated but is of lesser strength; since the time of its occurrence is not certain, it is not certain whether it will appear after two, three, or many lifetimes, depending on whether or not it encounters the catalysts of similar virtue or non-virtue. This is what is meant by "experienced in another lifetime." Even negative karma that is certain to be experienced can be suppressed by antidotes. In this text, the statement that the result of negative karma does not ripen immediately refers to most karma, excluding karma that is experienced in the current lifetime. If one asks, among those results of virtuous and non-virtuous karma that are ready to ripen immediately, which ripens first? Venerable Ananda said: "Regarding karma in cyclic existence, whichever is heavier, whichever is closer, whichever has been practiced, or whichever was performed first, from among these, the former will ripen first." The meaning is that among the karma of both virtue and non-virtue that is ready to ripen, the karma that has greater strength ripens first. If the strength of virtue and non-virtue is equal, the one supported by the state of mind at the time of death—whichever is more clear—ripens first. If their clarity is equal, the one for which there was greater habituation in the past ripens first. If that is also equal, whichever was performed first ripens first, in accordance with the order of the time it was performed. If non-virtue is equal, and virtue...

# The Dragon Plays with the Spider

A hunter, while lying in wait in the mountains at night, saw a small man about two feet tall walking alone along the bottom of a ravine. Shortly after, another person arrived, similar in height. As they met, they asked each other where they were going. The first replied, "I am going to look at Yang Scar-Face. I see that his complexion is dim and dark, which is a sign of bad luck." The second person replied, "I was going for the same reason, and your words are correct." The hunter realized they were not humans and shouted loudly. The two figures vanished. That night, he caught a fox, and on its forehead, there was a scar as large as a coin.

# The Dragon Plays with the Spider

In the government office of Qidong, where Magistrate Xu worked, there was an upper-story room used to store food and snacks. Often, these items were stolen by some creature, leaving the floor in a mess. The servants were frequently scolded, so they hid to watch. They saw a spider as large as a bushel basket. Terrified, they fled to report this to the Magistrate. Finding this strange, the Magistrate later ordered his maids to offer it food. The spider became more accustomed to them; whenever it was hungry, it would come out to lean [against the wall].

<summary>A hunter overhears supernatural beings discussing a fox's ill fortune, and Magistrate Xu discovers a giant spider in his office that he begins to feed.</summary>
<keywords>hunter, spirits, fox, Magistrate Xu, giant spider</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="166">
Once the spider was full, it would leave. After more than a year, the Magistrate was reading official documents when the spider suddenly appeared and crouched beneath the table. Suspecting it was hungry, he called his servants to bring food. Suddenly, he saw two snakes coil around the spider. They were as thick as chopsticks. The spider curled its legs and tucked in its abdomen, as if unable to withstand the fear. In an instant, the snakes grew suddenly, becoming thicker than eggs. The Magistrate was shocked and tried to flee. A massive thunderclap shook the entire household. After some time, the Magistrate regained consciousness. Seven or eight members of his family, including his wife and servants, had been struck dead. The Magistrate fell ill for over a month and eventually passed away. The Magistrate was a man of integrity who loved his people, and when he was appointed, the people collected money to see him off, with the sound of their weeping filling the fields.

The Historian Wu says: I always thought the story of "The Dragon Plays with the Spider" was just a baseless village rumor. How could it actually exist? I have heard that thunder strikes only the wicked. Why, then, did such a virtuous official meet with this tragic and poisonous fate? Is the Heaven above truly so filled with rage?

<summary>The giant spider is attacked by snakes, followed by a violent thunderstorm that kills the Magistrate and his household; the narrator reflects on the apparent injustice of this tragedy.</summary>
<keywords>Magistrate Xu, giant spider, snakes, thunder, tragedy, integrity</keywords>
</translation>

<header>Imperially Commissioned Complete Library of the Four Treasuries</header>

To "know words" and be able to know the right and wrong in people's speech, and to "exhaust the principles" of things, makes the heart like a clear mirror. Only then can one use the Sage's method of observing people to examine them.

○ The Master said: "Reviewing the old and learning the new, one may become a teacher."

"Reviewing" means to search out and trace. "Old" refers to what was previously heard. "New" refers to what is presently acquired. If a student can timely practice what was previously heard and thereby regularly acquire new understandings, then what is learned resides within oneself and one's response becomes inexhaustible. Therefore, one can become a teacher. As for <margin>pronounced "fu"</margin> "knowledge based on rote memory and questioning," one gains nothing in the heart <margin>Master Chen of Xin'an says: compared with</margin>, and what one knows is limited <margin>Master Chen of Xin'an says: compared with</margin>, which is the opposite of being inexhaustible. Thus, the <term>Xueji</term> <gloss>Record of Learning</gloss> criticizes such learning as insufficient to qualify one as a teacher, which mutually illuminates this very meaning. <margin>Master Zhu says: "Knowledge based on rote memory and questioning" is not "reviewing the old and learning the new." It is not searching for the principles within. If one remembers ten things, it is just ten things; if one remembers a hundred things, it is just a hundred things. This is dead and rigid. "Learning the new" means seeing something new within "reviewing the old."</margin>

<meta>Volume 2</meta>
<summary>This passage explains the Confucian educational method of "reviewing the old to learn the new," contrasting it with rote memorization to define the qualities of an effective teacher.</summary>
<keywords>Reviewing the old, Learning the new, Rote learning, Teacher, Principles</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="51">
<margin>Complete Commentary on the Analects</margin>

This principle becomes more refined, surpassing what was known before. By extending and broadening it, and by applying it to various categories, one remains constantly vibrant and not stagnant. The <term>Zhongyong</term> <gloss>Doctrine of the Mean</gloss> speaks of reviewing the old to learn the new. If one does not review the old to learn the new, it is not "reviewing the old to obtain the new." 

○ If one reviews the old but does not seek the new, then one cannot be a teacher. If one does not "learn the new," it is not enough to be a teacher. Thus, the question is decided: if one truly has nothing from the old that is reviewed, one is also not enough to be a teacher. The meaning of these words lies in "learning the new." It is only by reviewing the old that one can "learn the new." "New" does not mean a principle that was not there before. When one practices and learns something until it is familiar, it gradually reveals itself. For instance, the principles are all within oneself. When someone comes to ask, one uses this principle to explain it to them. When several people come to ask, one deduces the answer based on this principle, and the response is inexhaustible. 

For instance, "knowledge based on rote memory and questioning" means remembering one fact and speaking of ten, which does not go beyond the initial scope. This departs from the meaning of "reviewing the old and attaining the new." Is this not the principle of "learning what is low and reaching what is high"? The principles recorded in the Six Classics are the same as those recorded in the Analects and the Mencius. When one practices them time and again, one feels the taste is deep and lasting, and one naturally attains new insights. 

○ Another source says: What was previously acquired...

<summary>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of internalizing knowledge, emphasizing that learning must be a continuous process of discovery rather than mere memorization, ultimately connecting to the concept of moving from foundational studies to higher understanding.</summary>
<keywords>Doctrine of the Mean, Learning, Principles, Analects, Mencius</keywords>
</translation>

After Yang Huo fled to Qi, and from Qi fled to Jin, he made his way to the Zhao clan. Upon hearing of this, Confucius said to Zilu, "The Zhao clan will surely have chaos for generations." Zilu said, "Power does not reside there, so how could they cause chaos?" Confucius replied, "This is not something you understand. Yang Huo is close to those who are powerful but not close to those who are benevolent. He gained favor with the Jisun clan and even plotted to kill them. Having failed, he fled to Qi. The people of Qi imprisoned him, so he escaped to Jin. Thus, the two states of Qi and Lu have rid themselves of their scourge. Zhao Jianzi loves profit and kills many; he will surely be misled by his speech and follow his schemes. That the disasters and failures will last for more than one generation is something that can be known."

Jisun Kangzi asked Confucius, "At present, the twelfth month of the Zhou calendar is the tenth month of the Xia calendar, yet there are still locusts. Why is this?" Confucius replied, "I have heard that only after the fire star <note>Antares, a star used to track seasons</note> descends do the hibernating insects finish their work. Now the fire star is still moving toward the west." <margin>Zhengqitang edition</margin>
</translation>

<translation page="62">
The failure of the calendar official is the cause." Jisun Kangzi asked, "By how many months is it off?" Confucius said, "In the tenth month of the Xia calendar, the fire star should have already set. Seeing it now means the intercalary month was also missed." <margin>See Zuo Zhuan, 12th year of Duke Ai</margin>

King Fuchai of Wu intended to use Duke Ai to meet with the Marquis of Jin. Zifu Jingbo replied to the envoy, "When the King convenes the feudal lords, the hegemon leads the marquises and pastors to have an audience with the King. When the hegemon convenes the feudal lords, the marquises and viscounts lead the sons and barons to have an audience with the hegemon. Now, if the feudal lords are meeting and you wish to have my humble ruler meet with the ruler of Jin, then Jin becomes the hegemon. Furthermore, if you, the officers, call upon the feudal lords in the name of the hegemon, what benefit is there in having a marquis act as one?" The people of Wu then desisted. Later, they regretted it and imprisoned Jingbo. Jingbo said to the Grand Minister Pi, "Lu is about to perform ceremonies for the Supreme Deity and former kings in the tenth month, on the day of *shangxin*. Following this, they will conclude on the day of *jixin*. In every generation, there are those who hold these offices. Since the founding of Lu, this has not been changed. If we do not attend the meeting, the prayer masters and ancestral temple officials will say that Wu is truly without ritual." He spoke to Fuchai and was allowed to return. Zigong heard of this and went to see Confucius, saying, "The son of the Zifu family is clumsy in his speech."

If it is a condition that can be remedied by a doctor, then it should be treated accordingly; if it can be remedied by the power of these methods, then apply them. For those who are poor and cannot obtain wealth, one might borrow from the rich or pretend to be a relative or friend, leaving food and supplies at their bedside, offering this as a source of joy. This is the primary strategy for curing the illness of poverty. For those who have not yet obtained office, one might hurry to purchase a rank for them or falsely claim a recommendation; for those who already hold office, one might provide genuine assistance in their appointments or feign reports of promotion. For the elderly who wish to gain a few years of life, one might produce positive words from the mouths of astrologers, shamans, or healers. If I have these things, why should I be stingy with them? This is simply a matter of treating a person by their own standards. However, while treating various illnesses is easy, treating poverty is difficult. In this world, those who worry about poverty to the point of illness, and whose illness becomes incurable, are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. If everyone could distribute the grain of the Great Granary and loan out the gold of Guo Kuang, then everyone would be able to dwell in the Mustard Seed Garden.
</translation>

<translation page="106">
<header>Collected Works, Volume 6</header>
<sig>4</sig>

How can one be made to recover instantly through the occurrence of something joyful?

### The Third Category: Medicine for the Object of One’s Heart’s Affection

The third category is that the person one’s heart is deeply attached to can serve as medicine. A person’s private affection must have a target. There are often cases where a ruler cannot obtain it from a minister, or a father cannot obtain it from a son, yet someone extremely distant and unworthy of love becomes the object of their spirit and life force. This is precisely an object of deep attachment. It might be a pampered wife or beautiful concubine, an intimate companion or a page boy, or perhaps a close and trusted friend. To miss them and be unable to see them, or to see them but be unable to be close to them, can lead to illness. Even if the person fell ill due to this reason, once the moment of illness and despair arrives, they will inevitably think of their beloved. Suddenly bringing them into close contact is like a fish finding water. There is never a case where the ears do not clear, the eyes do not brighten, and the spirit does not suddenly become vigorous.
</translation>

<summary>Li Yu continues his discussion on unconventional medicine, advocating for the relief of poverty and the role of deep interpersonal affection in restoring physical and mental health.</summary>
<keywords>poverty, charity, social status, medicine, affection, psychology, emotional connection</keywords>

<translation page="24">
<header>Essentials of Buddhist Study</header>

Fayu heard of this from afar. He took a bamboo tube, placed a bramble staff inside, sealed it, and sent it to Fayu. When Fayu opened the seal and saw the staff, he immediately said, "This is because of the monk who drank alcohol. My teaching and guidance were not diligent, and I have caused concern from afar." He then struck the wooden clapper to assemble the community. He placed the tube before them, burned incense to show respect, prostrated himself on the ground, and ordered the <term>vinaya-master</term> <gloss>an officer in charge of monastic discipline</gloss> to strike him three times with the staff. He shed tears and blamed himself. There was no one among the monastics and laypeople in the region who did not sigh in pity. Because of this, many were inspired to be diligent in their own practice.

Eulogy: Oh, if today's people were to open such a parcel from an elder like Fayu, few would not break the tube and snap the staff, or speak in defiance. A holy teacher and a virtuous disciple. Even a thousand years later, I still praise these two men highly.

### Repentance Out of Respect for the Teacher

During the Jin dynasty, Fakuang was from Xiapi. He lost his parents early and was known for serving his stepmother with filial piety. Later, he left home and studied under the <term>shramana</term> <gloss>monk</gloss> Tanyin. Tanyin once became critically ill. Fakuang prayed with sincerity and performed rituals of repentance for seven days and seven nights. On the seventh day, he suddenly saw a five-colored light illuminating the door and room of Tanyin. Tanyin felt as if someone had shaken him with their hand, and his ailment was subsequently healed.

### Standing in the Snow Up to the Knees

During the Wei dynasty, Shenguang’s scholastic understanding surpassed that of his age. When the Great Master Bodhidharma arrived from the Western Regions, Shenguang went to study under him, but Bodhidharma never spoke to him. One evening, there was a heavy snowfall. Shenguang stood in the courtyard until dawn, with the snow rising above his knees. Bodhidharma looked at him and said, "You have stood in the snow for a long time; what is it you seek?" Shenguang wept and said, "I only wish for the Master to open the gate of nectar <note>a metaphor for the teachings of immortality or enlightenment</note> and broadly save the masses." Bodhidharma said, "The supreme, wonderful path of the Buddhas requires diligent exertion over countless <term>kalpas</term> <gloss>vast eons</gloss>. It requires doing what is difficult to do and enduring what is difficult to endure. Even that is sometimes not enough to reach the goal. You, with your light and shallow heart, wish to hope for the true vehicle? It is only vain toil and hardship." Hearing this instruction, Shenguang...
</translation>

<translation page="25">
<header>Record of Noble Conducts of the Monastic Community: Conduct of Respecting the Teacher, Part Three</header>

...was inspired. He took a blade and severed his own arm, placing it before Bodhidharma. *Bodhidharma* said, "The Buddhas of the past sought the path by forgetting their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma. Since you have severed your arm, your request may be fulfilled." *Shenguang* said, "My mind is not yet at peace. I beg the Master to pacify my mind." *Bodhidharma* said, "Bring your mind here, and I will pacify it for you." *Shenguang* said, "I have searched for my mind, and it is ultimately unattainable." *Bodhidharma* said, "I have finished pacifying your mind." Thereupon, he transmitted the Dharma, and Shenguang became the *Second Patriarch*.

> Eulogy: The *Second Patriarch* attained the Dharma truly because of his essence and sincerity. The opportune conditions were already ripe. Thus, it was like the meeting of needle and mustard seed; it was not necessarily about severing an arm. Foolish people who imitate this will only end up using knives and chopping blocks. Alas, if transmitting the Dharma required severing an arm, then none of the patriarchs would have had intact skin. If becoming a Buddha required burning the body, then none of the sages would have left descendants. Sever the arm of afflictions and burn the body of ignorance. May the practitioners of meditation strive for this.

### ->Reproaching Oneself Upon Leaving the Teacher<-

During the Tang dynasty, Qingjiang realized early on that things are like illusions and bubbles. He studied under the Vinaya Master Tanyi as his primary teacher. He recited scriptures and mastered them at a glance. Those who knew him said, "This is a thousand-mile steed of the monastic community." He once disagreed slightly with his teacher, left him, and traveled to study elsewhere. Having traveled widely to various seats of Dharma, he blamed himself, saying, "Having traveled half the world, I realize that one like my original teacher is rare." He returned. When the monks were gathered at his teacher's place, he carried a bramble bush on his back and declared, "I, <term>moujia</term> <gloss>a formal way of saying 'this person' or 'I'</gloss>, have come to surrender to the Master again. I only wish to be accepted." At that time, the *Master* scolded him severely. *Jiang* wept and confessed his gratitude. "Previously, I was ignorant. Now, I have attained realization in my heart. I hope the Master, with his great compassion, will grant me joy." He begged for mercy again and again. *Master Tanyi* pitied him and accepted him as his student again as before. After *Master Tanyi* passed away, he exhausted his devotion to *National Teacher Zhong* and secretly received the essence of the mind.

> Eulogy: To realize one's error after leaving a sage, and not to retreat even when scolded, can be called bright and sincere. Is there any reason why he eventually received the mind-seal? Those with shallow faith go away at the slightest offense and never return; they harbor resentment at the slightest rebuke. They meet a bright teacher in vain and gain nothing. It is like meeting an emperor and failing to secure even a single official post. How sad.

<summary>This page describes various accounts of students demonstrating profound sincerity and self-reproach to their teachers, including the legend of Bodhidharma and Shenguang's severed arm and the narrative of the monk Qingjiang.</summary>
<keywords>Bodhidharma, Shenguang, Second Patriarch, monastic discipline, repentance, devotion, teacher-student relationship</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="134">
<meta>continues from previous page: ...Wind above the Lake forms the image of Inner Truth. The superior person embodies the virtue of Heaven and Earth in loving life, therefore they deliberate on legal cases and delay the execution of death sentences.</meta>

Inner truth is an intention. When a legal case is about to be concluded, one deliberates on it; when it is about to be finalized, one delays it, so as to exhaust the possibilities of human sentiment. To speak of deliberating on a case is to seek life within death; to speak of delaying an execution is to seek life within death. Consider Emperor Shun’s compassionate concern regarding punishments, Emperor Yu’s weeping over criminals, King Tang’s prayer for the opening of his nets, and King Wen’s act of covering exposed bones. If these had not arisen from the sincerity of their original hearts, who could have been moved? The way of utmost sincerity can tread upon fire and water, melt metal and stone, and influence Heaven and Earth; how much more so with people? How much more so with spirits? The King hears the case, the Three Councillors hear the case, and the Minister of Justice hears the case—this is the deliberation of a case. Every ten days the duties are reviewed, and after thirty days the case is submitted—this is the delaying of a death sentence. Deliberating on a case corresponds to the <term>Dui</term> <gloss>Joyous</gloss> trigram, while delaying death corresponds to the <term>Sun</term> <gloss>Gentle</gloss> trigram. Regarding the hexagram as a whole with its six lines, it is "hollow in the middle."

<summary>This page discusses the application of the hexagram Inner Truth to judicial leniency, emphasizing the rulers' moral sincerity in managing legal affairs to preserve life.</summary>
<keywords>Inner Truth, judicial leniency, moral sincerity, historical sages, administrative procedure</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="135">
Considering the two trigrams and the second and fifth lines, it is "full in the middle," both representing images of truth. Furthermore, being joyful below to respond to what is above, and being gentle above to comply with what is below, also contain the meaning of truth. "Inner truth" means faith within the heart. To have faith within the heart is to have faith in principle. Seeing the principle and believing in it is the way to have faith in the heart. Among the sixty-four hexagrams, there is not a single hexagram or line that does not take truth as its pivot; without truth, the center cannot be empty, and how then could it be full? Being empty is what allows it to be full; this is the soft being truthful to the hard. Being joyful and gentle is the means of attaining emptiness. "Faith reaches the pigs and fish," which is the mutual response of emptiness. "Riding a wooden boat," which is the mutual aid of emptiness. Its substance is principle. Principle is Heaven. It is the reason why the heart is the heart. This is what is meant by "beneficial for remaining correct."

# High-Minded Scholars Will Naturally Correct Themselves

## Instructions for Dong Zhiguang

Student Dong <note>referring to Dong Zhiguang</note> was born into a household of wealth and status, yet early on he developed a heart to seek liberation from life and death. This is undoubtedly the power of the internal cultivation of <term>prajna</term> <gloss>transcendent wisdom</gloss> and superior conditions from past lives. He previously studied under the Great Master Yunqi and received the Pure Land teachings. Recently, he came to visit this old man <note>referring to the author, Hanshan Deqing</note> at Shuangjing, expressing his wish to receive the <term>upasaka</term> <gloss>lay practitioner</gloss> precepts and sincerely confess his heavy karmic debts, wishing to find the essential method for escaping suffering and asking how he should practice to eliminate his past offenses. The old man, in response, instructed him: "A practitioner who knows the root of his sins is deep should follow the teachings of the ancient virtuous ones, eliminating old karma as opportunities arise, and resolutely avoiding the creation of new disasters. The Buddha opened the gate of repentance for sentient beings burdened by heavy karma, which is the most convenient method for escaping suffering." The verse says:

> All sins are like frost and dew,
> The sun of wisdom can eliminate them all.
> If you wish to repent,
> Sit upright and contemplate the <term>dharmata</term> <gloss>the true reality/true aspect of all things</gloss>.

"This is the proper practice; all else is but a helpful expedient. The self-nature of all sentient beings and that of the Buddha..."

<summary>Hanshan Deqing instructs the lay practitioner Dong Zhiguang on the necessity of repentance, emphasizing that true purification comes from contemplating the true nature of reality rather than merely relying on secondary methods.</summary>
<keywords>Dong Zhiguang, Hanshan Deqing, Repentance, Prajna, Upasaka, Pure Land</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="11">
<header>Mengyou Collection, Volume 3</header>

are equal, originally unstained, and possess no characteristics of life, death, coming, or going. It is only because of the initial lack of awareness that one loses their original self-nature, which is called <term>avidya</term> <gloss>ignorance</gloss>. Because of this ignorance, all sorts of deluded thoughts arise, leading to various inverted views, creating various forms of karma, and falsely grasping at the suffering of life and death within the three realms <note>the realms of desire, form, and formlessness</note>. This is all because of ignorance and failure to understand one's own mind, following the flow of deluded thoughts. It is like a person in a deep sleep, experiencing various nightmares, encountering various situations, feeling all kinds of terror, and enduring unbearable suffering. Yet when one wakes up and looks for the things in the dream, they cannot be found. Therefore, sentient beings are trapped in the dream of ignorance, following deluded and inverted thoughts, creating all kinds of karma, and bringing suffering upon themselves. Looking at it with awakened eyes, how could these inverted states actually exist? Even now, while still in the dream of ignorance, how can one eliminate old karma? One must use the light of wisdom to illuminate and break through ignorance, believing that one's own mind is originally pure and not driven by deluded and inverted thoughts. If so, all karma will have no cause, for deluded thoughts are the root of all karma. Why is this? Because from beginningless time, we have been lost to our own original minds, life after life...

<summary>This page explains the metaphor of ignorance as a dream, arguing that karma and suffering are products of a deluded mind and that enlightenment—the awakening from this dream—reveals the original purity of the self.</summary>
<keywords>Ignorance, Karma, Deluded thoughts, Self-nature, Light of Wisdom, Awakening</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="120">
<meta>continues from previous page: ...The concept of the generation and overcoming of the five elements is deeply detrimental to correct principles. <margin>Note: Among Song dynasty Confucians, only Shaozi <note>Shao Yong</note> does not discuss the five elements, using instead the sun, moon, stars, and constellations in his *Huangji Jingshi* <gloss>Supreme Principles Governing the World</gloss>.</margin></meta>

From the discussion of the Shao lineage <note>likely referring to Shao Yong</note>, the substances and functions of water, fire, earth, and stone are clearly distinct from those of other schools. Master Zhang <note>Zhang Zai</note> states in his *Zhengmeng* <gloss>Correcting Youthful Ignorance</gloss> that water and fire are <term>qi</term> <gloss>vital energy/matter</gloss>. Therefore, their nature to flame upward and moisten downward is not restrained by earth, despite the rising and falling of <term>yin</term> and <term>yang</term>. Wood and metal are the flowers and fruits of earth. Their nature contains a mixture of water and fire; thus, for wood to exist, it must be soaked in water and ignited by fire, yet it remains inseparable from them. This is because it captures the floral essence of earth, floating at the intersection of water and fire. Metal, as a substance, captures the refined energy of fire from the dryness of earth and the refined energy of water from the moisture of earth. Thus, water and fire wait upon one another without harming each other. When melted, metal turns to liquid without being consumed, because it captures the essential substance of earth at the boundary of water and fire. Earth is that through which things complete their beginning and their end. It is the substance of the ground, and the ultimate point of transformation. It is that by which water and fire rise and fall.

<summary>This page explores the physical nature and interaction of the five elements, drawing primarily on the philosophical framework of Zhang Zai regarding qi, earth, and the transformative boundaries of water and fire.</summary>
<keywords>Zhang Zai, Zhengmeng, Five Elements, Qi, Earth, Transformation</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="121">
It is that which encompasses the substances of things without omission. Master Zhang’s view on the birth of metal, wood, water, fire, and earth is an immutable principle.

Examination of the *Dayan* <gloss>Great Expansion</gloss> Imagery and Numbers
The method of manipulating stalks:
The one that is not used
The fifty that become forty-nine
The *Dazhuan* <gloss>Great Commentary</gloss> states: "The number of the *Dayan* is fifty, and its functional number is forty-nine." According to the numbers of heaven and earth, which total fifty-five, the *Dayan* stops at fifty because Liu Changmin argues this is because the five of heaven are not used. The method of manipulating stalks uses one, two, three, and four as the numbers for the remainder, and six, seven, eight... 

<margin>Questions regarding the *Zhouyi Chanshu* <gloss>Explication of the Zhou Changes</gloss></margin>

<note>A printer's mark indicating the page sequence appears at the bottom left corner.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the mathematical foundations of the I Ching, specifically the derivation of the number forty-nine used in the divination process through the manipulation of yarrow stalks.</summary>
<keywords>Dayan, Dazhuan, I Ching, Divination, Numbers of Heaven and Earth, Yarrow Stalks</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="14">Abu al-Hasan and Umar Bali have retracted their <term>fatwa</term> <gloss>legal opinion</gloss> of permissibility, and have followed the <term>fatwa</term> of the Mufti, Shaykh Muhammad Sa‘id Babasil. They have confirmed that the Mufti’s <term>fatwa</term> is in accordance with the Shafi‘i school of thought, regarding which there is no disagreement among the Shafi‘i scholars. This is evidence. From the response of the Mufti, it is clear that in the Shafi‘i school of thought, there is no disagreement. From this, it is known that the <term>fatwa</term> of those who opposed the Mufti’s <term>fatwa</term> is void. All those who issued a <term>fatwa</term> opposing that <term>fatwa</term> have retracted their <term>fatwa</term> and have acknowledged their error. This confirmation has been written above to verify the <term>fatwa</term> of the Mufti, so that it may be known by the brothers who see this response. I, Ahmad Khatib, Imam of the Shafi‘is, in the noble Masjid al-Haram. 1317. The Head Penghulu of Mentawai, Haji Marzuki, confirms the <term>fatwa</term> of the Mufti Shaykh Muhammad Sa‘id Babasil and invalidates [the opposing views].

<page-break/>

The <term>fatwa</term> of those who issued a <term>fatwa</term> [stating it is] <term>halal</term> <gloss>permissible</gloss> to sell chickens to the Chinese. This is evidence.

Praise be to Allah alone, and peace and blessings be upon the one after whom there is no prophet.

He has seen the <term>fatwa</term> of the Shaykh al-Islam and Mufti of mankind, Shaykh Muhammad Sa‘id Babasil, and several Shafi‘i scholars who signed under that <term>fatwa</term>, that it is definitely <term>haram</term> <gloss>forbidden</gloss> to sell chickens to the Chinese according to the correct opinion in the Shafi‘i school of thought, and that the words of those who claim it is <term>halal</term> are void. And Allah knows best. The one who is the Head Penghulu of the Mentawai public, Haji Marzuki bin Haji Ismail, 1319. Signed by the weak and humble one, who complains to Allah the Glorified and Exalted, who grants success to the truthfulness of the <term>fatwa</term>. This was in the year one thousand three hundred and seventeen, which has been established by the leaders of the scholars in Makkah. May Allah reward them with a great reward and keep them in high esteem. O Allah, grant us success in following them in the religion. Amen, Lord of the worlds. Praise be to Allah and thanks be to Allah, and peace and blessings [be upon the Prophet].

<term>Fatwa</term>

<summary>This page records the formal retraction of Abu al-Hasan and Umar Bali regarding their previous legal opinion and confirms the Shafi‘i prohibition on selling chickens to the Chinese.</summary>
<keywords>Fatwa, Shafi‘i school, prohibition, Haji Marzuki, Ahmad Khatib, legal retraction</keywords></translation>

<translation page="17">...upon the best of Allah’s creation, and upon his family and companions, the guides of the community, and upon the scholars who are the heirs [of the prophets], and those who follow them until the Day of Resurrection. Thereafter, in Makkah, in the year of the Prophet’s Hijra, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, 1317, I issued a <term>fatwa</term> in Belibu, Afdeling Mentawai, that it is <term>haram</term> to sell chickens to the Chinese. After I examined the matter, some of them rejected my <term>fatwa</term>. Their leader, named Haji Madi bin Machan, and his companions exerted pressure on Haji Abu al-Hasan, a Palembang man in Talu Bali, Makkah. So Haji Abu al-Hasan helped [them], and he also obtained support from two people, namely Muhammad Mansuri Maliki and Umar Bali Ampunan. Haji Abu al-Hasan then proceeded to issue a <term>fatwa</term> of permissibility (<term>halal</term>) for Haji Madi bin Machan, and he informed him that he had already submitted a question to Mufti Sayyid Ahmad bin Zaini Dahlan in the past, and the Mufti had issued a <term>fatwa</term> of permissibility. He had also asked this Mufti, who is Shaykh Muhammad Sa‘id Babasil, and the Mufti had issued a <term>fatwa</term> of permissibility, and he informed him that Muhammad Mansuri 

<page-break/>

Maliki and Umar Bali Ampunan also permitted it. In Makkah, the letter of Haji Abu al-Hasan reached Haji Madi bin Machan in Belibu. Then Haji Dat Mentawai, Radin Muhammad Arif Boyan, immediately returned Haji Abu al-Hasan’s letter and sent a copy to the Penghulu of Penang. He then immediately sent his letter to Makkah to the Head of the community in Mentawai. Then, on Friday, 8th of Ramadan, 323, the Head Penghulu of Mentawai, Haji Marzuki, showed the letter of Haji Abu al-Hasan from Makkah, informing him that he had issued a <term>fatwa</term> that selling chickens to the Chinese is <term>halal</term>, and that the <term>fatwa</term> of Mufti Sayyid Ahmad Dahlan is also <term>halal</term>, and the <term>fatwa</term> of Mufti Shaykh Muhammad Sa‘id Babasil is also <term>halal</term>, followed by the two letters of response from Mansuri Maliki and the response from Umar Bali. Both letters issued a <term>fatwa</term> of <term>halal</term>. Furthermore, it is stated that Haji Abu al-Hasan requested that the Head Penghulu show the two letters of response to [the people of] Belibu, so that their meaning could be explained to the people of Belibu, so that the people would not be deceived.

<summary>This page narrates the historical conflict regarding the sale of chickens to the Chinese, detailing the exchange of letters and conflicting fatwas between local leaders and scholars in Makkah.</summary>
<keywords>Haji Marzuki, Ahmad Khatib, Fatwa, Mentawai, legal dispute, religious authority</keywords></translation>

<translation page="15">
In this, both males and females are equal, because they are the mother’s brothers and sisters, and the maternal siblings of the father are the same as their siblings, as is known. If they were to divide the inheritance of a maternal sibling’s son and the maternal aunts among them, they would not divide it such that the male receives the share of two females. The matter ends here.

It is apparent from both the <term>Tuhfa</term> <gloss>a prominent Shafi'i legal text by Ibn Hajar al-Haytami</gloss> and the <term>Nihaya</term> <gloss>a major commentary on Shafi'i jurisprudence by al-Ramli</gloss> that their statement "they divide it equally" is a restriction applying to both the children of the maternal descendants and the maternal uncles and aunts. This is explicit in the <term>Sharh al-Rawd</term> <gloss>Commentary on the Rawd al-Talib</gloss>, as you have learned from its phrasing. However, the matter is not so; rather, their statement regarding equal division is a restriction that applies only to the children of the maternal descendants. The exception is then apparent. They then mentioned the reasoning for the exception until they said: "As for the maternal uncles and aunts, meaning the sisters of the deceased’s mother and her maternal sisters, they are exempt from the aforementioned rule," as you have learned. It follows from their exemption from that rule that they inherit such that the male receives the share of two females, because they are placed in the position of the mother, as is explicitly stated in the primary texts and others. If they were to inherit the mother’s share, had she been the deceased, they would have divided it according to the number of their heads.
<page-break/>
to the view of Jamal al-Ramli regarding that in his <term>Nihaya</term>, and he was preceded in this by their teacher Zakariyya al-Ansari in his <term>Sharh al-Rawd</term>. His phrasing is: "And exempt from that are the children of the maternal brother and the maternal uncles and aunts; they do not divide it such that the male receives the share of two females, but rather they divide it equally among themselves, as is known from what will follow in his speech." The matter ends here.

I have understood it likewise, so that we do not judge it to be a slip. The matter ends here, and God knows best. According to the Hanbalis, the maternal uncle takes precedence over all other non-sharers <term>dhawi al-arham</term> <gloss>heirs who are not primary sharers or agnatic residuaries</gloss>. If the male and female are from the same side, such as the children of a daughter, and are in the same degree, and one of them is closer to the heir, that one is given precedence. Otherwise, they inherit through both, such as the daughter of a daughter of a son of a daughter, if the son of a daughter of Zayd were to marry his other daughter and they had a daughter; or the daughter of a sister through the father, which is the daughter of a brother through the mother, if Zayd’s brother through the mother were to marry his sister through the father and they had a daughter; or the daughter of a maternal uncle, which is the daughter of his paternal uncle, if Zayd’s maternal uncle were to marry his paternal aunt and they had a daughter. A note: <insert>In this, it is equal</insert>—this is taken from our statement "a descendant."
</translation>

<translation page="16">
the daughter of the son descends to her descendant three times, then the share of the son descends to his daughter, and the share of the daughter to her son. And God knows best. The author—may God grant benefit through him—said: "This is the summary of what I wished to transcribe from the aforementioned book, along with my travel to the holy city of Mecca for Hajj in the year 1232 <note>1817 CE</note>, so that it may be a reference for me when needed, as it is the essence of that commentary’s argument. Since it was not possible for me to bring the original, it would have been better, for it contains additional clarification and explanation. It mentions sections on the examples of categories, their branches, their differences, the rulings of the return <term>radd</term> <gloss>the return of the remainder of the estate to the primary heirs</gloss>, the principles of its problems, and their examples, as well as the school of the relatives and its branches. In this, both males and females are equal, because they are the mother’s brothers and sisters, and the maternal siblings of the father are the same as their siblings, as is known. If they were to divide the inheritance of a maternal sibling’s son and the maternal aunts among them, they would not divide it such that the male receives the share of two females. The matter ends here.

It is apparent from both the <term>Tuhfa</term> <gloss>a prominent Shafi'i legal text by Ibn Hajar al-Haytami</gloss> and the <term>Nihaya</term> <gloss>a major commentary on Shafi'i jurisprudence by al-Ramli</gloss> that their statement "they divide it equally" is a restriction applying to both the children of the maternal descendants and the maternal uncles and aunts. This is explicit in the <term>Sharh al-Rawd</term> <gloss>Commentary on the Rawd al-Talib</gloss>, as you have learned from its phrasing. However, the matter is not so; rather, their statement regarding equal division is a restriction that applies only to the children of the maternal descendants. The exception is then apparent. They then mentioned the reasoning for the exception until they said: "As for the maternal uncles and aunts, meaning the sisters of the deceased’s mother and her maternal sisters, they are exempt from the aforementioned rule," as you have learned. It follows from their exemption from that rule that they inherit such that the male receives the share of two females, because they are placed in the position of the mother, as is explicitly stated in the primary texts and others. If they were to inherit the mother’s share, had she been the deceased, they would have divided it according to the number of their heads.

to the view of Jamal al-Ramli regarding that in his <term>Nihaya</term>, and he was preceded in this by their teacher Zakariyya al-Ansari in his <term>Sharh al-Rawd</term>. <translation page="534">in jars, in jars with alcohol! The heir to the All-Russian Tsars is swimming in alcohol like a little frog! he suddenly burst into a laugh so wild that a shudder ran through Peter's body. He thought again, "He is a madman," and felt that disgust, akin to an unearthly horror, which he always felt toward sciences, cockroaches, and other vermin.
But at the same instant, the horror turned into fury: it seemed to him that his son was laughing at him, "playing the fool" on purpose to lock himself away and hide his evil deeds.
"What else is in you?" he returned to the interrogation, as if not noticing what was happening to the Tsarevich.
The latter stopped laughing as suddenly as he had begun, leaned his head back against the back of the armchair, and his face turned pale and drawn, like that of a dead man. He silently looked at his father with a vacant gaze.
"When you had hope in the mob," Peter continued, raising his voice and trying to make it calm, "did you not send anyone to the mob to speak of that rebellion, or did you not hear from anyone that the mob wanted to revolt?"
Alexei was silent.
"Answer!" shouted Peter, and a convulsion twisted his face.
Something twitched in Alexei's face as well. He opened his lips with effort and uttered:
"I have said everything. I will say no more."
Peter struck the table with his fist and jumped up.
"How dare you!"
The Tsarevich also stood up and looked his father straight in the eyes. Once again they became alike, with an instantaneous and seemingly ghostly resemblance.
"Why do you threaten me, Father?" spoke Alexei</translation>

<translation page="535">quietly. I am not afraid of you, I am not afraid of anything. You have taken everything from me, you have ruined everything, both soul and body. There is nothing more to take. Unless you kill me. Well then, kill me! It is all the same to me.

And a slow, quiet smile twisted his lips. It seemed to Peter that there was infinite contempt in that smile.

He roared like a wounded beast, threw himself at his son, grabbed him by the throat, knocked him down, and began to strangle him, trample him with his feet, and beat him with a stick, all with that same inhuman roar.

In the palace, people woke up, bustled about, and ran around. But no one dared to enter the Tsar's quarters. They only turned pale and crossed themselves, approaching the doors and listening to the terrible sounds that echoed from within: it seemed as if a beast were tearing a man apart there.

The Tsarina was sleeping in the Upper Palace. They woke her. She arrived, half-dressed, but she too did not dare enter.

Only when everything had quieted down did she open the door slightly, peer in, and enter on tiptoe, sneaking behind her husband's back.

The Tsarevich was lying on the floor unconscious; the Tsar was in an armchair, also nearly fainted.

They sent for the physician-in-ordinary, Blumentrost. He reassured the Tsarina, who feared the Tsar had killed his son. The Tsarevich had been beaten severely, but there were no dangerous wounds or fractures. He soon came to his senses and seemed calm.

The Tsar was worse off than his son. When they moved him, almost carrying him in their arms to the bedroom, he had such convulsions that Blumentrost feared paralysis.

But by morning he felt better, and in the evening he had already risen and, despite the pleas of Katenka <note>A nickname for Catherine I</note> and the physician-in-ordinary's warnings, ordered a boat to be readied and set off for Saint Petersburg. The Tsarevich was carried alongside in another covered boat.

The following day, May 14th, a second manifesto concerning the Tsarevich was announced to the people, in which it was stated that the Sovereign had deigned to promise his son forgiveness, "provided that he brings true repentance for everything, and conceals nothing."</translation>

<summary>Following a confrontation regarding the death of his infant son, Peter I brutally assaults Tsarevich Alexei in a fit of rage, leading to physical collapse for both men and the subsequent issuance of a second imperial manifesto demanding the Tsarevich's full confession.</summary>
<keywords>Peter I, Tsarevich Alexei, violence, Kunstkamera, imperial manifesto, repentance, Blumentrost</keywords>

Consider this: if a sick person is capable of bearing hardship like the hardship of walking in rain and mud, as previously mentioned, then how can a healthy person not bear a hardship that is less than that, by way of <note>a fortiori</note> analogy? Indeed, if there were a distribution of <term>riyals</term> <gloss>currency</gloss> in the old mosque, do you think the one who claims hardship would stay away due to an inability to endure it, or would you find him the first to rush toward it? And with God is success in returning to the truth, Amen.

### The Ninth Matter: Clarifying the position on the impermissibility of multiplication in this specific case.
It is not hidden from any knowledgeable person that our Shafi'i Imams, may God be pleased with them, only permitted the multiplication of Friday prayers for the sake of necessity and exigency. This is the certainty of the difficulty of gathering, as will come later regarding *al-Tuhfah*, to avert the distress resulting from unbearable hardship. It is known that every necessity is measured by its extent. They have established causes for the difficulty of gathering, either due to fighting, the narrowness of the place for the large number of worshippers, or the distance between the ends of the town. They have established for each of these causes specific conditions that must certainly be met. The condition for the narrowness of the place is that there must certainly not be a place in the Friday-prayer town that can accommodate them. Furthermore, the authoritative position, as stated in *al-Tuhfah* and *al-Nihayah*, is that the criterion is those who are likely to attend the Friday prayer, not those who attend in reality, whether the place is a mosque or otherwise. The certainty of the non-existence of a place refers to there being no place for Friday prayer at all, or the impossibility of expanding the place that has become narrow, or the impossibility of roofing that which is unroofed if the prayer is in the sun,

<column-break/>

resulting in a necessity that is certainly unbearable. Therefore, the absence of what was mentioned here is certainly the excuse that our master al-Ghazali pointed out by his statement: "If it is impossible for them to gather in one mosque, it is permitted in two mosques, etc." The meaning of impossibility here is the complete inability, not just the mere suspicion of insufficient space, nor the mere claim of narrowness without verifying the meaning in the aforementioned manner of certainty. Rather, it is guessing at the unknown and seeking comfort and ease. Furthermore, the condition of the distance of the ends of the town is either that the distance is from dawn until the time of the Friday prayer, or that the call to prayer cannot be heard, as explained in the commentary on *al-Manarah* in the Seventh Matter, or by the presence of unbearable hardship in the sense mentioned in the Eighth Matter. Thus, the certainty of the difficulty of gathering is not obtained except through these mentioned restrictions and conditions. The statement in *al-Tuhfah*, "and the difficulty of their gathering is certain," means through the existence of one of those causes with its conditions. Likewise is every statement by al-Ghazali, "And if the necessity is realized," meaning by the existence of what we have mentioned. They have defined the difficulty of gathering arising from one of those causes by the "unbearable hardship." It states in *al-Tuhfah*: "The criterion for difficulty is that it contains a hardship that is unbearable." The end. This hardship is what contains distress and necessity, as previously mentioned in the Eighth Matter, and it will come here from *al-Qamuli*, stating that for you with its evidence. Among the legal opinions of our master, Sayyid Abdallah bin Umar bin Yahya, is that *al-Qamuli* in *al-Jawahir*, when mentioning the permissibility of multiplication due to difficulty, supported it with the Quranic verse: "He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship." This indicates that our permission for the scholars to multiply is to negate hardship. The end, with omissions. This is also a declaration that the existence of hardship and necessity is what is meant by the unbearable hardship.</translation>

<translation page="13">that defines the difficulty of gathering which permits multiplication. This is because the habit of hardship in going to the mosque is [avoided] in pursuit of comfort and ease. **So when you know** and have verified everything mentioned here, and have known what was mentioned in the Fifth Matter regarding the description of the old mosque, its capacity, and the capacity of its courtyard, you will then know and verify the non-existence of the cause permitting multiplication, which is the lack of a place that accommodates them—that is, accommodates those who are likely to attend, as previously stated that the authoritative position according to Ibn Hajar, al-Ramli, and others is based on the capacity of this mentioned mosque and the capacity of its courtyard, upon looking at it. **And when you know** what was mentioned in the Seventh Matter regarding the distance between the two mosques, that it does not contain the hardship defined in the Eighth Matter, and that the call to prayer is heard between the two ends of the districts of the two mosques, let alone that they are [far apart]—that the distance between the two mosques is not the distance from before dawn to the time of the Friday prayer—**you will know** and verify then the non-existence of the cause permitting multiplication, which is the distance of the ends of the town, due to the short distance between the two ends of the districts of the two mosques, along with the absence of the aforementioned hardship. **It has thus appeared** and become clear to you now, through what was mentioned and written, that the case at hand does not allow for the multiplication of Friday prayers due to the certain absence of any of its causes, let alone the certainty of the existence of any of them. Therefore, all the texts of the Imams stating the permissibility of multiplication under its conditions cannot be used as evidence for the permissibility of multiplication in this case, which is devoid of those conditions. Likewise, the response of the Mufti of Mecca cannot be made into evidence for the validity of multiplication in this case, because it contains the mention of the condition of necessity and hardship, which

<column-break/>

does not exist in the case itself, as has been established in these matters repeatedly, and it will be known clearly from the coming Eleventh Matter. And with God is success. **The Tenth Matter:** Disclosing the signs of defiance that occurred in this case from the claimants of the permissibility of multiplication. These signs indicate a clear defiance of the truth, and that they had no motive other than to bring about multiplication, regardless of how, by what path, by which school of thought, and even if by invalid means, as will be known from their own words, along with what their motives were of defiance, rivalry, arrogance, and assisting in falsehood. As for the signs of defiance: **Among them** is, firstly, what happened from the builder of the new mosque, as mentioned in the Sixth Matter—what he himself previously claimed regarding building a mosque and holding Friday prayer in it, and that the previous judge forbade him in the presence of the scholars, and that he seized the opportunity at this time, and that he and the judge wrote to us and asked us for some of the scholars' texts that they could use as evidence for the validity of the multiplication of Friday prayer in the new mosque, by any means possible. **Among them** is what is in the fifth sheet from Sayyid Alawi bin Ahmad mentioned above, which is his saying: "So the request from you, sir, is [to find] any path, statement, or perspective that you know to advise the judge not to prevent the Friday prayer in the new mosque, may God seal [your deeds]—do not offer an excuse." **Among them** is also his saying in that sheet: "And the name of knowledge, what is the intention of the scholars in forbidding multiplication? [If it is] their right, if there is no path in the Shafi'i school, they ask the scholars about..."</translation>

<summary>This section concludes the argument against the legitimacy of performing multiple Friday prayers in the same town, emphasizing that the conditions for "unbearable hardship" or "lack of space" are not met in the current case. It also begins a critique of the claimants' motives, characterizing their actions as motivated by personal defiance and a disregard for established legal conditions.</summary>
<keywords>Friday prayer, Shafi'i school, unbearable hardship, necessity, jurisprudence, defiance, mosque capacity</keywords>

And what is more wondrous than the magpie, the truth of its senses, the intensity of its caution, and its sharp knowledge? Yet, there is no bird on earth that protects its eggs more diligently, with greater caution, and with more obscure knowledge than it. Uthman ibn Affan, may God be pleased with him, said: "Everything loves its offspring, even the bustard," which is proverbial for its stupidity. Then, the magpie, despite its cleverness with causes and the speed of its snatching, does not use this for what is beneficial. How many precious, grave necklaces and noble, exquisite earrings have been snatched from the hands of people! It either tosses them away after circling in the air, or hides them and never pays attention to them again. Al-Asma’i claimed that a magpie once snatched a precious necklace (*sakhāb*) from some people. The owners of the necklace took a Bedouin woman who was with them, and while she was being beaten, dragged, and insulted, the magpie passed by with the necklace in its beak. They shouted at it, so it dropped it. The Bedouin woman said, recalling safety after she had been afflicted with another calamity, she said:

And the day of the necklace was one of the wonders of our Lord,
As if it saved me from the town of evil.

She means the town-dwellers who had descended upon them. There is no harm in mentioning what occurs, as long as it is not from the long chapters that contain nothing but dry logical syllogisms and pure speculative speech, for that is something whose listening is not light, and souls do not feel lively at its reading. The practitioner and the seeker of reward and good deeds might tolerate it, so whenever we find a chapter that can be adorned with witty, eloquent poetry and curious anecdotes, we take the trouble to do so and report it all for the reader's benefit. For this reason, we deemed it permissible to say in the chapter on fire what we said. I am writing to you after this, since I have bored you with lengthiness and carried you upon the most difficult of mounts and the roughest of roads, as we have mentioned therein a goodly amount of the speech of the theologians. I do not see fit to add to your weariness and burden you to the exhaustion of your energy by starting the discourse on camels, cattle, sheep, lions, wolves, donkeys, gazelles, and the like, which I am writing for you. Rather, I will focus on the small, short, concise, and pleasant chapters so that you do not leave the first chapter without being energized for the second, and likewise the third and fourth, until the end of what I am writing for you, God willing. We will start with what is in the sparrow, then we will take up the mention of the mouse</translation>

Before we mention this chapter, we will mention chapters of witty poetry that are suitable for discussion, stimulate energy, and deserve, along with it, the reading of long, extensive books. Were it not for my poor opinion of those who appear to seek knowledge in this age and who appear to patronize books in this era, I would not have needed, in pacifying them, swaying them, conciliating their souls, and encouraging their hearts—despite the many benefits of this book—to undergo this long training and this frequent apologizing, until it is as if the benefit I bestow upon them is what I derive from them, and until it is as if my desire for their well-being is the desire of one who craves their worldly goods. This is even though I have not mentioned any of the long chapters. I have arrived at mentioning the differences between the jinn and mankind, between the angels and the prophets, the differences between the female and the male, and the differences between them and that which is neither female nor male, until the discourse extends for us into the virtue of man over all varieties of animals, the mention of nations and eras, the mention of fate and lifespans, and the mention of the measures of intellects through sciences and crafts. Then the discourse on the nature of man from the time he is a drop of semen until anxieties destroy him. If you grow weary of the book and find the reading burdensome, you are then excused. I am writing to you after this, since I have bored you with lengthiness and carried you upon the most difficult of mounts and the roughest of roads, as we have mentioned therein a goodly amount of the speech of the theologians. I do not see fit to add to your weariness and burden you to the exhaustion of your energy by starting the discourse on camels, cattle, sheep, lions, wolves, donkeys, gazelles, and the like, which I am writing for you.
