<header>OF POLYBIUS</header>

But when they are driven by the desire for leadership, and are unable to obtain it through themselves or their own virtue, they squander their estates, bribing and corrupting the masses in every way. From this, once they have made the multitude hungry for bribes and accustomed to living off the wealth of others through the abundance of their appetite for glory, then the democracy is destroyed and changes into rule by force and violence. For the multitude, having become accustomed to feeding on the property of others and to placing their hopes of survival in the possessions of their neighbors, when they find a leader who is ambitious and daring, and who is excluded from the honors of the state due to poverty, then he brings about rule by force. Then, gathering together, they perform massacres, banishments, and redistributions of land, until they have become like beasts again and find a master and a monarch. This is the cycle of governments; this is the economy of nature, according to which these things change, shift, and eventually return to the same state. Anyone who has clearly understood these things may perhaps miss the mark in terms of time when speaking of the future of a government, but he will rarely be mistaken about the stage of growth or decay of each, or in what direction it will shift, provided he makes his judgment without bias. Moreover, as for the Roman government, by this method of observation we would most certainly come to a knowledge of its constitution, its growth, and its peak, and likewise the change that will subsequently occur from these. For if any other government, as I said just now, happens to have its constitution, growth, and nature of change into the opposite state according to nature from the beginning, this one will as well. And it will be possible to observe this through the things that will be said hereafter. Now, however, we shall make a brief mention of the legislation of Lycurgus. For the discussion is not foreign to our purpose. For he organized each of the aforementioned things
</translation>

<translation page="20">
<header>SIXTH</header>
<sig>B ii</sig>

as necessarily and naturally fulfilled, and having reasoned that every form of government that is simple and consists of only one power becomes precarious, due to the fact that it quickly deviates into its own naturally inherent vice. For just as rust is the natural corruption of iron, and woodworms and borers are for wood, from which, even if they escape all external harm, they are destroyed by their own inherent ones; in the same way, a certain vice is naturally associated with and follows each of the governments. For kingship is followed by the form called monarchy, aristocracy by oligarchy, and democracy by the bestial and violent rule, into which all the aforementioned changes must necessarily come about in time according to the preceding argument. Foreseeing this, Lycurgus did not organize the government as simple or uniform, but brought together all the virtues and characteristics of the best governments, so that nothing growing beyond what is necessary would deviate into its inherent vices, but with each power held in check by the others, nothing would incline in any direction or collapse too far. Rather, being in equilibrium and held in balance, the government would remain for a long time according to the principle of sailing against the wind. For the kingship is prevented from arrogance by the fear of the people, since they are also given a sufficient share in the government. And the people, in turn, are prevented from daring to despise the kings due to the fear of the elders, who, being chosen by election, were always intended to lean toward justice in all things. Consequently, the portion of those who were inferior, because they adhered to the customs, would always become greater and carry more weight with the elders
</translation>

<summary>Polybius details the cyclical nature of governments (the anacyclosis), explaining how each form inevitably devolves into its corrupt counterpart. He then introduces the Roman and Spartan (Lycurgan) constitutions as examples of mixed governments that resist this natural decay by balancing power between different social classes.</summary>

However, knowledge is of two types: one which is called knowledge according to common custom, and another which is not called so according to common custom. Yet, in the view of the masters of <term>Haqiqat</term> <gloss>Truth/Ultimate Reality</gloss>, both categories belong to the genus of knowledge, because they witness the permeation of the Essential knowledge of the Truth—glory be to Him—in all existing things. It is from the perspective of the second type, for instance, that someone who is not considered knowledgeable by common custom is yet observed to distinguish between height and depth, avoiding the high and flowing toward the low. Furthermore, it penetrates into the body, arranges the outer surface of the body of the one who experiences the <term>Mukashafa</term> <gloss>unveiling/revelation</gloss>, and so on. Thus, it is a property of knowledge to flow according to the capacity of the recipient and not to oppose it. In the realm of nature, it has appeared in the form of nature, and by this analogy, the permeation of knowledge is in all other existents, rather, [it is] the permeation of all perfections.
</translation>

| Existence with the attributes that were hidden within it | And became manifest in all the essences of the world |
| The secret of the attribute of each one that was capable of it | Became manifest according to the measure of the acceptance of the essence |

Just as the reality of existence, due to its pure absoluteness, permeates the essences of all existing things in such a way that in those essences it is identical to those essences, just as those essences were identical to it in Him, likewise, His perfect attributes, in their totality and absoluteness, permeate all the attributes of existing things. This is to the extent that, within their attributes, they are the very essence of their attributes, just as their attributes were, in the essence of those perfect attributes, the very essence of those perfect attributes. For example, the attribute of knowledge, within the knowledge of the knower of particulars, is identical to the knowledge of particulars, and within the knowledge of the knower of universals, it is identical to the knowledge of universals.
</translation>

The son, having entered the footsteps of his dear father,
Bestows many advantages upon my fatherland.
He presides over the afflicted, and kindly assists needy men,
And is prepared to bring aid to the miserable.
He once offered green pastures to my Muses,
And was always beneficial to my studies.
For which, may God Almighty grant him one day
The heavenly joys of eternal life.
Skillfully you will imitate these examples of your kin,
Express your ancestors, noble bridegroom.
Thus your praise will grow, thus your lineage will become
Brighter, and thus your fame will be perennial.
But since you reflect on these things more wisely through yourself,
Let our songs cease at your admonition.
Just as a strong horse born of strong seed
Does not fear the din, nor flee from sorrowful weapons.
Not otherwise do you follow the deeds of your famous parents,
Nor do you allow your genius to degenerate.
Great joys deservedly sustain your mind,
Bride, because that man comes into your chambers.
I, even if I were to surpass Pylian Nestor <note>A legendary Greek king known for his great age and wisdom</note> in speaking,
Even if I were greater in eloquence than Cicero,
Could not commemorate everything according to merit
Which the glory of such a groom demands to be brought forth.
Why therefore does my Muse rather desert the young husband,
And seek the face of the chaste maiden.</translation>

<translation page="14">
Hail, renowned nymph of feminine modesty,
Hail, great glory of the virginal choir.
May He himself prosper the most holy rights of your bed,
Who was the first patron and author of the marriage chamber.
Who first discovered the marriages of the sweet torch,
And who is said to love the sacred flames of the bed.
May He placidly fortune the pacts of your bed,
Euphrosyne <note>The Greek goddess of joy and mirth</note>, a girl worthy of such a man.
Rare is your face, and the excellence of your form
Is so great that it makes you surpass the rest.
You raise your azure eyes to the lofty breezes
Quite often, and you shine entirely with a glowing color.
Such as the clouds are wont to be, colored
By the shining light of the opposing Sun.
Or like the frosty mother <note>Aurora, the goddess of dawn</note>, who drives away
The stars of the sky, and leads the day from the eastern axis.
Such a color is seen on your face, hardly do lilies
Stained with purple blood glow so much to me.
Divine modesty adorns your beautiful countenance:
You are gentle, and lack all rusticity.
Your ivory neck lets down golden-haired tresses,
And flowery garlands polish your hair.
Your arms are whiter to you than snowy privets:
Each of your limbs bears its own adornment.
You also be cheerful, be glad with your whole heart,
Bridegroom, because she seeks your embraces.</translation>

<summary>These pages from an epithalamium honor the bridegroom's noble heritage and character before shifting focus to the physical beauty, modesty, and grace of the bride.</summary>
<keywords>epithalamium, marriage, virtue, nobility, praise, beauty, classical allusions</keywords>

## Report of Master Johannes Waser, Pastor at Dinhard.
->A Jesu Medico, non aliunde salus!<- <gloss>From Jesus the Physician, salvation comes from nowhere else!</gloss>

<note>A large ornamental initial E features floral and leaf motifs.</note>
**Honored** and most learned brother-in-law, Doctor Ziegler, etc.
Since I have learned that the third description of the bath at Urdorff is to be sent to the press, I also want to share what has been observed by me during the time of my 15-year pastoral service at Urdorff. This famous bath is heartily good for <term>calculus</term> <gloss>kidney or bladder stones</gloss>, as it softens and drives out kidney and bladder stones, sand, and grit, as many other honest persons beside myself have experienced in fact. It is also excellently convenient for <term>cholericis</term> <gloss>those with bilious or yellow-jaundice conditions</gloss>, from whom it has removed a great quantity <note>abbreviation: f. b.</note>, of which the witnesses are for the most part still alive at this time. It was useful to <term>febricitanten</term> <gloss>those suffering from fevers</gloss> (of whatever kind they may be): many emaciated, consumption- and lung-sick people have been brought there in a gentle manner because of their weakness, who, after finishing the cure, could ride home fresh and healthy on horseback. It brings an excellent appetite back to the ruined, listless stomach and creates a desire to eat. It <term>acuire</term> <gloss>sharpens</gloss> and sharpens the eyes most wonderfully, so that many persons who must use glasses or spectacles before the bath cure can afterwards write, read, and perform other business without them. I also well remember respectable, honorable people who visited it because of infertility and afterwards highly praised its <term>efficaciam</term> <gloss>efficacy</gloss> and delightful effect. My successor, Master Pastor Wirtz, also gives testimony to this blessing of God. A precious thing at the location of the bath is a serviceable, gracious, friendly, and loving host and innkeeper; where that is lacking in a place, all appeal is lost.

<summary>This page concludes a general description of the Urdorff bath's benefits, followed by a personal testimonial from Pastor Johannes Waser regarding its medicinal successes.</summary>

**Honored** and most learned brother-in-law, Doctor Ziegler, etc.
Since I have learned that the third description of the bath at Urdorff is to be sent to the press, I also want to share what has been observed by me during the time of my 15-year pastoral service at Urdorff. This famous bath is heartily good for <term>calculus</term> <gloss>kidney or bladder stones</gloss>, as it softens and drives out kidney and bladder stones, sand, and grit, as many other honest persons beside myself have experienced in fact. It is also excellently convenient for <term>cholericis</term> <gloss>those with bilious or yellow-jaundice conditions</gloss>, from whom it has removed a great quantity <note>abbreviation: f. b.</note>, of which the witnesses are for the most part still alive at this time. It was useful to <term>febricitanten</term> <gloss>those suffering from fevers</gloss> (of whatever kind they may be): many emaciated, consumption- and lung-sick people have been brought there in a gentle manner because of their weakness, who, after finishing the cure, could ride home fresh and healthy on horseback. It brings an excellent appetite back to the ruined, listless stomach and creates a desire to eat. It <term>acuire</term> <gloss>sharpens</gloss> and sharpens the eyes most wonderfully, so that many persons who must use glasses or spectacles before the bath cure can afterwards write, read, and perform other business without them. I also well remember respectable, honorable people who visited it because of infertility and afterwards highly praised its <term>efficaciam</term> <gloss>efficacy</gloss> and delightful effect. My successor, Master Pastor Wirtz, also gives testimony to this blessing of God. A precious thing at the location of the bath is a serviceable, gracious, friendly, and loving host and innkeeper; where that is lacking in a place, all appeal is lost.

For the dwellers of heaven, while piety was not yet scorned,
Were accustomed to visit chaste homes in person,
And to show themselves to mortal gatherings.
Often the father of the gods, visiting his gleaming temples,
When the annual sacred rites had come on festive days,
Beheld the chariots of the Cretans racing across the land.
Often the wandering Liber <note>Bacchus</note>, from the highest peak of Parnassus,
Drove the Thyades <note>the Maenads</note> with disheveled hair,
When all the people of Delphi, rushing from the city in rivalry,
Happily received the god with smoking altars.
Often in the death-dealing contest of war, Mars,
Or the mistress of swift Triton <note>Minerva</note>, or the Rhamnusian maiden <note>Nemesis</note>,
Encouraged the armed troops of men in person.
But after the earth was soaked with unspeakable crime,
And all drove justice from their greedy mind,
Brothers stained their hands with a brother's blood,
The son ceased to mourn his dead parents,
The father wished for the funeral of his firstborn son,
So that he could enjoy the flower of an unmarried stepmother,
The impious mother, casting herself under her unknowing son,
Did not fear to defile the divine household gods with her impiety.
All things right and wrong, mixed by wicked madness,
Turned the just mind of the gods away from us.
Therefore they do not deign to visit such gatherings,
Nor do they suffer themselves to be touched by clear light.

<summary>The author laments the loss of divine favor, explaining that the gods once walked among men until humanity's pervasive crimes and moral decay alienated them.</summary>
<keywords>divine, piety, justice, crime, corruption, gods, antiquity</keywords>
</translation>

or one due circumstance is sufficient neglect, which they express in the common saying of <term>Dionysius</term>: "Any single defect causes evil, yet good is caused only by an integral cause." Here, however, one must note the distinction between the circumstances themselves, of which some transfer the moral act into a new genus of malice, while others leave it in the same genus, yet increase the gravity of the sin. Thus, the example of fornication, which <term>Aquinas</term> brings forward, consists in this: that a man approaches one who is not his own. But if this circumstance is added, that he exerts his lust upon another man's wife, it is then transferred into another genus of sin, namely into injustice, in as much as a man usurps the thing of another. Whence adultery is considered a graver offense than fornication. Let the example of the latter be some angry person, who gets angry when he ought not, and at whom he ought not, and with an inconvenient gesture, which triplet of circumstances certainly makes this anger graver than if at least one of them were violated. Just as a sickness is graver which infects more parts of the body. It happens, however, sometimes, that some circumstance does not add a new deformity, but only increases that which had come from elsewhere. Just as taking another's property constitutes theft: but if this is added, that he takes much of another's property, it will be a graver sin. Nor is there any reason for someone to say that a circumstance, if it is evil, constitutes a certain species of sin by itself. For this is false, or at least not universal, since it can add a reason for malice within the same species. About which see <term>Thomas</term>. We add at least this, since it can also be referred to among circumstances, how often, or properly—which <term>Cajetan</term> denies—or by analogy, that also in the weighing of an offense is not to be passed over. Whence <term>Grotius</term>:
<margin>1. 2. qu. 73. art. 8. ad 2. <gloss>1st Part of the 2nd Part, question 73, article 8, reply to 2nd objection.</gloss></margin>
<margin>l. c. <gloss>in the place cited</gloss></margin>
> "A greater depravity also appears if someone has sinned more often: because habits are worse through evil acts."

# TH. XI.

## Eighth, the gravity of vices differs according to the dignity of the virtues to which they are opposed.

<margin>3. 2. q. 73. art. 4. <gloss>3rd part of the 2nd part, question 73, article 4.</gloss></margin>
*This, <term>Thomas</term> proves from <term>Aristotle</term>: The Philosopher says that the worst is contrary to the best. The best in moral matters, however, is the greatest virtue; the worst is the gravest sin.* Since, however, the dispute regarding the mutual comparison of virtues among themselves, and which holds the first place among them, is not yet settled, it will be impossible to determine anything regarding vices in this respect. Certainly, all virtues shine like stars, and our world of darkness is made illustrious by their rays. Yet <term>Piccolomineus</term> admits that it is not easy to judge which of them shines more brightly or stands in relation to the others like the sun.

<margin>Phil de Mor. Gr. 4. c. 47. & 49. <gloss>Philosophy of Moral Grades, book 4, chapters 47 & 49.</gloss></margin>
And for each one, he himself offers something, by which they might quite probably claim the primacy for themselves, which he confirms both by arguments and the assent of the wise; and he warns first of all that, according to the diverse condition of men, judgments concerning this prerogative vary greatly: those placed in magistracy prefer justice, leaders of armies and soldiers prefer fortitude, men born and educated in splendor prefer magnificence, etc. Notwithstanding these things, however, we believe a judgment regarding the absolute preeminence of one can be fixed. We prefer to express this in the words of the most celebrated moral doctor in Italy, already praised, rather than our own:

<margin>Phil Mor. Gr. 4. c. 51. <gloss>Philosophy of Moral Grades, book 4, chapter 51.</gloss></margin>
> "Because that virtue must be judged absolutely best, to which belongs the best reason for excellence—the reason of dignity, which must be sought especially from the end. The end of virtue is action; the most excellent of actions are those which proceed from justice; therefore, by right, justice obtains the primacy. That the action of justice is the best is evident: for its duty is to compose our actions toward others, to govern the rest appropriately, to gather together scattered men, to preserve those gathered, to bind republics and assemblies of men, both small and great, with golden ligaments, to benefit all, and to harm no one, which is the property of virtue in the highest degree."

These are

<summary>This page addresses the hierarchy of virtues and their corresponding vices, arguing, via Piccolomineus and Aristotle, that justice holds the primary position among the virtues.</summary>
<keywords>virtue, vice, gravity, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, Piccolomineus, justice, primacy of virtue</keywords>
</translation>

76. Item, whether a mother is excluded from her legal portion by an express pupillary substitution <gloss>substitution for a minor heir</gloss>? And we affirm this.

<note>Donellus on the law "by petitions," Code regarding substitutions for minors and others.</note>

77. A soldier can make a testament by military law as much for himself as for his son, and for the son alone even if he has not made one for himself: which testament will be valid if, by chance, the father died either in military service or within a year of military service.

<note>Law "in fraud" 15, paragraph "item as much for himself," Digest regarding military testament.</note>

78. Finally, a soldier can, by mere will, appoint an heir even to those known <note>i.e., specified individuals</note>, in whatever way he wishes or is able, and another for a time after that time.

<note>Law "in fraud" 15, paragraph 1, and paragraph "a soldier" 4, Digest on this title.</note>

79. Here a question may be proposed: Why can an heir be written by a civilian under a condition, but not from a certain day or until a certain day? We shall investigate the reason.

<note>Law "under a condition" 73, Digest regarding the institution of heirs, law "inheritance" 3, 4. Digest regarding the institution of heirs: Cujacius in the commentary on the Code regarding military testament, folio 325.</note>

80. Hence, although soldiers have neither employed the legal number of witnesses nor observed other formalities of testaments, they nevertheless make a will correctly, provided it is established that the testament was made.
<margin>In the beginning of the Institutes regarding military testament.</margin>

81. If, therefore, a soldier regarding whose goods inquiry is made before you, having summoned men for this purpose so that he might testify his will, has spoken in such a way that he declares whom he would want to be his heir, and to whom he grants liberty, he can be seen to have testified in this manner even without writings, and his will must be held valid.

<note>Law 24, paragraph "if therefore," Digest regarding the testament of a soldier.</note>

82. Indeed, if he has noted anything on a scabbard or shield with letters glowing red with his own blood, or has inscribed it in the dust with a sword, at the very time when he abandoned the strength of his life in battle, such a will ought to be stable.

<note>Law "a soldier" 15, Code regarding the testament of a soldier.</note>
</translation>

<translation page="19">
83. Just as a soldier can give an inheritance by mere will, so too can he take it away.
Law "in fraud" 15, paragraph "just as" 5, Digest regarding the testament of a soldier.

84. Likewise, it is permitted for a soldier to make several testaments, but whether he made them at the same time or separately, they will certainly be valid if he specifically expressed this: nor will the former be broken by the latter.
Law "it was asked" 19, regarding the testament of a soldier.

85. An elegant question may here be debated by occasion: Is a prior, perfect testament of a civilian broken by a subsequent imperfect one, in which those coming from intestacy are instituted as heirs, if in the latter a son is passed over? In which, having inspected the legal truth, we shall try to defend the negative with our strength.
Law 7, Digest regarding children and posthumous heirs. Law 16, paragraph 1, Digest regarding ordinary substitution.

86. Furthermore, a soldier’s testament is not broken by the birth of a posthumous child, provided that when the soldier passed over the posthumous child, he knew that his wife was pregnant.
Law 9, Law 10, Code regarding the testament of a soldier.

87. Likewise, even if he did not know his wife was pregnant, if he was of the mind that he wanted whoever was born to him to be disinherited, the testament is not broken.
Law 7, Digest regarding the testament of a soldier.

88. A soldier’s testament is also not broken if he adopts a son, or if a grandson succeeds in place of a son.
Law "the same is" 8, Digest regarding the testament of a soldier.

89. Thus, if a soldier who is a <term>paterfamilias</term> <gloss>head of household</gloss> has testified only regarding his <term>castrense</term> <gloss>camp-acquired</gloss> property, and has given himself to be adopted, his testament is nonetheless valid, as if by a new will.
Law "the same" 23, Digest on this title.

90. However, only to those who are occupied in expeditions are the aforementioned benefits granted regarding the fulfillment of last wills.
Law "the penultimate," Code regarding the testament of a soldier.

91. Whether it is permitted by military law for those soldiers who are in camp, in a trench, in winter quarters, in stationary positions, or in garrisons—short of the battle line, short of the crisis of battle—to make a will is debated. And we judge it to be more true that it is permitted.
Cujacius in the commentary on the Code regarding the testament of a soldier.
</translation>

<summary>These pages continue the legal analysis of military testaments, specifically addressing the informality allowed for soldiers in designating heirs, the validity of testaments made under duress or in battle, and the conditions under which such testaments are revoked or remain valid, including the status of posthumous children and adopted heirs.</summary>
<keywords>military law, testament, soldier, inheritance, pupillary substitution, posthumous children, camp-acquired property, Cujacius</keywords>

Given from my study at <term>Altdorphium</term> <gloss>Altdorf</gloss>, on the eve of the Academic Festival in the church of the divine Peter and Paul, at which this most flourishing Academy was to transition into a University the very next day. In this flowering and honor, may it flourish and thrive eternally, I pray and vow from the deepest fibers of my soul.
In the year of restored salvation 1623.

-> To the Reader <-

I confess, indeed, kind reader, that there are many—even very many—errors in this collection, not only light ones but also serious ones that offend against grammatical purity (such as that one in the 5th decade regarding <term>τῆς εὐδαιμονίας</term> <gloss>happiness/well-being</gloss> in the introduction, where "infamous" is used for "the infamous"). These arose from the printer's haste and the corrector's shortcomings. Because of other tasks and frequently poor health, I have not yet been able to correct them even now at the end of the collection, nor to append a list of them here. Therefore, you will grant me pardon, and with your usual kindness, you will correct the errors yourself, especially since they will be very easy to fix from the coherence of the text, as I hope, and you will soon see the sense, even if it is often obscured by a shadowy veil of faults. Especially, however, where a <term>sphalma</term> <gloss>mistake/blunder</gloss> occurs in the very words of the authors, I would ask that you consult the sources themselves, particularly regarding the passage of <term>Aristotelis</term> <gloss>Aristotle</gloss> from the 2nd book on the parts of animals, chapter 4, in the 4th decade of <term>τῆς εὐδαιμονίας</term>, section 3, which is enormously corrupted. There you will soon have the truth in view. With these things, fare well and favor me kindly.

<summary>The author concludes his introductory material, apologizing for typographical errors due to poor health and haste, and asks the reader to consult original sources like Aristotle to clarify corrupted sections.</summary>

</translation>

# GEORG FRIDRICH BLINSIG,
## FRIEND AND PATRON.

<note>A large decorative initial Q begins the poem.</note>

What skilled man shall I call you, FRIDRICH?
With what titles, FRIDRICH, shall I adorn you
Worthy enough? Truly stunned,
I do not know, I hesitate, truly stunned.
More blessed in divine genius,
More blessed in divine judgment.
What? Are you called, perhaps undeservedly,
Who? The *second Tirynthian Hercules*?
By Pollux, you are not called that undeservedly,
Who? The *second Tirynthian Hercules*.
Do you want proof? I shall show it, and you will trust my words.
What, I ask, is celebrated <term>Sophia</term> <gloss>Wisdom</gloss>? Is she not the pious
Mother of the liberal arts,
And has she not brought forth more beautiful
Daughters, of more celebrated intellect,
Whom you grasp with more celebrated love?
In form, above all, sweeter,
And in other respects, more virtuous
Than <term>Dejanira</term> <gloss>wife of Hercules</gloss> in all your limbs.

<summary>This page contains a laudatory poem addressed to Georg Fridrich Blinsig, styling him a second Hercules and praising his wisdom and virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Georg Fridrich Blinsig, panegyric, Hercules, Sophia, liberal arts</keywords>
</translation>

### XLIV.

Moreover, the Jews, in order to maintain the same uniformity of seasons throughout each month, add an entire month as often as the number of <term>Epactae</term> <gloss>added days to align lunar and solar years</gloss> exceeds thirty days.

### XLV.

The <term>Epactae</term> are the eleven days that constitute the difference between the solar year of 365 days and the lunar year of 354 days. It is necessary for these to accumulate if we allow many such years to flow from one common starting point without compensation.

### XLVI.

And thus arises that lunar year which I previously called <term>Embolimaeus</term> <gloss>intercalary/leap year</gloss>. Since it is regulated by the motions of the Moon such that, even in common years, the months are in a certain way restored to the laws of solar revolutions for the sake of the enjoyment of permanent seasons, the entire form of such years is deservedly considered composite, and the years themselves are to be regarded as neither purely lunar nor even solar, but Luni-solar.

### XLVII.

Finally, some Civil years are more unrestricted than others. The Olympiadic years are completed sometimes in 360, sometimes in 361 or 362 days; likewise, others are completed in 390, 391, or 392 days. The Nabonassarean or Egyptian years indeed have 365 days, like the Common Julian year, but without any intercalation.

### XLVIII.

Therefore, this method of years is quite erratic if it is compared with the Julian form. For the Egyptian year does not find a fixed and perpetual beginning there; rather, once any four-year period has elapsed, it differs by an entire day from the Julian years because of the intercalary day, which every fourth Julian year receives, but which the [Egyptian year] does not admit.

### XLIX.

Hence, the head of its year runs through all the months of the Julian year in reverse, until, after 1460 Julian years have passed, 1461 Egyptian years are completed. For then, both return to one common starting point.

<summary>This page explains methods of calendar synchronization, specifically addressing how lunar years are adjusted through the addition of intercalary months and days, and describing the divergence between Julian and Egyptian calendar systems.</summary>
<keywords>Epactae, Embolimaeus, Lunar-Solar, Julian Calendar, Egyptian Calendar, Nabonassarean Year, Intercalation</keywords>
</translation>

These are the things I had to say about Time, according to the nature of my undertaking, concluding with the verses of D. Cramer:

> If you always measure fleeting time to the very fingernail,
> Time will never pass away inert.
> Tomorrow’s hour is not yet here, nor can yesterday’s
> Be recovered by a thousand talents: if you wish to live, live today.

---

You burn with the love of piety and wisdom, and also of virtue;
For this reason you discourse on TIME, well done!

->Endure and persevere, this labor will one day profit you.<-

->JO. FRID. SCHARFIUS, D.<-
->Dean of the College of Philosophy at this time.<-

---

The matter is indeed true; most choice virtue is pressed,
Yet it is not suppressed, but finally rises on high.
This, FIDLER, you attest abundantly by your example,
While you yield to no one, even though your resources are meager.
I praise your efforts. May the Divine power make your undertakings fruitful,
So that your native soil, by whose sweetness all are drawn,
May welcome back both you and your labors.

->MICHAEL VVALLTHERUS,<-

### XLIV.

Moreover, the Jews, in order to maintain the same uniformity of seasons throughout each month, add an entire month as often as the number of <term>Epactae</term> <gloss>added days to align lunar and solar years</gloss> exceeds thirty days.

### XLV.

The <term>Epactae</term> are the eleven days that constitute the difference between the solar year of 365 days and the lunar year of 354 days. It is necessary for these to accumulate if we allow many such years to flow from one common starting point without compensation.

### XLVI.

And thus arises that lunar year which I previously called <term>Embolimaeus</term> <gloss>intercalary/leap year</gloss>. Since it is regulated by the motions of the Moon such that, even in common years, the months are in a certain way restored to the laws of solar revolutions for the sake of the enjoyment of permanent seasons, the entire form of such years is deservedly considered composite, and the years themselves are to be regarded as neither purely lunar nor even solar, but Luni-solar.

### XLVII.

Finally, some Civil years are more unrestricted than others. The Olympiadic years are completed sometimes in 360, sometimes in 361 or 362 days; likewise, others are completed in 390, 391, or 392 days. The Nabonassarean or Egyptian years indeed have 365 days, like the Common Julian year, but without any intercalation.

### XLVIII.

Therefore, this method of years is quite erratic if it is compared with the Julian form. For the Egyptian year does not find a fixed and perpetual beginning there; rather, once any four-year period has elapsed, it differs by an entire day from the Julian years because of the intercalary day, which every fourth Julian year receives, but which the [Egyptian year] does not admit.

### XLIX.

Hence, the head of its year runs through all the months of the Julian year in reverse, until, after 1460 Julian years have passed, 1461 Egyptian years are completed. For then, both return to one common starting point.

They prepare everything: the house stirs on all sides with unusual work.
Then Father Abraham, with everything now duly prepared,
Wraps raw leather straps around the tender soles of his feet,
And takes the death-bringing sword with its gleaming hilt.
This, as they say, with his clever mind, <term>Lamecho</term> <gloss>Lamech</gloss>,
Born of <term>Sella</term> <gloss>Zillah</gloss>, having first discovered the craft,
Had fashioned beautifully from solid iron: and had handed it
To his father: Father Noah: He then,
When GOD overwhelmed the vast globe with all its peoples
With waves, had saved it in the safe ark.
From there, all his descendants happily received it:
And he himself thus left it to his son Abraham.
When things were thus, he entrusts the faithful reins to Sarah:
And orders her to guard the remaining house: She nods to his command:
And seeks her son: she detains him with her voice
As he is now trying to follow his dear father.
Now she commands him to veil his blonde hair, now his chest:
Now to care for the Gods above: and to carry God before all things
In his frequent thoughts. To the upright, she says, their rewards remain:
He loves these: the Ruler of high Olympus cares for these.
Thus she speaks, and sheds tears between each word.
But the son: Now farewell dear, farewell best mother:
Behold, he calls, behold, father calls: farewell you roofs.
When he had said this: he turns his steps away together,
Leaving behind his mother weeping, and often wanting
(Whether love persuaded her: or perhaps the forebodings of a troubled
Mind) to wrap her arms around his snowy neck.
</translation>

<translation page="13">
But she followed the departing one with such a voice:
Go, our glory, go: use the favorable gods:
May you leave your home while they accompany you, and may you return with them.
   Thus, therefore, with the dear city of his country now left behind,
The son and the father enter the green fields.
Behind them follow the servants, leading the bending
Beast of burden: and they urge it on much with staff and knot.
From here they enter the joyful valleys: and are covered by various
Trees: and they ply their path under high branches.
The Zephyrs accompany them going from behind:
And the charming birds rise up and greet them with their voice.
   Meanwhile Father Abraham, through the pleasant green lawns,
Recounts many things about the first religion and faith.
At the beginning, he recounts the origins of the spacious world:
How GOD fashioned the spheres of heaven from nothing,
And once separated the earth from the wandering waves:
And bound all things so beautifully in concordant peace.
Then he sings of the crime of Satan, and the offenses of the first parent,
And the seed that is to come, as the years roll on,
Which would avenge itself upon Satan: and turn him to the lowest hell.
And he sings of his crushed head, and the chest of the Serpent,
Flowing with much corruption, which he would gather through dark caves.
Then how he submerged the whole world in the sea
On account of the sins of men, and the foul heats of lust.
And in what manner, with what voice GOD had presented himself
To the fathers and great-grandfathers, and with what mouth he spoke to them:
And he unfolds the remaining deeds of the ancients in long order.
</translation>

-> IOANNES OSVVALDVS à ZIMMERN, Doctor of Sacred Theology, <-
-> Professor, Licentiate of Both Laws <gloss>Canon and Civil Law</gloss>, Academic <-
-> Pro-Chancellor, and currently Theological Dean. <-

---

*This Disputation on Universals in general and in particular proposes a solid and clear doctrine of the same, and at the same time, together with the annexed parerga, presents rich material for further disputation; therefore, it is worthy to be printed for this purpose.*

-> LEONARDVS LERCHENFELDT of the Society <-
-> of JESUS, Professor of Moral Philosophy, and <-

</translation>

<translation page="24">
<note>A horizontal decorative border at the top of the page is composed of repeating ornamental floral or knotwork patterns.</note>

# TO THE REVEREND, RELIGIOUS, AND MOST LEARNED MASTER, DEFENDER OF UNIVERSAL PHILOSOPHY IN UNIVERSALS.

*Others bedeck themselves with beautiful wisdoms,*
*As if they were shining Rachels,*
*They build up their brows and fashion them with a needle,*
*They polish their cheeks with learned trifles,*
*And paint their brides with sterile labor.*
*My Sage laughs at this; he takes the sister,*
*Leah, the fruitful mother.*
*Rachel does not please: the Universals,*
*He says, are the dowry Leah gives; she brings forth all things.*
*I have seen forms swelling under the Daedalian chisel,*
*Born to stir up envy.*
*I have seen bulls ordered to be silent*
*By the Sarmatian wound: the threatening piers*
*Of the harbors, built by the wave-flowing Three Cities <gloss>reference to the Triple City, perhaps Rome or a symbolic construct</gloss>:*
*The Causes propped up by the favor of demigods:*
*Gods playing in a physical bath:*
*The particles of a more blessed*
*Urn: the Pellaean worlds <gloss>referring to Alexander the Great</gloss> with Asia in awe.*
*I have seen clouds bring forth great things;*
*The pious heirs of the celestial spheres.*

<column-break/>

*The Lion of Stagira <gloss>Aristotle</gloss> will roar like a pygmy.*
*The Lyceums <gloss>schools of philosophy</gloss> will learn the price of shadows.*
*Our man says, I want the bleary-eyed sister.*
*Although Leah is not bleary-eyed, even if one who is bleary-eyed*
*Believes her to be, she is not bleary-eyed.*
*How does it happen that she produces the Species? Charming*
*Is Leah to us, and a noble Nymph:*
*And the mother of the Genus, and of lineages:*
*The goddess of beautiful Differences.*
*Now let Rachel boast of the light favors of the Graces,*
*And glass dolls, and Roses of Accidents*
*On a parchment brow,*
*The brief riches of youth.*
*Not so, not Leah; she offers from her own store.*
*She has no need of borrowed smoke;*
*She has learned to shine with native cultivation;*
*Taught not to blush with any other rouge,*
*She possesses and holds that which is Proper to each one.*
*Rachel does not please. Rich Leah*
*Promises the universals, and you give back the universals.*

---

->Out of duty of religious honor and love.<-

->Applauded by<-

P. GREGORIVS MAGIVS, Canon Regular of the Order
of Saint Augustine, professed at Gars, student of Sacred
Theology and Canon Law.
</translation>

<keywords>Philosophy, Universals, Approbation, Scholasticism, Leah and Rachel, University of Bavaria, Jesuit Philosophy</keywords>

## LORD RESPONDENT, a friend to be honored among the few.

<note>A large decorative initial S at the start of the first poem.</note>

**S**o, at last, provident fame forbids that the monuments of your tireless work
And the gifts of a noble mind be entrusted to the earth;
Nor does she threaten small names.
Alas, beloved, she looks upon your endeavors, when the chosen cohort
Of both young and old men spontaneously climb the pulpits,
And contemplates them with a silent mind, [to see] the rewards
With which, that she may see you adorned, your whole [friend] desires.

->M. Samuel Schultetus, of Hamburg.<-

Is it thus, friend, that all discover the omen of your generous name,
While you provide the pledges of your ready genius? Just as a Phrygian lion, led by cruel
Savagery, does not at all harm the whole miserable race of beasts,
To whom wise nature has granted the strengths of the body with moderation, but rather
Pursues those maddened with fierce ardor,
So that he may test his fame through deeds that prove it.
So too, friend, you bring forth the monuments of your manly genius,
Defending the swollen matter regarding the Being of Spirit,
And spurning all things with lesser investigation.
Well done, I pray, for your undertakings, and may the fates favor your studies!

->*I wrote these in gratitude for our most sincere friendship.*<-

->**Otto Helle, of Lübeck.**<-

<translation page="12">a false god, or indeed a true one, but not in the way one ought to, therefore it will be permissible to use external worship, provided we use it in a way other than theirs.

58. Those things by which God is worshiped both interiorly and exteriorly, by body and soul at the same time, are mixed, such as prayer, praise, thanksgiving, reading, and honorable speech about divine matters.

<margin>Luke 10.</margin>
59. He errs, therefore, who, content with mental prayer, throws away vocal prayer as useless, and dares to prefer every prayer done by the mind alone to every prayer that is also expressed by voice. For although Magdalene is said to have chosen the better part than Martha, because the latter gave herself to action and the former to contemplation: nevertheless, the Church most truly proclaims about the most blessed Virgin Mary that which is said of her, as she who joined both and excelled most in both. Thus, clearly, he who prays with affection alone does indeed better than he who only murmurs with his lips. Yet he who offers prayers to God in both ways surpasses him without doubt.

<margin>
Prov. 30.
Jer. 22.
</margin>
60. **THESE ARE THREE** things by which the earth is moved, to which the third Jeremiah acclaims. For sobriety receives the man approaching God, justice leads him, and piety conducts him to the end toward which he tends.

<margin>Eccl. 25.</margin>
61. Who denies that these three are indeed difficult? Yet they are beautiful, in which even the Spirit of God takes pleasure, approved before God, whom sobriety invites, justice holds, and piety places upon the throne; and just as before God, so too before men, among whom, indeed, the first wins admiration, the second goodwill, and the third reverence. For we admire the chaste and sober, we love the beneficent, and we consider the religious worthy of special honor.

<margin>
Eccl. 25.
Prov. 30.
Eccl. 4.
</margin>
62. There are three other species, which I wish our soul hated as God does. Three insatiable things: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life; a triple wedge advancing with a hostile front against the armies of the God of Israel, a triple cord drawing toward certain ruin, which can undoubtedly be broken through with difficulty (if it can be broken at all) by those who trust in their own strength.

63. But (thanks be to God) this our strength that draws us back from destruction is no less strong, while temperance extinguishes the lust of the flesh, liberality reins in the lust of the eyes, and humility prostrates the pride of life.

<summary>The author argues for a combination of internal and external worship, emphasizing that while internal devotion is primary, external acts like vocal prayer and pious living are necessary; he then warns against the three vices of lust and pride while advocating for sobriety, justice, and piety.</summary>
<keywords>worship, prayer, sobriety, justice, piety, vices, lust, pride</keywords></translation>

<translation page="13">64. Man (over whom they contend) is established in the middle between these battle lines, and the victory is certain for whomever he inclines toward.

65. This is the order of the struggle: that first of all, the flesh must come to be tamed, for he who serves it still clings to the beginnings; pride always remains the last, which, even if it is cast down a thousand times, nevertheless rises again, and sometimes all the stronger the more powerful the forces by which it was prostrated.

<margin>

58. Those things by which God is worshiped both interiorly and exteriorly, by body and soul at the same time, are mixed, such as prayer, praise, thanksgiving, reading, and honorable speech about divine matters.

<margin>Luke 10.</margin>
59. He errs, therefore, who, content with mental prayer, throws away vocal prayer as useless, and dares to prefer every prayer done by the mind alone to every prayer that is also expressed by voice. For although Magdalene is said to have chosen the better part than Martha, because the latter gave herself to action and the former to contemplation: nevertheless, the Church most truly proclaims about the most blessed Virgin Mary that which is said of her, as she who joined both and excelled most in both. 60. **THESE ARE THREE** things by which the earth is moved, to which the third Jeremiah acclaims. For sobriety receives the man approaching God, justice leads him, and piety conducts him to the end toward which he tends.

Prov. 30.

Three insatiable things: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life; a triple wedge advancing with a hostile front against the armies of the God of Israel, a triple cord drawing toward certain ruin, which can undoubtedly be broken through with difficulty (if it can be broken at all) by those who trust in their own strength.

dies when his children, who are both of age and minors, are still alive. Guardians and curators are immediately appointed for them by the Magistrate. But the children, having become adults, depart for other lands for the sake of the business which they had begun to learn in their fatherland. In the meantime, the curators of the minors sell the houses of their wards, which are the only property they possess, under urgent necessity and not without the decree of the Magistrate of that place.
*It is now asked, whether in such a state of affairs, a tax or deduction can be taken from the received price or money, which has been immediately placed at interest and is still subject to contributions, and which the minors neither seek to have transmitted to themselves, nor do the curators and debtors wish to transmit to them at any time without the prior knowledge of the Magistrate.*

### CASE XX.

Titius leaves behind his son as the successor to a fief. When the son seeks the renewal of his investiture after a year and twenty days, the Lord of the fief opposes him with the exception of <term>fatalia</term> <gloss>legal deadlines</gloss>; that is, that the time for seeking the renewal of the investiture has elapsed, and consequently, the Vassal has forfeited the fief.
*It is asked, whether this exception can be defeated, notwithstanding the text of the second book of the Feudal Law, title 24, and similar laws.*
I affirm it.

### I.

<note>A large ornamental initial N begins the text.</note>Those who, while rightly attributing power over sacred matters to the Princes of the <term>Augustanae Confessionis</term> <gloss>Augsburg Confession</gloss>, say that the episcopal right is possessed by them, do not explain themselves with sufficient consideration.

Likewise, that our Princes bear a dual role: namely, the ecclesiastical and the secular.

### III.

But also that episcopal rights are exercised by them by way of a fiduciary contract, or as if by deposit, or as a usufruct.

Finally, that the right of our Princes concerning sacred matters consists in the diocesan law and the law of jurisdiction. Add the DISSERTATION of the SAME on Statutes by the Supreme Prince, and the Digest book regarding Imperial Constitutions, paragraph 36.

Lutherans and Calvinists are not proven heretics from the fact that they are greeted by the names of their authors. THE SAME in his public manuscript lectures on law 6 of the Code concerning heretics and Manichaeans, against the Dillingen scholars.

</translation>

<translation page="102">The natural state of the mind: although it is primordial and lacks nothing, identify the root of the viewer and what is being viewed. The natural state of the mind: although it is primordial and has no meditation, leave the essence of the consciousness that meditates in the great all-pervading expanse. The natural state of the mind: although it is primordial and has no activity, there is no duality between activity and what to accept or reject. Leave it uncontrived and relaxed. The natural state of the mind: although it is primordial and spontaneously present, abandon the desire to achieve a result. Remain in the state free from complexity. The yogi who practices in this way, if they obtain stability in the natural state, purifies the delusions of kleshas <note>afflictive emotions</note> and obtains the result of Buddhahood. This is what was said. Furthermore, this was spoken for the great master Nyima Drakpa, drawing upon the thirty syllables of the alphabet: Ka is the unborn realization arising naturally. Kha is the state of the nature that is as clear as the sky. Ga is the consciousness that lacks any negation or affirmation. Nga is the state of the real essence of non-existence. Cha is the practice of having no contrivance. Cha is until the fruit of the dharmakaya is obtained. Ja is...
<leaf-break/>
Accomplish the meaning. This melody of practice based on the thirty syllables was written as it arose in my mind. This is what was spoken. Furthermore, in the Year of the Monkey, when the <term>Nangso</term> <gloss>local official</gloss> Sonam Gyalpo passed away at Lhalung, the <term>Chömdzey</term> <gloss>ritual practitioner</gloss> and the mother and son requested that I come to lead the funeral rites. Although I could not manage to go at that time, I provided them with one of my own tooth relics and wrote this series of instructions for consolation to the <term>Chömdzey</term>, the mother, and the son. I prostrate and take refuge in the Three Jewels, the object of refuge upon whom one can rely. The leader, mother and son, with whom I have had a deep karmic connection from before, look anywhere in the directions, in the center or at the edge, under the sky or on the earth. For all sentient beings of the three realms, there is no time to be liberated from all the suffering that comes. Everything is a place of departure. Like a father...
<leaf-break/>
Just like that. Gradually arising, the suffering is endless. When you have obtained the precious human body, cast aside all business and strive in the Dharma. This is the ultimate plan. All temporary great activities are of the nature of illusion. There is no benefit in whatever you do, so contemplate impermanence in your mind. By casting aside the business of this life, accomplish the eternal plan. If you are to accomplish a great purpose, do it now. There is no certainty what will happen in the next life. In this time when you have your own freedom, abandon distracting activities and strive in the practice of this deep instruction of the self-arisen Great Perfection. Happiness here and happiness in the next life. Even this current kingship should be protected by the Dharma of loving-kindness. If you benefit all sentient beings, happiness will come to you yourself. This is the instruction of the mendicant Pema Lingpa. Let it sink into the center of your heart. I will also be present around the monkey month. At that time, we will discuss the details of the offerings and the teachings. </translation>

<translation page="103">A memorial service. In the great residence of the <term>vidyadhara</term> <gloss>wisdom-holder</gloss> who practiced begging for flowers, in the southwest outskirts of the Pema Ling monastery, in a place called the Pleasant Land, he spoke this introduction to the <term>Khampa</term> <gloss>person from Kham</gloss> Jachral Rinchen Zangpo through the medium of poetry. The uncompounded nature of mind is the great sky. The natural state is like a chain of thoughts of complexity. The six objects show the form of illusion on the ground. By this non-truth, the path of happiness is scattered. O <term>Khampa</term>, do you see how it is like a moon in water or a magic illusion? This is what was said. Furthermore, he requested: Upon the earth of unwavering and stable faith, let the wish-fulfilling tree of devotion grow its branches. May the fruit of compassion and desired needs ripen. Upon this request, he answered with this: The king of birds, the wings...
<leaf-break/>
The king of birds, the wings... Engage in study and reflection without partiality of direction. Cut the root of doubt in the mind. Know what to accept and reject regarding Dharma and non-Dharma. The summit of the ultimate plan is not mistaken. Through the urging of the impermanent death, the renunciation and weariness that arise toward the nature of the deluded samsara is the summit of the ultimate plan that is not mistaken. Know that all the activities and doings of the world are meaningless. Resting in the state of non-doing is the summit of the ultimate plan that is not mistaken. See the suffering of all who possess wealth. It is a great ornament for the mind that has no wealth. Being endowed with the noble wealth of contentment is the summit of the ultimate plan that is not mistaken. Hold the object of support for the consciousness of your own benefit. Train in the bodhicitta that benefits others. Turn the mind of yourself and others toward the Dharma. The summit of the ultimate plan is not mistaken. The <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>expanse of reality</gloss> is free from complexity. The unborn consciousness is free from limits. To have attained the measure of realizing the view is the summit of the ultimate plan that is not mistaken. The natural essence of bliss, clarity, and non-thought is the object to be meditated upon and the meditator...
<leaf-break/>
Because of the merit, there are some yogis in the Land of Snows who primarily manifest the pure appearance of the awakening of fortunate karmic imprints. I request that you offer a little praise to them. This time, I, the yogi, have reached the difficult-to-reach Manbum Plain. I have met one like you, the lord Pema Lingpa, whom it is difficult to meet. You have granted the instruction that gathers all the deep Dharma meanings, and I have consumed the sacred substance that liberates upon tasting. How happy I am! How joyful I am! I, the yogi Lhawang Drakpa, have come onto the path of emptiness, clarity, and non-attachment. From the mountain pass of seeing nakedness free from extremes, I looked back at the unhindered, unobstructed, and transparent state. I met the guru of primordial, spontaneous presence. I requested the oral instructions of the inseparability of appearance and emptiness. I offered the mandala of the relaxed six sense collections. Through the pure merit of past times, I have met with this essence of the <term>Kuntuzangpo</term> <gloss>Samantabhadra</gloss> realization. Through the prayer I have requested now, it is impossible to be separated until the end of time. How happy I am!</translation>

<summary>This page contains a series of instructional verses and personal correspondences from Pema Lingpa, focusing on the nature of mind, the impermanence of worldly life, and the importance of practice, including specific consolations offered to a local official's family after a bereavement.</summary>
<keywords>Pema Lingpa, natural state of mind, impermanence, bodhicitta, Great Perfection, Dzogchen, funeral instructions, spiritual advice</keywords>

<translation page="47">
(2) Table of Positions, Dharmas, and Contemplative Practices

| Scripture Text | Interpretation | Position | By Dharma | By Contemplative Practice |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| No birth, no death | Ordinary people before the path. This death and that birth constitute the position of birth and death, which true emptiness departs from. | | Conditioned arising, conditions ceasing. | Conceptualized emptiness <note>original: "偏計空"</note>, nothing can be born or die. (Contemplation of non-birth) Delusional phenomena |
| No defilement, no purity | Bodhisattvas on the path. Defilement barriers not yet exhausted, pure conduct already cultivated, constitute the position of defilement and purity, which true emptiness departs from. | | Following the flow, exiting barriers. | Dependent-arising <note>original: "依他"</note> defilement and purity, lacking essence due to conditions. (Contemplation of non-characteristics) Conditioned arising |
| No increase, no decrease | Buddha-fruit after the path. Delusions exhausted is cessation, virtues perfected is increase, which true emptiness departs from. | | Barriers exhausted, virtues perfected. | The previous two are seen via contemplation └─┘ no increase or decrease. (Contemplation of non-self-nature) True emptiness |

(3) Table of the "Eight Negations" from the <term>Madhyamaka-shastra</term> <gloss>Treatise on the Middle Way</gloss>

No birth: All phenomena are unborn. Why? Because it is witnessed by worldly eyes. For example, the grain at the beginning of the kalpa is not born. Why? Separated from the initial grain, the current grain cannot be attained. If one says the current grain exists separated from the initial grain, then birth should exist, but it is not so in reality; therefore, it is no birth.

No death: The grain at the beginning of the kalpa does not die. Why? If it died, there should be no grain now, yet grain truly exists; therefore, it is no death.

No permanence: All things are not permanent. As when grain sprouts, the seed changes and decays; therefore, it is not permanent.

No cessation: All things do not cease. As there is a sprout from the grain, it does not cease; if it ceased, it could not continue.

No oneness: All things are not one. For example, the grain does not become the sprout, and the sprout does not become the grain. If they were one, it would not be so in reality; therefore, it is not one.

No difference: All things are not different. If they were different, why do we distinguish grain sprouts, grain stalks, and grain leaves, rather than saying tree sprouts, tree stalks, and tree leaves? Therefore, they are not different.

No coming: All things do not come. Like the sprout in the grain, it has nowhere it comes from. If it came, the sprout should come from elsewhere, like a bird coming to perch in a tree, but it is not so in reality; therefore, it is no coming.

No exiting: All things do not exit. If there were exiting, one should see the sprout exit from the grain, like a snake exiting from a hole, but it is not so in reality; therefore, it is no exiting.

<meta>continues from previous page: ...the stage of the Buddha, meaning it surpasses the causal state and is called "most supreme."</meta> Because the obstructions are exhausted, virtues are perfected, and the result reaches the ultimate position, it is called "most supreme." As for "karma," this summarizes the activities of the three modes of karma of all Buddhas. That is to say, "most supreme karma" means the supreme [nature] is exactly the karma, and "karma is supreme" means the karma is exactly the supreme nature. These two interpretations are understandable. This refers to the all-knowing intent-karma, the supreme and unimpeded physical-karma, and the supreme, compassionate, and salvific speech-karma. "The one who is supreme" refers to attributing these virtues to a person, meaning one who possesses the aforementioned virtues; this is what is called a Buddha.

Second, regarding the distinction through the two benefits: "Most supreme karma" is a general reference that covers all-knowing wisdom and other specific qualities, revealing the virtue of self-benefit. Within this, there is the wisdom of all-knowing internally, and the unimpeded physical form externally. The <term>Srimaladevi Simhanada Sutra</term> <gloss>Lion's Roar of Queen Srimala Sutra</gloss> states: "The Thus Come One's physical form is inexhaustible; wisdom is also the same." This and other similar passages correspond to this. "Saving the world" and other terms explicitly reveal the virtue of benefiting others. One who has perfected these two benefits is called a Buddha.

Third, regarding the distinction through the three virtues:
1. "Most supreme karma" is the general heading. 
2. "All-knowing" reveals the Buddha's virtue of great wisdom.
3. "Unimpeded physical form" clarifies the Buddha's virtue of great concentration, as it is based on concentration that supernatural powers are manifested, allowing the physical form to be unimpeded.

<summary>This page defines the "most supreme karma" of the Buddha through the lens of the three modes of karma, the two benefits (self and others), and the three virtues (wisdom, concentration, and compassion).</summary>
<keywords>most supreme karma, three modes of karma, self-benefit, altruism, three virtues, Buddha</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="53">
<header>Treatises for Common Use, Part 2</header>

3. "Saving the world" and other phrases explain the Buddha's virtue of great compassion. The <term>Mahayana-samparigraha-shastra</term> <gloss>Compendium of the Mahayana</gloss> explains the merits of the Buddha's enjoyment body <note>the sambhogakaya or reward body of the Buddha</note> by only mentioning these three.

4. Regarding the interpretation based on the text, this section only clarifies the reward body and the transformation body, because the dharma body is included within the Dharma Jewel. "Most supreme" is explained as before. The karma of "all-knowing" has two aspects: 
First, the all-knowing of true wisdom, relating to the gate of "mind as suchness," which contains virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. 
Second, the all-knowing of worldly wisdom, relating to the gate of "mind as birth-and-death," which covers the differentiations of dependent origination. Both reason and quantity are simultaneously illuminated, resulting in an all-knowing that is unerring.

"Unimpeded physical form" means the physical body of the Thus Come One is free and unobstructed. There are many types of this; as stated in the chapter on "Inconceivable Dharma" in the <term>Avatamsaka Sutra</term> <gloss>Flower Adornment Sutra</gloss>, we will briefly distinguish four kinds:
1. Unimpeded between large and small: Each sense organ extends throughout the entire dharma realm, yet it does not destroy the nature of the organs, nor does it confuse the characteristics of the organs.
2. Unimpeded in mutual usage: All sense organs function for each other without obstruction.
3. Unimpeded between principle and phenomenon: The manifest form is distinct and bright, yet this does not obstruct the fact that its entire essence is empty. This is the wondrous principle.

<summary>This page discusses the Buddha's bodies, distinguishing between the reward and transformation bodies, while detailing the "all-knowing" nature of wisdom and the four types of physical unimpededness as described in the Avatamsaka Sutra.</summary>
<keywords>Buddha bodies, great compassion, Mahayana-samparigraha-shastra, mind as suchness, dependent origination, unimpeded physical form, Avatamsaka Sutra</keywords>
</translation>

Moses says, by way of the literal interpretation, that this verse indicates a great and very broad matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created for His glory. Everything He created, He created with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, and there is nothing in the world that is in vain at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created only for His glory." This is a great and very broad subject, and a person needs to contemplate it at all times and at every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, may His name be blessed and His memory exalted forever and to all eternity.

And it can also be said that this verse indicates another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created by measure, by weight, and by limit, and there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by measure, by weight, and by limit." This is a great and very broad subject, and a person needs to contemplate it at all times and at every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, may His name be blessed and His memory exalted forever and to all eternity.

And it can also be said that this verse indicates another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created through the path of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, and there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only through the path of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge." This is a great and very broad subject, and a person needs to contemplate it at all times and at every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, may His name be blessed and His memory exalted forever and to all eternity.

<margin>Note on the subject of Creation</margin>
And it can also be said that this verse indicates another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created through the path of loving-kindness, mercy, and truth, and there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only through the path of loving-kindness, mercy, and truth." This is a great and very broad subject, and a person needs to contemplate it at all times and at every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, may His name be blessed and His memory exalted forever and to all eternity.

Moses says, by way of the literal interpretation, that this verse indicates a great and very broad matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created for His glory. Everything He created, He created with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, and there is nothing in the world that is in vain at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created only for His glory." This is a great and very broad subject, and a person needs to contemplate it at all times and at every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, may His name be blessed and His memory exalted forever and to all eternity.

And it can also be said that this verse indicates another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created by measure, by weight, and by limit, and there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by measure, by weight, and by limit." This is a great and very broad subject, and a person needs to contemplate it at all times and at every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, may His name be blessed and His memory exalted forever and to all eternity.

<translation page="61">
<header>Shat Chakra Nirupana</header>

Therefore, he clarifies the "Lord of all" <note>Sanskrit: *Sarvesha*</note> as *Hamsa*. This *Hamsa* is the form of the mantra that follows the *Sarvesha*. This is stated in the *Prapanchasara*: "That which is known as *Tattva* <gloss>principle/reality</gloss>, being mere consciousness, becomes dense due to the proximity of light, and eventually reaches the state of a dot <term>Bindu</term> <gloss>point/drop</gloss>. In time, that *Bindu*, being divided, becomes twofold. The right part is the *Bindu* and the left part is the *Visarga* <gloss>the two dots of the visarga punctuation mark</gloss>. With that, the right and left parts are characterized as male and female. The letter *Ha* is called the *Bindu*, and the *Visarga* is remembered as *Sa*. The *Bindu* is called the Male <term>Purusha</term> <gloss>spirit/consciousness</gloss>, and the *Visarga* is remembered as the Female <term>Prakriti</term> <gloss>matter/nature</gloss>. The *Hamsa* is of the nature of the Male and Female, and this world is of that nature." 

The *Mahakali Tantra*, in its first chapter, clearly states: "In the center of the thousand-petaled lotus, in the void, decorated by celestial arches, in the middle of the lunar mandala, above the two colors of *Hamsa* <note>referring to the subtle duality of the Hamsa mantra</note>, brilliant like pure crystal, illuminated by pure nectar, and so on." Here, the phrase "above the two colors of *Hamsa*" is very clear. Alternatively, *Hamsa* is known by the name of the Supreme <term>Parama</term> <gloss>Supreme</gloss>. For this reason, the author himself stated in the forty-eighth verse, "some say this is the form of *Hamsa*," thereby declaring its name to be *Hamsa*. Or, through the grammatical compound <term>Karmadharaya</term>, where *Hamsa* is at the end, it becomes *Hamsa-anta*, and since it is also the Supreme, by the rule of *Shakaparthivad* <note>a grammatical rule for dropping middle words in a compound</note>, it is established as *Hamsa-Parama* <note>meaning the Supreme Hamsa</note>. Therefore, it is known by the name *Paramahamsa*. As it is said in the *Agama Kalpadruma*: "This is the form of the *Paramahamsa*, connected with both the moving and the unmoving." "The flow of the stream of all-faces-bliss" <note>referring to *Sakalamukha-santana-lahari*</note> means the expansion of the stream of all-pervading happiness. It is raised in all ways, manifesting as the enduring quality of successive time. Thus, it is all-pervading and characterized by happiness of every kind. It was stated previously that this *Hamsa* resides below the Supreme Shiva <term>Parama Shiva</term>. 43.

<summary>This page discusses the nature of the Hamsa as the unity of Shiva and Shakti within the thousand-petaled lotus, referencing various Tantric texts to establish its identity as the Paramahamsa.</summary>
<keywords>Hamsa, Bindu, Visarga, Purusha, Prakriti, Mahakali Tantra, Paramahamsa, Parama Shiva</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="62">
<header>Shat Chakra Nirupana</header>

17

The Shaivas call this the place of Shiva, the groups of Vaishnavas call it the place of the Supreme Person <term>Parama Purusha</term>, and some others call it the abode of Harihara <note>a combined deity of Vishnu and Shiva</note>. The great sages, who delight in the lotus-feet of the Goddess, call it the pure place of Nature and Spirit <term>Prakriti-Purusha</term>. 44.

Having known this place, the noble man whose mind is fixed there shall not be born again in the world; he is not bound in the three worlds. Total power <term>Shakti</term> shall be... <note>The text is interrupted here.</note>

Since all deities such as *Hamsa* and others reside in the pericarp of this lotus, he explains that it is the place of worship for all followers of Shiva, Shakti, and others. "Place of Shiva": The Shaivas, or worshippers of Shiva, call this lotus the place of Shiva. "Supreme Person": By the use of the suffix of possession, it is established that this is the place of the Supreme Person, Vishnu. "Some others": Those who are worshippers of Harihara, whether Shaiva or Vaishnava, or others who are not exclusively worshippers of Shiva or Vishnu, call it the place of Harihara. Therefore, the meaning is that not all Shaivas and Vaishnavas say it is only the place of Shiva or only the place of Vishnu; rather, others who are devoted to the worship of the pair speak of it as such. Or, other great sages who are worshippers of the *Hamsa* mantra call it the place of *Prakriti* and *Purusha*, because *Hamsa* is the embodiment of both. This is merely an indication. It should be understood that because the Supreme *Bindu* resides there, this place is full of all deities, and whoever is a worshipper of a particular deity calls it the place of that deity. 44.

He states the result of the knowledge of the *Sahasrara* <note>the thousand-petaled lotus</note> as "having known this place." The sense is that the knowledge of this place, with its parts and appendages, is attained. "Whose mind is fixed": One whose mind is fixed there. "Shall not be born again": He becomes liberated, this is the meaning. "Because he is not bound in the three worlds": This is a causal adjective. Bound means tied by the snares of illusion, which are the forms of merit and demerit. This is stated in the *Bhagavata*: "While the action is being performed, one considers oneself as the body of qualities. This is his bondage in the world and his dependency."

<summary>This page explains that the Sahasrara lotus is perceived differently by various sectarian traditions—Shaivas, Vaishnavas, and others—based on their specific theological focus, while noting that the liberation attained through this knowledge removes the practitioner from the cycle of rebirth.</summary>
<keywords>Shat Chakra Nirupana, Sahasrara, Shiva, Vishnu, Harihara, Prakriti-Purusha, Hamsa mantra, liberation</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="62">
# Twenty-first Chapter

->Twenty-first Chapter. 48<-

She has beautiful teeth, is eternal, and has full and elevated breasts. 
She is positioned at the intersection of limbs, the slayer of the demon Mahishasura. (25)
She is as soft to the touch as a lotus stalk and possesses ten arms. 
One should meditate on the trident on the right, followed by the sword and the discus in order. (26)
She bears sharp weapons, including the <term>shakti</term> <gloss>divine power/spear</gloss> on the left arm. 
She is marked by the shield, the full bow, the noose, and the goad. (27)
One should also place the bell on the left side, or perhaps the supreme weapon. 
Her body is anointed with red sandalwood paste, and she is clad in red garments. (28)
She is the supreme Goddess, stationed upon a lion, worshipped by Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva. 
She is the great <term>Maya</term> <gloss>illusory power</gloss> dwelling upon a corpse, situated upon a red lotus seat. (29)
One should meditate upon this Durga, who is mounted on a lion and is the giver of supreme liberation. 
Shiva is the corpse, the great Lord, while Brahma is the red lotus. (30)
Vishnu is known as the lion; these are the mighty vehicles. 
O Goddess, the invocation of them through their own forms is not practiced. (31)
Having transformed into the respective forms, they have attained the state of being vehicles. 
Sometimes she is on the Shiva-corpse, sometimes on the red lotus. (32)
Sometimes she resides on the back of the lion, O supreme Lady. 
When the time of desire <note>Kama-kala</note> arrives, the one with the lion-vehicle resides upon the Shiva-corpse. (33)
Hear now of the beloved circle of companions of this slayer of the buffalo-demon. (34)

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the holy Kamivilasa Tantra.

<summary>This chapter provides the iconographic description and meditation (dhyana) instructions for the goddess Durga, the slayer of Mahishasura, detailing her ten-armed form, weapons, and symbolic vehicles.</summary>
<keywords>Durga, Mahishasuramardini, Tantra, iconography, meditation, Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma</keywords>

Shri Tatpurusha said:

Chanda, Chandavati, the <term>vidya</term> <gloss>knowledge/incantation</gloss> Chamunda, Chandanayika, (1)
Ugrachanda, Prachanda, Chandogra, and Chandanasika.
Surrounded by these powers, victorious and riding a lion, (2)
Hear the mantra I shall proclaim, which is the giver of liberation to the mortals.
Having uttered the <term>Maya-bija</term> <gloss>seed syllable Hrim</gloss>, then the words 'Durge Durge'. (3)
Then, O gentle one, the word 'Raksha', and at the end of that, the beloved of fire <note>Svaha</note>.
There is no mantra greater than this, nor a more auspicious one in the Tantras, O beautiful-eyed one. (4)
I proclaim to you the ten-syllabled great mantra.
Having uttered the <term>Maya-bija</term>, then the word 'Durge', O beloved one. (5)
With the spouse of fire <note>Svaha</note> at the end, it is known to grant all successes.
Having uttered the <term>Maya-bija</term>, then 'Durgyai', and after that, (6)
Having placed the spouse of fire at the end, if one repeats this once,
Having attained a billion states, he goes to <term>Vaikuntha</term> <gloss>the abode of Vishnu</gloss>. (7)
'Durge Durge', and then stated, with the spouse of fire after that.
This <term>vidya</term> is the great knowledge, the grantor of the fruits of the four aims of life. (8)

'Hrim Durge', that is the mantra, the grantor of the four aims of life.

Having uttered the <term>Maya-bija</term>, and then the spouse of fire after that.

'Hrim Durge', that is the mantra, the grantor of the four aims of life.
