pages.62:
# Twenty-first Chapter

->Twenty-first Chapter. 48<-

She has beautiful teeth, is eternal, and has full and elevated breasts. 
She is positioned at the intersection of limbs, the slayer of the demon Mahishasura. (25)
She is as soft to the touch as a lotus stalk and possesses ten arms. 
One should meditate on the trident on the right, followed by the sword and the discus in order. (26)
She bears sharp weapons, including the <term>shakti</term> <gloss>divine power/spear</gloss> on the left arm. 
She is marked by the shield, the full bow, the noose, and the goad. (27)
One should also place the bell on the left side, or perhaps the supreme weapon. 
Her body is anointed with red sandalwood paste, and she is clad in red garments. (28)
She is the supreme Goddess, stationed upon a lion, worshipped by Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva. 
She is the great <term>Maya</term> <gloss>illusory power</gloss> dwelling upon a corpse, situated upon a red lotus seat. (29)
One should meditate upon this Durga, who is mounted on a lion and is the giver of supreme liberation. 
Shiva is the corpse, the great Lord, while Brahma is the red lotus. (30)
Vishnu is known as the lion; these are the mighty vehicles. 
O Goddess, the invocation of them through their own forms is not practiced. (31)
Having transformed into the respective forms, they have attained the state of being vehicles. 
Sometimes she is on the Shiva-corpse, sometimes on the red lotus. (32)
Sometimes she resides on the back of the lion, O supreme Lady. 
When the time of desire <note>Kama-kala</note> arrives, the one with the lion-vehicle resides upon the Shiva-corpse. (33)
Hear now of the beloved circle of companions of this slayer of the buffalo-demon. (34)

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the holy Kamivilasa Tantra.

<summary>This chapter provides the iconographic description and meditation (dhyana) instructions for the goddess Durga, the slayer of Mahishasura, detailing her ten-armed form, weapons, and symbolic vehicles.</summary>
<keywords>Durga, Mahishasuramardini, Tantra, iconography, meditation, Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="10"/><note>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' at the beginning of the dedication.</note>

**N**o one can deny that Lord Philipp, Count, your father, because of his most celebrated virtues and the singular piety with which he shone toward God, should be honored with the praises of a hero and with Latin <note>original: "Ausonio"</note> verse. However, since I am not endowed with such eloquence as to be able to adorn his shade in accordance with his dignity, and yet I have descended into this arena, I pray that no one attributes this to me as a fault. For it is fitting to favor even modest talents, even if they do not achieve everything. To you, generous Counts, I have chosen to dedicate this poem, although it is but a slight gift, and I pray that you receive it with a calm and serene countenance. If you persevere in such a way that you do not decline from your fatherly virtues in any matter, you will one day be celebrated with a similar encomium. Therefore, apply yourselves so that, not degenerating, you do not stray from your father's footsteps. From Mühlberg, on the 11th of May, in the year of the Virgin's birth 1544.

### FUNERAL POEM FOR THE OBITUARY OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS
### AND FAMOUS COUNT, etc.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' at the beginning of the poem.</note>

**L**amenting elegy, put on your garments again now,
   And may you wish to hold the name that is properly yours.
From the high lineage of the Gleichen family, Philipp
   Has departed from the living, who was a father among the rest.
Therefore, a new grief occupies the brothers from that place, and their cheeks
   And whole faces are now once again drenched in tears.
And thus at home, in the ancestral castle of the Sigismunds <pb n="11"/>
He mourns his brother, full of sorrowful love.
But you, Ernst, having set out for the household gods of Speyer,
Groan for the fate of your brother under a foreign sky.
And just as you were recently following the pious arms of the Saxon,
A pugnacious man with joined forces, Hessen, with yours.
Meanwhile, that brother whose name is Grace, the cruel
Fate snatched away with an unfair death at home.
With the Emperor now also holding a council, I pray that it
May bring health and peace, the desired gifts.
While you were visiting him with the Duke of Saxony, you lose
Philipp at home now in a similar manner.
Therefore, you shed heavy tears by right, Ernst,
And you have a just and heavy cause for weeping.
You also, sons, sad at the death of your parent,
Weep, and heavy grief possesses your breasts.
A just cause produces huge complaints for you,
Which, if anyone finds fault with, has no reason for the truth.
Until now you have wept for your deceased mother and your uncle Johann;
You weep for both of them now along with your father.
And each sad fortress now grieves, its father having been taken away,
And the Ora <note>a river near Thonna/Gleichen</note> mixes its waters with your tears.
What need is there of many words; all things are full of grief,
And every subject has cause to weep as is deserved.
We too, who inhabit the shores of the nearby Wipper <note>original: "VVcite"</note>,
Weep for you, famous Philipp, with a complaining lyre.
We weep, and we sing the proclamations of your praise in these
Verses, even though they may be unrefined and rude.
</translation>

<summary>This text is a Latin funeral poem and dedication by Wendelin von Helbach, mourning the death of Philipp, Count of Gleichen, and addressing his sons and brother, Ernst, while reflecting on the collective grief of their lands and family.</summary>
<keywords>Philipp of Gleichen, funeral elegy, Helbach, lamentation, Saxon nobility, genealogy, grief, Speyer, Mühlberg</keywords>

...those who acknowledged nothing unless it were subject to the senses, we maintain that [the knowledge of universals] exists: for sciences of things considered universally need not exist for the reason that their total mutability and mortality are converted by the intuition of the mind into an eternal and perpetual constancy in reality and in every part—since no contemplation of our mind, however accurate, could achieve this—but because things understood universally are freed from the shackles of individuals, by which they are made unstable, and embrace only the essence and its inherent affections, which in themselves bear no mutation.

## XVIII.

For we do not consider it sufficient that some people hold that the <term>ousiae</term> <gloss>essences</gloss> of things, and the propositions formed from them, are necessary because they have existed from eternity in God, the Best and Greatest, as in one who knows, and as their idea and primary cause. For if by that reasoning all things are and have been in God, then all individuals, and even all statements which we call <term>contingentes</term> <gloss>contingent</gloss>, would be of exactly equal eternity and certainty.

## XIX.

Although in the very same moment, universals begin to exist with individuals, yet in the order of nature, as far as their existence is concerned, the latter are prior to them, since they can possess their existence as universals from nowhere else but from individuals: if, however, you consider their essence, you will find them to be prior to the individuals themselves, because they assist the constitution of singular things and communicate their own <term>quiddity</term> <gloss>whatness/essence</gloss> to them.

From what we have established thus far, it also becomes manifest in what way the treatment of universals pertains to different faculties. The wretched mother, suspecting nothing evil, sent him. Ten days had not yet passed when that other infant son was killed. And so, Sassia married Oppianicus, with a mind now rejoicing and fortified by the best hope; and no wonder, for she saw herself softened not by wedding gifts, but by the funerals of sons. I perceive, judges, that you, in your humanity, are vehemently moved by these great crimes which I have briefly set forth. With what state of mind, therefore, do you think those men were affected, who not only had to listen to these matters, but also to render a verdict upon them? You hear of a man regarding whom you are not the judges; of a man whom you do not see; of a man whom you can no longer hate; of a man who has satisfied both nature and the laws, whom the laws punished with exile and nature with death. <pb n="10"/>

### XL.

A pact is further considered either in itself, or insofar as it is confirmed by law, or as it is added to a contract in the immediate moment of its formation.

### XLI.

The former is called a naked <term>pactum</term> <gloss>pact</gloss>, while the latter are not called naked; since these do not rest upon the mere terms of a pact, but rather either adhere to a contract or have an assisting law, no one fails to see that they cannot be held in the class of naked pacts. *Bachovius in his notes to the Disputations of Treutler.*

### XLII.

And these can also be called clothed <term>pacta</term> <gloss>pacts</gloss> without inconsistency; for although these words do not exist in the Law, it can hardly be denied that the thing itself exists; but where it is established concerning the thing, we ought to be easy regarding the words, by the argument of <term>law 17</term>, Digest on laws.

### XLIII.

A naked convention is that which stands in the end of a simple agreement, <term>law "si tibi" 27</term>, Code on letting and hiring; or, which is the same thing, that which consists within the pure and simple boundaries of a convention.

### XLIV.

It is called so because it is naked of a cause or business transaction, <term>law "solent" 15</term>, Digest on prescribed words; which also formally distinguishes this convention from a contract, whence it is also called a simple convention in <term>law "avia" 6</term>, Code on the law of dowries, and merely a pact in <term>law "major" 23</term>, Code on pledges and mortgages.

### XLV.

For example, if it is agreed that you should sell me your house, this convention stands in the naked terms of an agreement: but if you agree concerning the thing and the price, it is no longer <pb n="11"/> called a naked convention, because a business transaction has been added which produces a civil obligation, and a contract has been celebrated, which is called buying and selling, <term>law "principio" on buying and selling</term> and <term>law "pacta conventa" 72</term>, in the beginning of the Digest on contracting a purchase.

### XLVI.

Thus, if I make a pact with you that you should give me money as a loan, or that you should exchange your Cornelian estate for my buildings, nothing has been done so far beyond a naked convention and a naked agreement. But as soon as you count out the money for me, or deliver the Cornelian estate to me, or I deliver my buildings to you, a transaction intervenes alongside the convention, and in that case, a loan contract is made, <term>law "principio" on the ways by which an obligation is contracted by a thing</term>; but if it is an exchange, see <term>law "naturalis" 5, paragraph 1</term>, Digest on prescribed words.

### XLVII.

It is doubted whether the name of pact, uttered simply, signifies a naked pact? I affirm this through <term>law "Jure gentium" 7, paragraph 5</term>, Digest on pacts. Those who feel the contrary are moved by the aforementioned <term>law "traditionibus" 20</term>, Code on pacts, where it states "not by naked pacts." But Hunnius satisfies these points in his resolutions to Treutler, Disputation 9, question 5.

### XLVIII.

A naked pact is either express or tacit, which is understood to be gathered from the deeds of the contracting parties, and is said to be entered into by the thing itself in <term>law 2</term>, Digest on pacts, and <term>law 32</term>, Digest on partnership; of which we have one example in <term>law 2, paragraph 1</term>, Digest on pacts: he who returned a bond to a debtor is understood to have tacitly agreed not to sue. Another is in <term>law 3</term>, Digest on the said title, where one who returns a pledge is believed to have remitted the right of the pledge, not the debt itself.

</translation>

<summary>This text distinguishes between naked and clothed pacts, defining a naked convention as one lacking a formal business transaction, and explains how subsequent actions transform simple agreements into binding contracts.</summary>
<keywords>Naked pact, clothed pact, convention, contract, obligation, Roman law, Digest, Code, business transaction</keywords>

the matter should be recounted in such a way that it appears that the scourges were inflicted upon Christ by the actual person of *Pilate*, not by his soldiers, since they are only mentioned later in verse 2. Blessed *Gerhard* indicates that *Beda*, while clinging too much to the letter, remained stuck in this opinion. But who, nevertheless, could so easily believe that such a man, established in such dignity and authority among the Romans as well as the Jews, would have submitted himself so far as to perform this duty, which was as if proper for soldiers and lictors to carry out? It is more probable that this butchery was carried out primarily by those who were most sent and destined by *Pilate* to perform it. However, the flagellation is imputed here to *Pilate* himself, the Governor of Judea, as the principal moral cause, because by his order and command the whole thing was done. It is therefore not absurd, but very convenient, to explain the words of the Evangelists in this way. For is it not, according to the common canon, that what a person does through another or others must be considered and said to have been done by himself?

XXVII. Furthermore, inquiring into the ministerial cause, we judge it not irrelevant to ask who and what kind of men were especially admitted to scourge JESUS? If we look at the more corrected Greek codices here, we do not find that they are mentioned separately in the text regarding this; however, we gather not incorrectly from the words both preceding and following that the Roman soldiers and lictors—by some called <term>Brutiani</term> <gloss>a type of Roman military police</gloss> or <term>Brutii</term>—and these being Gentiles, were the primary actors in this tragedy. For the added particle, <term>Eis</term> <gloss>to them</gloss>, looking back to the Jews, which is read in certain copies after the word <term>tradidit</term> <gloss>he handed over</gloss>, is not genuine: hence, as *Erasmus* notes, it hinders the sense somewhat.
<margin>Annotations on Matthew, ch. 27.</margin>
For (he adds) *Pilate* did not hand JESUS over to the Jews, but to his own soldiers, the ministers of the punishment. For these very men previously seized Christ, bound the seized one, brought the bound one to judgment, stood the brought one, scourged the stood one, clothed the scourged one in purple, crowned the clothed one, mocked the crowned one, beat the mocked one, led away the beaten one, and crucified the led-away one: just as we see this inculcated not once, but very often, in the history of the entire passion.

XXVIII. But perhaps a doubt could arise for someone, whether the Jews might have offered their own helping hands to the Heathens in this business? Certainly, with *Judas* the traitor carrying the torch ahead, these men handed over Christ, seeking nothing else than that JESUS be taken from their midst by the Gentiles, after various tortures, and finally lifted onto the cross itself. Therefore, who of us ever doubts that the blame for the far greatest part of the entire passion, and thus also of the flagellation, redounds upon the Jews as the morally efficient causes? Indeed, that the Jews played the part of some physical cause in any work, we neither read nor believe: especially since the SAVIOR himself, patiently suffering on his last journey to Jerusalem, foretold this of himself to his disciples, that it would happen that the Chief Priests and Scribes would hand over the Son of Man to the Gentiles to be mocked and <term>εἰς μαστιγῶσαι</term> <gloss>to be scourged</gloss>. Compare *Mark* and *Luke*. You will see that in both cases it is stated of the Gentiles, or (which is the same in these and many other places) the heathens, but by no means the Jews: <term>μαστιγώσουσιν</term> <gloss>they will scourge</gloss> and <term>μαστιγώσαντες αὐτόν</term> <gloss>having scourged him</gloss>. Hence, in order that this most truthful prediction of TRUTH might be fulfilled, the Gentiles alone had to scourge JESUS.
<margin>Matthew XX, v. 18, 19; ch. XV, 39, 40; ch. XVIII, v. 32 & 33.</margin>

XXIX. But even if we look at the very mind of the Jews, it is not difficult to understand why they did not wish to afflict JESUS with lashes. For, since according to the divine law it was not permitted for the Jews to inflict more than forty blows, or, as they themselves wrongly interpreted, thirty-nine, with scourges; hence, without a doubt, because of their sharp
<pb n="15"/>
<margin>John XVIII, v. 31; v. 18.</margin>

hatred against CHRIST, this punishment seemed too *lenient* if it were inflicted by his own people upon this JESUS, their *seducer*, as they blasphemed. They preferred, therefore, to choose the Gentiles to inflict this punishment, as they were not restricted to any certain number and were accustomed to beating criminals *beyond measure*, sometimes even *to the point of death*. Nor did they intend the flagellation for its own sake, but *only* demanded the crucifixion. Hence, not content with that punishment inflicted by *Pilate*, they shouted that Christ must also be punished by the cross, nor did they stop shouting until they obtained by the very act what they so strongly requested. For they did not want *life*, they wanted *death*, and that to be paid for by the cross: which capital punishment, however, it was not permitted for them to exercise, although the *Romans exercised the same at will among the Jews*. This is most supported by their own confession, uttered with one voice before *Pilate*: *It is not permitted for us*, they say, *to kill anyone*; understand in particular, as authors of no small note imply, by the punishment of the cross. So restricted was the power of the Jews at that time under the Romans. Indeed, perhaps for this reason also, the Jews refused to offer themselves as partners to the Romans in scourging Christ, because they thought that any one of their own would be contaminated if someone entered the praetorium, with Passover imminent, and so much more if they were to become an accomplice in the same punishments. See *John XVIII*.

<margin>Matthew XXVII, v. 27; Mark XV, v. 16.</margin>

XXX. But what of it? From what cause it was done by them, it matters little to us to know. We return more rightly to the act of flagellation itself. We gathered before from the text of Scripture that it was demanded by *Pilate*, from the merciless soldiers and satellites of *Pilate*, that they should scourge Jesus. How many lictors there were precisely, we have not said, nor can we say; with Scripture and antiquity remaining silent. Yet it is beyond controversy that more than one, indeed many, if not most, participated in this act, who by their help and labor assisted in the business of the flagellation. The place where the flagellation was to be instituted was set as the *atrium or praetorium, the house in which the provincial Governor not only lived but also administered justice*. For there the soldiers of the Governor had withdrawn, having called together and gathered the entire cohort into it.

<margin>L. 2. on Crucifixion, ch. 4, p. 63.</margin>

XXXI. There, indeed, Jesus was forced to undergo the individual fates of those to be scourged. Why should we deny that he was *deprived of his clothes*, having heard above that this custom remained *most common* among the Romans in this infliction of punishments? We also willingly grant some belief to the opinion by which it is asserted that *Jesus was bound to a column*; not so much because *Lipsius* tried to confirm this rite with certain examples and foreign testimonies, but because the pious and ancient Fathers of the religion did not entirely doubt that they should assert such a thing about the column of the scourged Savior. Clearly and illustriously, the most prudent of Poets sang in his own age:

<margin>Prudentius, Enchiridion of the New Testament on this column. See Library of the Fathers, Vol. 4, p. 924.</margin>

the matter should be recounted in such a way that it appears that the scourges were inflicted upon Christ by the actual person of *Pilate*, not by his soldiers, since they are only mentioned later in verse 2. Blessed *Gerhard* indicates that *Beda*, while clinging too much to the letter, remained stuck in this opinion. But who, nevertheless, could so easily believe that such a man, established in such dignity and authority among the Romans as well as the Jews, would have submitted himself so far as to perform this duty, which was as if proper for soldiers and lictors to carry out? It is more probable that this butchery was carried out primarily by those who were most sent and destined by *Pilate* to perform it. However, the flagellation is imputed here to *Pilate* himself, the Governor of Judea, as the principal moral cause, because by his order and command the whole thing was done. It is therefore not absurd, but very convenient, to explain the words of the Evangelists in this way. For is it not, according to the common canon, that what a person does through another or others must be considered and said to have been done by himself?

XXVII. Furthermore, inquiring into the ministerial cause, we judge it not irrelevant to ask who and what kind of men were especially admitted to scourge JESUS? If we look at the more corrected Greek codices here, we do not find that they are mentioned separately in the text regarding this; however, we gather not incorrectly from the words both preceding and following that the Roman soldiers and lictors—by some called <term>Brutiani</term> <gloss>a type of Roman military police</gloss> or <term>Brutii</term>—and these being Gentiles, were the primary actors in this tragedy. For the added particle, <term>Eis</term> <gloss>to them</gloss>, looking back to the Jews, which is read in certain copies after the word <term>tradidit</term> <gloss>he handed over</gloss>, is not genuine: hence, as *Erasmus* notes, it hinders the sense somewhat.
<margin>Annotations on Matthew, ch. 27.</margin>
For (he adds) *Pilate* did not hand JESUS over to the Jews, but to his own soldiers, the ministers of the punishment. For these very men previously seized Christ, bound the seized one, brought the bound one to judgment, stood the brought one, scourged the stood one, clothed the scourged one in purple, crowned the clothed one, mocked the crowned one, beat the mocked one, led away the beaten one, and crucified the led-away one: just as we see this inculcated not once, but very often, in the history of the entire passion.

XXVIII. But perhaps a doubt could arise for someone, whether the Jews might have offered their own helping hands to the Heathens in this business? Certainly, with *Judas* the traitor carrying the torch ahead, these men handed over Christ, seeking nothing else than that JESUS be taken from their midst by the Gentiles, after various tortures, and finally lifted onto the cross itself. Therefore, who of us ever doubts that the blame for the far greatest part of the entire passion, and thus also of the flagellation, redounds upon the Jews as the morally efficient causes? Indeed, that the Jews played the part of some physical cause in any work, we neither read nor believe: especially since the SAVIOR himself, patiently suffering on his last journey to Jerusalem, foretold this of himself to his disciples, that it would happen that the Chief Priests and Scribes would hand over the Son of Man to the Gentiles to be mocked and <term>εἰς μαστιγῶσαι</term> <gloss>to be scourged</gloss>. Compare *Mark* and *Luke*. You will see that in both cases it is stated of the Gentiles, or (which is the same in these and many other places) the heathens, but by no means the Jews: <term>μαστιγώσουσιν</term> <gloss>they will scourge</gloss> and <term>μαστιγώσαντες αὐτόν</term> <gloss>having scourged him</gloss>. Hence, in order that this most truthful prediction of TRUTH might be fulfilled, the Gentiles alone had to scourge JESUS.
<margin>Matthew XX, v. 18, 19; ch. XV, 39, 40; ch. XVIII, v. 32 & 33.</margin>

XXIX. But even if we look at the very mind of the Jews, it is not difficult to understand why they did not wish to afflict JESUS with lashes. For, since according to the divine law it was not permitted for the Jews to inflict more than forty blows, or, as they themselves wrongly interpreted, thirty-nine, with scourges; hence, without a doubt, because of their sharp
pages.15:
<margin>John XVIII, v. 31; v. 18.</margin>

hatred against CHRIST, this punishment seemed too *lenient* if it were inflicted by his own people upon this JESUS, their *seducer*, as they blasphemed. They preferred, therefore, to choose the Gentiles to inflict this punishment, as they were not restricted to any certain number and were accustomed to beating criminals *beyond measure*, sometimes even *to the point of death*. Nor did they intend the flagellation for its own sake, but *only* demanded the crucifixion. Hence, not content with that punishment inflicted by *Pilate*, they shouted that Christ must also be punished by the cross, nor did they stop shouting until they obtained by the very act what they so strongly requested. For they did not want *life*, they wanted *death*, and that to be paid for by the cross: which capital punishment, however, it was not permitted for them to exercise, although the *Romans exercised the same at will among the Jews*. This is most supported by their own confession, uttered with one voice before *Pilate*: *It is not permitted for us*, they say, *to kill anyone*; understand in particular, as authors of no small note imply, by the punishment of the cross. So restricted was the power of the Jews at that time under the Romans. Indeed, perhaps for this reason also, the Jews refused to offer themselves as partners to the Romans in scourging Christ, because they thought that any one of their own would be contaminated if someone entered the praetorium, with Passover imminent, and so much more if they were to become an accomplice in the same punishments. See *John XVIII*.

<margin>Matthew XXVII, v. 27; Mark XV, v. 16.</margin>

How many lictors there were precisely, we have not said, nor can we say; with Scripture and antiquity remaining silent. Yet it is beyond controversy that more than one, indeed many, if not most, participated in this act, who by their help and labor assisted in the business of the flagellation. The place where the flagellation was to be instituted was set as the *atrium or praetorium, the house in which the provincial Governor not only lived but also administered justice*. For there the soldiers of the Governor had withdrawn, having called together and gathered the entire cohort into it.

<margin>L. 2. on Crucifixion, ch. 4, p. 63.</margin>

muscles are marked by this character in general, so it happens especially to the muscles of the thorax, so that they can no longer lift the ribs; thus, of necessity, the equilibrium between the pressing air and our body is removed, whence breathing becomes difficult, with which the anxiety of the <term>precordia</term> <gloss>the region over the heart</gloss> walks in equal step.

> *Often the sick do not dare to speak, indeed they are scarcely able to, which must be deduced from the vehemence of the pains, or from the paralytic state of the organs dedicated to speech.*

> *A fever is present, insofar as the circulation of the humors, on account of the languid nerves and the abundance of morbific matter, does not succeed as desired; hence it happens that they conceive a fermentation or internal motion.*

The *Inaugural Dissertation on Malignant Fever by the most Clarissimi Domini* <term>Licentiatus</term> <gloss>a licensed practitioner</gloss> J. C. Wolff of Servest, formerly my most pleasant companion, held at Wittenberg under the most Excellent Lord Doctor Berger, Professor Publicus and my venerable teacher there, will shed light on this opinion.

For a more moderate degree of fermentation, however, the sick person does not feel its disturbances.

The propensity to sleep is also an effect of viscosity, thickness, and a lack of animal spirits and other fluids, or even of compression of the brain. However, somnolence is not an inseparable attribute of <term>Hemicrania</term>, as the previously praised Piso seems to hint. But excessive vigils otherwise urge, and that on account of the atrocity of the pains. A cold sweat occurs, insofar as the glandular context and tone on the surface of the body is too relaxed, whence an easy exit for the serum is open by any given gate; and it is cold where the humors, and especially the blood, pass through the small canals so slowly, due also to the solid parts, among which the heart holds primacy, relaxing from a constrictive motion, that they cannot produce that agitation which represents heat to the mind. With the nervous genus corrupted, and the humors also corrupted, what good shall we hope for from the stomach? Appetite is the offspring of the animal spirits; therefore, with the use of these denied, nausea arises. What is more, the corrupted gastric lymph is not suitable for dissolving food. The stomach, thus burdened and now sufficiently weak, contracts itself spasmodically and ejects the indigested mass again, which we call <term>Vomiting</term>. Whence a tumor on the surface of the head derives its birth, let it be sought from the preceding section. It should be noted moreover that it does not seem improbable to me that such a tumor can sometimes be nourished by caries of the skull itself.

### XI.
But as to why <term>Hemicrania</term> sometimes remits, or even torments the sick person only at certain interpolated intervals of time, <pb n="13"/> and from that a *periodic* pain results (examples of which can be read in Tulp, Linden, Bellini, and others), this depends upon various vicissitudes of the fluid surrounding us, and upon the peculiar constitution of the head introduced by the causes mentioned in section IX. For in such a way we easily conceive that the peccant matter, consumed in the course of time, is restored anew and insinuates itself again into the injured part (always, like a folded piece of paper, returning to its traces), until it grows into such a mass that it brings about a new distension of the frequently mentioned parts, whence the disease assumes its former face.

XII. If we recall to mind all the things now said with a little more curiosity, what dangers do we not see present for the sick? And what even greater ones do we not fear, not without the support of reason? We do not hesitate to affirm that <term>Hemicrania</term> is a most dangerous disease, in whatever way it behaves. Indeed, the affected part must provide aid to the highly sensitive economy of the body, and the producing causes are extremely grave. Moreover, the disease is most difficult to cure, both because its various causes must be torn out by the roots before it can be removed, and because one can scarcely find an equal remedy to restore the solid parts that have been twisted <term>praeter naturam</term> <gloss>contrary to nature</gloss> back to their natural state. But the evil is rendered especially stubborn because only half of the head is affected. For a remedy, however much it may wash the affected place, will operate sparingly, seeking an exit where it finds the least resistance of all. I pass over the fact that what is taken is not specifically determined here or there, but is distributed throughout the entire body by the law of circulation. Wherefore, *External Hemicrania*, where medicines immediately touch the affected part, bids us be more secure, unless a caries of the skull is joined to it. With respect to the duration of the disease, the sex, age, temper of the air, and the idiosyncrasy of the body, one prognosis after another will have to be formed. The evil must be called more or less ferocious according to the greater or lesser number of symptoms. I knew a friend (which it is to the point to mention here) who, on that side on which he had lain during the night, contracted *Hemicrania* with a languor of the limbs, which was happily resolved shortly, and, if I am not mistaken, within eight days. Alas, the worms nesting in the brain make for a more serious care, while small stones and calculi generated in the same entirely defy it! For confirmation of this, see the *Dissertation on Atherapeusia* <note>original: "Dissert. de Atherapeusia", meaning a condition incurable by standard treatment</note>
</translation>

<keywords>Hemicrania, animal spirits, gastric lymph, periodic pain, prognosis, hemicrania externa, medical theory</keywords>

XVII. Whoever denies that being insofar as it is being is the object of metaphysics, because all things that are treated in this discipline, such as first principles, axioms, hypotheses, and primary definitions, the doctrine of primary substance and its operations and attributes cannot be reduced to this, should also deny that a natural body insofar as it is natural is the object of physics, because not all things that are treated in physics are natural bodies, for example, matter, form, nature, place, time, quantity, quality, sound, sight, and so forth. Although not everything pertains to some discipline, which this or that person claims.

XVIII. Whoever said that someone who wishes to use abstractions in other philosophical disciplines besides mathematics abstracts the mind from the truth, because things must be known as they are found in the nature of things, not as certain things are wont or able to be abstracted from them, was either playing with ambiguity or did not understand abstraction.

XIX. There is great debate among the ancients whether virtue can be learned, with some affirming that it is given by nature to the good and denied to the wicked, while others maintain it is acquired through practice and doctrine. Plato seems at times to side with the former, at times with the latter. But there is no doubt that both a nature not depraved in itself, and precepts, and exercise, and training establish and perfect virtue. This is what the ancients called nature, reason, and practice <note>original: "Φύσιν, λόγον καὶ ἄσκησιν"</note>. These are as necessary in virtue as they are in the arts, and even in crops, where rich soil, good seeds, and the diligence of the farmer are required. Ludovicus Vives, *on chapter 1, book 19 of The City of God, column 1141; add Augustine in the aforementioned book, chapter 4, column 1148.* The Philosopher throughout his works: Plutarch, *the treatise* Is Virtue Teachable? <note>original: "εἰ διδακτὸν ἡ ἀρετή"</note>, *page 370.*

XX. Everyone always desires the good: Plato in *Hipparchus*. For all good things are useful: the same in *Meno*.

XXI. Poverty, the sister of a good mind, as Petronius says in the *Satyricon, page 94*, seems preferable to riches; for it teaches all the arts, wherever it touches anyone, says Plautus in *Stichus. Add Seneca, epistle 15, and Theocritus.* For usually Necessity and Sobriety accompany them, and render men attentive and circumspect, whereas second fortune and opulence beget negligence. Hence the intellect is sharpened, from which the arts arise. Indeed, as Apuleius says, pride has never inflated anyone, impotence has never depraved anyone, and tyranny has never brutalized anyone who neither desires nor is able to have the delights of the belly and loins. For these and other disgraces are usually the pupils of riches. And although we read that even the poorest men have committed the greatest crimes, many of them were not poor, but beggars. Aristophanes provides this distinction in *Plutus, page 11:*

> For the life of a beggar, which you speak of, is to live having nothing,
<pb n="13"/>
or of a poor man, to live sparingly and attending to his work,
so that nothing remains for him, yet he does not lack.

### XXII. Hesiod teaches in these verses that the care of human affairs lies with the spirits <term>Genii</term> <gloss>guardian spirits</gloss> by the permission of the Supreme Commander:

> For there are good spirits on earth,
> holy, warders of evil, guardians of mortal men,
> who watch over justice and cruel deeds,
> clothed in mist, wandering everywhere over the earth.

It is therefore probable that certain of these spirits, as legates or tribunes, care for peoples and regions; and Theodoretus records that these are archangels, on chapter 10 of Daniel, as cited by Besoldus. Certainly, even the fact that Saint Michael was seen in Poland before the victory against the Lithuanians, which was obtained without a single Pole being killed, makes it credible that he presides over my Poland, as history testifies; hence, a basilica was finally built to him in Lublin. What of the fact that this vast kingdom extends towards the North, and from there, according to the pronouncement of Scripture, comes evil; that is, the greatest part of the <term>Alastores</term> <gloss>avenging spirits</gloss> are stabled there. Hence Nicephorus Gregoras writes that the Chaldeans consider Hades to be the prince of the furthest and adjacent earthly inheritance, which fell to him by lot <note>original: "τῆς ἐσχάτης καὶ περιγείου λήξεως ἀρχηγόν"</note>.

### XXIII. Among men, whoever is raised by the gift of fortune to opulence, and elevated up to the changeable dais of the kingdom and the hanging tribunal, rarely allows access and dwells with far removed witnesses in certain inner chambers of his dignity, says Apuleius in his *On the God of Socrates*.

And that the person of the King among the Persians was hidden under the guise of majesty, Justin is a witness, book 1, page 10, and Herodotus <note>original: "κλει."</note>, a custom they seem to have received from the Chaldeans; for among them, Ninus, the son of Semiramis, content with the empire elaborated by his parents, laid aside the studies of war, and, as if he had changed sex with his mother, he was rarely seen by men and grew old in a crowd of women. His successors also followed this example and gave responses to the nations through intermediaries: Justin, in the aforementioned place, page 4. They, of course, indulged only in the pleasures of the body, and especially those that are more than others immersed in matter, which the sense of touch and taste provides, and they led a life not unlike that of a sea squirt. Much more rightly, Emperor Leo, *Tactica*, chapter 16, section 21, page 245, says: those who are procrastinating and inaccessible, and who command their servants to beat away those approaching in such a way, reasonably miss out on many and great things. Nor is there reason for Apuleius, in the same place, to say that familiarity breeds contempt, and that rarity itself confers admiration upon things; let us hear Synesius, *Oration on Kingship*, page 20, arguing as Petavius translates: *No one has yet looked down upon the sun, although what is it that is seen more frequently?* Therefore, the King, if he is to be true, and otherwise cannot...

### XXX.

Nor is it an obstacle that in this life the Church is subject to great
tribulations and is disfigured by many scandals, and is still weak, carrying about many signs of guilt; wherefore it has need of constant prayer, as witnessed by Psalm 32, verse 6, and concerning which it is said in the Lord’s Prayer, Matthew 6, verse 12: "forgive us our debts." For it is adorned with the remission of sins, with the Son of God sanctifying Himself for it (John 17, verse 19), and covering its remaining filth by His own merit, applying His own righteousness to it, and bestowing upon it the Holy Spirit, who kindles new light and life in the hearts of the faithful. This adornment is that gilded garment in which, according to Psalm 45, verse 10, the queen stands at the right hand of this king; and it is a glory which the same Psalm affirms, in verse 14, to be internal and not visible to human eyes.

### XXXI.

But other members are called rotten and dead, and they are like arid and sterile trees (Ezekiel 20, verse 47); a fruitless fig tree <term>συκῆ ἄκαρπος</term> <gloss>barren fig tree</gloss>, having nothing except leaves alone (Matthew 21, verse 19); foolish virgins who, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them (Matthew 25, verse 2); tares, and children and seed of the Devil (Matthew 13, verse 38; Genesis 3, verse 15); indeed, men not reborn nor sanctified, even if they agree concerning the doctrine regarding the foundation. For they live without repentance and faith, nor are they enlivened and governed by the spirit of Christ, even if they dwell in the external society of the pious. Yet, who would call those in whom Christ does nothing members of Christ and the Church, unless they be dead ones?

### XXXII.

But if they are not only secure hypocrites, but also dissent from the foundation and doctrine of truth, and become either defenders or approvers of false doctrine that overturns the foundation, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3, verse 5), and if they stubbornly persist in those manifest errors, condemned by the judgment of the true Church according to the norm of the Prophetic and Apostolic writings, then we must hold them not even as dead members, but entirely as <term>ἀναθέμασι</term> <gloss>anathemas/accursed ones</gloss> <pb n="15"/> and blasphemers, and we assert that they are outside the Church, even if they dare to arrogate to themselves the title and name of the Church, which indeed the <term>Pontificij</term> <gloss>Papists</gloss> diligently do. Because it is written, Galatians 1, verses 8 and 9: "If anyone preaches another Gospel, let him be <term>ἀναθέμα ἔστω</term> <gloss>anathema/accursed</gloss>."

### XXXIII.

That the saints may also have some errors, however, which do not overturn the articles of faith (for some build upon the foundation gold, silver, and precious stones; others wood, hay, and stubble, as witnessed by Paul in 1 Corinthians 1, verse 12), is manifest from the example of the Apostles, in whom, before and after the resurrection—even though they had seen before them the beginnings of new and eternal life and the restoration of our nature in the glorified body of Christ—there was such darkness and weakness that they still dreamed that the Kingdom of the Messiah would be political (Acts 1, verse 6), and many wished for Levitical worship to be retained (Acts 15, verse 5).

### XXXIIII.

And the arrogance and <term>φιλαυτία</term> <gloss>self-love</gloss> with which many labor is all too blind and unhappy, if we think that there is no infirmity in us, that we are ignorant of nothing, but that we are perfect and omniscient. For it is very true what Paul says in 1 Corinthians 13, verse 9: "We know in part, and we prophesy in part." And verse 12: "Now we see through a glass and in a riddle."

### XXXV.

But the pious, and those who are teachable, when admonished, return to the way, just as it is evident that the Apostles eventually cast aside their dreams about the corporal kingdom of the Messiah and the necessity of circumcision and other Levitical rites, having received the Holy Spirit, whom they did not contradict against their conscience and so many great testimonies of truth, as the stubborn Jews did.

### XXXVI.

Nor indeed, by differing from the Church in the manner described, do we dream of some Platonic <term>Idea</term> <gloss>archetypal form</gloss> or city existing nowhere on earth, and which consists only in the image of the mind, nor do we judge it to wander in the shadows among <term>Andabatas</term> <gloss>blindfolded gladiators</gloss>.</translation>

<summary>This passage explores the distinction between the true, sanctified Church and those who are spiritually dead or apostate, emphasizing that while the Church contains imperfect saints, it does not include those who reject the fundamental doctrines of Christ.</summary>
<keywords>Ecclesiology, true Church, remission of sins, anathema, Papists, Levitical rites, doctrine of Christ</keywords>

## Q. III.

### *Does quantitative number apply to Intelligences?*

The substances that theologians call Angels, metaphysicians name Intelligences. And it is debated here regarding them: whether a quantitative number can be attributed to them. We stand firmly on the side of the negative, using this shield: Where there is no quantity, there is no quantitative number. In Intelligences, there is no quantity. Therefore. Do you doubt the minor premise? You do well: for always to doubt is always to inquire into a greater truth. But do you oppose it? Oppose, provided you do not overcome it. For does quantity not belong only to material and corporeal things? Do you deny it? You strike against philosophical principles; you rise up against Aristotle himself; against truth itself. Look at the species of quantity: the continuous is that whose parts are joined by some common boundary; discrete, on the contrary, are those whose parts are neither joined nor fitted together by any such boundary, as Aristotle states in his book of Categories on quantity. But where, I ask, are there any parts in Intelligences? If these existed, they would certainly make the very substance of the Angels either partible or divisible, they would certainly give the Intelligences themselves an extension of parts, they would certainly consist of body, and they would certainly participate in matter along with form, all of which are absurd. I add this also: Quantitative number is classified among the common sensibles, as Aristotle states in book 2 of *On the Soul*, chapter 6, thesis 64. If, therefore, Intelligences are sensible, they must be perceived by the senses. Otherwise, with the removal of the thing that falls under the senses, it is necessary that the sense itself be removed. But sense does not exist except in a body, and it operates around bodies, as Aristotle states in his book of Categories on quantity. Yet who, gifted with sound reason, has ever said that Angels are bodies? Therefore, a quantitative number ought not to be attributed to them either. You infer that quantity, although not predicamental, is nevertheless given as intelligible in <pb n="10"/>Angels, so that our intellect might conceive one thing in them which is not another? You proceed poorly. For as things are, so are they conceived, which is the distinction that exists between the divine and the human intellect. Indeed, the divine intellect makes things conform to its own concept; the human, however, is itself conformed to the things. How, therefore, will you be able to form quantity for yourself, where there is no quantity at all? How will you be able to conceive one part distinct from another, where there are absolutely no parts given, and why therefore should there be distinct ones? Certainly, when you conceive a thing in this way, your intellect represents to you not the thing, but a figment of the brain and imagination.

## Q. IV.

### *Are there five intellectual habits?*

This question is taken from book 6 of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, where the Philosopher discourses quite prolixly on intellectual habits. It must be noted above all that these habits are twofold: some are instrumental, which serve the principal ones as ministers, and these are Grammar, Rhetoric, Poetics, and Logic; others are principal, concerning which the present question is proposed. We have said with the Philosopher that they are five in number, namely *intelligence, scientific knowledge, wisdom, prudence*, and *art*; we recognize neither more nor fewer. If there are more, I do not see by what argument those who are pleased with them are led, unless perhaps they classify the aforementioned instrumental habits among the principal ones, or comprehend them under the term Art. But who is so blind that he does not see the distinction between both types of habits? Or who is so utterly abandoned by all thought,</translation>

<keywords>Intelligences, Angels, quantity, intellectual habits, Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics</keywords>

For the passion of CHRIST was efficacious through faith before it existed. Compare Hebrews 13, verse 8. Finally, regarding the fifth point: that will be made manifest from a weighing of the sayings in Genesis 22, verse 16, Galatians 3, verses 16 and 22. You will say: 1 John 1, verse 17, *The Law was given by Moses, but grace was delivered by CHRIST.* The answer is: the consequence from the inclusion of one to the exclusion of the other is not valid. Here, at least, the office of Moses the Legislator is compared with the benefit of CHRIST the Savior. You will say: 2 Romans 16, verse 25, *The Gospel is said to have been hidden from eternal times, but manifested at the time of the Apostles.* The answer is: it is nonetheless made known through the Prophetic Scriptures. Therefore, it was not simply unknown, but only in respect of clarity, knowledge, exhibition, revelation, and promulgation. Certainly, therefore, the Fathers of the Old Testament possessed the doctrine of the Gospel, although not as clearly as we do in the New Testament. But they had it (1.) in the promises, because the promises concerning CHRIST were made to them; (2.) in the prophecies of the prophets; (3.) in the sacrifices and Levitical <pb n="13"/>types, which sustained the shadow of the antitype of the body of CHRIST.

## Question IX.
### Is CHRIST true man?

Entirely. For whoever is the seed of the woman, he is also truly and really man, <term>homoousios</term> <gloss>of the same substance</gloss> with our nature. But CHRIST is... and so forth. Therefore, CHRIST is true man. The entire Gospel history proves this very thing not only evidently; but moreover, it is clear 1. From the various names and epithets which are attributed to CHRIST in Holy Scripture. For He is called man in 1 Timothy 2, verse 5. Compare Luke 23, verse 47. <term>genomenos ek gynaikos</term> <gloss>made of a woman</gloss> (Galatians 4, verse 4). Son of Man (Hebrews 1, verse 14 <note>Note: The original text cites Hebrews 1:14, though this is likely a typographical error for Hebrews 2:14 or a similar reference to the Son of Man</note>). Made flesh (John 1, verse 14). Manifested in the flesh (1 Timothy 3, verse 16). Having assumed the seed of Abraham (Hebrews 2, 13). <term>genomenos ek spermatos David kata sarka</term> <gloss>made of the seed of David according to the flesh</gloss> (Romans 1, verse 3). 2. From the definition of man: to whomever the definition applies, to him the defined also applies. But the definition of man applies to CHRIST. Therefore, etc. The minor premise is proved: Because CHRIST was truly a rational animal consisting of body and soul. 3. From the proper human operations and affections which apply to CHRIST, for example, becoming a participant of flesh and blood (Hebrews 2, verse 14). Being born of a Virgin (Luke 1, verse 31). Being born of a woman and made subject to the Law (Galatians 4, verse 4). Having suffered and been crucified (Acts 3, verse 14). Having been seen by the eyes of the Apostles and touched by their hands (1 John 1, verse 2). Since, therefore, we see that all these things are not idioms of the Deity, which in itself is neither born of a Virgin, nor obeys the Law, nor suffers, nor is crucified, nor is seen, nor is palpated, it is absolutely necessary that, to preserve the truth of these statements, the <term>Logos</term> <gloss>Word</gloss> be said to be united with a nature that is visible, touchable, and so forth, not through a mere <term>parastasis</term> <gloss>juxtaposition/presence</gloss>, but through a <term>koinonia</term> <gloss>communion/participation</gloss> of Himself.
</translation>

From pharmacy, metallics are touted by many, which, as they are more noble, should restore almost every sick person to health, much less one with hectic fever. J. They melt it, pulverize it, extract it with spirit of salt, and abstract it to the consistency of oil. This they instill into one drachm of pulverized pearl salt. <pb n="19"/>OF MARRIED PRIESTS

In the name of the Lord, Amen. Let it be known to all and singular who inspect these presents, and significantly to those whom the business written below concerns, might concern, or could affect in any way in the future. That in the year from the Nativity of the Lord one thousand five hundred and twenty-four, in the twelfth indiction, on the Tuesday which was the fifth day of the month of April, in the first year of the pontificate of our most holy father in Christ and lord, Lord Clement VII, by divine providence Pope. In the presence of me, the notary public, and the witnesses subscribed below, specifically called and requested for this purpose, there appeared in person the honorable Lord <term>Wolfgang Sculteti</term> <gloss>Schultheiß</gloss>, a presbyter of Strasbourg, in his own name and also in the name of the venerable lords <term>Matthäus Zell</term> from Keysersberg, pastor of St. Lawrence, <term>Anton Firn</term>, pastor of St. Thomas, <term>Johannes Nubling</term>, chaplain of the chapel of St. Erhard, all churches of Strasbourg, and <term>Lucas Hackfurt</term>, <term>Konrad Spaczinger</term>, and <term>Alexander</term>, formerly a member of the <term>Order of St. John</term> <gloss>Hospitallers</gloss>, all presbyters, who were likewise appearing in person before me, the notary, and the witnesses subscribed below. Having and holding in his hands a certain paper document of appeal or provocation, which with the spirit and intention of provoking and appealing, protesting, seeking <term>apostoli</term> <gloss>letters of dismissal/appeal documents</gloss>, and causing other things to be done as he said were contained more fully in the same document, he delivered and assigned to me, the notary public subscribed below, of the tenor prescribed. That no violence be done, etc.
After the interposition of which provocation, appeal, and <pb n="20"/>petition for <term>apostoli</term> <gloss>letters of appeal</gloss> from the paper document, the said Lord <term>Wolfgang Sculteti</term>, in his own name and in the name of the aforementioned appealing principals, requested of me, the notary public subscribed below, that one or more public instruments be made and drawn up for him, as many as might be necessary for him or for any of them. These things were done at Strasbourg in the parochial court of the parish of St. Lawrence, Strasbourg, under the year of the Lord, indiction, day, month, hour, and pontificate as stated above, present there as witnesses to the premises, and called and requested for the same, the honorable and discreet men Lord <term>Wilhelm Beltinger</term>, assistant in divine matters, and <term>Melchior Schell</term>, sacristan of the church of St. Lawrence, Strasbourg.

And I, <term>Michael Schwencker</term> of Gernspach, of the Diocese of Speyer, notary public by sacred imperial authority. Because I was present in person, together with the aforementioned witnesses, to all and singular these things while they were done and transpired as is set forth above, and I saw and heard them being done thus. Therefore, I have taken them from there into a note, fashioned, published, and reduced into this public form this present public instrument, faithfully written by the hand of another at my instruction. And I have signed and subscribed it with my usual and customary sign, name, and surname.

<note>A circular library stamp of the National and University Library of Strasbourg obscures part of the final paragraph.</note>

In faith and testimony of all and the premises, I am requested and required.

->Strasbourg, from the house of <term>Wolfgang Cephaleus</term> <gloss>Köpfel</gloss><-
->near the horse market, 12 April<-
->YEAR 1524.<-

</translation>

<pb n="23"/> in the ancient contests of Greece, garlands made of parsley were customarily awarded to the victors. Pindar is a witness to such use of parsley in the Isthmian and Nemean games. Aeneas, too, when brought to Italy, built and arranged a table spread with parsley on the ground <note>original: "libro 1. Antiquitatum Romanarum"</note>. Similarly, Horace confirms that parsley was used for garlands in celebrating the birthday of Maecenas <note>original: "Carminum IV. Ode 11."</note>.

§. 18. Furthermore, it is reported and testified with one voice that garlands woven from flowers were placed upon the dead: *Xenophon in the 5th book of the Expedition of Cyrus, the commentator of Euripides in the Phoenissae, Lucian in his dialogue On Mourning; and among the Church Fathers, Justin Martyr in his Second Apology, and Clement of Alexandria in the Instructor, book 2, chapter 8*. Moreover, *Sophocles in Electra, Plutarch in Numa, and Tranquillus [Suetonius] in Nero, chapter 53* indicate that burial mounds were sprinkled with flowers. For they carried fronds and flowers to the sepulchers, and they scattered flowers at funerals, a custom which the early Christians in the age of Prudentius did not disapprove of, and which they retained for some time, even though in the first centuries of the Christian era, they not only did not use garlands at sepulchers

<pb n="24"/> but also rejected them out of a righteous hatred for the rites of the pagans, as is evident from *Tertullian* and *Minutius Felix*, who inveighed against garlands and wreaths as empty and impious gifts of the givers.

§. 19. It remains to be discussed, and I do not think it should be passed over, what is written regarding the *hyacinth inscribed with letters*, which had a use in decorating tombs with every kind of flower. I consider it all the less to be omitted because the hyacinth inscribed with letters is celebrated in the records of the ancients, and especially in those of the poets. It is termed by *Theocritus* in the Doric dialect *grapta*, that is, "inscribed," from which *Vergilius* drew in his own way, naming them "inscribed flowers," or those marked with certain letters, whose shape is depicted and noted as A I. This mark belongs to *Ajax*, the bravest of the Greek leaders, or kings, from whose blood the hyacinth flower is said in the myths of Greece to have been born. Others, however, imagine it arose from the blood of the boy whom *Apollo* loved, as found in *Pliny, book 21, chapter 11* and *Lucian* in his *Dialogues of the Gods*. This hyacinth the poets [celebrate] in their monuments

### XXVII.

Item: if he does not administer justice to the Vassal, he is narrowed by the same loss.

### XXVIII.

And regularly, if the lord commits a felony against the Vassal, from which, if the Vassal had perpetrated it, he would lose the fief, he loses the ownership of the feudal property.

### XXIX.

However, since mention is made by us primarily concerning that loss of a fief which deprives the Vassal, it is not inconvenient to subjoin here that there are some cases in which the Vassal does not lose the fief, although the fidelity that joins both the Vassal and the Lord may not intervene and be performed.

### XXX.

As for example, if the lord of the fief is excommunicated, banished, a condemned heretic, guilty of high treason, etc.

### XXXI.

Item: if [the lord commands] against honesty, possibility, or another immoderate command

<pb n="17"/>

the Lord commands to be done by the Vassal, the Vassal is freed from obedience.

### XXXII.

With fiefs lost for various reasons, it is a question: Do fiefs open to the Lord in every way and without distinction? Or, according to the variety of causes, sometimes to the lord, sometimes to others? Which is the truer [view].

### XXXIII.

It is asked whether there is a free power of resigning a fief, or whether it should depend upon the consent of the lord? Which seems uncivil: for it is permitted to renounce gains.

### XXXIIII.

Therefore, when the fief is resigned, it returns, in the case where it is new, to the Lord, notwithstanding that harm may happen to the children thereby; but in the case where it is paternal or ancient, it devolves to the male children, or to the <term>agnati</term> <gloss>relatives through the male line</gloss>, upon their failure.

### XXXV.

A brother resigning a fief in favor of a brother, to whom it is afterward assigned, and who dies without heirs, is not excluded from the fief.

and glassy, poured forth in abundance, in which whatever settles is commendable, or by an abscess worthy of mention, or by the bowels discharging mucous and bloody material, and suddenly bursting forth, and vomitings which do not occur in a foul manner, leading to a <term>crisis</term> <gloss>a decisive point in the course of a disease</gloss>. That the resolution happens through hemorrhage of the nostrils, as <term>Galen</term> recounts in <term>To Glaucon, Book 1, Chapter 15</term>, is indicated by headache, which did not set in immediately from the beginning as some accident of the illness, but during the disturbance which occurs before the crisis: delirium, difficult breathing, a retracted hypochondrium, and the neck becoming aggravated along with the head. Explanation of the text.
The inscription of the book *On Memory and Recollection* indicates its subject matter: the chapter is completed in two parts.

First part
He treats of memory.
I. To remember and to recollect are not the same: for those who are good at remembering, like the gifted, are not good at recollecting.
II. Memory is not of the future or the present, but of the past: for of the future there is hope or opinion; of the present, sensation; but memory is of a past act, which is neither sensation nor opinion.
III. Memory is a passion of something when time has passed.
<margin>Corollary: Supposition</margin>
IV. Only those who know time remember.
V. Understanding does not occur without a <term>phantasma</term> <gloss>mental image</gloss>, and therefore the intellect does not understand without continuous time.
VI. Memory is a passion of the primary sensitive [power]. He proves this because it is its [the power's] role to know time; therefore, its role is to remember: for sense knows time through motion, and magnitude. Hence, he admits memory to be an attribute <note>original: "per accidens"</note> of the intellect itself, insofar as it receives a mental image from the senses.
VII. The statements are proven; because even those who do not understand, such as brute animals, remember.
VIII. Not all animals possess memory.
IX. Although the species <note>original: "species" (an image or mental representation)</note> of a thing may be present, memory is not of that species, but of the absent thing: he proves this because if a painting or seal represents a past thing, so does a species in the imagination. He proves this firstly because those existing in great motion do not remember, such as the drunk or the infirm, because the species are impeded. 2. Children do not remember because the species are impeded due to flux. 3. The aged do not remember well because, due to excessive dryness, they do not receive the species well. 4. Because those who understand quickly retain and remember poorly.
X. Memory is not of that species, because then it would be of the present.
XI. It seems that memory is of the present, because memory is of the sense itself; now, sense is of the present. 2. Because the species in the imagination is like a painting on a wall; now, a painting is present to the one seeing it. 3. If the common sense can be of the absent, then so can the external sense.
XII. He solves the aforesaid; because although the species as a certain thing may be present in the thing, yet as it is representative of another, it is thus of an absent thing; he extends this concerning the mode of representing of the species as in the text.
XIII. Memory increases and is preserved through frequent meditation: for the soul is made more capable if it remembers many times.

Second part concerning recollection.
XIV. Recollection is not memory, nor is it to sense or understand something anew: according to what is proven; because memory does not occur when one understands or senses something anew; therefore, neither does recollection. The antecedent is clear because memory requires an interruption of past time; and thus memory presupposes that an act or habit existed beforehand. But it differs from memory because in recollection, forgetfulness intervenes.

XV. To remember or to recollect is not to know something again, but to know that one had known or seen this before.
XVI. The mode of recollecting occurs through this, that just as one motion of the soul happens after another, so one apprehends one thing after another. And thus when we recollect, we are moved from one act to another by meditating through a similar or contrary thing.
XVII. Why do we sometimes recollect easily from a long time ago, and not what happened yesterday or the day before? He answers that this is because recollection occurs through an apprehension of something that avails for apprehending.
XVIII. First corollary: we recollect from that principle from which what is to be recollected began. Second corollary: we recollect things that are well-ordered more easily than those that are disordered.
XIX. Why can one who wishes to recollect sometimes not do so, and then, not seeking, recollect spontaneously? He answers that the one wishing has many apprehensions that do not avail for that recollection, and spontaneously afterward comes an apprehension that does avail for apprehending.
XX. One wishing to recollect should think of the places in which he was.
XXI. The best mode of recollecting is through division, such as "that week I was there," by dividing through days I will easily find what I did from one to another.
XXII. Why do those who have the principle of recollection not recollect? He answers because that principle is indifferent to many things.
XXIII. Why do we sometimes recollect defectively? It is answered that just as in natural things, so it happens also in voluntary ones.
XXIIII. Time contributes to recollecting, such that one knows past time to be past; yet both memory and recollection occur without certain time, although things are understood in proportion to time.
XXV. It happens to err in recollection, and this on the part of the thing and on the part of time.
XXVI. Memory differs from recollection because although animals other than man remember, they do not recollect; the reason for which is because recollection occurs with discourse.
XXVII. Recollection is a bodily passion. The first sign of this is that many wishing to recollect and being unable to are troubled, especially the melancholic; and it is as in the angry, whose motions cannot easily be stilled; and because of strong imagination, we do not cease from the memory of certain things.
XXVIII. The second sign is that those having grosser upper parts remember poorly. The third sign is that children and the elderly are poor at remembering; children because of excessive motion, the elderly because of a lack of motion.

## Single Question
### Whether memory and recollection differ:
### Article I.

Note I. That we may run through in a true order this mode of remembering: when one sees (for example), then one species and likeness of the king is imprinted on the soul, as a seal imprints its form in wax; that species is reserved in the soul; and he who has seen can think about it, and then he is said to remember. This being supposed, know that there is a way of receiving memory: for the memorative power itself is called memory; similarly, the organ reserving the species is called memory; and fourthly, memory is used for the act of remembering; and thus we speak here of memory. And thus there is a twofold memory, i.e., intellectual and sensitive. And for memory, six things are required: three representational and three represented, according to Buridan. Represented in the prior example are the king seen, the vision, and the past time in which he saw; it is necessary that the soul have the species, images, and likenesses of all these if it wishes to remember.
Note II. That foundation being laid, the difference between remembering, recollecting, and forgetting can easily stand. For if species are strongly imprinted and reserved totally in the soul, so that upon immediately noticing, they at once move the power to the repeated cognition of the thing, and through these species memory is made; or these species are weakly imprinted, or lost by the duration of time or another cause, and corrupted and totally abolished and removed from the corporeal power of the species, and then we are said to forget; or they are only diminished, not fully lost, but confused and fragile, still clinging a little in the memorative organ, not sufficient by themselves to move the power unless with the apprehension of another and with aid, by which it is elevated and actuated; and then through these species we recollect. Take this symbol: you saw a painting on a wall; after an interval you return, where part of the painting is erased, and part remains; now from the part of the painting remaining, you discourse toward the knowledge of the erased part: thus it happens in recollection. Corollary: Recollection does not presuppose total forgetting, but partial; but re-learning <note>original: "readdiscentia"</note> presupposes total forgetting. Corollary: Thus Averroes is to be understood, that recollection is interrupted memory, i.e., partial forgetting; this is the mind of the Brussels and Ifennach schools. Add, however, that generally, memory extends itself to recollection.
Note III. From these, the definition of memory given by Aristotle is clear. Memory is a passion or habit of something when time has passed; it is a judgment of past acts through the mode of pastness. Doctors do not agree here as to whose power memory is; Aristotle concludes it is a passion of the primary sensitive, i.e., the common sense. Avicenna, *Physics* book 6, part 5, chapter 6, denies that memory is in the intellect. William of Ockham, q. 12 of the fourth book, denies memory is in the intellect; he is moved by this, that for memory, complex knowledge is required, but sense does not know complexly. Also, because by remembering, the power is reflected upon its own act, but no sense reflects upon its own act. More on these in Scotus, dist. 45 of the fourth, q. 3. But Gregory of Rimini, dist. 2, q. 2, art. 2, dub. 3, correctly objects because, first, memory is the common sense of sensibles, and per accidens or consequently it is in the intellect; yet the memory of intelligibles is primarily in the intellect. William of Ockham does not stand, because Gregory and Cameracensis, q. 3 of the first, clearly show sensitive knowledge to be complex, of which [I have spoken] in the prologue of logic. Secondly, although the external sense is not reflexive, because no one sees himself seeing, yet the common sense is indeed reflexive upon external senses, because it feels itself seeing. Wherefore we have posited a twofold memory: sensitive and intellectual.
Note IV. From this, the definition of recollection is clear: Recollection is the resumption of knowledge lapsed from memory from some principle retained in memory; take this as in the second note. It is a consequence that one wishing to recollect must have recourse to some rememorative principle, from which another might follow in order, so that thus he may find what is sought. And it does not matter whether it be a natural order or a habitual one, just as when I cannot say the verses of a psalm or a proverb unless I recite some preceding ones. And thus there is a twofold memory, i.e., intellectual and sensitive. And for memory, six things are required: three representational and three represented, according to Buridan. Represented in the prior example are the king seen, the vision, and the past time in which he saw; it is necessary that the soul have the species, images, and likenesses of all these if it wishes to remember.
Note II. That foundation being laid, the difference between remembering, recollecting, and forgetting can easily stand. For if species are strongly imprinted and reserved totally in the soul, so that upon immediately noticing, they at once move the power to the repeated cognition of the thing, and through these species memory is made; or these species are weakly imprinted, or lost by the duration of time or another cause, and corrupted and totally abolished and removed from the corporeal power of the species, and then we are said to forget; or they are only diminished, not fully lost, but confused and fragile, still clinging a little in the memorative organ, not sufficient by themselves to move the power unless with the apprehension of another and with aid, by which it is elevated and actuated; and then through these species we recollect. Take this symbol: you saw a painting on a wall; after an interval you return, where part of the painting is erased, and part remains; now from the part of the painting remaining, you discourse toward the knowledge of the erased part: thus it happens in recollection. Corollary: Recollection does not presuppose total forgetting, but partial; but re-learning <note>original: "readdiscentia"</note> presupposes total forgetting. Corollary: Thus Averroes is to be understood, that recollection is interrupted memory, i.e., partial forgetting; this is the mind of the Brussels and Ifennach schools. Add, however, that generally, memory extends itself to recollection.
Note III. From these, the definition of memory given by Aristotle is clear. Memory is a passion or habit of something when time has passed; it is a judgment of past acts through the mode of pastness. Doctors do not agree here as to whose power memory is; Aristotle concludes it is a passion of the primary sensitive, i.e., the common sense. Avicenna, *Physics* book 6, part 5, chapter 6, denies that memory is in the intellect. William of Ockham, q. 12 of the fourth book, denies memory is in the intellect; he is moved by this, that for memory, complex knowledge is required, but sense does not know complexly. Also, because by remembering, the power is reflected upon its own act, but no sense reflects upon its own act. More on these in Scotus, dist. 45 of the fourth, q. 3. William of Ockham does not stand, because Gregory and Cameracensis, q. 3 of the first, clearly show sensitive knowledge to be complex, of which [I have spoken] in the prologue of logic. Secondly, although the external sense is not reflexive, because no one sees himself seeing, yet the common sense is indeed reflexive upon external senses, because it feels itself seeing. Wherefore we have posited a twofold memory: sensitive and intellectual.
Note IV. From this, the definition of recollection is clear: Recollection is the resumption of knowledge lapsed from memory from some principle retained in memory; take this as in the second note. It is a consequence that one wishing to recollect must have recourse to some rememorative principle, from which another might follow in order, so that thus he may find what is sought.
