<pb n="11"/> Civil law may originate from statutes, plebiscites, decrees of the Senate, edicts of Princes, and the authority of the learned (Digest, On Justice and Law, Law 7, in the beginning). It is not sufficiently certain from which of these parts our action draws its birth. That it is free from doubt that its words and the solemn formula, which it was necessary to propose in ancient times, must be referred to the learned in the law, is argued by the Digest, On the Origin of Law, Law 2, paragraph 6.

### §. VII.

The proximate efficient cause, or foundation, is the right established in another's property, or servitude, and that both personal and real; or rather the harm and injury which is inflicted when one person strives either to deprive another entirely of the exercise of a servitude belonging to him, or at least acts as an impediment so that he cannot exercise his right quietly. For since an action is a complaint (Digest, On Summoning to Court, final law), and no one can complain unless he suffers something unjust which he desires to be corrected by a judge, it follows that the foundation of the Confessory action is not so much the right in another's property itself, as it is the injury inflicted concerning that right.

### §. VIII.

The person who may proceed with this action is he who, while having a right in another's property, whether competent to himself or to his thing, is either entirely deprived of its exercise or at least impeded in its quiet use. For just as he who is an owner, lacking the exercise of his dominant power while another is possessor, vindicates a corporeal thing, similarly it is intact for him to use a Confessory action, for whom the exercise of the right in another's property is either completely intercepted or at least its quiet use is blocked by the deed of another. Since, however, <pb n="12"/> servitudes are either of persons or of things (Digest, On Usufruct, Law 1), it is manifest that this action is given as much to him who has a right in another's property through himself as to him who has it through his own thing. Therefore, when <term>Ulpianus</term> <gloss>a Roman jurist</gloss> says (Digest, If a servitude is vindicated, Law 2, § 1 and Law 6, § 3) that the action is competent to no one other than the owner of the estate, it is clear that he is speaking only of Real servitudes, since in personal ones, the right in another's property suffices without an estate. But if there are several owners of the dominant estate, each vindicates it in full, not for a part (Digest, If a servitude is vindicated, Law 6, § 4). It is not given to the <term>USUMFRUCTUARIUS</term> <gloss>usufructuary, one having the right to use and enjoy the fruits of another's property</gloss> (Digest, If a usufruct is sought, Law 1, pr. and Law 5, § 1), for even though he also has a right in another's property, because the dominant estate does not belong to him by right of ownership, he cannot therefore vindicate the servitude competent to that estate, yet he can seek it against those impeding the usufruct. This, however, must be understood regarding the direct <term>vindicatio</term> <gloss>claim of ownership or right</gloss>; for that he can proceed with a useful action is declared by (Digest, On Remissions, Law 1, § 4). Although others interpret it regarding the usufructuary who, as if a procurator for the owner of the property, vindicates the servitude in his name; yet others prefer to resolve this conflict by thinking that the opinion of <term>Julianus</term> <gloss>a Roman jurist</gloss> (in the aforementioned Law 1, § 4) reported by <term>Ulpianus</term> was rejected by <term>Marcellus</term> (in Law 1, If a usufruct is sought) and <term>Ulpianus</term> (in Law 5, § "whether"). Furthermore, since it happens that he who has a right in another's property is either entirely deprived of the exercise of his right, or indeed exercises it but not securely and quietly, it results that this action is given to the owner whether he is possessing or not possessing (Digest, If a servitude is vindicated, Law 6, § 1), to the latter so that he may recover lost possession, to the former so that he may exercise the servitude securely (arguing from Digest, If a usufruct is sought, Law 5, § last).</translation>

<summary>This passage details the legal foundations and the parties eligible to bring a Confessory action, distinguishing between real and personal servitudes and the roles of the owner and the usufructuary in seeking legal redress.</summary>
<keywords>Confessory action, servitudes, Roman Law, usufruct, ownership, dominant estate, legal injury</keywords>

Since the education of the youth is the foundation of the entire Republic, a careful concern for education, as for the foundation itself, prohibits and prevents the structure built upon it from developing cracks, threatening ruin, being shaken entirely, or collapsing completely. Whoever has not seen or heard the public specimens of such great and provident care for the Schools published by the most Amplest Senate must be considered to be in deep ignorance of affairs in <term>Vratislavia</term> <gloss>Wrocław</gloss>. I am not unaware of what was done six years ago at our Magdalenean School. While in other places things were either becoming sparse or people were bitterly lamenting their own emptiness, ours was seen to be built up and expanded more highly and amply, not only the Scholastic building—with added stories exhibiting a pleasant and agreeable third heating room <note>a hypocaust or warming room for the school</note> as well as rooms for the students <term>Convictorum</term> <gloss>boarders/students living in a college</gloss>, facing South and North—but the number of students was also seen to be increasing, to our delight. I will not mention other perceived experiments of care regarding the School, among which you might not undeservedly count the convenient separation of the lower ranks: by which it was brought about that the students could not obstruct one another or the teachers, and that a confusion of languages or voices would not avert the ears or minds of some from the study of letters, as those two Emperors, Theodosius and Valentinian, say. (Code, Book 11, Title 18.) I shall say here, or touch upon only lightly, those things which, long deliberated, were recently and very prudently and usefully established concerning the two principal Schools, namely our Magdalenean one. There, one truly perceives matters concerning the divine and the human, to use the word of Plautus. They very piously instruct at the beginning of the Constitutions that divine worship and prayers for the health of the public Schools should be religiously continued no less in the public assemblies of the Temples than of the Schools: for all things are rightly and competently managed if the beginning of the matter is made decent and pleasing to **GOD**. (Novellae VI, Justinian, in the Preface to Epiphanius, Patriarch of Constantinople.) The human things, which are established, are committed for execution both to the civil Magistracy and to the order of Scholastic teachers. <pb n="10"/>19. But it is manifest that this reasoning concludes nothing other than that the Angels did not exist before the third day; it by no means proves they were created on it.
20. Since, therefore, none of these opinions rests on certain foundations, we conclude with Origen in Book 1 of <term>Περὶ ἀρχῶν</term> <gloss>On First Principles</gloss>:
> It is held in ecclesiastical preaching that there are certain Angels of GOD; but when these were created, it is not distinguished with sufficient clarity.

## APHORISM III.

->*Angels are spirits, intelligent and wise, good, holy, powerful, destined for the service of GOD, for the salvation of men.*<-

### I. EXPOSITION.

1. Since human language stammers when dealing with matters removed from the senses, let some description of the Angels—those most blessed minds, which are removed from the senses to the greatest degree—suffice for us, namely that which our aphorism has just provided.
2. It describes the Angels as they were from their first origin, and it establishes their <term>genus</term> <gloss>class/kind</gloss> as *Spirit*.
3. It attributes to them concrete <term>accidentia</term> <gloss>accidents/non-essential properties</gloss> or <term>qualitates</term> <gloss>qualities</gloss>, such as intelligence, wisdom, goodness, holiness, and power. We wish for these predicates to be understood restrictively and in their own kind, not absolutely. For as soon as you compare these to the spirituality, intelligence, goodness, etc., of GOD, there appears a difference as great as that which exists between the infinite and the finite, the essential and the accidental, the Creator and the created, the immutable and the mutable—in terms of holiness, goodness, and so forth.
4. *It reports their office to be twofold; one is considered with respect to GOD, the other with respect to men.*

->CONFIRMATION.<-

5. Scripture itself confirms this nature of the Angels, and indeed that they *are Spirits*. 1. By simply calling them *Spirits*, in Psalm 104:4 and Hebrews 1:14 <note>The Latin text cites "the last verse."</note>: Are they not all (the Angels) ministering spirits? 2. By denying them *matter*, in that they do not have flesh and blood, Ephesians 6:12; nor flesh and bones, Luke 24:39.
6. II. It attributes *concreated qualities* to them: And the woman of Tekoa says that *the Angels are intelligent*: My lord, she says, is wise according to the wisdom of the Angel of GOD, to know everything that is on earth, 2 Samuel 14:20.
7. They are called *good* by the Creator Himself. For GOD saw everything that He had made, and behold, they were all very good, Genesis 1:31. The Angels, however, were made by GOD, as seen above in Aphorism 1. Therefore, they are also good, by the goodness of creation, as theologians like to speak.
8. They are called *holy*, Luke 9:26, Acts 10:22.
9. They are *powerful* in virtue, Psalm 103:20: not to mention here the works of the Angels, which sufficiently demonstrate their power—those admirable works mentioned above in Aphorism 1, thesis 9—and the names of principalities, powers, virtues, and thrones, which they receive in Scripture.
10. III. The *office* which they perform with respect to GOD is the celebration of His name. For the Cherubim and Seraphim sing: Holy, Holy, Holy, etc., Isaiah 6:3. And the execution of His commands. Hence thousands of thousands serve Him, and ten times a hundred thousand stand before Him, Daniel 7:10. Psalm 103:20–21 speaks of both these offices.</translation>

<summary>The text concludes that the precise day of angelic creation remains unverified by scripture, then moves to define the nature of angels as spirits possessing created, non-divine qualities, divided into offices serving both God and humanity.</summary>
<keywords>Angels, Creation, Origen, On First Principles, Spiritual nature, Divine service, Theology</keywords>

For it does not follow from this that the cultivation of the Christian religion, which is diametrically opposed to paganism, is less necessary for the happiness of a Republic. For even if we should grant that the religion of the heathens was not only not harmful, but actually contributed no small measure of fortune to their Republics, it cannot therefore be concluded that that same religion rendered the Republics, of which we are speaking, truly happy. Nor do we deny that religion benefited the Romans and other nations greatly, yet we deny that paganism brought them any advantage at all.

XIX. Since it is incumbent upon the supreme Powers to preserve the true worship of God and to protect the people under true religion, and since protection often cannot be afforded without the aid of arms, those who govern can scarcely afford to lack the virtue of fortitude. *A Republic ought to be fortified and adorned not only by religion and justice but also by arms and military discipline,* according to Isaac Pontanus in *Florilegii*, ch. 3. Therefore, it is manifest that the expression is improper, yet it is said of the whole person on account of the other nature, to which these things are proper. For the <term>λόγος</term> <gloss>Word</gloss> was the Son in heaven before he was incarnate, so that the same <term>λόγος</term> <gloss>Word</gloss> descended from heaven to assume flesh; these things are attributed here to the Son of Man through communication, that is, to Christ the man, because he is also God: and the divine and human nature constitute the same person. Hence the predicates are exchanged, and it is said that God suffered and redeemed the Church with his own blood: and conversely, that Christ the man is in heaven, and "before Abraham was, I am," and similar things. *And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.*

He shows how the merit of the Son of God becomes useful to us, namely through his death and our faith, which firmly <pb n="196"/> apprehends that merit. He uses an argument from a similarity. He took the comparison from Moses, Numbers 21, concerning the bronze serpent, which, lifted up by the command of the Lord, saved those gazing upon it from the bites of the fiery serpents.

The correspondence is added by the Lord Christ himself, which shows how the parts correspond to the parts. The <term>antitypa</term> <gloss>antitypes</gloss> here are Christ and the serpent; the exaltation and death of Christ; gazing at the serpent and firmly apprehending Christ by faith. The bites of the serpents and the power of sin; this temporal life and eternal salvation. From this, a coherent and timely <term>allegoria</term> <gloss>allegory</gloss> is taken. First, the bronze serpent was instituted by the authority of God when matters were desperate among the Israelites: thus Christ was given as mediator when matters were desperate among us. For no one among men, or even among the Angels, was found suitable. Next, the bronze serpent cures those struck by serpents: Christ [cures] those struck by the serpent Satan, having been made a serpent of the serpent himself, as if you would say poison of poison. Thirdly, it benefits by sight alone; thus Christ cures us by faith alone. Fourthly, the mystery of the cross is manifest in the exaltation. Things that are lifted up are seen more easily and are of use to more people. Thus the merit of Christ is proposed in the open to all nations; he who, while walking, had already sanctified the earth, consecrates while hanging, and extending his hands, he calls together.

<margin>Num 21:8-9</margin>
<margin>Antitypes</margin>

<pb n="11"/>And with this constitution repealed, by the constitution of <term>Marcus Antoninus</term> <note>original: "Marci Antonini"</note>, a special praetor who is also called the tutelary <term>praetor</term> <gloss>magistrate</gloss> was appointed, so that for the rest, the praetor might provide guardians for those of senatorial rank after an inquiry, require security, and compel them to the administration. Paragraph 3 of this title, which constitution of Marcus, custom finally abolished, by which at Rome either the prefect of the city gave guardians, indeed for the sons of illustrious persons—Law 1, <term>Code on the guardianships and curators of illustrious persons</term> <gloss>original: "Codice de tutelis et curatoribus illustrium"</gloss>—or the praetor according to his jurisdiction; but in the provinces, the governors or magistrates [did so] by order of the governor. Paragraph 4 of this title, which custom <term>Justinian</term> <gloss>original: "Iustinianus"</gloss> later changed again, and transferred that right to the defenders of the cities together with the bishop of the same city or other magistrates. Paragraph 5 of this title, Law 30, <term>Code on Episcopal Hearing</term> <gloss>original: "Codice de Episcopali audientia"</gloss>; <term>Cuiacius</term> <gloss>a prominent French jurist</gloss> in the later notes on this.

Today, however, the ordinary magistrate of each place gives a guardian, and not only when the guardianship has ended, as in the civil law—Law 5, "If a guardian," <term>Code on the risk of guardians</term> <gloss>original: "Codice de periculo tutorum"</gloss>, paragraph "The end" of this title—but also yearly by the constitution of <term>Charles V</term> <gloss>original: "Caroli V"</gloss>, published in the year 1548, he demands an account from the guardians, to which the Canon law does not resist, <term>Clementina 1</term> <gloss>a book of canon law</gloss> "On religious houses," chapter 1, "On sick clerics." But by Saxon law, the nearer heirs demand an account every year. Book 1, <term>Landrecht</term> <gloss>Saxon regional law</gloss>, article 23; <term>Fachsius</term> <gloss>a jurist</gloss> difference 17; <term>Reinhardus</term> <gloss>a jurist</gloss> difference 7. (e) Because it is neither of imperial power nor of jurisdiction—Law 6, paragraph 2, "On guardianships," Law 23 at the end, "On the excuses of guardians"—but that of him alone to whom either the law, or a decree of the Senate, or the prince has granted it. The beginning of the Institutes of this title, Law 1, paragraph 2, Law 8, "On guardians and curators," Law 1, "On his office." A dissertation of the Doctors after the gloss to the said Law 6, while they attribute this to mixed power. Otherwise, <term>Muscornius</term> <gloss>a jurist</gloss> in his treatise on jurisdiction says it is sometimes of jurisdiction, sometimes of power. Otherwise, <term>Bellonus</term> <gloss>a jurist</gloss> 1, *Supputationes* 2, maintains it is of permission. (f) And therefore neither for the prodigal nor the madman, paragraph "Of madmen," "Who can give guardians by will," Pragmatic question 3, number 33, 63. Nor for the minor, in the said question, number 8, 10. Nor for the mute or the deaf. Law 1, paragraph "Mute," "On guardianships," which also, according to <term>Brunnus</term> <gloss>a jurist</gloss> in the said paragraph "Mute," holds for him who contracted such an infirmity after assuming the guardianship, for the reason [given in] the said paragraph "Mute." Nor for a cleric, in the chapter "Let them be denied" <note>original: "capite negentur"</note>, distinction 88, unless he wishes to undertake it of his own accord. Law "Generally," with the following <term>Authentica</term> <gloss>an excerpt from Justinian's novels</gloss>, <term>Code on bishops and clerics</term>. Nor for a slave, because he is held as dead by civil law, Law 32, <term>On the Rules of Law</term> <gloss>original: "de Regulis Juris"</gloss>. Nor for a debtor nor a creditor. <term>Authentica</term> "of the minor," <term>Code on who can give guardians</term>. Nor for a husband. Law "Husband," <term>Code on guardianship</term>. It is otherwise by Saxon law, by which a wife is found under the guardianship of her husband, Book 1, <term>Landrecht</term>, article 31. These therefore being excepted, guardianship can be deferred to anyone, and since it is a public duty—beginning of the Institutes "On the excuses of guardians"—necessarily so much so that even by taking pledges, a guardian can be compelled, Law 5, <term>Code on who can give guardians</term>, which Saxon law also approves, Book 1, <term>Landrecht</term>, article 47, where the gloss is received. Law "Final," in the beginning, <term>Code on the administration of guardians</term>, by argument of Law 28, <term>Code on decurions</term>, book 10, and indeed for free, unless the guardian is a pauper. Law 33, "From guardians," paragraph "Final," "On the administration of guardians"; it makes for Law 15, but also if he has [matters] regarding the *ad exhibendum* <gloss>a type of legal action for production</gloss> or other excuses of which [we shall speak] in the following disputation. (g) Not only from office but also at the request which relatives, kin by marriage, and friends offer out of free will. <pb n="13"/>constructed in a square shape, with silk and most precious garments, and surrounded on all sides by railings, outside of which the spectators stand. To this tower or chapel a small door provides entrance, to which another is joined, where on one side there are twenty, and on the other twenty-five, books bound very preciously, which contain the life and laws of Muhammed and his companions. In the lowest part of the tower, the aforementioned man adds, the underground sepulchre of Muhammed is shown, in which certain of his friends are likewise buried, namely Haly, Othmann, Abubecer, and Homar; the top two of whom were associates of Muhammed. These things, I say, Varthema testifies as an eyewitness. Moreover, regarding the fact that others have commonly persuaded people—perhaps more out of hatred for the religion than a pursuit of the truth—that the sepulchre of Muhammed hangs from a magnet under the vault of the temple, or was driven to the underworld by a thunderbolt, the most consistent testimony of men returning every year from Medina to Egypt, and the accepted accurate floor plan of the whole temple, complete with an explicit illustration, proves this to be far from the truth. Prosper Alpinus also mentions this in the following way: It was built alongside the sepulchres of his father-in-law and his son-in-law, with a simple but precious stone; then it was fortified by a surrounding wall of a square circuit, of which the one that most closely encircles the tombs is of a lower structure, and contains a diamond inserted into the inner face of the wall, which they proclaim to be the most noble of all that the sun sees in size and appearance, and which, by the reflection of rays captured from the sun, touches the coffin of the lying Muhammed as if with a celestial radiance. An intermediate partition is adorned with a veil splendid with gold and gems. The Byzantine Emperors send this solemnly to Medina, and when it is carried through the city of Cairo as a public spectacle, the Viceroy of Egypt and the nobles, then some myriads of the people, follow it outside the gates in veneration. Outside these enclosures of the sepulchre, the monument <pb n="14"/>of Fatima, the daughter of Muhammed, and the chests of several sacred books are seen. Philippus Lonicerus, Doctor of Sacred Theology, adds his own calculation regarding the place, writing on the sepulchre of Muhammed: When Muhammed was dead, his body was carried by the <term>Sculperi</term> <gloss>grave-diggers</gloss> or disciples to Modinum or Medina, and there, as he himself had ordered, the sepulchre was dug for him in the middle of the temple. The body was enclosed in a wooden chest and then covered with marble, with a height almost that of a man. Two tablets rise from the sepulchre, one higher, attached to the head, and another lower, applied to the feet. # What kind of contest is the Pancratium?

The <term>Pancratium</term> <gloss>an ancient Olympic contest combining boxing and wrestling</gloss> also flourished, above other Olympic contests, and that not only at the Olympics, a) but also in the Isthmian, Nemean, and Pythian games. # The Division of Nobility

§. 1. A single division of Nobility does not occur. <term>Plato</term> divided it into four species, the first of which is of those who were born from clear, good, and just ancestors. Then, those whose parents had been nobles and princes; he called them by the same name. Thirdly, he wanted those to be called noble whose ancestors had been famous by report and opinion, and that either from martial deeds clearly performed, or from the crowns of contests. Finally, he esteemed the most excellent kind of Nobility, when someone excelled through himself by greatness of soul. Compare <term>Plutarch</term>, book 10, *Against Nobility*.

§. 2. <term>Aristotle</term> distinguishes between the Nobility of the race and of the city, along with the private, in book I, *Rhetoric to Theodectes*, chapter 5, in such a way that he says the splendor of the former is to be indigenous and very ancient, and to be the first illustrious leaders; many from that race also to have been outstanding in matters that are sought after. But private nobility is either from men or from women, and a legitimate procreation from them.

...and as many daughters to his brother Danaus. When they contended with each other for the kingdom, Danaus, with the help of his daughters, killed the sons of Aegyptus, save for one or two; for he had received an oracle that his death was imminent at the hands of one of them. Struck by fear, and following the counsel of Minerva, he was the first to construct a ship, which he named from the number of his daughters a <term>pentekontoros</term> <gloss>fifty-oared ship</gloss>. Placing his daughters upon it, he fled. Then, putting in at Rhodes, he dedicated a statue to Minerva of Lindus. From there, he betook himself to Argos, and Helanor, who was then reigning at Argos, handed over the kingdom to him; (but he himself, having taken possession of that region, named the inhabitants Danaans after his own name). But because that region suffered from a scarcity of water, as Neptune, in his anger, had dried up the springs because he had testified that the land belonged to Minerva, he sent his daughters out to fetch water. One of these, Amymone, while searching for water, cast a spear at a deer and struck a sleeping Satyr. Awakened from sleep, he was seized with a wondrous desire to possess the girl. But upon the arrival of Neptune, the Satyr took flight. Amymone, however, lay with him, and in return, Neptune pointed out the springs of Lerna to her. Furthermore, the sons of Aegyptus journeyed to Argos, and in order to settle the mutual hostility between them, they exhorted one another and begged that the daughters of Danaus be given to them in marriage. Then Danaus, partly because he had little faith in their promises, and partly because he remembered the injury of his flight and exile, pledged the marriages and began to distribute the girls by lot. Therefore, he selected Hypermnestra, the eldest of his daughters, for Lynceus, and Gorgophone for Proteus. For Aegyptus had fathered these from his wife, Queen Argyphia. From that point, each drew their lot.

<margin>Danaus was the first to construct a ship.</margin>

<margin>Some matters omitted which do not appear in the text.</margin>

Busiris, indeed, and Enceladus, Lycus, and Daiphro took Automate, Amymone, Agaue, and Scaea, who were born to Danaus from the royal matron Europa. But from those born of Elephantis came Gorgophone and Hypermnestra, but Lynceus drew Calyces. Ister took Hippodamia; Chalcodon, Rhodia; Agenor, Cleopatra; Chaetus, Asteria; Diacorytes, Hippodamia; Alcis, Glauce; Alcmenon, Hippomedusa; Hippothous, Gorgo; Euchenor, Iphimedusa; Hippolytus, Rhode. These ten were born from his wife, who was from Arabia. But the girls 
<pb n="552"/>
<header>OF APOLLODORUS</header>

born of the Hamadryad nymphs, others born of Atlantea, and others of Phoebe, were wed as follows: Pirene to Agaptolemus; Dorion to Cercestes; Pharte to Eurydamas; Mnestra to Aegius; Argio to Euhippe; Archelaos to Anaxibia; Nelo to Menachus. These seven were born of a Phoenician wife. But the girls who were Ethiopian, because they were of the same name as Memphis, by no means wished to be joined among themselves by lot. For Clitus, born of a Tyrian mother, took Clite; Sthenelus took Sthenele; Chrysippus took Chrysippe. And from the nymph Caliadis and a Naid were born twelve sons, along with as many daughters of Polyron the Naid. Their names are these: Eurylochus, Phantes, Peristhenes, Hermus, Dryas, Potamon, Cilleus, Lixus, Imbrus, Bromius, Polyctor, Chthonius. These others were born of the nymph Autonoe: Theano, Electra, Cleopatra, Eurydice, Glaucippe, Anthelea, Cleodora, Euippe, Erato, Stygne, Bryce. Those, however, who were born of Aegyptus from the Gorgons took as their wives those who were born of Pieria. For Actaea fell to Periphantes; Podarce to Oeneus; Dioxippe to Aegyptus; Adyte to Menalces; Lampo to Ocypete; Idmon to Pylarge. There are, however, eight most recent: Idas, who took Hippodice; Daiphron, who took Adiante, born of the mother Herse; Pandion, who took Callidice; Arbelus, who took Oeme; Hyperbius, who took Celaeno; Hippocorystes, who took Hyperipte. These originate from Hephaestine, but the girls were from the mother Crinone.

Afterwards, when each had drawn his lot and taken his wife, the daughters of Danaus, having taken them into the banquet with daggers provided by their father, killed their husbands as they were buried in sleep, except for one alone, Hypermnestra. For she alone kept Lynceus safe, because he had spared her virginity. For this reason, Danaus ordered her to be thrown into chains and kept in custody. The remaining daughters of Danaus buried the severed heads of their husbands in Lerna, but they arranged for their bodies to be lamented and buried before the city. Minerva and Mercury, by the command of Jupiter, purified them. Finally, afterwards, Danaus gave Hypermnestra to Lynceus in marriage, and he brought out the others for a gymnastic contest and gave them to the victors. Amymone</translation>

has made. Not only things that exist in reality can be sold, but also those that exist in hope. Exceptions are made, among other things, for sacred and spiritual items, which cannot be sold by themselves without sacrilege and simony. An agreement for resale and the resale itself, if done without fraud, is approved by law. A sale under a forfeiture clause or a conditional award by a specific day are considered absolute.

### XVI. Other Onerous Contracts.

Not only a real <term>census</term> <gloss>a ground rent or annuity secured by real estate</gloss> but also a personal one is licit, and not only an irredeemable one, but also one redeemable by the part of either the buyer or the seller. A dry exchange <note>a fictitious bill of exchange used to disguise usurious lending</note> does not know how to produce a just profit. The justice of a real exchange, whether local, manual, or by letter, is easily preserved. A contract of partnership can be made so that one contributes the capital, the other his industry. For a valid game, among other things, it is required that the risk be equal on both sides; and for a wager, that the condition of the bettors be equal. A lessor must primarily ensure the preservation of the leased property. A depositary is sometimes held liable for slight negligence, Law 12, Digest on deposit. A loan for use cannot be recovered by its nature before the time has elapsed for which it was granted. If a borrowed item perishes by accident without the fault of the borrower, it perishes for the owner, Law final, Digest on loan for use. A precarious grant is not ended by the death of the grantor. A guarantee not under oath by a woman for her husband is void. Even rights can be pledged or mortgaged.

### XVII. Injury and Restitution.

Injury is the violation of another’s right. One type is real, which is committed through an unjust laying on of hands; another is verbal, which is committed through insulting words, letters, writing, or images, Law 15, Digest on injuries and libelous writings. One type is slight, another atrocious; the nature of which must be determined from the act, the place, the person, and other circumstances, § Atrocious, Institutes on injuries. Injury is not done to one who is willing, unless

<pb n="15"/>where positive or natural law resists the cession of a right; hence, one who drags a cleric unwillingly to a secular tribunal still commits an injury. Indeed, an inflicted injury is repaired either by satisfaction or by restitution. Restitution is an act of commutative justice, necessary for salvation not by the necessity of the medium, but only by precept; this is both Divine and natural, partly affirmative, partly negative. The obligation to restore arises either from unjust acceptance or from the thing itself having been accepted; hence, restitution differs greatly from payment, since the obligation to pay proceeds from contracts.

## T H E   E N D.

<pb n="15"/>§. 2. Since there are two classes of arguments by which we can arrive at the investigation and discovery of the truth: I. Inartificial <note>meaning external evidence</note>, or authorities and testimonies; II. Artificial <note>meaning derived from logic</note>, or reasons and arguments. All these things, given the nature of this topic, are so arranged that they, on one hand, directly and explicitly <term>katá thésin</term> <gloss>according to a thesis/affirmative</gloss> construct the antiquity and <term>theopneustian</term> <gloss>divine inspiration</gloss> of the points, which we seek; on the other hand, <term>kat’ ársin kaì athétesin</term> <gloss>by denial and rejection</gloss>, insofar as they deny that the Tiberian Masoretes were the authors of the points and remove them from the equation, or they are silent about them altogether. Hence, having already cited the testimonies, we shall now provide the following reasons to support the antiquity and divine inspiration of the points.

§. 3. To obtain the truth of our assertion, we urge: I. *The most certain danger of uncertainty and ambiguity.* If we assume that the vocal points were added by the Rabbis only after the passage of several centuries, would we not render the clarity of meanings and the origin of words thoroughly ambiguous, or rather, plainly uncertain? Indeed, the Hebrew language, due to its own rather narrow limits, does not abound in many primitive and radical words, and for that reason, it is for the most part forced to represent and explain several discrepant things using a single derivative. I ask, therefore, that you explain to me: does the diversity of meanings depend upon the consonants alone, or upon the vowels? It cannot depend solely upon the consonants, because consonants occur in the same way under the most diverse meanings of words. The matter is made clearer by examples. Thus, <term>HWH</term> if pointed <term>Hawah</term> signifies "he was"; if in this way <term>Howah</term>, it denotes "misery"; if in another way <term>Hawwah</term>, it signifies "substance." Likewise, <term>BQR</term> if pointed <term>Baqar</term> denotes "he investigated"; if <term>Baqqer</term>, "examine" and "to investigate"; if <term>Boqer</term>, "morning"; if <term>Baqar</term>, "cattle," and similar ones. Who, truly, among these words descending from one root, would conveniently distinguish and discern one meaning from another, unless the diversity of vowels came to one's aid?

§. 4. Furthermore, we urge: II. *The inevitable duty of the points.* For that traditional saying is valid here also:
> the symbols in speech are of the passions in the soul, and written things <pb n="16"/>are symbols of those in the soul <note>Aristotle, *De Interpretatione*, ch. 1</note>. Indeed, the reason for vowels is held to be prior and more important than that of consonants. Since vowels are an essential part of reading and writing, and constitute the primary part, who would believe that language lacked them from the beginning? Especially since any language that is deprived of them is rendered lame, mutilated, and imperfect. Therefore, vowels are called by the Hebrews not only <term>tenu'ot</term> <gloss>motions</gloss>, and by the Greeks <term>phōnéenta</term> <gloss>vowels/voiced sounds</gloss>; but they are also called the souls of words, which vivify them, and as in other languages, they hold the primacy. Moreover, every speech, for which literature serves to record, consists of words; words consist of syllables; syllables consist of consonants and vowels. If, therefore, no syllable can consist without vowels, then neither can any speech. And what is more, no letter can be pronounced without vowels. Hence, Johannes Isaac, a convert Jew, said well: he who reads Scripture without points and accents is like a man riding a horse that is <term>achálintōn</term> <gloss>unbridled</gloss>. There are some who call the <term>ammot ha-qeri'ah</term> <gloss>mothers of reading</gloss> to their aid here, in that they can supply the functions of the vowels. But while we do not deny that the reading of an unpointed text can be helped in some way by those letters, neither do we completely reject their use in Rabbinic and Talmudic books. But neither are they present everywhere, nor where they are present do they always judge them to be certain and the same.

### §. 5. Furthermore, we add: III. The contrary opinion is absurd.

Because they posit that the vowels were recently invented by the Masoretes, they incur this mark of absurdity, so that from their hypothesis, every most false thing and what is contrary to reason seems to flow: 1. That a necessary means of interpreting Scripture was missing for some thousands of years; because, just as for pronunciation, so also for the certain and indubitable transcription of sacred things, vocal points are undeniably required. 2. That sacred Scripture is offered to be corrupted by enemies; for if the points were not divinely handed down, it would truly be easy to interpret a voice otherwise than is right. 3. That the venerable and pious antiquity of the Jews is either charged with ignorance or accused of envy; if they knew the points and did not communicate them, it is of the latter; but if they did not know them, to whom...

</translation>

<summary>The author argues for the necessity and antiquity of Hebrew vocalization points, claiming they are essential for clarifying meanings that consonants alone cannot distinguish and that they are integral to the divine nature of the text.</summary>
<keywords>Hebrew vocalization, Masoretes, Tiberian, orthography, divine inspiration, theopneusty, linguistics, semantics, Johannes Isaac</keywords>

<pb n="15"/>because Holy Scripture cannot deceive, whoever fears being deceived should consult that same Church regarding the obscurity of this question, which Holy Scripture demonstrates without any ambiguity. If, however, you doubt that this Holy Scripture commends the Church which is spread abroad throughout all nations in most copious numbers (for if you did not doubt, you would not still be in the party of <term>Donatus</term> <note>a 4th-century North African bishop whose followers, the Donatists, believed the efficacy of sacraments depended on the holiness of the minister</note>), I will burden you with many and most manifest testimonies brought forth from that same authority (Scripture), so that from your own concessions, if you are not willing to be too stubborn, you may be led to this conclusion (namely, that the Church from which the Donatists had separated themselves is the true Church).

II. Regarding the passage in Matthew 18:17, to which the Protestor appeals several times, it likewise has the same <term>kene asikopa</term> <gloss>empty and aimless</gloss> <note>original: "κενεῖ ἄσκοπα"</note> as that of <term>Augustine</term>. It does not speak of the Church's interpretation of Scripture and controversies at its own pleasure, but precisely of private injuries and offenses. But let it be so; let us grant some Papist objectors that it can also be understood as referring to injuries done to the whole Church and to God himself, namely, through the perverse interpretation of Scripture and through heresies. We must indeed hear the Church; but it is not to be heard simply and in all things; rather, only insofar as it follows Christ the head and the Holy Spirit as guide while speaking, interpreting, and judging in the Word. No less must the leaders and pastors of the churches be obeyed reverently in the Lord (2 Thessalonians 3:3, 14; Hebrews 13:17), yet not absolutely, but conditionally, insofar as and for as long as they hear the voice of the Chief Shepherd, Christ Jesus, rightly propose His word, and keep themselves within the bounds of their calling. One must not simply and in all things, without any <term>dokimasia</term> <gloss>examination/testing</gloss> <note>original: "δοκιμασίᾳ"</note> (that is, an examination of interpretations, dogmas, and rites proposed by others according to the norm of the divine Word) and without any selection of all things, believe or obey as if with closed eyes. Not otherwise than as the Pharisees were teachers and interpreters who were to be heard in part, insofar as they sat in the seat of Moses (Matthew 23:2), but in part were not to be heard, but avoided, insofar as they spread the leaven of their doctrine and human traditions, infecting the healthy sense of Scripture (Matthew 16:6, 12).

Therefore, we maintain that there is absolutely no Church on earth, whether it be particular or universal, which is not perpetually and simply bound to the written Word of God, and which is not bound to derive from thence the account of both its dogmas and <pb n="16"/>all its rites, and to explain them to others who ask. Thus, pastors are to be obeyed only at the altars, or not otherwise than in the Lord, as the Holy Scriptures speak, nor is any dogma of theirs to be held as a fundamental article of faith whose solid and open foundations we have not first discovered in the Word of God itself. Even if we know that the Church in which we live is true, and that the pastors whom we hear are orthodox, yet one must not believe either these or those absolutely; for it is possible that even a true Church, and even orthodox teachers, may hallucinate while interpreting the Scriptures, gradually deviate from the truth, and begin to put forward erroneous opinions, just as happened to many churches in the times of the Old and New Testaments.

III. Thus (to say something about the Pauline passage), the *Church is the pillar and foundation of the truth*, but because of the Holy Scripture which it faithfully embraces, guards, commends, teaches, explains, and propagates. If it recedes from this, it is not only not the foundation of truth, but it even loses the truth itself.

Whence the true Church also interprets Scripture from Scripture. If, however, you doubt that this Holy Scripture commends the Church which is spread abroad throughout all nations in most copious numbers (for if you did not doubt, you would not still be in the party of <term>Donatus</term> <note>a 4th-century North African bishop whose followers, the Donatists, believed the efficacy of sacraments depended on the holiness of the minister</note>), I will burden you with many and most manifest testimonies brought forth from that same authority (Scripture), so that from your own concessions, if you are not willing to be too stubborn, you may be led to this conclusion (namely, that the Church from which the Donatists had separated themselves is the true Church).

II. Regarding the passage in Matthew 18:17, to which the Protestor appeals several times, it likewise has the same <term>kene asikopa</term> <gloss>empty and aimless</gloss> <note>original: "κενεῖ ἄσκοπα"</note> as that of <term>Augustine</term>. It does not speak of the Church's interpretation of Scripture and controversies at its own pleasure, but precisely of private injuries and offenses. But let it be so; let us grant some Papist objectors that it can also be understood as referring to injuries done to the whole Church and to God himself, namely, through the perverse interpretation of Scripture and through heresies. We must indeed hear the Church; but it is not to be heard simply and in all things; rather, only insofar as it follows Christ the head and the Holy Spirit as guide while speaking, interpreting, and judging in the Word. No less must the leaders and pastors of the churches be obeyed reverently in the Lord (2 Thessalonians 3:3, 14; Hebrews 13:17), yet not absolutely, but conditionally, insofar as and for as long as they hear the voice of the Chief Shepherd, Christ Jesus, rightly propose His word, and keep themselves within the bounds of their calling. One must not simply and in all things, without any <term>dokimasia</term> <gloss>examination/testing</gloss> <note>original: "δοκιμασίᾳ"</note> (that is, an examination of interpretations, dogmas, and rites proposed by others according to the norm of the divine Word) and without any selection of all things, believe or obey as if with closed eyes. <translation>
<pb n="14"/> invite us to such great sobriety that we would not suffer drunkenness to be even named among us. AP. Moreover, the most shameful deeds of drunkards and their most absurd behavior should above all deter us from the immoderate habit of drinking. For from what wicked acts do they abstain? They cast aside all modesty, they are inflamed with illicit lust, they reveal the secrets of their minds, they wallow in the mire, they walk without any control of their steps, they stagger, they vomit like beasts, they assail all the best men with slanders, and they do not look to the work of God, nor do they consider the works of his hands. Now, indeed, when they have weakened their bodies by immense gluttony, and have become exhausted from the performance of the works of darkness, they fall down as if lifeless, lying prostrate on the ground like pigs, so that it may most truly be said, A DRUNKARD IS A LIVING CORPSE. Finally, let us be moved by the profane men, the <term>Ethnici</term> <gloss>Heathens/Gentiles</gloss>, who entirely condemned this detestable and abominable vice, so much so that Solon held that a prince should be punished with death if he were found drunk. And it was not permitted for a king among the Indians to reach the point of drunkenness while drinking. Among the Persians, however, this was granted to the king on only one day, the day on which they offered sacrifices to the sun. NEPH. And I remember reading that Pittacus of Mytilene, not the least of the seven Greek Sages, enacted a law that if any person committed any wickedness while drunk, he should be punished with a penalty twice as severe. AP. If, therefore, those who were ignorant of God so highly condemned this crime, avoided it, and punished it, what do you think we Christians must do, I ask? NEPH. Let us strive that we may never be intoxicated with wine, in which there is <term>asōtia</term> <gloss>profligacy/debauchery</gloss>: let us despise and avoid drunkenness, which takes away the heart and memory, which scatters the senses and confuses the intellect, and which makes a beast out of a man, an invalid out of a robust person, and a fool out of a prudent one. Let us, however, burn with a zeal for sobriety and temperance, and let us consider that these are now the final times; let us revere and fear the long-suffering of God, lest we despise the riches of his goodness and patience <pb n="15"/> and his forbearance. Let us also remember that our bodies are the temple of God, and the instrument of the Holy Spirit, who dwells within us. AP. Sobriety and temperance are the fruits of the Spirit; but drunkenness and luxury are the nurses and promoters of all vices, and the receptacles of every kind of filth. Just as smoke drives away bees, so excessive drinking drives away the Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts. NEPH. And just as clouds and rain always follow the south wind, so the diseases of the soul and the animal spirit follow drunkenness. COM. Therefore, is it clearly not permitted to drink? AP. Certainly, if the limit is missing. However, honor must be shown to the body so that it may be fed with sufficient, not immoderate and superfluous, sustenance, and we must be careful that we are not found to be the murderers of our own bodies. COM. I understand now at last that nothing is more destructive to man than drunkenness. AP. Therefore, heal this disease within yourself, brother, and separate this vice from yourself, and flee the company of wine-drinkers as you would a reef. TRIC. Alas! Are you not ashamed, Comasta, to allow yourself to be corrupted by the persuasion of these men? AP. Come, arise Comasta, let us go; do not listen to them. COM. Farewell, fellow drinkers, I must be off and be wary, so that I may become a man; but if you are wise, take an example from me.

## THE END.

<note>A woodcut tailpiece features symmetrical scrollwork and floral designs, possibly acanthus leaves, forming a heart-like central shape.</note>

<pb n="19"/>if anything has come to him on the occasion of the mandate, he must restore it, <note>Digest 16.3.10.2; Digest 17.1.20 pr.</note>.

### XXXIII.

As regards the case concerned in paragraph 30, there the cause of the litigation is the detention of a thing, which Paul seeks back from Maevius, and he assigns the reason for seeking it because he mandated that Maevius should carry his property to Pomponius so that he might keep it, and if Pomponius refused, Maevius should guard it for as long as he sought it back. Paul’s intention is founded in <note>Digest 16.3.1.12 "On Deposit,"</note> where the action of mandate, not strictly deposit, is granted to him. We shall propose other examples still.

### XXXIV.

The actions discussed so far have exhibited to us those arising from contracts; now a case must be seen where a contract in part and a tort in part produces an action. For Sempronius leased his house to Titius, and once this consensual business was completed, they went together to inspect the leased house. <pb n="13"/>a base person has been instituted by a deceased uncle, does the complaint of an undutiful testament <note>original: "querela inofficiosi testamenti"</note> accrue to the children of the brothers by virtue of this right of representation? It might seem so from the decision of the aforementioned Novella 118, which generally substitutes children into the place of their parents; however, with Zoesius on the title of the Digest, *On the Undutiful Testament*, number 26, we shall sustain the negative through the law *Frater* 21, Code, *On the Undutiful Testament*, and § 1, Institutes, of the same. For although in the Novellae children of brothers are admitted to the inheritance of an uncle along with brothers, that nevertheless proceeds if he dies intestate simply, but not if the testament is overturned through the complaint of being undutiful. Furthermore, the children of brothers succeed to a deceased uncle by the right of representation only then, if they were conceived while he was alive; otherwise, they will not be admitted to his goods, whom they do not reach by any kinship, law 1, § *Si quis proximior*, Digest, *Whence the relatives are called*. Unless a path to the succession lies open from the right of transmission, and that from the right of deliberating (namely, if their parent dies within the annual period from the day of knowledge that the inheritance had been deferred to him), law *Cum in antiquioribus* 19, Code, *On the right of deliberating*, and there Brunnemannus.

### I.

Since the right of receiving tithes of newly cultivated land <term>novalia</term> <gloss>newly cleared or cultivated lands</gloss> must be granted through a special privilege, and is not contained in the right of receiving old tithes, chapter 2, *On Tithes*, in the Sext; hence it follows that if wood for felling is brought to cultivation, he who exercises the right of tithing through prescription <pb n="14"/>or any other just title in that place cannot seek tithes from the newly born fruits. By the customs of the Empire today, these tithes belong to the lord of the territory in recognition of supreme jurisdiction; see Myler, *On the State of the Empire*, page 2, chapter 70, number 5.

#### Paragraph I.

Just as a real census <note>a permanent annual income or rent</note> that is redeemable on the part of the seller alone (provided it is purchased for a just price, namely, by force of Imperial constitutions, 5 florins of annual rent for one hundred florins) is a licit and non-usurious contract, *Extravagantes* 1 and 2, *On Buying and Selling*; so a census that is irredeemable on the part of the seller (given that the aforementioned price intervenes) is not alien to the stain of usury. Emperor Charles V confirmed this in the constitution published at Augsburg in the year 1548, under the title **On usurious contracts, paragraph "and after the redemption florins."** For this quality is inherent in such censuses: that the seller may redeem even if the buyer is unwilling, nor can one contract to the contrary, nor can the faculty of redeeming be prescribed ever, not even in the space of one hundred years, at least by Canon Law. If, therefore, in the instrument of obligation, mention of perpetuity (Unablößlich <gloss>irredeemable</gloss>) has been made, then the irredeemability must be understood and accepted in relation to the buyer or creditor, not the seller or debtor.

### From Civil Law.

#### Paragraph I.

The question is famous in law: does the profit of a dowry by reason of pact or statute yield to the survivor, if the other dies before the marriage is consummated? For the negative, it is commonly brought up that a dowry is not owed where there are no burdens of marriage, law *Si pater* 76, at the end, Digest, *On the Law of Dowries*. We shall answer in the affirmative, however, if nothing has been expressly provided in the pact or statute by reason of time. For it is not intercourse that makes a marriage, but consent; for this part, the text in the law *Cum fuerit* 15, Digest, *On Conditions and Demonstrations*, serves, where a legacy left under the condition of marriage is owed immediately as soon as the woman is led to the husband. Just as a real census <note>a permanent annual income or rent</note> that is redeemable on the part of the seller alone (provided it is purchased for a just price, namely, by force of Imperial constitutions, 5 florins of annual rent for one hundred florins) is a licit and non-usurious contract, *Extravagantes* 1 and 2, *On Buying and Selling*; so a census that is irredeemable on the part of the seller (given that the aforementioned price intervenes) is not alien to the stain of usury. Emperor Charles V confirmed this in the constitution published at Augsburg in the year 1548, under the title **On usurious contracts, paragraph "and after the redemption florins."** For this quality is inherent in such censuses: that the seller may redeem even if the buyer is unwilling, nor can one contract to the contrary, nor can the faculty of redeeming be prescribed ever, not even in the space of one hundred years, at least by Canon Law. He is truly with us, he sees and knows all things, he also rules and governs all things, and since he favors all who believe in him and call upon him in faith, he does not grant nor permit any adversity to happen to them unless he knows that this very thing is salutary for them and useful for attaining heavenly goods. If, therefore, we are in danger in water, in fire, in prisons, or are overwhelmed by any calamity, we can and must always awaken our faith and our invocation to God in this manner: that we know that Christ, true God and man, is not far from us in some peculiar place of this outer heaven distant from us, and perhaps having no care for us, but that he is with us, both in humanity and in divinity, in the water, in the fire, in the prison, and in every calamity, and provided that we embrace him with true faith and call upon him, he will never allow us to perish.

<margin>III.</margin>
Finally, the knowledge of the majesty of Christ, in that he is everywhere and fills all things not only by his divinity but also by his humanity, brings us also this use and this benefit: that we may walk all the more religiously in the fear and obedience of God, and avoid sins and crimes with all the greater diligence. Meanwhile, they do not consider that Christ himself is present, who sees all things, and who, without doubt, will not leave evil deeds unpunished. Who would not say that the servant is foolish to a high degree who thinks it is going well for him if the things he does treacherously against his master escape the conscience and eyes of his fellow servants and other members of the household, and in the meantime, he does not care about the conscience and sight of his master, who is present and sees all things? Wherefore, let us not confuse or disturb the presence and sight of Christ our savior, but rather affect him with honor and joy. And so that his presence may be more for our consolation than for terror and destruction, let us endeavor not to offend the present eyes of that majesty with sins and crimes,

§. 3. Truly, in Franconia and the Palatinate, the word <term>Centena</term> seems to have a different meaning today, while by <term>Centena</term> they understand criminal jurisdiction and absolute authority, and thus the adjudication of capital offenses. Hence: what is called elsewhere <term>Hals-</term> or <term>hohe Gerechtigkeit</term> <gloss>capital or high justice</gloss>, they call <term>Centgerechtigkeit</term> <gloss>hundred-justice</gloss>; they call him to whom such judgment pertains <term>Centherrn</term> <gloss>hundred-lord</gloss>, and the assessors of that same criminal court <term>Zentschöpffen</term> <gloss>hundred-jurors</gloss>, and those who are finally subject to such judgment <term>Zentbare Unterthanen</term> <gloss>hundred-liable subjects</gloss>. Regarding this matter, <term>Berneggerus</term> should be consulted. But it is so far from the truth that modern customs have imposed a meaning other than and different from the ancient use of the word <term>Centena</term>, that it rather accurately reflects the most ancient institution of the Germans, by which they divided the <term>Pagi</term> into <term>Centenae</term>, or as we just said, and placed over each <term>Centena</term> a judge whom they called <term>CentGraffen</term>, along with his <term>Centenarii</term> and <term>Scabini</term> <gloss>jurors/magistrates</gloss>. For what prevents one from calling a Count of a <term>Centena</term> a <term>Zentherrn</term>, or a judgment held in a <term>Centena</term> before the Count and <term>Centenarii</term> a <term>Zentgericht</term> <gloss>hundred-court</gloss> or <term>Zentgerechtigkeit</term>? By this, we arrive at the explanation of the appointed time within which the creditor has agreed with the debtor that he is not held to receive the debt, which, in the style of the <term>Jurisconsults</term> <gloss>legal experts</gloss>, is known to be called a day. *By the argument of Law 213, Digest, On Verbal Obligations, paragraph 2; [and] 7 of the same.*

---

However, this depends upon the decision of the contracting parties, so that either a certain day is determined, before the lapse of which the debtor does not have the freedom of paying, *by the argument of the cited paragraph 2; 7, On Verbal Obligations*, or the payment is deferred to an uncertain time, *by the argument of Law 48, Digest, On Verbal Obligations; Law 85, Digest, On Conditions and Demonstrations.*

---

->§. 24.<-

But since in both cases the entire importance lies in the fact that the day is added for the benefit of the creditor, it is therefore necessary that he act cautiously in determining it.

---

->§. 25.<-

For regarding the time that is certain, as often as <pb n="12"/><note>Two handwritten diagonal ink strokes in the left margin, likely reader marks or a cancellation mark.</note> <margin>/</margin> <margin>/</margin> a day is simply added in the instrument of obligation, it is presumed as often that it was added for the benefit of the debtor, to the end, namely, that he may use the thing in the meantime as he pleases, and may not be sued by the plaintiff throughout that intermediate time which was left free for him to make payment, according to the argument of Law 117, Digest, On the Rules of Law; Law 41, paragraph 1; Law 42, On Verbal Obligations; Law 44, paragraph 1, Digest, On Obligations and Actions; paragraph 2, Institutes, On Verbal Obligations. From which it simultaneously follows that, although he may be able to pay even before the day, if the creditor is unwilling, Law 70, Digest, On Payment; Law 50, Digest, On Obligations and Actions, provided however that general security is applied, so that the payment is offered without any detriment to the creditor, and not at an inopportune time or place, Law 39, Digest, On Payment; Law 122, preamble, Digest, On Verbal Obligations.

->§. 26.<-

Hence, if every opportunity to pay within the appointed day is to be taken away from the debtor, those words must primarily be employed from which it may clearly appear that it was agreed by the contracting parties that the debtor wished to renounce this benefit, which pertains to him by law, and to transfer the same to the creditor; so that, indeed, a contract which is otherwise regarded as odious because it impedes release, is not interpreted more openly against the creditor, in whose power it was [to stipulate otherwise].

Finally, the dispute and expostulation of the Jews regarding the changing of the writing. For if it had been without the <term>yod</term> and <term>vav</term> <note>Hebrew letters י and ו</note>, the writing would have remained doubtful, and the crowd of high priests would have had a handle and opportunity to excuse themselves regarding the explanation.

XIII. <term>Iησȣ͂ς</term> <gloss>Jesus</gloss>, in its origin is Hebrew, said to be either from <term>Yehoshua</term> or from <term>Yeshua</term>. For he who was called <term>Yehoshua</term> in Haggai and Zechariah, is elsewhere called <term>Yeshua</term> (Ezra 2:2, Nehemiah 7:7), and Joshua, or <term>Yehoshua</term>, is elsewhere called <term>Yeshua</term> (Nehemiah 8:17). Moreover, it is derived from the verb <term>yasha</term> in the <term>Hiphil</term> <gloss>causative conjugation</gloss>, which means to make safe, to save, to preserve, and to vindicate. It has its name from the deed performed. Just as we read many such things in Scripture, as <term>Jacob</term> was called a supplanter from <term>aqeb</term>, because he had supplanted his brother in the birthright. By the same reasoning, Christ receives His name from the admirable and truly stupendous work of salvation, so that He might be called <term>Iησȣ͂ς</term>, Savior, or <term>Soter</term>, which signifies more than the Latin <term>servator</term> <gloss>preserver</gloss>, as Cicero himself acknowledges (Second Action Against Verres). I have seen Him inscribed at Syracuse not only as the patron of that island but also as <term>Soter</term>. How great is this? It is so great that it cannot be expressed by one Latin word. He is undoubtedly the <term>Soter</term>, who gave salvation. Hence the Greek <term>Iησȣ͂ς</term> was born, which is read and written in Latin with two syllables, the letter S being added. For the Greeks add the same letter to foreign names at the end.

XIV. Here, if it pleases anyone, let someone venerate the religion and subtlety of the <term>Jesuits</term>, who write JHESUS for JESUS, or by abbreviation with three letters, IHS, and so that no superstition is lacking, even with a cross placed above it. These good fellows incorrectly insert the Latin H, not attending to the fact that there is no aspiration of H in the Greek or Hebrew language. And since in all things the first and last moments have the greatest power, they wanted Janus to be the leader in sacrificing, says Cicero (<note>Book 1, On the Nature of the Gods</note>).

We, who are called Christians, and who are such, are far from simply subscribing to the formulas of the pagans, as if we did not have things as good or better. Rather, we seriously condemn everything erroneous that the idolatry of the Gentiles attracted, and we judge that only that which seems to be derived and composed from the year itself should be retained, especially in this vow. But if we obtain through our prayer what we are vowing, each of us will have that for which he may congratulate himself and rejoice after the passing of the year.

And we know that vows of this kind were observed in the temples, especially through the <term>Flamines</term> <gloss>priests of ancient Rome</gloss>. But what were those who sat at the helm of the Republic doing around this time? Consuls and senators were ordained; once ordained, they entered upon their offices and, for the sake of good omens, performed a <term>delibatio</term> <gloss>a preliminary offering or tasting</gloss>. This can be seen in the election of the father of <term>Symmachus</term>, a man of marvelous eloquence and knowledge. In the country and in retirement, his parent, digesting the injury of a lost house, was finally summoned by the Senate to a new honor through frequent votes and by sent orators. And it was then the Kalends, when the year is opened, as the son himself testifies, and rejoices (<note>Book 1, Epistle 44</note>). He is seconded by <term>Naso</term> <gloss>Ovid</gloss>, the prolific recorder of the <term>Fasti</term> <gloss>Roman calendar and festive records</gloss>, who introduces this rite gracefully when he says:

> With garments untouched, they go to the Tarpeian Heights,
> And the people themselves are of one color with their festival.
> Now the new fasces march before, new purple shines,
> And the ivory chair feels new weight. (<note>Book 1, Fasti, verse 10</note>)

<pb n="4"/>There was also a custom of making a preliminary offering, and of as it were dedicating and auspiciously commencing duties on that very day. <term>Drusus</term>, the Prefect of the City, ascended the tribunal to take the auspices; <term>Nero</term> took the auspices on the Kalends of January; what the Emperor <term>Maximianus</term> had wished for the future, he made immediately accomplished. The historian of the Augustan history, <term>Tacitus</term> (<note>Book 4, Annals, chapter 36</note>), writes this of the former; <term>Suetonius</term> (<note>chapter 46</note>) of that; and the panegyrists testify to the latter. The habit and custom of Christians does not differ from this time; in some places, around these same turnings of the year, they complete and restore their councils and senates. And indeed they seem to do this more correctly than the ancients. For we believe that at that time was born the eternal Son of GOD, the <term>Logos</term> <gloss>Word</gloss> of the eternal Father, who by His merit and satisfaction designated and established us as heavenly citizens and nobles. We transmit the other custom of making a preliminary offering and dedicating the tasks and occupations assigned to each person, the <term>aparchas</term> <gloss>first fruits/initial offerings</gloss>, and, if I may say so, into disuse. We are aware that the paternal grace of GOD, implored by our prayer, can, if He wills, make every month and every day of the month prosperous for us, and that the certain commencement of work on the first or any other day does not help us at all.

This, too, the most praised Emperors, the divine <term>Valentinianus</term>, <term>Theodosius</term>, and <term>Arcadius</term>, seem to have acknowledged, for they willed by a salutary rescript that the days of the January Kalends should be consigned to leisure and should be an <term>apodeixis</term> <gloss>a demonstration/exhibition</gloss>, a fact which is not unknown to the priests of the law and the learned (<note>Novellae 8, Law "All Days," 7, chapter on Holidays XII, Book 3</note>). Perhaps, so that for divine worship and sacred things, there...

when you look for a magnificent one, what is more magnificent than this King, to whom the Angels applaud from the heavens, whom Kings adore in the cradle, and to whom they offer Gold, Frankincense, and Myrrh, the gifts of Kings? <pb n="11"/>and the Prophets, and the remaining books of the Old Testament, and you will have removed the entire scripture of the Old Testament. For if all parts are removed, the whole itself is removed. I, however, will demonstrate to you the true divinity of those books themselves from those very books in such a way that you will not depart without most just confusion: and then I will also demand from you that, if you can and wish to, you show the contrary. I will observe the same method in the books of the New Testament, and I will set before you the statement in John 21:24: "This is the disciple who testifies of these things, and wrote these things. And we know that his testimony is true." But then I will add a collation of the Old and New Testaments and of parallel passages, and the mutual testimony of the books regarding themselves, and finally I will ask of you: Do you believe that out of all these one thing is true, or do you hold all these as false? I will assert, Papist: Tell the Church. If he acknowledges it as true, I have what I want. But if he denies it, he destroys the primary foundation of all the Pontiff's followers. Whatever you answer, Pistorius, will redound to the disgrace of this argument of yours. 5. That faith which Pistorius describes here is not justifying faith, but historical faith, which many have lacked, and can lack without the loss of salvation. For that number of Biblical books, or their order, contributes nothing to the justice of faith, provided that you sincerely believe what scripture proposes to be believed concerning Christ the redeemer. See thesis 24 of the first disputation.

29. Note here, p. 15, the extreme impudence of Pistorius, who writes expressly: "Our position concerning the perfection and sufficiency of Holy Scripture leads gradually to the abnegation of all sacred scripture, and makes one a Turk or an Epicurean." His argument is as follows: Whoever believes nothing except what is held in sacred scripture is led gradually to the abnegation of all scripture, and turns into a Turk or an Epicurean. Lutherans believe nothing except what is held in sacred scripture. Therefore, Lutherans are led gradually to the abnegation of all scripture and turn into Turks and Epicureans. Who would not judge such an impudent apostate worthy of universal hatred? For are not "to believe" and "to abnegate" contraries? How, therefore, do they coincide in the singular Lutherans? For whoever believes in the sole scripture, surely does not abnegate it. And he who abnegates <pb n="12"/> does not believe. Regarding the Papists, the conclusion is most true: a fact that will be demonstrated most clearly in its proper place.

30. Argument 2. Nothing is to be believed unless it exists in writing in the word of God. But that which is not explicitly <term>bekandtlich</term> <gloss>known/evident</gloss> in scripture is nowhere found. Therefore, not even this itself ought to be believed, p. 16.

31. I respond. These are 4 terms. The proposition speaks generally of that which in any way exists in the word of God, whether expressly, that is, in distinct words, or implicitly, that is, through a certain, firm, and necessary consequence. And thus far it is true. The assumption speaks only of that which exists openly. Whence the argument is narrower than the question, when it ought to be either broader or equally broad. 2. The assumption of Pistorius is most false, which is evident from thesis 4 and primarily from these clearest testimonies: "You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left," Deut. 5:32. "To the law and to the testimony; if they do not speak according to this word, there will be no morning light for them," Isa. 8:20. "Let him be anathema who has preached another Gospel," Gal. 1:8. "Do not teach other doctrines" <note>original Greek: μὴ ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν</note>, 1 Tim. 1:3. And ch. 6:3. "Whoever shall walk according to this Rule, peace be upon them and mercy," Gal. 6:16. Conversely: "Whoever shall depart from this rule, wrath and damnation be upon them." 3. If all things are implicitly in scripture, as Pistorius says on page 35, then this too must be held implicitly in it: that nothing is to be believed outside the word of God. 4. For Christian faith and the word of God stand in relation to one another. 5. Which Pistorius will not deny, who has written distinctly that he will prove all his points from one sacred scripture. 6. And Bellarmine, although he speaks insidiously, nevertheless admits in book 1, *On the Word of God*, ch. 1, that the Prophetic and Apostolic books are the certain and stable rule of faith. 7. And today, nothing in the matter of religion is put forward by the Pontiff's followers that the Jesuits do not attempt to prove from some scripture: a fact which is evident from their disputations. Thus, clearly, these men say one thing and do another.

32. Argument 3, p. 30. The Apostles preached many things about which they wrote nothing, and yet these ought to be believed. Therefore, scripture is not perfect. He proves the antecedent on p. 31, because Paul refers his listeners not only to scripture, but primarily also to traditions.
</translation>

<summary>This text addresses specific theological challenges posed by Pistorius regarding the sufficiency and authority of Scripture, specifically concerning the canon and the necessity of traditions versus the sole authority of the written word of God.</summary>
<keywords>Scripture, Canon, Pistorius, Lutheranism, faith, traditions, divine revelation, Bellarmine, Jesuits</keywords>

<pb n="14"/>

### X L I I.

This pleasure is nothing other than a certain perfection following human functions, recommending them with a singular sweetness.

### X L I I I.

Just as, therefore, theoretical happiness excels practical, so also does theoretical pleasure surpass practical pleasure.

### X L I I I I.

<margin>See the last chapter of Book 1 of the Ethics and Chapter 7 of Book 10 of the Nicomachean Ethics.</margin>
Furthermore, from the preceding it is also clear that Aristotle perceived both the excellence and the dignity of human nature, as well as its corruption: while he surely confesses that a desire for divinity and immortality is implanted in man by nature, yet he says that divinity does not belong to man, as he is man. But indeed, he did not know the cause of this, much less the method of obtaining immortality through <term>MESSIAH</term> <gloss>the Anointed One</gloss>; for this whole matter is owed to revelation, as the most learned Zwinger has most beautifully noted on Chapter 7 of the 10th book of the Ethics.

### X L V.

Nor is there any reason why we should reject Aristotle’s doctrine regarding human happiness on the grounds that it is less in agreement with our Christian religion.

### X L V I.

For besides what we have said above <pb n="15"/> <margin>Homily to the young on how they might profit from Greek literature.</margin> regarding the philosopher arguing philosophically about this matter, his opinion ought to be commended to us for this reason alone: namely, that either the philosopher says the same things, that is, things congruent with heavenly truth, and the consensus is beneficial; or he says different things, and the comparison is beneficial, to use the words of St. Basil the Great, a witness in this matter greater than any exception.

### X L V I I.

Finally, the philosopher does not contradict himself, even though in the first book of the Nicomachean Ethics he asserts that practical happiness is the highest good, yet in the last book he maintains and argues that theoretical happiness <note>original: "θεωρητικὴν εὐδαιμονίαν"</note> is superior to it.

### X L V I I I.

For just as in the first book, with respect to practical happiness, he considers the composite man <note>original: "τὸν σύνθετον ἄνθρωπον"</note>, so in the tenth book, regarding theoretical blessedness, he considers the mind <note>original: "τὸν νοῦν"</note>, which he calls the "man most of all" <note>original: "μάλιστα ἄνθρωπον"</note>.

### X L I X.

From all of which, I think, it appears clearer than the midday sun, as the saying goes, that it is most true what Cicero used to say: that the entire authority of philosophy, that is, of the doctrine concerning life and morals, consists in attaining a blessed life, and that therefore its dignity and excellence are supreme and admirable.
</translation>

<summary>This text concludes the discussion of Aristotelian ethics, reconciling his views on human happiness with Christian doctrine and confirming the primacy of theoretical contemplation over practical life.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Happiness, Ethics, Contemplation, Christianity, Cicero, Zwinger, Basil the Great</keywords>

For just as in the first book, with respect to practical happiness, he considers the composite man <note>original: "τὸν σύνθετον ἄνθρωπον"</note>, so in the tenth book, regarding theoretical blessedness, he considers the mind <note>original: "τὸν νοῦν"</note>, which he calls the "man most of all" <note>original: "μάλιστα ἄνθρωπον"</note>.

### X L I X.

From all of which, I think, it appears clearer than the midday sun, as the saying goes, that it is most true what Cicero used to say: that the entire authority of philosophy, that is, of the doctrine concerning life and morals, consists in attaining a blessed life, and that therefore its dignity and excellence are supreme and admirable.
