For we see in the states of all Republics that various kinds of men are found, who by their own inclination depart into different classes, as it were, such that one constitutes the illustrious and wealthy; another the humbler and poorer; and a third, finally, those who walk the middle path and exist as a sort of temperament between the illustrious and the poor. But by what reason these classes are to be composed, so that the city may be rendered quiet, and each part of the city may rejoice in its own happiness—this is the task, this is the labor.

<margin>5. Pol. 1.</margin>
The illustrious or wealthy persuade themselves that, because they surpass the rest in splendor, they are simply superior and that, by right and merit, unequal things are owed to the unequal. Conversely, the poor, measuring all things by liberty, concede no inequality. By this vain persuasion of men, as if justice is not attributed to each one's own, the state of Republics is most greatly changed, a fact already proven long ago in excellent fashion by Aristotle.

Writers record of Solon that, in order to make the citizens friendly to himself and to be declared legislator by them, he said: he would propose laws equal to all, and for that reason, the decision of proposing laws was permitted to him by the highest zeal and will of all. For the common people thought he spoke of the middle of the affair—to borrow this from the schools—while the aristocrats thought he spoke of the middle of the person. If citizens remain at these precipices and are unwilling to remit anything of their own right, which they boast of so laboriously, it is easily evident that contentions of this kind are joined with the internal destruction of the Republic, and do not cease until one party is oppressed.

Truly, neither party, whether the poor or the wealthy be considered, is accustomed to derive equality and inequality from true principles. It is a common assertion of philosophers that only virtue makes a distinction between the plebeians and the illustrious, so that the latter may shine forth among the rest, while the former live content with their humbler lot. But who could persuade this to minds that are blinded by self-love and agitated on every side? Nor is the matter so clear that it no longer has any doubt.

<margin>6. Pol. c. 3.</margin>
Aristotle himself, in dealing with Democracy, confesses that it is very difficult to organize the people in such a way that all share equally in the communion of rights. For although the humbler sort look to nothing else in this equality of theirs than that they not be oppressed by the wealthier, nevertheless you will notice the diverse purposes, pursuits, propensities, inclinations, inventions, arts, and rules of the more powerful.

So that we may not dwell longer on this question, and may explain in few words the mind of the philosopher, which is found more than once in his work <term>Politico</term> <gloss>Politics</gloss>, <pb n="13"/>these things must be added: that harmony can certainly be obtained between the poor and the wealthy if the legislator always has greater care for the middle citizens than for the extremes, for then the Republic will be maintained as if in equilibrium. If this proceeds less according to one's wish, another path must be undertaken, namely, that the laws themselves be properly mixed, that both parties preside over affairs, and that each concedes something to the other. Let other duties of humanity also be added, and signs of benevolence, whether in gesture or in conversation; let one party promote the advantages of the other and decline its disadvantages; perhaps such a Republic will fare well enough in this way, provided that no one can complain of being oppressed or despised, but all live among themselves with equal right.

What we have said so far regarding the mixing of the Popular state with the Aristocratic is explained more fully by Greek and Latin writers, who treat Democratic and Aristocratic matters even to the point of nausea, beyond the political works of Aristotle and Plato. For to repeat our opinion again: among the ancients, a Popular state was never found unless it was tempered by the arts of the Optimates <gloss>Aristocrats</gloss>. Not to mention at present the changes and various attempts by which the Attic Republic was vexed. Therefore, Thucydides, Demosthenes, and Isocrates must be diligently studied. In Roman history, Halycarnasseus, Plutarch, and Dionysius are to be commended; but no one surpasses the labors of Livy in learning the characters of the Aristocrats.

§. 13. The signs for recognizing the state of a Republic are not rarely confused. If power were contained by external apparatus and splendor, the King of Poland, whom the nobles venerate like slaves, would certainly surpass all Princes of Europe in Majesty. Yet his power is enclosed within narrow limits. For it is very little that is permitted to him in ecclesiastical matters; it is a crime to condemn a knight to death, except in the assemblies; concerning waging war or entering into a treaty, the care is common with the Senate; to promulgate new laws, to command an extraordinary tribute, to coin money, to nominate a successor, and other things that most adorn the Royal dignity, he cannot do even in the Senate without the consent of the rest of the nobility. And to conclude in a few words: the rights of Majesty are exercised by the aristocrats rather than by the King. Cromer has executed this diligently and happily.

<pb n="24"/>you will find yourself admonished, and you will be excited toward a surpassing desire for all honorable arts. Whatever is contrary to these arts, you will cast aside and despise. You will judge those things unworthy not only of the man you ought to show yourself to be in the future, and the kind of man we all augur you will be, but unworthy of any man at all. You have always lived praiseworthily before this; there was modesty in the boy, there is integrity in the youth, there is a perfect sense of duty, and a knowledge of things to be sought and avoided. The occasion seemed to be lacking in which you might display yourself. It has been bestowed by heaven, the greatest of all, by the singular counsel of the supreme Pontiff, Paul IV. Since he is the brother of your father, since he has loved you not a little from your earliest years, and since he is accustomed to embrace all his own with a certain incredible affection, he nevertheless followed certain other principles in honoring you. He gave the honor not to kinship or to family, but to you yourself, you who strive to illuminate the family name; and as the beginnings show themselves, the outcome will confirm the endeavor. Behold, Alfonso, you have a field in which your virtue, acquired by vigils and already confirmed by the habit of acting well, may run. This is that very province most worthy of your genius, your best thoughts, and your studies, toward which you were exercising yourself, and toward which your cares were directed. Show what the excellence of your will, and indeed of your industry, is; and bring forth from your soul those brilliant things that you have gathered from boyhood, so that you may reflect the ancient glory of your race and the present virtue of your house. It is not, believe me, a labor for one who thinks well to act 
<pb n="25"/>well. For that which is placed within ourselves does not depend on anything else, nor is it taken from outside; in that regard, what stands in the way of the deed following the will? Now, virtue itself invites, entices, and affects those who are devoted to it with every desire and every reward; and I do not doubt that the excellent force of your spirit will overcome all difficulties and all human obstacles. Therefore, I congratulate you on your own account for that highest degree of honor to which the divine wisdom of the Pontiff Paul has raised you. But I am moved somewhat more by the public cause, which you will defend throughout your life, having been entrusted to you along with that dignity and commended to you, especially now when it is in such great need of the help of such men. In you, there will be a most firm protection situated against injustice and impiety. If these things seem great and glorious to you, you must so prepare and moderate your spirit that you refer nothing to yourself, that you claim nothing for yourself, and that you expect nothing from yourself. Think that all things have flowed from God, who is the perennial and eternal fountain of all goods. For we, as ourselves, are nothing; but we are something, and indeed a great deal, insofar as we can be from God and through God. Farewell.

On the impediments of this work, on the part of the artist's body. Chapter IV.

We have already determined for you, in a general way, the impediments to this work. Now, however, we shall address you with more specific discourse in this chapter, and we shall narrate to you all those impediments most fully and in order. We say, therefore: that if anyone does not have his organs complete, he will not be able to reach the completion of this work by himself, such as if he were blind or maimed in his extremities, since he is not helped by the members through which this art is perfected, as if they were ministers of nature. But if the artist’s body is weak and sick, like the bodies of those suffering from fevers or leprosy, whose limbs are failing, or those who labor in the extremes of life, or the decrepit old, he will not arrive at the completion of the art. By these natural impotencies of the body, therefore, the artist is hindered in his intention.

On the impediments on the part of the artist's soul. Chapter V.

We have provided you with one chapter in which we narrated, in absolute and manifest speech, the impediments depending on the part of the artist's body. It remains for us to narrate briefly the impediments on the part of the soul itself, which most greatly hinder the completion of this work. We say, therefore, that he who does not have a natural talent and a soul that subtly scrutinizes natural principles, the foundations of nature, and the crafts that can follow nature in the properties of its action, will not find the true root of this most precious science. Such are many who have a stiff neck, void of talent in every investigation, who can scarcely understand common speech, and who learn even common works with difficulty. Besides these, we also find many who have a soul that easily opines any fantasy whatsoever, but what they believe they have found to be true is entirely fantastic, deviant from reason, full of error, and removed from natural principles, since their brain, filled with many vapors, cannot receive the true intention of natural things. There are also, besides these, others who have a mobile soul, shifting from opinion to opinion and from will to will, like those who now believe this and desire the same, without any foundation of reason. Yet, a little while after, they believe something else and desire something else similarly. And these are so mobile that they can scarcely complete the least part of that which they intend, but rather leave it diminished. There are likewise others who cannot see any truth from natural things, no more than beasts, like those who are deranged, insane, and children. There are also others who contemn the science and do not believe it exists; this science likewise contemns them and repels them from the end of this most precious work. And there are those who are slaves, serving money, while affirming this admirable science, yet they fear to interpose the necessary expenses; therefore, even if they affirm it and investigate it according to reason, they do not arrive at the experience of the work because of greed for money. To these, therefore, this science of ours does not reach. For how would one who is ignorant, or who has neglected to investigate the science, easily arrive at it?

On external impediments, hindering the work of this art. Chapter VI.

We have reduced to two chapters all the impediments delaying the end of this art, which are from the radical principles according to the nature of the artist of this most precious business. It is necessary, therefore, that we finally narrate the impediments coming from the outside, and from contingent fortunes and chances, by which this most glorious work is hindered. We see, therefore, some who are astute and talented, not at all ignorant of the works of nature and its <pb n="139"/> principles and works, in which there is also an investigation that is not fantastic, in all things that are regulated by the movements and actions of nature within the lunar circle. These, however, oppressed by extreme poverty, from lack of funds, are nonetheless compelled to postpone this excellent <term>magisterium</term> <gloss>mastery/the Great Work</gloss>. There are also many others besides those just mentioned, curious, detained by various cares and anxieties of this world, occupying themselves entirely with every secular business, from whom this precious science of ours again flees. Now, therefore, it is sufficiently clear to you from the aforementioned chapters what the impediments are that distract from this art.

<note>A decorative drop cap C begins the paragraph.</note> We conclude, therefore, from what has already been said, that it is necessary for the artist of this work to be learned and perfect in the sciences of natural philosophy, because no matter how much money and naturally profound talent and desire he has for this art, he will not acquire its end unless he has attained natural philosophy through doctrine, because that which is not attained by natural talent is assisted in its defect by doctrine. It is necessary, therefore, that the artist be helped by the deepest scrutiny and industry. For because of doctrine, no matter how much science he has acquired, unless he is also helped by natural industry, he will not be invited to such precious banquets. For he would amend his error in an instant by his industry, for which he would not know how to apply a remedy if he were founded only on doctrine; and likewise, he would correct an error in an instant from science acquired through natural doctrine, which he could not avoid by industry alone; for art is helped by talent, and talent is likewise helped by art. And it is likewise necessary for him to have a constant will in the work, so that he does not presume to attempt this one moment and that the next; for our art does not consist in a multitude of things, nor is it perfected in them. There is, indeed, one stone, one medicine, in which the <term>magisterium</term> <gloss>mastery</gloss> consists, to which we add no extraneous thing, nor do we diminish, except that we remove what is superfluous in preparation. It is also necessary for him to insist upon the work steadily until its consummation, so that he does not leave the work truncated; for he would acquire neither science nor profit from a diminished work, but rather despair and loss. It is also expedient that he not be ignorant of the principles and main roots of this art, which belong to the essence of the work; for he who ignores the beginning will not find the end. And we shall tell you all those principles in complete speech, and sufficiently open and manifest to the prudent, according to the requirement of this art of ours. It is likewise expedient for the artist to be temperate and slow to anger, lest suddenly, because of the impulse of anger, he dissipate and destroy what has already been begun. Likewise, let him guard his money, and let him not presumptuously distribute it in vain, lest, if by chance he does not find the art, he be left in misery and the despair of poverty; or lest, perchance, when he has already approached the end of this <term>magisterium</term> <gloss>mastery</gloss> through his investigation, his funds be consumed, and the poor man violently abandons the true end because of poverty. Just as those who, in the beginning of their investigation, prodigally exterminate their entire treasure, and when they are near the end, they have nothing further from which to labor. Whence such men are buried in sorrow twofold: both because they dissipated their money on useless things, and because they lose the most noble science which they were about to have investigated. For it is not necessary to consume your goods, since for a vile price (if you have not ignored the principles of the art, and have correctly understood those things which we have handed down to you) you will arrive at the completion of the <term>magisterium</term> <gloss>mastery</gloss>. If, therefore, you have lost your money by not heeding our warnings, which we have written for you in this booklet, open and manifest, do not unfairly gnaw at us nor heap blasphemies upon us, but impute it to your own ignorance and presumption. Therefore, this science does not suit the poor or the needy well, but rather it is</translation>

A danger no less to be feared from that Avarice is perceived in private matters, namely, when either individuals among the Magistrates, or the whole order of Magistrates, draw the goods of private citizens to themselves by force, deceit, and under some pretext.

## XIII.
Indeed, since this **Avarice** exists as a frequent cause of ruin above others, a King will act most safely if he demands small tributes in parts, with the consent of the estates, having demonstrated the necessity of the treasury, keeps the ordinary ones, and does not easily command new ones. Adam Contzen, in Book 9 of his *Politics*, chapter 8, § 4. Especially since, among Princes and those governing the Commonwealth, no vice is found more hideous than **Avarice**. *For to hold the Commonwealth for profit is not only shameful, but also wicked and nefarious,* says Cicero. Indeed, it even fights against nature; hence the same man says:

> To take something away from another, and to increase one's own advantage by the discomfort of a human being, is more contrary to nature than death, than poverty, than pain, or than other things that can happen either to the body or to external affairs. For it removes the fellowship and society of men: If we are so affected that each person despoils or violates another for his own benefit, it is necessary that this society of the human race, which is most in accordance with nature, be torn asunder.

## XIV.
Not rarely does **Ambition** of those who hold the scepter usually produce a pestilence in Commonwealths equal to, or indeed almost greater than, **Avarice**; from it, as if from a Lernaean hydra of evils, besides wars, the torch of which it is, countless other evils also spring forth, and it often tends to bring the greatest pestilence and destruction upon the ambitious men themselves. For although **Avarice** also exists as a frequent cause of war, it is far <pb n="10"/> more persistent in it is Ambition. *Indeed, their own wicked causes drag each man into battles, yet the lust for ruling holds the primacy,* says Adam Contzen, in *Book 10 of his Politics, chapter 8.* Hence Thucydides rightly said: *The cause of all evils is the desire for power arising from ambition.* And Polybius, a most serious writer, says that after some city has overcome and struggled through many and great dangers, and has already risen to sovereignty and power: *It is manifest that where fickle fortune is not used with moderation and has fixed its seat therein, luxury creeps into the morals, and ambition and stubbornness into the minds of men, both concerning the magistracy and concerning others: where these evils have once prevailed, they will be the beginning of change for the worse, through honors sought or denied by ambition.*

XV. Many, however, only judge themselves happy in every respect when, by adding new provinces to the old, they can expand their Kingdom, ignorant that, according to Seneca's 113th Epistle, *to rule over oneself is the greatest empire.* Nor do they attend to the very certain destruction of their provinces resulting from that: for while they are not content with their own boundaries and covet many provinces, they often lose those which they have already placed in safety. By the example of the cities of Greece, which, while each desired to rule, all lost their empire. *Justinus, Book 8, chapter 1.*

XVI. Therefore, that saying of Thucydides in his description of the Corcyrean sedition is from the mouth of Truth: *The cause of all evils is the desire for power and ambition.* From these affections every calamity is born. Thence atrociously waged wars have continued in a perpetual series from the beginning of the world. Inflamed by this, Alexander pursued all of Asia with fire and sword, and Cyrus had previously devastated Ionia. Demosthenes is said to have once said: if two paths were open; one to the underworld, the other to the throne, he would choose the one that led to the underworld. I believe he did not speak sincerely, but it nonetheless shows the most miserable ambition of those who, through labors, dangers, and wounds, ascend to a slippery, tottering summit, agitated by lightning and winds, where one can neither stand firm nor depart from there.

You might not incongruously call its daughter or sister <term>PICTORIA</term> <gloss>the art of painting</gloss>, the true and genuine one in which Zeuxis, Apelles, and Parrhasius once excelled, and in our age, Dürer. Indeed, other craftsmen—sculptors, goldsmiths, architects, military commanders, captains, and musketeers—cannot lack these same proportions for the skillful discharge of projectiles toward fixed targets.

L. I come finally to <term>CANONICA</term> <gloss>music theory</gloss> or <term>MUSICA</term> <gloss>music</gloss>, specifically <term>HARMONICA</term> <gloss>harmonics</gloss>, which is the science of sound estimable by number. That is, it is the contemplation and practice of harmony or order composed from sounds and intervals, with the considered ratio of perceived harmonies, and with the judgment of the senses applied everywhere, so that the ears might seem to have been placed before the mind, according to Plato. Whatever this <term>HARMONICA</term> theory teaches, it demonstrates everything by mathematical principles. Among the ancients, many excelled in this, such as Euclid, Aristoxenus, Ptolemy, and Boethius, the musicians.

LI. But from those theoretical foundations, another <term>PRACTICA</term> <gloss>practical application</gloss> composes songs which possess grace in sound or harmony and elegance in singing. In this, many emulate the supreme artist Orlando <note>referring to Orlando di Lasso</note>.

LI. Finally, <term>ASTROLOGIA</term> <gloss>astrology</gloss> also does not wish to be separated from the mixed mathematical disciplines. For astronomy itself is present, whether as a servant or a mistress, teaching to what end those astronomical observations and contemplations may be useful, if we look at the distinction of times, just as it has wonderfully and uniquely aided us in <pb n="21"/>chronographic matters. For from the diligent consideration of the situations, positions, and configurations of the stars and planets, it conjectures and divines certain events, as much in elementary matters, such as storms and the like, which we call <term>PROGNOSTICA</term> <gloss>forecasting</gloss>, as in humans, such as matters of life, diseases and death, temperament, character, morals, and the like, which is called <term>GENETHLIACA</term> <gloss>natal astrology</gloss>, often true, often false, often vain, often impious. There is no need to reject it, if many superstitions of the Arabs and many other less solid minor precepts are pruned away, and only those things are retained which admit either reason or experience, or both together.

LIII. In this class, others count both <term>CHIROMANTIA</term> <gloss>palmistry</gloss> and <term>METOPOSCOPIA</term> <gloss>physiognomy by the forehead</gloss>, of which the former teaches the method of recognizing signs and characters in a person’s hand and judging them skillfully; the latter, however, is the art of divining from the forehead. Of these, we have primary patrons and writers: Taisnier, Johannes de Indagine, Rothmann, and Thaddaeus Haggetius.

LIV. Truly, we do not wish to either highly commend or harshly impugn these in this place, lest we slip outside this scope of mathematics into the camp of the physicists to argue about signatures.
</translation>

**We therefore maintain, not inconveniently, that it is not a peculiar form, but the specific and communicated power of matter, that possesses the capacity to individuate within itself.**

We have not yet investigated with sufficient clarity what that thing is by which a man is what he is, as Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), Renaissance scholar</note> says in *Exercises*, section 6, number 1. But the Theorem says that it is form. Since the office of form is to bestow being, quiddity <note>the "whatness" or essence of a thing</note>, and the totality of quiddity, as attested by Armando de Bello Visu <note>Armandus de Bellovisu, a 14th-century Dominican theologian</note> in *Treatise 2 on Causes*, chapter 142, a distinction must be considered between giving being and the act of a thing. This being is twofold, and therefore the act is also twofold: one is the being of <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence</gloss>, <pb n="10"/> the other of <term>hyparxis</term> <gloss>existence</gloss>. Therefore, the act can also be taken either for the degree of essence which form bestows, since the form of an animal constitutes an animal and the form of a human constitutes a human, or for the act of existence outside the soul, which the form likewise bestows, though not just any form, but only that final and specific one, which is directed to no other thing than to make the thing exist individually. This is what Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> explains as skillfully as he does elegantly in Part 1 of the *Summa*, Question 3, articles 2 and 3, and in other places, when he says: "Being is the actuality of form, for form implies potentiality before it is placed into being; therefore being is compared to essence as act is to potency." ->X.<-

The <term>constitutio, de expeditione Romana</term> <gloss>constitution concerning the Roman expedition</gloss> of Charles the Fat, for the year 890, is spurious and devoid of both credit and truth. Even if this were not already apparent from the clause added to the constitution, which clearly betrays its defect, the mere insertion of the word <term>Feudi</term> <gloss>fief/feudal tenure</gloss>, and the remaining character of the style, which is abhorrent to that age, would clearly demonstrate it.

->XI.<-

The <term>constitutio de torneamentis</term> <gloss>constitution concerning tournaments</gloss> of Henry the Fowler, the first King of Germany among the Saxons, for the year 938, is supposititious. This is because the style is repugnant and does not conform to the conditions of the times, and also because there are named in it circles not yet known and illustrious dignities not yet instituted, such as the Burgraviate, the Palatinate of Thuringia, and the Principality of Pomerania, not to mention other signs of forgery.

->XII.<-

The origin of the Electors is not correctly ascribed to the age of Otto the Great, as done by <term>Christoph. Gewoldus</term>, a Bavarian Councilor and otherwise a very learned man, who undoubtedly followed <term>Martinus Polonus</term>, whom many believe to have been the primary author of that opinion.

->XIII.<-

The tradition regarding <term>Fridericus Aenobarbus</term> <gloss>Frederick Barbarossa</gloss> being trampled underfoot by the Pope <term>Alexander III</term> must be deservedly rejected, just as the tale that the common people relate concerning his death, that he was drowned in a river, must be counted among fables. For the contrary is clear from the <term>Diario Thagenonis</term> <gloss>Diary of Thageno</gloss>, in which no such thing is reported. As far as I know, only <term>Otto de Sancto Blasio</term> <gloss>Otto of St. Blasius</gloss> stands <pb n="10"/><note>Small leaf-like typographic ornaments flanking the page number.</note> for the opinion of the masses. The others, whoever they may be, are either silent or dissent.

### XIV.

That Hatto, Archbishop of Mainz, was devoured by mice is false, and the argument concerning the tower still visible on the Rhine today, which they generally bring forward to confirm their opinion, is entirely inept and in no way holds the weight of proof.

### XV.

The common opinion is that the Emperor Henry VII of Luxembourg was taken off by Francis Paulinus, a monk of the Order of St. Bernard, with a poisoned sacramental host; and it is not without reason that one doubts it, because Conrad Vecerius, who described his life most diligently, recorded no such thing.

### XVI.

It cannot be proven by certain and undoubted monuments that the Emperor Charles IV alienated the Kingdom of Burgundy Transjurana, or Arelatense. Nor are the assertors of the contrary opinion able to produce or demonstrate a document of such alienation, although it is otherwise agreed that he was a little too liberal not only toward the French but also toward the Rhenish Princes.

### XVII.

<margin>Germ. c. 28. in the book on the Origin of Bohemia.</margin>
Those who think that the Bohemians received their name from a certain King Bohemus are absurd. This also encompasses the error of those who write that they were a Gallic people, among whom are Cornelius Tacitus and Johannes Matthias à Sudetis, to whom Melchior Goldastus otherwise owes a great deal. But there are just causes that exhort us not to agree with them.</translation>

<keywords>Charles the Fat, Henry the Fowler, Frederick Barbarossa, Hatto of Mainz, Henry VII of Luxembourg, Charles IV, Bohemians, historical criticism, forgery</keywords>

Even if this were not already apparent from the clause added to the constitution, which clearly betrays its defect, the mere insertion of the word <term>Feudi</term> <gloss>fief/feudal tenure</gloss>, and the remaining character of the style, which is abhorrent to that age, would clearly demonstrate it.

->XI.<-

The <term>constitutio de torneamentis</term> <gloss>constitution concerning tournaments</gloss> of Henry the Fowler, the first King of Germany among the Saxons, for the year 938, is supposititious. This is because the style is repugnant and does not conform to the conditions of the times, and also because there are named in it circles not yet known and illustrious dignities not yet instituted, such as the Burgraviate, the Palatinate of Thuringia, and the Principality of Pomerania, not to mention other signs of forgery.

->XII.<-

The origin of the Electors is not correctly ascribed to the age of Otto the Great, as done by <term>Christoph. Gewoldus</term>, a Bavarian Councilor and otherwise a very learned man, who undoubtedly followed <term>Martinus Polonus</term>, whom many believe to have been the primary author of that opinion.

->XIII.<-

The tradition regarding <term>Fridericus Aenobarbus</term> <gloss>Frederick Barbarossa</gloss> being trampled underfoot by the Pope <term>Alexander III</term> must be deservedly rejected, just as the tale that the common people relate concerning his death, that he was drowned in a river, must be counted among fables. For the contrary is clear from the <term>Diario Thagenonis</term> <gloss>Diary of Thageno</gloss>, in which no such thing is reported. As far as I know, only <term>Otto de Sancto Blasio</term> <gloss>Otto of St. Blasius</gloss> stands
pages.10:
<note>Small leaf-like typographic ornaments flanking the page number.</note> for the opinion of the masses. The others, whoever they may be, are either silent or dissent.

### XIV.

That Hatto, Archbishop of Mainz, was devoured by mice is false, and the argument concerning the tower still visible on the Rhine today, which they generally bring forward to confirm their opinion, is entirely inept and in no way holds the weight of proof.

### XV.

The common opinion is that the Emperor Henry VII of Luxembourg was taken off by Francis Paulinus, a monk of the Order of St. Bernard, with a poisoned sacramental host; and it is not without reason that one doubts it, because Conrad Vecerius, who described his life most diligently, recorded no such thing.

### XVI.

It cannot be proven by certain and undoubted monuments that the Emperor Charles IV alienated the Kingdom of Burgundy Transjurana, or Arelatense. Nor are the assertors of the contrary opinion able to produce or demonstrate a document of such alienation, although it is otherwise agreed that he was a little too liberal not only toward the French but also toward the Rhenish Princes.

### XVII.

<margin>Germ. c. 28. in the book on the Origin of Bohemia.</margin>
Those who think that the Bohemians received their name from a certain King Bohemus are absurd. This also encompasses the error of those who write that they were a Gallic people, among whom are Cornelius Tacitus and Johannes Matthias à Sudetis, to whom Melchior Goldastus otherwise owes a great deal. But there are just causes that exhort us not to agree with them.

Who Samson was, can be gathered from the preceding, namely a Nazirite, who from birth was dedicated to GOD as a redeemer of Israel. (2) That they should not shear their heads, but nourish their hair throughout the entire Nazirite state. (3) That they should not contaminate themselves with funeral mourning, and this not even at the death of a father. Such a vow Paul also seems to have had, as in Acts 21. Thus, Samson was a holy and public person from his very birth, and he was also such in his death. (2) What Samson did, not a few things have already been said about that in the doctrine regarding the object; namely, after he had judged the Israelite people for some time, he was captured by the Philistines, deprived of his eyes, and thrown into prison. Where he recovered the grace of GOD and the virtue of his Nazirite state, and thus, in his recovered vocation, he redeemed the people of Israel and liberated his fatherland from the enemies by whom it was oppressed. He fought bravely, he conquered, and he sealed his victory with his own <pb n="19"/>private death. For three thousand men were in the upper part of the house. Therefore, the place was not narrow; which proves all the more that those extraordinary powers were so immense that they must be considered plainly incomparable. (4) By what aids he did this is clear from the prayers, namely by supernatural aid, the special grace of GOD, and plain divine assistance. (5) Finally, it must be seen how that man of GOD, the judge of the people and thus a public person, liberated his own people, and avenged the deprivation of his eyes and the injury brought upon himself and GOD through this. Surely, he seized the occasion given to him: for when he saw that all hope of victory was vain without his own death, he preferred to perish in mutual destruction rather than leave the glory of GOD stained, the fatherland without liberty, and the enemies without vengeance. Thus, he sought victory with concomitant death, as if called to it, and he preferred to return the life deposited and granted to him to GOD and his fatherland, rather than to retain it unjustly.

->§. 19.<-

Samson, therefore, did not kill himself properly, as he would have done if he had stabbed himself with a sword, or had dashed his head against a column; but he allowed himself to be crushed with the enemy. Nor did he kill himself by moral imputation, because primarily he intended to kill the Philistines and to seek vengeance for his eyes. Secondarily, however, and only permissively, he involved himself in that same slaughter, which he could not evade. > *Samson conquered himself in death; and although he was incomparable in this life, yet in death he conquered himself, and bore an insuperable spirit, so that he despised, and held as if for nothing, the end of life which is fearful to all.*

### X.

The theologians in the villages of Bärsdorf and Cuniz judged no differently concerning Krentzheim, and in the sight of all, when the MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE, moved by their prayers, around this ninety-first year, called the pastors of the Duchy of Legnica into a public judgment with Krentzheim, which was instituted on the fifteenth day of January, they were consistent in voices and writings in this opinion. Acts, page 87. Indeed, our man also responded with many words to the charges brought against him and attempted to clear himself of the crime, but the Prince by no means approved of the response, and he sent the interposed testimony of his contrary will, presented in writing, back to the Academy of Frankfurt. Krentzheim, having been summoned to the hall on the twentieth day of June, and with the permission of the Judge, who was the Prince's Prefect, took home the sentences of this University and the Questions, which had been sent back from Frankfurt on the third day of May of the same year, and on the seventh hour of the morning of the following day, he returned them with a written and speciously colored

<pb n="11"/>response. *Acts, pages 102, 103.* But this plausible response was vehemently protested by all, for the fact that both the explanations and the modes and formulas of explaining the Article concerning the Holy Supper, which *Martin Gosky*, formerly pastor of the Marian church, had excerpted from Krentzheim’s orations delivered in the assemblies of pastors and had publicly read aloud in the presence of all the pastors, argued him to be entirely suspect and taught [as much]. Wherefore the Frankfurt theologians were consulted by the Most Illustrious Prince for a third time through letters written on the eleventh day of July; when, however, Krentzheim had responded with little integrity even in this writing to those things which were asked, they could not acquiesce to him, but on the thirty-first day of June <note>Note: There is no 31st of June; likely an error in original text for July or June 30th.</note>, having transmitted their judgments to the Prince, they again judged him suspected of Calvinism. *Acts, pages 109, 110b.*

XI. Scarcely had this judgment been sent back when not only did the reformation instituted by the Administrator of the Electorate of Saxony, Frederick William, reach the ears of the Most Illustrious Prince, but he was simultaneously made certain that certain letters of Leonhard Krentzheim, written to Master Urbanus Pierius, pastor of Wittenberg and General Superintendent of the Electorate of Saxony—who was himself vehemently suspected of Calvinism <note>(k)</note>—had been found in his study and kept in the archives of Duke FREDERICK WILLIAM. Provoked by these, the MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE decided to refer this controversy to the Saxon theologians as well, and in order that Krentzheim might be evidently convinced of his errors, the Most Illustrious Prince first most lovingly demanded his letters from the Administrator twice, and upon obtaining them through the second letter, he read them avidly, and at the same time discovered in them the most certain indications of a perverse doctrine. *Acts, page 116.* Therefore, after FREDERICK IV saw that this dissension could in no way be suppressed by tolerating and prolonging it, but would cause great detriment to the Church unless it were quickly appeased, he called Master Martin Mirus and Master Georg Müller from Saxony to compose this controversy in letters written on the VI of February in the year [15]93 to the Most Illustrious Duke of Saxony, Frederick William. *Acts, pages 141, 142.* However, there departed for Legnica, by the order and mandate of Duke FREDERICK WILLIAM, Master Aegidius Hunnius, formerly a most celebrated Doctor and Professor of Theology at this Wittenberg Academy, and Wolfgang Mamphrasius, Superintendent of Wurzen, to whom our man was ordered to render an account of his doctrine in a public colloquy on the very ample stone floor of the Castle, to which Duke FREDERICK IV had summoned the councilors, the two delegates of the Oels people, the leaders of the Equestrian Order and the urban Senate, and all the pastors of this Duchy, with many from the lower classes looking on. The theologians in the villages of Bärsdorf and Cuniz judged no differently concerning Krentzheim, and in the sight of all, when the MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE, moved by their prayers, around this ninety-first year, called the pastors of the Duchy of Legnica into a public judgment with Krentzheim, which was instituted on the fifteenth day of January, they were consistent in voices and writings in this opinion. Acts, page 87. Indeed, our man also responded with many words to the charges brought against him and attempted to clear himself of the crime, but the Prince by no means approved of the response, and he sent the interposed testimony of his contrary will, presented in writing, back to the Academy of Frankfurt. Krentzheim, having been summoned to the hall on the twentieth day of June, and with the permission of the Judge, who was the Prince's Prefect, took home the sentences of this University and the Questions, which had been sent back from Frankfurt on the third day of May of the same year, and on the seventh hour of the morning of the following day, he returned them with a written and speciously colored
pages.11:
response. *Acts, pages 102, 103.* But this plausible response was vehemently protested by all, for the fact that both the explanations and the modes and formulas of explaining the Article concerning the Holy Supper, which *Martin Gosky*, formerly pastor of the Marian church, had excerpted from Krentzheim’s orations delivered in the assemblies of pastors and had publicly read aloud in the presence of all the pastors, argued him to be entirely suspect and taught [as much]. Wherefore the Frankfurt theologians were consulted by the Most Illustrious Prince for a third time through letters written on the eleventh day of July; when, however, Krentzheim had responded with little integrity even in this writing to those things which were asked, they could not acquiesce to him, but on the thirty-first day of June <note>Note: There is no 31st of June; likely an error in original text for July or June 30th.</note>, having transmitted their judgments to the Prince, they again judged him suspected of Calvinism. *Acts, pages 109, 110b.*

Scarcely had this judgment been sent back when not only did the reformation instituted by the Administrator of the Electorate of Saxony, Frederick William, reach the ears of the Most Illustrious Prince, but he was simultaneously made certain that certain letters of Leonhard Krentzheim, written to Master Urbanus Pierius, pastor of Wittenberg and General Superintendent of the Electorate of Saxony—who was himself vehemently suspected of Calvinism <note>(k)</note>—had been found in his study and kept in the archives of Duke FREDERICK WILLIAM. Provoked by these, the MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE decided to refer this controversy to the Saxon theologians as well, and in order that Krentzheim might be evidently convinced of his errors, the Most Illustrious Prince first most lovingly demanded his letters from the Administrator twice, and upon obtaining them through the second letter, he read them avidly, and at the same time discovered in them the most certain indications of a perverse doctrine. *Acts, page 116.* Therefore, after FREDERICK IV saw that this dissension could in no way be suppressed by tolerating and prolonging it, but would cause great detriment to the Church unless it were quickly appeased, he called Master Martin Mirus and Master Georg Müller from Saxony to compose this controversy in letters written on the VI of February in the year [15]93 to the Most Illustrious Duke of Saxony, Frederick William. *Acts, pages 141, 142.* However, there departed for Legnica, by the order and mandate of Duke FREDERICK WILLIAM, Master Aegidius Hunnius, formerly a most celebrated Doctor and Professor of Theology at this Wittenberg Academy, and Wolfgang Mamphrasius, Superintendent of Wurzen, to whom our man was ordered to render an account of his doctrine in a public colloquy on the very ample stone floor of the Castle, to which Duke FREDERICK IV had summoned the councilors, the two delegates of the Oels people, the leaders of the Equestrian Order and the urban Senate, and all the pastors of this Duchy, with many from the lower classes looking on. For both a difference and a univocal term have a genus, and they differ through something of their own—namely, a specific difference. But some Disparates grasp neither of those. Indeed, God and primary matter are counted among Disparates, but yet they have no univocal genus, nor do they differ through something of their own. For the entire essence of God is distinguished from the essence of primary matter; whence they are named by metaphysicians not as differences, but as diverse things. # PARADOX VII.

## The <term>Lunula</term> <gloss>lune or crescent-shaped figure</gloss> (a part of a circle), although it has long since been reduced to a square space by Hippocrates of Chios, the <term>quadrature</term> <gloss>squaring</gloss> of the circle has nevertheless not yet been discovered to this day.

### DECLARATION.

<term>Tetragonism</term> <gloss>the squaring of a figure</gloss>, or the <term>quadrature</term> of the circle, has hitherto been attempted by two principal methods, either geometrically through lines, or arithmetically through numbers. By the former method, the <term>lunula</term> has long since been reduced to a square space by Hippocrates of Chios; however, the circle, by no means, neither geometrically nor arithmetically, has been able to be squared to this day.

### DEMONSTRATION.

That the quadrature of the <term>lunulae</term> was most correctly discovered by Hippocrates of Chios, no one, if they have properly grasped his demonstration, will deny; for it is as follows: Let a circle *a, b, c, d* be drawn, and upon its diameter *b, c* let a square *b, e, f, c* be constructed, whose <term>diagonius</term> <gloss>diagonal</gloss> <pb n="13"/> is *b, d, f* (see Figure VI). Let the semidiameter *g, i, d* also be drawn, perpendicular to *b, e*, which will cut in half both the semicircle *b, d, c* and the diagonal *b, d, f* at point *d*. Therefore, having made *d* the center and *d, b* the interval, let another circle be described through points *b, e, f*, and let the straight line *d, c* be connected. Since, however, in the right-angled triangle *b, e, f*, the side *b, f* subtends the right angle *b, e, f*, its square will be double the square of *b, e* or *e, f* according to the 47th [proposition] of the first [book] of Euclid. And consequently, the circle *b, e, f* will be double the circle *a, b, d, c* according to the 2nd [proposition] of the twelfth [book] of Euclid, and the semicircle *b, e, f* will be double the semicircle *b, a, c*, and the quadrant *b, g, d, c* will be equal to the same semicircle *b, a, c*. With the common segment *b, g, c, i* therefore removed, there remains the lunula *b, a, c, g*, equal to the triangle *b, i, d*. If that triangle is squared according to the last [proposition] of the second [book] of Euclid, the lunula *b, a, c, g* will be squared. But that the circle has not been reduced to a square space to this day, neither through lines nor through numbers, is clearly evident from the most recent writings of geometers. Hippocrates indeed persuaded himself that by the same reasoning with which he had completed the quadrature of the lunula (a part of the circle), the whole circle could also be squared, and therefore he attributed to himself the very invention of tetragonism, or the quadrature of the circle. But in truth, as ingeniously as he had reduced the lunula to a square space, so foully did he hallucinate in squaring the circle, as is plain to anyone from Father Caspar Schott’s <term>Technica Curiosa</term> <gloss>Curious Technique</gloss>, Book VIII, §. 1, my page 600, 601, and Christopher Clavius's *Mathematical Works*, Volume II, Book VIII, page 189. Indeed, it is credible, says Blancanus in the *Mathematical Places of Aristotle*, that Hippocrates recognized this fallacy (which he used in squaring the circle), and concealed it on account of the subtlety of the discovery. The same thing happens with the most recent attempts at the quadrature of the circle, in which, when properly examined, a paralogism <note>logical fallacy</note> is for the most part detected, so that many today judge the tetragonism to be absolutely impossible; see the <term>Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensium</term> <gloss>Acts of the Learned of Leipzig</gloss>, Month of September, Year 1687, page 524. Therefore, although the lunula (a part of the circle) has long since been reduced to a square space, the quadrature of the circle has nevertheless not yet been discovered to this day. Which Was To Be Demonstrated.

<pb n="12"/>For behold the wonderful apotheosis; by which the wolf turned into a lamb, the beast into a man, and from a single kiss of the hand, peace, sought on land and sea, was finally captured. For scarcely had Holofernes undergone the sight of URSULA when he already assumed the spirit of Ethereus <note>referring to the noble convert/suitor</note>; scarcely had he greeted the one present in spirit when he already changed his mind toward divine things; scarcely had he kissed her hand with a chaste kiss when he changed the decreed war into peace. And nothing further remains but that the treaties of virginal peace be confirmed by the end of life itself. Come then, fierce spirit of the barbarians! And subscribe to the kiss of perpetual peace with the blood of those who make the pact, and grant to the banks of the Rhine that privilege, so that they may glory until our own age in the peace concluded by Saint URSULA.

-><-

But why do we implore barbarous minds with anxious prayer? They conspire of their own accord for the slaughter of Christians, to whom no one is a greater enemy than he who is distinguished by the Christian name; they uniquely desire to satiate their iron, thirsty for the blood of those whose life is hostile to them; they deem those unworthy of the earth who deny the many gods of heaven.

As URSULA stood with Ethereus; so, for the sake of the faith and the love of virginal peace, she saw her fellow Virgin soldiers fall in their station and their life: with the same spirit with which she embraced her Ethereus spouse, she received the deadly weapon; with the same love with which she panted for this peace, she expired in testimony of peace. She expired! That mind, of course, corrupted by the weapon, which could not be conquered by any engines: the Virgin fell as prey to the barbarous hand, she who resolved by an inviolable vow to always stand in the perpetual verdure of virginity. She gave her blood, she who had dedicated the purest milk of virginity to the Heavenly ones alone.

But thus it was fitting for the Virgin, that in one kiss she should unite both the laurel of virginity and the <pb n="13"/>martyrdom. Let there be, then, faith in the fantastic chronicles of the poets, who proclaim the wonderful power of the caduceus rod, while with a single touch, as if a kiss, it settled the poisoned wrath of serpents into an amiable treaty of friendship. Let there be, then, the amiable force of the Lyre of Orpheus, which by sound alone compelled beasts and stones to perpetual peace with spontaneous violence. For the same praise that fable has fashioned for them, the kiss of peace of Saint URSULA deserves. Indeed, it would have been little to deserve it, had not the Rhine also given it, a year ago, with the public applause of Peace. Well, therefore, was Peace concluded by the Saintly Virgin for herself and her own: that peace, namely, which sings the canticle granted to virgins alone in the sight of the lamb; that Peace whose condition is perpetual virginity; whose desired fruit is virginity; whose consummation is virginity.

That peace, in which the Rhine and the shores of the Rhine drank the blood of divine ones; the City of Cologne received the bodies, and Heaven received the souls. Hence, let it be a wonder to no one that peaceful laurels flourish on the banks of the Rhine, which can indeed be shaken but cannot be uprooted; for the peace which Saint URSULA obtained there with a kiss and her own blood, the same she bestowed upon this land as a peace that would last forever; nor would she believe herself happy in peace, unless she bestowed peace upon her own fortunate land. Let Alexandria now glory in the prerogative of its name from Alexander, Rome from Romulus, Constantinople from Constantine, and Leopoldopolis from the most august Leopold reigning most happily: our Rhine also has that which it takes from Saint URSULA as a sweet name of peace, as if by hereditary right. Let rivers be carriers of gold and gems, most fitting instruments of commerce, and famous throughout entire kingdoms for their course and utility; the renowned Rhine is made so by a single peace concluded many centuries ago;

The author contrasts the destructive, barbarous nature of war with the divine endurance of virginity and the lasting influence of the peace Ursula established.</summary>

*But to return from this digression to the path, although that speed of execution may contribute to the public good;* it cannot be denied that in this way *innocent people also often perish: as Ammianus Marcellinus writes in book 14, chapter 28, regarding what was done by Constantius Gallus Caesar; and Aurelius Victor writes in his Life of Carus regarding Carinus Caesar; and Tacitus in book 1 of his Histories regarding Gaius Fonteius Capito under Galba.*

Nor is it always safe for a <term>Jurisconsult</term> <gloss>legal expert</gloss> to respond in favor of that opinion, *Julius Clarus in his Criminal Practice, § on High Treason, number 17.*

*And Calenus, in Dio, book 46, inveighs against what was done in Cicero’s case on the advice of Cato.*

*Scipio Gentilis* also criticizes it in his disputation on the *Lex Cornelia*; the *Lex Porcia*; and the *Lex Clodia*. That *Cicero* himself tacitly repented of it is made quite clear in his *letters to Atticus throughout; and he confesses somewhere expressly that the world of the Republic was turned upside down by the fault of Cato.*

Thus, for the highest Princes, this excessive haste, the stepmother of wise counsel, often created the greatest dangers and destruction. *Antipater, the Prefect of Greece and Macedonia under Alexander the Great,* who in his absence governed both provinces rightly and with great authority, when he heard that *Parmenion* had been killed by *Alexander*, said: "If *Parmenion* plotted against *Alexander*, whom then can one trust? If not, what is to be done?" (from *Plutarch* in his *Apophthegms*, *Erasmus*, book 5). Everyone in the entire camp also began to murmur, lamenting the fall of the guiltless old man and his son *Philotas*, sometimes saying that they themselves should not expect any better. *Antipater*, however, when he judged himself to be not so much pleasing to the King as he was envied, due to his great deeds in Greece and the accusations of *Olympias*, the mother of *Alexander*, and thought that he was being summoned from Macedonia not for the companionship of the military, but for his death, became the author of plots against the life of *Alexander*. He suborned his son *Cassander*, who, with his brothers *Philippus* and *Iollas*, was accustomed to serving the King. The friends later disseminated the cause of the illness as intemperance from drunkenness, and the infamy of the plot suppressed the power of the successors. *Justin, book 12; Diodorus Siculus, books 17 and 19; Plutarch in his Life of Alexander; Curtius and Arrian, book 7.* Regarding *Perennis*, *Dio* testifies in book 72 that he was unworthy of dying by that type of death, both for his own sake and for the sake of the *Roman Empire*: that he had never set his mind on wealth and glory, but had been most continent and modest, and had kept the reign of *Commodus* secure: and upon his death <pb n="19"/>the Caesar-factions, of whom Cleander, who had deeply hated Perennis, was the leader, began to commit every kind of crime, to set fire to everything, to harm everyone with injury, and to vex them with insults, while in the meantime Commodus had indulged in his pleasures. And regarding Georgius Martinusius, Thuanus says in the aforementioned place, book 7: that he was a man famous in peace and in war, and of profound prudence, comparable to few. While he had accommodated that prudence to the times, and although he had almost always been compliant with the will of the Turks for the good of his fatherland, Hungary, he had incurred the envy of many, and finally, a fatal hatred toward himself. By these, it was finally brought about that, with a constant rumor spread about his immense treasures, they armed Castaldus, an assassin, with the hope of gain. With his henchmen, he persuaded the Emperor Ferdinand that Georgius had been agitating secret plots with the Turks to the ruin of the Christian Republic; in truth, however, he had been panting after his slaughter because of the treasures, which nevertheless were found afterward to be modest. All that money, which they had believed was set aside, had been consumed in public works and armies by a liberal man who, with no private affection, had administered the care of the Republic with exact faith and diligence, and could have been diverted.

However, to put an end to our disputation, and that the mind may have a place to rest at this crossroads of opinions: the former [opinion], that indeed even in this most serious crime of treason or high treason one must not proceed without a prior cognitive investigation, has its place when the accused, or the one denounced, has not occupied fortresses, has not seduced the populace, has not been armed with cohorts, and no evident act appears simultaneously. The latter [opinion], however, applies when the opposites are in the open, or are detected from no light signs. And that we may establish this, the opinion of Cicero in Dio, book 45, suggests it to us when he says: "Punishments must be inflicted immediately upon unjust citizens: by judgment, indeed, if it is permitted to cast votes against them: <note>by voice, not by ballot, according to the Lex Cassia regarding voting, passed in the year 616 from the Founding of the City. Everyone in the entire camp also began to murmur, lamenting the fall of the guiltless old man and his son *Philotas*, sometimes saying that they themselves should not expect any better. *Antipater*, however, when he judged himself to be not so much pleasing to the King as he was envied, due to his great deeds in Greece and the accusations of *Olympias*, the mother of *Alexander*, and thought that he was being summoned from Macedonia not for the companionship of the military, but for his death, became the author of plots against the life of *Alexander*. He suborned his son *Cassander*, who, with his brothers *Philippus* and *Iollas*, was accustomed to serving the King. ### XXI.

Therefore, parents succeed to their children who have died without children, brothers, and sisters; if there are surviving brothers or sisters connected to the deceased on both sides, they succeed per capita <gloss>individually</gloss>, but with the children of these, they succeed per stirpes <gloss>by right of representation of their parent</gloss>.

### XXII.

Parents of different lines, from the paternal and maternal, placed in an equal degree, divide the inheritance of the deceased today, not in proportion to their strength <note>i.e., not by person</note>, but having regard for the branch, and without distinction of the goods left by the deceased.

### XXIII.

It is a well-known point of law that brothers and the children of brothers connected to the deceased by only one side are excluded by all ascendants.

### XXIV.

An adoptive father cannot be the heir of his adopted son, whom he does not have in his power, although such a son succeeds to him.

### XXV.

I would say otherwise concerning the one into whose power the adopted person passes, to whom, just as to the <term>arrogator</term> <gloss>one who adopts a person already in his own right</gloss> regarding the property of the emancipated son, succession is granted as to a legitimate and natural father.

### XXVI.

Natural parents succeed to their children, whom they have legitimized by a subsequent marriage, or by a rescript of the prince, or by an offering to the Curia, equally as if they were natural and legitimate.

### XXVII.

In the same way that natural children and illegitimate children succeed to their parents, so do these succeed to them in turn; namely, the natural father and his ascendants succeed to their natural son for two ounces <note>a fraction of the inheritance</note>, but the mother and those ascending from the maternal line succeed to the whole.

### XXIIX.

I believe there is no doubt that those born from an incestuous and condemned union, if they cease to be among the living, have neither father nor mother, nor any of the ascendants as a successor.

### XXIX.

Thus much concerning the succession of those standing in the direct line; failing these, collaterals succeed in the oblique line, whose succession extends to the tenth degree.

### XXX.

But whether the succession of agnates <gloss>relatives on the male side</gloss> in the succession of an ancient fief is circumscribed by certain degrees, or whether it proceeds to infinity, the opinions of doctors vary because of the discrepant texts, which I think should be reconciled by the bond of distinction.

### XXXI.

Brothers and sisters <term>ἀμφιθαλεῖς</term> <gloss>born of the same father and mother</gloss> connected on both sides, with those connected by only one side excluded, are called to the inheritance of the previously deceased brother per capita, and the children of the previously deceased brothers connected on both sides, but not others, are called concurrently with them per stirpes.

### XXXIII.

Brothers succeed one another in a paternal fief; in a new one, this is not the case, but the fief reverts to the lord: however, the sisters of either are incapable.

If the deceased has left no brothers or sisters connected on both sides, nor their children, but only uterine <gloss>born of the same mother</gloss> or paternal siblings, then these are admitted to the inheritance of the brother.

Indeed, not so that paternal property is deferred to the paternal side and maternal to the maternal, as in the old law, but the inheritance of the deceased is divided equally between the paternal and uterine; if only one exists, he obtains the whole inheritance.

<pb n="682"/> barricaded doors and watched over their own, whom I could sometimes see from the height of my horse, huddled together in the courtyards in anxious tension. From afar, one could occasionally hear the cries of fear from women and children when unscrupulous marauders had forced access to their hiding places and were plundering them or taking them captive.

In their outward appearance, the <term>Pâlem</term> do not differ essentially from the <term>Somraï</term> and <term>Gâberi</term>. They are strong, well-proportioned, and often tall figures with a more or less black skin color, which generally shows no shades tending toward reddish or yellowish hues, and for the most part, they also seem to understand the <term>Bagirmi</term> language.

The sky had become heavily clouded, and thunder rolled on all sides as we set up our night camp at the feet of some <term>Delêb</term> palms without any other tree cover. I spent half the night with the surgical treatment of the wounded. I stitched the flesh wounds together with horsehair and bandaged the more serious injuries as well as I could. Yet some had penetrating chest and abdominal wounds or exposed shoulder and hip joints, and a few gave up the ghost that very night.

The next morning (June 1st), we broke camp an hour before sunrise and, also moving in a roughly easterly direction, crossed a low-lying area with lush grass, which was described to me as <term>Komodûgu</term>. It showed swampy ground in the deepest parts and small pools of water here and there, and according to the locals, it is said to extend north toward <term>Mul</term> and northwest toward the <term>Ba Ili</term> river. We had passed a similar grassy, treeless valley, which was rich in water in the summer and seemed to extend from southeast to northwest, the previous evening. Both, as well as the valley-like depression near <term>Murki</term> and another one situated south-southwest of <term>Gundi</term> that we saw later, seem to be parts of the swamp network from which the <term>Ba Ili</term> eventually develops. An hour after sunrise, we turned south, passed numerous scattered and barricaded homesteads that already belonged to <term>Gundi</term>, traveled beyond the center of this main village of the <term>Tummok</term> tribe, and made camp at 8 o'clock in the morning. Everyone immediately headed into the <pb n="683"/> surrounding area to search for roofs and wall coverings from huts, poles and fences, wooden mortars, and other household equipment, in short, all the necessary living requisites. The shameless slaves of the King and his highest dignitaries also returned heavily laden, but my people had only captured a piece of a straw fence that sufficed at most for the wall of one hut, and we had to make do for the time being with a shelter made of leafy branches. While the morning had been overcast with a light southeast wind, the sky cleared around midday, so that I indulged in the hope of a rain-free night. But the rains had become so frequent over time, and I could bear damage to my few belongings so poorly, that when neither <term>Almâs</term> nor <term>Hammu</term> had managed to find a hut roof in the vicinity by the afternoon, I lay down to sleep not without worry.

An evil night followed, the beginning of which has remained in particularly repulsive memory for me. Without suspecting it, we had built my provisional hut on a termite mound that did not yet rise above the level of the surrounding area, and at night, the hated little creatures paid me a most unpleasant visit. I had barely spent half an hour in restless sleep on my bedding, which was always laid out on the bare ground—I had been suffering from severe rheumatic pains since <term>Somraï</term>—when I awoke and felt a strange sensation on the skin of my whole body. At first, I tried not to pay attention to it and to fall back asleep, but since my pains promised me no rest anyway, I decided to get up and light a lamp. The latter was no easy procedure, for even if I had prepared a lamp from a little bowl of butter by means of a scrap of <term>Châm</term> cloth rolled into a wick, our cooking fire had gone out, and I had to ignite dry rags on the priming powder of one of our flintlock muskets. Finally, I had light and, in the dim glow of the primitive lamp, saw my bedding swamped by thousands upon thousands of white termites, a large portion of which I had already crushed. My shirt and the surface of my sleeping blanket were covered with the insects crushed into a mush, and ever more swarms of them...

<summary>This passage describes the aftermath of the attack on the village of Kolî, the journey toward Gundi, and a harrowing night spent in a temporary shelter infested with termites.</summary>

They are strong, well-proportioned, and often tall figures with a more or less black skin color, which generally shows no shades tending toward reddish or yellowish hues, and for the most part, they also seem to understand the <term>Bagirmi</term> language.

The sky had become heavily clouded, and thunder rolled on all sides as we set up our night camp at the feet of some <term>Delêb</term> palms without any other tree cover. I spent half the night with the surgical treatment of the wounded. I stitched the flesh wounds together with horsehair and bandaged the more serious injuries as well as I could. Yet some had penetrating chest and abdominal wounds or exposed shoulder and hip joints, and a few gave up the ghost that very night.

The next morning (June 1st), we broke camp an hour before sunrise and, also moving in a roughly easterly direction, crossed a low-lying area with lush grass, which was described to me as <term>Komodûgu</term>. It showed swampy ground in the deepest parts and small pools of water here and there, and according to the locals, it is said to extend north toward <term>Mul</term> and northwest toward the <term>Ba Ili</term> river. We had passed a similar grassy, treeless valley, which was rich in water in the summer and seemed to extend from southeast to northwest, the previous evening. Both, as well as the valley-like depression near <term>Murki</term> and another one situated south-southwest of <term>Gundi</term> that we saw later, seem to be parts of the swamp network from which the <term>Ba Ili</term> eventually develops. An hour after sunrise, we turned south, passed numerous scattered and barricaded homesteads that already belonged to <term>Gundi</term>, traveled beyond the center of this main village of the <term>Tummok</term> tribe, and made camp at 8 o'clock in the morning. Everyone immediately headed into the
pages.683:
surrounding area to search for roofs and wall coverings from huts, poles and fences, wooden mortars, and other household equipment, in short, all the necessary living requisites. The shameless slaves of the King and his highest dignitaries also returned heavily laden, but my people had only captured a piece of a straw fence that sufficed at most for the wall of one hut, and we had to make do for the time being with a shelter made of leafy branches. While the morning had been overcast with a light southeast wind, the sky cleared around midday, so that I indulged in the hope of a rain-free night. But the rains had become so frequent over time, and I could bear damage to my few belongings so poorly, that when neither <term>Almâs</term> nor <term>Hammu</term> had managed to find a hut roof in the vicinity by the afternoon, I lay down to sleep not without worry.

An evil night followed, the beginning of which has remained in particularly repulsive memory for me. Without suspecting it, we had built my provisional hut on a termite mound that did not yet rise above the level of the surrounding area, and at night, the hated little creatures paid me a most unpleasant visit. I had barely spent half an hour in restless sleep on my bedding, which was always laid out on the bare ground—I had been suffering from severe rheumatic pains since <term>Somraï</term>—when I awoke and felt a strange sensation on the skin of my whole body. At first, I tried not to pay attention to it and to fall back asleep, but since my pains promised me no rest anyway, I decided to get up and light a lamp. The latter was no easy procedure, for even if I had prepared a lamp from a little bowl of butter by means of a scrap of <term>Châm</term> cloth rolled into a wick, our cooking fire had gone out, and I had to ignite dry rags on the priming powder of one of our flintlock muskets. Finally, I had light and, in the dim glow of the primitive lamp, saw my bedding swamped by thousands upon thousands of white termites, a large portion of which I had already crushed. My shirt and the surface of my sleeping blanket were covered with the insects crushed into a mush, and ever more swarms of them...

The medicine is prepared from eight thousand roots,

To liberate all sentient beings of the six realms,

To the brothers and sisters of the Bodhisattvas,

To the gatekeepers, Father and Mother, and the circle of <term>Dakinis</term> <gloss>sky-goers</gloss>,
I offer this pure nectar and sacred substance as a pleasing offering.
Through compassion, contemplate and be fully pleased,
And grant the accomplishment of the magical, pure realms.
In the stainless and pure nature of the sky,
Many false concepts are like masses of clouds.

I have realized the meaning of purity and make this offering.

<pb n="88"/>...concerning these grievances: because a woman's grievance is considered low, if one enters and another also enters, they will inevitably kill each other. What was said, that "whoever enters must pay five hundred <term>karshapana</term> <gloss>gold coins</gloss>," is also true; she must undoubtedly have clothes and ornaments for that. What was said, that "after seven days pass, the house should be vacated," is also true; what harm is there in doing it earlier or later? What was said, that "one should not examine those arriving and entering for the sake of men," is also true; for this is a courtesan, and if one were to examine everyone arriving for the sake of men, who would enter her house? Then the assembly granted her these five supreme conditions, and she was enjoyed by the assembly. As the <term>Lichchhavi</term> <gloss>a clan of Vaishali</gloss> of Vaishali began to enter her house to enjoy themselves as they wished, some, due to intense attachment to the sense objects, became detached from desire the moment they saw her. Others, by mere touch, were satisfied; no one actually performed the act of a man with her. She thought, "These are not men; I shall devise a method," and she <leaf-break/>
Amrapali, a woman of supreme beauty and youth, possessed of sixty-four arts, and suitable only for the enjoyment of a king, was present. She said, "Your Majesty, if that is the case, I shall go to Vaishali and enjoy myself with him as I wish." The King said, "The <term>Lichchhavi</term> of Vaishali have long been troublesome, aggressive enemies; they will harm you." The King replied, "Wise ones, people are courageous, so I shall go." She said, "Your Majesty, if you insist on going for no reason, then please depart." He boarded a chariot and set off for Vaishali with the King. Gradually arriving in Vaishali, the King remained in the pleasure grove. The King entered Amrapali’s house. After a while, the sound of a bell arose. The <term>Lichchhavi</term> of Vaishali became agitated, saying, "Wise ones, a man unfriendly to us has entered; ring the bell." As the sound became clear and loud, King Bimbisara asked Amrapali, "Lovely one, what is this?" "Your Majesty, the city guards are patrolling." "Why?" "For your sake." "What should I do? Should I flee?" "Your Majesty, do not be displeased. Your Majesty, since the city guards are patrolling, enjoy yourself for seven days. <pb n="89"/>Enjoy yourself as you wish, stay for seven days, and I will see to the time."

She played, rejoiced, and enjoyed herself with him. After some time, Amrapali became pregnant, and she said to King Bimbisara, "Your Majesty, I am carrying a child." He gave her a cloth and a signet ring, saying, "If it is a girl, she is yours. But if it is a boy, wrap him in this cloth, hang the signet ring around his neck, and bring him to me." He departed, boarded his chariot, and left with the King. As he did, the bell rang. They said, "Wise ones, the enemy has appeared; pursue him!" Five hundred <term>Lichchhavi</term> archers pursued King Bimbisara. Seeing them, the King asked, "Your Majesty, the <term>Lichchhavi</term> of Vaishali are coming. Your Majesty, will you fight them, or shall I drive the chariot?" He replied, "I am exhausted; you drive the chariot, and you alone fight them." As he began to fight with them, the <term>Lichchhavi</term> of Vaishali <leaf-break/>
recognizing him, they struck even harder, saying, "Wise ones, he is the father of our enemy!" She told her son what had happened over time. She thought, "The <term>Lichchhavi</term> of Vaishali are violent and powerful; if he is killed, there is a place where that could happen." While she was thinking this, she saw many merchants carrying goods, traveling to Rajagriha. She said, "With this signet ring, take these goods and depart; you will not have to pay customs duties. Also, take this boy to the King's palace, hang this signet ring around his neck, and leave him at the gate of Rajagriha." They promised to do so, saying, "It shall be done." She gave the boy a pearl necklace and said, "Son, go to where the King is staying, place the pearl necklace at his feet, and sit in his lap, fearing nothing. If someone says, 'This boy is ignorant of fear,' you should say, 'Does a son have anything to fear from his father?'" He traveled gradually to Rajagriha with the merchants. They bathed, tied the signet ring to him, and left him at the gate of the King's palace. He went to where the King was, and...</translation>

<summary>This text describes the courtesan Amrapali's interactions with the assembly of Vaishali, her romance with King Bimbisara, and the subsequent efforts to protect their son from the hostile Lichchhavi clan by sending him to the King's court in Rajagriha.</summary>
<keywords>Amrapali, King Bimbisara, Vaishali, Lichchhavi, courtesan, royal intrigue, Rajagriha, genealogy</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="386"/>...1,008 times, or even 100 or 8. After having recited [it], and having fasted day and night, offer the rosary to the seventh Arya <note>noble one</note>. Recite it just as before. Perform it equal to that standard. Then, recite fully upon the rosary. That very night, sit down. On ground covered with <term>kusha</term> <gloss>sacred grass</gloss>, the mantra-practitioner should sleep there. Whatever dreams are seen, if one sees an auspicious dream, that is the dream being surely shown. Accomplish the <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>attainment</gloss> by that. If the practitioner sees Buddhas, <term>shravakas</term> <gloss>listeners/disciples</gloss>, or <term>pratyekabuddhas</term> <gloss>solitary realizers</gloss> in a dream, [the practitioner] will succeed with the fruit. Surely perform the ritual for that. If one sees the beautiful forms of a monk or a Brahmin, if one sees that dream, [you] should offer the rosary in the same way. The one who accomplishes all purposes of mantra will likewise succeed without fail. The sutra of the <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss> known as the <term>Gandavyuha</term> <gloss>Array of Virtues</gloss>, from the root tantra of the Bhagavati Arya Tara with hair bound up <note>Ushnisha-Vijaya-Tara</note>, the exhaustive chapter on the ritual of counting rosaries from the exhaustive ritual of the painted cloth <term>patala</term> is completed. Then, the Bhagavati Shakyamuni, having looked again at the great <term>mandala</term> <gloss>circle/sphere</gloss> of the assembly endowed with everything, spoke to the great bodhisattva, the noble Avalokiteshvara: "Great Bodhisattva, you have the specific ritual for the completion of the chapter on the mantra of awareness, and the performance of the ritual of fire offerings <term>homa</term>."
<leaf-break/>
The one who has abandoned living beings and [is] joined perfectly with sand, that then [has] a lotus-like rim <note>referring to the shape of the fire hearth</note> that is the form of the <term>mandala</term> from all sides. Or, with effort, a four-sided one, or one to be made with three petals. The <term>shantika</term> <gloss>pacifying</gloss> and <term>paushtika</term> <gloss>increasing</gloss> [rituals], these are also correctly proclaimed. For <term>abhichara</term> <gloss>wrathful/violent actions</gloss>, in the middle of the ground, make a <term>vajra</term> <gloss>thunderbolt/diamond</gloss>, and it is to be made with two points, [or] three points.
