In the directions of one teaching, and in empty charnel houses or buildings, perform the fire offering well. Likewise on a mountain peak, and always in an empty temple, and in a great wilderness in that same way. Whatever directions of accomplishment, those that the supreme person has spoken, for all <term>homa</term> actions, those are spoken as the places. Sitting near on a mat of <term>kusha</term> grass measuring one cubit, the mantra-knower should specifically perform the action of <term>homa</term>. By residing in that very place, there is no doubt of swift accomplishment. By facing east and north, perform <term>shantika</term> and <term>paushtika</term>. The <term>raudra</term> <gloss>wrathful</gloss> actions are in the south; the mantra-practitioner should avoid that. Facing east is the <term>siddhi</term> of pacifying; the increasing one is also faced to the north. By that, the mantra-practitioner should always begin the recitation of the awareness [mantra]. For <term>paushtika</term> actions, use <term>bilva</term>, <term>arga</term>, <term>shala</term>, and <term>nyagrodha</term> <gloss>banyan</gloss>. <pb n="387"/>
<term>paushtika</term>, [use] moist wood, which is auspicious. Likewise for wrathful actions, [use] dry wood. Those [which are] hot, acidic, and sharp—if those sacrificial woods are not available, always make those [others] into the wood. The points should be checked to be two. Likewise, always consider [the use of] dry [wood] for performing sinful actions; here the supreme Victorious One has forbidden it. In pure, stainless water, always [use] those abandoned by insects. With the base of pure grass, make the lamp of proper measure, and then, having formed the fist <term>mudra</term>, make the fire blaze with effort. Do not do it with the breath of the mouth, and always not even with the edge of a garment. Clearly abandon the lower garment and upper robe. It is not with joy for the extinguishing of the hand's air with other garments. Similarly, [use] a clean fan, or a garment. Even with a jewel, one should make a fan. <leaf-break/>

By changing the three types of colors, these are the three types of <term>siddhi</term>. Other colors, such as cloud-color, or
<note>on that same ground of the teachings, for that mantra-practitioner, there is no <term>siddhi</term>. If one sees the fire blazing like those colors, or of various colors, then one should begin the work again.</note>
Perform the recitation again. If the mantra is accomplished, by seeing the ritual of the action, one enters well into the <term>homa</term>. <pb n="214"/>The bodhisattva does not focus on his own mind, nor does he focus on the minds of others. Why is that? Because the bodhisattva’s mental continuum is known through pristine wisdom. The mental continuum is known through mindfulness. It is known through intellect. The mental continuum is known through realization. The mental continuum is known through wisdom. The mental continuum is known through the mind. The mental continuum is free from defilements, the bonds of karmic propensities are perfectly severed, it is pure, stainless, luminous, blameless, not harsh, unclouded, and it perceives the appearance of all phenomena. It is known as following the mental conduct of all sentient beings. Shariputra, the entry into knowing the minds of others in this manner is called the bodhisattva’s supernormal cognition of the minds of others and the perfection of the activity of pristine wisdom. Shariputra, what is the bodhisattva’s supernormal cognition of recollecting previous states of existence, and what is the perfection of the activity of the pristine wisdom of supernormal cognition? Shariputra, in this regard, a bodhisattva [recollects] all the births of all sentient beings throughout the infinite and limitless realms of the ten directions: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty
<leaf-break/>
He recollects his own roots of virtue that arose from previous causes. He also recollects the causes of the roots of virtue of others. He dedicates his own roots of virtue to enlightenment. After recollecting the roots of virtue of other sentient beings, he generates the mind set upon enlightenment. He reflects on the causes of previous pleasure and pain as impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless. By relying on their impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, he is not arrogant due to physical form. He is not arrogant due to material wealth. He is not arrogant due to servants. He is not arrogant due to power. He is not arrogant due to desiring a wheel-turning monarch. He is not arrogant due to desiring an Indra. He is not arrogant due to desiring a Brahma. He is not arrogant due to desiring a world protector. He is not arrogant due to desiring all births. He does not have a mind that desires all pleasures of desire, kingly rule, and power, except for when he intentionally takes on existence for the sake of maturing sentient beings. Because he relies on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, his previous
<pb n="215"/>actions of defiled conduct lead him to feel shame and embarrassment, and he criticizes them. Even for the sake of his life, he does not perform actions that would become roots of non-virtue through current objects. He also dedicates his previous roots of virtue to the unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment and causes them to increase. Because he gathers all current roots of virtue, he abandons mismatched dedications. In order to ensure that the lineage of the Buddha, the lineage of the Dharma, and the lineage of the Sangha are not interrupted, he dedicates all to omniscience through the power of correctly generated mindfulness. That mindfulness is also completely blessed by the power of the <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>the realm of phenomena/absolute reality</gloss>. Because it is thoroughly correct, it is unmoving. Because the <term>dhyana</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> has been perfected, it is not agitated. Because it is thoroughly blessed by <term>shamatha</term> <gloss>calm abiding</gloss>, it is harmless. Because it is correctly grasped by <term>vipashyana</term> <gloss>special insight</gloss>, it is without error. Because it is direct, it is not ordinary. Because mindfulness does not deteriorate, there is no forgetting
<leaf-break/>
He possesses the <term>riddhipada</term> <gloss>feet of miraculous manifestation</gloss>—desiring, being affectionate, exercising power, and [the fourth]—and because he has thoroughly meditated on these, he attains the manifestation of miracles, and he experiences various miraculous displays. Those miraculous displays are also thoroughly familiarized for the sake of looking after sentient beings. He manifests those specific miraculous displays that will tame sentient beings through whichever form, power, blessing, or miraculous display is appropriate. He displays those specific forms and colors that will tame sentient beings, such as appearing in the form and color of a Buddha, or appearing in the form and color of a <term>pratyekabuddha</term> <gloss>solitary realizer</gloss>, or appearing in the form and color of a <term>shravaka</term> <gloss>disciple</gloss>, or appearing in the form and color of an Indra, or appearing in the form and color of a Brahma, or appearing in the form and color of a world protector</translation>

<summary>This passage describes the bodhisattva's mastery of the supernormal cognitive powers, including knowing the minds of others and recollecting previous lives, while emphasizing that these abilities are grounded in non-attachment and the dedication of all virtues toward ultimate enlightenment.</summary>
<keywords>bodhisattva, supernormal cognition, mental continuum, emptiness, dedication of merit, meditative states, miraculous displays, taming sentient beings</keywords>

<pb n="107"/>You will become untouchable by all attackers, enemies, malicious beings, and sins. Even if you have been afraid, all fear will vanish and you will be completely liberated. Furthermore, you will not be stained by the filth of sin. If you mix <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pills with sesame oil and smear it on your face before appearing before a king, you will be embraced like a child and gain great joy; all fears of a wrathful king will be pacified. If smeared on the body, even if the body were to be executed, weapons will not strike it, and they will break into pieces. If an arrow is shot, it will not hit the body and the bow will break. If you tie a <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pill around your neck and enter difficult paths in wild areas, mountains, or dense forests, all fear of bandits, deceivers, thieves, <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>, <term>rakshasas</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, humans, non-humans, malicious wild animals, poisonous snakes, and poisons will not arise, and they will not be encountered. If tied to the right shoulder, you will be victorious over enemies everywhere. You will also become a great object of worship in all places. You will have great power and diligence.
<leaf-break/>
All those food items will be summoned and will arrive; they will come to wherever you desire. If you enter a spice shop, all the goods in the shop will come to you. If you clap your hands at the door of a beer seller, all the pots of beer will come. If you clap your hands at the door of a granary, all the grain will be summoned. If you enter the house of a honey-maker and touch the equipment, all the honey syrup and slabs of sugar will come. They will be directed to wherever you desire. If you clap your hands in the bustle of a city gate, all who dwell in the city will have their sleep disturbed. If you strike at the door of an enemy, they will be driven away. If you cast it into the house of an armorer, all weapons and armor will become rigid and useless. If you strike at the door of a king, all opposing attackers, enemies, and malicious sentient beings will be bound, made rigid, and paralyzed. If you smear it on a conch and blow it in a high place, wherever the sound is heard, one will be liberated from conflict, fighting, harm, quarrels, spells, prepared poisons, toxins, and diseases. If you blow it at the gate of a city, epidemics, harm, and the misery of
<pb n="108"/>low status will not exist, and you will suppress the power of others. If tied to the left shoulder, you will become highly regarded by all men, women, boys, and girls, and all will desire to see you. You will become a great object of worship. Many purposes will be accomplished. If tied to the right calf, you will travel a thousand leagues without fatigue. If you hold a <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pill in your mouth and, with your right hand, recite the iron hook mantra of white mustard seeds <note>a ritual to attract or draw someone toward the practitioner</note>, and then, without speaking other words, go to a high place, you can scatter white mustard seeds in the direction of any man, woman, boy, or girl you contemplate, and they will be summoned instantly and will arrive. Even if they are a hundred leagues away, there is no doubt they will arrive in three days. If you tie a <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pill to your right or left hand, wherever you touch, all wealth, grain, jewels, precious stones, pearls, <term>shankhshila</term> <gloss>conch-shell-like stone</gloss>, coral, gold, silver, clothing, and ornaments will be summoned and come to you; whatever you desire will come. If you enter a kitchen and clap your hands at the door, all the cooking and the cooking...
<leaf-break/>
All will be completely pacified. If you blow it in a cattle pen, all the milk will be yielded up. They will come to wherever you desire. If you blow it in a goat or sheep pen, the milk of the goats and sheep will be yielded up, and they will come to wherever you desire. If you blow it in the middle of a great crowd of people, all will become naked and all their clothing will be summoned. If you smear it on a clay drum and beat it on a high veranda, all cold, wind, and hail will be bound and destroyed; they will not be able to strike. Hail will be stopped in a hundred-league radius. If you blow it throughout a city or a region, all diseases, epidemics, harm, and violence will be pacified. All conflict, fighting, disputes, and quarrels will be completely pacified. All fear of low status and famine will be completely pacified. Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of various purposes will be accomplished; it should be applied to everything. Then, it will be shared with all sentient beings to pacify all diseases, destroy all sins, completely pacify all epidemics and harms, completely pacify all famine-stricken areas, and pacify all <term>bhutas</term> <gloss>spirits</gloss> and <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>.</translation>

low status will not exist, and you will suppress the power of others. If tied to the left shoulder, you will become highly regarded by all men, women, boys, and girls, and all will desire to see you. You will become a great object of worship. Many purposes will be accomplished. If tied to the right calf, you will travel a thousand leagues without fatigue. If you hold a <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pill in your mouth and, with your right hand, recite the iron hook mantra of white mustard seeds <note>a ritual to attract or draw someone toward the practitioner</note>, and then, without speaking other words, go to a high place, you can scatter white mustard seeds in the direction of any man, woman, boy, or girl you contemplate, and they will be summoned instantly and will arrive. Even if they are a hundred leagues away, there is no doubt they will arrive in three days. If you tie a <term>giwang</term> <gloss>bezoar</gloss> pill to your right or left hand, wherever you touch, all wealth, grain, jewels, precious stones, pearls, <term>shankhshila</term> <gloss>conch-shell-like stone</gloss>, coral, gold, silver, clothing, and ornaments will be summoned and come to you; whatever you desire will come. If you enter a kitchen and clap your hands at the door, all the cooking and the cooking...
<leaf-break/>
All will be completely pacified. If you blow it in a cattle pen, all the milk will be yielded up. They will come to wherever you desire. If you blow it in a goat or sheep pen, the milk of the goats and sheep will be yielded up, and they will come to wherever you desire. If you blow it in the middle of a great crowd of people, all will become naked and all their clothing will be summoned. If you smear it on a clay drum and beat it on a high veranda, all cold, wind, and hail will be bound and destroyed; they will not be able to strike. Hail will be stopped in a hundred-league radius. If you blow it throughout a city or a region, all diseases, epidemics, harm, and violence will be pacified. All conflict, fighting, disputes, and quarrels will be completely pacified. All fear of low status and famine will be completely pacified. Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of various purposes will be accomplished; it should be applied to everything. Then, it will be shared with all sentient beings to pacify all diseases, destroy all sins, completely pacify all epidemics and harms, completely pacify all famine-stricken areas, and pacify all <term>bhutas</term> <gloss>spirits</gloss> and <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>.

Attachment, ignorance, fear, and anger, and the fruit of shame, one should abandon. Having abandoned the two by oneself, one should perform the conduct without doubt. Having given the body as a gift, one then truly practices the conduct. Because one practices based on capacity and lack of capacity, therefore one should not give gifts. Eat and chew in that same way, and drink. Eat whatever is obtained. For the sake of the thoughts of pleasant and unpleasant, one should not engage in mere attachment. Eating and non-eating conduct, and likewise drinking and non-drinking; moving and non-moving, the practitioner of mantra should not create thoughts. The disciple who has obtained the <term>siddhi</term> <gloss>attainment</gloss>, who is truly...
<leaf-break/>
...when showing the robe, its three points are well-shown. Whoever shows the breasts, its boundary is well-shown. Whoever shows the teeth, its mouth is well-shown. Whoever shows a frown, one should speak of untying the topknot. Whoever shows the forehead, its back is well-shown. Whoever shows the soles of the feet, one should play with the heels. By the answer of the <term>mudra</term> <gloss>hand gesture</gloss> to a <term>mudra</term>, one is distinguished by the <term>samaya</term> <gloss>vow/sacred commitment</gloss>. To that, the <term>yogini</term> <gloss>female practitioner of yoga</gloss> said: "Ah, son, great compassion! If one shows the hands with a garland, it is said that one should gather. If one specifically offers the garland, one has good conduct residing in the <term>samaya</term>. That which is called the 'outer gathering' is the place of good conduct. By the <term>yogini</term>, whatever is said to that, one should do all of it." "Oh, Blessed One, what is the place of gathering?" The Blessed One spoke: "Places, near-places, fields, near-fields, <term>chandohas</term> <gloss>sacred sites</gloss> and near-<term>chandohas</term>, likewise gatherings and near-gatherings, <term>athung-cho</term> <gloss>sacred sites of consumption</gloss> and near-<term>athung-cho</term>, charnel grounds and near-charnel grounds. These are the twelve lands. The lord of the ten lands, the Protector: this should not be spoken of by others. Oh, Blessed One, the places..."

<pb n="353"/>and so forth, what are they?" The Blessed One spoke: "The place is taught as <term>Jalandhara</term>. Likewise, <term>Oddiyana</term>. The place is <term>Kollagiri</term>. Likewise, <term>Kamaru</term>. The near-place is spoken of as <term>Malava</term>. It is the city of <term>Sindhu</term>. The field is taught as <term>Mumnir</term>. The field is the number of 'the doer'. <term>Devikota</term> is likewise a field. The field is the number of 'the locker'. The near-field is spoken of as <term>Kuluta</term>. Likewise <term>Arbuta</term>, and the best bestower <term>Khava</term> mountain. The near-field is summarized. The <term>chandoha</term> is <term>Harikela</term>, and the one born in the salt sea, <term>Lampaka</term> and <term>Kanchi</term>. Likewise, <term>Saurastra</term>. The near-<term>chandoha</term> is <term>Kalinga</term>, the island containing gold, and <term>Konkana</term> is also a near-<term>chandoha</term>. In brief, it should be spoken. The <term>athung-cho</term> of the city, and the one residing at the edge of the <term>athung-cho</term> village, <term>Caritra</term> and <term>Kosala</term>, <term>Bindha</term> is the city of the youth. <term>Vajra-garbha</term> is great compassion. The near-<term>athung-cho</term> is that which is near. The charnel ground is the perfected <term>sangha</term> <gloss>monastic community</gloss>, and the edge of the charnel ground sea. The edge of the pond in the garden enclosure is spoken of as the near-charnel ground. For the sake of all sentient beings, the <term>vajra</term> of the <term>yogini</term> tantra, the good gathering of the <term>yogini</term>, even in the daytime..."
<leaf-break/>
"...the sentient beings become subject to those. This is the seventh chapter, the Chapter on Determining Signs and Places. Then, the Mandala of the <term>yogini</term> will be explained. In the space of the sky, meditate on the <term>bhaga</term> <gloss>womb/source</gloss>. Meditating in the center is the mandala, beginning as appropriate. How the gods appear: the mandala of earth and water is first. As appropriate, the <term>Agni</term> <gloss>fire</gloss> and the gods, the great wind, and how the meditator also appears, is the mandala born from the source of phenomena. The two additional ones are without fault. From the pistil, one becomes. It is spoken of as the outer part of the triangle. In its center, meditate on the essence of the seat of the fifteen deaths. Upon that is the moon. Upon the moon is the seed syllable. Afterward, press down with the victor over demons. From the bowing of the two, great bliss. It resides in the form of the moon for the vowels. It manifests in the form of the consonants. From the gathering of the moon and sun, the white one and so forth are well-known. The moon possesses mirror-like wisdom. The seventh of the seven possesses equality. The seed syllable and hand-symbol of one's own deity are spoken of as discriminating. All becoming one, this is the diligence. Perfection is the pure <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>realm of reality</gloss>. By the ritual spoken by the wise, the five types..."
</translation>

<keywords>Vajra conduct, Yogini Tantra, Mandala, sacred sites, samaya vows, seed syllables</keywords>

<pb n="198"/>[They] do not benefit others through the four <term>so-so yang-dak-par rik-pa</term> <gloss>individual perfect discernments</gloss>, and do not benefit others through great love, and do not benefit others through great compassion, and do not benefit others through the eighteen distinct qualities of a Buddha, and do not benefit others through the fruit of being a stream-enterer, and do not benefit others through the fruit of being a once-returner, and do not benefit others through the fruit of being a non-returner, and do not benefit others through arhatship, and do not benefit others through self-enlightenment, and do not benefit others through the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and do not benefit others through omniscience, and do not act in accordance with the perfection of wisdom, and do not act in accordance with the perfection of meditative concentration, and do not act in accordance with the perfection of diligence, and do not act in accordance with the perfection of patience, and do not act in accordance with the perfection of morality, and do not act in accordance with the perfection of generosity, and do not act in accordance with internal emptiness
<leaf-break/>
and do not act in accordance with the powers, and do not act in accordance with the factors of enlightenment, and do not act in accordance with the noble eightfold path, and do not act in accordance with the noble truths, and do not act in accordance with the meditative concentrations, and do not act in accordance with the immeasurables, and do not act in accordance with the formless absorptions, and do not act in accordance with the eight liberations, and do not act in accordance with the nine serial absorptions, and do not act in accordance with the gateways of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. They do not act in accordance with the clairvoyances. They do not act in accordance with the meditative concentrations. They do not act in accordance with the gateways of <term>dharani</term> <gloss>retention/incantation</gloss>. They do not act in accordance with the ten powers of the Tathagata. They do not act in accordance with the four fearlessnesses. They do not act in accordance with the four individual perfect discernments. They do not act in accordance with great love. They do not act in accordance with great compassion. They do not act in accordance with the eighteen distinct qualities of a Buddha.
<pb n="199"/>They do not act in accordance with the fruit of being a stream-enterer. They do not act in accordance with the fruit of being a once-returner. They do not act in accordance with the fruit of being a non-returner. They do not act in accordance with arhatship. They do not act in accordance with self-enlightenment. They do not act in accordance with the knowledge of the aspects of the path. If they do not act in accordance with omniscience, then they will dwell in one of the two stages, either the stage of the <term>shravaka</term> <gloss>disciple/hearer</gloss> or the stage of the <term>pratyekabuddha</term> <gloss>self-enlightened one</gloss>. Why is that? It is because those sons or daughters of noble family did not write down, did not teach, did not recite, did not contemplate properly, and did not benefit others through this profound perfection of wisdom in the past. <leaf-break/>
and does not ask about or teach the perfection of meditative concentration, does not recite it, does not contemplate it properly, and does not rely upon it. They do not ask about or teach external emptiness, do not recite it, do not contemplate it properly, and do not rely upon it. They do not ask about or teach internal and external emptiness, do not recite it, do not contemplate it properly, and do not rely upon it. They do not ask about or teach the emptiness of emptiness, do not recite it, do not contemplate it properly, and do not rely upon it. They do not ask about or teach great emptiness, do not recite it.

<keywords>perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva path, shravaka, pratyekabuddha, emptiness, dharani, buddha qualities</keywords>

<pb n="10"/>adorned with a wheel of light. She whose own masses of light are turbulent. Homage to her whose splendor is utterly joyful, spreading a garland of light from her crown. By the laughter of <term>Tuttare</term>, she brings the <term>maras</term> <gloss>demonic forces</gloss> and the world under her control. Homage to her with the power to summon all hosts that protect the earth. By the letter <term>Hum</term> of her furrowed brow, she completely liberates all from poverty.
Homage to her whose crown is adorned with a crescent of the moon, she who is always intensely blazing. Amidst her hair, from the <term>Amitabha</term> <gloss>Buddha of Boundless Light</gloss> at her crest, she constantly emits great beams of light. Homage to her who dwells in the midst of a garland of fire like the fire at the end of an aeon. Right leg extended,
<leaf-break/>
left bent, she rejoices in circling in every way. She who completely destroys the army of enemies. Homage to her who strikes the surface of the earth with her palm and beats it with her feet. With the letter <term>Hum</term> and a furrowed brow, she crushes the seven levels. Homage to her who is bliss, virtue, and peace, whose sphere of activity is the peace of <term>nirvana</term> <gloss>extinction of suffering</gloss>. She who is perfectly endowed with <term>Svaha</term> and <term>Om</term>. She who is the destroyer of great sins. Homage to her who rejoices in circling in every way, who completely destroys the bodies of the enemies. Through the mantra of ten syllables, she is the <term>Tara</term> <gloss>Liberator</gloss> born from the <term>Hum</term> of wisdom. Homage to her who stomps her feet with <term>Ture</term>, whose seed-syllable is in the form of <term>Hum</term>, she who causes Mt. Meru, 
<pb n="11"/>Mandara, and the Vindhya mountains to tremble, causing the three worlds to shake. Homage to her who holds in her hand a deer-marked moon, like the ocean of the gods. By reciting <term>Tare</term> twice and the syllable <term>Phat</term>, she eliminates all poisons without exception. Homage to her whom the host of gods, the kings of gods, and the <term>gandharvas</term> <gloss>celestial musicians</gloss> serve. By the splendor of her joy and her protective armor, she eliminates disputes and bad dreams. 
Homage to her whose two eyes—the sun and the moon—are bright with brilliant light. By reciting <term>Hara</term> twice and <term>Tuttare</term>, she eliminates highly virulent epidemics. Homage to her who is perfectly endowed with the power of peace by setting the three suchnesses in order. She who destroys the <term>bhuta</term> <gloss>spirits</gloss>, the <term>vetala</term> <gloss>zombies</gloss>, 
<leaf-break/>
and the hosts of <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>—she is the supreme <term>Ture</term>. This praise of the root mantra and these twenty-one homages. 
Any intelligent person who, with perfect devotion to the Goddess, recites this with great faith, at twilight or upon rising at dawn, will be given total fearlessness by remembering her. All sins will be thoroughly pacified, and all lower realms will be destroyed. The seven tens of millions of Buddhas will quickly grant her empowerment. By attaining greatness beyond this, she will proceed to that ultimate state of <term>Buddhahood</term> <gloss>enlightenment</gloss>. Her potent, great poison—whether it remains in the seat or moves elsewhere— 
</translation>

Homage to her who dwells in the midst of a garland of fire like the fire at the end of an aeon. Right leg extended,
<leaf-break/>
left bent, she rejoices in circling in every way. She who completely destroys the army of enemies. Homage to her who strikes the surface of the earth with her palm and beats it with her feet. With the letter <term>Hum</term> and a furrowed brow, she crushes the seven levels. Homage to her who is bliss, virtue, and peace, whose sphere of activity is the peace of <term>nirvana</term> <gloss>extinction of suffering</gloss>. She who is perfectly endowed with <term>Svaha</term> and <term>Om</term>. She who is the destroyer of great sins. Homage to her who rejoices in circling in every way, who completely destroys the bodies of the enemies. Through the mantra of ten syllables, she is the <term>Tara</term> <gloss>Liberator</gloss> born from the <term>Hum</term> of wisdom. Homage to her who stomps her feet with <term>Ture</term>, whose seed-syllable is in the form of <term>Hum</term>, she who causes Mt. Meru,
pages.11:
Mandara, and the Vindhya mountains to tremble, causing the three worlds to shake. Homage to her who holds in her hand a deer-marked moon, like the ocean of the gods. By reciting <term>Tare</term> twice and the syllable <term>Phat</term>, she eliminates all poisons without exception. Homage to her whom the host of gods, the kings of gods, and the <term>gandharvas</term> <gloss>celestial musicians</gloss> serve. By the splendor of her joy and her protective armor, she eliminates disputes and bad dreams. 
Homage to her whose two eyes—the sun and the moon—are bright with brilliant light. By reciting <term>Hara</term> twice and <term>Tuttare</term>, she eliminates highly virulent epidemics. Homage to her who is perfectly endowed with the power of peace by setting the three suchnesses in order. She who destroys the <term>bhuta</term> <gloss>spirits</gloss>, the <term>vetala</term> <gloss>zombies</gloss>, 
<leaf-break/>
and the hosts of <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>—she is the supreme <term>Ture</term>. This praise of the root mantra and these twenty-one homages. 
Any intelligent person who, with perfect devotion to the Goddess, recites this with great faith, at twilight or upon rising at dawn, will be given total fearlessness by remembering her. All sins will be thoroughly pacified, and all lower realms will be destroyed. The seven tens of millions of Buddhas will quickly grant her empowerment. By attaining greatness beyond this, she will proceed to that ultimate state of <term>Buddhahood</term> <gloss>enlightenment</gloss>. Her potent, great poison—whether it remains in the seat or moves elsewhere—

<pb n="19"/>The highly respected Apa Layla offered one unit of meat and one offering of southern beer and spirits. May his wealth and human resources increase. Kye! From this royal district of Phyimtsang: The emanation of Gesar, Koche Gedun, and the intelligent Lady Drukmo and Orgyen Wangzom, along with their retinue, offered meat and southern beer once. May they obtain the Buddhahood of that virtuous offering. From the compassionate Apa Natrong, who has developed great enthusiasm for the Holy Dharma, a connection was established through one offering of southern beer. May he be born in the field of Avalokiteshvara. From the good land of Churi, Wengkhar, and Yulmo: Sonam Tenpa, who has entered the path of the Holy Dharma, and the Gesar-flower Tashi Zangmo established a connection with one offering of meal and spirits. May they be born in the presence of Orgyen Pema. The master of scholars who has descended in a lineage from old, the teacher Pema Karpo and the two from Taktshar Khyipo, offered meal and spirits as a service to the Dharma. May their merit expand like the sky. From the cold land of Them-gang-bi: The youthful Taktshar Kunzang established a connection to the Dharma with meal and spirits. The Kumuda-flower Karma Wangmo offered a small gathering of spirits to the Dharma. May she be rich in inexhaustible wealth. The talkative elder Tsang Koche Dawa offered one serving of meal and spirits as a service to the Dharma. May he have long life, no illness, and flourishing resources. From the isolated mountain-dwelling of Takchu Monastery: The one who masters the elephant of mindfulness, the renouncer of the expanse of the Great Perfection, the master Sangdag Norbu—with him as the leader, the yogi Ten-dzin Guru, the renunciate yogi Tashi, the one who abandoned mind-clinging yogi Karma, and the yogi Ngawang Trinley—these have great merit and offered service to the Holy Dharma. May they be born in the presence of Kuntuzangpo. From the Yulmo area, where the elephant descends: Pema Tsewang, who has greatness and Dharma, and the pure-visioned Apa Druk Tsering, the strong-minded Apa Druk Phuntsok, and the heaven-ordained Taktshar Kun-le—all of these offered meal and spirits individually. Through the great blessing of these offerings, may their humans, wealth, and food flourish. The yogi Ten-dzin Guru’s
<leaf-break/>
three offered southern beer once as a service. May they have resources and may their humans and wealth increase. Apa Tsewang, who is possessed of good conduct, and the Manjushri-flower Pema Wangmo offered southern beer once as a service to the Dharma. The buffalo-strong Sonam Trinley, the unmoving faithful Bukri, and the conch-flower girl Sonam, these two established a connection with the Dharma through two offerings of southern beer. May they be born in the field of the pure Dakini. The great treasure of intelligence, Apa Dondrup, offered southern beer once to the profound Dharma. The lion-strong Norbu Trinley offered the dried-fish offering of the Indian river-region once as a service to the Dharma. Based on the merit of this virtuous offering, may all be victorious and attain the state of health. Kye! From the very white mountain, Tsan-khar Monastery: The strong-speaking Apa Druk Norbu and the mountain-flower girl Chomo, the two of them perform one offering of southern beer as a service. May they be born in the blissful land of Pema. Surrounded by rows of forest trees, the beautiful white-haired one from the high-lying mountain of Rowa-li-pung: The powerful Trinley, Konchok, the swift-footed Sridtal Tashi, the respectful-minded Chodang Lhamo, the white-soft flower Lhadang Dronma, and their retinue offered southern beer and one piece of meat. May they be born in the presence of the Buddhas in the field of bliss. From the tree-trunk Taktshar Tshe-chu, the sandalwood tree Lhakshar Ngonla, each established a connection by offering southern beer once. Apa Tsewang, Ngawang Druk Norbu, Sonam Trinley, and Ngonla Tshe-chu, from the collective offering, the one who is the mother offered one piece of meat. Through the great merit of this single offering, may they be born in the field of Dewachen. The highly clear-resulted Drukkhyi Lhamo and the <note>flower</note> girl Karmo performed a gathering of spirits and established a connection with the Dharma. May they obtain the rank of the Vidhyadhara Victor. The mountain-dwelling renunciate yogi Tsondru and the very compassionate Rinchen Wangmo, along with southern beer and spirits <pb n="20"/> with them as the leaders, the realized-being Dolma, the very compassionate Dechen Chodzom, and the Gur-gum flower girl Yang-dzin, established a connection to the Dharma with meal and spirits. May they be born in Dewachen in the future. Kye! From the beautiful white-flowing Kur-tod region, the perfect city of Tashi-drak: The faithful mother Kunga Wangmo, the golden-flower Norbu Dzompa, and the pleasant Wangchen Dondrup—these three offered southern beer and spirits twice, along with one portion of pork, as a service to the Holy Dharma. May they be born in the presence of Pema Lingpa. Those who have emptied their minds for the Holy Dharma, the great meditator Orgyen Ten-dzin and the Dharma-remembrance girl Dzompa Lhamo, these two offered southern beer once. May they be born in the field of Kuntuzangpo. Kye! From the great plain of the beautiful water-mountain, the Yulmo-let-shig-gang with its piled terraces: The silver-flower Chakdor Wangmo offered meal and spirits once to the scriptural Dharma. Her servants, Ngatse Rinpoche and the very faithful mother Sangdron, these two offered one connection of grand southern-rice. May they obtain the rank of the high-reaching paradise. The unmoving faithful Apa Tsewang and the sandalwood tree Lhakshar Kowlala and the faithful and good-faced girl Naka and the father Pema, these three offered southern beer and tea; may they be reborn miraculously in the presence of the Victorious One. The very virtuous mother Nyida offered a serving of fragrant tea once. May she be born in the presence of Orgyen Pema. Kye! From the great cool land, the high-lying Yulmo Odom-khar city: Led by the compassionate Dechen Wangmo, the Udum-flower Tashi Wangmo, the Kumuda-flower girl Pema, the joyful-flower girl Dechok-mo, the clear-flower Tsewang Lhamo, the sky-flower Dondrup Zangmo, and the sun-flower girl Khymo, these girls performed one gathering of spirits. <leaf-break/>
offered once. May they be born in the field of the great Ganden. The workers of the forest-tree paper-making, Sonam Trinley, Norbu Trinley, Nagpo-la, Tamdrin Ngon-ser, the great gatekeeper Ten-dzin Chodar, Dorje Phuntsok, Rinchen Wangmo, Tashi Drukgyal, the great gatekeeper Dor-phan, Konchok Wangyal, Tshe-chu-la, and Gnae-la—these eleven, having abandoned the fatigue and weariness of the physical work, offered the scriptural-Dharma paper as a service. Through the merit of this offering, may they be born miraculously before the Buddhas and obtain the prophecy. Kye! From the white eastern Tashi-gang and the cold, bright Yulmo Bhagi: The sky-soaring Purgshe Trinley Norbu offered southern beer twice with a faithful mind. May he be born in the field of the Joyous One. The meditator Rigdzin, who has realized the meaning of emptiness, established a connection by offering southern beer six times. May he be born in the Ngayab field of Pema. <translation>
<pb n="14"/>Just as one who is not pacified is like that, please understand that attachment to desires is similar. A person suffering from the torture of worms moving under the skin because of an affliction of leprosy might, for the sake of comfort, rely entirely on the light of a fire. Although this appears to provide a moment of comfort, the illness does not subside; rather, the heat increases the serum and the agony intensifies. Similarly, by relying on the virtues of desire, one might appear satisfied for a moment, yet desire grows and one becomes insatiable. Therefore, please realize that being attached to desires is like this, and turn away from the craving for objects of desire from the very beginning.
Thus, craving increases, <leaf-break/>
and since there is no escape, following the explanation of the focus on being attached to desires, the actual path is explained. This involves a detailed explanation of the common path and a brief indication of the uncommon Mahayana path and the entrance to the result. The first of these consists of identifying the object of meditation in a summarized way and explaining the sequence of the five paths in detail. The first of these is: To see the ultimate truth, cultivate mental engagement toward things as they are. There is no other virtuous quality similar to that. Seeing and understanding the reality of the ultimate purpose <leaf-break/>
Things composed by mind and consciousness are conditioned because they are assembled by causes and conditions. Because they arise in a fleeting moment and cease, they are impermanent, constantly changing and disintegrating. Correspondingly, conditioned things other than the Truth of the Path are contaminated. This refers to the container world of the three realms, the body of the senses, and the mental consciousness, which are all accompanied by outflows. Feelings associated with suffering are the suffering of pain. Feelings associated with happiness are the suffering of change. Feelings associated with equanimity are the suffering of conditioned existence. The suffering of pain is known even by animals and the like. The suffering of change is seen by those with wisdom. Although the suffering of conditioned existence is the basis for all suffering, it is not known by others and is realized by noble beings. All phenomena are empty means that although many generally take emptiness to mean the absence of elaborations, here the aspect of the Truth of Suffering being empty refers to being empty of incompatible causes. Therefore, creators such as the Lord <term>Ishvara</term> <gloss>a creator deity</gloss> and those who speak of time as the cause are impossible in the nature of things. Thus, one knows it is empty of a creator, and through overcoming the various suitable causes and conditions <leaf-break/>
The essence of the wisdom of the Truth of the Path, which is free of contamination and accompanied by meditative concentration and ethical discipline, possesses the power to abandon afflictions and enables one to attain the state of cessation. Having certainty in this way is mental engagement with the aspect of the Truth of the Path. Regarding the detailed explanation of the division of the five paths, there are two parts: the sequence of the path of common beings and the path of the noble ones along with its results. The former includes the teachings related to the path of accumulation and the path of preparation. The first of these, which teaches that one must rely specifically on ethical discipline and wisdom on the path of accumulation, is: Even a person endowed with high birth, beauty, and learning is not respected if they lack wisdom and ethical discipline. Therefore, one who possesses these two qualities is worshipped even if they lack other virtues. Although a person may be of the royal caste like a great sal tree, or of the brahmin caste like a great sal tree, thus being of the highest lineage; even if they are handsome, healthy, and the like; and even if they are well-versed in the eighteen sciences and conventional arts; if they lack the wisdom that understands the nature of reality and the path of liberation, and are devoid of the ethical discipline that remains pure in what to adopt and abandon, they are not worthy of honor and respect by the world, including the gods.
<pb n="15"/>And if one is endowed with the virtues of lineage, beauty, and learning, what need is there to speak further? If one possesses those two—the wisdom that understands the nature of reality and the path of liberation, and the perfection of ethical discipline—they become the supreme object of worldly offerings and reverence. Regarding wisdom, there are three types: the wisdom born of hearing, the wisdom born of reflection, and the wisdom born of meditation. On this path of accumulation, the wisdom born of hearing and reflection are of primary importance. Although there are limitless bodhisattva ethical disciplines, in this context, it refers to the ethical discipline of individual liberation. Teaching that those on the path of accumulation must equalize the conceptualization of the eight worldly concerns: Those who know the world, equate gain and loss, happiness and unhappiness, praise and blame, and pleasant and unpleasant talk—these eight worldly concerns—must be equalized so that they do not become objects of the mind. The Buddha, who perfectly understood the world, taught that one must equalize the eight worldly concerns. This means that whether one gains abundant resources or suffers from lack, whether one has a healthy body and a happy mind or suffers, whether one hears pleasant or unpleasant rumors passed from one person to another, or is directly praised or criticized <leaf-break/>
because they do not become companions. For the sake of others, never commit evil deeds. The hidden meaning of this verse: If one thinks that the result of committing evil deeds does not happen immediately, so it is not necessary to abandon them, [know that] although the result of some committed evil deeds does not cut like a weapon at that very moment, when the time of death arrives, the result of the karma of the evil deeds will become manifest. Most results of committed evil deeds do not ripen or cut immediately like a wound inflicted by a sharp weapon, but when the time of death arrives, or in the intermediate state, or when the time of the next birth occurs, the results of the maturation of the karma of the evil deeds will be experienced and become manifest. If you ask when the result of karma will ripen, there are two types: karma that is not certain to be experienced and karma that is certain to be experienced. Regarding the first, there are two: deeds done but not accumulated, and deeds not done but accumulated. Deeds done but not accumulated are of three types: great, medium, and small. Entering into the engagement of virtuous or non-virtuous karma but not reaching the main act is small; entering the engagement but stopping due to regret after reaching half of the main act is medium; and completing the main act but feeling intense regret before the aftermath is deeds done but not <leaf-break/>
The ripening in other lifetimes refers to deeds done and accumulated that have weak power, and because the time of their occurrence is not fixed, it is not determined whether they will occur in two, three, or many lifetimes depending on whether one meets the supporting conditions of virtue or non-virtue. This is what is experienced in other lifetimes. Even the karma of non-virtue that is certain to be experienced can be overcome by antidotes. The text says that the result of evil karma does not ripen immediately, referring to most karma other than that which is to be experienced in this very life. If you ask, among those that are ripe for immediate maturation for both virtuous and non-virtuous karma, which ripens first? The noble Ananda said: "Whichever karma is heavy, whichever is near, whichever is habitual, and whichever was done first—among those, the former ones will ripen." The meaning is that among those ripe for both virtuous and non-virtuous karma, the one with greater karmic power ripens first. If the powers of virtue and non-virtue are equal, the one that is reinforced by whichever thought, virtuous or non-virtuous, is clearer at the time of death will ripen first. If they are equally clear or unclear, the one with the greater habituation to virtue or non-virtue ripens first. If they are also equal, the one that was done first among the two will ripen first, according to the order of time in which they were performed. Equal non-virtue, and virtue</translation>

<summary>This text details the Buddhist path, emphasizing the abandonment of desires, the understanding of the four truths (suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path), and the karmic laws that govern the maturation of actions over various lifetimes.</summary>
<keywords>desire, four noble truths, path of accumulation, karma, ripening of deeds, ethical discipline, wisdom, emptiness</keywords>

Feelings associated with equanimity are the suffering of conditioned existence. The suffering of pain is known even by animals and the like. The suffering of change is seen by those with wisdom. Although the suffering of conditioned existence is the basis for all suffering, it is not known by others and is realized by noble beings. All phenomena are empty means that although many generally take emptiness to mean the absence of elaborations, here the aspect of the Truth of Suffering being empty refers to being empty of incompatible causes. Therefore, creators such as the Lord <term>Ishvara</term> <gloss>a creator deity</gloss> and those who speak of time as the cause are impossible in the nature of things. Thus, one knows it is empty of a creator, and through overcoming the various suitable causes and conditions <leaf-break/>
The essence of the wisdom of the Truth of the Path, which is free of contamination and accompanied by meditative concentration and ethical discipline, possesses the power to abandon afflictions and enables one to attain the state of cessation. Having certainty in this way is mental engagement with the aspect of the Truth of the Path. Regarding the detailed explanation of the division of the five paths, there are two parts: the sequence of the path of common beings and the path of the noble ones along with its results. The former includes the teachings related to the path of accumulation and the path of preparation. The first of these, which teaches that one must rely specifically on ethical discipline and wisdom on the path of accumulation, is: Even a person endowed with high birth, beauty, and learning is not respected if they lack wisdom and ethical discipline. Therefore, one who possesses these two qualities is worshipped even if they lack other virtues. Although a person may be of the royal caste like a great sal tree, or of the brahmin caste like a great sal tree, thus being of the highest lineage; even if they are handsome, healthy, and the like; and even if they are well-versed in the eighteen sciences and conventional arts; if they lack the wisdom that understands the nature of reality and the path of liberation, and are devoid of the ethical discipline that remains pure in what to adopt and abandon, they are not worthy of honor and respect by the world, including the gods.
pages.15:
And if one is endowed with the virtues of lineage, beauty, and learning, what need is there to speak further? If one possesses those two—the wisdom that understands the nature of reality and the path of liberation, and the perfection of ethical discipline—they become the supreme object of worldly offerings and reverence. Regarding wisdom, there are three types: the wisdom born of hearing, the wisdom born of reflection, and the wisdom born of meditation. On this path of accumulation, the wisdom born of hearing and reflection are of primary importance. Although there are limitless bodhisattva ethical disciplines, in this context, it refers to the ethical discipline of individual liberation. Teaching that those on the path of accumulation must equalize the conceptualization of the eight worldly concerns: Those who know the world, equate gain and loss, happiness and unhappiness, praise and blame, and pleasant and unpleasant talk—these eight worldly concerns—must be equalized so that they do not become objects of the mind. The Buddha, who perfectly understood the world, taught that one must equalize the eight worldly concerns. This means that whether one gains abundant resources or suffers from lack, whether one has a healthy body and a happy mind or suffers, whether one hears pleasant or unpleasant rumors passed from one person to another, or is directly praised or criticized <leaf-break/>
because they do not become companions. For the sake of others, never commit evil deeds. The hidden meaning of this verse: If one thinks that the result of committing evil deeds does not happen immediately, so it is not necessary to abandon them, [know that] although the result of some committed evil deeds does not cut like a weapon at that very moment, when the time of death arrives, the result of the karma of the evil deeds will become manifest. Most results of committed evil deeds do not ripen or cut immediately like a wound inflicted by a sharp weapon, but when the time of death arrives, or in the intermediate state, or when the time of the next birth occurs, the results of the maturation of the karma of the evil deeds will be experienced and become manifest. If you ask when the result of karma will ripen, there are two types: karma that is not certain to be experienced and karma that is certain to be experienced. Regarding the first, there are two: deeds done but not accumulated, and deeds not done but accumulated. Deeds done but not accumulated are of three types: great, medium, and small. Entering into the engagement of virtuous or non-virtuous karma but not reaching the main act is small; entering the engagement but stopping due to regret after reaching half of the main act is medium; and completing the main act but feeling intense regret before the aftermath is deeds done but not <leaf-break/>
The ripening in other lifetimes refers to deeds done and accumulated that have weak power, and because the time of their occurrence is not fixed, it is not determined whether they will occur in two, three, or many lifetimes depending on whether one meets the supporting conditions of virtue or non-virtue. This is what is experienced in other lifetimes. Even the karma of non-virtue that is certain to be experienced can be overcome by antidotes. The text says that the result of evil karma does not ripen immediately, referring to most karma other than that which is to be experienced in this very life. If you ask, among those that are ripe for immediate maturation for both virtuous and non-virtuous karma, which ripens first? The noble Ananda said: "Whichever karma is heavy, whichever is near, whichever is habitual, and whichever was done first—among those, the former ones will ripen." The meaning is that among those ripe for both virtuous and non-virtuous karma, the one with greater karmic power ripens first. If the powers of virtue and non-virtue are equal, the one that is reinforced by whichever thought, virtuous or non-virtuous, is clearer at the time of death will ripen first. If they are equally clear or unclear, the one with the greater habituation to virtue or non-virtue ripens first. If they are also equal, the one that was done first among the two will ripen first, according to the order of time in which they were performed. Equal non-virtue, and virtue

<pb n="124"/>...are just the same as having attainments. How is this different from the old views? Furthermore, this is even worse than the views of others. Why? Because formerly they grasped the old interpretations of the Treatise on Numbers <note>the Abhidharma tradition</note>, and now they grasp the new wisdom of the Three Treatises. This only adds one more layer of view. The Master says: "This is merely adding feet to a snake <note>an idiom meaning to add something unnecessary that ruins the original</note>." It may be said that the more one learns, the more inverted one becomes. However, the intent of the sutras and treatises lies in quieting the mind to reach the original source, which is why one is called a <term>shramana</term> <gloss>ascetic/renunciant</gloss>. Moreover, one should quiet the mind until there is no more quieting. As for the statement that one should not refute the "Middle-Provisional," those who embody the Way understand that this "provisional nature" is originally the Way itself; there is no need to refute it. Since you wish to refute it, are you not refuting the Way? One must most deeply perceive this meaning. Now, when we speak of "refuting," it is because they do not know that the "provisional nature" they establish is originally the Way. Therefore, they treat the Way as "not-the-Way." Now, we simply cause them to awaken to the fact that "not-the-Way" is actually the Way. Therefore, we speak of "refutation," but in reality, there is no refutation. Second, one must also know that nature <term>svabhava</term> is itself provisional. Ordinary people, in their inversion, think that the provisional becomes nature. The Buddhas observe it, and nature is always provisional. Therefore, it is said that all worldly truths, if in the eyes of the Thus-Come-One,
<pb n="125"/>
<header>Commentary on the Madhyamaka-shastra, Volume 4</header>
<sig>Gui</sig>
are always the First Principle Truth. Third, those who embody the Way know that this Way has never been a provisional nature. Provisional nature arises from dual conditions, just as the One Way has never been "truth" or "convention," but arises from two conditions. Fourth, those who seek to understand the teachings must recognize that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess unobstructed contemplation within, and inexhaustible eloquence without. They speak of the provisional as nature, and speak of nature as not being provisional. They speak of nature as not being nature, and the provisional as nature. <pb n="165"/> A hunter lay in wait in the mountains at night when he saw a small person, about two feet tall, walking alone along the bottom of a ravine. A short while later, another person appeared, similar in height. When they met, they asked each other where they were going. The first one said, "I am going to visit Yang the Scarred. I have seen his complexion; it is dark and lacks luster, which is very inauspicious." The second one replied, "I am also here for this reason. What you say is correct." The hunter realized they were not human, so he shouted loudly. Both figures immediately vanished. That night, he caught a fox, and on its forehead, there was a scar as large as a coin.

**The Dragon Plays with the Spider**

Master Xu was an official in Qidong. There was a building in his office used to store food and delicacies, which were often stolen and scattered on the floor by some creature. The household servants were frequently scolded for this, so they laid an ambush to observe. They saw a spider as large as a bushel measure and fled in terror to inform the master. Master Xu considered this strange and began to send servants to offer food to it. The spider became increasingly tame, emerging whenever it was hungry to lean against...

<pb n="166"/> ...a person, satiated, before leaving. After more than a year, the master was reading official documents when the spider suddenly came and crouched under his desk. Suspecting it was hungry, he called for his servants to bring food. Suddenly, he saw two snakes pinning the spider down, their bodies as thick as chopsticks. The spider curled its legs and shrunk its abdomen as if unable to bear the fear. In an instant, the snakes grew violently, becoming thicker than eggs. The master was terrified and wanted to flee, when a massive thunderclap occurred. The whole house was shaken and shocked. After some time, the master regained consciousness, but seven or eight people, including his wife and servants, had been struck dead. The master was ill for over a month and soon passed away. Master Xu was an upright and honest man who loved the people dearly. When news of his death spread, the people collected money to send off his funeral, and the sound of their weeping filled the wilderness.

Historian Wu says: I always thought "The Dragon Plays with the Spider" was just a rumor from the streets. Could it really have happened? I have heard that lightning strikes must target wicked people. Why then did such a virtuous and benevolent official suffer such a tragic and poisonous fate? Is the Lord of Heaven so endlessly resentful of many things?
</translation>

<summary>This page recounts two supernatural tales: one involving mountain spirits predicting an ill-fated man's future, and a tragic story where an official named Master Xu is killed by a supernatural lightning strike while dealing with an oversized spider and mysterious snakes.</summary>
<keywords>Master Xu, folklore, supernatural, portents, morality, destiny, spirits, lightning, tragedy</keywords>

"Knowing words" means being able to know the right and wrong in people's speech; "exhausting the principles" means to fully investigate the principles of things. Only then can the mind be like a bright mirror and be able to use the Sage's method of observing people to examine them.

○ The Master said, "If a man keeps warm what he has learned and deduces new things from it, he may become a teacher."

"Warm" means to search out and trace. "Old" refers to what one has heard in the past; "new" refers to what one obtains in the present. If, through constant practice, one can grasp the old, and with each instance acquire new insights, then what is learned resides within oneself and the application becomes inexhaustible. Therefore, one is fit to be a teacher. As for <margin>pronounced *fu*</margin> learning that is merely for the purpose of reciting and asking, one has nothing realized in the heart, <margin>Master Chen of Xin'an says: [compared] with</margin> and what one knows is limited. <margin>Master Chen of Xin'an says: [compared] with</margin> This is the opposite of being inexhaustible in application. Thus, the *Book of Rites* <note>original: "Xueji"</note> criticizes such learning as insufficient to qualify one as a teacher. This exactly corroborates the meaning here. <margin>Master Zhu says: "Keeping warm the old" is not</margin> merely looking inside to find a principle. If you remember ten things, you only have ten; if you remember a hundred, you only have a hundred. That is dead knowledge. "Knowing the new" means that within the process of warming the old, one perceives 
<pb n="51"/>
<margin>Complete Commentaries on the Analects</margin>
this principle becoming more refined, surpassing what was known before. By extending and expanding upon it, and by touching upon categories and letting them grow, it remains constantly alive and not dead. In the *Doctrine of the Mean*, it is noted that keeping warm the old and knowing the new is not merely keeping warm the old and waiting for the new. Seeking beauty—if one keeps warm the old but only seeks the new, one still cannot "know the new." If one does not keep warm the old, one is not fit to be a teacher. This is why the question makes a definitive judgment. If one truly does not "keep warm the old," one is also not fit to be a teacher. The meaning of this utterance lies in "knowing the new." Only by keeping warm the old can one know the new. The new is not an external principle; through constant practice, one becomes familiar, and it gradually emerges. For example, the principles all come from within oneself. When people come to ask, one uses these principles to explain them. Even if several people come to ask, one uses these principles to reason them out, and the application is inexhaustible. For instance, the learning of mere recitation: if one remembers one matter, one can only speak of that one matter. It does not go beyond that. This departs from the meaning of "keeping warm the old and reaching understanding." Is this not the principle of "learning from what is below and reaching what is above"? What is contained in the Six Classics is one principle; what is contained in the Four Books is one principle. When one constantly reviews them, one feels the flavor is profound and lasting, and one naturally attains new insights. Also, one says: what was obtained in the past
</translation>

It connects these pedagogical principles to the concepts of "knowing words," "exhausting principles," and the Confucian ideal of continuous, self-reflective growth.</summary>
<keywords>Confucius, Master Zhu, learning, pedagogy, Analects, Doctrine of the Mean, knowledge, teacher-student relationship</keywords>

One must ensure that the denominator of the fraction and the resulting numerator each have an origin to be able to extract the root. <pb n="61"/>...from the words of the Marquis of Chen. The Marquis of Chen said to Zigong, "Only now do I know the value of a sage." Zigong replied, "It is not as good as specializing in his way and practicing his teachings, for that is the true excellence." <margin>Revision follows the commentary on "You"</margin>
After Yang Huo had fled to Qi and then from Qi to Jin, he sought refuge with the Zhao clan. Confucius heard of this and said to Zilu, "The Zhao clan will likely suffer chaos for generations." Zilu asked, "The power does not reside there, so how could he cause chaos?" Confucius replied, "This is not something you would know. Yang Huo is intimate with those who are powerful but not intimate with those who are humane. He had the favor of the Jisun family, and later attempted to kill them but failed, fleeing to Qi. The people of Qi imprisoned him, yet he escaped and returned to Jin. Thus, the two states of Qi and Lu have already removed their ailment. Zhao Jianzi loves profit and kills many; he will inevitably favor Yang Huo’s rhetoric and follow his stratagems. That the disasters and failures will last for more than one generation is predictable."
Ji Kangzi asked Confucius, "In the current twelfth month of the Zhou calendar, which is the tenth month of the Xia calendar, there are still locusts. Why is this?" Confucius replied, "I have heard that once the fire star <note>Antares, which signals the transition of seasons</note> descends, hibernating creatures should all be hidden. Now, the fire star is still moving toward the west. <margin>Zhengqi Hall</margin>
<pb n="62"/>It is a failure of the calendar official." Ji Kangzi asked, "By how many months is it off?" Confucius said, "In the tenth month of the Xia calendar, the fire star should have already set. Now that it is still visible, it means the intercalation is missed by two months." <margin>See the Zuo Zhuan, 12th year of Duke Ai</margin>
The King of Wu, Fuchai, was planning to present Duke Ai to the Marquis of Jin. Zifu Jingbo replied to the envoy, "When the King convenes the feudal lords, the hegemon leads the lords and pastors to appear before the King. When the hegemon convenes the feudal lords, the lords lead the viscounts and barons to appear before the hegemon. Now that the feudal lords are meeting, and you plan to have our humble ruler appear before the Marquis of Jin, you are essentially making Jin the hegemon. Moreover, if your office uses the authority of the hegemon to summon the feudal lords, what benefit is there in having the lords do this for you?" The people of Wu then stopped. <pb n="105"/>If the illness is such that no ordinary doctor can save the patient, one must treat it using this method of satisfying their needs. If one has the ability to provide what they need, one should provide it; if one lacks the ability, there is no harm in providing it through trickery. For those who are poor and cannot obtain wealth, one may borrow in their name from the rich, or falsely claim to be a relative or friend offering charity for their hunger, and place the money by their bedside. If I can provide this, it is the first step in curing the "illness of poverty." For those who have not yet obtained official rank, one might urgently pay the grain contribution <note>a historical method of purchasing official titles</note> on their behalf, or falsely claim they have been recommended for a post. For those who already hold office, one might truly scheme for their appointment or falsely report an official transfer. For the elderly who wish to attain a certain age, one can use the words of astrologers, shamans, or physicians to provide them. If I can give them this, what is there to begrudge? This is simply a matter of "using the person's own way to govern their own body." However, while it is easy to treat most illnesses, it is difficult to treat poverty. The people of this world who suffer from poverty to the point of illness, and whose illness becomes incurable, are almost as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. How can one borrow the grain from the great granaries or the gold from the wealthy Guo Kuang <note>a historical figure noted for immense wealth</note> for every person? If I could do so, everyone would be able to feel joy, and all would be cured, as if in the <term>Jieziyuan</term> <gloss>Mustard Seed Garden</gloss> <pb n="106"/><header>Collected Works, Volume 6</header> <sig>4</sig>

where one is made happy and thus suddenly and completely healed.

The third category: those one is deeply attached to can serve as medicine. A person's heart and private affections must have a focus. There are often rulers who cannot obtain this from their ministers, or fathers who cannot obtain it from their sons, yet they may focus their spirit and life force entirely upon someone who is extremely distant, remote, and unworthy of such love; this is what is meant by "fixing one's passion." It might be a beautiful wife or concubine, a close companion, a handsome youth, or a most intimate friend. To long for them and not obtain them, or to obtain them but not be close to them, can all cause illness. Even for those whose illness is not related to this, once they reach a point of pain and despair, they will inevitably think of the person they love. If one then suddenly brings them together, they will be like fish finding water; there has never been a case where the ears do not become clear, the eyes bright, and the spirit suddenly invigorated.
</translation>

<summary>Li Yu continues his discussion of "medicine" for the soul by suggesting that alleviating poverty through artifice and satisfying deep-seated personal attachments can cure physical ailments that standard medicine cannot reach.</summary>
<keywords>psychological healing, poverty, social status, emotional attachment, desire, unconventional medicine</keywords>

<pb n="24"/>Fayu heard of this from afar. He took a bamboo tube, placed a thorn-wood staff inside, sealed it, and sent it to Dao'an. When Dao'an opened the seal and saw the staff, he immediately said, "This is because of the monk who drank alcohol. My teaching and instruction have not been diligent, and I have caused concern from afar." He then struck the bell to assemble the monks and placed the tube before them. Burning incense, he paid his respects and prostrated on the ground, ordering the <term>vinaya-master</term> <gloss>monk in charge of discipline</gloss> to strike him with the staff three times. Shedding tears, he repented and blamed himself. There was no one among the monastics and laypeople in the region who did not sigh in sorrow. Because of this, many were inspired to apply themselves to their practice.

Eulogy: Alas, if someone today were to open an envelope like the one from Elder Dao'an, few would not break the tube, snap the staff, and speak insolently. A sage teacher and a virtuous disciple; even a thousand years later, I still praise these two masters highly.

### Repentance and Prostration for the Teacher

During the Jin dynasty, Fakuang was from Xiapi. He lost his parents at an early age and served his stepmother with such devotion that he was known for his filial piety. Later, he left the home life and studied under the <term>shramana</term> <gloss>Buddhist monk</gloss> Tanyin. Tanyin once became critically ill. Fakuang prayed with sincerity and performed repentance rituals for seven days and seven nights. On the seventh day, he suddenly saw a five-colored light shining upon Tanyin’s room. Tanyin felt as if someone had shaken him with their hand, and his illness was cured.

### Standing in the Snow Up to the Knees

During the Wei dynasty, Shenguang’s scholarly understanding surpassed the world. When Grand Master Bodhidharma arrived from the Western Regions, Shenguang went to study under him, but Bodhidharma never spoke to him. One night, there was a heavy snowfall. Shenguang stood in the courtyard until dawn, with the snow rising above his knees. Bodhidharma turned and asked, "You have stood in the snow for a long time; what do you seek?" Shenguang wept and said, "I only wish for the Reverend to open the gate of sweet dew <note>a metaphor for the teachings of the Dharma, which nourish the spirit</note> and widely liberate all sentient beings." Bodhidharma said, "The supreme, subtle path of all Buddhas requires diligent exertion over countless eons. It requires doing what is difficult to do and enduring what is difficult to endure. Even that is not enough to attain it. Yet you, with a light and shallow mind, hope to reach the true vehicle. It is a futile effort." Hearing this encouragement, Shenguang <pb n="25"/> took a blade and severed his own arm, placing it before Bodhidharma. Bodhidharma said, "All Buddhas sought the path by sacrificing their physical forms for the sake of the Dharma. You have now severed your arm; your request may be fulfilled." Shenguang said, "My heart is not yet at peace. I beg the Master to pacify my heart." Bodhidharma said, "Bring your heart here, and I will pacify it for you." Shenguang said, "I have searched for my heart, but it is ultimately unattainable." Bodhidharma said, "I have finished pacifying your heart." He then transmitted the Dharma, and Shenguang became the <term>Second Patriarch</term> <gloss>of the Chan school</gloss>.

> Eulogy: The Second Patriarch attained the Dharma due to his sincere dedication. The conditions were ripe and his potential was already fully developed. Like a needle and a mustard seed meeting, it was not specifically about the act of severing the arm. Foolish people mimic the action and think they must wield the blade. Alas, if one must sever an arm to transmit the Dharma, the various patriarchs would have no intact skin. If one must burn the body to attain Buddhahood, then the sages would have no survivors. One should sever the arm of defilements and burn the body of ignorance. I urge practitioners of Chan to strive for this.

### ->Leaving the Teacher and Self-Reproach<-

During the Tang dynasty, Qingjiang realized the illusory nature of life as a bubble from a young age. He received ordination under the Vinaya Master Tanyi as his primary teacher. He memorized scriptures and mastered them at a glance. Those who knew him said, "This is a thousand-mile steed of the monastic community." Once, having a slight disagreement with his teacher, he left to travel for study, visiting various halls of the Dharma. He later reproached himself, saying, "I have traveled half the world, and there is rarely anyone like my original teacher." He then returned. While the community was gathered, he carried a thorn-wood branch on his back and declared, "I, your student, have come to rely upon you again. I only pray for your acceptance." At that time, the Master scolded him harshly, and Qingjiang wept as he repented and thanked him. He realized that his previous thoughts were based on ignorance, while his later thoughts brought him understanding. He looked toward the Master with great compassion, asking him to bestow joy upon him. He pleaded four times. Master Tanyi took pity on him, and their relationship as teacher and student resumed as before. After Master Tanyi passed away, he exhausted himself serving National Teacher Zhong, from whom he secretly received the essence of the mind.

> Eulogy: To realize one's errors after leaving a sage teacher, and to remain steadfast despite being scolded, is to be both enlightened and sincere. Did the final transmission of the mind-seal not result from this? As for those of shallow faith, they leave permanently over a minor grievance, or nurse hatred over a slight reprimand. Though they encounter an enlightened teacher, what is the gain? It is like meeting an emperor and failing to receive even a single official post. How lamentable.

<summary>This text chronicles the extreme devotion of disciples such as Fakuang, Shenguang (Huike), and Qingjiang, emphasizing that true commitment to the Dharma transcends physical sacrifice and requires internal humility.</summary>
<keywords>Dao'an, Fakuang, Bodhidharma, Shenguang, Qingjiang, Tanyi, repentance, filial piety, transmission of Dharma, Chan Buddhism</keywords>

<pb n="134"/>...is like the wind, which is the image of inner truth. The superior person embodies the virtue of Heaven and Earth, which delights in the birth of things; thus, they deliberate on legal cases and delay death sentences. Inner truth is a state of mind. When a legal case is near completion, one deliberates on it; when a verdict is to be passed, one delays it, so that it may reach the human heart. To speak of "deliberating" on a case is to seek life within the verdict; to speak of "delaying" an execution is to seek life within the sentence of death. Shun’s concern for punishment, Yu’s weeping over the condemned, Tang’s prayer at the net, and King Wen’s burial of skeletal remains—if these did not arise from the sincerity of their original hearts, who would have been moved by them? The way of utmost sincerity can traverse water and fire, melt metal and stone, and influence Heaven and Earth; how much more so with humans, and how much more with spirits? The King listens, the Three Ministers listen, and the Minister of Justice listens—this is the deliberation of cases. To listen to reports every ten days, and to submit to the throne every thirty days—this is the delay of death sentences. <note>The text refers to the administrative protocols for reviewing capital cases as described in the Rites of Zhou.</note> The hexagram <term>Dui</term> <gloss>Joy/Marsh</gloss> represents the deliberation, while different symbols represent the delay of death. Regarding the six lines of the single hexagram, it is the center that is empty; 

<pb n="135"/>regarding the two sections of the hexagram, it is the center that is full—both are images of sincerity. Furthermore, the lower part is pleased to respond to the upper, and the upper part is changed to follow the lower; this also contains the meaning of sincerity. Inner truth is the belief within the heart. To believe in the heart is to believe in <term>li</term> <gloss>principle/universal order</gloss>. To see <term>li</term> and believe in it is the method of believing in the heart. Among the sixty-four hexagrams, there is not one hexagram or one line that does not take sincerity as its pivot. Without sincerity, the center cannot be empty; how then could it be full? The empty is that which gains fullness; it is the soft being sincere to the hard. To be pleased and to change is how one achieves emptiness. To have trust reach even pigs and fish is for the empty to move the empty. To board a wooden boat is for the empty to assist the empty. That which is full is <term>li</term>. <term>Li</term> is Heaven. It is that which makes the heart the heart. It is what is meant by "beneficial for remaining correct."

<note>A woodcut depicts the hexagram of Thunder below and Mountain above, known as the hexagram of "Developing" (Jian).</note>
