<translation>
# High-minded individuals will naturally rectify these matters

## An instruction for Dong Zhiguang

Student Dong <note>original: "董生", refers to Dong Zhiguang</note> has grown up in a wealthy family, yet early on developed a heart seeking to transcend birth and death. This is the power of the internal cultivation of <term>prajna</term> <gloss>transcendent wisdom</gloss> from past lives. He first studied under Master Yunqi <note>original: "雲棲大師", likely referring to Yunqi Zhuhong</note> and received the Pure Land method. Recently, he visited this old man <note>original: "老人", refers to the author, Hanshan Deqing</note> at Shuangjing and expressed a wish to receive the <term>upasaka</term> <gloss>lay practitioner</gloss> precepts. He also confessed that his karmic offenses were heavy and asked for the essential method to escape suffering and how to cultivate it to extinguish his past errors. The old man then instructed him, saying: "Since you, as a student, know that your root of offenses is deep and heavy, the ancient virtuous ones taught people to eliminate old karma as they go, and strictly avoid creating new disasters. The Buddha opened the single gate of repentance for sentient beings burdened with heavy karma, which is the most convenient method for escaping suffering." The verse says:

> All sins are like frost and dew,
> The sun of wisdom can eliminate them.
> If one wishes to repent,
> Sit upright and contemplate the <term>tathata</term> <gloss>true reality/essential nature</gloss>.

This is the correct practice; all else is but auxiliary. The <pb n="11"/> original nature of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddhas, fundamentally unstained, and devoid of the phenomena of birth, death, coming, or going. It is only because, at the very beginning, there was a failure to awaken, leading to the obscuration of one’s own nature, that it is called "ignorance" <note>original: "無明" (avidya)</note>. Because of this ignorance, all sorts of delusions arise, leading to various inverted views and the creation of various karmas, resulting in the misguided grasping of the suffering of life and death within the three realms. All this is due to ignorance and a failure to understand one’s own mind, allowing oneself to be turned by delusions. It is like a person in a deep sleep having various nightmares, seeing all sorts of terrifying realms and enduring unbearable suffering; yet upon waking, if they try to find the things from the dream, they are utterly unattainable. Therefore, sentient beings have fallen into the dream of ignorance, following delusions and inverted views, creating various karmas, and bringing suffering upon themselves. When viewed with awakened eyes, how could the conditions of these inverted views be found? Since you are presently within this dream of ignorance, how can you eliminate old karma? You must use the light of wisdom to illuminate and break through ignorance, believing that your own mind is fundamentally pure and not driven by delusions and inverted views. Then, all karma will be without a cause, for delusion is the cause of all karma. Why is this so? It is because, from beginningless time, we have been lost to our own original mind, life after life.
</translation>

<summary>Hanshan Deqing instructs the lay practitioner Dong Zhiguang on the necessity of repentance and the cultivation of wisdom to break the "dream" of ignorance, which he identifies as the root cause of karmic suffering.</summary>

pages.10:
# High-minded individuals will naturally rectify these matters

## An instruction for Dong Zhiguang

Student Dong <note>original: "董生", refers to Dong Zhiguang</note> has grown up in a wealthy family, yet early on developed a heart seeking to transcend birth and death. This is the power of the internal cultivation of <term>prajna</term> <gloss>transcendent wisdom</gloss> from past lives. He first studied under Master Yunqi <note>original: "雲棲大師", likely referring to Yunqi Zhuhong</note> and received the Pure Land method. Recently, he visited this old man <note>original: "老人", refers to the author, Hanshan Deqing</note> at Shuangjing and expressed a wish to receive the <term>upasaka</term> <gloss>lay practitioner</gloss> precepts. He also confessed that his karmic offenses were heavy and asked for the essential method to escape suffering and how to cultivate it to extinguish his past errors. The old man then instructed him, saying: "Since you, as a student, know that your root of offenses is deep and heavy, the ancient virtuous ones taught people to eliminate old karma as they go, and strictly avoid creating new disasters. The Buddha opened the single gate of repentance for sentient beings burdened with heavy karma, which is the most convenient method for escaping suffering." The verse says:

> All sins are like frost and dew,
> The sun of wisdom can eliminate them.
> If one wishes to repent,
> Sit upright and contemplate the <term>tathata</term> <gloss>true reality/essential nature</gloss>.

This is the correct practice; all else is but auxiliary. The
pages.11: original nature of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddhas, fundamentally unstained, and devoid of the phenomena of birth, death, coming, or going. It is only because, at the very beginning, there was a failure to awaken, leading to the obscuration of one’s own nature, that it is called "ignorance" <note>original: "無明" (avidya)</note>. Because of this ignorance, all sorts of delusions arise, leading to various inverted views and the creation of various karmas, resulting in the misguided grasping of the suffering of life and death within the three realms. All this is due to ignorance and a failure to understand one’s own mind, allowing oneself to be turned by delusions. It is like a person in a deep sleep having various nightmares, seeing all sorts of terrifying realms and enduring unbearable suffering; yet upon waking, if they try to find the things from the dream, they are utterly unattainable. Therefore, sentient beings have fallen into the dream of ignorance, following delusions and inverted views, creating various karmas, and bringing suffering upon themselves. When viewed with awakened eyes, how could the conditions of these inverted views be found? Since you are presently within this dream of ignorance, how can you eliminate old karma? You must use the light of wisdom to illuminate and break through ignorance, believing that your own mind is fundamentally pure and not driven by delusions and inverted views. Then, all karma will be without a cause, for delusion is the cause of all karma. Why is this so? It is because, from beginningless time, we have been lost to our own original mind, life after life.

<meta>continues from previous page: ...The concept of the generation and overcoming of the five elements is deeply detrimental to correct principles. <margin>Note: Among Song dynasty Confucians, only Shaozi <note>Shao Yong</note> does not discuss the five elements, using instead the sun, moon, stars, and constellations in his *Huangji Jingshi* <gloss>Supreme Principles Governing the World</gloss>.</margin></meta><pb n="120"/>The words from "less than a catty" <note>This refers to the phrase "Shaohao" <term>少昊</term>, literally "less than a catty" or "less than a metal," a pun often found in critical commentaries on the Five Elements.</note> regarding water, fire, earth, and stone—all these define the substance and function of heaven and earth—stand prominently apart from other schools of thought. Master Zhang <note>Zhang Zai (1020–1077), a prominent Neo-Confucian philosopher.</note> states in his *Zhengmeng* <gloss>Correcting Youthful Ignorance</gloss> that water and fire are <term>qi</term> <gloss>vital energy/breath</gloss>. Therefore, their nature to flame upward and moisten downward is something that earth cannot control. Wood and metal are the flowers and fruits of the earth. Their nature contains a mixture of water and fire. As for the nature of wood, if it is soaked in water, it thrives; if it catches fire, it burns, yet it never departs from either. It essentially obtains the brilliance of the earth and floats at the intersection of water and fire. As for the nature of metal, it obtains the essence of fire from the dryness of the earth and the essence of water from the moisture of the earth. Thus, water and fire wait upon each other without harming one another. Even when melted, metal flows back into its liquid state without being consumed. It essentially obtains the solid essence of the earth at the juncture of water and fire. Earth is the means by which all things complete their beginnings and reach their ends. It is the substance of the ground and the culmination of transformation. It is the reason why water and fire rise and fall. <pb n="121"/>It is what encompasses the substances of all things without omission. That Master Zhang explains the generation of metal, wood, water, fire, and earth in this way is an immutable principle.

The method of manipulating stalks uses one, two, three, and four to represent the remainder numbers, and six, seven, eight <margin>Questioning the *Zhouyi Chanshu* <gloss>Explication of the Book of Changes</gloss></margin> <note>A woodcut or typographical mark exists in the bottom left corner.</note>

It further critiques the numerical foundations of the "Great Expansion" method from the Book of Changes, specifically focusing on why the total number is fifty and how the stalks are manipulated.</summary>

<pb n="13"/>The retraction of Abu al-Hasan and Umar Bali from the fatwa of permissibility, and following the fatwa of the Mufti Shaykh Muhammad Sa'id Babasil, and stating that the Mufti's fatwa is according to the Shafi'i school, in which there is no disagreement among the Shafi'i scholars. Such is the proof. And from the Mufti's answer, it is that which is in the Shafi'i school, there is no disagreement in the school. From that, it is known that the fatwa of those who oppose the fatwa is void. So all the people who issued fatwas opposing that fatwa have retracted their fatwa and have acknowledged their error. And this signature has been written above to confirm that fatwa of the Mufti <note>so that it is known by the brothers</note> who see this answer. By Ahmad Khatib, Imam of the Shafi'is in the glorious Makkah, from the Sacred Mosque <note>al-Masjid al-Haram</note>. End of the signature of the Chief of Mentawai, Hajj Marzuqi, confirming the fatwa of the Mufti Shaykh Muhammad Sa'id Babasil and invalidating 

<pb n="14"/>the fatwa of the person who issued a fatwa that it is permissible to sell rice to the Chinese. Such is the proof.
Praise be to Allah alone, and may blessings and peace be upon him after whom there is no prophet.

I have seen the fatwa of the Shaykh al-Islam and Mufti of Mankind, Shaykh Muhammad Sa'id Babasil, and several Shafi'i scholars who have signed below that fatwa, that it remains forbidden to sell rice to the Chinese according to the correct opinion of the Shafi'i school, and the statement of those who claimed it is permissible is void. And Allah knows best. By the servant of the Chief of the Mentawai community, Hajj Marzuqi bin Hajj Isma'il. Signed by the one who is weak and lowly, out of complaint to Allah the Glorified and Exalted, who grants success. Success in the correctness of the fatwa of the scholars, which is in the year one thousand three hundred and seventeen <note>Hijri year 1317, or 1899/1900 CE</note>. May Allah reward them with a great reward and keep them in a high status. O Allah, grant us success in following them in the religion. Amen, Lord of the Worlds. Thus, all praise is due to Allah, and thanks be to Allah, and blessings and peace.

Fatwa

<pb n="15"/>May blessings and peace be upon the best of Allah's creation, his family, and his companions, the guides of the community, and upon the scholars who are the heirs <note>of the prophets</note> and those who follow them until the Day of Resurrection. And after: Makkah, in the year of the Prophet's Hijra, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, [one thousand three hundred and seventeen], I issued a fatwa in Belibu, Afdeling Mentawai, that it is forbidden to sell rice to the Chinese. After I had inquired into its matter, some of them rejected my fatwa, [namely Hajj Madi bin Machan], and he sought support from Hajj Abu al-Hasan, Palembang, Talang Bali. So Hajj Abu al-Hasan assisted, and he also obtained support from two people, namely Muhammad Mansuri Maliki and Umar Bali Ampunan. [Then Hajj Abu al-Hasan immediately issued a fatwa of permissibility to Hajj Madi bin Machan, and he informed him that he had already submitted a question to the Mufti Sayyid Ahmad bin Zaini Dahlan in the past, and the Mufti issued a fatwa of permissibility, and he had already consulted this Mufti, who is Shaykh Muhammad Sa'id Babasil, and the Mufti issued a fatwa of permissibility, and he informed him that Muhammad Mansuri

<pb n="16"/>Maliki and Umar Bali Ampunan also permitted it in Makkah. The letter of Hajj Abu al-Hasan in Makkah to Hajj Madi bin Machan in Belibu arrived. Then Hajj Dat Mentawai <note>Radin Muhammad Arif Boyan</note> immediately returned that letter of Hajj Abu al-Hasan and sent a copy of it to the head of Penghulu in Penang. Then he immediately sent his letter to Makkah to the Hajj who was in Mentawai. On Friday, 8 Ramadan 323, the Chief of Mentawai, Hajj Marzuqi, showed the letter of Hajj Abu al-Hasan from Makkah, informing him that he had issued a fatwa that it is permissible to sell rice to the Chinese, and that the fatwa of Mufti Sayyid Ahmad Dahlan is also permissible, and the fatwa of Mufti Shaykh Muhammad Sa'id Babasil is also permissible, and included were the two letters of the answer from Mansuri Maliki and the answer from Umar Bali, both letters issuing a fatwa of permissibility. Furthermore, Hajj Abu al-Hasan requested that the Chief Penghulu bring those two letters of answer to Belibu, and that their meaning be explained to the people of Belibu so that the people would not be deceived.</translation>

<summary>This text contains a series of religious rulings (fatwas) and retractions concerning the sale of rice to Chinese merchants, with scholars in Makkah and Mentawai affirming the prohibition based on the Shafi'i school.</summary>
<keywords>Fatwa, Shafi'i school, rice trade, Aḥmad Khatib al-Minangkabawi, Hajj Marzuqi, religious law</keywords>

<pb n="15"/>their males and females are equal, because they are her brothers and sisters through her mother, and the brothers of the mother through the father alongside their sisters, as is known. If they divide the inheritance of the son of a sister through the mother and the maternal aunts related through her, they do not divide it such that the male receives the portion of two females. The discussion ends here.

The apparent meaning of both <term>al-Tuḥfah</term> <gloss>The Masterpiece</gloss> and <term>al-Nihāyah</term> <gloss>The End</gloss> is that their statement "it is divided equally" is a qualification for all of the children of the uterine descendants and for the maternal uncles and aunts through her, which is explicit in <term>Sharḥ al-Rawḍ</term> <gloss>Commentary on the Garden</gloss>, as you know from its wording. That is not the case; rather, their statement "it is divided equally" is a qualification for the children of the uterine descendants only. The exception then becomes apparent. They then mentioned the reasoning for the exception until they said: "As for the maternal uncles and aunts through the mother—meaning the sisters of the mother of the deceased and her sisters through her mother—they are excluded from the aforementioned rule, as you know." It follows from their exclusion from that rule that they inherit such that the male receives the portion of two females, because they descend into the position of the mother, as is stated explicitly in the legal texts <term>mutūn</term> <gloss>foundational legal manuals</gloss>, let alone others. If they were to inherit the share of the mother, had she been the deceased, they would have divided it according to the number of heads. 

<pb n="15b"/>
...according to <term>Jamāl al-Ramlī</term> in his <term>Nihāyah</term> <gloss>The End</gloss>, and he was preceded by his teacher <term>Zakariyyā al-Anṣārī</term> in his <term>Sharḥ al-Rawḍ</term> <gloss>Commentary on the Garden</gloss>. His phrasing is: "The children of the brother through the mother and the maternal uncles and aunts through her are excluded from that, so they do not divide it such that the male receives the portion of two females; rather, they divide it among themselves equally, as is known from what will follow in his speech." The matter ends here.

I understood it that way so that we do not rule that it was a slip of the pen. The matter ends here. And God knows best. According to the <term>Ḥanbalīs</term>, the maternal uncle is given priority over all other <term>dhawī al-arḥām</term> <gloss>uterine relatives</gloss>. If the male and female are from one side, such as the children of the daughter at the same degree, and one of them is earlier in reaching the heir, they are prioritized by that; otherwise, they inherit through both. Like the daughter of a daughter of a daughter of a son of a daughter: it is as if the son of the daughter of Zayd had married the daughter of his other daughter, and she gave birth to a daughter; and the daughter of a sister through the father is like the daughter of a brother through the mother: it is as if the brother of Zayd through his mother had married his sister through his father and she gave birth to a daughter; and the daughter of a maternal uncle is like the daughter of his paternal uncle: it is as if the maternal uncle of Zayd had married his paternal aunt and she gave birth to a daughter. Note: <insert>it is equal in it</insert> is taken from our saying "descendant."

<pb n="16"/>
The daughter of the son descends to her descendant three times, then the share of the son descends to his daughter, and the share of the daughter descends to her son. And God knows best. The author—may God grant benefit through him—said: "This is what I wanted to copy from the aforementioned book during my journey to the honored Makkah for the Hajj in the year 1232 [AH], so that it may be a reference for me when needed, as it is a summary of the statement of that commentary. Because it was not possible for me to accompany the original, otherwise it would have been preferable, for he mentioned in it additional clarification and explanation. He mentioned chapters on the examples of the categories, their branches, their differences, the rulings of the return <term>radd</term>, the principles of its problems and their examples, and the school of the people of affinity and its branches. I ask God Almighty to make them beneficial for the people of Islam, and may God bless our master Muhammad, his family, and all his companions, and grant them peace. Amen."

<pb n="16b"/>
...when descending generation after generation, etc., to the intermediary between the <term>dhawī al-arḥām</term> <gloss>uterine relatives</gloss> and the nearest heir, which is considered in the primary cases. He said in <term>Kashf al-Ghawāmiḍ</term> <gloss>The Uncovering of Obscurities</gloss> by the grandson: "The father of the mother descends into the position of the mother, the father of the father of the mother descends into the position of the mother of the father, and the mother of the father of the mother descends into the position of the father of the mother." If the intermediary were not considered, the mother of the father of the mother would descend into the position of the heir, which is the mother, so she would be equal to the father of the mother, and no one says this. Therefore, what is in the legal opinions <term>fatāwā</term> of the scholar <term>Ibn Ḥajar</term> regarding his making the son of the maternal aunt equal to the maternal uncle has an element of scrutiny, which is halted by our saying "according to his inheritance from him," [because of] difficulty, assuming that the intermediary is considered in determining the share of the heir for the uterine relative, since agnation and fixed shares are a reality in the connected descendants. He said in <term>al-Fatḥ</term> <gloss>The Opening</gloss>: "The result of this is that you raise the one lower by a generation, and for the higher, it is the reverse." The discussion ends here. That is why I said after that: "Meaning the share of the heir descends to his connected descendants, etc." Also, there might be a uterine relative at the end of the descendants, such as the daughter of the son of the daughter of the son, and the son of the daughter of that daughter. If the intermediary were not considered, he would be excluded because he is not an heir of this heir, but it is not so; rather, the share of the daughter of the son...
</translation>

<summary>This text concludes a discussion on the inheritance rights of uterine relatives (dhawī al-arḥām) and the methodology for assigning shares based on the status of the heirs through whom these relatives are connected. The author provides a concluding note regarding his compilation of these rules during his pilgrimage to Makkah in 1232 AH.</summary>
<keywords>Islamic inheritance law, dhawī al-arḥām, uterine relatives, heirs, jurisprudence, Hajj, Makkah, Ibn Ḥajar, Zakariyyā al-Anṣārī</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="534"/>in a jar, in a jar with alcohol! The heir to the All-Russian Tsars swimming in alcohol like a little frog! he suddenly burst into such a wild laugh that a shudder ran through Peter’s body. He thought again, "He is insane!" and felt a revulsion, similar to a supernatural horror, which he had always felt toward science, cockroaches, and other vermin.
But at that very moment, the horror turned into fury: it seemed to him that his son was mocking him, deliberately "playing the fool" to shut himself off and hide his evil deeds.
— What else is in you? — he proceeded to interrogate him again, as if not noticing what was happening to the Tsarevich.
The latter stopped laughing as suddenly as he had begun, leaned his head back against the back of the armchair, and his face turned pale and gaunt, like a dead man’s. He looked at his father silently with a vacant gaze.
— When you had hope in the rabble, — Peter continued, raising his voice and trying to make it sound calm, — did you not send anyone to the rabble to speak of that uprising, or did you not hear from anyone that the rabble wanted to revolt?
Alexei was silent.
— Answer! — shouted Peter, and a convulsion twisted his face.
Something twitched in Alexei’s face as well. He forced his lips apart and pronounced:
— I have said everything. I will not speak any more.
Peter struck his fist against the table and jumped up.
— How dare you!..
The Tsarevich also stood up and looked his father straight in the eyes. Again they became like each other, in a fleeting and seemingly spectral resemblance.
— Why do you threaten me, father? — said Alexei<pb n="535"/> quietly. I am not afraid of you, I am not afraid of anything. You have taken everything from me, you have ruined everything, both soul and body. There is nothing left to take. Unless you kill me. Well then, kill me! It is all the same to me.

And a slow, quiet smile twisted his lips. It seemed to Peter that there was infinite contempt in this smile.

He roared like a wounded beast, threw himself at his son, grabbed him by the throat, knocked him down, and began to strangle him, trample him with his feet, and beat him with his cane, all with that same inhuman roar.

In the palace, people woke up, bustled about, and ran back and forth. But no one dared to enter the Tsar’s presence. They only turned pale and crossed themselves, approaching the doors and listening to the terrible sounds that echoed from within: it sounded as if a beast were gnawing on a man.

The Empress was sleeping in the Upper Palace. She was awakened. She ran over, half-dressed, but she also did not dare to enter.

Only when everything had quieted down did she open the door slightly, peek in, and enter on tiptoe, sneaking behind her husband’s back.

The Tsarevich was lying on the floor unconscious, and the Tsar was in an armchair, also almost in a swoon.

They sent for the court physician, <term>Blumentrost</term> <gloss>the Tsar’s personal doctor</gloss>. He calmed the Empress, who feared that the Tsar had killed his son. — What else is in you? — he proceeded to interrogate him again, as if not noticing what was happening to the Tsarevich.
The latter stopped laughing as suddenly as he had begun, leaned his head back against the back of the armchair, and his face turned pale and gaunt, like a dead man’s. He looked at his father silently with a vacant gaze.
— When you had hope in the rabble, — Peter continued, raising his voice and trying to make it sound calm, — did you not send anyone to the rabble to speak of that uprising, or did you not hear from anyone that the rabble wanted to revolt?
Alexei was silent.
— Answer! — shouted Peter, and a convulsion twisted his face.
Something twitched in Alexei’s face as well. He forced his lips apart and pronounced:
— I have said everything. I will not speak any more.
Peter struck his fist against the table and jumped up.
— How dare you!..
The Tsarevich also stood up and looked his father straight in the eyes. Again they became like each other, in a fleeting and seemingly spectral resemblance.

Rather, what led the claimant to it was ignorance of its meaning, combined with deception in the question, as will be explained later, along with a lack of desire for reward and a love for comfort and ease. Consider this: if a sick person is able to endure hardship that is like the hardship of walking in rain and mud, as previously mentioned, how can a healthy person not endure a hardship that is less than that, by analogy? Yes, if the old mosque were distributing riyals, would you see the one who claims [the presence of] hardship staying away because he cannot bear it? Or would you find him the first to rush toward it? And by God is the granting of success to return to the truth. Amen.

### The Ninth Matter: Clarifying the position on the impermissibility of multiplication [of Friday prayers] in this specific case
It is not hidden from any knowledgeable person that our Shafi'i Imams, may God be pleased with them, only permitted the multiplication of Friday prayers due to the existence of need and necessity, which is the certainty of the difficulty of gathering, as will follow from *al-Tuhfah*, to repel the hardship resulting from "unbearable hardship." It is known that every necessity is estimated according to its extent. They established causes for the difficulty of gathering, whether due to fighting, the narrowness of the place due to the multitude of worshippers, or the distance of the city's outskirts. They established for each of these causes conditions that restrict it, which must exist with certainty. The condition for the narrowness of the place is that there is certainly no place in the city of Friday prayer that can accommodate them. Furthermore, the authoritative position, as in *al-Tuhfah* and *al-Nihayah*, is that the standard is those who are likely to attend Friday prayer, not those who actually attended, regardless of whether the place is a mosque or otherwise. The certainty of the non-existence of [a suitable] place is true when there is no place for Friday prayer at all, when it is impossible to expand what has become narrow of the Friday prayer place, and when it is impossible to roof over what is unroofed of it, if the prayer is in the sun, <column-break/> causing a hardship that is certainly unbearable. Therefore, the absence of what is mentioned here with certainty is the impossibility that our master al-Ghazali pointed to by his saying: "If their gathering in one mosque is impossible, it is permitted in two mosques, etc." For the meaning of impossibility is the absolute inability to do so, not merely a conjecture of lack of space, nor merely a claim of narrowness without verification of the aforementioned meaning with certainty; rather, it is conjecture in the unknown and a pursuit of comfort and luxury. Furthermore, the condition of the distance of the outskirts is either that the distance is from dawn until the time of Friday prayer, or that from which the call to prayer is not heard, as explained in the *Sharh* of the minaret in the Seventh Matter, or through the existence of the "unbearable hardship" in its meaning which passed in the Eighth Matter. Thus, the certainty of the difficulty of gathering is not obtained except through these mentioned conditions and requirements. So the statement of *al-Tuhfah*, "and the difficulty of their gathering with certainty," means through the existence of one of those causes with their conditions. Likewise, every statement of al-Ghazali: "And when the need is verified," meaning through the existence of what we have mentioned, for they have defined the difficulty of gathering arising from one of those causes as the "unbearable hardship." He said in *al-Tuhfah*: "The criterion for difficulty is that it contains a hardship that is unbearable." The end. And this hardship is that which contains hardship and necessity, as previously mentioned in the Eighth Matter. It will come here from al-Qamuli, explicitly mentioning its evidence. From the legal opinions of our master, Sayyid Abdallah bin Umar bin Yahya, is that al-Qamuli, in *al-Jawahir*, when he mentioned the permissibility of multiplication due to difficulty, supported it with the Almighty's saying: "He has not placed upon you any hardship in the religion," which indicates that our permission for the scholars for multiplication is to negate hardship. The end, with omissions. This is also a clarification that the existence of hardship and necessity is what is intended by the hardship <pb n="13"/> that is unbearable, which is the definition of the difficulty of gathering that permits multiplication, [which is contrary to] what has become the habit of [claiming] hardship in going to the mosque to seek comfort and luxury. **So when you know** and have verified everything mentioned here, and you know what was mentioned in the Fifth Matter regarding the description of the old mosque, its vastness, and the vastness of its courtyard, you will then know and verify the non-existence of the cause that permits multiplication, which is the non-existence of a place that can accommodate them, meaning those who are likely to attend, as previously mentioned that this is the authoritative position according to Ibn Hajar, al-Ramli, and others, and that is due to the vastness of this aforementioned mosque and the vastness of its courtyard, for those who look at it. **And when you know** what was mentioned in the Seventh Matter regarding the distance between the two mosques, that there is no "unbearable hardship" in it, in its meaning mentioned in the Eighth Matter, and that the call to prayer is heard between the two ends of the neighborhoods of the two mosques, let alone them being a distance between the two mosques [equivalent to] the time from before dawn to the time of Friday prayer, **you will know** and verify then the non-existence of the cause that permits multiplication, which is the distance of the outskirts, due to the short distance between the ends of the two mosques' neighborhoods, along with the absence of the aforementioned hardship. **It has thus become apparent** and clear to you now, by what has been mentioned and what has been recorded, that the situation as it stands does not permit the multiplication of Friday prayer due to the non-existence of any of its causes with certainty, let alone the certainty of the existence of any of them. Thus, all the texts of the Imams stating the permissibility of multiplication with its conditions cannot be used to argue for the permissibility of multiplication in this case, which is stripped of those conditions. Likewise, the answer of the Mufti of Mecca cannot be taken as evidence for the validity of multiplication in this case, because it contains the condition of "need and hardship," which <column-break/> did not exist in the reality of the case, as has been established in these matters repeatedly. And it will be known clearly from the coming Eleventh Matter. And by God is the granting of success. **The Ninth Matter** [Correction: Tenth Matter] in exposing what took place in this case by those claiming the permissibility of multiplication in it, regarding the traits of opposition. These traits indicate with a clear indication their stubbornness against the truth and that they have no motive other than causing multiplication, by any means possible, by any path, and by any school of thought, indeed, even on the basis of falsehood, as will be known from their own words, along with what they had as motives of stubbornness, rivalry, arrogance, and cooperation in falsehood. As for the traits of opposition, **among them** is, first, what took place from the builder of the new mosque, as mentioned in the Sixth Matter, what he himself claimed previously regarding building a mosque and holding Friday prayer in it, and that the previous judge forbade him in the presence of scholars, and that he seized the opportunity at this time, and that he and the judge wrote to us and asked us for some of the texts of the scholars that they could use as evidence for the validity of the multiplication of Friday prayer in the new mosque, even by any means possible. **And among that** is what is in the fifth paper from the aforementioned Sayyid Alawi bin Ahmad, which is his saying: "It is requested of you, sir, that by any path, statement, or opinion, you inform the judge not to forbid the Friday prayer in the new mosque. May God... you do not present an excuse." **And among that** is also his saying in that paper: "And what is the intent of the scholars regarding the multiplication if it is their right? If there is no path in the Shafi'i school, they ask the scholars in..."</translation>

<summary>The text concludes its argument against the multiplication of Friday prayers in a specific locality, asserting that none of the conditions for "unbearable hardship" or necessity—such as lack of space or extreme distance—are present. It further critiques the motives of those pushing for a new mosque as driven by stubbornness, arrogance, and a desire for personal comfort rather than legitimate religious necessity.</summary>
<keywords>multiplication of Friday prayer, Shafi'i jurisprudence, hardship, mosque expansion, religious authority, legal controversy</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="533"/>they are clever ministers, but Alexander Nikolaevich <note>referring to Tsar Alexander II</note> does not trust them fully. For their aid, he has summoned the famous Dr. Liprandi, who treats with heroic measures and will undoubtedly hasten the tragedy. A great consolation for government-aligned Petersburg now is the people and the attachment of the people to the Tsar. They threaten the revolutionary youth with the people. "The Tsar only has to wave his hand, and the students will be no more." Yes, without a doubt they would be no more; but by the next day, the nobility in all of Russia would also be no more, and with the nobility, the entire bureaucracy would fall under the axe; you yourselves, my dears, would perish. Go ahead, try waving your hand! And there will remain only the people and the Tsar. But what will this Tsar do with these people? After all, our Tsar is bureaucratic and aristocratic, not a <term>Zemsky</term> <gloss>land-based/national</gloss> one. He would drown himself in noble blood, only to give way to some sort of Pugachev! Might you not try the Nicholas-era methods instead: the knout, the gallows, and Siberia? These are good methods. But it is doubtful they will help you now. After all, fear has been killed in Russia. Nowadays people will walk to the scaffold laughing at you. And even for the greatest cowards, there is no calculation in shrinking before your fear. In Russia, there is now a fear that is more terrible: the fear of popular retribution. And if one must choose between the axe or the gallows, then, of course, it is better to fall with the consciousness of a high deed than as a victim of a fatal misunderstanding by the people.

You have one more tool: war. A national war against the Germans, in alliance with Italy and France, perhaps even for the freedom of the Slavs, if only not to grant freedom to the Russian people. Yes, in fact, going to war against the Germans is a good, and above all, a necessary Slavic cause, in any case better than strangling the Poles to please the Germans. Rising for the liberation of the Slavs from under the Turkish and German yoke will be a need, a necessity, and a holy duty of the liberated Russian people. But you, the enemies of Russian and Polish freedom, what freedom will you give the Slavs? Or do you wish to repeat the old, shameful deception for the hundredth time? Having satisfied no one and resolved nothing at home, upon what will you lean? Even the army you will have <pb n="534"/> to maintain on a pittance with foreign subsidies. And you will only serve as a means for the goals of others, you yourselves will acquire nothing, and Russia you will ruin completely. Perhaps you are even counting on her exhaustion? Perhaps you think to pacify her with hunger? Take care not to be mistaken in your calculation: war did not prevent the Pugachev rebellion or the Novgorod riot in our history.

But all our efforts are in vain. Neither war, nor the ruses of a supposedly liberal (?) ministry, nor open reaction will help you. The people have awakened and are awaiting their hour; you yourselves contributed to their awakening. By flirting with them and inciting them against the young, educated generation, you yourselves are awakening in them a consciousness of strength, and they will take by force what you do not wish to give them voluntarily.

For a peaceful resolution of the present, inevitable crisis, there is only one means: a <term>Zemsky Sobor</term> <gloss>National Assembly</gloss> and the resolution of the people's land affairs there. This is the only salvific means in the hands of the Tsar. But he does not want to use it. That means he wants blood.

When rulers ruin a country, private individuals must take up the work of salvation. To all true conservatives who have the wit to understand and foresee necessary events, to all merchants, priests, and nobles, to military and civil officials who love tranquility and peace and wish to preserve their lives, property, wives, sisters, and children, to everyone for whom the prosperity and glory of Russia are dear, I would advise thinking hard about this. After all, not much time remains for free reflection. And it would not be a bad thing if they, having agreed among themselves, formed a massive conservative society, which I would propose they call: "Society for the Salvation of Russia from the Tsar's Myopia and from Criminal Ministerial Charlatanism," and let them raise their voice in a chorus in favor of the <term>Zemsky Sobor</term> as the only means for preventing a bloody, destructive catastrophe.

And as for us, the revolutionary party, what are we to do? We will also unite and stand under the banner of the "People's Cause."</translation>

<summary>Bakunin analyzes the precarious state of the Russian monarchy, dismissing the Tsar's reliance on bureaucracy and repressive tactics, and argues that a Zemsky Sobor is the only peaceful alternative to an inevitable, violent popular revolution.</summary>
<keywords>Alexander II, Zemsky Sobor, popular revolution, Russian bureaucracy, political crisis, revolutionary party, People's Cause</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="56"/>melodious song, in noble character, in the delicate craft of the hand, in strange guidance, in useful service, or in harm that calls for extreme caution and precise cunning. For such reasons, it is given priority in mention. And what is more astonishing than the magpie, with its keen sense, its intense caution, and its good knowledge? Yet, there is no bird on earth that guards its eggs more thoroughly, with more intense watchfulness, or with more profound understanding than it. Uthman ibn Affan, may God be pleased with him, said: "Everything loves its young, even the houbara <gloss>bustard</gloss>," which is used as a proverb for stupidity. Yet the magpie, despite its skill in affairs and its speed in snatching, does not utilize this for anything beneficial. How many precious and valuable necklaces, and noble and costly earrings, have been snatched from people's hands! It either throws them away after circling in the air, or hides them and never pays attention to them again. Al-Asma'i claimed that a magpie once stole a precious necklace (*sakhāb*) from some people. The owners of the necklace seized an Arab woman who was with them. While she was being beaten, dragged, and cursed, the magpie passed by with the necklace in its beak. They shouted at it, so it dropped it. The Arab woman said, remembering safety after she had been afflicted with another calamity:

> The day of the necklace is one of the wonders of our Lord,
> It is as if it saved me from the town of evil.

She meant those of the city dwellers who had descended upon her. There is no harm in mentioning what occurs, provided it does not fall into the long chapters that contain nothing but abstract measures and purely speculative discourse; for such things are not light to hear, nor do souls feel eager to read them. The seeker of knowledge and the one who desires reward and merit may endure that. Whenever we find a chapter that can be embellished with elegant, eloquent poetry and interesting anecdotes, we take the trouble to do so and narrate it in its entirety for the benefit of the reader. For this reason, we deemed it permissible to say what we said in the chapter on fire. I am writing for you after this, since I have bored you with length and burdened you with the most difficult of paths and the roughest of roads, having already mentioned a fair amount of the speech of the theologians. I do not think I should add to your weariness and exhaust your energy by beginning the discourse on camels, cows, sheep, lions, wolves, donkeys, gazelles, and similar things about which I am writing for you. Instead, I will turn to the small, brief, concise, and pleasant chapters so that you will not emerge from the first chapter without being energized for the second, and likewise for the third and fourth, until the end of what I am writing for you, God willing. We will begin with what is in the sparrow, then we will start mentioning the mouse,

<pb n="57"/>and the scorpion, and the mediation between them along with their other traits. Then, the discourse on the scorpion and the beetle, and the friendship between them, along with their other traits. Then, the discourse on the cat, then the discourse on the hedgehog, then the discourse on mosquitoes and fleas, then the discourse on lice and children, then the discourse on the monitor lizard and the mastigure, then the discourse on the jerboa and the hedgehog, then the discourse on vultures and Egyptian vultures, then the discourse on the eagle and the hare, then the discourse on ticks and frogs, then the discourse on the houbara and the like. Before we mention this chapter, we will mention some elegant chapters of poetry that are suitable for discussion, stimulate energy, and deserve that one read the long books associated with them. Were it not for my low opinion of those who pretend to seek knowledge in this time and pretend to author books in this age, I would not have needed, alongside the many benefits of this book, to resort to this long training, to this abundance of apology, as if the benefit I give them is something I gain from them, and as if my desire for their improvement were the desire of one who craves their worldly goods. This, even though I have not mentioned any of the long chapters, and I have arrived at mentioning the differences between jinn and humans, between angels and prophets, between the female and the male, and between what is neither female nor male, until the discourse extends for us into the excellence of man over all types of animals, into the mention of nations and eras, into the mention of destiny and life spans, and into the mention of the measures of intellects through sciences and crafts. Then follows the discourse on the nature of man from the time he is a drop of semen until worries consume him. If you grow tired of the book and find reading it a burden, you are then excused. I have no strategy for you except to present it to you in the best form and turn you through various arts, so that you do not exit from argumentation by the Wise Quran without entering into the transmitted tradition, and you do not exit from the tradition without entering into authentic poetry, and you do not exit from elegant, authentic poetry without entering into a widespread, factual proverb, and you do not exit from the widespread, factual proverb without entering into philosophy and the rarities that experience has verified, that testing has brought to light, that demonstration has unveiled, and that the wonders for which souls have a passion and sound intellects have a strong struggle are revealed. For this reason, I wrote it for you, led it to you, and sought reward for you. Look into it with the eye of an equitable peer and scholar, or the eye of a seeker being guided among the learners and followers. If you find the book I have written for you to be contradictory
</translation>

<summary>Al-Jahiz discusses the importance of balancing scholarly inquiry with engaging anecdotes and poetry to maintain the reader's interest. He outlines the structure of the forthcoming chapters, which will focus on various animals and natural phenomena, before justifying his pedagogical approach to a modern audience.</summary>
<keywords>Al-Jahiz, Book of Animals, animal behavior, pedagogical method, literary style, theology, nature of man</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="19"/>OF POLYBIUS

But when they are driven by the ambition for power, and cannot achieve it through their own means and through their own personal merit, they squander their estates by baiting and corrupting the masses in every way. When they have once made the multitude greedy for bribes and accustomed to living at the expense of others, due to their <term>doxophagia</term> <gloss>craving for reputation/public acclaim</gloss>, then the democracy is destroyed and transformed into rule by force and by the hand. For the multitude, having become accustomed to feeding on the property of others and to placing their hopes of livelihood in their neighbors, when they find a leader who is bold and high-minded, but excluded from public honors because of his poverty, then they establish rule by force. Then, they assemble and carry out massacres, banishments, and the redistribution of land, until they have become like wild beasts again and find a master and monarch. This is the cycle of constitutions, this is the arrangement of nature, according to which things change, are transformed, and return again to the point where they started in their constitutions. Whoever has clearly perceived these things will perhaps be mistaken in his predictions about the future of a constitution in terms of time, but he will rarely be wrong about where each state is in its growth or decline, or how it will change, provided he makes his judgment without being swayed by excessive emotion. And indeed, regarding the Roman constitution, through this understanding we might best arrive at knowledge of its formation, its growth, its peak, and likewise the reverse transformation that will follow from these. For if any other constitution, as I have just said, happens to have its formation, its growth, and its nature, and even its change to the contrary, in accordance with nature, it will be possible to observe this through what is to be said hereafter. For the present, we shall make brief mention of the legislation of Lycurgus. For the discussion is not irrelevant to our proposed subject. For he took each of the aforementioned <pb n="20"/> things, which were accomplished by necessity and nature, and reasoned that every form of constitution that is simple and consists of only one power becomes precarious, because it quickly turns into the specific vice that follows it by nature. For just as rust is the inherent corruption of iron, and woodworms and shipworms are the inherent corruptions of timber, by which, even if they escape all external damage, they are destroyed by the very things that grew up within them; in the same way, each constitution has a specific vice that naturally grows with it and accompanies it. Monarchy has the method called tyranny, aristocracy has oligarchy, and democracy has the savage and violent rule of the hand. It is impossible that these constitutions should not, over time, undergo these transformations according to the argument just made. Lycurgus, foreseeing this, did not construct the constitution to be simple or uniform, but he gathered together all the virtues and characteristics of the best governments, so that no part, by growing beyond what is proper, might degenerate into its inherent vices. Since the power of each is checked by the others, none of them inclines or falls too far in one direction. Instead, the government remains in balance and stability for a long time, like a ship sailing against the wind, with the monarchy being prevented from arrogance by fear of the people, who are given a sufficient share in the constitution. And again, the people are not tempted to despise the kings due to fear of the elders, who, having been selected by choice, were all expected to always side with justice. Thus, the side that was at a disadvantage, by adhering to these customs, would always become greater and more influential, thanks to the elders
</translation>

<summary>Polybius describes the natural cycle of political decay, wherein pure forms of government inevitably devolve into their corrupt opposites (monarchy to tyranny, aristocracy to oligarchy, and democracy to mob rule). He introduces Lycurgus of Sparta as a model who mitigated this instability by creating a balanced, mixed constitution that prevents any single power from becoming dominant.</summary>
<keywords>Polybius, Roman constitution, cycle of constitutions, Lycurgus, monarchy, aristocracy, democracy, political decay, stability</keywords>

# Fifth Chapter

|| 189 || By constant practice, he will surely see it within three days. By that vision alone, the practitioner burns away the mass of his sins. || 190 ||

Commentary—One should meditate upon that <term>Niranjana</term> <gloss>the stainless</gloss>, known as the Swan, endowed with sixteen digits and nectar-rays, within the cavity of the skull. Through three days of constant practice, this <term>Niranjana</term> will certainly manifest to the practitioner. By that vision alone, the practitioner will burn away all accumulated sins. || 189 || 190 ||

Root Text—The future becomes manifest, and purity of mind surely arises. Even by performing it for an instant, one burns away the five great sins. || 191 ||

Commentary—By performing this meditation, the future will manifest, meaning that things which have not yet occurred will be revealed. Purity of mind will be achieved, and by merely meditating, the practitioner will instantly burn away the five great sins <note>original: "panchamahapataka"</note>. || 191 ||

Root Text—All the planets become favorable, and all disturbances perish. Obstacles find peace, and one attains victory in battle. The <term>khechari</term> <gloss>moving in the void</gloss> and <term>bhuchari</term> <gloss>moving on the earth</gloss> <note>These refer to specific advanced yogic powers.</note> <pb n="184"/> siddhis are attained through the nectar-rayed Moon. Through meditation alone, everything is attained; there is no need for doubt in this matter. || 192 || 193 ||

Through constant practice of yoga, a human becomes a <term>siddha</term> <gloss>perfected being</gloss>. I declare it true, true, and true again: he will certainly become equal to me. This supreme yoga science is the bestower of success to yogis. || 194 ||

Now, the description of <term>Raja Yoga</term> <gloss>the royal yoga</gloss>.

Root Text—Above this exists the divine-formed thousand-petaled lotus. It resides outside the body, which is called the <term>brahmanda</term> <gloss>the microcosm or cosmic egg</gloss>, and it grants liberation. || 195 || It is called <term>Kailasa</term>, where <term>Mahesha</term> <gloss>the Great Lord Shiva</gloss> resides. He is known as <term>Akula</term> <gloss>the absolute/beyond lineage</gloss>, the imperishable, devoid of growth and decay. || 196 ||
</translation>

<summary>The text details the spiritual benefits of meditating on the lunar nectar within the skull, asserting that this practice purifies the mind, grants foresight, and leads to the attainment of yogic powers and liberation. It concludes by introducing the thousand-petaled lotus, Sahasrara, as the divine seat of the Lord.</summary>
<keywords>Niranjana, meditation, five great sins, khechari, bhuchari, Raja Yoga, Sahasrara, Kailasa</keywords>

<pb n="54"/>Now, knowledge is of two types. One is that which is called knowledge by custom, and the other is that which is not called knowledge by custom; but both types, according to the masters of <term>Haqiqat</term> <gloss>Truth/Reality</gloss>, belong to the category of knowledge, because they witness the permeation of the essential knowledge of the Truth—glory be to Him—in all existents. From the second type, for instance, there is that which is not considered knowing by custom; however, we see that it distinguishes between height and depth, turning away from the height and flowing toward the depth. Similarly, it penetrates into the body and arranges the outer appearance of the body for the one who experiences <term>mukashafa</term> <gloss>unveiling</gloss>, and so on. Therefore, it is a property of knowledge to flow according to the requirements of the receptacle's capacity without opposing it. However, at the level of nature, it has appeared in the form of nature, and by this analogy is the permeation of knowledge in all other existents, nay, the permeation of all perfections.

<pb n="55"/>

| | |
|---|---|
| That which follows existence in all existents | |
| Existence with the attributes that were hidden within it | And became manifest in all the entities of the world |
| The secret of the attribute of the Essence that was receptive to it | Became apparent according to the measure of the acceptance of the entity |

Just as the reality of existence, by virtue of its pure absoluteness, permeates the essences of all existents in such a way that in those essences it is the very essence of those existents, just as those existents were the same within it; likewise, His perfect attributes, in their totality and absoluteness, permeate all the attributes of existents, in such a manner that within their attributes they are the very essence of their attributes, just as their attributes were the same as those perfect attributes. For example, the attribute of knowledge, within the knowledge of one who knows particulars, is the very essence of knowledge of particulars, and within the knowledge of one who knows universals, is the very essence of knowledge of universals.
</translation>

<translation>
<pb n="13"/>The son, having entered upon the footsteps of his dear father,
Bestows many benefits upon my fatherland.
He presides over the afflicted, and kindly assists the needy,
And is prepared to bring aid to the miserable.
He once offered green pastures to my Muses,
And was always helpful to my studies.
For which, may the Almighty God at some time grant him
The heavenly joys of eternal life.
Skilful bridegroom, you will imitate these examples of your clan,
Represent your ancestors.
Thus your praise will grow, thus your generation will become
More illustrious, and thus your fame will be perennial.
But because you revolve these things more wisely by yourself,
Let my songs cease at your own admonition.
Just as a strong horse born of strong seed
Does not fear noises, nor does it flee sorrowful arms,
In no other way do you follow the deeds of famous parents,
Nor do you allow your intellect to degenerate.
Great joys deservedly sustain your mind,
Bride, because that man comes into your chambers.
I, even if I were to surpass the Pylian <note>Nestor, the wise counselor of Greek legend.</note> Nestor in speaking,
If I were more eloquent than Cicero:
I could not recount everything according to the merit
Which the glory of such a groom demands to be brought forth.
Why, therefore, does my Muse rather
Desert the young husband, and seek the face of the chaste virgin.
<pb n="14"/>Hail, illustrious nymph, ornament of feminine modesty,
Hail, great glory of the virginal chorus.
May He himself make prosperous the most holy rights of your bed,
He who was the first patron and author of the wedding chamber.
He who first discovered the marriages of the sweet torch,
And who is said to love the sacred flames of the marriage bed.
May He placidly bring fortune to the pacts of your bed,
Euphrosyne <note>The name means "Mirth" or "Joy" in Greek.</note>, a girl worthy of such a man.
Rare is your face, and the excellence of your beauty
Is so great that it makes you surpass the rest.
You lift your sky-blue eyes to the sublime breezes
More often, and you shine entirely with a glowing color.
Such as the clouds are wont to be, colored more frequently
By the shining light of the opposing Sun.
Or like the frosty mother <note>Aurora, the dawn.</note>, who drives the stars
Of heaven away, and leads the day from the eastern axis.
Such a color is seen on your face, lilies stained with purple
Blood scarcely appear so red to me.
Divine modesty decorates your beautiful face:
You are gentle, and lack all rusticity.
Your ivory neck lets down golden hair,
And flowery garlands polish your tresses.
Your arms are whiter than snowy privet:
Every single limb reflects its own adornment.
You also be cheerful, be glad with your whole heart,
Groom, because she seeks your embraces.
</translation>

<summary>This text concludes the praise of the groom's lineage and virtues, urging him to emulate his ancestors, before shifting focus to the bride, Euphrosyne, praising her modesty, physical beauty, and grace in the context of their upcoming marriage.</summary>
<keywords>epithalamium, wedding poetry, marriage, beauty, modesty, genealogical honor, bride, groom</keywords>

<pb n="13"/>to return: We may likewise say with truth of the Urdorff bath and that entire region that it is a collector of many delights and is so constituted that it lacks nothing to refresh not only the body but also the spirit and the mind. Which we would rather let the favorable reader experience from ocular inspection and use of the bath than detain him further with a longer historical narrative.

There is no grass nor herb so small that it does not praise the Creator of its own, so natural reason tells us finally how highly we have to thank the wondrous goodness of God for this and many similar healing waters in our Zurich territory. But we will give him the best thanks when we not only count them among the wonders of nature and gifts of God, but also use them to the honor of God and do not stain the use of the same through any intemperate, arrogant, unbridled, and ungrateful misuse; <margin>(e) Psalm 104, v. 24</margin> also in and with every use, to the praise of God and in owed gratitude, we shall many times repeat after Saint David:

> How many are your works, O Lord, you have wisely ordained them all, and the earth is full of your goods.

## Report of Herr Johannes Waser, Pastor at Dynhart.
->From Jesus the Physician, salvation comes from nowhere else!<-

<note>A large ornamental initial E features floral and leaf motifs.</note>
**Honored** and highly learned brother-in-law, Doctor Ziegler, etc.
Since I have heard that the third description of the bath at Urdorff is to be prepared for the press, I also wish to share what I have observed during the time of my 15-year pastoral service at Urdorff. This famous bath is heartily good for <term>calculus</term> <gloss>stone disease</gloss>, for it softens and expels kidney and bladder stones, sand, and grit, as besides myself, many other honest persons have experienced in practice. It is also excellently suited for <term>cholericis</term> <gloss>those suffering from yellow bile or jaundice</gloss>, from whom it has discharged a mass (f. b.), of which the witnesses are for the most part still alive at this time. For <term>febricitanten</term> <gloss>those suffering from fevers</gloss>, of whatever type they may be, it was useful. Many emaciated, consumption- and lung-sick people have been brought there in carriages due to weakness, and after completion of the cure, they have been able to ride home on horseback, fresh and healthy. To a spoiled and ailing stomach, it brings an excellent appetite once again and creates a desire for food. It <term>acuire</term> <gloss>sharpens</gloss> and clears the eyes most wonderfully, so that many persons who had to use glasses or spectacles before the bath cure can afterwards write, read, and perform other tasks without them. I also remember well notable honorable people who visited it due to infertility and afterwards highly praised its <term>efficaciam</term> <gloss>efficacy</gloss> and joyful effect. My successor, Herr Pastor Wirtz, also gives testimony to this blessing of God. A serviceable, gracious, friendly, and loving landlord and host is a precious thing at the site of the bath; where that is missing, all comfort is lost.

<pb n="14"/>
<note>An elaborate horizontal typographic ornament is composed of symmetrical leafy scrolls, fleurons, and stylized floral motifs.</note>

### I.

Come here, friends, come here! It is shown to you here
An excellent bath; which has long been praised
By the highly learned Stumpff; who remembered it with fame
Kircherus world-famous, highly regarded by scholars
In his book of wonders; Doctor Gessner also wrote of it
Since then it has kept its ancient price and fame. It has three springs
Therein to see how manifold is
The grace of the great Physician. The first carries sulfur,
The second copper, from the third spring flows
The healthy good alum. There one finds at all times
Food, drink, and everything that gladdens the mind and sense.

->Affectionately added by his beloved brother<-
->From<-
->**Christoph Ziegler, Doctor.**<-

<note>A horizontal border of repeating small floral and decorative fleuron patterns.</note>

### II.

After God the Lord had raised up at Urdorff
Three healthy waters, the foundation was laid.
<margin>1526.</margin> For its proper use, indeed by Herr Steiner,
<margin>1583.</margin> Herr Johann Ziegler, however, was the true master builder.
Who guided this precious bath and fitted it out,
And for bathing guests of honor, he adorned it excellently
With its amenities, just as one could desire.
Herr Jacob Ziegler, who was a highly learned Doctor
<margin>1620.</margin> And well-experienced, has two times shown us
<margin>1662.</margin> In print, from what kind of minerals
From three springs this water is powerful:
He knew this through the wondrous chemistry.
</translation>

Will make the deep rivers warm, mixed with slaughter.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Finally, the prey given over to death will also be a witness,
When the smooth tomb, heaped up with a high mound,
Will receive the snow-white limbs of the struck maiden.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
For as soon as fate gives the exhausted Achaeans the opportunity
To loosen the Neptunian chains of the Dardanian city <note>Troy</note>,
The high tombs will be wetted with the slaughter of Polyxena,
Who, like a victim succumbing to the double-edged iron,
Will cast her headless body down with bent knee.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Therefore come, join your desired loves of heart,
Let the spouse receive the goddess in a happy pact,
Let the bride be given to her eager husband at long last.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Her nurse, visiting her at the rising light,
Will not be able to put her thread <note>a symbol of domestic duty</note> around her neck.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Nor will her anxious, grieving mother, because of the discord
Of the maiden sleeping apart, cease to hope for dear grandchildren.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Such songs did the Fates once sing with divine hearts,
Foretelling the happy things of Peleus.

<pb n="197"/>For the dwellers of heaven <term>Cœlicolæ</term> <gloss>heaven-dwellers</gloss> were formerly accustomed to visit
The chaste homes of men, and to show themselves to mortal gatherings,
Before piety was scorned.
Often the father of the gods, visiting his shining temples,
While the annual sacred rites had come on festive days,
Beheld the chariots of the Cretans racing across the earth.
Often the wandering Liber <note>Bacchus</note> from the highest peak of Parnassus
Drove the Thyads <note>Bacchantes</note> with hair flowing in celebration,
When the people of Delphi, rushing from the whole city,
Gladly received the god at the smoking altars.
Often in the deadly contest of war, Mars,
Or the mistress of swift Triton <note>Minerva</note>, or the Rhamnusian maiden <note>Nemesis</note>,
Were present and encouraged the armed crowds of men.
But after the earth was soaked with unspeakable crime,
And all drove justice from their greedy minds,
Brothers stained their hands with brotherly blood,
The son ceased to mourn for his dead parents,
The father wished for the funeral of his first-born son,
So that he might possess the flower of an unwed stepmother,
And the impious mother, casting herself under her unknowing son,
Did not fear to pollute the divine household gods.
All things, lawful and unlawful, mixed by evil madness,
Turned the just mind of the gods away from us.
Therefore they do not deign to visit such gatherings,
Nor do they suffer themselves to be touched by the clear light.
</translation>

<keywords>Fates, Peleus, Thetis, Trojan War, Polyxena, decline of piety, divine absence, gods, mythology</keywords>

<pb n="21"/>or one due circumstance is neglected, which they express with the common saying of <term>Dionysius</term>: "Any single defect causes evil, yet good is caused by an integral cause." A distinction must be noted here between the circumstances themselves, some of which transfer the moral act into a new genus of malice, while others leave it in the same genus but increase the degree of sin. Thus, the example of fornication, which <term>Thomas</term> <gloss>Aquinas</gloss> brings into the middle, consists in this: that a man approaches one who is not his own. But if this circumstance is added, that he exerts lust upon the spouse of another, it is transferred into another genus of sin, namely, injustice, in as much as a man usurps the thing of another. Whence adultery is called a graver offense than fornication. Let the example of the latter be some angry person, who gets angry when he ought not, and at whom he ought not, and with an inconvenient gesture; this triplet of circumstances certainly makes this anger graver than if at least one of them were violated. Just as a sickness is graver which infects more parts of the body. It happens, however, sometimes, that some circumstance does not add a new deformity, but only increases that which had come from elsewhere. Just as taking another's property constitutes theft; but if this is added, that he takes much of another's property, it will be a graver sin. Nor is there any reason for someone to say that a circumstance, if it is evil, constitutes a certain species of sin by itself. For this is false, or at least not universal, since it can add a reason for malice within the same species. About which see <term>Thomas</term>. We add at least this, since it can also be referred to among circumstances, how often, or properly—which <term>Cajetan</term> denies—or by analogy, that also in the weighing of an offense <margin>1. 2. q. 73. art. 8. ad 2. <gloss>First part of the second part, question 73, article 8, response to point 2</gloss></margin> is not to be passed over. Whence <term>Grotius</term>: <margin>l. c. <gloss>in the same place</gloss></margin>
> "A greater depravity also appears if someone has sinned more often: because habits are worse through evil acts."

<pb n="22"/># TH. XI.

## Eighthly, the gravity of vices differs according to the dignity of the virtues to which they are opposed.

<margin>3. 2. q. 73. art. 4. <gloss>Third part of the second part, question 73, article 4</gloss></margin>
*This, which <term>Thomas</term> proves from <term>Aristotle</term>: The Philosopher says that the worst is contrary to the best. But the best in moral matters is the greatest virtue; the worst is the gravest sin.* Since, however, the dispute concerning the mutual comparison of virtues among themselves, and which one obtains the leading place among them, has not yet been settled, it would be improper to determine anything about vices in this respect. Indeed, all virtues shine like stars, and our orb of shadows is made illustrious by their rays. Yet which of them shines more brightly, and relates to the others like the sun, <term>Piccolomineus</term> admits it is not easy to judge. 

<margin>Phil. de Mor. Gr. 4. c. 47. & 49. <gloss>Philosophy of Moral Grades, book 4, chapters 47 and 49</gloss></margin>
And for each one, this same author brings forth something in view of which they might claim the primacy for themselves quite plausibly, which he confirms both by reasons and the assent of the wise; and he warns primarily that judgments about this prerogative vary greatly according to the different condition of men, since those who are established in magistracy prefer justice, commanders of armies and soldiers prefer fortitude, and those born and educated in splendor prefer magnificence, etc. Nevertheless, these things notwithstanding, we believe a judgment about the absolute preeminence of some one virtue can be fixed. This we prefer to express in the words of the most celebrated doctor of morals in Italy, already praised, rather than our own: 

<margin>Phil. Mor. Gr. 4. c. 51. <gloss>Philosophy of Moral Grades, book 4, chapter 51</gloss></margin>
> "Because that virtue must be judged absolutely best to which the best standard of excellence, the most excellent standard of dignity, is to be sought especially from the end; the end of virtue is action; the most excellent of actions are those which proceed from justice; therefore, by right, justice holds the primacy. That the action of justice is the best is certain: for its duty is to compose our actions toward others, to govern the rest fittingly, to gather scattered men, to preserve those gathered, to bind republics and groups of men, whether small or great, with golden ligaments, to benefit all, and to harm no one, which is the peculiar mark of virtue above all."

76. Item, is a mother excluded from her legal portion by an express pupillary substitution <gloss>substitution for a minor heir</gloss>? We affirm this.

->Donellus on the law "by petitions," Code on impuberes <gloss>those not yet of age</gloss> and other substitutions.<-

77. And a soldier can make a testament both for himself and for his son by military law, and for his son alone even if he has not made one for himself: which testament will be valid if, by chance, the father died either on an expedition or within a year of military service.

->Law "in fraud," 15, paragraph "item, as for himself," Digest on military testament.<-

78. Finally, a soldier may make an heir by mere will, even to those known to him, in whatever manner he wishes or is able, and likewise for a time and another after a time.

->Law "in fraud," 15, paragraph 1, and paragraph "the soldier," 4, Digest on this title.<-

79. Here a question can be proposed: Why can an heir be written by a civilian under a condition, but not from a day certain or until a day certain? We shall investigate the reason.

->Law "under condition," 73, Digest on the institution of heirs; Law 3 [and] 4.<-
->Digest on the institution of heirs: Cujacius in the commentary on the Code regarding<-
->military testament, folio 325.<-

80. Hence, although soldiers may neither have employed the lawful number of witnesses nor observed the other solemnities of testaments, they nevertheless testify correctly, provided it is established that the testament was made.
<margin>in the beginning of the Institutes on the military testament.</margin>

81. If, therefore, a soldier concerning whose goods it is inquired before you, having called together men for this purpose so that he might testify his will, has spoken in such a way that he declares whom he wished to be his heir, and to whom he granted liberty, he can be seen to have testified in this manner even without writings, and his will is to be held valid.

->Law 24, paragraph "if therefore," Digest on the testament of a soldier.<-

82. Nay, if he has noted anything in a scabbard or shield with letters gleaming in his own blood, or has inscribed it in the dust with his sword, at the very time when he abandoned the fortune of life in battle, such a will as this ought to be stable.

->Law "the soldier," 15, Code on the testament of a soldier.<-

<pb n="19"/>83. Just as a soldier can grant an inheritance by mere will, so too can he take it away.
Law "in fraud," 15, paragraph "just as, however," 5, Digest on the testament of a soldier.

84. Likewise, it is permitted to a soldier to make several testaments, but whether he made them together or separately, they will certainly be valid if he has specially expressed this: and the former shall not be broken by the latter.
Law "it was asked," 19, on the testament of a soldier.

85. An elegant question may here be discussed by way of opportunity: Is the prior, perfected testament of a civilian broken by a subsequent, imperfect one, in which those coming from intestacy are instituted as heirs, if in the latter a son is passed over? In which, having inspected the legal truth, we shall endeavor to defend the negative with all our strength.
Law 7, Digest on children and posthumous children. Law 16, paragraph 1, Digest on ordinary substitution.

86. The testament of a soldier is not broken by the birth of a posthumous child, provided that when the soldier passed over the posthumous child, he knew the wife was pregnant.
Law 9, Law 10, Code on the testament of a soldier.

87. Likewise, even if he did not know the wife was pregnant, yet he had this intention, that he wished whosoever was born to him to be disinherited, the testament is not broken.
Law 7, Digest on the testament of a soldier.

88. The testament of a soldier is also not broken if he has adopted a son, or if a grandson has succeeded into the place of a son.
Law "the same is," 8, Digest on the testament of a soldier.

89. Likewise, if a soldier who is a head of a household has testified only regarding camp-acquired goods, and has given himself to be adopted, his testament is nevertheless valid, as if by a new will.
Law "the same," 23, Digest on this title.

90. However, these privileges mentioned regarding the making of last wills are granted only to those who are occupied on expeditions.
Law the penultimate, Code on the testament of a soldier.

91. Is it permitted for those soldiers who are in camp, in a trench, or in winter quarters, or at static posts, in garrisons, apart from the battle line, apart from the danger of battle, to testify by military law? This is disputed. And we judge it more true that it is permitted.
Cujacius in the commentary on the Code on the testament of a soldier.
</translation>

<summary>This text details the legal standing of military testaments, exploring how soldiers may bequeath property, bypass standard inheritance formalities, and execute wills even in unconventional ways such as writing in blood or dust. It further distinguishes between the rights of soldiers on active expedition versus those in static garrisons and discusses the impact of adoption or posthumous heirs on these unique military wills.</summary>
<keywords>Military testament, Soldiers, Inheritance, Pupillary substitution, Camp-acquired goods, Roman Law, Testaments, Last will</keywords>

### XLIV.

Furthermore, the Jews, in order to maintain the same seasonal trend throughout individual months, add an entire month as often as the number of <term>epacts</term> <gloss>the excess of the solar year over the lunar year</gloss> exceeds thirty days.

### XLV.

The epacts, moreover, are the eleven days that represent the difference between the solar year of 365 days and the lunar year of 354 days. It is necessary for these to increase if we allow several such years to flow from a certain common beginning without compensation.

### XLVI.

And thus arises that lunar year, which I previously called <term>Embolimæus</term> <gloss>intercalary/leap year</gloss>. Since this is adjusted by the motions of the Moon such that the months of common years are also, by its benefit, brought back to the laws of solar revolutions with respect to the enjoyment of perpetual seasons, the entire form of such years is deservedly considered composite, and the years themselves are to be held as neither merely lunar, nor solar, but lunisolar.

### XLVII.

Finally, some civil years are more flexible than others. The Olympiadic years are completed sometimes in 360, sometimes in 361 or 362 days, and others in 390, 391, or 392 days. The Nabonassarean or Egyptian years have 365 days, just like the common Julian year, but without any intercalation.

### XLVIII.

Therefore, that system of years is quite erratic if it is compared with the Julian form. For the Egyptian year does not find a fixed and perpetual beginning there; but after every four years, it differs by an entire day from the Julian ones, on account of the intercalary day that every fourth Julian year receives, while the former does not admit it.

### XLIX.

Hence, its beginning travels through all the months of the Julian year in retrograde until, after 1460 Julian years are completed, 1461 Egyptian years are fulfilled. For then both return to one common beginning.

<pb n="11"/>

These things I had to say concerning Time, according to the requirements of the task, concluding with the verses of Dr. Cramer:

> If you always measure fleeting time to the very fingertip,
> Time will never pass by idle.
> Tomorrow's hour is not yet here; yesterday's cannot be regained 
> By a thousand talents: if you wish to live, live today.

---

You burn with the love of piety, wisdom, and virtue;
For this reason you discuss TIME, well done!

->Endure and persist, this labor will benefit you one day.<-

->JO. FRID. SCHARFIUS, Doctor.<-
->Dean of the College of Philosophy at this time.<-
