The matter is indeed true; the most excellent virtue is pressed,
Yet it is not suppressed, but finally rises on high.
This, FIEDLER, you attest abundantly by your own example,
While you yield to no one, even though your resources are meager.
I praise your efforts. May the Divine favor make your undertakings fruitful,
So that your native soil, by whose sweetness all
Are led, may welcome you and your labors back again.

->MICHAEL WALLTHER,<-
->Professor Publicus.<-

<translation>
<pb n="12"/>They prepare everything; the house is astir everywhere with unusual work.
Then Father Abraham, with all things now duly prepared,
Wraps raw leather bands around the tender soles of his feet,
And takes the fate-bearing sword with its gleaming hilt.
This once (as they say) through the skilled mind of Lamech
And the son of Sella, the craft of the smith first discovered,
Had beautifully fashioned from solid iron; and he
Had handed it to his father; Father Noah; and he himself then,
When GOD overwhelmed the vast world and all nations
With waves, had kept it safe in the ark.
Since then all his descendants happily received it;
And he himself thus left it to his son Abraham.
When things were thus, he entrusts the faithful reins to Sarah:
And orders her to guard the rest of the house: She, to the one ordering,
Nods: and seeks her son: Him she detains with her voice
As he is now about to follow his dear father.
Now she commands him to cover his yellow hair, now his chest:
Now to care for the Gods above: and before all things to carry
God with frequent eyes. To the upright, she says, their rewards remain:
These he loves: these the Ruler of high Olympus cares for.
Thus she speaks, and sheds tears between every word.
But the son: Now farewell dear, farewell best mother:
Behold he calls, behold he calls, father: farewell, you roofs.
Thus when he had spoken: he turns his footsteps in equal measure,
Leaving the mother weeping, and often wishing
(Whether love persuaded, or perhaps forebodings of a mind
Troubled) to wrap her arms around his snowy neck.
<pb n="13"/>She, however, followed him as he departed with such a voice:
Go, our glory, go: may you use happy gods:
May you leave the house with them accompanying, and with them return.
   Thus, therefore, with the dear city of his country now abandoned,
Both son and father enter the flourishing fields.
Whom the servants, leading behind the bowing
Beast of burden, follow: and they tire it much with staff and knot.
Then they enter joyful valleys: and are covered by various
Trees: and they wend their way beneath high branches.
The Zephyrs accompany them as they go from behind:
And the gentle birds rise up and greet them with their voice.
   Meanwhile Father Abraham, through the pleasant green meadows,
Relates many things concerning the first religion and faith.
At first he recalls the origins of the spacious world:
How GOD fashioned the spheres of heaven out of nothing,
And once divided the earth from the wandering waves:
And bound all things so beautifully in concordant peace.
Then he sings of the crime of Satan, and the transgressions of our first parent,
And the seed that would come, as the years rolled by,
Which would avenge itself upon Satan: and turn hell upside down.
And crush the head, and gather the chest of the Serpent,
Flowing with much corruption, through dark caves.
Then how he submerged the whole world under the sea
On account of the sins of men, and the foul heats of lust.
And in what manner, with what voice GOD revealed himself
To the fathers and grandfathers, and with what mouth he spoke to them:
And he unfolds the remaining things of the ancients in a long order.
</translation>

## THEOLOGICAL APPROBATION.

*These Universals, with their supplementary theses taken from the whole of Philosophy, most learnedly proposed and illuminated by the splendors of the most serene House of Bavaria, may most rightly be published in print for the common benefit of the studious youth and the most useful exercise of the religious lord defending them.*

-> JOHANN OSWALD von ZIMMERN, Doctor & Professor of Sacred Theology, Licentiate of Both Laws, Academic Vice-Chancellor, & currently Theological Dean. <-

---

## PHILOSOPHICAL APPROBATION.

*This Disputation concerning Universals in general and in particular proposes a solid and clear doctrine of the same, and at the same time, with the annexed supplementary theses, provides abundant material for further disputation; therefore, it is worthy to be printed for this purpose.*

-> LEONARD LERCHENFELDT of the Society of JESUS, Professor of Moral Philosophy & currently Dean. <-

<pb n="24"/>
<note>A horizontal decorative border composed of repeating ornamental floral or knotwork patterns.</note>

# TO THE REVEREND, RELIGIOUS, AND MOST LEARNED LORD, CHAMPION OF THE WHOLE OF PHILOSOPHY IN UNIVERSALS.

*Others bedeck themselves with beautiful Wisdoms,*
*As if they were shining Rachels,*
*They build up their brows, and shape them with needles,*
*They polish their cheeks with learned trifles,*
*And paint their brides with sterile labor.*
*My Wise Man laughs at this; he seizes the sister,*
*The fruitful Leah, the mother.*
*Rachel is displeasing: he says, Leah gives the dowry,*
*She gives all things, she begets all things.*
*I have seen shapes swelling under the Daedalian chisel,*
*Born to stir up envy.*
*I have seen bulls, ordered by the Sarmatian*
*Wound, grow silent: the threatening piers*
*Of the harbors, built in the wave-flowing city of three,*
*Supported by the favor of demigods:*
*Gods playing in a physical bath:*
*The urn of the more blessed particles:*
*Worlds of Pella <note>an allusion to Alexander the Great</note> while Asia stood amazed.*
*I have seen clouds bring forth grand things;*
*Pious heirs of the spheres of the gods.*

<column-break/>

*The Lion of Stagira <note>Aristotle</note> will roar with a Pygmy voice.*
*The Lyceums will learn the price of shadows.*
*My man says: I want the blear-eyed sister.*
*Although Leah is not blear-eyed, though to the one*
*Who is blear-eyed she may be believed to be, she is not blear-eyed.*
*How does it happen that she brings forth Species? Leah is charming*
*To us, a noble Nymph:*
*And the mother of the Genus, and of lineages:*
*The goddess of beautiful Differences.*
*Now let Rachel boast of the light favors of the Graces,*
*And glass dolls, and roses of cheeks on*
*An Accident-prone parchment brow,*
*The brief riches of youth.*
*Not so, not Leah; she offers from her own store.*
*She does not need borrowed smoke;*
*She has learned to shine with native elegance;*
*Taught not to blush with any other rouge,*
*Having for herself that which is her own.*
*Rachel is displeasing. The rich Leah*
*Promises all things, you return all things.*

---

-> Out of the duty of religious honor & love. <-

-> Applauded by <-

P. GREGORY MAGIUS, Canon Regular of the Order
of Saint Augustine, professed at Gars, Student
of Sacred Theology & the Canons.
</translation>

### To the Very Excellent & Most Distinguished
## LORD RESPONDENT, a friend to be honored by me among few.

<note>A large decorative initial S at the start of the first poem.</note>

**S**o at length, the monuments of untiring labor
And the gifts of an excellent spirit, discerning fame
Forbids to entrust to the earth; nor does it threaten small names,
Alas! O beloved, to your undertakings, when a select cohort
Of both young and old men sees you, of their own accord,
Ascending the pulpits; and weighs in a silent mind the prizes
With which, that it might see you adorned, your whole self hopes.

->M. Samuel Schultetus, of Hamburg.<-

Is this, friend, how all discover the omen of your generous name,
While you present the pledges of your ready
Genius? Just as the Phrygian lion, led by atrocious
Savagery, does not at all harm the wretched race of beasts
To which wise nature has granted the strengths of a relaxed
Body, but rather pursues those rabid with fierce heat,
By which he tests his deeds, proving his fame.
Thus also, friend, you bring forth the monuments of your manly
Genius, defending the tumid matter concerning the Essence of Spirit,
And scorning all things with a lesser investigation.
Bravo, I pray, to your undertakings, and may the fates favor your studies!

->*These I wrote for the grace of our most sincere friendship.*<-

->**Otto Helle, of Lubeck.**<-

pages.23:
### To the Very Excellent & Most Distinguished
## LORD RESPONDENT, a friend to be honored by me among few.

<note>A large decorative initial S at the start of the first poem.</note>

**S**o at length, the monuments of untiring labor
And the gifts of an excellent spirit, discerning fame
Forbids to entrust to the earth; nor does it threaten small names,
Alas! O beloved, to your undertakings, when a select cohort
Of both young and old men sees you, of their own accord,
Ascending the pulpits; and weighs in a silent mind the prizes
With which, that it might see you adorned, your whole self hopes.

->M. Samuel Schultetus, of Hamburg.<-

Is this, friend, how all discover the omen of your generous name,
While you present the pledges of your ready
Genius? Just as the Phrygian lion, led by atrocious
Savagery, does not at all harm the wretched race of beasts
To which wise nature has granted the strengths of a relaxed
Body, but rather pursues those rabid with fierce heat,
By which he tests his deeds, proving his fame.
Thus also, friend, you bring forth the monuments of your manly
Genius, defending the tumid matter concerning the Essence of Spirit,
And scorning all things with a lesser investigation.
Bravo, I pray, to your undertakings, and may the fates favor your studies!

->*These I wrote for the grace of our most sincere friendship.*<-

->**Otto Helle, of Lubeck.**<-

<pb n="12"/>a false God, or perhaps the true God but not in the manner that one ought. Therefore, it will be permissible to use external worship, provided we use it in a different manner than they do.

58. Mixed are those things by which God is worshiped simultaneously by body and soul, internally and externally, such as prayer, praise, thanksgiving, reading, and honorable speech about divine things.

<margin>Luke 10.</margin>
59. He therefore errs who, content with mental prayer, casts aside vocal prayer as useless, and dares to prefer every prayer whatsoever that is done by the mind alone to all prayer that is also expressed by the voice. For although Magdalene is said to have chosen the better part than Martha, because the latter gave herself to action and the former to contemplation, nevertheless the Church most truly preaches of the most blessed Virgin Mary that which is said of the former, as one who joined both and excelled most in both. It is clearly better indeed for one to pray with affection alone than for one to murmur with the lips only. Yet he who offers prayers to God in both ways surpasses the former without doubt.

<margin>
Prov. 30.
Jer. 22.
</margin>
60. **THERE ARE THREE THINGS** by which the earth is moved, to which the third Jeremiah acclaims. For sobriety receives the man approaching God, justice leads him on, and piety brings him to the end toward which he strives.

<margin>Eccl. 25.</margin>
61. Who denies that these three things are difficult? Yet they are beautiful, in which even the spirit of God finds pleasure, approved before God, whom sobriety invites, justice holds, and piety places upon the throne. And just as they are before God, so they are before men, among whom, indeed, the first attracts admiration, the second benevolence, and the third reverence. For we admire the chaste and sober, we love the beneficent, and we hold those who are religious to be worthy of special honor.

<margin>
Eccl. 25.
Prov. 30.
Eccl. 4.
</margin>
62. There are three other species, which I wish our soul, like the soul of God, would hate. Three insatiable things: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. A triple wedge advancing with a hostile face against the ranks of the God of Israel, a triple cord drawing into certain destruction, which could undoubtedly be broken with difficulty (if indeed it can be broken at all) by those who trust in their own strength.

63. But (thanks be to God) this one of ours, which draws us back from destruction, is no less strong, while temperance extinguishes the lust of the flesh, generosity curbs the lust of the eyes, and humility prostrates the pride of life.

<pb n="13"/>64. Placed in the middle between these battle lines, the man (about whom they contend) belongs to the one toward whom he has inclined.

65. This is the order of the struggle: that first of all, the flesh must be tamed; he who serves it still lingers in the beginnings. Pride always remains the last, which, if it be cast down a thousand times, nonetheless rises again, and sometimes it is all the stronger for having been prostrated by more powerful forces.

<margin>
Isa. 22.
1 Cor. 15.
</margin>
66. BUT WHEN there is mention of labor and battle, the memory of reward and stipend immediately occurs. We are compelled to say this: that we worship God in vain, and act in vain, and act foolishly if we do not eat and drink, for tomorrow we die, if there is no reward for a right deed, and if no punishment is prepared for the sinner.

<margin>Ps. 61.</margin>
67. Furthermore, God can be judged more cruel than just or merciful (far be such blasphemy from the word) if He becomes angry, is not moved by grace, if He inflicts punishments upon the unjust, the impious, and the sinners, while establishing no rewards for the just, the pious, and the industrious.

<margin>
Prov. 24.
Eccl. 35.
Rom. 2.
2 Cor. 5.
Apoc. 22.
</margin>
68. If, however, a premium and reward will be given to each one according to the fruit of his works, it is a wonder why the merits of good works are denied.

> Let us therefore live soberly, justly, and piously, that is, let us strive vigorously in every kind of good work in this age, awaiting the blessed hope, namely the reward of eternal beatitude, which He who is the beginning, fountain, and origin of all good things, and likewise their end and scope, God blessed forever, may deign to grant to us, and indeed to our merits first. Amen.

<note>A second small decorative trifoliate ornament.</note>

->**Praise to God.**<-
</translation>

<note>continues from previous page</note> passes away, leaving behind children, both those of legal age and those under age. Immediately, tutors and curators are appointed for them by the magistrate. But the adolescents, for the sake of the business they had begun to learn in their homeland, depart for other parts of the land. In the meantime, the curators of these minors, due to pressing necessity and not without the decree of the magistrate of that place, sell the houses of the minors, which are the only property they possess.
*It is now asked, since matters stand thus, whether a tax may be taken or deducted from the received price, that is, the money immediately placed at interest and still subject to levies, which the minors neither seek to have transmitted to themselves, nor do the curators and debtors wish to transmit to them at any time without the prior knowledge of the magistrate.*

### CASE XX.

Titius leaves a son as heir to a fief, to whom, when he petitions for the renewal of the investiture after a year and twenty days, the Lord of the fief opposes the exception of fatal days <note>original: "fatalium exceptionem"; referring to the expiration of a set legal time limit</note>, that is, that the time for requesting the renewal of the investiture has elapsed, and consequently the vassal has lost the fief.
*It is asked whether this exception can be defeated, notwithstanding the text in the second book of the fiefs, chapter 24, and similar [legal authorities].*
I affirm it.

<header>MISCELLANEA.</header>

### I.

<note>A large ornamental initial letter N begins the text.</note>They do not conduct themselves with sufficient consideration who, while rightly attributing to the Princes of the <term>Augustana Confessio</term> <gloss>Augsburg Confession</gloss> authority regarding sacred matters, say that the <term>jus Episcopale</term> <gloss>episcopal right/bishopric power</gloss> is possessed by them.

### II.

And likewise [they err who claim] that our Princes bear a double person, namely, the ecclesiastical and the secular.

### III.

But also [they err who claim] that episcopal rights are exercised by them by way of a fiduciary contract, or as if from a deposit, or in the manner of a usufruct.

### IV.

Finally, the right of our Princes regarding sacred matters consists in the diocesan law and the law of jurisdiction. See the public manuscript lectures of the Magnificent Lord <term>Strauchius</term> <gloss>Johann Strauch, a 17th-century jurist</gloss> on Ecclesiastical Government, in the special part under title 1, paragraph 3 and following, where he pursues this argument with his customary subtlety. Add the Dissertation by the same author on Statutes by the Supreme Prince, in the Digest <note>original: "ff."; referring to the Pandects or Digest of Justinian</note>, title on the Constitutions of Princes, paragraph 36.

### V.

Lutherans and Calvinists are not proved to be heretics from the fact that they are addressed by the names of their authors. THE SAME author [argues this] in his public manuscript lectures on law 6 of the Code concerning heretics and Manichaeans against the Dillingen theologians.

<translation>
<pb n="102"/>The natural state of the innate mind, although from the beginning it is without appearance, cut through the root of whoever is the one looking at the view. The natural state of the innate mind, although from the beginning it is without meditation, leave the essence of the awareness that mediates in the great all-pervading expanse. The natural state of the innate mind, although from the beginning it is without action, there is no duality of action and adopting or abandoning; leave it in its unfabricated, relaxed state. The natural state of the innate mind, although it is self-perfected from the beginning, leave it as the equality of beyond-elaboration, without any desire for a fruit to be achieved. The yogi who maintains it in this way, if he attains stability in the natural state, will purify the delusions of kleshas and attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus it was said. Again, this was offered to the Great Master Nyima Drakpa, compiled into thirty syllables of the alphabet:
K: The unborn realization is self-arising.
Kh: From the nature that is as clear as the sky,
G: That awareness without negation or affirmation,
Ng: Is the state of reality without substantial existence.
C: Through the practice without fabrication,
Ch: Until the body of reality is attained,
J: Accomplish the purpose of beneficial practice.
This song of experience of the thirty syllables was written as it arose in the mind. Thus it was said. Again, in the year of the Monkey, when the <term>Nangso</term> <gloss>official/steward</gloss> Sonam Gyalpo passed away at Lhalung, the <term>Nangso</term>’s wife and children requested that the Guru come to lead the funeral rites. Although at that time he was not free to attend, along with one relic that arose from his teeth, he wrote down and gave this series of instructions to console the <term>Nangso</term>’s wife and children.
I prostrate to and take refuge in the Three Jewels, who are the reliable source of refuge.
<leaf-break/>
To the <term>Nangso</term>, wife and children, with whom there is a profound connection from the past, look wherever you may look—to the ends of the earth or the corners of the sky, or toward the center—there is no time when all sentient beings of the three realms are liberated from the suffering that comes upon them; everyone is headed that way.
<leaf-break/>
Like the passing of time, rising up one by one, the suffering is endless. When you have attained the precious human body, cast aside all worldly activities and exert yourselves in the Dharma. It is the only long-term provision. All temporary activities are of the nature of illusion. Nothing you do is of any benefit, so contemplate impermanence in your mind. Cast aside the activities of this life and achieve your lasting purpose. If you are to achieve a great purpose, do it now, for there is no certainty as to what will happen in the next life. In this time when you have your own freedom, cast aside the activities of distraction and exert yourselves in the practice of this profound instruction of the self-arisen Great Perfection. If you are happy here, you will be happy in the next life. As for this present kingdom, protect it with a mind of love and Dharma. If you benefit all sentient beings, happiness will come to you yourself. This is the advice of the beggar Pema Lingpa. Keep it in the center of your heart. I will be around in the year of the Monkey; at that time we can discuss the offerings and the teachings in detail.

<pb n="103"/>The great <term>vidyadhara</term> <gloss>knowledge-holder</gloss> was practicing begging in the flowers, to the southwest of the Pema Ling monastery, in a place called Nyam-ga. He spoke this poetic introduction to the Khampa yogi Rinchen Zangpo:
The unconditioned mind is the great sky. Its nature is the chain of thoughts of conceptual elaboration. The six objects manifest as the forms of illusion upon the ground. This unreality destroys the path of happiness. Do you see the Khampa, who is like the magical illusion of the moon in water?
Thus he spoke, and again he requested: To the ground of unwavering faith, may the wish-fulfilling tree of devotion branch out. May the fruit of compassion that satisfies all needs ripen.
Thus he requested, and in reply he spoke this:
<leaf-break/>
Again, engage in study and reflection without partiality of direction. Cut the root of the mind’s doubt. Know what is Dharma and what is not, and what to adopt or abandon. Do not err in the pinnacle of your future prospects!
Through the urging of the impermanent death, to realize the nature of the delusion of cyclic existence and to develop renunciation and weariness is the pinnacle of your future prospects, do not err.
Knowing that all the activities and deeds of the world are meaningless, and resting in the state of non-action is the pinnacle of your future prospects, do not err.
Seeing the suffering of all who possess wealth, and realizing that lack of wealth is a great ornament of the mind, and possessing the noble wealth of contentment is the pinnacle of your future prospects, do not err.
Holding onto the object of support that realizes one’s own benefit, training in the mind of enlightenment that benefits others, and turning one’s own and others' minds toward the Dharma is the pinnacle of your future prospects, do not err.
The expanse of Dharma beyond elaboration, the awareness that is unborn and without limits, and attaining the measure of understanding the view is the pinnacle of your future prospects, do not err.
The innate nature of bliss, clarity, and non-thought, and the meditation of the one who meditates...
<leaf-break/>
...because there are some yogis in Tibet, the Land of Snows, who rely on diligence and bring forth the pure vision that awakens their fortunate karmic connections, I request that a little praise be offered to them. This time, I, the yogi, have arrived in the difficult-to-reach Manbum Thang. I have met with you, the Lord Pema Lingpa, whom it is difficult to meet. You have granted the profound instructions of the Essence of All Intentions, and I have eaten the sacred substance that liberates upon tasting. How happy I am, how joyous I am! I, the yogi Lhawang Drakpa, have arrived on the path of empty, clear, non-grasping. From the mountain pass of seeing the naked reality beyond limits, I looked inward at the unceasing, pervasive clarity, and I met the guru of innate self-perfection. I requested the oral instructions on the non-duality of appearance and emptiness. I offered the mandala of the relaxed six consciousnesses. Because of the pure merits of the past, I have met with this essence of the Samantabhadra’s intention. Because of the aspirations I have made now, it is impossible that we will be separated until the end of time. How happy I am!

</translation>
<summary>This text contains Pema Lingpa’s spiritual instructions, including verses on the nature of the mind, advice to a bereaved family, a poetic dialogue with a Khampa yogi, and a personal testimony of a disciple.</summary>
<keywords>Pema Lingpa, innate mind, impermanence, Great Perfection, Dzogchen, spiritual advice, funeral consolation, non-duality, view and meditation</keywords>

Through the urging of the impermanent death, to realize the nature of the delusion of cyclic existence and to develop renunciation and weariness is the pinnacle of your future prospects, do not err.
Knowing that all the activities and deeds of the world are meaningless, and resting in the state of non-action is the pinnacle of your future prospects, do not err.
Seeing the suffering of all who possess wealth, and realizing that lack of wealth is a great ornament of the mind, and possessing the noble wealth of contentment is the pinnacle of your future prospects, do not err.
Holding onto the object of support that realizes one’s own benefit, training in the mind of enlightenment that benefits others, and turning one’s own and others' minds toward the Dharma is the pinnacle of your future prospects, do not err.
The expanse of Dharma beyond elaboration, the awareness that is unborn and without limits, and attaining the measure of understanding the view is the pinnacle of your future prospects, do not err.
The innate nature of bliss, clarity, and non-thought, and the meditation of the one who meditates...

...because there are some yogis in Tibet, the Land of Snows, who rely on diligence and bring forth the pure vision that awakens their fortunate karmic connections, I request that a little praise be offered to them. This time, I, the yogi, have arrived in the difficult-to-reach Manbum Thang. I have met with you, the Lord Pema Lingpa, whom it is difficult to meet. You have granted the profound instructions of the Essence of All Intentions, and I have eaten the sacred substance that liberates upon tasting. How happy I am, how joyous I am! I, the yogi Lhawang Drakpa, have arrived on the path of empty, clear, non-grasping. From the mountain pass of seeing the naked reality beyond limits, I looked inward at the unceasing, pervasive clarity, and I met the guru of innate self-perfection. I requested the oral instructions on the non-duality of appearance and emptiness. I offered the mandala of the relaxed six consciousnesses. Because of the pure merits of the past, I have met with this essence of the Samantabhadra’s intention. Because of the aspirations I have made now, it is impossible that we will be separated until the end of time. How happy I am!

(3) Table of the Eight Negations from the <term>Madhyamaka-shastra</term> <gloss>Treatise on the Middle Way</gloss>

No birth: All phenomena have no birth. Why? Because it is manifest to worldly eyes. For example, the grain at the beginning of the kalpa <gloss>eon</gloss> does not have birth. Why? If one departs from the grain of the beginning of the kalpa, the present grain cannot be obtained. If there were a present grain apart from the grain at the beginning of the kalpa, then there should be birth, but in reality, this is not so. Therefore, there is no birth.

No death: The grain from the beginning of the kalpa does not die. Why? If it died, there should be no grain today, yet in reality, there is grain. Therefore, there is no death.

No permanence: All things are not permanent. For example, when a grain produces a sprout, the seed changes and decays. Therefore, it is not permanent.

No interruption: All things are not interrupted. For example, there is a sprout coming from the grain. Therefore, it is not interrupted; if it were interrupted, there should be no continuity.

No oneness: All things are not one. For example, the grain does not act as the sprout, and the sprout does not act as the grain. If they were one, yet in reality, this is not so. Therefore, it is not one.

No difference: All things are not different. If they were different, why would one distinguish between grain sprouts, grain stalks, and grain leaves, but not speak of tree sprouts, tree stalks, and tree leaves? Therefore, it is not different.

No coming: All things do not come. For example, the sprout within the grain comes from nowhere. If it came, the sprout should come from another place, like a bird coming to perch on a tree, but in reality, this is not so. Therefore, there is no coming.

No going: All things do not go. If there were a going, one should see the sprout coming out of the grain, like a snake coming out of a hole, but in reality, this is not so. Therefore, there is no going.

<pb n="52"/>"Little" refers to "supreme." "Surpassing the cause" refers to "most." Because the obstacles are exhausted, the virtues are perfected, and the fruit has reached the ultimate level, it is called "most supreme." "Karma" refers to the collective activities of the Three Wheels <note>original: "三輪" - the physical, verbal, and mental actions of a Buddha</note> of all Buddhas. That is, "most supreme karma" means the most supreme is the karma. The second interpretation is understandable: it refers to the mental karma of pervasive knowledge, the physical karma of supreme unimpededness, and the verbal karma of supreme compassionate salvation. "The one who possesses" refers to connecting the virtues to a person, meaning one who possesses the aforementioned virtues, which is the Buddha. Secondly, distinguishing by the two types of benefit <note>original: "二利" - self-benefit and benefiting others</note>: "most supreme karma" refers generally to pervasive knowledge and the other specific types, manifesting the virtue of self-benefit. Within this, there is internal wisdom of pervasive knowledge and external form that is unimpeded. The <term>Srīmālādevī Simhanāda Sūtra</term> <gloss>Lion's Roar of Queen Srīmālā Sūtra</gloss> says: The Thus Come One's form is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise. This is also the same. "Saving the world" and the rest specifically manifest the virtue of benefiting others. The one who has perfected these two benefits is the Buddha. Thirdly, distinguishing by the three virtues: first, "most supreme karma" is the general designation. Pervasive knowledge manifests the Buddha's virtue of great wisdom. Second, "form is unimpeded" clarifies the Buddha's virtue of great meditative concentration <note>original: "大定" - the stable, unmoving state of profound focus</note>. This means relying on concentration to manifest supernatural powers and presenting form without impediment.
<pb n="53"/>
<header>Common Commentary on Treatises, Part Two</header>

Third, "saving the world" and the rest clarify the Buddha's virtue of great compassion. The <term>Mahāyāna-saṃgraha</term> <gloss>Summary of the Great Vehicle</gloss> clarifies the virtues of the Buddha's enjoyment body, and only mentions these three. Fourth, following the text for explanation: here, only the reward body and manifestation body are explained, because the Dharma body is included within the Dharma Jewel. "Most supreme" is as explained initially. "Karma" and "pervasive knowledge" have two meanings: first, the pervasive knowledge of true wisdom, which refers to the gate of the Thusness of the mind, the virtues as numerous as the Ganges sands, and so on. Second, the pervasive knowledge of conventional wisdom, which refers to the gate of birth and cessation of the mind, the various manifestations of dependent origination, and so on. Understanding both principle and quantity, this is the pervasive knowledge that is without error. "Form is unimpeded" means that the Thus Come One's physical body is free and unimpeded. There are many types. As described in the "Inconceivable Dharma" chapter of the <term>Avataṃsaka Sūtra</term> <gloss>Flower Adornment Sutra</gloss>, here I will briefly distinguish four types: first, unimpededness of large and small, meaning that each and every sense organ permeates the Dharma realm without damaging the nature of the various organs, and the text is not mixed; the characteristics of the various organs. Second, unimpededness of mutual usage, meaning the various sense organs perform each other's functions without mutual obstruction. Third, unimpededness of principle and phenomenon, meaning that the manifested form is bright and distinct, yet does not obstruct the essential voidness of its totality, the profound principle.
</translation>

<summary>This text explains the concept of a Buddha's "most supreme karma" through the lenses of three modes of action, the two types of benefit (self and others), and the three virtues, eventually detailing the unimpeded nature of the Buddha's physical and mental manifestations.</summary>
<keywords>Buddha, karma, Three Wheels, two benefits, three virtues, pervasive knowledge, unimpeded form, Thusness, dependent origination</keywords>

<pb n="45"/>Moses said, by way of the literal meaning, that this verse indicates a great and very broad matter. It is that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created for His glory; and everything He created, He created with wisdom, with understanding, and with knowledge, and there is nothing in the world created in vain at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created only for His glory." This is a great and broad matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know their Creator, blessed be His name and may His memory be exalted forever and ever.

And further, one may say that this verse indicates another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created by measure, by weight, and by capacity, and there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by measure, by weight, and by capacity." This is a great and broad matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know their Creator, blessed be His name and may His memory be exalted forever and ever.

And further, one may say that this verse indicates another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created by way of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, and there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by way of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge." This is a great and broad matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know their Creator, blessed be His name and may His memory be exalted forever and ever.

<margin>Note on the subject of Creation</margin>
And further, one may say that this verse indicates another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created by way of kindness, mercy, and truth, and there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by way of kindness, mercy, and truth." This is a great and broad matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know their Creator, blessed be His name and may His memory be exalted forever and ever.

<summary>This text explores the nature of creation as an expression of divine wisdom, measure, and kindness, and discusses the spiritual qualifications, such as wisdom, strength, and integrity, required for a prophet to attain the level of communion with the Divine Presence, exemplified by Moses.</summary>
<keywords>Creation, divine wisdom, prophet, prophecy, Divine Presence, Shekhinah, Moses, shining mirror, purification, righteousness, integrity</keywords>

Moses said, by way of the literal meaning, that this verse indicates a great and very broad matter. It is that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created for His glory; and everything He created, He created with wisdom, with understanding, and with knowledge, and there is nothing in the world created in vain at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created only for His glory." This is a great and broad matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know their Creator, blessed be His name and may His memory be exalted forever and ever.

And further, one may say that this verse indicates another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created by measure, by weight, and by capacity, and there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by measure, by weight, and by capacity." This is a great and broad matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know their Creator, blessed be His name and may His memory be exalted forever and ever.

And further, one may say that this verse indicates another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created by way of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, and there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by way of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge." This is a great and broad matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know their Creator, blessed be His name and may His memory be exalted forever and ever.

<margin>Note on the subject of Creation</margin>
And further, one may say that this verse indicates another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created by way of kindness, mercy, and truth, and there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by way of kindness, mercy, and truth." This is a great and broad matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know their Creator, blessed be His name and may His memory be exalted forever and ever.

<pb n="61"/>Therefore, it specifies the Lord of all <note><term>Sarvesha</term></note> as the <term>Hamsa</term> <gloss>swan; the soul or life-breath</gloss>. This Lord of all is the <term>Hamsa</term>, in the form of a mantra consisting of that sequence. This is stated in the <term>Prapanchasara</term>. That which is named <term>Tattva</term> <gloss>Reality</gloss>, being mere Consciousness, then, due to the proximity of the Light, desiring to manifest, becomes dense and attains the state of a <term>Bindu</term> <gloss>point/drop</gloss>. In time, that <term>Bindu</term> splits and becomes twofold. The right part is the <term>Bindu</term>, and the left part is the <term>Visarga</term> <gloss>the two vertical dots representing release or emission</gloss>. Through this, the right and left parts are characterized as male and female. The letter 'Ha' is called the <term>Bindu</term>, and the <term>Visarga</term> is known as 'Sa'. The <term>Bindu</term> is called the Purusha <gloss>the Cosmic Man/Spirit</gloss>, and the <term>Visarga</term> is known as Prakriti <gloss>Nature/Creative Power</gloss>. The <term>Hamsa</term> is of the nature of both Purusha and Prakriti, and this universe is of its nature. This is stated very clearly in the first chapter of the <term>Mahakali Tantra</term>: "In the void within the thousand-petaled lotus, which is adorned with divine archways, in the middle of the lunar mandala, above the two letters of the <term>Hamsa</term>, it shines like pure crystal, resplendent with pure nectar," and so on. Here, "above the two letters of the <term>Hamsa</term>" is clear. Alternatively, <term>Hamsa</term> is the name known as the Supreme <gloss>Parama</gloss>, meaning it is famous by that name. Therefore, the author himself, in the forty-eighth verse, said "some call this the form of the <term>Hamsa</term>," thus naming it <term>Hamsa</term> himself. Or, that which has <term>Hamsa</term> at the end is <term>Hamsantah</term>, and since it is both the <term>Hamsa</term> and the Supreme, by the compound rule of <term>Karmadharaya</term> and the omission of the middle word <note>a linguistic rule for compounding words</note>, "Hamsaparama" <gloss>the Supreme Hamsa</gloss> is established. Thus, it is known by the name <term>Paramahamsa</term> <gloss>the Supreme Swan/Self-realized soul</gloss>. Hence it is said in the <term>Agama Kalpadruma</term>: "This is the form of the <term>Paramahamsa</term>, united with all that is stationary and moving." It is the flowing stream of all happiness. The expansion of that total happiness, which is the series of waves, is manifest everywhere and is revealed through its persistence in successive times. Therefore, it is characterized by all-pervading, all-encompassing happiness. This <term>Hamsa</term> has been mentioned previously as being situated below the Supreme Shiva. 43.

<pb n="62"/>The Shaivas call this place the Supreme Purusha <gloss>Spirit</gloss>, the Vaishnavas describe it as the abode of Hari-Hara <gloss>Vishnu and Shiva united</gloss>, and some others call it the abode of the Goddess. The greatest of sages, who delight in the lotus feet of the Goddess, call it the pure abode of Prakriti and Purusha. 44.

He explains that because all deities, the <term>Hamsa</term>, and others reside in this pericarp, it is the place of worship for all devotees, including Shaivas and Shaktas. "The abode of Shiva" <note>This explains the first line of the verse</note>: Shaivas, the worshippers of Shiva, call this lotus the abode of Shiva. The "Supreme Purusha" <note>referring to Vishnu's abode</note> is established through the secondary suffix. "Some" refers to those who worship Hari-Hara; they are Shaivas and Vaishnavas. Others, those who are not exclusive worshippers of only Shiva or Vishnu, call it the abode of Hari-Hara. Therefore, the meaning is that not all Shaivas and Vaishnavas say it is only the abode of Shiva or only the abode of Vishnu. Others, who are devoted to the dual worship, speak of it this way. Or, other sages who are devoted to the <term>Hamsa</term> mantra call it the abode of Prakriti and Purusha because the <term>Hamsa</term> is the form of both. This is just an illustration; it should be understood that because the supreme <term>Bindu</term> resides in that place, which is full of all deities, whoever is a worshipper of a certain deity calls it the abode of that deity. 44.

He states the result of the knowledge of the <term>Sahasrara</term> <gloss>the thousand-petaled lotus</gloss> in the words "this place." The meaning is that one gains knowledge of this place along with its secondary parts and limbs. "With his mind fixed": one whose mind is engaged there. "Shall not be in the world": the meaning is that he becomes liberated. The reason is given in the phrase "he is not bound in the three worlds." "Bound" means bound by the snares of Maya <gloss>illusion</gloss> in the form of merit and demerit. It is stated in the <term>Bhagavata</term>: "While performing actions due to the qualities, the soul considers itself the doer; this is its worldly bondage and dependence."</translation>

<summary>This section discusses the identity of the Hamsa as the Supreme Lord within the thousand-petaled lotus, explaining why different religious traditions associate this space with their respective deities, such as Shiva, Vishnu, or the union of Prakriti and Purusha.</summary>
<keywords>Hamsa, Sahasrara, Paramahamsa, Bindu, Visarga, Purusha, Prakriti, Shaiva, Vaishnava, Tantra, Liberation</keywords>

pages.61: Therefore, it specifies the Lord of all <note><term>Sarvesha</term></note> as the <term>Hamsa</term> <gloss>swan; the soul or life-breath</gloss>. This Lord of all is the <term>Hamsa</term>, in the form of a mantra consisting of that sequence. This is stated in the <term>Prapanchasara</term>. That which is named <term>Tattva</term> <gloss>Reality</gloss>, being mere Consciousness, then, due to the proximity of the Light, desiring to manifest, becomes dense and attains the state of a <term>Bindu</term> <gloss>point/drop</gloss>. In time, that <term>Bindu</term> splits and becomes twofold. The right part is the <term>Bindu</term>, and the left part is the <term>Visarga</term> <gloss>the two vertical dots representing release or emission</gloss>. Through this, the right and left parts are characterized as male and female. The letter 'Ha' is called the <term>Bindu</term>, and the <term>Visarga</term> is known as 'Sa'. The <term>Bindu</term> is called the Purusha <gloss>the Cosmic Man/Spirit</gloss>, and the <term>Visarga</term> is known as Prakriti <gloss>Nature/Creative Power</gloss>. The <term>Hamsa</term> is of the nature of both Purusha and Prakriti, and this universe is of its nature. This is stated very clearly in the first chapter of the <term>Mahakali Tantra</term>: "In the void within the thousand-petaled lotus, which is adorned with divine archways, in the middle of the lunar mandala, above the two letters of the <term>Hamsa</term>, it shines like pure crystal, resplendent with pure nectar," and so on. Here, "above the two letters of the <term>Hamsa</term>" is clear. Alternatively, <term>Hamsa</term> is the name known as the Supreme <gloss>Parama</gloss>, meaning it is famous by that name. Therefore, the author himself, in the forty-eighth verse, said "some call this the form of the <term>Hamsa</term>," thus naming it <term>Hamsa</term> himself. Or, that which has <term>Hamsa</term> at the end is <term>Hamsantah</term>, and since it is both the <term>Hamsa</term> and the Supreme, by the compound rule of <term>Karmadharaya</term> and the omission of the middle word <note>a linguistic rule for compounding words</note>, "Hamsaparama" <gloss>the Supreme Hamsa</gloss> is established. Thus, it is known by the name <term>Paramahamsa</term> <gloss>the Supreme Swan/Self-realized soul</gloss>. Hence it is said in the <term>Agama Kalpadruma</term>: "This is the form of the <term>Paramahamsa</term>, united with all that is stationary and moving." It is the flowing stream of all happiness. The expansion of that total happiness, which is the series of waves, is manifest everywhere and is revealed through its persistence in successive times. Therefore, it is characterized by all-pervading, all-encompassing happiness. This <term>Hamsa</term> has been mentioned previously as being situated below the Supreme Shiva. 43.

<translation>
<pb n="62"/>
# Twenty-first Chapter

->Twenty-first Chapter. 48<-

With beautiful teeth, eternal, with firm and raised breasts, situated in a graceful posture, she is the destroyer of the buffalo demon <note>Mahishasuramardini, a form of Durga</note>. (25)
Her touch is as soft as the lotus stalk, and she is endowed with ten arms. On the right, one should contemplate the trident, the sword, and the discus, in order. (26)
She holds sharp weapons in her left arms: the shield, the full bow, the noose, and the goad. (27)
One should also place the bell, or that which is supreme, on the left. Her body is anointed with red sandalwood, and she is draped in red garments. (28)
Mounted on a lion, the Supreme Goddess is worshipped by Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva. She rests upon a corpse, she is the Great Illusion <term>Mahamaya</term> <gloss>the creative power of the universe</gloss>, and she stands upon a red lotus. (29)
One should meditate upon Durga, who is mounted on a lion and grants supreme liberation. Shiva is the corpse, the great god; Brahma is the red lotus. (30)
Vishnu is known as the lion, and these are the mounts of the Great Power. Oh Goddess, the invocation of these by their own forms is not practiced. (31)
Having taken on those respective forms, they have attained the state of being mounts. Sometimes she resides on the corpse of Shiva, sometimes on the red lotus. (32)
Sometimes she resides on the back of the lion, Oh Supreme Goddess. In the time of desire, the lion-mounted one resides on the corpse of Shiva. (33)
Hear now of the beloved group of companions of this buffalo-destroying goddess. (34)

Thus ends the Twenty-first Chapter in the Shri Kamivilasa Tantra.

<pb n="63"/>

->Now the Twenty-second Chapter.<-

Shri Tatpurusha said:

Chanda, Chandavati, the knowledge <term>vidya</term> <gloss>divine wisdom/mantra</gloss>, Chamunda, Chanda-nayika, (1)
Ugra-chanda, Prachanda, Chandogra, and Chanda-nasika.
Surrounded by these powers, victorious and lion-mounted, (2)
Hear the mantra I will tell you, which is the granter of liberation for the destroyer of the buffalo demon.
Extract the <term>maya-bija</term> <gloss>seed syllable of illusion, Hrim</gloss>, then the words "Durge, Durge". (3)
Then, Oh virtuous one, the word "Raksha" <gloss>protect</gloss>, and at the end, the beloved of fire <note>Svaha</note>. (4)
There is no mantra greater than this, the most excellent in the tantras, Oh beautiful-eyed one. I will tell you the ten-letter great mantra. (5)
Extract the <term>maya-bija</term>, then the word "Durge", Oh Beloved.
At the end, the wife of fire <note>Svaha</note>; it is considered to grant all successes. (6)
Extract the <term>maya-bija</term>, then "Durgyai", and after that,
Adding the wife of fire at the end, if one chants it even once, (7)
Taking a path of ten million, he goes to Vaikuntha <note>the abode of Vishnu</note>.
"Durge, Durge", and thus spoken, the wife of fire after that. (8)
This knowledge <term>vidya</term> is the great knowledge <term>maha-vidya</term>, the granter of the four fruits of human life <note>virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation</note>.
Extract the <term>maya-bija</term>, and at the end, the beloved of fire. (9)
This knowledge <term>vidya</term> of yours is free from the faults of the buffalo-destroyer.
"Hrim, Durge", that supreme mantra, is the granter of the four fruits. (10)
"Hrim, Durge", then the word "Rakshani", then the syllable "Namah".
Extract the <term>maya-bija</term>, and the wife of fire after that. (11)
The fourteen-lettered knowledge is free from all faults.
"Hrim, Durge", that supreme mantra is the granter of the four fruits. (12)
</translation>

<summary>This text details the iconographic meditative form of the goddess Mahishasuramardini (Durga) and provides various powerful mantras associated with her worship for the attainment of liberation and success.</summary>
<keywords>Tantra, Mahishasuramardini, Durga, Mantras, Iconography, Meditation, Kamivilasa, Liberation</keywords>

<translation>
<pb n="214"/>The Bodhisattva does not focus intently on their own mind, nor do they focus intently on the minds of others. Why is that? Because in that way, the Bodhisattva’s continuum of mind is known through primordial wisdom <term>ye shes</term> <gloss>gnosis or original wakefulness</gloss>. The continuum of mind is known through mindfulness. It is known through intelligence. The continuum of mind is known through realization. The cause of the mind is known through transcendent setient wisdom <term>shes rab</term> <gloss>prajna</gloss>. The continuum of mind is known through the intellect. The continuum of mind is known as being without afflictions, having completely cut the connection to habitual tendencies, being pure, stainless, luminous, without fault, not harsh, unclouded, and as the cognition of the appearance of all phenomena. It is known through following the mental activities of all sentient beings. Shariputra, this entry of the mind’s knowledge into such phenomena is called the Bodhisattva’s clairvoyance of knowing the minds of others and the total perfection of the activity of primordial wisdom. Shariputra, in that regard, what is the Bodhisattva’s clairvoyance of the realization of recollecting previous lives, and what carries out the total perfection of the activity of the primordial wisdom of clairvoyance? Shariputra, here a Bodhisattva, throughout the entirely countless realms of the world in the ten directions, recollects all the births of all sentient beings: one, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty
<leaf-break/>
They also recollect their own roots of virtue arising from previous causes. They also recollect the causes of the roots of virtue of others. They dedicate their own roots of virtue toward enlightenment. Having recollected the roots of virtue of other sentient beings as well, they cause them to generate the mind set on enlightenment. Whatever causes of previous happiness and suffering existed, they rely on them as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and without a self. Because they rely on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, they are not conceited about their physical form; they are not conceited about their enjoyments; they are not conceited about their attendants; they are not conceited about their power. They do not desire and are not conceited about being a universal monarch <term>chakravartin</term>. They do not desire and are not conceited about being Shakra <note>the king of the gods</note>. They do not desire and are not conceited about being Brahma. They do not desire and are not conceited about being a world-protector. They do not desire and are not conceited about all types of rebirth. They do not possess a mind that desires all the pleasures of desire, royal dominion, or power; except, however, for intentionally taking on existence for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity. Because they rely on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness, their previous <pb n="215"/>conduct of afflictions causes them to feel shame, embarrassment, and regret. Even for the sake of their life, they do not perform actions with present objects that would become roots of non-virtue. They dedicate and expand those previous roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfectly complete enlightenment. In order to gather all present roots of virtue, they completely abandon discordant dedications. For the sake of not interrupting the lineage of the Buddha, the lineage of the Dharma, and the lineage of the Sangha, they dedicate everything toward omniscience through the power of perfectly generated mindfulness. That mindfulness of theirs is also deeply blessed by the blessing of the expanse of phenomena <term>dharmadhatu</term>. It is utterly unshakable through reason. Because they have practiced the purification of meditative concentration <term>dhyana</term>, it is beyond mere analysis. Because it is deeply blessed by calm abiding <term>shamatha</term>, it is without harm. Because it is deeply grasped by superior insight <term>vipashyana</term>, it is without error. Because it is direct perception, it is not ordinary. Because mindfulness is not impaired, it is without forgetfulness.
<leaf-break/>
Because they have deeply and completely meditated on these phenomena that have been mastered—the desires, the pleasures, the mastery, and the four bases of miraculous power—the miracles are actually attained. They experience various types of the renunciation of miraculous displays. Those miraculous displays of theirs are also practiced for the sake of looking after sentient beings. Whatever form, strength, blessing, or miraculous display is needed to tame sentient beings, they manifest that very miraculous display. Whatever appearance of form and color is needed to tame sentient beings, they manifest that very appearance of form and color. Whether it is the appearance of the form and color of a Buddha, or the appearance of the form and color of a Solitary Realizer <term>pratyekabuddha</term>, or the appearance of the form and color of a Listener <term>shravaka</term>, or the appearance of the form and color of Shakra, or the appearance of the form and color of Brahma, or the appearance of a world-protector
</translation>

<summary>This passage describes the advanced cognitive and miraculous abilities of a Bodhisattva, focusing on their mastery of mindfulness, recollection of past lives, and their ability to manifest various forms to benefit sentient beings. It emphasizes that these powers are rooted in the realization of impermanence and selflessness rather than personal ambition.</summary>
<keywords>Bodhisattva, primordial wisdom, mindfulness, past lives, miraculous powers, roots of virtue, enlightenment, dharmadhatu, shamatha, vipashyana</keywords>

<pb n="45"/>Moses said, according to the plain meaning <note>original: "al derekh ha-peshat"</note>, that this verse points to a very great and expansive matter. It is that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created entirely for His glory. Everything He created, He created with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge; there is nothing at all in the world created in vain. This is what our sages of blessed memory said: "Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created only for His glory." This is a very great and expansive matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, blessed be His name and exalted be His mention forever and for all eternity.

Furthermore, it can be said that this verse points to another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created entirely with measure, weight, and proportion <note>original: "bi-middah u-ve-mishkal u-ve-meshurah"</note>. There is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages of blessed memory said: "Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only with measure, weight, and proportion." This is a very great and expansive matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, blessed be His name and exalted be His mention forever and for all eternity.

Furthermore, it can be said that this verse points to another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created entirely by way of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge. There is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages of blessed memory said: "Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by way of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge." This is a very great and expansive matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, blessed be His name and exalted be His mention forever and for all eternity.

<margin>A note on the matter of Creation</margin>
Furthermore, it can be said that this verse points to another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created entirely by way of loving-kindness <term>Chesed</term>, mercy, and truth. There is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages of blessed memory said: "Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by way of loving-kindness, mercy, and truth." This is a very great and expansive matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, blessed be His name and exalted be His mention forever and for all eternity.

<pb n="46"/><margin>Two names <note>Refers to the divine names or the call of Abraham</note></margin>

Moses said, according to the plain meaning <note>original: "al derekh ha-peshat"</note>, that this verse points to a very great and expansive matter. It is that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created entirely for His glory. Everything He created, He created with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge; there is nothing at all in the world created in vain. This is what our sages of blessed memory said: "Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created only for His glory." This is a very great and expansive matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, blessed be His name and exalted be His mention forever and for all eternity.

Furthermore, it can be said that this verse points to another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created entirely with measure, weight, and proportion <note>original: "bi-middah u-ve-mishkal u-ve-meshurah"</note>. There is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages of blessed memory said: "Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only with measure, weight, and proportion." This is a very great and expansive matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, blessed be His name and exalted be His mention forever and for all eternity.

Furthermore, it can be said that this verse points to another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created entirely by way of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge. There is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages of blessed memory said: "Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by way of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge." This is a very great and expansive matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, blessed be His name and exalted be His mention forever and for all eternity.

<margin>A note on the matter of Creation</margin>
Furthermore, it can be said that this verse points to another matter: that everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created entirely by way of loving-kindness <term>Chesed</term>, mercy, and truth. There is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages of blessed memory said: "Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by way of loving-kindness, mercy, and truth." This is a very great and expansive matter, and a person must contemplate it at every time and every hour, for through this, a person will merit to know his Creator, blessed be His name and exalted be His mention forever and for all eternity.

<translation page="10">
<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'N' begins the dedication.</note>

**THERE IS NO ONE WHO WOULD DENY** that your father, the Lord Count Philipp, because of his most celebrated virtues and the singular piety toward God in which he shone, deserves to be honored with the praises of a hero and with Latin verse <note>original: "carmine Ausonio" referring to the tradition of Ausonius, a Latin poet.</note>. Since I am not endowed with such eloquence that I might be able to decorate his ghost as his dignity requires, and yet I have descended into this arena, I pray that no one holds it against me as a fault. For it is fitting to favor even modest talents, even if they do not achieve everything. However, generous Counts, it has pleased me to dedicate this poem, however humble a gift, to you, and I pray that you receive it with a calm and serene countenance. If you continue as you have, not yet deviating in any matter from your father's virtues, you will one day be celebrated with a similar eulogy. Therefore, apply yourselves so that you do not degenerate or stray from your father's footsteps. From Mühlberg, on the 11th of May, in the year from the birth of the Virgin.

Grieves for his brother, filled with sorrowful love.
But you, Ernst, having departed for the home of Speyer,
Groan for the fate of your brother under a foreign sky.
Just as you were recently following the pious arms of Saxony,
A fighter with united forces: yours, Hesse.
Meanwhile, the fates snatched away your brother at home,
Whose name was Gracia <note>likely referring to the deceased or a specific relative</note>, in a cruel and unjust death.
With the Emperor now also holding council, I pray
That it might bring salvation and peace, those welcome gifts.
With the Duke of Saxony and you visiting this, you lose
Philipp at home now for a similar reason.
Therefore, you deservedly pour out heavy tears, Ernst,
And you have just and grave cause for your weeping.
You too, children, sad about the death of your parent,
You weep, and heavy grief possesses your breasts.
Just cause produces huge complaints for you,
And anyone who criticizes them has no reason at all.
Until now you wept for your deceased mother and uncle Johann,
Now you weep for both, together with your father.
And now each sad fortress mourns its deprived
Father, and the Ora <note>a river near the Gleichen estates</note> mixes its waters with tears.

<header>PRO A. CLVENTIO.</header>

who had coveted the money of Sassia, thought that a remedy for the delay being imposed upon the marriage had to be sought at home. For since he had an infant son by Novia, while his other son, born of Pappia, was being raised by his mother at Teanum Apulum—which is eighteen miles away from Larinum—he suddenly, and without cause, sent for the boy from Teanum, something he was not in the habit of doing except during public games or festival days. The wretched mother, suspecting no evil, sent him. Although he had feigned that he was setting out for Tarentum, on that very day, after the boy had been seen in public in good health at the eleventh hour, he was dead before nightfall, and the following day, before dawn, he was cremated. And this great grief was reported to the mother by the rumor of men before anyone from the household of Oppianicus had informed her. When she heard at once that not only her son, but even the duty of performing the funeral rites had been snatched from her, she came to Larinum, having been rendered senseless, and there performed the funeral anew for her son, already buried. Not ten days had passed when that other infant son was killed. Therefore, Sassia married Oppianicus immediately, with a soul already rejoicing and strengthened by the best of hopes; nor is it a wonder, for she saw herself appeased not by wedding gifts, but by the funerals of her sons. And so, because others are accustomed to be more eager for money on account of their children, he considered it agreeable to lose his children for the sake of money. I sense, judges, that because of your innate humanity, you have been vehemently moved by these great crimes which I have briefly demonstrated. With what heart, therefore, do you think those men were, who not only had to listen to these things but also to judge them? You hear about a man against whom you are not the judges; about a man whom you do not see; about a man whom you can no longer hate; about a man who has satisfied both nature and the laws—whom the laws punished with exile and nature with death. You hear not from an enemy; you hear without witnesses,</translation>

<translation page="55">
<header>ORATIO</header>

you hear while those things, which could be told with great copiousness, are stated by me briefly and in summary. They heard about a man concerning whom they were obligated to deliver their verdicts under oath; about a man whose nefarious and wicked face they gazed upon as he was present; about a man they hated because of his audacity; about a man they considered worthy of every punishment. They heard from accusers; they heard the words of many witnesses; they heard while each point was discussed gravely and at length by P. Canutius, a most eloquent man. And is there anyone who, having learned these things, could suspect that Oppianicus was crushed by a trial and that an innocent man was outmaneuvered? I will state the remaining points in summary now, judges, so that I may arrive at those matters which are closer to this case and more relevant. I ask you to keep in mind that my purpose here is not to accuse a dead Oppianicus, but—since I wish to persuade you that the trial was not corrupted by this man—to use as the beginning and foundation of the defense that Oppianicus, a most wicked and guilty man, was indeed convicted. He gave a cup to his own wife, Cluentia, who was the paternal aunt of this man Habitus, and suddenly, in the middle of drinking, she exclaimed that she was dying with the greatest pain, nor did she live longer than she spoke; for she died in the very act of speaking and crying out. And besides this sudden death and the cry of the dying woman, all other signs and traces of poison that are usually present were found in the body of the dead woman; and with that same poison he killed his brother, C. <translation page="17">The greater, therefore, is the necessity incumbent upon us to examine this matter accurately, since the hinge of almost the entire controversy turns upon it. For, according to Vossius, the Vast Void <term>χαω</term> <gloss>Chaos</gloss> comes from the ancient <term>χαιω</term> <gloss>to gape/yawn</gloss>, which, according to Hornius, was made from the Mosaic <term>תהו</term> <gloss>tohu</gloss> or <term>בהו</term> <gloss>bohu</gloss> by the change of a single letter. But in the opinion of Riccioli, it descends from <term>παρα τω χεισθαι</term> <gloss>from the act of pouring</gloss>, a derivation that pleased the Stoics in particular, according to Philo <term>περί αφθαρσίας</term> <gloss>On Incorruptibility</gloss>, and the author Achilles Tatius, and Pherecydes.

<margin>In the Etymologicum. Hist. Phil. Book II. Ch. XI.</margin>
<margin>Loc. cit. Quest. V. p. 201. Isag. in Phan. Arati, Ch. III.</margin>

In this way, it signifies confusion and many things mixed together or aggregated at once. But writers vary greatly, not only in its origin but also in its meaning. Except for Aristotle, who interprets it as place, the Gentiles seem commonly to have held that it denotes uncreated matter, existing before all Gods, or, as Plato says, before all things were made. Indeed, almost everyone who mentions it agrees equally that it denotes the *principle of the World*. However, what that principle was, and how it was established and composed, is no more agreed upon among them than it is among clocks. Regarding this, as well as the order in which individual elements or bodies were separated or distinguished from it, see Riccioli or our own Roeschelius. Burnet sets it forth in such a way as to establish the firstborn—as it were, chaos—and its twins, Night and Tartarus, that is, the upper and lower body. He makes the former a dark air, impenetrable by the sun's rays, and the latter, Tartarus or the abyss. Then he posits that Night, being pregnant, likewise gave birth to twins: Earth, for instance, and Aether, or the sublunary Heaven, which is the region of the purer air. No one, I think, fails to perceive that in this, the most ingenious author adds much of his own to Aristophanes. For, besides the fact that neither sign nor trace appears in him of a distinction between aether and heaven, nor can an atmosphere be conceived at that time when the terrestrial globe was fashioned, with no vapors yet existing: furthermore, he says Night and Tartarus were not born from Chaos, but existed simultaneously with Chaos. Finally, he attributes immense gulfs to Erebus, whom he joins with the abyss and tartarus, such as he would certainly only incongruously pronounce of the terrestrial-aerial sphere, which hardly holds itself as a point with respect to the Universe. All these and other similar inconveniences are easily dissipated if it is said that Aristophanes held *Night and Tartarus and Erebus* not as the various offspring of Chaos, but as its parts, or rather as its adjuncts or affections. So that Chaos signifies the matter; Night, the darkness and privation of light; Tartarus, the horrific confusion; and Erebus, the immense vastness or interspace</translation>

<translation page="18">signify and denote. It is as if he had wished to say that Chaos was an immense and boundless, and likewise formless, vastness, not otherwise than the Author of the Book of Wisdom says, that God made the world out of invisible and formless matter; or, as the Doctor of the Gentiles speaks, that the ages were fitted to the word of God, so that visible things were made from invisible ones. Or, if one must speak from the corpuscular philosophy, supported by experience and the firmest reasoning, that primary and infinite Matter occupied an immense space with the power of atoms.

<margin>
Book I, On the Heavens, Ch. III.
Ch. II, t. s. p. 94.
</margin>

§. XVI. These things are clearly in conformity with the Mosaic narrative, and they agree excellently with the pronouncements and traditions of both Greek and barbarian philosophers. We will not be more laborious in bringing these forward, since Lord Master Tentzel has already occupied this entire province. We urge this instead: that Aristophanes clearly declares that the race of the Gods did not exist before Love had mingled all things. That the stars must be understood by these Gods, the formula of speaking <term>γένος ἀθανάτων</term> <gloss>race of immortals</gloss> proves more clearly than the meridian sun, which no one of the Ancients, neither Pythagoreans, nor Platonists, nor Peripatetics, ever applied to sublunary things. So much so that, although Pseudo-Hermes says and posits that nothing dies in the World, he nevertheless does not apply the word <term>ἀθάνατον</term> <gloss>immortal</gloss>. The passages by which the assertion could be demonstrated are infinite; however, two will suffice: one from Aristotle, who says that all nations attribute the supreme place to the Gods for the reason that <term>ὡς τῷ ἀθανάτῳ τὸ ἀθάνατον συνηρτημένον</term> <gloss>as the immortal is bound to the immortal</gloss>; another from Ocellus Lucanus, asserting with an elegant simile that the path of the Moon is the isthmus of mortality and immortality. Nor do the mythologists and cyclic poets say or teach anything else, for they all proceed in explaining the Theogonies in such a way that they recount the creation or production of the Gods and the Theogony in a continuous series, with no space of time interposed. Regarding Plato and the Platonists, the same is most evident, so that to wish to declare it laboriously would be a waste of effort.

<margin>
Book VI. 6. VI.
</margin>

We cannot, however, refrain from adding from Proclus that he calls the Gods the makers and producers of the novel and fresh animals; but elsewhere, he asserts that the same things are the <term>Ὀρφικὸν ᾠὸν</term> <gloss>Orphic egg</gloss> and the <term>τοῦ πλάτωνος ὄν</term> <gloss>being of Plato</gloss>. These latter things not only show that the ancients understood nothing else by the egg than Chaos itself, but they simultaneously reveal the foundation or the occasion for the opinion regarding the pre-existence of antemundane matter. Namely, because whatever they said of the Gods besides the supreme God—whom they called one, good, <term>ἀνουσίαον</term> <gloss>without substance/essence</gloss> and not endowed with essence—such as the stars, demons, or indeed even the mind itself and the Soul of the World, were entities produced by the supreme God, they believed that these freshly produced Gods accepted the matter from which they fashioned the sublunary bodies as already prepared and existing. They could not help but posit eternal matter, because before the time that began, as soon as the mundane bodies had been produced, there was mere eternity.

§. XVII. That Aristophanes says Night laid the first wind-egg does not hinder the truth at all, and it shows only that he did not sufficiently grasp the Mosaic doctrine, nor could he attain to the incubation or fostering of Divine Love: therefore, he adorned the sentiment according to the capacity of his own intellect. So that this single difficulty cannot by any means prevent us from subscribing to the opinion, leaving aside Burnet's archaeology, that has been sufficiently demonstrated by Hugo Grotius, Edmund Dickinson, Jacob Tollius, and Adam Tribbechovius.</translation>

<summary>This passage examines the etymology of "Chaos," linking it to Mosaic accounts, and discusses how various philosophers—including Plato and Aristophanes—conceived of the origins of the universe, matter, and the gods, ultimately arguing that these ancient views align with Mosaic doctrine when interpreted correctly.</summary>
<keywords>Chaos, Mosaic narrative, Aristophanes, Plato, Proclus, primary matter, creation, Theogony, Hugo Grotius</keywords>

Nor do the mythologists and cyclic poets say or teach anything else, for they all proceed in explaining the Theogonies in such a way that they recount the creation or production of the Gods and the Theogony in a continuous series, with no space of time interposed. Regarding Plato and the Platonists, the same is most evident, so that to wish to declare it laboriously would be a waste of effort.

Book VI. 6. VI.
</margin>

We cannot, however, refrain from adding from Proclus that he calls the Gods the makers and producers of the novel and fresh animals; but elsewhere, he asserts that the same things are the <term>Ὀρφικὸν ᾠὸν</term> <gloss>Orphic egg</gloss> and the <term>τοῦ πλάτωνος ὄν</term> <gloss>being of Plato</gloss>. These latter things not only show that the ancients understood nothing else by the egg than Chaos itself, but they simultaneously reveal the foundation or the occasion for the opinion regarding the pre-existence of antemundane matter. Namely, because whatever they said of the Gods besides the supreme God—whom they called one, good, <term>ἀνουσίαον</term> <gloss>without substance/essence</gloss> and not endowed with essence—such as the stars, demons, or indeed even the mind itself and the Soul of the World, were entities produced by the supreme God, they believed that these freshly produced Gods accepted the matter from which they fashioned the sublunary bodies as already prepared and existing. They could not help but posit eternal matter, because before the time that began, as soon as the mundane bodies had been produced, there was mere eternity.

§. XVII. That Aristophanes says Night laid the first wind-egg does not hinder the truth at all, and it shows only that he did not sufficiently grasp the Mosaic doctrine, nor could he attain to the incubation or fostering of Divine Love: therefore, he adorned the sentiment according to the capacity of his own intellect. So that this single difficulty cannot by any means prevent us from subscribing to the opinion, leaving aside Burnet's archaeology, that has been sufficiently demonstrated by Hugo Grotius, Edmund Dickinson, Jacob Tollius, and Adam Tribbechovius.
