### XL.

And a pact is considered either in itself, or insofar as it is confirmed by law, or is added immediately to a contract.

### XLI.

The former is called a bare <term>pactum</term> <gloss>pact</gloss>, but the latter are not called bare; since they do not stop at the bare terms of a pact, but either adhere to a contract or have the support of the law, it is evident to everyone that they cannot be held in the class of bare pacts. *Bachovius in notes to the Disputations of Treutler.*

### XLII.

And these also can be called "clothed" <note>meaning supported or evidenced by something other than mere words</note> without inconsistency; for although these words do not exist in the Law, it can hardly be denied that the thing itself exists; but where the matter is certain, we ought to be easy regarding the words, by the argument of *law 17, Digest on laws*.

### XLIII.

A bare convention is that which remains within the boundaries of a simple agreement. *Law "if to you" 27, Code on letting and hiring*; or, what is the same thing, that which consists within the pure and simple limits of a convention.

### XLIV.

It is called so because it is bare of a cause or business, *the aforementioned law "they are accustomed" 15, Digest on prescribed words*, which also formally distinguishes this convention from a contract, whence it is also called a simple convention in *law "grandmother" 6, Code on the law of dowries*, and merely a pact in *law "greater" 23, Code on pledges and mortgages*.

### XLV.

For example, if it is agreed that you should sell your house to me, this convention rests upon the bare terms of the agreement; but if it is agreed regarding the thing and the price, no longer is this convention...

<summary>This page defines the distinction between "bare" pacts, which consist only of simple agreements, and "clothed" pacts, which are supported by contracts or legal provisions.</summary>
<keywords>Pact, convention, bare pact, clothed pact, Bachovius, Treutler, law</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="11">
...called a bare convention, because a transaction has been added which produces a civil obligation, and a contract has been concluded, which is called buying and selling, in the beginning of the law on buying and selling, and law "agreed pacts" 72, in the beginning of the Digest on contracting a sale.

### XLVI.
Thus, if I make a pact with you that you lend me money, or exchange your Cornelian estate with my house, up to this point, besides a bare convention and a bare agreement, nothing has been done. But as soon as you count out the money to me, or deliver the Cornelian estate to me, or I deliver my house to you, a transaction intervenes beyond the convention, and in that case a loan has been contracted, in the beginning of the law on the ways an obligation is contracted by a thing; this, however, is an exchange, law "natural" 5, § 1, Digest on prescribed words.

### XLVII.
It is questioned whether the name of "pact," when stated simply, signifies a bare pact? I affirm this through the law of nations 7, § 5, Digest on pacts. Those holding the contrary view are moved by the aforementioned law "by traditions" 20, there, "not by bare pacts," Code on pacts. But Hunnius satisfies these points in his resolutions to Treutler, Disputation 9, question 5.

### XLVIII.
A bare pact, moreover, is either express or tacit, which is understood from the actions of the contracting parties, and is said to be entered into by the thing itself in law 2, Digest on pacts; law 32, Digest on partnership. We have one example of this in law 2, § 1, Digest on pacts: one who returns a bond to a debtor is understood to have tacitly agreed not to sue. Another example is in law 3, Digest on the said title, where one who returns a pledge is believed to have remitted the right of the pledge, not the debt itself.

<summary>This page clarifies the transition from a simple agreement to a formal contract and distinguishes between express and tacit bare pacts through legal examples.</summary>
<keywords>Contract, buying and selling, loan, exchange, tacit pact, express pact, Hunnius, debt</keywords>
</translation>

so that the matter is narrated in such a way that it appears the scourges were inflicted upon Christ by the person of Pilate himself, not by his soldiers, since they are only mentioned later in verse 2. Blessed Gerhard indicates that Bede clung to this opinion because he adhered too strictly to the letter. But who, nevertheless, would so easily believe that such a great man, established in such dignity and authority among both the Romans and the Jews, would have so lowered himself as to perform this duty, which was as if appropriate to be dispatched by soldiers and lictors? It is much more probable that this butchery was carried out primarily by those who were most sent and designated by Pilate to execute it. However, the scourging is imputed here to Pilate himself, the Governor of Judea, as the principal moral cause, because the whole affair was conducted by his order and command. It is therefore not absurd, but very appropriate, to explain the words of the Evangelists in this way. For is it not the case, according to the common canon, that what one does through another or others is to be considered and said to have been done by oneself?

XXVII. Furthermore, in investigating the ministerial cause, we judge it not irrelevant to ask, who and what kind of persons were especially admitted to scourge JESUS? If we look here at the more corrected Greek codices, we do not find mention of them made separately in the text regarding this; however, we gather not poorly from the words, both preceding and following, that the Roman soldiers and lictors—by some called *Brutiani* or *Brutii*—and those gentiles, were the principal actors in this tragedy. For the little word, *Eis* <gloss>to them</gloss>, which looks toward the Jews and is read in certain copies after the word, *handed over* <note>original: "tradidit"</note>, is not genuine: hence, as Erasmus notes, it detracts somewhat from the meaning.
<margin>
annot. in c. 27. Matth.
</margin>
For (he adds) Pilate did not hand JESUS over to the Jews, but to his own soldiers, the ministers of punishment. For these are indeed the same who had captured Christ earlier, bound him when captured, placed him in judgment when bound, scourged him when placed, clothed him in purple when scourged, crowned him when clothed, mocked him when crowned, struck him when mocked, led him away when struck, and crucified him when led away: just as we see this inculcated not once, but more often, in the history of the entire passion.

XXVIII. But perhaps a doubt could arise for someone, whether the Jews lent their own helping hands to the heathens in this business? hatred against CHRIST, this punishment seemed too *lenient*, if it were inflicted by his own people upon this JESUS, a *seducer* as they blasphemed. Nor did they intend the scourging for its own sake, but *only* demanded the crucifixion. Wherefore, not content with that punishment inflicted by Pilate, they shouted that Christ also be punished with the cross, nor did they cease to shout until they obtained that which they so greatly sought by the very fact itself. Namely, they did not want *life*, they wanted *death*, and that to be paid for by the cross: which capital punishment, however, they were not permitted to exercise, even though the *Romans exercised the same among the Jews at their pleasure*. So restricted was the power of the Jews under the Romans at that time. Indeed, perhaps it was for this reason too that the Jews refused to offer themselves as partners to the Romans in scourging Christ, because they thought anyone of their own would be defiled if he should merely enter the praetorium, with the Passover imminent, and so much more therefore if he should become an accomplice in the same punishments. are marked by this character, so it happens especially to the muscles of the thorax, so that they can no longer elevate the ribs; thus the equilibrium between the pressing air and our body is necessarily removed, whence difficulty of breathing arises, with which anxiety of the precordium walks in equal step.

> *Often the sick do not dare to speak, or indeed are barely able, which must be deduced from the vehemence of the pains, or from the paralytic state of the organs dedicated to speech.*

> *Fever is present insofar as the circulation of the humors, on account of the languid nerves and the abundance of morbific matter, does not succeed according to desire; hence it happens that they conceive a fermentation or intestinal motion.*

The *Inaugural Dissertation on Malignant Fever* by the most illustrious Licentiate, J. C. WOLFF of Servest, formerly my sweetest companion, held at Wittenberg under the most excellent Doctor BERGER, Public Professor and venerable teacher there, will shed light on this opinion.

For a milder degree of fermentation, however, the patient does not feel those discomforts. 

A proclivity toward sleep is also an effect of the viscosity, thickness, and shortage of animal spirits and other liquids, or even of compression of the brain. Yet somnolence is not an inseparable attribute of <term>Hemicrania</term>, as the previously praised Piso seems to hint. But excessive vigils otherwise urge, and that on account of the atrocity of the pains. A cold sweat occurs, insofar as the glandular context and tone on the surface of the body is too relaxed, whence an easy exit for the serum is open by any given gate; and it is cold where the humors, and especially the blood, pass through the small canals so slowly that they cannot produce that agitation which represents heat to the mind, then on account of the solid parts, among which the heart holds primacy, relaxing from a constrictive motion. With the nervous genus corrupted, and the humors also corrupted, what good shall we hope for from the stomach? XVII. If one denies that "being as being" is the object of Metaphysics because all things treated in this discipline—such as first principles, axioms, hypotheses, first definitions, and the doctrine of primary substance with its operations and attributes—cannot be reduced to it, then one must also deny that a natural body as such is the object of Physics, because not all things treated in Physics are natural bodies; for example: matter, form, nature, place, time, quantity, quality, sound, sight, and so forth. Although, in truth, not all things belong to any discipline that this or that person claims.

XVIII. Whoever said that one who wishes to use abstractions in philosophical disciplines other than Mathematics abstracts the mind from truth—because things must be known as they are found in nature, not as they are accustomed to be or can be abstracted from them—was either playing with ambiguity or did not understand abstraction.

XIX. There is great debate among the ancients whether virtue can be taught, with some affirming it is given by nature to the good and denied to the bad, while others hold it is acquired through use and instruction. Plato seems at times to side with the former, at times with the latter. There is no doubt, however, that both a nature not in itself depraved, and precepts, and exercise, institute and perfect virtue. The ancients called these <term>physin, logon kai askesin</term> <gloss>nature, reason, and practice</gloss>: these are as necessary for virtue as they are for the arts, and even for crops, which require rich soil, good seeds, and the farmer's diligence. Ludovicus Vives, <note>on chapter 1, book 19 of The City of God, column 1141; add Augustine, in the said book, chapter 4, column 1148</note>; the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> throughout; Plutarch, the treatise <term>Ei didakton he arete</term> <gloss>Whether Virtue can be Taught</gloss>, page 370.

XX. All men always desire the good: Plato in <term>Hipparchus</term>. For all good things are useful: the same in <term>Meno</term>.

XXI. Poverty is the sister of a good mind, according to Petronius in the <term>Satyricon</term>, page 94; it seems preferable to riches, for it teaches all arts wherever it touches one, says Plautus in <term>Stichus</term>. Add Seneca, epistle 15, and Theocritus. For usually Necessity and Sobriety accompany it, and it makes men attentive and circumspect, whereas second fortune and opulence beget negligence. Hence, the intellect is sharpened, from which the arts arise. Indeed, as Apuleius says, it has never puffed anyone up with pride, never corrupted anyone with impotence, never brutalized anyone with tyranny; it neither desires nor can tolerate the delicacies of the belly and the groin. Indeed, these and other vices are usually the foster-children of riches. And although we read that even very poor men have committed the greatest crimes, many were not poor, but beggars. Aristophanes provides this distinction in <term>Plutus</term>, page 11:

> For the life of a beggar, which you describe, is to live having nothing,
> but that of the poor man is to live sparingly and be attentive to his work,
> so that nothing remains for him, yet he is not in want.</translation>

<translation page="13">### XXII. Hesiod teaches in these verses that the care of human affairs lies with the Spirits, by the permission of the Supreme Commander:

> And these are the noble spirits upon the earth,
> holy, the protectors of mortal men,
> who guard justice and wicked deeds,
> clothed in mist, walking everywhere upon the earth.

It is therefore probable that some of the Spirits, as it were Legates or Tribunes, take care of peoples and regions; Theodoret teaches that these are Archangels <note>see Theodoret on Daniel, chapter 10; cited by Besold</note>. Certainly, what makes it credible that Saint Michael presides over my Poland is that, before the victory against the Lithuanians, which was obtained without a single Pole being killed, he was seen in Poland, as histories testify; hence, a Basilica was eventually built to him in Lublin. What of the fact that this vast kingdom stretches toward the North, and from there, according to the dictum of Scripture, comes evil? That is, the greatest part of the <term>Alastores</term> <gloss>avenging spirits/demons</gloss> are stabled there. Hence Nicephorus Gregoras writes, in his scholia on Synesius, <term>De insomniis</term> <gloss>On Dreams</gloss>, page 383, that the Chaldeans considered Orcus <note>the underworld</note> to be the prince of the furthest and adjacent earthly inheritance, which fell to him by lot: <term>tes eschates kai perigeiou lexeos archegon</term> <gloss>the leader of the outermost and earthly portion</gloss>.

### XXIII. Among men, he who has been raised by the gift of fortune to opulence, and elevated to the changeable throne of a kingdom and a pendulum tribunal, rarely appears, and lives with his judges far removed in certain inner chambers of his dignity, says Apuleius in <term>De Deo Socratis</term> <gloss>On the God of Socrates</gloss>.

And that among the Persians the person of the King was hidden under the guise of Majesty, Justin is the witness, book 1, page 10, and Herodotus <note>Clio</note>. This custom they seem to have received from the Chaldeans; for among them Ninus, the son of Semiramis, content with the Empire elaborated by his parents, laid aside the studies of war, and, as if he had changed his sex with his mother, was rarely seen by men and grew old in a crowd of women. His descendants also followed that example and gave answers to the nations through intermediaries; Justin, in the said place, page 4. They themselves indulged only in the pleasures of the body, and especially those which are more immersed in matter than others, which the senses of touch and taste provide, and they led a life not unlike that of a sea squirt. More correctly, Leo the Emperor, <term>Tactica</term>, chapter 16, section 21, page 245, says: "Those who are procrastinating and unapproachable, and order their servants to push away those who approach in such a way, rightly fail in many and great matters." Nor is there any reason why Apuleius, in the said place, should say that familiarity breeds contempt, and that rarity itself confers admiration. Let us hear Synesius, in his oration <term>De Regno</term> <gloss>On Kingship</gloss>, page 20, arguing thus, as Petavius translates: "No one has ever looked down upon the sun, even though what is it that is seen more frequently?" Therefore, if a King wishes to be true, and to be unable to be otherwise...</translation>

<summary>The text discusses the method of philosophical disciplines, the nature of virtue, the distinction between poverty and beggary, the role of spirits in human governance, and the proper conduct of rulers in relation to their accessibility.</summary>
<keywords>Metaphysics, Physics, Virtue, Poverty, Spirits, Archangels, Kingship, Political Philosophy</keywords>

<translation page="14">

### XXX.

It is no objection that in this life the Church is exposed to immense afflictions, is disfigured by many scandals, and remains weak, bearing many signs of guilt. For this reason, it has need of constant prayer, as witnessed by Psalm 32, verse 6, and as is stated in the Lord’s Prayer in Matthew 6, verse 12: "Forgive us our debts." For it is adorned with the remission of sins, with the Son of God sanctifying Himself for it (John 17, verse 19). He covers its remaining filth with His own merit, applies His righteousness to it, and gives it the Holy Spirit, who kindles new light and life in the hearts of the faithful. This adornment is that golden garment in which, according to Psalm 45, verse 10, the queen stands at the right hand of this King; and the same Psalm affirms, in verse 14, that this glory is internal and is not perceived by human eyes.

### XXXI.

Other members, however, are called rotten and dead; they are withered and sterile trees (Ezekiel 20, verse 47), a <term>συκῆ ἄκαρπος</term> <gloss>fruitless fig tree</gloss> having nothing <term>εἰ μὴ φύλλα μόνον</term> <gloss>except leaves only</gloss> (Matthew 21, verse 19). They are the foolish virgins who, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them (Matthew 25, verse 2); they are <term>Zizania</term> <gloss>tares/weeds</gloss>, and children and seed of the Devil (Matthew 13, verse 38; Genesis 3, verse 15). They are clearly men who are neither reborn nor holy, even if they agree regarding the fundamental doctrine. For they live without repentance and faith, and they are not vivified and governed by the Spirit of Christ, even if they move within the external society of the pious. Yet, who would call those in whom Christ does nothing but dead members of Christ and the Church?

### XXXII.

But if they are not only secure hypocrites, but also dissent from the foundation and doctrine of truth, and become either defenders or approvers of false doctrine that overturns the foundation, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3, verse 5), and if they stubbornly persist in those manifest errors—which the true Church condemns by judgment according to the norm of the Prophetic and Apostolic writings—then we assert that they are not to be held even as dead members, but as <term>ἀναθέμασι</term> <gloss>anathemas/accursed things</gloss> and blasphemers, and that they are outside the Church, even if they dare to arrogate to themselves the title and name of the Church, which indeed the <term>Pontificij</term> <gloss>Papists/Roman Catholics</gloss> busily do. Because it is written, Galatians 1, verses 8 and 9: "If anyone preaches another Gospel, let him be <term>ἀναθέμα ἔστω</term> <gloss>accursed</gloss>."</translation>

<translation page="15">and blasphemers, and we assert that they are outside the Church, even if they dare to arrogate to themselves the title and name of the Church, which indeed the Papists busily do. Because it is written, Galatians 1, verses 8 and 9: "If anyone preaches another Gospel, let him be accursed."

### XXXIII.

That the saints, however, can also have some errors—but not ones that overturn the articles of faith (for some build upon the foundation with gold, silver, and precious stones, others with wood, hay, and straw, as witnessed by Paul in 1 Corinthians 3, verse 12)—is manifest from the example of the Apostles. In them, before and after the resurrection, even though they had witnessed the beginnings of a new and eternal life and the restoration of our nature in the glorified body of Christ, there was such darkness and infirmity that they still dreamed that the kingdom of the Messiah would be political (Acts 1, verse 6), and many wished for the Levitical rites to be retained (Acts 15).

### XXXIIII.

And too blind and unhappy is the arrogance and <term>φιλαυτία</term> <gloss>self-love</gloss>, from which many suffer, if we think there is no infirmity in us, that we are ignorant of nothing, but that we are perfect and omniscient. For it is very true what Paul says, 1 Corinthians 13, verse 9: "We know in part, and we prophesy in part." And verse 12: "Now we see through a glass, and in a dark saying."

### XXXV.

But the pious, and those who are teachable, when admonished, return to the way. It is certain that the Apostles eventually abandoned their dreams about a bodily kingdom of the Messiah and the necessity of circumcision and other Levitical rites, having received the Holy Spirit, whom they did not contradict—as the stubborn Jews did—against their conscience and so many and such great testimonies of the truth.

### XXXVI.

Nor, indeed, do we dream of a certain Platonic Idea or city regarding the Church that differs from the way mentioned above, existing nowhere on earth and consisting only in the imagination of the mind, nor do we believe it wanders in the darkness like <term>Andabatae</term> <gloss>blindfolded gladiators</gloss>.</translation>

<summary>This text defines the nature of the Church, distinguishing between its internal holiness and external frailty, while condemning those who openly subvert foundational doctrine as being outside the Church. It further acknowledges that even true believers may hold erroneous views, provided they are teachable and do not reject the foundational articles of faith.</summary>

That the saints, however, can also have some errors—but not ones that overturn the articles of faith (for some build upon the foundation with gold, silver, and precious stones, others with wood, hay, and straw, as witnessed by Paul in 1 Corinthians 3, verse 12)—is manifest from the example of the Apostles. In them, before and after the resurrection, even though they had witnessed the beginnings of a new and eternal life and the restoration of our nature in the glorified body of Christ, there was such darkness and infirmity that they still dreamed that the kingdom of the Messiah would be political (Acts 1, verse 6), and many wished for the Levitical rites to be retained (Acts 15).

### XXXIIII.

And too blind and unhappy is the arrogance and <term>φιλαυτία</term> <gloss>self-love</gloss>, from which many suffer, if we think there is no infirmity in us, that we are ignorant of nothing, but that we are perfect and omniscient. For it is very true what Paul says, 1 Corinthians 13, verse 9: "We know in part, and we prophesy in part." And verse 12: "Now we see through a glass, and in a dark saying."

### XXXV.

But the pious, and those who are teachable, when admonished, return to the way. It is certain that the Apostles eventually abandoned their dreams about a bodily kingdom of the Messiah and the necessity of circumcision and other Levitical rites, having received the Holy Spirit, whom they did not contradict—as the stubborn Jews did—against their conscience and so many and such great testimonies of the truth.

### XXXVI.

Nor, indeed, do we dream of a certain Platonic Idea or city regarding the Church that differs from the way mentioned above, existing nowhere on earth and consisting only in the imagination of the mind, nor do we believe it wanders in the darkness like <term>Andabatae</term> <gloss>blindfolded gladiators</gloss>.

## Q. III.

### *Does quantitative number apply to Intelligences?*

The substances that theologians call Angels, metaphysicians name Intelligences. The point of controversy here is: can quantitative number be attributed to them? We stand firmly on the negative side, using this shield: where there is no quantity, there is no quantitative number. There is no quantity in Intelligences. Therefore. Do you doubt the minor premise? You do well: for always to doubt is always to inquire into a greater truth. But are you attacking it? Attack it, provided you do not overcome it. For does quantity not apply solely to material and corporeal things? Do you deny this? You are striking against philosophical principles; you are rising up against Aristotle himself; against truth itself. Look at the species of quantity: there is continuous quantity, whose parts are joined by some common boundary; and conversely, there is discrete quantity, whose parts are neither joined nor fitted together by any such boundary, as Aristotle states in his Categories, regarding quantity. Where, I ask, are there any parts in Intelligences? If they existed, they would surely make the very substance of the Angels either partible or divisible; the Intelligences themselves would have an extension of parts; they would consist of a body; they would participate in matter along with form—all of which are absurd. I add this as well: quantitative number is listed among the common sensibles, as Aristotle says in his work On the Soul, book 2, chapter 6, section 64. If, therefore, Intelligences are sensible, they must be perceived by the senses. Otherwise, if the object that falls under the sense is removed, the sense must necessarily be removed as well. But sensation exists only in a body, and revolves around bodies, as Aristotle says in his Categories, regarding quantity. Now, who has ever called angels bodies</translation>

### §. 22.

Regarding surgery, there is nothing that benefits those with hectic fever. Indeed, bloodletting and purging are equally harmful in all diseases of depletion, such as the hectic state, with which <term>Forestus</term> <gloss>Pieter van Foreest, a Dutch physician</gloss> agrees; in *Book 4, Observation*, he reports that he noted a noble matron with hectic fever who, having been bled by an empiric, died shortly thereafter. Another person held by hectic fever, having disregarded the interdictions of <term>Forestus</term> at the persuasion of a surgeon and a charlatan, also admitted to bloodletting, and on the following day, having taken one pill made of <term>precipitate</term> <gloss>a mercurial compound</gloss> from a quack, perished on that same day.

### §. 23.

In pharmacy, many praise metallic medicines, asserting that, as they are more noble, they restore almost every sick person to health, let alone one with hectic fever. But concerning what <term>Sennertus</term> <gloss>Daniel Sennert, a German physician</gloss> affirms in *On the Agreement and Disagreement of Chemists, Chapter 18, On Spirit of Salt*, <term>Salt</term>, and similar substances which can be exhibited more safely than metallic ones; that they can cause the greatest harm when used too frequently, while they consume the natural moisture by drying it out, and therefore their use must be cautious in dry bodies (such are the bodies of those with hectic fever)—this can be said with better right regarding the metallic substances with which many boast they have cured hectic patients, and which are everywhere in daily use. On the same foundation, <term>Bravo de Sobremonte</term> <gloss>Gaspar Bravo de Sobremonte, a Spanish physician</gloss>, in his *Medical Resolutions*, fol. Med., disapproves of the rashness of <term>Paracelsus</term>, who in every fever, and thus also in hectic fever, uses a single diaphoretic: this is against the indication that demands nutrition, not a violent dissipation of moisture. Nor can he help but find fault with <term>Helmont</term> <gloss>Jan Baptist van Helmont, a Belgian physician</gloss> for using the same diaphoretic</translation>

<translation page="15">of <term>Paracelsus</term>, seeing that it is drying and heating, and consumes the vital forces no less than the hectic fever itself; although he sanctimoniously affirms in his book on fevers that it performs its effects insensibly and without sweat, and that it cures the hectic patient within the course of a moon.

### §. 24.

<term>Poterius</term> <gloss>Pierre Potier, a French physician</gloss> also presses his thumb on this when he testifies from his own experience in *Book 2 on Fevers, Chapter 25*, that he cured a fifty-year-old man suffering from a slow fever of the hectic type for four years with <term>Magnetic Sugar</term> <gloss>a specific medicinal preparation of the period</gloss>. He restored another of the same ilk to health within a month, given twice a day his <term>antihectic</term> <gloss>fever-preventing</gloss> medicine in a conserve of roses. <term>P. J. Faber</term> joins him in asserting the same utility of metallic substances for hectic patients, who, in his *Curation of Various Diseases, Curation 14*, recounts a desperate case of hectic fever cured by the use of <term>Spirit of Acid Salt</term> and <term>Tincture of Gold</term> extracted with rectified <term>Oil of Salt</term>. I also know those for whom dried salt is in use for essentially moistening the wasting body of hectic patients. Others praise the <term>Balsam of Life</term>, as they call it, which they prepare thus: They take two ounces of salt and a half-ounce of the purest gold. They melt, pulverize, and extract it with <term>Spirit of Salt</term>, and distill it to the consistency of an oil. They instill this into one dram of pulverized <term>Pearl Salt</term>. Mix in a marble mortar, dry over a slow fire, and regenerate gradually until it acquires a purple color. They exhibit from five to ten grains in a restorative broth quite often. From this, they hope that the essential moisture consumed by the hectic heat will be restored, as if by a substance essentially moistening.

### §. 25.

But may a physician who walks on both legs of experience and reason be far from using drying agents in place of those that essentially moisten, as is indicated by hectic fever. For although hectic patients cured in that manner have often seemed to become somewhat fatter and entirely free from the disease, the unhappy outcome not infrequently revealed, and not long after, what the root of that cure was: namely, that the spirits having been rendered more fixed, the remaining serous and excrementitious moisture, intercepted by said drying and fixation from the regime of nature due to the service of the spirits, is left behind, putrefies, and thus, from a simple hectic fever, it becomes joined with a putrid one. We embrace the healthier opinion on curing hectic fever as much as possible, together with <term>Sennertus</term>. Indeed, he says in *On the Agreement and Disagreement of Chemists, Chapter 18, page 324*: "There are diseases in which one benefits more from nutrition than from medicine: such is hectic fever."</translation>

They melt, pulverize, and extract it with <term>Spirit of Salt</term>, and distill it to the consistency of an oil. They instill this into one dram of pulverized <term>Pearl Salt</term>. Mix in a marble mortar, dry over a slow fire, and regenerate gradually until it acquires a purple color. They exhibit from five to ten grains in a restorative broth quite often. From this, they hope that the essential moisture consumed by the hectic heat will be restored, as if by a substance essentially moistening.

### §. 25.

But may a physician who walks on both legs of experience and reason be far from using drying agents in place of those that essentially moisten, as is indicated by hectic fever. For although hectic patients cured in that manner have often seemed to become somewhat fatter and entirely free from the disease, the unhappy outcome not infrequently revealed, and not long after, what the root of that cure was: namely, that the spirits having been rendered more fixed, the remaining serous and excrementitious moisture, intercepted by said drying and fixation from the regime of nature due to the service of the spirits, is left behind, putrefies, and thus, from a simple hectic fever, it becomes joined with a putrid one. We embrace the healthier opinion on curing hectic fever as much as possible, together with <term>Sennertus</term>. Indeed, he says in *On the Agreement and Disagreement of Chemists, Chapter 18, page 324*: "There are diseases in which one benefits more from nutrition than from medicine: such is hectic fever."

### XXVII.

However, since the primary mention by us concerns that loss of the Fief which deprives the Vassal, it is not inconvenient to add here that there are some cases in which the Vassal does not lose the fief, even if the loyalty which binds both, Vassal and Lord, is not present or rendered.

### XXX.

For instance, if the lord of the fief is excommunicated, banished, a condemned heretic, guilty of lèse-majesté <note>original: "laesae Maiestatis"</note>, etc.

### XXXI.

### XXXII.

With fiefs lost for various reasons, the question is: Do fiefs always and indiscriminately open to the Lord, or, depending on the variety of the causes, sometimes to the lord, and sometimes to others? This is the more truthful view.

### XXXIII.

It is asked: is the faculty of renouncing a fief free, or must it depend upon the consent of the lord? The latter seems improper, for it is permitted to renounce gains.

### XXXIIII.

Therefore, once the fief is renounced, in the case where it is new, it reverts to the Lord, notwithstanding that loss may occur to his children. In the case, however, where it is paternal or ancient, it devolves to the male children, or to the agnates <note>paternal relatives</note> if those are lacking.

### XXXV.

A brother renouncing a fief in favor of a brother, to whom it is subsequently assigned, and who dies without heirs, is not excluded from the fief.</translation>

Likewise: *To those for whom the bowels are disturbed around the beginning, but urine is scanty, in the progress of time the bowels are indeed dried out, but thin urine abounds, for these, abscesses at the joints occur,* as the same observes in <term>Coan Prenotions 619</term>. *By diarrhea: If,* says Hippocrates again in the <term>Coan Prenotions</term>, *for one drinking with difficulty with a cough-inducing breath, there is a belch that brings back and revolves; it denounces labor of the lungs.* He writes in <term>Coan 142</term>: *To those for whom there are belches, flatulence, sound of the belly with inflation, for them the bowels are disturbed.* *By vomit*, it happens to those whom stomach disgusts vex, with biting of the mouth of the stomach and frequent spitting, <term>Coan 142</term>. Galen, <term>On Crises 3, chapter 11</term>, calls vomiting a sign of crisis when the lower lip is agitated. When the solution happens through other excretions, for example through the flow of hemorrhoids or menses, or through several at once, those too are manifested by their own signs, which can be seen in the works of Practitioners.

### XVII. I return to the Definition, the last words of which are: *which arises either from bile alone, or from other humors putrefying together in the larger vessels.* By which the difference of the <term>Causus</term> <gloss>burning fever</gloss> is partly expressed: For by reason of the cause, one burning fever is from bile alone, which suddenly tends toward the state with the vehemence of all symptoms, and is otherwise called *exquisite* or *legitimate*. Another is from other humors mixed together at the same time, and is called *bastard*. Bile, however, can be mixed and putrefy at the same time with *phlegm*, whence a *phlegmatic burning fever* arises, which has very mild symptoms, moves more slowly to the state, and sometimes worsens toward evening: Or with *melancholy*, and then the signs of melancholy are present: Or with *blood*, as <term>Galen</term> seems to hint in <term>Commentary 4 on Aphorism 59, when he teaches that burning fevers have yellow bile redundant in the veins together with blood;</term> and these fevers, by reason of the preeminence of the putrefying humor, are sometimes called <term>συνοχοὶ καυσώδεις</term> <gloss>continuous burning fevers</gloss>, sometimes <term>καύσοι συνεχεῖς</term> <gloss>continuous burning fevers</gloss>. Or if *Scorbutic Serum* <gloss>scurvy-related fluid</gloss> is present, a scorbutic burning fever arises. Malignity not rarely supervenes upon all these differences.

From the Natural, the *hot and dry Temperament* is accused. <term>ἡ ἐτοιμοτάτη μὲν δυσκρασία</term> <gloss>the most ready dyscrasia</gloss>, says <term>Galen</term> in <term>8. II. Memory is not of the future or the present, but of the past: because hope or opinion concerns the future; sense perception concerns the present: but memory concerns a past act, which is neither sense perception nor opinion.

<margin>Corollary: Supposition</margin>

VI. Memory is a state of the primary sensitive faculty. He proves this because its task is to know time; therefore its task is to remember: for sense perception knows time and magnitude by movement. Hence, he admits that memory belongs to the intellect only by accident, insofar as it receives a mental image from the sense.
VII. The statements are proven; because even those who do not understand, such as brute animals, remember.
VIII. Not all animals have memory.
IX. Although the species <gloss>the mental representative form</gloss> of a thing may be present, memory does not concern the species, but the absent thing. He proves this first because those who are in great agitation, like the drunk or the sick, do not remember, because the species are obstructed. 2. Children do not remember, because the species are obstructed due to their fluidity. 3. The elderly do not remember well, because due to excessive dryness, they do not receive species well. 4. Because those who understand quickly retain and remember poorly.
X. Memory is not of that species: because then it would be of the present.
XI. It seems that memory is of the present: because memory belongs to the sense, and sense perception is of the present. 2. Because the species is in the imagination as a painting is on a wall: and a painting is present to the one who sees it. 3. If the common sense can be of an absent thing, then so can the exterior sense.
XII. He solves the aforementioned; because although the species as a certain thing is present in a subject, nevertheless, as it is representative of another thing, it is thus of an absent thing: it extends itself in the manner of representing the different species as in the text.
XIII. Memory is increased and preserved through frequent meditation: for the soul becomes more capable if it remembers many times.

### Second part: On recollection
XIV. Recollection is not memory, nor is it sensing or understanding something anew: this is proven because memory does not occur when one understands or senses something anew; therefore neither does recollection. The antecedent is clear because memory requires an interruption of past time, and thus memory presupposes a prior act or habit. But it differs from memory because in recollection, oblivion intervenes.

XV. To remember or to recollect is not to know something repeatedly: but to know that one had known or seen this before.
XVI. The mode of recollecting occurs through the fact that just as one movement of the soul follows another, so it apprehends one thing after another. And thus, when we recollect, we move from one act to another by meditating through similarity or contrast.
XVII. Why do we sometimes recollect easily after a long time, and not what happened yesterday or the day before? He replies that this is because recollection occurs through some apprehension that is useful for apprehending.
XVIII. First corollary: we recollect from that principle from which what is to be recollected began. Second corollary: we recollect well-ordered things more easily than disordered ones.
XIX. Why can someone wanting to recollect sometimes not do so, and then, without looking, recollect spontaneously? He replies that the one who is searching has many apprehensions that are not useful for that recollection, and then, spontaneously, an apprehension comes that is useful for apprehending.
XX. He who wishes to recollect should think of the places in which he has been.
XXI. The best mode of recollecting is through division: such as "that week I was there," dividing by days so that I may easily find what I did from one to another.
XXII. Why do those who have the principle of recollection not recollect? He replies that this principle is indifferent to many things.
XXIII. Why do we sometimes recollect defectively? It is replied that just as it happens in natural things, so it also happens in those of the will.
XXIV. Time contributes to recollecting, such that one knows that past time is past. Nevertheless, both memory and recollection occur without certain time, although things are understood in proportion to time.
XXV. It happens that one errs in recollection, and this is on the part of the thing and on the part of time.

## APHORISM III.

### I. EXPOSITION.

1. Since human language stammers when dealing with matters removed from the senses, let a certain kind of description of the Angels—those most blessed minds removed as far as possible from the senses—suffice for us, namely the one our aphorism has just provided.

We intend these predicates to be understood with restriction and in their own kind, not absolutely. XIX. Since, however, it is the duty of supreme powers to preserve the true worship of God and to protect the people under the true religion, and since this protection cannot often be provided without the help of arms, those who rule can hardly be without the praise of fortitude. *A Republic ought to be fortified and adorned not only with religion and justice but also with arms and military discipline*, according to Isaias Pontanus in *The Flowers*, ch. 3. Consequently, a Queen, sufficiently protected by the shield of saving religion, must also be equipped with arms; if the aforementioned religion is defended by their use, the assaults of enemies are repelled, and stronger foes are driven away from the inferiors, these are not improperly called pious arms. *And this fortitude, which protects the fatherland from barbarians through war, or defends the weak, or protects allies from brigands, is full justice.* Ambrose, *On Duties*.

XX. Women who are not broken by the fortune of war, and who are magnanimous even in conflict, are praised everywhere. Tomyris, having gathered her forces, fought with Cyrus in such a way that this battle is said to have been the fiercest of all among the barbarians; Herodotus, book 1. The wonderful eagerness of her, Semiramis, to engage the enemy hand to hand appears from the words of Valerius Maximus, book 9, ch. 3.

The Argive women, by bravely repelling them, warded off the Spartan kings Cleomenes

And not without reason, for she performed great deeds, worthy of envy and scarcely to be emulated even by men and the strongest of emperors. The wonderful eagerness of her, Semiramis, to engage the enemy hand to hand appears from the words of Valerius Maximus, book 9, ch. 3.

<translation page="196">
<header>CAPVT III.</header>

He uses an argument from similarity. He took the simile from Moses, Numbers 21, regarding the bronze serpent, which, when lifted up at the command of the Lord, saved those looking upon it from the bites of the fiery serpents.

<margin>Nume. 21. 8.9</margin>

The application is added by the Lord Christ himself, which shows how the members correspond to the members. The <term>antitypa</term> <gloss>antitypes</gloss> here are Christ and the serpent; the exaltation and death of Christ; looking at the serpent and firmly grasping Christ by faith. The bites of the serpents and the power of sin; this temporal life and eternal salvation. A neat and timely allegory is taken from this. 

<margin>Antitypa</margin>
<margin>Allegoria</margin>

First, the bronze serpent was instituted by God as the author, when matters were desperate among the Israelites: thus Christ was given as mediator when matters were desperate among us. For among men, or even Angels, no one suitable was found. Next, the bronze serpent heals those struck by the serpents: Christ heals those struck by the serpent Satan, himself having become a serpent of the serpent, so to speak, as if one might say the poison of poison. Thirdly, it benefits by sight alone; thus Christ heals us by faith alone. Fourthly, the mystery of the cross is manifest in the exaltation. Things that are lifted up are seen more easily, and are of use to more people. Thus the merit of Christ is proposed in the open to all nations; he who now sanctifying the earth while walking, consecrates while hanging, extending his hands he calls together.
</translation>

<keywords>Communicatio idiomatum, Son of Man, justification, bronze serpent, antitype, allegory, mystery of the cross, faith</keywords>

### CHAPTER IV.
#### Of
# The Division of Nobility
# On the division of the nobility.

§. 1. There is not just one division of nobility. <term>Plato</term> divided it into four species, the first of which is of those who are born of famous, good, and just ancestors. Next, those whose parents had been nobles and princes; he called them by that name. Thirdly, he wished those to be called noble whose ancestors had been celebrated in fame and opinion, and this either from clearly performed military deeds or from the crowns of contests. Finally, he estimated the most excellent genus of nobility to be when someone excelled by his own greatness of soul. Compare <term>Plutarch</term>, book 10, *Against Nobility*.

§. 2. <term>Aristotle</term> distinguishes between the Nobility of the Race and that of the City along with the Private, in book I of the *Rhetoric to Theodectes* <note>original: "Rhetorica ad Theodectem"</note> chapter 5, to the extent that he says that the splendor of the former is for the indigenous and most ancient to be the first and illustrious leaders; many also from that race have emerged as famous in the matters which are sought after. Private nobility, however, is either from men or women and is a legitimate procreation from them.

§. 3. <term>Gregory of Nazianzus</term> makes a triple genus of nobility: one which draws its origin from above, as are all who are created in the image of God; the second, which proceeds from blood; the third is recognized from virtue and vice. Discourse 18; compare discourse 28.

§. 4. <term>Piccolomini</term> says that six degrees of Nobility can be established: (1) He makes the first of divine Nobility. (2) Metaphysical. (3) Inspecting <note>note: likely referring to intellectual or moral oversight</note>. (4) Civil. (5) Physical. (6) Of Fortune. Which, however, he contracts a little later to only four forms, namely to Divine, Moral, and the nobility of nature and fortune. Divine, as he speaks, approaches God most closely; Moral, which he also names the nobility of the mind, consists in the composition of manners and the habit of virtue. Of nature</translation>

<translation page="551"># BOOK TWO.

<margin>Danaus first constructed a ship.</margin>
<margin>Certain things omitted, which do not appear in the text.</margin>
<margin>The daughters of Danaus marry the sons of Aegyptus.</margin>
Aegyptus had fifty sons, and his brother Danaus had an equal number of daughters. When they contended among themselves for the kingdom, Danaus killed the sons of Aegyptus, save for one or two, through the agency of his own daughters. For he had received an oracle that his own death would come from one of them. Struck by fear, and by the counsel of Minerva, he was the first to construct a ship, named by him after the number of his daughters, a <term>pentēkontoros</term> <gloss>fifty-oared ship</gloss>, as one might say. Placing his daughters upon it, he fled. Then, putting in at Rhodes, he dedicated a statue to the Lindian Minerva. From there, he betook himself to Argos, and Helanor, who then reigned in Argos, handed the kingdom over to him. He himself, having taken possession of that region, called the inhabitants Danaans after his own name. But because that region suffered from a lack of water, since Neptune, in his anger, had dried up the springs for Inachus—for he testified that it was the land of Minerva—he sent his daughters out in the meantime to fetch water. One of these, Amymone, while searching for water, cast a weapon at a deer and struck a sleeping Satyr. Therefore, he, awakened from sleep, was seized by a marvelous desire to possess the girl. But at the arrival of Neptune, the Satyr took to flight. Amymone, however, had intercourse with him, and Neptune pointed out the Lernaean springs to her. Furthermore, the sons of Aegyptus, having set out for Argos to compose their mutual enmity, urged themselves on, and begged that the daughters of Danaus be given to them in marriage. Then Danaus, both because he little trusted their promises and because he remembered the injury of his own flight and exile, agreed to the nuptials and began to distribute the girls by lot. Therefore, he selected Hypermnestra, the eldest of his daughters, for Lynceus, and Gorgophone for Proteus. For Aegyptus had fathered these from his wife, Queen Argyphia. From there, each obtained their own by lot.</translation>

<translation page="552">Bufiris, Enceladus, Lycus, and Daiphro took Automate, Amymone, Agave, and Scaea, who were born to Danaus from the royal matron Europa, as wives. But Gorgophone and Hypermnestra were born from Elephantis, yet Lynceus obtained Calyce by lot. Ister took Hippodamia, Chalcodon took Rhodia, Agenor took Cleopatra, Chaetus took Asteria, Diacorytes took Hippodamia, Alcis took Glauce, Alcmenon took Hippomedusa, Hippothous took Gorge, Euchenor took Iphimedusa, and Hippolytus took Rhode. These ten were begotten from the Arabian wife. But the girls born from the Hamadryad nymphs, others from the Atlantean, and others from Phoebe, were wedded as follows: Pirene to Agaptolemus, Dorion to Cerceftis, Pharte to Eurydamas, Mnestra to Aegius, Argio to Euhippe, Archelao to Anexibia, and Nelo to Menachus. These seven were born from the Phoenician wife. But the girls who were Ethiopians, because they were namesakes to Memphis, were by no means willing to be joined to them by lot. For Clitus, born from the Tyrian mother, married Clite; Sthenelus married Sthenele; and Chrysippus married Chrysippe. And from Caliade, a Naiad nymph, twelve sons were born, along with twelve daughters of the Naiad Polyron. These are their names: Eurylochus, Phantes, Peristhenes, Hermus, Dryas, Potamon, Cilleus, Lixus, Imbrus, Bromius, Polyctor, and Chthonius. These others were born from the nymph Autonoe: Theano, Electra, Cleopatra, Eurydice, Glaucippe, Anthelea, Cleodora, Euippe, Erato, Stygne, and Bryce. Those who were born to Aegyptus from the Gorgons took as their wives those who were born from Pieria. For to Periphant fell Actaea, to Oeneus fell Podarce, to Aegyptus fell Dioxippe, to Menalce fell Adyte, to Lampo fell Ocypete, and to Idmon fell Pylarge. There are, however, eight more recent ones: Idas, who took Hippodice; Daiphron, who took Adiante, born from the mother Herse; Pandion, who took Callidice; Arbelus, who took Oeme; Hyperbius, who took Celaeno; and Hippocorystes, who took Hyperipte. These originate from Hephaestine, but the girls were from the mother Crinone. 

<margin>All the daughters of Danaus kill their husbands except one.</margin>
Afterwards, when each had obtained his own wife, the daughters of Danaus, having received daggers from their father, killed their own bridegrooms while they were buried in sleep—all of them, that is, with the sole exception of Hypermnestra. For she alone kept Lynceus unharmed because he had spared her virginity. For this reason, Danaus ordered her to be thrown into chains and guarded. The remaining daughters of Danaus buried the severed heads of their bridegrooms in Lerna, but took care to bury the bodies with lamentation before the city. # BOOK TWO.

<margin>Danaus first constructed a ship.</margin>
<margin>Certain things omitted, which do not appear in the text.</margin>
<margin>The daughters of Danaus marry the sons of Aegyptus.</margin>
Aegyptus had fifty sons, and his brother Danaus had an equal number of daughters. When they contended among themselves for the kingdom, Danaus killed the sons of Aegyptus, save for one or two, through the agency of his own daughters. For he had received an oracle that his own death would come from one of them. Struck by fear, and by the counsel of Minerva, he was the first to construct a ship, named by him after the number of his daughters, a <term>pentēkontoros</term> <gloss>fifty-oared ship</gloss>, as one might say. Placing his daughters upon it, he fled. Then, putting in at Rhodes, he dedicated a statue to the Lindian Minerva. From there, he betook himself to Argos, and Helanor, who then reigned in Argos, handed the kingdom over to him. He himself, having taken possession of that region, called the inhabitants Danaans after his own name. But because that region suffered from a lack of water, since Neptune, in his anger, had dried up the springs for Inachus—for he testified that it was the land of Minerva—he sent his daughters out in the meantime to fetch water. One of these, Amymone, while searching for water, cast a weapon at a deer and struck a sleeping Satyr. Therefore, he, awakened from sleep, was seized by a marvelous desire to possess the girl. But at the arrival of Neptune, the Satyr took to flight. Amymone, however, had intercourse with him, and Neptune pointed out the Lernaean springs to her. Furthermore, the sons of Aegyptus, having set out for Argos to compose their mutual enmity, urged themselves on, and begged that the daughters of Danaus be given to them in marriage. Then Danaus, both because he little trusted their promises and because he remembered the injury of his own flight and exile, agreed to the nuptials and began to distribute the girls by lot. Therefore, he selected Hypermnestra, the eldest of his daughters, for Lynceus, and Gorgophone for Proteus. For Aegyptus had fathered these from his wife, Queen Argyphia. From there, each obtained their own by lot.
pages.552:
Bufiris, Enceladus, Lycus, and Daiphro took Automate, Amymone, Agave, and Scaea, who were born to Danaus from the royal matron Europa, as wives. But Gorgophone and Hypermnestra were born from Elephantis, yet Lynceus obtained Calyce by lot. Ister took Hippodamia, Chalcodon took Rhodia, Agenor took Cleopatra, Chaetus took Asteria, Diacorytes took Hippodamia, Alcis took Glauce, Alcmenon took Hippomedusa, Hippothous took Gorge, Euchenor took Iphimedusa, and Hippolytus took Rhode. These ten were begotten from the Arabian wife. But the girls born from the Hamadryad nymphs, others from the Atlantean, and others from Phoebe, were wedded as follows: Pirene to Agaptolemus, Dorion to Cerceftis, Pharte to Eurydamas, Mnestra to Aegius, Argio to Euhippe, Archelao to Anexibia, and Nelo to Menachus. These seven were born from the Phoenician wife. But the girls who were Ethiopians, because they were namesakes to Memphis, were by no means willing to be joined to them by lot. For Clitus, born from the Tyrian mother, married Clite; Sthenelus married Sthenele; and Chrysippus married Chrysippe. And from Caliade, a Naiad nymph, twelve sons were born, along with twelve daughters of the Naiad Polyron. These are their names: Eurylochus, Phantes, Peristhenes, Hermus, Dryas, Potamon, Cilleus, Lixus, Imbrus, Bromius, Polyctor, and Chthonius. These others were born from the nymph Autonoe: Theano, Electra, Cleopatra, Eurydice, Glaucippe, Anthelea, Cleodora, Euippe, Erato, Stygne, and Bryce. Those who were born to Aegyptus from the Gorgons took as their wives those who were born from Pieria. For to Periphant fell Actaea, to Oeneus fell Podarce, to Aegyptus fell Dioxippe, to Menalce fell Adyte, to Lampo fell Ocypete, and to Idmon fell Pylarge. There are, however, eight more recent ones: Idas, who took Hippodice; Daiphron, who took Adiante, born from the mother Herse; Pandion, who took Callidice; Arbelus, who took Oeme; Hyperbius, who took Celaeno; and Hippocorystes, who took Hyperipte. These originate from Hephaestine, but the girls were from the mother Crinone. 

<margin>All the daughters of Danaus kill their husbands except one.</margin>
Afterwards, when each had obtained his own wife, the daughters of Danaus, having received daggers from their father, killed their own bridegrooms while they were buried in sleep—all of them, that is, with the sole exception of Hypermnestra. For she alone kept Lynceus unharmed because he had spared her virginity. For this reason, Danaus ordered her to be thrown into chains and guarded. The remaining daughters of Danaus buried the severed heads of their bridegrooms in Lerna, but took care to bury the bodies with lamentation before the city. Minerva and Mercury, by the command of Jupiter, purified these women. Finally, Danaus joined Hypermnestra to Lynceus in marriage and brought the others forth to a gymnastic contest, giving them to be possessed by the victors. Amymone

Not only those things that exist in reality, but also those that are held in hope can be sold: excepted, however, besides other things, are sacred and spiritual things, which cannot be sold by themselves without sacrilege and simony. An agreement for repurchase and the act of repurchase itself, if done without fraud, is approved by law. A sale with a forfeiture clause <note>original: "Lex Commissoria"</note> or an assignment subject to a time limit are absolute in nature.

### XVI. Other onerous contracts.

Not only a real ground rent <note>original: "Census realis"</note>, but also a personal one is licit; not only an irredeemable one, but also a redeemable one, both on the part of the buyer and the seller. A dry exchange <note>a form of credit transaction involving no actual movement of currency</note> is incapable of yielding just profit. The justice of a real exchange, whether local, manual, or by letter, is easily maintained. A contract of partnership can be made so that one contributes capital, the other industry. For a game to be valid, among other things, it is required that the risk be equal on both sides; and for a wager, that the condition of those wagering be equal. A lessor must, above all, provide for the preservation of the leased thing. A depositary is sometimes liable even for slight negligence. <term>Law 12, Digest on deposit</term>. A thing lent for use <note>original: "Commodatum"</note> cannot be reclaimed by the lender before the time has elapsed for which it was granted. If a borrowed thing perishes by accident without the fault of the borrower, it perishes for the owner. <term>Law last, Digest on commodatum</term>. A precarious loan is not terminated by the death of the grantor. A non-sworn suretyship of a woman on behalf of her husband is void. Even rights can be pledged or mortgaged.

### XVII. Injury and Restitution.

Injury <note>original: "Injuria"</note> is the violation of another's right: one type is real, which is committed through an unjust laying on of hands; another is verbal, which is committed through words, letters, writing, or contumelious pictures. <term>Law 15, Digest on injuries and libelous writings</term>. One type is light, another atrocious; this classification is to be derived from the deed, the place, the person, and other circumstances. <term>Paragraph "atrocious," Institutes on injuries</term>. No injury is done to a willing person, unless

where positive or natural law resists the yielding of a right: hence, one who drags a cleric unwillingly to a secular tribunal still commits an injury. Indeed, an inflicted injury is repaired either by satisfaction or by restitution. Restitution is an act of commutative justice, necessary for salvation not by the necessity of the medium, but only of the precept: which is as much Divine as it is natural; partly affirmative, partly negative. The obligation to restore arises either from unjust receipt or from the thing itself having been received: hence restitution differs greatly from payment, since the obligation to pay arises from contracts.

## THE END.

§. 2. Since there are two classes of arguments by which we can arrive at the investigation and discovery of truth: I. Unartificial [means], that is, authorities and testimonies; II. Artificial [means], that is, reasons and arguments. All of these, according to the nature of this subject, are so arranged that on one side they directly and explicitly <term>kata thesin</term> <gloss>according to a positive thesis</gloss> establish the antiquity and <term>theopneustian</term> <gloss>divine inspiration</gloss> of the points, which we seek; and on the other side <term>kat' arsin kai athetēsin</term> <gloss>by way of negation and rejection</gloss>, insofar as they deny that the Tiberian Masoretes were the authors of the points and remove them from consideration, or are entirely silent about them. Having thus cited the testimonies, we shall now finally set forth the following reasons to establish the antiquity and divine inspiration of the points.

§. 3. To obtain the truth of our assertion, we urge: I. *The most certain danger of uncertainty and ambiguity*. For if we posit that the vowel points were added by the Rabbis only after the passage of several centuries, shall we not render the clarity of meanings and the origin of words entirely ambiguous, indeed clearly uncertain? Truly, the Hebrew language, due to its own rather narrow limits, does not abound in so many primitive and radical words, and for that reason is forced, for the most part, to represent and explain several discrepant things by a single derivative. I ask, therefore, that you explain to me: does the diversity of meanings depend upon the consonants alone, or upon the vowels? It cannot depend upon the consonants alone, because the same consonants occur under the most diverse meanings of words. The matter is made clearer by examples. Thus, if <term>הוה</term> is pointed as <term>הָוָה</term>, it signifies "he was"; if it is pointed in this way, <term>הֹוָה</term>, it denotes "misery"; if in another way, <term>הַוָּה</term>, it signifies "substance." Likewise, if <term>בקר</term> is pointed as <term>בָּקַר</term>, it denotes "he investigated"; if <term>בַקֵּר</term>, "investigate" (imperative) and "to investigate"; if <term>בֹקֶר</term>, "in the morning"; if <term>בָּקָר</term>, "cattle"; and [other] similar [examples]. Who indeed would conveniently distinguish between these words descending from one root, and recognize one meaning from another, unless the diversity of vowels provided some aid?

§. 4. Furthermore, we urge: II. *The inevitable function of the points*. For this traditional saying holds true here as well:
> The things in the voice are symbols of the things in the soul, and the things written are [symbols of the things in the voice]. <note>Aristotle, *De Interpretatione*, ch. 1</note>
</translation>

<translation page="16">
Furthermore, the reason for vowels is held to be prior and more important than that of consonants. For since vowels are an essential part of reading and writing, and constitute the principal part, who would imagine that language was originally without them, especially since every language that is deprived of them is rendered lame, mutilated, and imperfect? Therefore, vowels are not only called <term>tenuot</term> <gloss>motions</gloss> by the Hebrews, and <term>ta phōnēenta</term> <gloss>the sounding ones</gloss> by the Greeks, but they are otherwise called the souls of words, which vivify them, and as in other languages, they obtain the place of highest importance. Moreover, every speech which writing serves to record consists of words, words of syllables, and syllables of consonants and vowels. If, therefore, no syllable can consist without vowels, so too no speech. And what is more, no letter can be pronounced without vowels. Hence, John Isaac, a convert from Judaism, said very well that he who reads Scripture without points and accents is like a man riding a horse <term>achalinōton</term> <gloss>unbridled</gloss>. There are some who call the <term>immot ha-keriah</term> <gloss>mothers of reading</gloss> [i.e., quiescent letters] here to their aid, for the reason that they can fulfill the functions of vowels. However, while we do not deny that reading an unpointed text can be helped in some way by those letters, neither do we completely reject their use in Rabbinic and Talmudic books. But they are not present everywhere, nor do they always indicate certain and identical [sounds] where they are present.

### §. 5. Furthermore, we add: III. The absurdity of the contrary opinion.

Those who maintain that the vowels were recently invented by the Masoretes incur this mark of absurdity, as if from their hypothesis flow all sorts of things that are most false and contrary to reason. 1. That for several thousands of years a necessary means of interpreting Scripture was lacking; because, just as for pronunciation, so also for the certain and indubitable transcription of sacred things, the vowel points are <term>anantirrētōs</term> <gloss>irrefutably</gloss> required. 2. That Holy Scripture is offered up to be corrupted by enemies; for if the points are not divinely handed down, it will easily be permitted to interpret the voice otherwise than is right. 3. That the venerable and pious antiquity of the Jews is either charged with ignorance or accused of malice; of the former, if it knew the points and did not communicate them; of the latter, if it did not know them, to whom [does the fault belong]?
</translation>

<summary>The author presents arguments for the divine origin and antiquity of Hebrew vowel points, emphasizing their necessity for the accurate interpretation and preservation of the sacred text against claims of later rabbinic invention.</summary>
<keywords>Hebrew vowel points, Masoretes, Theopneustia, divine inspiration, philology, textual criticism, linguistic structure</keywords>

One must obey the leaders and pastors of the churches reverently in the Lord, no less (2 Thessalonians 3:3, 14; Hebrews 13:17), yet not absolutely, but conditionally, insofar as and as long as they hear the voice of the supreme Pastor, Jesus Christ, correctly propose His Word, and keep themselves within the bounds of their calling. Even if we know for the greatest certainty that the Church in which we live is true, and that the pastors we hear are orthodox, nevertheless neither they nor the others are to be believed absolutely, because it is possible that even the true Church, even orthodox doctors, may hallucinate while interpreting the scriptures, deviate little by little from the truth, and begin to bring forth erroneous opinions, as happened to many churches in the times of the Old and New Testaments.

One must not simply and in all things, without any <term>δοκιμασία</term> <gloss>examination/testing</gloss>—that is, the testing of interpretations, doctrines, and rites proposed by others according to the standard of the divine Word—and without any discernment of all things, believe or obey as if with closed eyes. It is not otherwise than how the Pharisees were readers and interpreters who were to be heard in part, insofar as they sat in the chair of Moses (Matthew 23:2), but in part not to be heard, but to be avoided, insofar as they brought forth the leaven of their own doctrine and human traditions, infecting the healthy sense of Scripture (Matthew 16:6, 12).

Therefore, we maintain that there is absolutely no Church on earth, whether it be particular or universal, that is not perpetually and simply bound to the written Word of God, and that is not, therefore, required to derive the reason for both its doctrines and its...
pages.16:
rites, and to explain them to those who ask. Thus, pastors are to be obeyed only at the altars, or only in the Lord, as the Holy Scriptures speak, nor is any doctrine of theirs to be held as a fundamental article of faith whose solid and open foundations we have not first detected in the very Word of God. Even if we know for the greatest certainty that the Church in which we live is true, and that the pastors we hear are orthodox, nevertheless neither they nor the others are to be believed absolutely, because it is possible that even the true Church, even orthodox doctors, may hallucinate while interpreting the scriptures, deviate little by little from the truth, and begin to bring forth erroneous opinions, as happened to many churches in the times of the Old and New Testaments.

III. Thus (to say something about the Pauline passage), the *Church is the pillar and foundation of the truth*, but because of the Holy Scripture which it faithfully embraces, guards, commends, teaches, explains, and propagates. If it withdraws from this, it is not only not the foundation of the truth, but it also loses the truth itself.

Hence the true Church interprets Scripture from Scripture. With <term>Tertullian</term> in his book *On the Flesh of Christ*, it receives nothing that anyone brings in from outside of Scripture; with <term>Hilary</term>, it does not bring in an understanding of the sayings, but draws it from Scripture; it pronounces on articles of faith only from the one Holy Scripture and according to its perpetual analogy, in this way above others:

In the parables of Scripture, it does not rashly urge other matters beyond their scope; it does not allow <term>Allegorical Theology</term> to be argumentative, or rather, it does not establish and build doctrine from figures and allegories alone, according to <term>Jerome</term>. Whatever in divine speech can be referred neither to the honesty of morals nor to the truth of faith, it recognizes as figurative, with <term>Augustine</term> in *On Christian Doctrine*, book 3, chapter 10; or, when the absurdity of the letter clashes with other clearer places of Scripture, or with articles of faith, it corrects them by the benefit of figures, so that the meaning is retained, not the <term>ῥητὸν</term> <gloss>literal word</gloss>. Therefore, from figuratively spoken things, which treat a matter incidentally, it appeals to the seat of some article. For it extracts nothing from those more obscure matters that is not found to be spoken most plainly elsewhere, according to <term>Augustine</term>, *On Christian Doctrine*, book 2, chapter 6. <margin>*Drunkards*</margin>
sobriety, so that we would not suffer drunkenness to be even named among us. AP. Primarily, let the most shameful deeds of drunkards and their most inept manners also move us to cast aside the immoderate custom of drinking. For what crimes do they abstain from? They cast off all modesty, are inflamed by illicit lust, reveal the secrets of the mind, wallow in the mire like beasts, walk without any control of their gait, stagger, vomit like animals, and <margin>Isaiah 5</margin> attack all the best men with slanders; they do not look to the work of God, nor do they consider the works of his hands. Now, indeed, when they have weakened their bodies with immense gluttony and are exhausted from perpetrating the works of darkness, they fall down as if lifeless, lying prostrate on the ground <margin>Chrysostom, *On Prayer*, book 2</margin> like swine, so that it can most truthfully be said: A DRUNKARD IS A LIVING CORPSE. Finally, let us be moved by the profane men, the <term>Ethnici</term> <gloss>pagans/gentiles</gloss>, who condemned this entirely detestable and abominable vice, so much so <margin>Athenaeus, book 10</margin> that Solon felt a prince should be punished with death if he were found drunk. And it was not permitted for a king among the Indians to drink to the point of drunkenness. Among the Persians, however, this was granted to the king on only one day, when they sacrificed to the sun. NEPH. And I remember reading that Pittacus of Mitylene, not the least of the seven Greek Sages, passed a law that if any person committed any crime while drunk, he should be punished with a penalty twice as severe. AP. If, therefore, those who were ignorant of God condemned, avoided, and punished this wickedness so <margin>Ephesians 5; Hosea 4; Augustine; Origen</margin> highly, what, I ask, do you think we Christians must do? NEPH. Let us strive so that we are never intoxicated by wine, in which there is <term>asōtia</term> <gloss>dissoluteness/profligacy</gloss>: let us despise and avoid drunkenness, which takes away the heart and memory, which scatters the senses and confuses the intellect; and which makes a beast out of a man, a weakling out of a robust one, and a fool out of a prudent one. Let us burn, however, with a zeal for sobriety and temperance; and let us think that the last times are even now at hand; let us revere and fear the long-suffering of God, lest we despise the riches of his goodness and patience.

<summary>This page explores the moral and physical degradation caused by drunkenness, citing pagan historical examples to urge Christians toward sobriety.</summary>
<keywords>Drunkenness, Sobriety, Temperance, Solon, Pittacus of Mitylene, Ethics, Christian Morality</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="15">
of His. Let us also remember that our bodies are the temple of God and the instrument of the Spirit who dwells in us. AP. Sobriety and temperance <margin>1 Corinthians 3; 2 Corinthians 6; Galatians 5</margin> are fruits of the Spirit; but drunkenness and luxury are the nurses and promoters of all vices, and the receptacles of all manner of filth. Just as smoke puts to flight bees, so <term>crapula</term> <gloss>drunken excess</gloss> puts to flight the Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts. NEPH. And just as clouds and rain always follow the south wind, so the diseases of the soul and the body follow drunkenness. COM. Therefore, is one not to drink at all? AP. Certainly, if moderation is absent. However, honor must be shown to the body so that <margin>Colossians 2</margin> it is nourished with sufficient, not immoderate and superfluous, sustenance, and we must take care not to be found as the murderers of our own bodies. COM. I understand now at last that there is nothing more destructive to man than habitual drunkenness. AP. Therefore, heal this disease within yourself, brother, and separate this vice from yourself, and flee the company of wine-bibbers like a reef. TRIC. Alas! Are you not ashamed, Comasta, to let yourself be corrupted by their persuasion? AP. Come, rise, Comasta; let us depart, do not listen to them. COM. Farewell, you fellow drinkers; I must depart and take care that I may become a man. But if you are wise, take an example from me.

## THE END.

What if the peers, who were present at the time of the investiture, afterwards cease to be peers? When a dispute arises between the Lord and the Vassal, are they still held to be suitable witnesses? ### XXXIII.

As for the case in paragraph 30, the cause of the litigation there is the detention of the property, which Paul demands back from Maevius, and he assigns the reason for seeking it, because he mandated Maevius to carry his property to Pomponius, so that he might keep it, and if Pomponius refused, Maevius would guard it for so long until he [Paul] requested it back. Paul's intention is founded in *Digest 16.3.1.12, "On Deposit,"* where the action of mandate is granted to him, not indeed the action of deposit. We shall propose still other examples.

### XXXIV.

Thus far, the sayings have exhibited to us actions arising from contracts; now a case must be seen where a contract in part and a tort in part produces an action. For Sempronius leased his house to Titius; with this consensual business completed, they go together to visit the leased house, but after they are in the house, Sempronius, without any roundabout words, having placed a club behind the door out of hatred previously conceived against him, fulfills his deed: he throws the well-greased <note>This likely refers to Titius being forcibly and unceremoniously ejected</note> man outside and does not grant him power to inhabit [the house] any longer. Titius, because he suffered this against his own stomach <note>i.e., against his own will or inclination</note>, does not wish to bear the matter without any vengeance, and so he hurries to approach the judge and intends to convene Sempronius.

### XXXV.

However, because in the proposed case two different facts or acts present themselves, why should two separate legal remedies not also be obtained for pursuing the double scope or end of the intention? For two things are involved here, of which one is a contract and the other is a tort, which differ greatly and put forward two separate petitions; or, a double object of grievance and offense, from the fact and the double action performed, is brought into court, the first object of the dispute [is] the denied habitation of the house, which the plaintiff intends, and even for that reason, because it was agreed between them in such a way that he should inhabit them for a certain price, to be paid at a determined time; the intention of the plaintiff is founded in *Laws 7, 8, 9 of the Digest on the Locating and Hiring of Property*. The other matter of the litigation or the other object which makes the lawsuit is the beating, which the plaintiff pursues civilly and desires to bind the defendant to pay him this or that amount; this [is] because, without any reason or opportunity given, he [the defendant] received the plaintiff with beatings injuriously enough, hence his intention is founded in *Section 10 of the Institutes on Injuries*, and the estimatory action for injuries is granted to him.</translation>

Thus far, the sayings have exhibited to us actions arising from contracts; now a case must be seen where a contract in part and a tort in part produces an action. It might seem so from the decision of the said Novella 118, which generally substitutes children into the place of their parents. We will, however, with Zoesius on the title of the Digest, *On the Undutiful Will*, number 26, maintain the negative, by Law 21, *fratris*, Code, *On the Undutiful Will*, and § 1, Institutes, of the same title. For although in the Novellae the children of brothers are admitted to the inheritance of an uncle along with the brothers, this nevertheless proceeds if he dies intestate simply, and not if the will is overturned by a complaint of being undutiful. Furthermore, the children of brothers succeed to a deceased uncle by the right of representation only then, if they were conceived while he was alive; otherwise, they will not be admitted to his goods, for they are not joined to him by any kinship, Law 1, § *si quis proximior*, Digest, *Whence the Cognates*. Unless access to the succession lies open from the right of transmission, and that from the right of deliberating (namely, if their parent dies within a year from the day of knowing that the inheritance was deferred to him), Law *cum in antiquioribus* 19, Code, *On the Right of Deliberating*, and Brunnemann there.
