Under the customs of the Empire today, these tithes belong to the lord of the territory in recognition of supreme jurisdiction; see Myler, *On the State of the Empire*, page 2, Chapter 70, number 5.

#### Paragraph I.

Just as a real annuity <term>census realis</term> <gloss>a fixed annual charge on real property</gloss> that is redeemable on the part of the seller alone (provided it is purchased for a just price, namely, by force of Imperial constitutions: 5 florins of annual return for one hundred florins) is a lawful and non-usurious contract, *Extravagantes* 1 and 2, *On Buying and Selling*, so an annuity that is irredeemable on the part of the seller (with the same aforementioned price intervening) is not free from the taint of usury. This was confirmed by the Emperor Charles V in a constitution published at Augsburg in the year 1548, under the title **On usurious contracts. Paragraph: "And after the redeemable florins."** For this quality is inherent in such annuities: that the seller may redeem even against the will of the buyer, nor can one contract to the contrary, nor can the faculty of redemption ever be barred by prescription, not even in the space of one hundred years, at least according to Canon Law. If, therefore, in the instrument of obligation, a mention of perpetuity ("unredeemable") has been made, then the irredeemability is to be understood and taken in terms of the buyer or creditor, not the seller or debtor.

We shall reply in the affirmative, however, if nothing was expressly provided in the pact or statute regarding time. For it is not cohabitation that makes a marriage, but consent; for this part, the text in Law 15, *cum fuerit*, Digest, *On Conditions and Demonstrations*, speaks, where a legacy left under the condition of marriage is owed immediately, as soon as the woman is led as a wife. We will, however, with Zoesius on the title of the Digest, *On the Undutiful Will*, number 26, maintain the negative, by Law 21, *fratris*, Code, *On the Undutiful Will*, and § 1, Institutes, of the same title. For although in the Novellae the children of brothers are admitted to the inheritance of an uncle along with the brothers, this nevertheless proceeds if he dies intestate simply, and not if the will is overturned by a complaint of being undutiful. Furthermore, the children of brothers succeed to a deceased uncle by the right of representation only then, if they were conceived while he was alive; otherwise, they will not be admitted to his goods, for they are not joined to him by any kinship, Law 1, § *si quis proximior*, Digest, *Whence the Cognates*. Unless access to the succession lies open from the right of transmission, and that from the right of deliberating (namely, if their parent dies within a year from the day of knowing that the inheritance was deferred to him), Law *cum in antiquioribus* 19, Code, *On the Right of Deliberating*, and Brunnemann there.

### I.

Since the right of receiving tithes from newly cultivated lands <term>novalia</term> <gloss>newly cleared or cultivated lands</gloss> must be granted by a special privilege, and is not contained in the right of receiving ancient tithes, Chapter 2, *On Tithes*, in the Sext, it follows that if wood ready for cutting <term>sylva caedua</term> <gloss>coppice or timber woods</gloss> is brought into cultivation, he who exercises the right of tithing there by prescription
pages.14:
or by any other just title in that place cannot demand tithes from the newly produced fruits. Under the customs of the Empire today, these tithes belong to the lord of the territory in recognition of supreme jurisdiction; see Myler, *On the State of the Empire*, page 2, Chapter 70, number 5.

#### Paragraph I.

Just as a real annuity <term>census realis</term> <gloss>a fixed annual charge on real property</gloss> that is redeemable on the part of the seller alone (provided it is purchased for a just price, namely, by force of Imperial constitutions: 5 florins of annual return for one hundred florins) is a lawful and non-usurious contract, *Extravagantes* 1 and 2, *On Buying and Selling*, so an annuity that is irredeemable on the part of the seller (with the same aforementioned price intervening) is not free from the taint of usury. This was confirmed by the Emperor Charles V in a constitution published at Augsburg in the year 1548, under the title **On usurious contracts. Paragraph: "And after the redeemable florins."** For this quality is inherent in such annuities: that the seller may redeem even against the will of the buyer, nor can one contract to the contrary, nor can the faculty of redemption ever be barred by prescription, not even in the space of one hundred years, at least according to Canon Law. If, therefore, in the instrument of obligation, a mention of perpetuity ("unredeemable") has been made, then the irredeemability is to be understood and taken in terms of the buyer or creditor, not the seller or debtor.

### From Civil Law.

#### Paragraph I.

The question is famous in law: does the profit of a dowry <term>dos</term> <gloss>marriage portion</gloss> yield to the survivor by force of pact or statute, if the other died before the consummation of the marriage? To support the negative, it is commonly cited that a dowry is not owed where there are no burdens of marriage, Law 76, *si pater*, in the end, Digest, *On the Right of Dowries*. We shall reply in the affirmative, however, if nothing was expressly provided in the pact or statute regarding time. But if we are in danger in water, in fire, in prisons, or are overwhelmed by any calamity, we can and ought to always stir up our faith and our invocation to God in this way: by knowing that Christ, true God and man, is not far from us, absent in some peculiar place in this outer heaven far distant from us, having perhaps no care for us, but that He is with us, both in humanity and divinity, in the water, in the fire, in prison, and in every calamity. For he who was called <term>Yehoshua</term> in <note>Haggai and Zechariah</note>, is called <term>Yeshua</term> elsewhere <note>Ezra 2:2, Nehemiah 7:7</note>, and Joshua or <term>Yehoshua</term> is called <term>Yeshua</term> elsewhere <note>Nehemiah 8:17</note>. It is derived from the verb <term>yasha</term> in <term>Hiphil</term>, which means to make safe, to save, to preserve, and to vindicate. The name has its origin from the deed performed. Just as we read many things in Scripture, such as <term>Jacob</term>, who was called <term>supplanter</term> from <term>aqeb</term>, because he had supplanted his brother in the birthright. In like manner, Christ receives His name from the admirable and truly stupendous work of salvation, that He might be called *Iησȣ͂ς*, *Savior*, or *sōtēr*, which signifies more than the Latin *servator* <gloss>preserver</gloss>, as Cicero himself acknowledges in *Action 2 against Verres*: "I saw him inscribed at Syracuse not only as the patron of that island, but also as a Soter." How great is this? So great that it cannot be expressed by one Latin word. He is undoubtedly the Soter, who gave salvation. Hence was born the Greek *Iησȣ͂ς*, which is read and written in Latin likewise with two syllables, with the letter S added. For the Greeks add the same to foreign names at the end.

Here, if anyone likes, let him revere the religion and subtlety of the *Jesuits*, who write JHESUS instead of JESUS, or by abbreviation with three letters, IHS, and so that no superstition is missing, even with a cross placed on top. Those good companions wrongly introduce the Latin H, not attending to the fact that there is no aspiration H in either the Greek or the Hebrew language. For it is not a Latin word, but made in imitation of the Greek diction, whence it preserves almost the same inflection in the oblique cases. ### XV. Ναζωραιος <gloss>Nazarene</gloss>.

By a gentile name, JESUS is so called from Nazareth, a city of Galilee, and the fatherland of his parents. Regarding the application of this name to Christ, a threefold exposition is given. To some he is called a Nazarene, as if separated and consecrated to the Lord, from Judges 13:7 and Genesis 49:26. To others, it is supported by the head of Isaiah 11:1. The third group combines both passages. And here different people look to different roots. There is the root <term>natsar</term> <gloss>to guard, to form, to plant</gloss>; there is also <term>nazar</term> <gloss>to separate, to sanctify</gloss>. Whence <term>nazir</term> and the Chaldean <term>nazira</term> <gloss>Nazarene</gloss>. We do not deny that both are appropriate to the Lord, yet we feel that here He had this name derived from the city and common fatherland. It is also painted in various ways. Sometimes *Nazōraios* is used among Matthew, Luke, and John; Mark, however, presents it with another ending, *Nazārēnos*, as it is elsewhere. It is therefore used indiscriminately, just as I say *Essaio* and *Essēnos*. But let us assume that a comparison to a harlot and adulteress is intended in that passage of Proverbs; nevertheless, the word <term>‘almah</term> could there signify a virgin and be accepted <term>doxastikos</term> <gloss>in terms of opinion/repute</gloss> or <term>eironikos</term> <gloss>ironically</gloss>. Nor is that mode of speaking unusual in the Holy Codex, that someone should be called [something] not because they truly are that, but because they seem or are believed to be so, or because that is how they sell themselves, or what they had been before. Whence also our blessed Luther says:

> The Jews would gain nothing, he says, except for the fact that the name <term>‘almah</term> signifies there such a young girl as all might hold to be a virgin, who bears a virginal garland and name, and sells herself as a virgin, even if she is a harlot. Which abuse of the name will by no means take away its proper and genuine signification, even in that very place, as all those endowed with a sound mind will easily understand.

Therefore, we have so far proven that this passage in Proverbs contributes nothing to bringing forth the sense that the Jews attribute to the word <term>‘almah</term>. And since the same people, refusing to grant the palm to divine truth, expound this same word in Isaiah 7 with that perverse sense, and simultaneously appeal to the aforementioned passage of Proverbs, they do what most idle Sophists are accustomed to do, who, when they dispute about some controversial matter, assume what is in controversy and thus deceive their adversary. We conclude now with the once-great theologian and philosopher, Dr. Jacob Martini, that the word <term>‘almah</term> in our passage signifies nothing other than a virgin hidden, concealed, and obscured from the sights of men, and thus entirely untouched, concerning whose modesty and integrity there is no doubt, especially when the letter <term>he</term> is prefixed to it, which, as Galatinus rightly advises, makes the expression mean [it] specifically.</translation>

<translation page="16">For it is worthy of note, says the praised author, that in the whole *Holy Scripture* this expression <term>ha-‘almah</term>, written articulatively—namely with the letter <term>he</term>—is found only three times, and is always used of a virgin; <note>Genesis 24:43, Exodus 2:8, and Isaiah 7:14.</note> Because, therefore, the former two to whom <term>ha-‘almah</term> is attributed were virgins, who will doubt that this word, used in the same way by Isaiah in his prophecy, denotes a pure virgin, since the Jews cannot demonstrate from any other place that <term>ha-‘almah</term> is used of a married woman? Finally (which Rabbi Solomon also acknowledges), that sign given by Isaiah had to be highly miraculous; but for a young woman to conceive and bear a son by a man (and thus with the privation of virginity) is no miracle, since it happens naturally, and thus occurs daily. Let the Jews therefore concede, whether they like it or not, that the sign given by the Prophet was none other than that, beyond the manner of nature, by the miracle of GOD alone, a virgin would conceive and bear a son. *B. Jac. Martini, aforementioned book 3, page 243 and following.*

that the day had passed, he said: On this day, he says, the ancients were accustomed to hope and pray that they might be allowed to live through the year happily <note>Latin: "annare perannare", a ritual phrase meaning to live through the year successfully</note>, and they applied themselves diligently so that they would not even name anything dire, sad, or deadly. Instead, they would speak only words of good omen, abstain from all quarrels, and discuss only joyful and friendly matters among themselves.

Although this honor paid to the invocation of Anna Perenna was not considered worthless or despicable, the worship of <term>Janus</term> <gloss>the Roman god of beginnings</gloss> was preferred over it. We find in the archives of antiquity that Janus was the first to be invoked in all sacrifices and prayers, and that he was accustomed to be placed before all other gods, and even before Jupiter himself. Because he was the first in Italy to build temples to the gods and establish the rites of sacred things, he deserved perpetual prayer in sacrifices. And since the first and last moments have the greatest influence in all things, they wished for Janus to be the leader in sacrificing, says Cicero (<italic>Book 1 of On the Nature of the Gods</italic>).

We who are called, and are, Christians, are so far from simply subscribing to the formulas of the heathens, as if we did not have ones that were equally good or better, that we rather seriously condemn everything in them that the idolatry of the Gentiles introduced as erroneous. We judge that only that which seems to be derived and composed from the year itself should be retained, especially in this prayer. If we obtain our desires in our own prayer, each of us will have reason to congratulate and rejoice in himself after the passing of the year.

We know that such vows were curated mainly by the flamens <note>priests of ancient Rome</note> in the temples. But what did those who sat at the helm of the Republic do around this time? Consuls and senators were ordained: once ordained, they entered upon their offices and, for the sake of good omens, performed a preliminary sampling of their duties. This can be seen in the election of the father of Symmachus, a man of marvelous eloquence and knowledge. While he was in the country and in retirement, nursing the injury of his lost house, the Senate recalled him to new honor through frequent votes and, finally, by sending orators. And those were the Calends, on which the year is opened, as his son himself testifies and rejoices (<italic>1, Epistle 44</italic>).</translation>

Naso <note>Ovid</note>, the prolific recorder of the Fasti, agrees and introduces this rite gracefully when he says:

> The people go to the Tarpeian heights in untouched garments,
> And the people themselves are the same color as their festival.
> Now the new fasces go before, the new purple gleams;
> And the new ivory seat feels the weight of the distinguished one. (<italic>1, Fasti, v. 10</italic>)

It was also the custom to perform a preliminary act, as if to imbue and auspiciously initiate offices on that very day. Drusus, the Prefect of the City, ascended the tribunal to take the auspices; Nero took the auspices on the Calends of January; the Emperor Maximian immediately finished what he had hoped to accomplish for the future. Tacitus, the writer of the Augustan History, testifies to this regarding the former (<italic>Book 4, Annals, chapter 36</italic>); Suetonius regarding the latter (<italic>chapter 46</italic>); and the panegyrists regarding the third. The custom and habit of Christians does not differ from this time, for in certain places, around these same turns of the year, they integrate and restore their senatorial colleges. And they seem to do this more rightly than the ancients. For we believe that the eternal Son of God, the <term>Logos</term> <gloss>the Word/Reason of the eternal Father</gloss>, was born at that time, and by His merit and satisfaction, He designated and appointed us as citizens and nobles of heaven. that the day had passed, he said: On this day, he says, the ancients were accustomed to hope and pray that they might be allowed to live through the year happily <note>Latin: "annare perannare", a ritual phrase meaning to live through the year successfully</note>, and they applied themselves diligently so that they would not even name anything dire, sad, or deadly. Instead, they would speak only words of good omen, abstain from all quarrels, and discuss only joyful and friendly matters among themselves.

Although this honor paid to the invocation of Anna Perenna was not considered worthless or despicable, the worship of <term>Janus</term> <gloss>the Roman god of beginnings</gloss> was preferred over it. We find in the archives of antiquity that Janus was the first to be invoked in all sacrifices and prayers, and that he was accustomed to be placed before all other gods, and even before Jupiter himself. Because he was the first in Italy to build temples to the gods and establish the rites of sacred things, he deserved perpetual prayer in sacrifices. And since the first and last moments have the greatest influence in all things, they wished for Janus to be the leader in sacrificing, says Cicero (Book 1 of On the Nature of the Gods).

We who are called, and are, Christians, are so far from simply subscribing to the formulas of the heathens, as if we did not have ones that were equally good or better, that we rather seriously condemn everything in them that the idolatry of the Gentiles introduced as erroneous. We judge that only that which seems to be derived and composed from the year itself should be retained, especially in this prayer. If we obtain our desires in our own prayer, each of us will have reason to congratulate and rejoice in himself after the passing of the year.

We know that such vows were curated mainly by the flamens <note>priests of ancient Rome</note> in the temples. But what did those who sat at the helm of the Republic do around this time? Consuls and senators were ordained: once ordained, they entered upon their offices and, for the sake of good omens, performed a preliminary sampling of their duties. This can be seen in the election of the father of Symmachus, a man of marvelous eloquence and knowledge. While he was in the country and in retirement, nursing the injury of his lost house, the Senate recalled him to new honor through frequent votes and, finally, by sending orators. And those were the Calends, on which the year is opened, as his son himself testifies and rejoices (1, Epistle 44).

> The people go to the Tarpeian heights in untouched garments,
> And the people themselves are the same color as their festival.
> Now the new fasces go before, the new purple gleams;
> And the new ivory seat feels the weight of the distinguished one. (1, Fasti, v. 10)

It was also the custom to perform a preliminary act, as if to imbue and auspiciously initiate offices on that very day. Drusus, the Prefect of the City, ascended the tribunal to take the auspices; Nero took the auspices on the Calends of January; the Emperor Maximian immediately finished what he had hoped to accomplish for the future. <translation page="13">
GOD is worshipped either primarily and in Himself, as are the works of the first table of the Decalogue <note>original: "decalogi tabulae"; the first four of the Ten Commandments concerning man's duty to God</note>, or indirectly, as are the works of the second table.

### LXIII.
Of these, some are internal, others are external.

### LXIIII.
The internal are: to acknowledge the depravity and corruption of nature, to confess oneself guilty of divine wrath and eternal punishment, and to grieve for sins from the heart.

### LXV.
To flee to the mercy of GOD proposed in Christ, and to establish firmly and certainly that through Him, the remission of sins and the right to enter the heavenly inheritance are given.

### LXVI.
To dedicate oneself entirely to the obedience of GOD, and to apply oneself to this with the whole mind, so that all the counsels and actions of life may serve the glory of the divine name and the utility of the Church.

### LXVII.
The external, however, are those which fall upon the eyes and the exterior senses.

### LXVIII.
These relate either to words, such as to teach the Gospel, to call upon GOD in dangers, to give thanks to Him for benefits, and to issue a confession of faith.

### LXIX.
Or to deeds: such as to hear the Word, to use the sacraments ordained by GOD, to give alms, and to offer the body for the assertion of the truth and the glory of Christ, if there is need, through martyrdom.
</translation>

<translation page="18">
when you await a magnificent one, what is more magnificent than this King, to whom the Angels applaud from the heavens, whom Kings adore in the cradle, and to whom they offer Gold, Frankincense, and Myrrh, the gifts of Kings? If you desire one who fights and triumphs, what is stronger, what is more glorious than this Hercules, who already in the cradle has tamed the ancient serpent, and was born and revealed for this very purpose, that he might destroy the works of the devil, and restore to its proper place whatever the fury of the infernal Prince had shaken. You see a Lamb here indeed, but one who is to take away the sins of the world; a lamb, but one who is at the same time the greatest Lion of the tribe of Judah. You believe that the dry rod of Aaron blossomed, grew leaves, and bore fruit; why do you not also believe that a virgin could have given birth? You believe that the great Goliath was slaughtered by the little David, that the lion was torn apart by Samson, and that the Philistines were routed; why do you not also believe that the head of the serpent was crushed by this little Hercules in the cradle, the seed of the woman? Omnipotence accomplishes what human impotence cannot, nor does it grasp it with distrust. Rightly indeed does the Divine Augustine judge these cradles to be more august than your Jerusalem temple, repeating:

> *O manger, more august and holy than the very temple of Solomon! Let the Jerusalem temple glitter with gold, let it shine with Cherubim, the ark of God, candlesticks, tables, and golden vessels; let it be adorned with the most spacious courtyards, sacrifices, and the ministry of priests; yet it is inferior to the Bethlehem manger.*

Your fathers in the desert suffered many and deadly wounds from fiery serpents; and when Moses had raised up the bronze serpent and set it as a sign, whoever among those stricken looked upon it were healed. Behold, indeed, the tamer of those fiery serpents hides here in the cradle, as does the very bronze serpent, which was later raised up as the sign of the cross: look upon this and you will see! But alas, you seed of the snake, seed of vipers, you do not wish to recognize the blessed seed of Abraham, the seed of the woman. The most holy Infant complains of you incredulous ones: The ox has known</translation>

<translation page="19">
his owner, and the donkey his master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood. After the Jews, you too, born of the nations, approach the cradle of our Hercules, whom this infant, long desired by the nations, has called his people, when they were not a people. The Magi, whether Persians or Chaldeans, lead the way for you, and with a star as their guide, they approach the Savior of the nations as well. *Indeed, these cradles do not shine with precious paintings, here neither purple nor scarlet radiate, nor whatever* the Chinese <note>original: "Seres"</note> *have taught to spin with a learned hand, whatever* Babylon *has taught to weave with an ingenious comb, whatever* the Tyrians *have dyed, whatever* the Phrygians *have embroidered, whatever* the Milesians *have sheared;* yet these are nonetheless the cradles of the King of Kings and Lord of Lords, the King who shall crush the kings of the earth with an iron rod. If you believe, you Gentiles, that Minerva was born from the brain of Jove, then believe also that this God was born of God. If you believe that Jove rendered Danaë pregnant by means of a golden rain, believe also that the Spirit of God overshadowed the virgin so that she might bear a womb, and bring forth a son. If you believe that your Hercules has subdued the monstrous beasts of men and wild animals, has overcome the Erymanthian boar, has wrestled and suppressed the bull with Antaeus, has routed the Stymphalian birds, has fought with the Amazons, has conquered the three-bodied Geryon, has tamed the horses of Diomedes, has cleansed the stable of Augeas, has struggled with the dragon of the Hesperides, and has fought against the Lernaean Hydra and the three-headed Cerberus; believe also that this heavenly Hercules of ours has overcome the world, death, the devil, and hell, and has trampled our enemies and his own under his feet, has cast out evil spirits with a word, has calmed the winds and the waves with a command, has healed the lepers, the deaf, and the blind with a touch, and with a simple decree has put to flight all kinds of diseases and death.

I have called upon the Christians, then the Jews themselves, and I have called upon the nations to the cradle of our Hercules. It is time that I myself approach. Grant, O Child Jesus, that I might from afar only your manger</translation>

The proposition speaks generally of that which exists in the word of God in any way, whether explicitly, that is, in plain words, or implicitly, that is, through a certain, firm, and necessary consequence. The assumption of Pistorius is most false, which is clear from the 4th thesis and especially from these most clear testimonies: Do not turn to the right or to the left, Deuteronomy 5, verse 32. To the law and to the testimony. If they do not speak according to this word, there will be no morning light for them, Isaiah 8, verse 20. Let him be anathema who has preached another Gospel, Galatians 1, verse 8. Not to teach other doctrines <note>original: "μὴ ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν"</note>, 1 Timothy 1, verse 3. And chapter 6, verse 3. Whoever shall walk according to this Canon, peace be upon them and mercy, Galatians 6, verse 16. On the contrary: Whoever departs from this rule, wrath upon them and condemnation. 3. If all things are implicitly in scripture, as Pistorius says on page 35, then this too will be contained in it implicitly, that nothing is to be believed outside the word of God. 4. For Christian faith and the word of God relate to one another. 5. Which Pistorius will not deny, who wrote explicitly that he would prove all his points from sacred scripture alone. 6. And Bellarmine, although he speaks insidiously, nevertheless admits in book 1, chapter 1, on the word of God, that the prophetic and apostolic books are a certain and stable rule of faith. 7. And nothing today in the matter of religion is brought forward by the Papists that the Jesuits do not attempt to prove from some scripture: which is evident from their disputations. Thus, these men say one thing and do another.

The illustrious or wealthy persuade themselves that, because they surpass the rest in splendor, they are simply superior, and that by right and merit, unequal things are owed to unequal persons. Conversely, the poor, measuring all things by liberty, concede no inequality. By this vain persuasion of men, as if one's own right were not granted to each, the state of Republics is most greatly changed, which was long ago excellently proven by Aristotle.

Writers record of Solon that, in order to make the citizens friendly to himself and to be declared legislator by them, he said he would propose laws equal for all, and from that, the decision of proposing laws was permitted to him by the greatest zeal and will of all. If citizens remain at these precipices, and are unwilling to remit anything of their own right, which they boast of so laboriously, it is easily evident that such contentions are joined with the internal destruction of the Republic, and do not cease until one party is oppressed.

Indeed, neither party, whether the poor or the rich is observed, is accustomed to derive equality and inequality from true principles. It is a common assertion of philosophers that only virtue creates the difference between the plebeians and the illustrious; so that the latter may shine among the rest, and the former may live content with their own humbler lot. But who can persuade these minds of this, which, blinded by excessive self-love, are agitated here and there? Nor is the matter so clear that it no longer has any doubt.

<margin>6. Pol. c. 3.</margin>
Aristotle himself, when dealing with Democracy, confesses it is extremely difficult to organize the people so that all participate equally in the communion of rights. # LIB. I. SUMMAE

## Regarding the impediments of this work, on the part of the artist's body. Chapter IV.

We have now determined for you, in a general way, the impediments to this work. Now, truly, we shall address you with more specific discourse in this chapter, and we shall relate to you all those impediments most fully and in order, quite openly. We say, therefore: that if anyone does not have his organs complete, he will not be able to arrive at the completion of this work by himself, as if he were blind, or maimed in his extremities, since he is not helped by the members through which this art is perfected, as if they were the ministers of nature. But if the artist's body is weak and sick, such as the bodies of those suffering from fevers or lepers, whose limbs are falling off, or those laboring in the final stages of life, and elderly men of decrepit age, he will not arrive at the completion of the art. By these natural impotencies of the body, therefore, the artist is hindered in his intention.

## Regarding the impediments on the part of the artist's soul. Chapter V.

We have provided you with one chapter in which we related, in absolute and manifest speech, the impediments depending on the artist's body. It remains for us to relate briefly the impediments on the part of the soul itself, which most greatly hinder the completion of this work. We say, therefore, that he who does not have natural talent, and a soul that searches subtly into natural principles, the foundations of nature, and the crafts that can follow nature in the properties of its action, will not find the true root of this most precious science. Such are many who have a stiff neck, void of talent in every investigation, who can scarcely understand common speech, and who likewise learn common works with difficulty. Besides these, we also find many who have a soul that easily opines any fantasy whatsoever; yet what they believe they have found to be true is entirely fantastic, deviant from reason, full of error, and remote from natural principles, since their brain, filled with many <term>fumositates</term> <gloss>vapors or fumes</gloss>, cannot receive the true intention of natural things. Besides these, there are others who have a mobile soul, shifting from opinion to opinion, and from will to will, like those who now believe this and desire the same, without any foundation of reason. Yet, a little while after that, they believe something else similarly, and desire something else. And these are so mobile that they can scarcely finish the least bit of that which they intend, but rather leave it diminished. There are likewise others who cannot see any truth from natural things, no more than beasts, such as those captured by their mind, the insane, and children. There are also others who despise the science, and do not believe it to be: whom this science similarly despises, and repels them from the end of this most precious work. And there are those who are slaves, serving money, affirming this wonderful science themselves, but fearing to incur expenses; and therefore, although they affirm it, and investigate it according to reason, yet they do not arrive at the experience of the work because of the avarice of money. To these, therefore, our science does not come. For how could he who has been ignorant or has neglected to investigate the science easily arrive at it?

## Regarding external impediments hindering the work of this art. Chapter VI.

We have reduced to two chapters all the impediments delaying the end of this art, which are from the radical principles, according to the nature of the artist of this most precious business. It is therefore useful for us at last to relate the impediments supervening from the outside, and from contingent fortunes and chances, by which this most glorious work is hindered. We see, therefore, some who are astute and talented, in no way ignorant of the works of nature, and of those things in which it is possible</translation>

<translation page="139">
# PERFECTIONIS GEBERI.

to follow the principles and works, and for whom there is an investigation that is not fantastic in all things which are regulated by the motions and actions of nature within the lunar circle. These, however, oppressed by extreme poverty, from the need for expenses, are forced to postpone this excellent <term>magisterium</term> <gloss>mastery/the Great Work</gloss>. There are also many others besides those now mentioned, curious men, detained by the various cares and solicitudes of this world, occupying themselves entirely with every secular business, from whom this precious science of ours again retreats. Now, therefore, it is sufficiently clear to you from the aforementioned chapters what the impediments are that distract from this art.

<note>A decorative drop cap 'C' begins the paragraph.</note>We conclude, therefore, from what has already been said, that it is necessary for the artist of this work to be learned and perfect in the sciences of natural philosophy, because no matter how much money and naturally profound talent he may have, and desire in this craft, he will not acquire its end unless he has attained natural philosophy through doctrine, because what is not acquired by natural talent is relieved of its defect through doctrine. It is necessary, therefore, that the artist be helped by the deepest investigation and industry. For because of doctrine, no matter how much science he has acquired, unless he is also helped by natural industry, he will not be invited to such precious feasts. For in a moment he would correct his error through his industry, for which he would not know how to apply a remedy if he were founded on doctrine alone: and likewise he would provide for an error in a moment from the science acquired through natural doctrine, which he could not avoid by industry alone: since art is helped by talent, and talent is likewise helped by art. And it is likewise necessary for him to be of constant will in the work, so that he does not presume to attempt now this, now that: because our art does not consist in a multitude of things, nor is it perfected by it. For there is one stone, one medicine, in which the <term>magisterium</term> <gloss>mastery/the Great Work</gloss> consists, to which we add no extraneous thing, nor do we diminish anything, except what we remove as superfluous in the preparation. It is also necessary for him to persist diligently in the work until its consummation, so that he does not leave the work truncated: because he would acquire neither science nor profit from a diminished work, but rather despair and loss. It is also expedient that he not be ignorant of the principles and main roots of this art, which are of the being of the work: for he who is ignorant of the beginning will not find the end. And we shall tell you all those principles in complete speech, and also, for the prudent, sufficiently open and manifest, according to the requirements of this art of ours. It is likewise expedient for the artist to be temperate and slow to anger, lest suddenly, because of the impetus of anger, he dissipate and destroy what has already been begun. Likewise, let him guard his money, and not distribute it vainly as one who is presumptuous, lest if by chance he has not found the art, he be left in misery and the despair of poverty: or lest by chance, when he has already approached the end of this <term>magisterium</term> <gloss>mastery/the Great Work</gloss> through his investigation, his expenses be consumed, and the poor wretch violently abandon the true end because of poverty. Just as with those in the beginning who, in their investigation, prodigally exterminate their entire treasure, and when they are near to it, they have nothing further from which to labor. # LIB. I. SUMMAE

## Regarding the impediments of this work, on the part of the artist's body. Chapter IV.

We have now determined for you, in a general way, the impediments to this work. Now, truly, we shall address you with more specific discourse in this chapter, and we shall relate to you all those impediments most fully and in order, quite openly. We say, therefore: that if anyone does not have his organs complete, he will not be able to arrive at the completion of this work by himself, as if he were blind, or maimed in his extremities, since he is not helped by the members through which this art is perfected, as if they were the ministers of nature. But if the artist's body is weak and sick, such as the bodies of those suffering from fevers or lepers, whose limbs are falling off, or those laboring in the final stages of life, and elderly men of decrepit age, he will not arrive at the completion of the art. By these natural impotencies of the body, therefore, the artist is hindered in his intention.

## Regarding the impediments on the part of the artist's soul. Chapter V.

We have provided you with one chapter in which we related, in absolute and manifest speech, the impediments depending on the artist's body. It remains for us to relate briefly the impediments on the part of the soul itself, which most greatly hinder the completion of this work. We say, therefore, that he who does not have natural talent, and a soul that searches subtly into natural principles, the foundations of nature, and the crafts that can follow nature in the properties of its action, will not find the true root of this most precious science. Such are many who have a stiff neck, void of talent in every investigation, who can scarcely understand common speech, and who likewise learn common works with difficulty. Besides these, we also find many who have a soul that easily opines any fantasy whatsoever; yet what they believe they have found to be true is entirely fantastic, deviant from reason, full of error, and remote from natural principles, since their brain, filled with many <term>fumositates</term> <gloss>vapors or fumes</gloss>, cannot receive the true intention of natural things. Besides these, there are others who have a mobile soul, shifting from opinion to opinion, and from will to will, like those who now believe this and desire the same, without any foundation of reason. Yet, a little while after that, they believe something else similarly, and desire something else. And these are so mobile that they can scarcely finish the least bit of that which they intend, but rather leave it diminished. There are likewise others who cannot see any truth from natural things, no more than beasts, such as those captured by their mind, the insane, and children. There are also others who despise the science, and do not believe it to be: whom this science similarly despises, and repels them from the end of this most precious work. And there are those who are slaves, serving money, affirming this wonderful science themselves, but fearing to incur expenses; and therefore, although they affirm it, and investigate it according to reason, yet they do not arrive at the experience of the work because of the avarice of money. To these, therefore, our science does not come. For how could he who has been ignorant or has neglected to investigate the science easily arrive at it?

## Regarding external impediments hindering the work of this art. Chapter VI.

We have reduced to two chapters all the impediments delaying the end of this art, which are from the radical principles, according to the nature of the artist of this most precious business. It is therefore useful for us at last to relate the impediments supervening from the outside, and from contingent fortunes and chances, by which this most glorious work is hindered. We see, therefore, some who are astute and talented, in no way ignorant of the works of nature, and of those things in which it is possible

Gout rarely arises from <term>melancholia</term> <gloss>black bile</gloss>; if, however, it draws its origin from this dark humor, it is bad, both because it disturbs much more than others, and because it lasts longer and does not yield easily to medicines. Finally, if gout proceeds from a varied mixture of humors, signs of a mixed nature will arise in various ways.

Thus, the Phocians, having been accused by the Thebans and condemned in the common council of Greece to a sum of money so great that it could not be paid, were finally driven by desperation—having been deprived of their fields, children, and wives—to plunder that most famous Temple of Apollo which was at Delphi. From this later erupted the greatest wars, by which all of Greece was subjected to the yoke of the Macedonians. Justinus records this in book 8, chapter 1. A danger no less severe is to be feared from that Avarice in public affairs which is perceived in private matters, when, namely, either individual Magistrates or the whole body of Magistrates draw the goods of private citizens to themselves by force, deceit, and under some pretext.

## XIII.
Indeed, since this **Avarice** is a more frequent cause of ruin than the rest, a King will act most safely if he exacts small tributes in installments, with the consent of the estates, having demonstrated the necessity of the monetary matter; if he preserves the ordinary [tributes]; and if he does not easily command new ones. Adam Contzen, in book 9 of his *Politics*, chapter 8, § 4: Especially since there is no fouler vice to be found in Princes and those governing the Commonwealth than **Avarice**. *For to treat the Commonwealth as a source of profit is not only shameful, but also wicked and nefarious*, says Cicero. Indeed, it is contrary to nature itself; hence the same author says:

> To take something away from another, he says, and to increase one's own advantage at the inconvenience of a human being, is more contrary to nature than death, than poverty, than pain, or than other things that can happen either to the body or to external circumstances. For it destroys the fellowship and society of men: if we are so disposed that each person plunders or violates another for the sake of his own gain, then that society of the human race, which is most in accordance with nature, must necessarily be torn apart.

## XIV.
Often, **Ambition** in those who wield the scepter is accustomed to produce a plague in Commonwealths equal to, or indeed almost greater than, **Avarice**. From this, as if from a Lernaean hydra <note>a reference to the many-headed serpent of Greek myth; a source of endless trouble</note> of evils, besides the wars of which it is the torch, infinite other evils also spring forth, and it is often accustomed to bring the greatest plague and ruin even upon the ambitious themselves. For although **Avarice** also exists as a frequent cause of war, far</translation>

<translation page="10">more persistent in this is Ambition. *Indeed, their own wicked causes drive each man into battles, yet the lust for power holds the chief place at home*, says Adam Contzen, *Pol. lib. 10, cap. 8*. Hence Thucydides rightly said: *The cause of all evils is the desire for power arising from ambition.* And Polybius, a most serious writer, says that after some city has overcome and struggled through many and great dangers and has already ascended to leadership and power: *It is manifest that where favorable fortune is not employed with moderation, it fixes its seat there, and luxury creeps into customs, and ambition and stubbornness into the spirits of men, both regarding the Magistracy and regarding others. Once these evils have prevailed, they will be the beginning of a change for the worse, [arising] from honors sought through Ambition or denied.*

XV. Many, however, judge themselves to be happy in every respect only then, if they can enlarge their Kingdom by adding new provinces to the old, ignorant of the fact that, according to Seneca, *Epistle 113*, to rule oneself is the greatest Empire. Nor do they attend to the most certain ruin of their own provinces resulting from this: for while, not content with their own borders, they covet many provinces, they often lose those which they have already placed in safety. The cities of Greece are an example, which, while each desired to rule, all lost their power. *Justinus, book 8, chapter 1.*

XVI. Therefore, that saying of Thucydides in his description of the sedition at Corcyra is from the mouth of Truth: *The cause of all evils is the desire for power and Ambition.* From these affections is born every calamity. Thence come the atrocious wars continued in a perpetual series from the beginning of the founded world. Inflamed by this, Alexander pursued all of Asia with fire and sword, and Cyrus had previously devastated Ionia. Demosthenes is said to have once stated that if two paths were open—one to the underworld, the other to the throne—he would choose the one that led to the underworld. I believe he did not speak sincerely, but nevertheless, it shows the most miserable ambition of those who, through labors, dangers, and wounds, ascend to a slippery and tottering summit, agitated by lightning and winds, where they can neither stand nor depart from there.</translation>

<summary>This passage discusses the dangers of avarice and ambition in political leadership, illustrating how these vices—often compared to external plagues—lead to the destruction of both rulers and the commonwealths they govern.</summary>
<keywords>Avarice, Ambition, Thucydides, Cicero, Adam Contzen, Commonwealth, Political Corruption, Desire for Power, Tyranny</keywords>

the category of substance, an individual substance, which does not depend on accidents, and is in that prior state of Nature something distinct from all accidents, by which this human is an individual human, to such an extent that those accidents presuppose and follow singularity rather than constitute it, and Socrates is Socrates with all accidents mentally abstracted. Therefore, his statements must be understood either concomitantly, because the collection of accidents follows (as has been said) the individuation of substance, or notificatively, because through them, as notes and signs, we recognize the individual. See Zabarella, frequently elsewhere in book 2, chapter 2; Jakob Martini, *Metaphysical Exercises*, book 1, theorem 5.

->IV.<-

**We therefore posit, not inconveniently, that the power of individuating is held by the form, not as a peculiar property, but as a specific and communicated power of matter.**

What that is, through which a human is what he is, as Scaliger speaks in his *Exercises*, section 6, number 1, we have not yet investigated with sufficient clarity. The theorem says, however, that it is the form. Now, since it is the function of the form to bestow being, quiddity, and the totality of quiddity, as attested by Armando de Bello Visu, *Treatise 2 on Causes*, chapter 142, a distinction must be considered between giving being and the act of a thing. This being is twofold, and therefore the act is also twofold: one is the being of <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence</gloss>
</translation>

<translation page="10">
<header>Metaphysical Disputation.</header>

the other of <term>hyparxis</term> <gloss>existence</gloss>. Wherefore the act can also be taken either for the degree of essence, which the form bestows—since the form of an animal constitutes an animal, and the form of a human constitutes a human—or for the act of existence outside the soul, which the form likewise bestows. Truly, not just any form does this, but only that final and specific one, which is directed toward no other thing than causing the thing to exist individually. Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> explains this no less skillfully than elegantly in Part 1 of the *Summa*, Question 3, Articles 2 and 3, and in other places, when he says: "To be is the actuality of the form; for form implies potentiality before it is placed in being; therefore being is compared to essence as act is to potency." For this reason, we see that the form of an animal, and any other general form, constitutes the essence proper to that thing, such as the essence of an animal or a plant, yet it cannot bestow actual existence without the help of the specific form, which alone then constitutes the essence of the species and makes the thing exist in act. ### XIV.

It is false that Hatto, Archbishop of Mainz, was devoured by mice. The argument regarding the tower that can still be seen today on the Rhine, which they usually bring forward to confirm their opinion, is entirely inept and does not sustain the dignity of proof in the least.

### XV.

It is a common opinion that the Emperor Henry VII of Luxembourg was removed by Francis Paulinus, a monk of the Order of Saint Bernard, by means of a sacramental host soaked in poison. It is not without reason that this is doubted, because Conrad Vecerius, who described his life most diligently, recorded nothing of the sort.

### XVI.

That the Emperor Charles IV alienated the Kingdom of Burgundy Transjurane, or Arelatense, cannot be proven by certain and undoubted records. Neither can the proponents of the contrary opinion provide or demonstrate a diploma for such an alienation, although it is otherwise known that he was somewhat too liberal toward the French, and even the Princes of the Rhine.

### XVII.

<margin>Germany, chapter 28 in the book on the Origin of the Bohemians.</margin>
Those who think the Bohemians obtained their name from some King Bohemus are absurd. To this error also pertains that of those who write that they were a Gallic nation, among whom are Cornelius Tacitus and Johannes Matthias of the Sudetenland, to whom Melchior Goldastus otherwise owes a great deal. But there are just causes that urge us not to agree with them.

<summary>This page continues the investigation of historical legends and claims, disputing accounts of Archbishop Hatto's death, the poisoning of Henry VII, the alienation of Burgundy by Charles IV, and the origin of the Bohemian name.</summary>

However, the most numerous and principal aspects of Nazariteship seem to be able to be referred to these three heads: (1) That they should not drink wine or strong drink, or anything else that could intoxicate. <term>Sicera</term> <gloss>strong drink/cider</gloss> was called by the Jews, as Peter Martyr notes in his commentary, water that was poured onto pressed grapes after the wine was expressed, and where it had fermented, it retained some flavor of wine, and was the same as that which we call secondary wine, and which in Upper Saxony is called <term>Lauer</term> <gloss>a weak, secondary wine or mash</gloss>. (2) That they should not shave their heads, but keep their hair throughout the whole of their Nazariteship. (3) That they should not defile themselves with funeral mourning, and not even at the death of a father. A vow of such a kind Paul also seems to have had in Acts 21. Samson was, therefore, from his very first birth, a holy and public person, and he was such also in his death. (2) Concerning what Samson did, some things were said no less in the doctrine regarding the object; namely, after he had judged the Israelite people for some time, he was captured by the Philistines, deprived of his eyes, and thrown into prison. There he recovered the grace of God and the power of his Nazariteship, and thus in his recovered vocation, he redeemed the people of Israel and freed his fatherland from the enemies by whom it was oppressed. He fought bravely, conquered, and sealed the victory with his own death. (3) Where this deed happened, the sacred history teaches, namely in some public place where the Philistines had gathered to celebrate a festival to the false god Dagon, where God was mocked, and Samson, that chosen Prince of God, was held in derision. Not a few think that this house was the temple of Dagon itself, on account of its size, which is not to be presumed in a private house:

(4) By what aids he did this, is evident from the prayers, namely by supernatural aid, the special grace of God, and clearly divine assistance. (5) Finally, it must be seen how that man of God, a judge of the people and thus a public person, freed his own people and avenged the deprivation of his eyes and the injury brought upon himself and God through this. ->§. 19.<-

Samson, therefore, did not kill himself properly, as he would have done if he had run himself through with a sword or dashed his head against a column; but he allowed himself to be crushed along with the enemy. Nor did he kill himself by moral imputation, because primarily he intended to kill the Philistines and seek vengeance for his eyes. Secondarily, however, and only permissively, he involved himself in that same destruction which he could not escape. Which was, indeed, of great fortitude, as Cornel. à Lap. <note>Cornelius a Lapide, a prominent Jesuit biblical commentator</note> says on this passage. Not incongruously, therefore, Ambrose says of him in Epistle 70 on this passage: 
> *Samson conquered himself in death; and although he was incomparable in this life, nevertheless he conquered himself in death, and bore an insuperable spirit, so that he despised, and as if for nothing held, the end of life which is fearful to all.*

It was, therefore, of virtue that he closed his day with a number of victories, and found not a captive end, but a triumphal one. Finally, not by weapons,

<summary>This page concludes that Samson’s death was not suicide but a permitted act of martyrdom and military necessity, supported by the interpretation of Ambrose.</summary>
<keywords>Samson, suicide, fortitude, Cornelius a Lapide, Ambrose, Philistines, martyrdom</keywords>
</translation>

### V.
There is no less doubt among the interpreters of law: whether, besides the actions of good faith <note>original: "actiones bonaefidei"</note> enumerated in paragraph 28 of the Institutes on actions, others of the same kind are to be found? We similarly deny this: thinking that by that very fact the most absolute and perfect enumeration of all good faith actions is contained therein.
*The common Doctors, as Schneidewinus reports on the said paragraph, number 8, where Donellus speaks elegantly on the same. Cujacius on 11, observation 28. Lorius in the treatise on actions, axiom 20. Corasius on the said paragraph in "Differences."*

### VI.
Do we see very often that form alone serves as a dowry for girls? Hence, for a special reason, we think it has been received by the Doctors: that the condition of a virgin's face, if injured by deformity and visible scars, can be taken into account.
*Ravennas on the law "from this," law 3, Digest on whether a quadruped is said to have caused damage, whom Albericus commends in the same place.*

For Difference and the Univocal have a Genus, and they differ through something of themselves, such as a Specific Difference. But indeed, some Disparates grasp neither of those. ### XXVIII.

Furthermore, a feud established in this way is finally acquired through a proper investiture, which is usually called such, namely, a delivery made under some just title, <note>(a)</note> and thus the feudal contract is said to be consummated. The effects of this acquisition are considered both in the utilities <note>(b)</note> or advantages arising from the feudal thing, and in the burdens to be performed on the occasion of the thing granted in feud, and regarding the disposition, which is especially observed in alienation, otherwise, our discussion would grow too large.

<note>(a) Title 1, title 2, law 33, book 2 of feuds; Iacobinus in the verse "invested such," number 11; Vulteius, book 1, feuds, chapter 10, number 6. (b) Vulteius, book 1, feuds, chapter 10, number 17, with what follows; Rosenthal, whole chapter 8.</note>

### XXIX.

Regarding advantages, once the delivery of the thing is made, a quasi-dominion of the feudal thing is transferred to the vassal, which is commonly called useful <term>dominium utile</term> <gloss>beneficial ownership</gloss>: and so he obtains free power of administering and enjoying <note>(a)</note> it, saving however the substance of the thing, <note>(b)</note> with the ownership remaining with the Lord. <note>(c)</note>

<note>(a) § "But the thing," § "although," title 8, title 23, in the end, title 43, in the word "usefully," there the Doctors, book 2 of feuds; Iacobinus on the word "invested," number 10; Rosenthal, chapter 1, conclusion 4; Vulteius, chapter 10, number 8. (b) Title 8, book 2 of feuds. Like a usufructuary, law 1, § 3, Digest, on usufruct; how it is provided. Clarus, question 47 and 56; Vulteius, chapter 10, number 38. # PARADOX VII.

## Although the <term>Lunula</term> <gloss>crescent shape</gloss> (a part of the circle) has long since been reduced to a square space by Hippocrates of Chios, the <term>quadrature</term> <gloss>squaring</gloss> of the circle has not yet been discovered to this very day.

### DECLARATION.

The <term>Tetragonism</term> <gloss>squaring of a square/quadrature</gloss>, or <term>quadrature</term> of the circle, has been attempted hitherto by two principal methods, either Geometrically through lines, or Arithmetically through numbers: by the former method, the <term>Lunula</term> was long ago reduced to a square space by Hippocrates of Chios, but the circle itself, in no way, neither Geometrically nor Arithmetically, could be squared to this very day.

### DEMONSTRATION.

That the quadrature of <term>lunulae</term> was most correctly discovered by Hippocrates of Chios, no one will deny if they have properly grasped his demonstration, for it is as follows: Let there be drawn a circle *a, b, c, d*, and upon its diameter *b, c* let a square *b, e, f, c* be constructed, whose diagonal</translation>

<translation page="13">is *b, d, f*. (see Fig. VI.) Let there also be drawn a semidiameter *g, i, d*, perpendicular to *b, e*, which will bisect both the semicircle *b, d, c* and the diagonal *b, d, f* at point *d*. Therefore, having made *d* the center with interval *d, b*, let another circle be described through points *b, e, f*, and let the straight line *d, c* be connected. Since, however, in the right-angled triangle *b, e, f*, the side *b, f* subtends the right angle *b, e, f*, its square will be double the square of *b, e* or *e, f* according to the 47th proposition of the first book of Euclid. And consequently, the circle *b, e, f* will be double the circle *a, b, d, c* according to the 2nd proposition of the twelfth book of Euclid, and the semicircle *b, e, f* will be double the semicircle *b, a, c*, and the quadrant *b, g, d, c* will be equal to the same semicircle *b, a, c*. Therefore, with the common segment *b, g, c, i* removed, there remains the lunula *b, a, c, g*, equal to the triangle *b, i, d*. If that triangle is squared according to the last proposition of the second book of Euclid, the lunula *b, a, c, g* will be squared. But that the circle to this very day has not been reduced to a square space, neither through lines nor through numbers, is clearly evident from the most recent writings of geometers. Hippocrates indeed persuaded himself that by the same reasoning with which he had completed the quadrature of the lunula (a part of the circle), the whole circle could also be squared, and therefore he attributed the invention of the tetragonism, or quadrature of the circle, to himself. But indeed, how ingeniously he had restored the lunula to a square space, so foully did he hallucinate in squaring the circle, as is plain to anyone from Father Caspar Schott's *Technica Curiosa*, Book VIII, § 1, my page 600, 601, and Christopher Clavius's *Mathematical Works*, Volume II, Book VIII, page 189. Indeed, it is credible, says Blancanus in *Aristotle's Mathematical Places*, that Hippocrates recognized this fallacy (which he used in squaring the circle) and concealed it because of the subtlety of the invention. It happens no differently with the most recent attempts at the quadrature of the circle, in which, when properly examined, a paralogism is for the most part detected, so that many today judge the tetragonism to be absolutely impossible; see *Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensium* <gloss>Journal of the Learned of Leipzig</gloss>, month of September, year 1687, page 524. Therefore, although the lunula (a part of the circle) has long since been reduced to a square space, the quadrature of the circle has nevertheless not yet been discovered to this very day. Which was to be demonstrated.

### XXI.

Therefore, parents succeed to their children who have died without children, brothers, or sisters equally; they succeed per capita <gloss>by the head/individually</gloss> alongside surviving brothers or sisters connected to the deceased on both sides, but they succeed by the right of representation per stirpes <gloss>by branch/lineage</gloss> alongside the children of these.

### XXII.

Parents of a different line, from the paternal and maternal sides, established in an equal degree, divide the inheritance of the deceased today not according to the number of persons as a fair portion, but having regard for the branch, without distinction of the goods left by the deceased.

### XXIII.

It is a well-known point of law that brothers and the children of brothers connected to the deceased on only one side are excluded by all ascendants.

### XXIV.

An adoptive father cannot be an heir to his adopted son, whom he does not have under his power, although such a son succeeds to him.

### XXV.

I would say something different regarding the person into whose power the adopted party passes, to whom succession is granted just as it is to an <term>arrogator</term> <gloss>one who adopts a person already independent</gloss> in the goods of a son who has reached puberty and has been adopted, as to a legitimate and natural father.

### XXVI.

Natural parents succeed to their children, whom they have legitimized by subsequent marriage, by a rescript <gloss>written order</gloss> of the prince, or by presentation to the Curia, just as natural and legitimate parents do.

### XXVII.

In the same manner that natural children and illegitimate children succeed to their parents, so too do the parents succeed to them; namely, the natural father and his ascendants succeed to their natural son in two twelfths <gloss>a portion of the estate</gloss>, while the mother and ascendants from the maternal line succeed to the whole.

### XXIIX.

I believe there is no doubt that those born from incest and condemned coitus, if they cease to be among the living, have neither father nor mother, nor any of the ascendants as a successor.

### XXIX.

These are the rules concerning succession for those who stand in the direct line; when these are lacking, the collaterals succeed in the oblique line, whose succession extends to the tenth degree.

### XXX.

But whether the succession of agnates <gloss>relatives on the father's side</gloss> in the succession of an ancient fief is restricted to certain degrees or proceeds to infinity, the opinions of doctors vary due to conflicting texts, which I believe should be reconciled by a rule of distinction.

### XXXI.

Brothers and sisters <term>ἀμφιθαλεῖς</term> <gloss>born of the same father and mother</gloss> who are connected on both sides, with those connected on only one side excluded, are called to the inheritance of a pre-deceased brother per capita, while children of pre-deceased brothers connected on both sides, but not others, are called by the right of representation per stirpes.

</translation>

### XXXII.

Does a half-brother <term>consanguineus</term> <gloss>brother by the same father</gloss> also get excluded by those connected on both sides in the law of fiefs? The accepted opinion is that he is to be admitted to the fief of the deceased along with the brother connected on both sides.

### XXXIII.

Brothers succeed to one another in a paternal fief, but not so in a new one, as the fief reverts to the lord; however, sisters of both are incapable of succeeding.

### XXXIV.

If only children of brothers connected on both sides are present, and no paternal uncles survive, are they called to the succession of the deceased uncle per capita or per stirpes? It has been established that they are called per capita, both in new and old law, and this is true.

### XXXV.

If the deceased has left no brothers or sisters connected on both sides or their children, but only uterine <gloss>born of the same mother</gloss> or paternal siblings, then these are admitted to the brother’s inheritance.

### XXXVI.

Not, indeed, that paternal goods are assigned to paternal relatives and maternal to maternal, as in the old law, but the inheritance of the deceased is divided equally between the paternal and uterine relatives if they are present at the same time; if only one group is present, they shall obtain the entire inheritance.

### XXXVII.

Those adopted by ascendants from both the paternal and maternal lines succeed to one another transversally, as do those <term>arrogati</term> <gloss>those adopted under the power of another</gloss>, although they are not at all included under the name of blood relatives.

### XXXIIX.

Collaterals related to one another by a natural bond through the father enjoy no right of succession; however, it is certain law that those connected through the maternal line, even if one is natural and the other legitimate, succeed to one another.

### XXXIX.

Illegitimate children born of one and the same father, but different mothers, are prohibited from succeeding to one another; a fact that no one would affirm regarding <term>ὁμογαστρίοις</term> <gloss>those born of the same womb/mother</gloss> illegitimate children.

### XL.

Among incestuous brothers, and also those adopted by a stranger, there is no succession.

### XLI.

After brothers and brothers’ children, those who are closer in degree are called per capita, so that those equal in degree are admitted equally without difference of sex.

### XXX.

But whether the succession of agnates <gloss>relatives on the father's side</gloss> in the succession of an ancient fief is restricted to certain degrees or proceeds to infinity, the opinions of doctors vary due to conflicting texts, which I believe should be reconciled by a rule of distinction.

### XXXI.

Brothers and sisters <term>ἀμφιθαλεῖς</term> <gloss>born of the same father and mother</gloss> who are connected on both sides, with those connected on only one side excluded, are called to the inheritance of a pre-deceased brother per capita, while children of pre-deceased brothers connected on both sides, but not others, are called by the right of representation per stirpes.

<summary>This page details the laws of succession regarding parents, agnate relatives, and the specific rights of adopted, natural, and illegitimate children in both general inheritance and feudal systems.</summary>

### XXXII.

Does a half-brother <term>consanguineus</term> <gloss>brother by the same father</gloss> also get excluded by those connected on both sides in the law of fiefs? The accepted opinion is that he is to be admitted to the fief of the deceased along with the brother connected on both sides.

### XXXIII.

Brothers succeed to one another in a paternal fief, but not so in a new one, as the fief reverts to the lord; however, sisters of both are incapable of succeeding.

### XXXIV.

If only children of brothers connected on both sides are present, and no paternal uncles survive, are they called to the succession of the deceased uncle per capita or per stirpes? It has been established that they are called per capita, both in new and old law, and this is true.

### XXXV.

If the deceased has left no brothers or sisters connected on both sides or their children, but only uterine <gloss>born of the same mother</gloss> or paternal siblings, then these are admitted to the brother’s inheritance.

### XXXVI.

Not, indeed, that paternal goods are assigned to paternal relatives and maternal to maternal, as in the old law, but the inheritance of the deceased is divided equally between the paternal and uterine relatives if they are present at the same time; if only one group is present, they shall obtain the entire inheritance.

### XXXVII.

Those adopted by ascendants from both the paternal and maternal lines succeed to one another transversally, as do those <term>arrogati</term> <gloss>those adopted under the power of another</gloss>, although they are not at all included under the name of blood relatives.

### XXXIIX.

Collaterals related to one another by a natural bond through the father enjoy no right of succession; however, it is certain law that those connected through the maternal line, even if one is natural and the other legitimate, succeed to one another.

### XXXIX.

Illegitimate children born of one and the same father, but different mothers, are prohibited from succeeding to one another; a fact that no one would affirm regarding <term>ὁμογαστρίοις</term> <gloss>those born of the same womb/mother</gloss> illegitimate children.

### XL.

Among incestuous brothers, and also those adopted by a stranger, there is no succession.

### XLI.

After brothers and brothers’ children, those who are closer in degree are called per capita, so that those equal in degree are admitted equally without difference of sex.

### XLII.

So much for the succession of those related to the deceased by kinship: to whom

In their outward appearance, the <term>Pâlem</term> do not differ essentially from the <term>Somraï</term> and <term>Gâberi</term>. They are powerful, well-proportioned, and often tall figures, with a more or less black skin color that generally shows no hues leaning toward reddish or yellowish, and they also seem to understand the <term>Bagirmi</term> language for the most part.

The sky had become densely covered with clouds, and thunder rolled on all sides as we set up our night camp at the feet of a few <term>Delêb</term> palms without any other tree cover. I spent half the night performing surgical treatments on the wounded. I sutured flesh wounds with horsehair and bandaged the more serious injuries as best I could. Yet some had penetrating chest and abdominal wounds or exposed shoulder and hip joints, and a few gave up the ghost that very night.

The next morning (June 1st), we set off an hour before sunrise and moved, also in an approximate easterly direction, across a low-lying area with lush grass growth, which was identified to me as the <term>Komodûgu</term>. In the deepest places, it showed swampy ground and small pools of water here and there, and according to the people, it is said to stretch north toward <term>Mul</term> and northwest toward the <term>Ba Ili</term>. We had passed a similar grassy, treeless, and (in summer) water-rich valley, which seemed to extend from southeast to northwest, the previous evening. Both, as well as the valley-like depression near <term>Murki</term> and another one situated south-southwest of <term>Gundi</term> that we saw later, seem to be parts of the swamp network from which the <term>Ba Ili</term> eventually develops. An hour after sunrise, we turned south, passed numerous scattered and barricaded homesteads that already belonged to <term>Gundi</term>, moved past the center of this main village of the <term>Tummok</term> tribe, and made camp at 8 o'clock in the morning. Immediately, everyone set out into the

surroundings to look for roofs and wall coverings from huts, poles and fences, wooden mortars, and other household utensils—in short, all the necessary residential requirements. <translation page="88">As for the complaints, they are as follows: It is a low state for a woman to be a common object, so that if one person enters and another also enters, they will undoubtedly kill one another. What was said—that one must pay five hundred <term>karshapana</term> <gloss>ancient Indian coins</gloss> to enter—is also true; it is necessary for her clothing and adornments without doubt.

What was said—that the house must be vacated after seven days—is also true; whether it is done sooner or later, what conflict is there in that? What was said—that one does not inquire about the coming and going of men—is also true; because this is a courtesan, if one were to inquire about the coming and going of all the men, who would ever enter her house?

Then, the assembly granted her the five supreme conditions, and she began to be enjoyed by the assembly. As the Licchavis of Vaishali began to enter her house to enjoy themselves as they wished, some, due to an intense attachment to worldly things, became free of desire the moment they saw her. Others were satisfied by mere touch, and none of them performed the act of a man. She thought, "Since these are not men, I must prepare a strategy." Having settled in various places,

<leaf-break/>

there was one named Amrapali, who possessed perfect beauty and youth, and was skilled in the sixty-four arts; she was a woman worthy of being enjoyed by the gods alone. She said, "Your Majesty, if that is the case, I shall go to Vaishali and enjoy myself with him as I please." The King said, "The Licchavis of Vaishali have long been enemies who cause harm and strike back; they will bring harm upon you." The King said, "Wise ones, these men are brave in heart, so I will go." She said, "Your Majesty, if you insist on a matter that has no purpose, then you may go." She boarded a chariot and set out for Vaishali with the King. Gradually arriving in Vaishali, the King stayed in the pleasure grove.

The King entered Amrapali's house, and after a short time, the sound of a bell arose. The Licchavis of Vaishali became agitated and said, "Wise ones, a person who is not our friend has entered, and the bell has rung." As the sound became clear and grew loud, King Bimbisara asked Amrapali, "Lovely one, what is this?" "Your Majesty, someone is checking the residence." "For what reason?" "For your sake." "What shall we do? Shall we flee?" "Your Majesty, do not be displeased. Your Majesty, when seven days have passed and..."</translation>

<translation page="89">...I am checking the residence, so for the time being, for seven days, enjoy yourself as you wish. Enjoy yourself to your heart’s content, and when the seven days have passed, you will know the time."

He played with her, delighted with her, and enjoyed himself as he pleased. After some time, Amrapali became pregnant and said to King Bimbisara, "Your Majesty, I am with child." He gave her a piece of linen and a signet ring, saying, "If it is a girl, it is yours. But if it is a boy, wrap him in this linen, place the signet ring around his neck, and bring him to my presence." That passed, and as she boarded the chariot to depart with the King, the bell rang. They said, "Wise ones, the enemy has appeared, so follow and search!" As five hundred Licchavis with arrow-spoke wheels pursued King Bimbisara, the King saw them and said, "Your Majesty, if the Licchavis of Vaishali are coming, will you fight them, or shall I drive the chariot?" He said, "I am exhausted, so drive the chariot and you alone engage in battle with them." As he began to fight with them, the people of Vaishali recognized him

<leaf-break/>

and said, "Wise ones, the one who is our enemy is the father of this child," and they struck him even more fiercely. When she eventually told her mother what had happened, she thought, "The Licchavis of Vaishali are cruel and powerful. If he is killed, there is a place for that." As she sat thinking such thoughts, she saw many merchants loaded with goods heading toward Rajagriha. She said, "Take this signet ring; by showing it, you will obtain passage and will not be charged tolls. Lead this boy to the royal palace as well, place this signet ring around his neck, and leave him at the gate of Rajagriha." They agreed, saying they would do so. She also gave the boy a pearl necklace and said, "Son, when you meet the King, place the pearl necklace on your feet and sit in his lap, appearing afraid. If anyone says, 'This boy does not know how to be afraid,' then say to them, 'Is there any boy who does not fear his father?'" He traveled gradually with the merchants to Rajagriha. They bathed, tied the signet ring on him, and left him at the gate of the royal palace. He went to where the King was...</translation>

<summary>This passage recounts the history of the courtesan Amrapali, her relationship with King Bimbisara, and the birth of their son, who is sent to Rajagriha to escape the hostility of the Licchavis of Vaishali.</summary>
