It is therefore prioritized in mention. What is more astonishing than the magpie, in the veracity of its senses, the intensity of its caution, and its keen awareness? Yet there is no bird on earth that protects its eggs as abundantly, as intensely, or with as profound knowledge as it does. Uthman ibn Affan, may God be pleased with him, said: "Everything loves its young, even the bustard," which is used as a proverb for stupidity. However, the magpie, despite its mastery of causes and its speed in snatching, does not utilize this for what is beneficial. How many precious and significant necklaces, or noble and fine earrings, have been snatched from the hands of people! It would either toss them away after circling in the air, or stash them away and never look at them again. Al-Asma‘i claimed that a magpie once snatched a valuable necklace from some people. The owners of the necklace seized a Bedouin woman who was with them. While she was being beaten, dragged, and cursed, the magpie passed by with the necklace in its beak. They shouted at it, and it dropped it. The Bedouin woman said, referring to her safety after having been afflicted by another calamity:

> The day of the necklace was one of our Lord’s wonders,
> As if He saved me from the town of evil.

She meant those of the city dwellers who had been afflicted. There is no harm in mentioning what occurs, provided it is not from those long chapters that contain nothing but dry measurements and purely speculative speech; for that is something whose hearing does not lighten the spirit, nor do souls feel eager to read it. The craftsman and the seeker of reward and virtue may endure such things, so whenever we find a chapter that can be adorned with elegant, eloquent poetry and interesting anecdotes, we take the trouble to do so and narrate it in full, for the reader to benefit. For this reason, we have permitted ourselves to say what we have said in the chapter on fire. I am writing for you after this, since I have already wearied you with length and burdened you with the most difficult tasks and roughest paths, as we have mentioned therein a goodly amount of the speech of the dialecticians. I do not wish to increase your boredom or tax your strength by starting the discourse on camels, cows, sheep, lions, wolves, donkeys, gazelles, and the like, which I intend to write for you. Rather, I will provide small, short, concise, and pleasant chapters, so that you do not finish the first chapter without being energized for the second, and likewise the third and fourth, until the end of what I am writing for you, God willing. We will begin with what pertains to the sparrow, then we will take up the mention of the mouse.</translation>

This, even though I have not yet mentioned anything of the long chapters. I have proceeded to mention the differences between jinn and humans, between angels and prophets, between the female and the male, and between them and that which is neither female nor male, until our discourse extends to the superiority of man over all types of animals, the mention of nations and eras, the mention of divisions and lifespans, and the mention of the scales of intellects through sciences and crafts. These are the wonders for which souls have a craving and toward which sound intellects have an intense yearning. For this reason, I have written it for you, driven it toward you, and sought reward in you. If you find the book I have written for you to be contrary...</translation>

<translation page="19">
<header>OF POLYBIUS</header>

But when they are driven by the desire for command, and cannot achieve this through themselves and their own virtue, they squander their estates, enticing and corrupting the masses in every way. When they have once made the multitude greedy for gifts and accustomed to living on the property of others, the democracy is destroyed and transforms into rule by force and violence. For the multitude, accustomed to feeding on the property of others and to finding their hope of survival in the possessions of their neighbors, when they find a leader who is ambitious and daring, but excluded from political honors due to poverty, they then establish rule by force. Then, gathering together, they perform massacres, exiles, and re-distributions of land, until they have become savage once more and find a new master and monarch. This is the cycle of governments, this is the arrangement of nature, according to which they change, shift, and eventually return to the same state. Anyone who has clearly understood these things may perhaps miss the mark in terms of time when speaking about the future of a government, but he will rarely be mistaken about whether it is growing or decaying, or in what direction it will shift, provided he makes his judgment without excess passion. Indeed, regarding the Roman government, through this sort of scrutiny we would come to the greatest knowledge of its constitution, its growth, its peak, and likewise the change that will happen in the opposite direction. For if any other government, as I have just said, happens to have its constitution and growth according to nature from the start, it will also have the nature of changing into its opposite. It will be possible to observe this through what will be said hereafter. Now, we shall make a brief mention of the legislation of Lycurgus. For the account is not irrelevant to the intended goal. For he examined each of the previously mentioned
</translation>

<translation page="20">
<header>THE SIXTH</header>

<sig>B ii</sig>

things that are accomplished necessarily and according to nature, and concluded that every form of government which is simple and established upon a single power becomes precarious, because it quickly slips into its own innate and naturally accompanying vice. For just as rust is the inherent corruption of iron, and wood-worms and wood-borers are the inherent corruption of wood, even if they escape all external harm, they are destroyed by the very things that grow within them. In the same way, a certain vice naturally accompanies and follows each form of government: kingship has its monarchy, aristocracy its oligarchy, and democracy its savage rule by violence. It is impossible that these governments will not, in time, undergo the shifts mentioned above according to the argument just made. Foreseeing this, Lycurgus did not establish a government that was simple or uniform, but gathered together all the virtues and characteristics of the best governments, so that no part, by growing beyond what is proper, would slip into the vices naturally inherent to it. Since the power of each is restrained by the others, none of them will incline or drift too far in any direction, but will remain balanced and on an even scale, so that the state may remain stable for a long time according to the principle of sailing against the wind. The arrogance of the kings is restrained by fear of the people, as the latter are given a sufficient share in the government. The people, in turn, do not dare to despise the kings due to fear of the elders, who, being selected by choice, were always intended to apply themselves to justice. Thus, the portion of the disadvantaged, by adhering to custom, always becomes greater and more influential through the elders
</translation>

<summary>Polybius describes the cyclical degradation of simple government forms into their corresponding vices, advocating for a mixed constitution as a means of preservation, with the Spartan system of Lycurgus as an initial example of this structural balance.</summary>
<keywords>Polybius, cycle of governments, democracy, oligarchy, kingship, Lycurgus, mixed constitution, political stability</keywords>

In the same way, a certain vice naturally accompanies and follows each form of government: kingship has its monarchy, aristocracy its oligarchy, and democracy its savage rule by violence. It is impossible that these governments will not, in time, undergo the shifts mentioned above according to the argument just made. Foreseeing this, Lycurgus did not establish a government that was simple or uniform, but gathered together all the virtues and characteristics of the best governments, so that no part, by growing beyond what is proper, would slip into the vices naturally inherent to it. Since the power of each is restrained by the others, none of them will incline or drift too far in any direction, but will remain balanced and on an even scale, so that the state may remain stable for a long time according to the principle of sailing against the wind. The arrogance of the kings is restrained by fear of the people, as the latter are given a sufficient share in the government. The people, in turn, do not dare to despise the kings due to fear of the elders, who, being selected by choice, were always intended to apply themselves to justice. Thus, the portion of the disadvantaged, by adhering to custom, always becomes greater and more influential through the elders

However, knowledge is of two types. One is that which, according to common usage, is called knowledge; the other is that which, according to common usage, is not called so, yet it is considered by the masters of <term>Haqiqat</term> <gloss>ultimate reality</gloss> to be of the category of knowledge. This is because they have witnessed the pervasion of the essential knowledge of the Truth, may He be glorified, in all existing things. And it is from the second category, for example, that although one is not considered learned by common usage, one sees that he distinguishes between high and low, deviates from the high, and proceeds toward the low. In the same way, it penetrates into the body, arranges the appearance of the body of the one who experiences the unveiling <note>referring to the process of <term>mukashafa</term> or mystical unveiling</note>, and performs other things besides these. Therefore, it is a property of knowledge to flow according to the requirements of the capacity of the recipient, without opposition to it. However, at the level of nature, it has appeared in the form of nature. And by this analogy, [there is] the pervasion of knowledge in all other existing things, nay, the pervasion of all perfections.</translation>

<translation page="55">
| | |
|---|---|
| That which follows existence in all existing things | |
| Existence with the attributes that were hidden within it | And it permeated all the essences of the world |
| The secret of the quality of this manifestation, which is capable of it | Became manifest according to the measure of the acceptance of the essence |

Just as the reality of existence, due to its pure absoluteness, is pervasive in the essences of all existing things in such a way that it is identical to those essences within them, just as those essences were identical to it within itself, so too are His perfect attributes, in their totality and absoluteness, pervasive in all the attributes of existing things. They are such that, within their attributes, they are identical to their attributes, just as their attributes were identical to those perfect attributes within those perfect attributes. For example, the attribute of knowledge, within the knowledge of the learned concerning particulars, is identical to the knowledge of particulars; and within the knowledge of the learned concerning universals, it is identical to the knowledge of universals.</translation>

<summary>This passage discusses the metaphysical extension of divine knowledge and perfections into all existing things, asserting that such attributes manifest according to the capacity of the recipient, similar to the way existence itself pervades all essences.</summary>

<translation page="13">
The son, having entered the footprints of his dear father,
Bestows many advantages upon my fatherland.
He presides over the afflicted, and kindly assists needy men,
And is prepared to bring aid to the miserable.
He once offered green pastures to my Muses,
And was always helpful to my studies.
For which, may God Almighty one day grant him
The heavenly joys of eternal life.
Skillful bridegroom, you will imitate these examples of your family,
Express your ancestors.
Thus your praise will grow, thus your generation will become
Brighter, and thus your fame will be perennial.
But since you reflect on these things more wisely through yourself:
Let my poems cease at his admonition.
Just as a strong horse born from strong seed
Does not fear the noise, nor flee from sorrowful weapons.
In no other way do you follow the deeds of famous parents,
Nor do you allow your character to degenerate.
Great joys deservedly sustain your mind,
Bride, because that man comes into your chambers.
I, even if I were to conquer Pylian <term>Nestor</term> <gloss>the wise king of Pylos in the Iliad</gloss> in speaking:
If I were greater in eloquence than <term>Cicero</term> <gloss>the Roman statesman and orator</gloss>:
I would not be able to commemorate all things according to merit,
Which the glory of such a groom demands to be brought forth.
Why therefore does my Muse rather desert the young husband,
And seek the face of the chaste maiden.
</translation>

<translation page="14">
Hail, renowned nymph, the glory of feminine modesty,
Hail, great glory of the maiden choir.
May He himself prosper the most holy laws of your marriage bed:
Who was the first patron and author of the bridal chamber.
Who first discovered the marriages of the sweet torch,
And who is said to love the sacred flames of the marriage bed.
May He placidly favor the compacts of your couch,
<term>Euphrosyne</term> <gloss>one of the Graces in Greek mythology</gloss>, a girl worthy of such a man.
Rare is your face, and the excellence of your form
Is so great that it makes you surpass the rest.
You lift your blue eyes into the sublime breezes
More often, and you shine entirely with a glowing color.
Such as it is accustomed to be from the shining light of the opposing
Sun, with the clouds frequently colored.
Or of the frosty mother <note>referring to Aurora, the dawn</note>, who drives the stars of heaven,
And leads the day from the eastern axis.
Such a color is seen on your face, lilies stained with purple
Blood scarcely redden so much for me.
Divine modesty decorates your beautiful countenance:
You are gentle, and you lack all rusticity.
Your ivory neck lowers hair the color of gold,
And flowery garlands polish your locks.
Your arms are whiter to you than snowy privets:
Each of your limbs reports its own adornment.
You also be cheerful, be glad with your whole heart,
Bridegroom, because she seeks your embraces.
</translation>

<summary>Page 13 praises the bridegroom's virtuous lineage and character, while page 14 shifts to a detailed, flowery description of the bride's physical beauty and grace.</summary>
<keywords>Epithalamium, marriage, virtue, beauty, bride, bridegroom, praise</keywords>

come again: We may likewise truthfully say of the Urdorff bath, and that entire region, that it is a gatherer of many delights, and so constituted that it lacks nothing to refresh not only the body but also the spirit and the mind. Which we prefer to let the favorable reader experience from visual inspection and use of the bath, rather than detaining him further with a longer historical narrative.

There is no grass or herb so small that it does not praise its Creator, so natural reason concludes for us how highly we must thank the miraculous goodness of God for this and many similar healing waters in our Zürich region. But we will give Him the best thanks when we not only count them among the wonders of nature and the gifts of God, but also use them to the honor of God, and do not sully the use of them through any immoderate, arrogant, profligate, and ungrateful misuse;
<margin>(e) Ps. 104, v. 24</margin>
also, in and with every use, to the praise of God and due thanks, we shall often repeat after holy David:

> How many are thy works, O Lord! In wisdom hast thou made them all, and the earth is full of thy riches.

## Report of Herr Johannes Waser, Pastor at Dinhard.
->From Jesus the Physician, salvation from nowhere else!<-

<note>A large ornamental initial E features floral and leaf motifs.</note>
**Honorable** and most learned Brother-in-law, Doctor Ziegler, etc.
Since I have heard that the third description of the bath at Urdorff is to be prepared for the press, I also wish to share what has been observed by me during the time of my 15-year pastoral service at Urdorff. This famous bath is heartily good for <term>calculus</term> <gloss>kidney or bladder stones</gloss>, as it softens and drives out kidney and bladder stones, sand, and grit, as many honorable persons besides myself have experienced in deed. For <term>cholericis</term> <gloss>those suffering from bile or jaundice</gloss>, it is also excellently suitable, of which it has carried out a great deal (f.b.), of which witnesses are for the most part still alive at this time. For <term>febricitanten</term> <gloss>those suffering from fevers</gloss> (of whatever kind they may be), it was beneficial. Many emaciated people, and those suffering from consumption or lung ailments, were brought there in weakness on soft litters, who, after completion of the cure, could ride home fresh and healthy on horseback. To the corrupted and ailing stomach, it brings back an excellent appetite and creates a desire for food. It <term>acuire</term> <gloss>sharpens</gloss> and sharpens the eyes most miraculously, so that many persons who had to use glasses or spectacles before the bath cure can afterwards write, read, and perform other business without them. I also well remember distinguished honorable people who visited it due to infertility and afterwards have highly praised its <term>efficaciam</term> <gloss>efficacy</gloss> and delightful effect. My successor, Herr Pastor Wirtz, also gives testimony to this blessing of God. A precious feature of this place is a helpful, gracious, friendly, and loving landlord and host for the bath; where the flaw is in the location, all inclination is lost.
</translation>

He will lay low the bodies of those born of Troy with hostile steel.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
The wave of the Scamander <note>a river in the Troad</note> will be a witness to his great virtues,
Which is poured out everywhere into the swift Hellespont,
And which, narrowing its course with heaped-up piles of bodies,
Will make the deep rivers warm, mixed with slaughter.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Finally, the spoil given to death will also be a witness,
When the polished tomb, heaped up with a high mound,
Will receive the snow-white limbs of the struck maiden <note>Polyxena, daughter of Priam, sacrificed at the tomb of Achilles</note>.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
For as soon as fortune grants the weary Achaeans the opportunity
To loosen the Neptunian chains <note>the walls built by Neptune</note> of the Dardanian city,
The high tombs will be drenched with the slaughter of Polyxena,
Who, like a victim succumbing to the double-edged steel,
Will throw down her trunk-like body with bended knee.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Wherefore come, join the desired loves of your heart,
Let the husband receive his divine bride in a happy union,
Let the bride be surrendered to her eager husband without delay.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
No nurse, revisiting her in the morning light,
Will be able to place the thread <note>the marriage-thread, worn as a sign of chastity</note> around her neck.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Nor will her anxious mother, mourning the lonely bed
Of her daughter, cease to hope for dear grandchildren.
*Run, drawing the threads, run, spindles.*
Such songs, foretelling the future happiness of Peleus,
The Fates <term>Parcae</term> <gloss>the goddesses of destiny</gloss> sang with divine hearts.

<summary>This page concludes the wedding song of Peleus and Thetis, detailing the future glory of their son Achilles, his role in the Trojan War, and the eventual sacrifice of Polyxena.</summary>
<keywords>Achilles, Polyxena, Trojan War, Fates, Peleus, Thetis, wedding song</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="197">
<header>ON CATULLUS</header>

For in days of old, the dwellers of heaven <term>Coelicolae</term> <gloss>inhabitants of heaven</gloss>
Were accustomed to visit chaste homes more often,
And to show themselves to mortal gatherings, before piety was scorned.
Often the father of the gods, revisiting his shining temples,
When the annual sacred rites had come on festival days,
Observed the chariots of the Cretans racing forward.
Often the wandering Liber <note>Bacchus</note> from the highest peak of Parnassus
Drove the Thyads <note>maenads/followers of Bacchus</note> with streaming hair,
When the people of Delphi, rushing from the whole city,
Joyfully received the gods at the smoking altars.
Often in the death-dealing contest of war, Mars <term>Mauors</term> <gloss>Mars</gloss>,
Or the mistress of the swift Triton <note>Minerva/Athena</note>, or the Rhamnusian maiden <note>Nemesis, goddess of vengeance</note>,
Were present, urging on the armed ranks of men.
But after the earth was stained with unspeakable crime,
And all drove justice from their greedy minds,
Brothers stained their hands with a brother's blood,
A son ceased to mourn his dead parents,
A father wished for the death of his firstborn son,
So that he might enjoy the bloom of a maiden stepmother,
A mother, wickedly placing herself beneath her ignorant son,
Did not fear to defile the divine household gods <term>Penates</term> <gloss>guardian spirits of the home</gloss>.
All things, permitted and forbidden, mixed with evil madness,
Turned the just mind of the gods away from us.
Wherefore they do not deign to visit such gatherings,
Nor do they suffer themselves to be touched by the clear light.

<summary>This passage laments the corruption of the world, explaining that the gods have abandoned humanity because of the prevalence of greed, violence, and taboo-breaking crimes.</summary>
<keywords>gods, justice, corruption, human depravity, myth, piety</keywords>
</translation>

or neglect of one required circumstance is enough; which they express in the common saying of <term>Dionysius</term>: "Any single defect causes evil, yet good is caused by an entire cause." A distinction must be noted here among the circumstances themselves, some of which transfer the moral act into a new genus of malice, while others leave it in the same genus but nevertheless increase the gravity of the sin. Thus, the example of fornication, which <term>Aquinas</term> brings forward, consists in this: that a man approaches one who is not his own. But if this circumstance is added, that he exercises his lust upon the spouse of another, it is then transferred into another genus of sin, namely injustice, in as much as a man usurps the thing of another. Whence adultery is called a graver offense than fornication. Let the example of the latter be some angry person, who gets angry when he ought not, at whom he ought not, and with an inconvenient gesture; this triplet of circumstances certainly makes this anger graver than if at least one of them were violated. Just as a sickness is graver which infects more parts of the body. It happens, however, sometimes, that some circumstance does not add a new deformity, but only increases that which had come from elsewhere. Just as taking another's property constitutes theft: but if this is added, that he takes much of another's property, it will be a graver sin. Nor is there any reason for someone to say that a circumstance, if it is evil, constitutes a certain species of sin by itself. For this is false, or at least not universal, since it can add a reason for malice within the same species. About which see <term>Thomas</term>. We add at least this, since it can also be referred to among circumstances, how often, or properly—which <term>Cajetan</term> denies—or by analogy, that also in the weighing of an offense is not to be passed over. Whence <term>Grotius</term>:

<margin>l. c. <gloss>the same place</gloss></margin>
> "A greater depravity also appears if someone has sinned more often: because habits are worse through evil acts."

# TH. XI.

## Eighthly, the gravity of vices differs according to the dignity of the virtues to which they are opposed.

<margin>3. 2. q. 73. art. 4. <gloss>First part of the second part, question 73, article 4.</gloss></margin>
<note>Thomas proves this from Aristotle: The Philosopher says that the worst is contrary to the best. The best in moral matters is the greatest virtue; the worst, however, is the most grievous sin.</note> Since, however, the dispute concerning the mutual comparison of virtues among themselves, and which of them holds the place of prince, has not yet been settled, nor is it possible to determine anything concerning vices in this respect, it will remain a complete matter. Truly, all virtues shine like stars, and our world of darkness is rendered illustrious by their rays. Yet which of them shines more, and relates to the others like the sun, <term>Piccolomineus</term> admits is not easy to judge.

<margin>Phil. de Mor. Gr. 4. c. 47. & 49. <gloss>Philosophy of Moral Grades, book 4, chapters 47 and 49.</gloss></margin>
And for each one, this same author brings forward something, by whose intuition they claim the principate for themselves quite probably, which he confirms both by reasons and the assent of the wise; and he warns first that, according to the diverse condition of men, judgments about this prerogative vary much, with those established in magistracy preferring justice, leaders of armies and soldiers preferring fortitude, men splendidly born and educated preferring magnificence, etc. Yet, these things notwithstanding, we believe that an opinion about the superiority can be fixed absolutely in some one virtue. This we prefer to express in the words of the most celebrated doctor of morals in Italy, already praised, rather than our own:

<margin>Phil. Mor. Gr. 4. c. 51. <gloss>Philosophy of Moral Grades, book 4, chapter 51.</gloss></margin>
> "Because that virtue must be judged absolutely best, to which the best reason for excellence—the most outstanding reason of dignity—must be sought especially from the end: the end of virtue is action, the most excellent of actions are those which proceed from justice; therefore, by right, justice holds the principate. That the action of justice is the best is evident: for its duty is to compose our actions toward others, to govern the rest appropriately, to gather together dispersed men, to preserve those gathered, to bind together Republics and the gatherings of men, both small and great, with golden ligaments, to benefit all, and to harm no one, which is most highly proper to virtue."

85. An elegant question can be discussed here by way of opportunity: Is a prior, perfected testament of a civilian broken by a later, imperfect one, in which those succeeding from intestacy are instituted as heirs, if in the later one a son has been passed over? Law 7, Digest on children and posthumous heirs. Law 16, paragraph 1, Digest on ordinary substitution.

Law 7, Digest on the testament of a soldier.

# M. GEORG GEORG FRIDERIC BLINSIG,
## FRIEND AND PATRON.

<note>A large decorative initial Q begins the poem.</note>

What skilled man, Fridericus, shall I call you?
With what titles, Fridericus, shall I adorn you
Dignified enough? Stunned, indeed,
I know not, I doubt, stunned indeed
That you are blessed with divine genius,
Blessed with divine judgment.
What? Should you be called undeservedly
Who? A second *Tirynthian Hercules* <note>A reference to Hercules, who was born in Tiryns.</note>
By Pollux! Not undeservedly are you called that,
Who? A second *Tirynthian Hercules*
Do you wish? I will demonstrate it, and you will give faith to my words.
What, I ask, is celebrated *Sophia* <gloss>Wisdom</gloss>? Is she not the mother
Of the liberal arts, and has she not brought forth
More beautiful daughters; whom you grasp
With a more celebrated love of genius?
And you, through all your limbs, [have] *Deianira* <note>The wife of Hercules, whose name is used here to signify the personification of beauty and virtue.</note>
Most sweet above all,
And more virtuous than the rest.</translation>

<translation page="10">

### XLIV.

Moreover, the Jews, in order to maintain the same cycle of seasons in each month, add an entire month as often as the number of <term>epactae</term> <gloss>added days to align lunar and solar calendars</gloss> exceeds thirty days.

### XLV.

The <term>epactae</term> are, in fact, the eleven days that represent the difference between the solar year of 365 days and the lunar year of 354 days. These must eventually accumulate if we allow such years to flow from a single common starting point without compensation.

### XLVI.

And thus arises that lunar year which I previously called <term>embolimaeus</term> <gloss>intercalary/leap year</gloss>. Since it is so regulated by the motions of the Moon that even the months of common years, through its benefit, are in a way restored to the laws of solar revolutions regarding the enjoyment of perpetual seasons, the entire form of such years is deservedly considered composite, and the years themselves are to be held as not merely lunar, nor indeed solar, but lunisolar.

### XLVII.

Finally, some civil years are more flexible than others. Olympiadic years are completed sometimes in 360, sometimes in 361 or 362 days, and others in 390, 391, or 392 days. The Nabonassar, or Egyptian, years do indeed have 365 days, like the Common Julian year, but without any intercalation.

### XLVIII.

Therefore, this method of years is quite erratic if compared with the Julian form. For the Egyptian year does not find a fixed and perpetual beginning there; but once every four years have elapsed, it differs from the Julian by an entire day because of the intercalary day which every fourth Julian year receives, but which that one does not admit.

### XLIX.

Hence, its beginning travels backwards through all the months of the Julian year, until 1460 Julian years are finished and 1461 Egyptian years are completed. For then both return to one common starting point.</translation>

<translation page="12">
They prepare everything: the house is bustling everywhere with unaccustomed work.
Then Father Abraham, with all things now duly prepared,
Fastens raw bonds around the tender soles of his feet,
And takes the death-bringing sword with its gleaming knots.
This sword once (as they relate) Lamech, born of Sella,
Had crafted with a skilled mind, through art first discovered by a smith,
From solid iron beautifully: and he had handed it over
To his father: Father Noah: then he himself,
When GOD overwhelmed the vast world with all its peoples
With waves, had kept it safe in the ark.
Thence all his descendants happily received it:
And he himself thus left it to his son Abraham.
When these things were done, he entrusts the faithful reins to Sarah:
And commands her to protect the rest of the house: She nods to the one commanding:
And seeks her son: she detains him with her voice
As he is now trying to follow his dear father.
Now she commands him to cover his yellow hair, now his chest:
Now to care for the Gods above: and before all things to keep GOD
Before his frequent eyes. To the righteous, she says, their rewards remain:
He loves them: the Ruler of high Olympus cares for them.
So she speaks, and sheds tears between every word.
But the son: Now farewell dear, farewell best mother:
Behold he calls, behold he calls, father: farewell, house.
So when he had spoken: he turns his steps equally,
Leaving his mother weeping, and often wishing
(Whether love persuaded her: or perhaps the forebodings of a worried
Mind) to wrap her arms around his snowy neck.
</translation>

<translation page="13">
But she followed him as he was leaving with such a voice:
Go, our glory, go: use the favorable gods:
May you leave the house with these accompanying you, and may you return with them.
   Thus therefore, the city of his dear fatherland now left behind,
The son and father enter the flourishing fields.
Whom the servants, leading the curved beast of burden, follow behind:
And weary it much with stick and knot.
Thence they enter pleasant valleys: and are covered by various
Trees: and they wind their way under high branches.
The Zephyrs accompany them from behind as they go:
And gentle birds rise up and greet them with their voice.
   Meanwhile, father Abraham, through the pleasant green lawns,
Relates many things concerning the first religion and faith.
At the beginning, he recounts the origins of the spacious world:
How GOD fashioned the orbs of the heavens from nothing,
And once separated the earth from the wandering waves:
And bound all things so beautifully in concordant peace.
Then he sings of the crime of Satan, and the transgressions of the first parent,
And the seed that would come, as the years roll by,
Which would avenge itself upon Satan: and overturn hell from the depths.
And crush the head, and gather the chest of the Serpent, flowing
With much gore, through dark caves.
Then how he submerged the whole world in the sea
Because of the sins of men, and the foul heats of lust.
And in what way, with what voice GOD revealed Himself to the fathers and ancestors,
And with what mouth He spoke to them:
And he unfolds the remaining things of the ancients in a long order.
</translation>

<summary>Abraham prepares for his journey to sacrifice Isaac, taking a historic sword and bidding an emotional farewell to Sarah, before setting out into the countryside where he instructs his son in the history of creation, the fall of Satan, and the divine covenants.</summary>
<keywords>Abraham, Isaac, Sarah, sacrifice, Lamech, Noah, Satan, creation, faith, theology</keywords>

(Whether love persuaded her: or perhaps the forebodings of a worried
Mind) to wrap her arms around his snowy neck.
pages.13:
But she followed him as he was leaving with such a voice:
Go, our glory, go: use the favorable gods:
May you leave the house with these accompanying you, and may you return with them.
   Thus therefore, the city of his dear fatherland now left behind,
The son and father enter the flourishing fields.
Whom the servants, leading the curved beast of burden, follow behind:
And weary it much with stick and knot.
Thence they enter pleasant valleys: and are covered by various
Trees: and they wind their way under high branches.
The Zephyrs accompany them from behind as they go:
And gentle birds rise up and greet them with their voice.
   Meanwhile, father Abraham, through the pleasant green lawns,
Relates many things concerning the first religion and faith.
At the beginning, he recounts the origins of the spacious world:
How GOD fashioned the orbs of the heavens from nothing,
And once separated the earth from the wandering waves:
And bound all things so beautifully in concordant peace.
Then he sings of the crime of Satan, and the transgressions of the first parent,
And the seed that would come, as the years roll by,
Which would avenge itself upon Satan: and overturn hell from the depths.
And crush the head, and gather the chest of the Serpent, flowing
With much gore, through dark caves.
Then how he submerged the whole world in the sea
Because of the sins of men, and the foul heats of lust.
And in what way, with what voice GOD revealed Himself to the fathers and ancestors,
And with what mouth He spoke to them:
And he unfolds the remaining things of the ancients in a long order.

# TO THE REVEREND, RELIGIOUS, AND MOST LEARNED MASTER, DEFENDER OF ALL PHILOSOPHY IN ITS UNIVERSALS.

Others adorn for themselves beautiful Sophias,
Shining like Rachels,
They build up brows, shape them with needles,
Polish their cheeks with learned trifles,
And paint their brides with sterile labor.
My Sage laughs at this; he seizes the fertile sister,
Leah, the mother.
He says: Rachel displeases; Leah gives the dowry,
She brings forth all things.
I have seen forms swelling under a Daedalean chisel,
Born to stir up envy.
I have seen bulls ordered to be silent
By a Sarmatian wound: threats of harbors,
Piers built by the wave-flowing Three-cities:
Causes supported by the favor of demigods:
Gods playing in a physical bath:
Particles of a more blessed urn:
Pellaean worlds, with Asia standing in awe.
I have seen clouds bring forth grand things;
Pious heirs of the spheres of the gods.

<column-break/>

The Lion of Stagira <note>Aristotle</note> will roar like a pygmy.
The Lyceums will learn the price of shadows.
My master says, I want the weak-eyed sister.
Although Leah is not weak-eyed,
Even if she is believed to be so by the bleary-eyed, she is not weak-eyed.
How does she beget the Species? To us,
Leah is charming and a noble Nymph:
And the mother of both Genus and lineages:
The goddess of beautiful Differences.
Now let Rachel boast of the light favors of the Graces,
And glass dolls, and roses of cheeks
On a parchment forehead, the brief riches of youth.
Not so, Leah does not offer from what is another's.
She does not need borrowed smoke;
She has learned to shine with native adornment;
Taught to redden without any other cosmetic,
Having and holding that which is uniquely her own.
Rachel displeases. The rich Leah promises all things,
You restore all things.

---

-> Out of the duty of religious honor and love. <-

-> Applauded by <-

Father GREGORY MAGIUS, Canon Regular of the Order of Saint Augustine, professed at Gars, student of Sacred Theology and Canon Law.
</translation>

## LORD RESPONDENT, a friend to be honored by me among the few.

<note>A large decorative initial S at the start of the first poem.</note>

Thus, providence and fame forbid that the monuments of your tireless labor
and the gifts of your outstanding spirit be entrusted to the earth at last;
nor does it threaten small names,
Alas! Beloved, it looks upon your attempts, when a select
cohort of both young and old men sees you,
ascending the pulpit of your own accord;
and they weigh in silent mind the prizes,
so that it may see how you are adorned with them, all your own desires.

->M. Samuel Schultetus, Hamburgian.<-

Is it thus, friend, that all people discover the omen
of your generous name, while you provide pledges of
your easy genius? Just as a Phrygian lion, led by fierce
savagery, does not at all harm the entire wretched race of beasts,
to whom wise nature has granted the strengths of the body
sparingly, but rather pursues those that are rabid with fierce
ardor, by which he might test his fame, proving his deeds.
Thus also, friend, you bring forth monuments of your manly
genius, defending the swollen matter concerning the Being of Spirit,
and spurning all things with lesser investigation.
Bravo, I pray, for your undertakings, and may the fates favor your studies!

->*I wrote these things for the sake of our most sincere friendship.*<-

->**Otto Helle of Lübeck.**<-

<margin>Eccl. 25.</margin>

Eccl. 25.
Prov. 30.
Eccl. 4.

### CASE XX.

Titius leaves a son as successor to a fief, to whom, when he petitions for the renewal of his investiture after a year and twenty days, the Lord of the fief opposes the exception of the fatal terms <note>original: "fatalium exceptionem"; a legal term referring to the expiration of time limits for an action</note>, that is, that the time for seeking the renewal of investiture has elapsed, and consequently the Vassal has lost the fief.

I affirm it.

<leaf-break/>
Because there are some yogis in the land of Tibet who bring forth only pure perceptions, having awakened their fortunate karmic connections through practice, I request that you offer a little praise to them. (3) Table of the Eight Negations from the <term>Madhyamaka-shastra</term> <gloss>Treatise on the Middle Way</gloss>

No birth: All phenomena have no birth. Why? Because worldly eyes perceive it as such. For example, the grain at the beginning of the kalpa does not have birth. Why? Apart from the grain at the beginning of the kalpa, present grain is unattainable. If there were present grain apart from the initial grain, then birth should exist, but this is not the reality; therefore, there is no birth.

No death: The grain from the beginning of the kalpa does not have death. Why? If it perished, there should be no grain today, but grain actually exists; therefore, there is no death.

No permanence: All things are not permanent. As when grain produces a sprout, the seed changes and decays, therefore it is not permanent.

No interruption: All things are not interrupted. For instance, because the sprout comes from the grain, it is not interrupted; if it were interrupted, it should not continue in succession.

No identity: All things do not have identity. For instance, the grain does not become the sprout, and the sprout does not become the grain. If they were one, it would contradict reality; therefore, there is no identity.

No difference: All things have no difference. If there were a difference, why distinguish between grain-sprout, grain-stalk, and grain-leaf, and not call them tree-sprout, tree-stalk, and tree-leaf? Therefore, there is no difference.

No coming: All things do not come. For example, the sprout in the grain comes from nowhere. If it came, the sprout should arrive from elsewhere, like a bird arriving to perch in a tree, but this is not the reality; therefore, there is no coming.

No going: All things do not go. If there were a going, one should see the sprout emerge from the grain, like a snake emerging from a hole, but this is not the reality; therefore, there is no going.

<meta>continues from previous page: the accomplishments of all beings.</meta> "Small" is termed supreme. Transcending the causal stage is termed most. Because obstructions are exhausted, virtues are perfected, and the result reaches the ultimate stage, it is therefore called "most supreme." "Karma" refers to the collective action of the three modes of karma <note>body, speech, and mind</note> of all Buddhas. That is to say, the most supreme karma is the karma that is most supreme. The two explanations are as follows: It refers to the omniscient mental karma, the supreme unimpeded physical karma, and the supreme compassionate verbal karma that saves others. "The one who is supreme" links the virtues to the person, meaning the one who possesses the aforementioned virtues is called a Buddha. 

Second, distinguishing by the two benefits <note>self-benefit and benefiting others</note>: "Most supreme karma" is a general reference to omniscience and the other distinct qualities, manifesting the virtue of self-benefit. Within this, internally there is the wisdom of omniscience, and externally there is the form of unimpededness. Third, distinguishing by the three virtues: First, "most supreme karma" is the general designation. "Omniscience" manifests the Buddha's virtue of great wisdom. "Form of unimpededness" clarifies the Buddha's virtue of great meditative concentration, meaning that based on concentration, supernatural powers are manifested, revealing the unimpededness of form.

<translation page="53">
<header>Common Treatises, Volume 2</header>
"Saving the world" and the following terms clarify the Buddha's virtue of great compassion. The <term>Mahāyānasaṃgraha</term> <gloss>Compendium of the Great Vehicle</gloss> clarifies the virtues of the Buddha's reward-body and manifested-body, speaking only of these three. 

Fourth, explaining according to the text: This passage only clarifies the reward-body and the manifested-body, because the Dharma-body is included within the Dharma-jewel. "Most supreme" is as explained initially. The "karma and omniscience" have two aspects: First, the true wisdom of omniscience, related to the aspect of the mind as suchness <term>tathātā</term> and the virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Second, the conventional wisdom of omniscience, related to the aspect of the mind as arising and ceasing, such as the differentiation of dependent origination. Principle and manifestation are discerned equally, with no error in this omniscience. 

"Form of unimpededness" means the Tathagata's physical body is autonomous and unimpeded, of which there are many types. As the <term>Avataṃsaka Sūtra</term> <gloss>Flower Adornment Sutra</gloss>, chapter on Inconceivable Qualities, says, I will now briefly distinguish four types: 

First, the unimpededness of large and small: This means each of the sense faculties pervades the entire dharma-realm, yet they do not destroy the nature of the various faculties, nor do they mix the characteristics of the various faculties. 

Second, the unimpededness of mutual usage: This means the various faculties function for one another without obstructing each other. 

Third, the unimpededness of principle and phenomenon: This means that while form is clearly manifest, it does not obstruct the realization that its entire substance is empty in nature. <note>The text cuts off at the word "subtle principle."</note>

</translation>

Moses said, by way of the plain meaning, that this scripture points to a great and vast matter: everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created for His glory. Everything He created, He created with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, and there is nothing at all in the world created in vain. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created, He created only for His glory." This is a very great and vast matter, and a person must contemplate it at all times and at every hour, for through this a person will merit to recognize his Creator, may His name be blessed and His memory exalted forever and ever.

It may further be said that this scripture points to another matter: everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created by measure, by weight, and by limit, and there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by measure, by weight, and by limit." This is a very great and vast matter, and a person must contemplate it at all times and at every hour, for through this a person will merit to recognize his Creator, may His name be blessed and His memory exalted forever and ever.

It may further be said that this scripture points to another matter: everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created by way of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, and there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous in the world at all. This is what our sages, of blessed memory, meant when they said: "Everything that the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only by way of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge." This is a very great and vast matter, and a person must contemplate it at all times and at every hour, for through this a person will merit to recognize his Creator, may His name be blessed and His memory exalted forever and ever.

<header>Shat Chakra Nirupana</header>

Therefore, he clarifies the "Lord of All" as <term>Hamsa</term>. This <term>Hamsa</term> is the "Lord of All," in the form of a mantra consisting of the sequence of these letters. This is stated in the <term>Prapanchasara</term>: "That existence, the pure consciousness, becomes manifest near the light. Wishing to create, it becomes dense and attains the state of a <term>bindu</term> <gloss>point/drop</gloss>. In time, that <term>bindu</term>, splitting, becomes twofold. The right part is the <term>bindu</term> and the left part is the <term>visarga</term> <gloss>emanation/two points</gloss>. Through that, the right and left parts are characterized as male and female. The letter 'Ha' is called the <term>bindu</term>, and the <term>visarga</term> is remembered as 'Sa'. The <term>bindu</term> is called the <term>purusha</term> <gloss>cosmic person/male principle</gloss>, and the <term>visarga</term> is considered <term>prakriti</term> <gloss>nature/female principle</gloss>. The <term>Hamsa</term> is the embodiment of the male and female principles, and this universe is of its nature." This is stated very clearly in the first chapter of the <term>Mahakali Tantra</term>: "In the void within the thousand-petaled lotus, which is adorned with the <term>dinya</term> arch, in the middle of the lunar mandala, above the two letters of <term>Hamsa</term>, is the one resembling pure crystal, illuminated by the pure <term>Soma</term> <gloss>nectar</gloss>," and so on. Here, "above the two letters of <term>Hamsa</term>" is very clear. Alternatively, <term>Hamsa</term> is also known by the name <term>Parama</term> <gloss>Supreme</gloss>. For this reason, the author himself stated in the forty-eighth verse, "Some say this is the form of <term>Hamsa</term>," declaring its name as <term>Hamsa</term> by his own words. Or, "Hamsa" at the end of which is "Antah" <gloss>Inner</gloss>, making it "Hamsantah"; and because that "Hamsantah" is also the "Parama" <gloss>Supreme</gloss>, by the rule of <term>karmadharaya</term> <gloss>appositional compound</gloss>, and through the middle-word-elision rule of <term>shakaparthivadi</term>, the term <term>Paramahamsa</term> is established. Thus, it is known by the name <term>Paramahamsa</term>. Hence it is said in the <term>Agama Kalpadruma</term>: "This is the <term>Paramahamsa</term> form, connected with the stationary and the moving." "The flow of the waves of all-encompassing happiness" means: that which is all-encompassing happiness, its expansion is the series of waves, and in that, it is raised in every way, illuminated as existing in successive times. Therefore, it is characterized by all-encompassing happiness in the form of a sequence. It was said previously that this <term>Hamsa</term> is situated below the Supreme Shiva. 43

<summary>This page explains the etymology and symbolic identity of Hamsa as the Lord of All, connecting it to the union of Purusha and Prakriti within the thousand-petaled lotus.</summary>
<keywords>Hamsa, Bindu, Visarga, Purusha, Prakriti, Mahakali Tantra, Paramahamsa</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="62">
<header>Shat Chakra Nirupana</header>

17

<center>The Shaivas call it the abode of Shiva, the Vaishnavas call it the Supreme Person <note>Vishnu</note>, and others, the Hari-Hara <note>Vishnu-Shiva</note> position. But those sages who delight in the lotus-feet of the Goddess <note>Shakti</note> call it the immaculate abode of Nature and the Person <note>Prakriti-Purusha</note>. 44</center>

Knowing this place, a man of excellence with a focused mind shall not be reborn into the world. He is not bound in the three worlds. He possesses the entire power, how—

He explains that because all the deities, beginning with <term>Hamsa</term>, reside in the pericarp of this <term>lotus</term>, it is the place of the chosen deity for all practitioners, such as Shaivas and Shaktas. "Abode of Shiva" means: the Shaivas, the worshippers of Shiva, call this lotus the abode of Shiva. "Supreme Person" means: this is the abode of the Supreme Person, Vishnu, which is established by the <term>taddhita</term> <gloss>possessive</gloss> suffix. "Some say" means: those who are worshippers of both Vishnu and Shiva, the Shaivas and Vaishnavas, and others who are neither just Shiva-worshippers nor Vishnu-worshippers, call it the position of Hari-Hara. Therefore, all Shaivas and Vaishnavas do not say it is only the abode of Shiva or only the abode of Vishnu; with this intention, it is said that others, devoted to the worship of the pair, speak thus. Or, other great sages, the worshippers of the <term>Hamsa</term> mantra, call it the abode of Nature and the Person because <term>Hamsa</term> is of the form of both Nature and the Person, and thus it is the place presided over by that. This is merely an indication; it should be understood that because the <term>bindu</term> presides there, it is filled with all deities, and whoever worships a particular deity speaks of it as the abode of that deity. 44

He states the fruit of the knowledge of the <term>Sahasrara</term> <gloss>thousand-petaled lotus</gloss> in the words "Knowing this place." The meaning is that one gains knowledge of this place with all its parts and subdivisions. "Focused mind" means: one whose own mind is fixed on that. "Shall not be reborn" means: he becomes liberated. This is because "he is not bound in the three worlds," which is a qualifier pregnant with the reason. "Bound" means bound by the bonds of illusion in the form of merit and sin. This is stated in the <term>Bhagavata</term>: "While actions are being performed, one considers the self to be the qualities. This is his worldly bondage and dependence."

<summary>This page discusses the various sectarian perspectives on the Sahasrara lotus, identifying it as the abode of the specific deity worshipped by the practitioner, and describes the state of liberation achieved through focused meditation there.</summary>
<keywords>Sahasrara, Shiva, Vishnu, Hari-Hara, Prakriti, Purusha, Hamsa mantra, Liberation, Maya</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="62">
# Twenty-first Chapter

->Twenty-first Chapter. 48<-

She has beautiful teeth, is eternal, and possesses full, high breasts. She is established in a posture of elegant grace, the destroyer of the buffalo demon <note>Mahishasuramardini</note>. (25)
Her touch is as soft as a lotus stalk, and she is adorned with ten arms. One should meditate upon the trident in the right hand, and then the sword and discus in order. (26)
She holds sharp weapons, and on the left arm, she carries the power. She is adorned with the shield, the full bow, the noose, and the goad. (27)
One should also place the bell and the supreme weapon on the left side. Her body is anointed with red sandalwood, and she is clad in red garments. (28)
She is mounted upon a lion, the supreme Goddess, worshipped by Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva. She rests upon a corpse, the Great Illusion <term>Mahamaya</term> <gloss>the supreme creative power</gloss>, and stands upon a red lotus seat. (29)
One should thus meditate upon Durga, who is mounted upon a lion and is the giver of supreme liberation. Shiva is known as the corpse; Mahadeva, Brahma is the red lotus. (30)
Vishnu is known as the lion; these are the vehicles of the highly powerful one. O Goddess, no invocation is performed for them in their own forms. (31)
Having transformed into the respective forms, they have attained the state of being the vehicle. Sometimes she rests upon Shiva as a corpse, sometimes upon the red lotus. (32)
Sometimes, O supreme Goddess, she dwells upon the back of a lion. In the time of desire, she dwells upon Shiva as a corpse, and she is the lion-rider. (33)
Hear now, O beloved, of the host of companions belonging to the buffalo-slaying queen. (34)

Here ends the twenty-first chapter in the glorious Kamivilasa Tantra.

<summary>This page describes the iconography and meditative visualization of the goddess Mahishasuramardini, detailing her ten-armed form, weapons, and various vehicles including the lion, the corpse, and the lotus.</summary>
<keywords>Mahishasuramardini, Durga, iconography, meditation, Kamivilasa Tantra, Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma</keywords>
</translation>

<translation page="63">
->Now, the Twenty-second Chapter.<-

The glorious Lord of Beings <term>Tatpurusha</term> <gloss>Shiva</gloss> said:

Chanda, Chandavati, the <term>vidya</term> <gloss>knowledge/deity</gloss> Chamunda, the leader of the Chanda host, (1)
Ugrachanda, Prachanda, Chandaya, and Chandanasika.
Surrounded by these powers, victorious and riding a lion, (2)
Hear the mantra I shall proclaim, which grants liberation to the slayer of the demon <note>Mahishasura</note>.
Extract the <term>maya-bija</term> <gloss>seed of illusion</gloss> <note>Hrim</note>, then the words "Durge Durge." (3)
Then, O beautiful one, the word "Raksha" <note>protect</note>, and at the end of that, the beloved of fire <note>Svaha</note>.
There is no mantra greater than this, O clear-eyed one, to be found in the Tantras. (4)
I shall now declare the great ten-syllabled mantra after extracting it.
Extract the <term>maya-bija</term>, then the word "Durge," O beloved. (5)
At the end, the beloved of fire <note>Svaha</note>; this is known to grant all successes.
Extract the <term>maya-bija</term>, then "Durgyai," and after that (6)
Add the beloved of fire; if one repeats this once,
Having attained a crore <note>ten million</note> of abodes, he goes to Vaikuntha <note>the celestial realm of Vishnu</note>. (7)
"Durge Durge," and then stated is the beloved of fire after that.
This <term>vidya</term> is the great knowledge, which grants the fruits of the four goals of life <note>virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation</note>. (8)
Extract the <term>maya-bija</term>, and at the end, the beloved of fire.
This is the supreme <term>vidya</term>, free from all defects. (9)
"Hrim Durge," this is the mantra that grants the four goals of life.
"Hrim Durge Rakshani," then the word "Namah" <note>obeisance</note>, after that the syllable. (10)
Extract the <term>maya-bija</term>, and the beloved of fire after that.
This fourteen-syllabled <term>vidya</term> is devoid of all defects. (11)
"Hrim Durge," this is the mantra that grants the four goals of life.

---

<note>1. "Vahini" has the variant reading "Samsthita."</note>
<note>2. "Lachyam" has the variant reading "Lachytame."</note>
<note>3. "Tadante" has the variant reading "Tadante" <note>Note: the source text indicates a variant for the same word; likely referring to orthographic or nasalization differences in the original manuscripts.</note></note>

<summary>This chapter introduces various mantras associated with Durga and her emanations, detailing their structure, syllables, and the spiritual benefits they provide, including the attainment of liberation and celestial realms.</summary>
<keywords>Mantra, Durga, Chamunda, Vidya, Vaikuntha, Kamivilasa Tantra, spiritual liberation</keywords>
</translation>
